listeningParts.title: Planning a microplastics project
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two marine science students, Leon and Hana, discuss their research project with their tutor, Dr Morris.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've been working on the outline for your microplastics project. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've decided to compare the amount of microplastics in sand at two beaches: the town beach near the river mouth and the beach at Kelly Bay, which is much more remote.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: That's a nice clear comparison. What do you expect to find?

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Well, my first thought was that the town beach would have far more, because of all the visitors. But Hana pointed out that the river probably matters more than the tourists. A lot of plastic fibres come from washing machines, and they travel down the river into the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Good. So your hypothesis is about the river rather than the beach users. Make sure that's stated clearly in your introduction. Now, how are you planning to collect the samples?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: We'll mark out squares on the beach, half a metre on each side, and take the top five centimetres of sand from each one. We were going to sample just along the high-tide line, where you can actually see rubbish collecting.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Hmm. The trouble is that the high-tide line changes from day to day. I'd suggest you take samples at three distances from the water instead: the high-tide line, the middle of the beach and the back near the dunes. Then you can see whether the particles are spread evenly.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: That would triple the number of samples, though. Is that realistic?

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: If you cut the number of squares at each distance from ten to five, it's about the same amount of work. And you'll have a much more interesting result.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Okay, that makes sense. The other thing we wanted to ask about was contamination. We've read that people's clothes can shed fibres into the samples.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Yes, it's a real problem in this field. The simplest solution is to wear cotton lab coats and leave a clean dish of filtered water open beside you while you work. Anything that lands in that dish tells you how much contamination there is, and you can subtract it from your results.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: That's clever. We hadn't thought of measuring it rather than just trying to avoid it.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Now, your reading. Which sources have you looked at so far?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Quite a few. The government report on coastal pollution was useful for background, but honestly, it's ten years old, so a lot of the figures are out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Then there's the Thompson study. I found it really useful because she explains her laboratory method step by step, so we could almost copy her procedure for separating plastics from sand.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: I wasn't so sure about Thompson. Her sample was very small, only two beaches, like ours. I preferred the review by Castillo, which brings together results from more than sixty studies around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Castillo is excellent for comparison. You could use her figures to say whether your beaches are typical. What about the article in the newspaper you mentioned in your email?

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Oh, that one. It had some striking photographs, but when I checked, the numbers it quoted didn't seem to come from any published research.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Then leave it out. A newspaper can give you an idea, but it isn't evidence. And the citizen science website?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: The Beach Watch site. Volunteers all over the country record what they find. The data isn't as precise as a lab study, but there's an enormous amount of it, and it's updated every month, so it's the most current source we have.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Exactly. Use it, but explain its limitations. Right, I'd like a draft of your method section by next Thursday, please.

listeningParts.title: A short history of wind power
listeningParts.contextDescription: Part of a lecture in an engineering history course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're continuing our series on energy history, and I want to look at wind power. We tend to think of wind turbines as a modern technology, but people have been using the wind to do work for well over a thousand years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The earliest windmills that we have clear records of were built in Persia, in what is now eastern Iran, probably in the ninth century. These looked very different from the windmills most of us picture. The sails were arranged around a vertical shaft, a bit like a revolving door, and they were surrounded by walls that directed the wind onto one side. Their main job was grinding grain, though some were also used to pump water for irrigation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In Europe, windmills appear in the late twelfth century, and these had a horizontal shaft, with the sails facing into the wind. The early European design was called the post mill, because the whole wooden body of the mill sat on a single large post. When the wind changed direction, the miller had to push the entire building round to face it, using a long beam at the back. As you can imagine, that limited how big a post mill could be.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The solution was the tower mill. Here, the body was a fixed tower of stone or brick, and only the cap at the top, which carried the sails, needed to turn. That meant the mills could be much taller, catching stronger winds. Then, in the eighteenth century, an English inventor added the fantail: a small wheel at the back of the cap that automatically turned the sails into the wind. The miller no longer had to watch the weather all day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, the place where windmills had their greatest impact was probably the Netherlands. A large part of the country lies below sea level, and from the fifteenth century onwards, thousands of windmills were used for drainage, pumping water out of the land so that it could be farmed. By the mid-nineteenth century, there were around nine thousand windmills in the country. They also powered sawmills, which helped the Dutch build the ships that made them a major trading nation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Windmills declined in the late nineteenth century, when steam engines, and later electric motors, became cheap and reliable. But the idea of using wind to make electricity is older than many people realise. In 1887, a Scottish professor, James Blyth, built a wind turbine in the garden of his holiday cottage and used it to charge batteries that lit the house. Local people apparently refused his offer to light the main street, because they thought electricity was the work of the devil.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the United States, small wind turbines were common on farms in the 1920s and 1930s, before the national electricity grid reached rural areas. Once farms were connected to the grid, most of these turbines were abandoned. So for much of the twentieth century, wind power was seen as a curiosity, something for remote places only.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What changed that? The oil crisis of the 1970s. When oil prices rose sharply, governments began to look for other sources of energy, and Denmark in particular invested heavily in wind research. Danish engineers settled on the design you now see everywhere: three blades, facing into the wind, on a tall steel tower. Three blades turned out to be the best balance between efficiency and stability. Two-bladed turbines wobble more as they turn, and four or more blades add weight and cost without producing much extra power.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Since then, the main trend has simply been size. A typical turbine in the 1980s had blades about fifteen metres long. Today, the largest offshore turbines have blades of over a hundred metres, and a single rotation can power an average home for a couple of days. Moving out to sea has been important, because the wind there is stronger and steadier, and turbines don't face the same opposition from people who object to the view.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, size brings its own problems. Blades this long are extremely difficult to transport by road, and at the end of their life, they're hard to recycle, because they're made from a mixture of glass fibre and resin. Several companies are now developing blades that can be broken down and reused, and that, I think, will be one of the key challenges of the next decade. Next week, we'll move on to solar energy.

readingPassages.title: The return of the sail
paragraphs: For most of human history, ships crossed the oceans by sail. Then, in the nineteenth century, steam engines and later diesel engines made sailing ships seem hopelessly old-fashioned. A motor ship could keep to a timetable regardless of the weather, and by the 1930s commercial sail had almost disappeared. Today, around ninety per cent of world trade travels by sea, and almost all of it is carried by ships burning heavy fuel oil. Shipping produces roughly three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, about the same as a large industrial country, and international rules now require the industry to cut those emissions sharply by the middle of the century.

One of the more surprising responses to this pressure is the return of wind power. Engineers are not proposing a return to the clipper ships of the past, which needed large crews to handle hundreds of square metres of canvas. Instead, they are developing what is known as wind-assisted propulsion: equipment fitted to ordinary cargo ships that uses the wind to reduce, rather than replace, the work done by the engine. Because the engine remains on board, the ship can still keep to its schedule when the wind drops. Crucially, most of these systems are largely automated, so they do not require additional crew members, which would quickly cancel out any savings on fuel.

Several technologies are competing. The oldest of them, the rotor sail, was first tested in the 1920s by the German engineer Anton Flettner. It consists of a tall vertical cylinder that is spun by a small electric motor. When wind blows across the spinning cylinder, the air moves faster on one side than the other, creating a difference in pressure that pushes the ship forward. This is the same effect that makes a football curve when it is kicked with spin. Flettner's rotor ship crossed the Atlantic in 1926, but the low price of oil at the time meant that there was little commercial interest in the idea.

A second approach uses rigid wing sails, which look rather like aircraft wings standing on end. Made of composite materials, they can be angled automatically by computer to make the best use of the wind, and some designs can be folded down when the ship enters port or passes under a bridge. A third option, the kite, is perhaps the most unusual: a large parafoil flies several hundred metres above the ship, where winds are stronger and more constant, and pulls the vessel along by a cable attached to the bow.

How much fuel can these devices save? The answer depends heavily on the route and the type of ship. Trials on vessels fitted with rotor sails have reported fuel savings of between five and twenty per cent, and developers claim that wing sails could achieve more than that on routes with steady winds, such as parts of the North Atlantic. Routes through regions with weak or unpredictable winds offer much smaller gains. Critics also point out that many published figures come from the manufacturers themselves, and independent long-term data is still limited.

There are practical obstacles as well. Rotors and wing sails take up deck space, which on a container ship is valuable, since every container that cannot be carried represents lost income. Tall structures can also interfere with the cranes used to load and unload ships in port. For this reason, early adopters have mostly been bulk carriers and tankers, which carry cargo inside the hull and have relatively clear decks. Ship owners must also weigh the cost of installation, which can run into millions of dollars per vessel, against uncertain future fuel prices.

Despite these difficulties, interest is growing quickly. In the past decade, the number of large ships fitted with some form of wind-assisted propulsion has risen from a handful to several dozen, and many more are on order. Some analysts believe that the greatest benefit will come from combining wind power with other measures, such as slower sailing speeds and improved hull designs. Even a saving of ten per cent, multiplied across tens of thousands of ships, would represent a significant cut in global emissions. After a century in the background, the wind may be returning to the centre of world trade.

readingPassages.title: Meadows beneath the sea
paragraphs: Seagrasses are often mistaken for seaweed, but the two are quite different. Seaweeds are algae, which absorb nutrients directly from the water through their surfaces. Seagrasses, by contrast, are true flowering plants, related to the grasses and lilies that grow on land. They have roots, leaves and veins, and they produce flowers and seeds, all underwater. Around seventy species are found in shallow coastal waters on every continent except Antarctica, where they form dense green meadows that can stretch for many kilometres.

These meadows are among the most productive habitats on Earth. A single hectare of seagrass can support tens of thousands of fish and millions of small invertebrates, and many commercially important species, including cod and some kinds of prawn, spend the early part of their lives sheltering among the leaves. Seagrass is also the main food of animals such as dugongs and green turtles. One study estimated that a fifth of the world's largest fisheries depend on seagrass meadows at some stage of the life cycle of the fish they catch.

In recent years, however, it is the role of seagrass in tackling climate change that has attracted most attention. Like all plants, seagrasses take carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they grow. What makes them unusual is what happens to that carbon. The dense leaves slow the movement of water, so fine particles settle on the seabed, and the roots bind these sediments together. Because the sediment contains little oxygen, dead plant material decays very slowly, and carbon can remain locked in the seabed for centuries or even thousands of years. Although seagrass covers less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, it is thought to be responsible for around ten per cent of the carbon buried in ocean sediments each year.

Unfortunately, seagrass is disappearing. A global assessment published in 2009 concluded that around seven per cent of the world's meadows were being lost every year, a rate comparable to the destruction of tropical rainforests. The causes are varied. Fertiliser and sewage washing off the land encourage the growth of algae, which cloud the water and block the sunlight that seagrass needs. Dredging, boat anchors and coastal construction physically tear up meadows, and in some places disease has killed large areas. When seagrass dies, the sediment it was holding can be washed away, releasing stored carbon back into the water.

Restoring lost meadows has proved difficult. Early attempts involved digging up plants from healthy meadows and replanting them elsewhere, but this damaged the donor sites and many transplants failed. Researchers at the University of Virginia took a different approach in the coastal bays of the eastern United States, where seagrass had been wiped out by disease and a hurricane in the 1930s. Beginning in 1999, they scattered more than seventy million seeds over the bare seabed. Progress was slow at first, but the meadows eventually began to spread by themselves, and today they cover more than three thousand six hundred hectares. The project's leader, Professor Robert Orth, has described the result as evidence that 'if you give nature a helping hand, it can do remarkable things'.

Elsewhere, projects have adopted other methods. In Wales, a project known as Seagrass Ocean Rescue collected seeds by hand, with the help of volunteer divers, and planted them in small hessian bags filled with sand, which were then lowered onto the seabed in rows. Marine biologist Dr Richard Unsworth, one of the project's founders, argues that local involvement is just as important as the technique: in his view, a meadow is far more likely to survive if the surrounding community understands its value and supports efforts to reduce pollution.

Not all scientists are convinced that restoration should be the priority. Dr Carlos Duarte, who has studied seagrass for decades, has pointed out that protecting existing meadows is far cheaper and more reliable than creating new ones, since a damaged meadow may take decades to recover its full carbon store. Others warn against treating seagrass simply as a way to cancel out emissions, a concern raised by the economist Dr Lena Fischer, who fears that companies might pay for planting projects instead of reducing their own pollution. What most experts agree on is that seagrass deserves far more attention than it has received in the past.

readingPassages.title: Why we misjudge our energy use
paragraphs: If you ask people how much energy different household activities use, their answers are often surprisingly inaccurate. In a well-known study in the United States, the psychologist Shahzeen Attari asked several hundred participants to estimate the energy used by everyday devices and activities, from running a dishwasher to drying clothes. On average, participants underestimated energy use by a factor of almost three. More strikingly, the errors were not random. People slightly overestimated the energy used by small, visible devices such as light bulbs, but dramatically underestimated the energy used by large appliances, particularly those that produce heat, such as water heaters and tumble dryers.

Why should this be? One explanation lies in the way people make judgements when they lack precise information. Rather than calculating, they rely on mental shortcuts, and one of the most common is to judge the size of something by how noticeable it is. A light is switched on and off many times a day; it is in plain view, and we are constantly reminded to turn it off. A water heater, by contrast, sits out of sight in a cupboard and works silently. It is therefore easy to assume that the light matters more, even though heating water typically uses many times as much energy.

A second factor is that energy is, for most people, invisible. When we buy food or petrol, we see exactly how much we are getting, and the price is displayed at the moment of purchase. Electricity and gas, however, arrive continuously through wires and pipes, and the bill comes weeks later as a single figure that combines dozens of activities. It is almost impossible to connect a particular choice, such as taking a longer shower, with its cost. Economists describe this as a problem of feedback: without clear and timely information about the consequences of our actions, we cannot learn to adjust them.

This analysis suggests an obvious remedy: give people better feedback. In recent years, millions of homes in Europe and North America have been fitted with smart meters, which can display energy use in real time on a small screen in the kitchen. Early trials produced encouraging results, with some households cutting their consumption by ten per cent or more. However, larger and longer studies have generally found smaller effects, typically around two or three per cent. One reason appears to be that the novelty wears off: many people look at their display frequently in the first few weeks, and then rarely, if ever. In my view, this does not mean that feedback is useless, but rather that simply providing data is not enough.

Some of the most effective interventions have combined information with social comparison. In a series of experiments, an American energy company sent customers letters that compared their consumption with that of similar neighbours, adding a smiling face for those who used less than average. Households receiving these letters reduced their energy use by around two per cent, a small figure for an individual home, but a large one across a whole country, and achieved at very low cost. Interestingly, the researchers found that households who were already using less than their neighbours sometimes increased their consumption after learning this, an effect that was reduced when the letters included the smiling face.

Defaults offer another powerful tool. Psychologists have long known that people tend to accept whatever option is presented as standard. In one German study, when a town's electricity supplier made green energy the default tariff, so that customers had to take action to switch away from it, more than ninety per cent of households stayed with it, even though it was slightly more expensive. When the same option had to be chosen actively, only a small minority selected it. Critics argue that such techniques can be manipulative, but I believe that when the default is clearly explained and easy to change, it simply makes the sustainable choice the easy one.

None of this means that behaviour change alone can solve the problem of energy demand. Better insulation, more efficient appliances and cleaner sources of electricity will matter far more in the long run. But buildings and appliances are used by people, and the way they are used depends on what people understand and notice. Policies that ignore human psychology are likely to deliver less than their designers expect, while those that take it into account may achieve a great deal at surprisingly little cost.

listeningParts.title: Renting a flat
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a letting agency about a flat advertised online.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Riverside Lettings, Mia speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm calling about one of the flats on your website. It's the two-bedroom one in Albert Street.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Ah yes, number twelve. It's a lovely flat, just been redecorated. Are you looking for yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: For me and a friend. We're both starting a master's course in September, so we need somewhere for at least a year.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That fits nicely. The landlord prefers a twelve-month tenancy anyway. Can I take your name first?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Sure. It's Tomás Ruiz. R-U-I-Z.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks, Tomás. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's oh-seven-seven-one-four, three-six-two, nine-eight-five.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. So, let me tell you a bit about the flat. It's on the second floor of a converted Victorian house. There's no lift, I'm afraid, but there are only two flights of stairs.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. Is it quiet? My friend is a light sleeper.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a residential street, so there's not much traffic at night. The flat at the back looks over the gardens, and that's where both bedrooms are, so I'd say it's very quiet. The previous tenants were there for three years and never complained.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good to hear. And is there a washing machine?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a washing machine in the kitchen, and a small drying rack, but no dryer.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. The advert said the rent was eight hundred and fifty pounds a month. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It was, but the landlord has just put in a new kitchen, so it's now nine hundred and twenty a month. That's for the whole flat, not each.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay, so four hundred and sixty each. Does that include bills?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Water is included, but you'd pay for gas and electricity yourselves. Internet's included too; the landlord has a contract with a provider for the whole building.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good. And is it furnished?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Partly furnished. Both bedrooms have a bed and a wardrobe, and there's a sofa and a dining table in the living room. But there are no desks, so if you're students, you'd probably want to buy those.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Right, desks. I'll note that. What about the area? I don't really know that part of town.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's very convenient. There's a supermarket on the corner, and the train station is about ten minutes' walk. If you're at the university, you can get the number fourteen bus, which goes right past the main library.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Perfect. Is there anywhere to keep a bike? I cycle most places.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's no garage, but there's a shed in the back garden that tenants share. Most people keep their bikes there.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. And what would we need to pay at the start?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's a deposit equal to five weeks' rent, which is protected in a government scheme and returned at the end of the tenancy, as long as there's no damage. You'd also pay the first month's rent in advance. We don't charge any agency fees; that's not allowed any more.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's good to know. Would we need a guarantor?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: For students, yes, usually. That's someone who agrees to pay the rent if you can't, normally a parent. If you don't have anyone in the UK, the landlord will accept six months' rent paid in advance instead.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: My parents are abroad, so we might have to do that. Can we see the flat?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. I've got viewings on Wednesday afternoon. Could you do three o'clock?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Wednesday's difficult, I've got a class. Is Thursday possible?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thursday at eleven? I'm meeting another tenant nearby, so that works for me.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Eleven on Thursday is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. Please bring some photo identification, a passport is best, and if you can, a letter from the university confirming your place. It speeds things up if you decide to take it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. Passport and university letter. Thanks so much, Mia.

listeningParts.title: A new city bike-sharing scheme
listeningParts.contextDescription: A local radio presenter interviews a transport officer about a bike-sharing scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And now on Morning City, we're talking about the new bike-sharing scheme that starts next month. With me is Rachel Lim from the city council's transport department. Rachel, welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Thanks for having me.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: So, for listeners who haven't heard about it, what exactly is the scheme?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Well, from the first of May, people will be able to hire a bicycle from any of our docking stations around the city, ride it wherever they want to go, and leave it at another station. It's designed mainly for short journeys, the kind of trip that's a bit too far to walk but where taking the car is a waste of time and fuel.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: How many bikes are we talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: We're starting with six hundred bikes at forty stations. A third of them are electric, which should help people who are worried about the hills on the north side of the city. If the first year goes well, we'd like to double the number of stations.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Why start with this number? Some people have said it's rather small for a city of our size.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: It's deliberately what we call a pilot scheme. We'd rather start with fewer stations in the right places and learn from how people use them than spread the bikes too thinly. Other cities have found that if a station is often empty when people need a bike, they quickly give up on the scheme altogether. The operator will also move bikes around in vans during the day to stop the busiest stations running out.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And how do people pay?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Everything is done through a phone app. You can pay per ride, which costs one pound to unlock the bike and then ten pence a minute, or you can buy an annual membership for sixty pounds, which gives you unlimited rides of up to forty-five minutes. Electric bikes cost a little more on both options. For people without a smartphone, we'll also have a card, available from the main library.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, a lot of cities have tried schemes like this, and some have had problems. Bikes left everywhere, blocking pavements...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Yes, that's mostly with what are called dockless schemes, where you can leave the bike anywhere. We deliberately chose a system with fixed stations. You have to return the bike to a dock, otherwise the app keeps charging you. That should keep the streets tidy.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Where will the stations be?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: We looked at where people actually travel. So there are stations at both railway stations, at the hospital, at the university campus, in the main shopping streets and in several residential areas. The busiest, we expect, will be the one outside Central Station.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: What about safety? Some people say our roads just aren't safe for cyclists.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: That's a fair point, and it's the thing people raised most often in our public consultation. Alongside the scheme, we're building eight kilometres of new protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by a kerb. The first section, along the riverside, opens at the same time as the scheme. We also recommend helmets, although they're not compulsory, and every bike has lights that switch on automatically.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Who's paying for all this?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: The bikes and stations are provided by a private operator, which collects the fees. The council's main contribution is the cycle lanes, which are funded by a national government grant, so there's no increase in local taxes.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And finally, Rachel, what would count as success?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Our target for the first year is a million rides. But really, what we'd like to see is fewer short car journeys in the city centre. We'll be measuring traffic levels before and after, and we'll publish the results.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Rachel Lim, thank you very much.

listeningParts.title: Analysing a commuting survey
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Kofi and Emma, discuss the results of a survey they carried out on commuting.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Right, Kofi, I've put all the questionnaire results into the spreadsheet. Shall we go through them before we start writing?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Yes, please. How many people did we get in the end?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Two hundred and thirty-four. Fewer than we'd hoped, but more than enough for the assignment.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Okay. And what did we find on journey times? I remember a lot of people complaining when we were handing out the forms.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: The average one-way journey was thirty-eight minutes. But that hides a big difference. People who drove took about thirty minutes on average, while bus users took nearly fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That's not surprising. The buses go round every housing estate. What about satisfaction? We asked people to rate their commute from one to ten.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: This is the interesting bit. You'd expect drivers to be happiest, since they're quickest. But actually, the cyclists and walkers were the most satisfied, even though some of them had journeys of forty minutes or more.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That fits with what I read in that study from Canada. The researchers said that active commuting makes people feel more relaxed when they arrive at work. Drivers spend their whole journey worrying about traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: And bus users were the least satisfied of all. In the comments, the main complaint wasn't the journey time but the reliability. People said they never knew when the bus would actually come.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Did the train users say anything similar?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Not really. There weren't many of them, only about twenty, and they were mostly positive, apart from the price of tickets. A few mentioned that trains were crowded at peak times, but they still said they'd rather take the train than drive into the centre and pay for parking.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Twenty is too few to say much, though. We should point that out rather than make claims about train users in general.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: We should definitely include some of those comments. They make the numbers more real. Now, what about our question on flexible working?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Forty-one per cent said their employer let them work from home at least one day a week. And most of those said they'd moved further from their workplace in the last five years.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: So working from home might actually be making commutes longer on the days people do go in. That's a nice point for our discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: I thought so too. Though we can't prove that one causes the other from a survey like ours.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi

listeningParts.title: The history of public parks
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an urban history course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today I'd like to talk about the public park, something most of us take completely for granted. But the idea that a city should provide open green space, free for everyone to use, is actually quite recent. For most of history, the large gardens in and around cities belonged to kings, aristocrats or the church, and ordinary people were either kept out or allowed in only on certain days.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The modern public park really begins in the nineteenth century, and the main driving force was not beauty but health. Industrial cities in Britain were growing at an astonishing rate. Manchester's population, for example, increased about six times in the first half of the century. Housing was crowded, the air was full of smoke, and diseases such as cholera spread rapidly. Doctors and reformers believed, partly correctly, that fresh air and open space would reduce disease. Parks were often described at the time as the lungs of the city.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There was also a moral argument. Many reformers worried that working people spent their only free day, Sunday, in pubs. A park, they argued, would offer a healthier and more respectable alternative. So from the start, parks came with a lot of rules: no gambling, no drinking, and in some cases no walking on the grass.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the first parks created specifically for the public was Birkenhead Park, near Liverpool, which opened in 1847. It was designed by Joseph Paxton, who later designed the Crystal Palace. What was unusual about Birkenhead was the way it was paid for. The town bought far more land than it needed for the park itself and then sold plots around the edges for expensive houses. The sale of those plots covered the cost of building the park.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Birkenhead had a direct influence across the Atlantic. In 1850, an American farmer and journalist called Frederick Law Olmsted visited it and was very impressed, particularly by the fact that rich and poor used it equally. A few years later, Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux won the competition to design Central Park in New York. Central Park was enormous, over three hundred hectares, and although it looks natural, almost everything in it was planned. The lakes were dug by hand, millions of trees were planted, and the roads for carriages were sunk below the level of the paths so that walkers wouldn't see the traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, the purpose of parks changed. Instead of quiet walking, the emphasis moved to active recreation: sports fields, playgrounds and swimming pools. During the two world wars, many parks in Britain were dug up and turned into allotments where people grew vegetables, because of food shortages.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then, from the 1970s, many cities faced budget cuts, and parks were often among the first things to suffer. Park keepers were removed, and some parks became neglected and were seen as unsafe. More recently, however, there's been a revival of interest. Research has linked access to green space with lower stress and better mental health, and cities are now looking at parks as a way to cope with climate change, because trees and grass reduce temperatures and absorb rainwater that would otherwise cause flooding.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the most talked-about recent examples is the High Line in New York, which opened in 2009 on an old elevated railway line. Instead of demolishing the structure, the city turned it into a long, narrow park above the streets. It's been hugely popular, but it's also been criticised, because it pushed up property prices in the surrounding area, so that some long-term residents could no longer afford to live there. That tension between parks as a public good and parks as a driver of rising prices is something we'll come back to next week.

readingPassages.title: Going underground
paragraphs: In the middle of the nineteenth century, London was the largest city in the world, and its streets were close to gridlock. Every morning, hundreds of thousands of workers poured into the City, the financial district, on foot, by horse-drawn omnibus or in private carriages. The mainline railway companies, which had built their terminals around the edge of the centre, were not permitted to bring their lines further in, so passengers arriving by train simply added to the crowds trying to cross the city by road. One survey in the 1850s counted more than seven hundred thousand people entering the City each day, and journeys of a few kilometres could take well over an hour.

The idea of solving this problem by putting a railway beneath the streets was promoted above all by Charles Pearson, a lawyer who worked for the City of London. Pearson argued for years that an underground line linking the mainline stations would relieve congestion and allow working people to live in healthier suburbs and travel to their jobs. Many people regarded the plan as absurd. Critics warned that tunnels would collapse, that passengers would be poisoned by smoke, and that the noise of trains would disturb the dead in the cemeteries the line would pass close to.

Construction of the Metropolitan Railway began in 1860. Rather than boring deep tunnels, the engineers used a method known as cut and cover. A deep trench was dug along the line of an existing road, the track was laid at the bottom, and the trench was then roofed over with a brick arch and the road rebuilt on top. The method was relatively cheap and avoided the need to buy expensive buildings, but it caused enormous disruption to traffic and businesses while the work was going on, and it meant that the line could only follow the routes of streets wide enough to be dug up.

The line opened on 10 January 1863, running about six kilometres between Paddington and Farringdon. It was an immediate success: almost forty thousand passengers used it on the first day, and in its first year it carried nine and a half million people. The trains were pulled by steam locomotives, and although they were designed to reduce smoke in the tunnels, the stations were notoriously dirty and the air unpleasant. Some passengers nevertheless claimed that the sulphurous atmosphere was good for their health. Charles Pearson did not live to see the result; he had died a few months before the opening.

Over the following decades, further lines were built, but cut and cover had clear limits. The next great advance came with the tunnelling shield, a large iron cylinder that protected workers as they dug through the London clay, allowing tunnels to be bored deep below the surface without disturbing the streets above. These deep tubes, which gave the system its popular nickname, could not have used steam engines, because there was no way to remove the smoke. The first deep line, the City and South London Railway, opened in 1890 and used electric trains from the start.

Electricity transformed the system. By the early years of the twentieth century, the older lines had also been converted to electric power, and a series of new tube lines was built, many of them financed by the American businessman Charles Yerkes. Investors, however, often lost money, because fares were kept low and the lines were expensive to build. In 1933, the various private companies were brought together into a single public body, the London Passenger Transport Board, which was responsible for the Underground as well as buses and trams.

The London Underground served as a model for cities around the world. Budapest opened a line in 1896, followed by Paris in 1900, Berlin in 1902 and New York in 1904. Today more than one hundred and eighty cities have metro systems, and the largest of them, in cities such as Shanghai and Beijing, now carry far more passengers than London. Yet many of the basic features of underground railways, from the shape of tunnels to the use of a simplified diagrammatic map, can still be traced back to the system that began beneath the streets of Victorian London.

readingPassages.title: Forests in the sky
paragraphs: When the two residential towers known as the Bosco Verticale, or Vertical Forest, were completed in Milan in 2014, they attracted attention from around the world. The buildings, designed by the architect Stefano Boeri, are covered with around nine hundred trees and more than twenty thousand smaller plants, growing on large balconies that project from every floor. Boeri has said that the total planting is equivalent to about two hectares of forest, squeezed onto a footprint of less than a quarter of a hectare. Since then, similar projects have been built or planned in cities from Sydney to Singapore, and the image of a tower draped in greenery has become a familiar symbol of the sustainable city, appearing in architectural competitions and property advertisements alike.

Supporters of such buildings point to a range of benefits. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and some air pollutants, and they release moisture through their leaves, which cools the air around them. On a hot summer day, a planted facade can be several degrees cooler than bare concrete or glass, reducing the need for air conditioning in the apartments behind it. Trees and shrubs also provide shelter from wind and noise, and they create habitats for birds and insects in places where nature is otherwise scarce. Surveys of residents suggest that many people simply enjoy living surrounded by plants, and there is growing evidence that contact with greenery reduces stress.

Building a forest in the sky, however, is far from simple. Trees are heavy, especially when their soil is wet, and balconies must be designed to carry much greater loads than usual, which requires extra concrete and steel. The Milan towers needed specially reinforced structures, and engineers tested the trees in a wind tunnel to make sure that they would not be blown over in storms. Each tree is attached to the building with steel cables, and its roots grow in containers rather than in open ground, which limits how large it can become.

Maintenance is another major issue. The plants must be watered, fed and pruned, and dead trees must be replaced. In Milan, this work is carried out by specialist gardeners who abseil down the outside of the buildings several times a year, and the costs are included in the residents' service charges. An automatic irrigation system delivers water to every container, much of it recycled from the buildings themselves. Critics argue that this level of care makes vertical forests an option only for wealthy residents, and indeed apartments in the Milan towers are among the most expensive in the city.

There are also questions about the environmental balance. The extra concrete and steel needed to support the trees have a substantial carbon footprint, since producing cement is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions. Some researchers have calculated that the trees on a single tower absorb only a small fraction of the carbon released in constructing the reinforced structure, and that it may take many decades, if ever, for the planting to make up the difference. From this perspective, a park at ground level, or trees planted along streets, may deliver far greater benefits for the same cost.

Defenders of the concept respond that the comparison is unfair, because the purpose of vertical forests is not simply to store carbon. In dense cities, they argue, land at ground level is extremely scarce, and a planted tower adds green space where none would otherwise exist. They also point to newer designs that reduce the structural cost, for example by using lighter timber frames, choosing smaller species of tree or concentrating planting on lower floors. Boeri himself has developed versions of the idea for social housing in the Netherlands, with the aim of showing that vertical greenery need not be a luxury.

What seems clear is that vertical forests are not a solution on their own. Their greatest contribution may be symbolic: by making greenery highly visible in the skyline, they have encouraged city authorities, developers and the public to think more seriously about integrating nature into urban design. Whether the next generation of buildings will be covered in trees, or simply surrounded by better streets and parks, will depend on careful assessment of costs and benefits rather than on striking images alone.

readingPassages.title: The wisdom and madness of crowds
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant view of crowds was deeply pessimistic. Its most influential source was a book published in 1895 by the French writer Gustave Le Bon, who argued that individuals who join a crowd lose their capacity for reason. Submerged in the mass, he claimed, a person descends several rungs on the ladder of civilisation, becoming impulsive, suggestible and potentially violent. Le Bon's ideas were enormously popular, and they shaped how police forces, politicians and the public thought about crowds for decades. Even today, news reports routinely describe crowds as 'stampeding' or 'panicking' in emergencies, as though people in large groups behave like frightened animals.

Over the past forty years, however, researchers have assembled a very different picture. A key figure in this work is the British psychologist John Drury, who has studied how people actually behaved in emergencies ranging from fires and shipwrecks to terrorist attacks. His conclusion, based on interviews with survivors and analysis of video footage, is that mass panic is extremely rare. In most disasters, people do not trample one another in a selfish rush to escape. Instead, they tend to help strangers, wait their turn and cooperate, often at considerable risk to themselves. Where deaths do occur in crowds, they are usually caused by the physical pressure of too many bodies in a confined space, not by irrational behaviour.

To explain this, Drury and his colleagues draw on what is known as social identity theory. According to this approach, a crowd is not simply a collection of individuals who happen to be in the same place. When people face a shared threat, they often begin to see themselves as part of a common group, a 'we' rather than a collection of separate 'I's. This shared identity encourages people to trust one another and to care about what happens to others in the group. In other words, far from losing their identity in a crowd, people often gain a new one, and it is this that guides their behaviour.

These ideas have important practical consequences. If authorities assume that crowds are likely to panic, they may withhold information in an emergency, fearing that the truth will cause chaos. Research suggests the opposite approach is more effective: people respond better when they are given clear, honest information about what is happening and what they should do. Similarly, if police treat an entire crowd as a threat because of the actions of a small minority, they risk creating the very conflict they wish to avoid. Studies of football crowds and protests have found that heavy-handed policing can cause previously peaceful participants to unite against the police, whereas approaches that distinguish between troublemakers and the majority tend to reduce violence.

A separate line of research has focused on a more surprising idea: that crowds can sometimes be wiser than individuals. The classic illustration dates from 1906, when the scientist Francis Galton attended a country fair where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox. Galton, who had expected ordinary people to perform poorly, collected around eight hundred guesses and found that their average was within one per cent of the true weight, closer than almost any individual guess. Later research has repeated this effect for many kinds of estimate, from the number of sweets in a jar to the outcome of elections.

The wisdom of crowds, however, depends on certain conditions. The most important is independence: each person must make their own judgement without being influenced by others. When people can see each other's answers, or are exposed to the same misleading information, their errors stop cancelling out and instead reinforce one another. In one experiment, participants who were shown the estimates of others became more confident while their collective accuracy actually fell. This helps to explain why groups that discuss a problem at length can sometimes reach worse decisions than the same people would have reached alone, a phenomenon sometimes called groupthink.

I would suggest that the two bodies of research share an important lesson. Neither the old idea of the mindless mob nor a naive faith in collective wisdom captures how groups really work. Crowds can be cooperative or hostile, accurate or deeply mistaken, depending on how their members see themselves and how they are treated. Understanding those conditions is not merely of academic interest; it is essential for anyone who has to manage large gatherings or make decisions on behalf of others.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Then you'd probably want our Spanish Level Two course, which is for people who've had some contact with the language but aren't confident. If you're not sure, you can do a short placement test online before you enrol. It only takes about twenty minutes.

listeningParts.title: A guided walk through the botanical garden
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a botanical garden and explains its history and layout.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Morning, everyone. Welcome to the Halton Botanical Garden. I'm Josh, and I'll be showing you around this morning. Before we start walking, let me give you a bit of background and point out where things are, because the garden is bigger than it looks from the gate.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The garden was founded in 1820 by the university, originally as a place to grow plants for medical students to study. Back then, most medicines came from plants, so future doctors had to be able to recognise them. Today, our main work is conservation. We grow over twelve thousand species, and around four hundred of them are threatened in the wild.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, if you look at the map on the board here, we're at the main gate, at the bottom. The path in front of us leads straight up the middle of the garden to the lake. On your left as you walk up, the first area you come to is the herb garden, which is the oldest part of the site and still laid out in the original pattern from the 1820s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Opposite the herb garden, on the right of the main path, is the rock garden, where we grow alpine plants from mountain regions around the world. It's at its best in late spring, so you've come at a good time.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Carry on up the main path and you'll reach the lake. The glasshouses are on the far side of the lake, at the very top of the map. There are three of them: one for tropical plants, one for desert plants and one for plants from temperate regions like Australia and South Africa. The tropical house is very warm and humid, so you may want to leave your coats in the cloakroom before you go in.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: To the left of the lake is the woodland walk, a circular path through trees from North America and Asia. It's very peaceful and takes about twenty minutes. And to the right of the lake, between the lake and the east wall, you'll find the visitor centre, with the café, the shop and the toilets.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few words about what goes on behind the scenes. Perhaps the most important part of our work isn't visible at all. In a building behind the glasshouses, we have a seed bank, where seeds of rare species are dried and stored at minus twenty degrees. Stored like this, many seeds can stay alive for decades or even centuries. If a species dies out in the wild, we can grow it again and, in some cases, return it to its natural habitat. That has already happened with a small flowering plant from a Mediterranean island, which we reintroduced in 2015.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: We also run a training programme for gardeners. Each year we take on six trainees, who spend two years working in every part of the garden. Many of them go on to work in other botanical gardens around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A couple of practical points. The garden closes at five, but the glasshouses close half an hour earlier, at half past four, so if you want to see them, don't leave them till last. Please stay on the paths, because some of our plants are very rare, and a few, especially in the medicinal section of the herb garden, are poisonous, so please don't touch or pick anything.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And if you have children with you, they can collect a free activity sheet from the visitor centre. It's a sort of treasure hunt, and anyone who completes it gets a small prize. Okay, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start in the herb garden.

listeningParts.title: A seminar on bilingual children
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two education students, Mei and Joseph, discuss an article on bilingualism with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay, let's get started. Last week I asked you both to read the review article on bilingual children. Mei, what was your overall impression?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I found it really interesting, partly because I grew up speaking Cantonese at home and English at school. The main argument seemed to be that a lot of the fears parents have about bilingualism aren't supported by the research.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Which fears in particular?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Mainly the idea that learning two languages will confuse children or delay their speech. The article says that bilingual children reach the main milestones, like saying their first words, at about the same age as monolingual children.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Although it did say that if you test them in just one language, bilingual children often seem to know fewer words. That's what worries a lot of parents.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how does the article explain that?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Well, the point is that their vocabulary is split between two languages. A child might know the word for kitchen things in Spanish because that's what they speak at home, and school words in English. If you count the words in both languages together, their total vocabulary is usually the same as, or larger than, a monolingual child's.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. So what's the lesson for teachers?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That you shouldn't assess bilingual children only in the school language, or you might wrongly think they have a language problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, the article also discusses the so-called bilingual advantage. Joseph, what did you make of that section?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: That was the part I found most surprising. I'd always heard that being bilingual makes you smarter, especially at what they call executive function, things like switching between tasks and ignoring distractions. The idea is that bilinguals constantly have to control which language they're using, so they get extra practice.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: But the article said that the evidence is much weaker than people think. Some early studies found big advantages, but they were small studies, and when researchers repeated them with larger groups, the effect often disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: And there's the problem of publication. Apparently, studies that found an advantage were more likely to be published than ones that didn't, which made the effect look stronger than it was.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important general point about research. So where does that leave us?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I think the article's conclusion was quite balanced. It said there may be some small cognitive benefits, but the main reasons for bilingualism are cultural and practical. Being able to talk to your grandparents, for instance.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: I agree. Though the article also said researchers are still arguing about it, so it's probably too early to say there's no advantage at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Which brings us to heritage languages. What did the article say about children of immigrants?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: That many of them gradually lose their parents' language as they grow up, especially once they start school. Often by the third generation, the family language has disappeared completely.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That happened to some of my cousins. They can understand Cantonese, but they can't really speak it. And the article said that some parents actually stop using their own language at home because a teacher told them it would help the child's English.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, which is advice the research doesn't support. Okay. For next week, I'd like each of you to find one study on how schools can support heritage languages, and be ready to summarise its method and findings in five minutes. Mei, perhaps you could look at weekend community schools, and Joseph, at bilingual programmes within ordinary schools?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Sure. That sounds really interesting. Should we include our own opinions as well?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Briefly, at the end, but focus on the evidence first.

listeningParts.title: The invention of writing
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory course on the history of communication.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. In this lecture, I'm going to talk about one of the most important inventions in human history: writing. Humans have been speaking for perhaps a hundred thousand years or more, but writing is only around five thousand years old. And unlike speech, which every human community has, writing was invented independently only a few times, perhaps as few as three or four.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The earliest known writing system developed in Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq, about five thousand two hundred years ago. Interestingly, it wasn't created to record stories, poems or laws. The earliest texts are almost all administrative records: lists of goods, such as grain, sheep and beer, and the names of the people who owed or received them. As cities grew and trade expanded, officials needed a reliable way of keeping track of who owed what.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Many researchers believe writing grew out of an older system of small clay tokens, which had been used for thousands of years to count goods. Different shapes represented different things: a cone might stand for a measure of grain, a sphere for a larger measure. These tokens were sometimes sealed inside clay containers, and the shapes were pressed into the outside so that people could see what was inside without breaking the container. Eventually, people realised they could simply make the marks on a flat piece of clay and do without the tokens altogether.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The Mesopotamian script is known as cuneiform, which means wedge-shaped, because the signs were made by pressing a cut reed into soft clay, producing marks shaped like wedges. At first, many signs were pictures of the things they represented, but over time they became more abstract, and scribes began to use signs for their sound rather than their meaning. This was a crucial step, because it meant writing could record any word in the language, including names and grammatical endings.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Clay turned out to be an excellent material for preserving information. Tablets that were baked, either deliberately or accidentally when buildings burned down, became as hard as pottery, and hundreds of thousands have survived. One famous example is the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, where around thirty thousand tablets were preserved when the palace was destroyed by fire in the seventh century BC.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Writing seems to have appeared in Egypt at around the same time as in Mesopotamia, though whether the Egyptians borrowed the idea or developed it independently is still debated. Writing was invented quite separately in China, where the earliest examples, from about three thousand two hundred years ago, are inscriptions on bones used to predict the future. And in Mesoamerica, the Maya developed a sophisticated script that was only fully deciphered in the late twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Early writing systems were extremely complicated. Cuneiform used several hundred signs, and Egyptian hieroglyphs even more, so reading and writing were skills restricted to a small group of professional scribes, who trained for many years. The development that made writing accessible to ordinary people was the alphabet, in which each sign represents a single sound. The first alphabet was created around three thousand eight hundred years ago by people speaking a Semitic language, possibly workers in Egypt who adapted some Egyptian signs. Because it needed only about two dozen letters, it was far easier to learn.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This early alphabet was adopted and adapted by the Phoenicians, who were great traders and spread it around the Mediterranean. The Greeks then made an important change: the Phoenician alphabet had no letters for vowels, so the Greeks added them. The Greek alphabet in turn gave rise to the Latin alphabet, which most European languages use today. Next week, we'll look at the next great revolution in communication: printing.

readingPassages.title: Cracking the code of the Rosetta Stone
paragraphs: For more than fourteen hundred years, no one could read the writing of ancient Egypt. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in the year 394, and after that the knowledge of how the script worked was gradually lost. Later scholars, including Arab writers in the Middle Ages and European scholars of the Renaissance, were fascinated by the mysterious signs carved on temples and monuments, but most assumed that each sign was a symbol expressing a philosophical or religious idea rather than a way of writing the sounds of a language. This assumption, as it turned out, was the main obstacle to decipherment.

The key to the problem was discovered in 1799, when French soldiers who were rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, known in Europe as Rosetta, in the Nile Delta, found a broken slab of dark stone covered with writing. The stone carried the same text, a decree issued by a council of priests in 196 BC, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in demotic, a cursive script used for everyday purposes in Egypt, and in ancient Greek. Since scholars could read Greek, it seemed that the stone might provide the means to understand the other two scripts. When the French were defeated by the British in Egypt, the stone was handed over under the terms of the peace agreement and taken to the British Museum in London, where it remains today.

Copies of the inscriptions were circulated among scholars across Europe, and several made progress. One of the most important early contributions came from Thomas Young, an English scientist and doctor who was also a gifted linguist. Young noticed that some hieroglyphs were enclosed in oval rings, now known as cartouches, and argued correctly that these contained the names of rulers. By comparing the cartouches with the Greek text, he identified the name of the king Ptolemy and worked out the sound values of several signs. However, Young believed that the hieroglyphs were used for sounds only when writing foreign names, such as Ptolemy, which was Greek, and that the rest of the script was symbolic.

The breakthrough came from Jean-François Champollion, a young French scholar who had been obsessed with ancient Egypt since childhood. Unlike Young, Champollion had a deep knowledge of Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, which had survived as the language of the Egyptian Christian church. In 1822, he examined copies of inscriptions from temples in Egypt and found cartouches containing names that were not Greek, but Egyptian, such as that of the pharaoh Ramesses. Using his knowledge of Coptic, he was able to read them. He realised that the hieroglyphic system was a mixture: some signs represented sounds, while others represented whole words or indicated the general category of a word's meaning.

According to a well-known story, when Champollion understood what he had found, he ran to his brother's office, shouted 'I've done it!' and promptly fainted. Whether or not this is true, his announcement in a letter to the French Academy later that year is generally taken as the moment when hieroglyphs were deciphered. Champollion continued to work on the script until his death in 1832, at the age of only forty-one, and published a grammar and dictionary of ancient Egyptian.

The relationship between Young and Champollion has been the subject of debate ever since. Young felt that his contribution had not been properly acknowledged, while Champollion insisted that he had reached his conclusions independently. Most historians now accept that Young made important early discoveries, but that it was Champollion who understood the system as a whole. National rivalry between Britain and France, which had recently been at war, undoubtedly made the dispute more bitter.

The decipherment of hieroglyphs opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history, literature and religion that had been silent for centuries. Thousands of texts, from royal inscriptions to private letters and medical manuals, could now be read. The Rosetta Stone itself has become a symbol of the key that unlocks something previously incomprehensible, and its name has even been borrowed by a well-known language-learning company. In recent years, Egypt has formally requested the return of the stone, arguing that it was removed from the country without the consent of its people.

readingPassages.title: The dance language of honeybees
paragraphs: Among the many ways in which animals communicate, few have attracted as much interest as the dance of the honeybee. When a forager bee discovers a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. Other bees cluster around her, following her movements closely, and soon afterwards many of them leave the hive and fly directly to the food source, even if it is several kilometres away. The dance, it seems, contains precise information about where the food can be found.

This remarkable behaviour was decoded by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for more than fifty years and was awarded a Nobel Prize in 1973 for his work. Von Frisch identified two main types of dance. When food is close to the hive, generally within about fifty metres, bees perform what he called the round dance, running in small circles and frequently changing direction. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction, and they search the area around the hive, using the scent of flowers carried on the dancer's body to help them.

When food is further away, bees perform the waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking her abdomen rapidly from side to side, then circles back to her starting point, first to one side and then the other, so that her path forms a figure of eight. The straight run carries the key information. Its angle relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun: if the bee runs straight upwards, the food is in the same direction as the sun; if she runs at an angle of forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies forty degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of the waggle run indicates distance, with longer runs signalling food that is further away.

Even more impressively, bees take account of the movement of the sun. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a bee that dances for an extended period gradually changes the angle of her waggle run to match. Von Frisch also showed that bees can locate the sun even when it is hidden by clouds, as long as a patch of blue sky is visible, by detecting patterns of polarised light that are invisible to humans.

Not everyone accepted von Frisch's interpretation. In the 1960s, some researchers argued that bees found food not by decoding the dance but simply by following the scent of flowers carried by the dancer. This led to a long and sometimes bitter debate. The question was largely settled in the 2000s, when scientists attached tiny radar transponders to bees that had watched a dance and tracked their flights. Most of the bees flew directly towards the area indicated by the dance, confirming that they were using the information it contained, although they then relied on scent to find the exact flowers.

More recent research has revealed that the dance is not perfectly accurate. The angle of the waggle runs varies slightly each time the bee repeats them, so that the information is somewhat imprecise. Some scientists have suggested that this variation may actually be useful, because it spreads the recruited bees over a wider area of flowers rather than concentrating them on a single spot. Others think it is simply a limitation of the system. Studies have also shown that the relationship between the length of the waggle run and distance differs between populations of bees, suggesting that bees in different regions use slightly different 'dialects'.

The dance is also used for purposes other than food. When a colony becomes too large, part of it leaves the hive with the old queen to establish a new nest. Scout bees search for suitable sites, such as hollow trees, and report back using the waggle dance. Different scouts advertise different sites, and over a period of hours or days, more and more scouts come to support the best site, until a kind of consensus is reached and the whole swarm flies off. The biologist Thomas Seeley has argued that this process is a highly effective form of collective decision-making from which human groups might learn.

readingPassages.title: Does language shape thought?
paragraphs: Does the language we speak affect the way we think? The question is an old one, but it is most closely associated with the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, who argued in the 1930s that speakers of different languages perceive and understand the world in fundamentally different ways. Whorf claimed, for example, that the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammatical forms referring to time, and that Hopi speakers therefore had a completely different conception of time from speakers of European languages. This idea, often called linguistic relativity or the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, became extremely popular, and it remains so outside academic circles.

Within linguistics, however, Whorf's ideas gradually fell out of favour. Later research showed that his claims about the Hopi language were simply wrong: Hopi does in fact have many ways of talking about time. More fundamentally, the dominant approach to language in the second half of the twentieth century, associated with Noam Chomsky, emphasised the features that all human languages have in common rather than their differences. From this perspective, languages were seen as variations on a single underlying system, and the idea that they might shape thought in deep ways seemed implausible. Few linguists, I suspect, regretted the decline of a theory built on such questionable evidence.

In the last thirty years, though, the question has returned, this time investigated with careful experiments rather than anecdotes. Researchers now generally reject the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis, the idea that language determines thought so that some concepts are impossible without the right words. Nobody seriously believes, for instance, that speakers of a language without a word for 'blue' cannot see the colour. But many accept a weaker version: that the habits of a particular language may influence attention, memory and perception in subtle but measurable ways.

One of the most striking lines of research concerns space. In English, we usually describe the location of objects relative to our own bodies: the cup is to the left of the plate. But some languages, such as Guugu Yimithirr, spoken in north-eastern Australia, rarely use words like 'left' and 'right'. Instead, speakers use compass directions, saying that the cup is to the north of the plate, even when talking about objects on a table. To speak like this, people must keep track of their orientation at all times, and studies have found that speakers of such languages are remarkably good at knowing which direction they are facing, even in unfamiliar places or inside buildings.

Colour has also been extensively studied. Russian has two separate basic words for what English speakers call blue: one for lighter shades and one for darker ones. In one experiment, Russian and English speakers were shown three squares of blue and asked which of the bottom two matched the top one. Russian speakers were faster when the two shades came from different categories in Russian, while English speakers showed no such difference. Interestingly, the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they were asked to repeat a series of numbers silently during the task, suggesting that language was actively involved in their judgements.

Grammar may matter too. In languages such as Spanish and German, nouns have grammatical gender, being classified as masculine or feminine. Some studies have reported that speakers describe objects in ways that reflect this gender: for example, that German speakers, for whom the word for 'bridge' is feminine, are more likely to describe bridges as elegant or beautiful, while Spanish speakers, for whom it is masculine, describe them as strong. These findings have been widely reported in the media, but attempts to repeat some of them have failed, and I would treat them with considerable caution.

What should we conclude? It seems clear that language does not imprison thought, as Whorf's more enthusiastic followers suggested. People can think about things they have no words for, and they can learn new languages and new ways of describing the world. Yet the evidence also suggests that the language we speak trains us to pay attention to certain aspects of experience more than others. In this modest sense, Whorf may have been more right than his critics allowed, even if many of his own examples were mistaken.
