listeningParts.title: Reporting a lost item at a conference centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A conference delegate calls the lost property office at an international conference centre.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Lost property, Harbour Conference Centre, Nadia speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I'm hoping you can help. I was at the climate science conference yesterday and I think I left my laptop bag somewhere in the building.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let's see what we can do. Can you describe the bag?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: It's a black leather bag, quite slim, with a shoulder strap. Actually, no, sorry, it's dark brown. It looks black under artificial light, but it's brown. And it has a small metal badge on the front with a koala on it. My daughter gave it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: A dark brown leather bag with a koala badge. And what was inside?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: My laptop, obviously, which is silver, and the charger. There was also a notebook, a couple of pens and a paper copy of my presentation. Oh, and my reading glasses in a red case.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Was there anything with your name on it?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: The notebook has my name inside the front cover, and there's a luggage label on the handle with my email address.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: That's helpful. Could I take your name?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: It's Dr Fiona Atherton. A-T-H-E-R-T-O-N.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Thank you, Dr Atherton. And do you know where you might have left it?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: I've been trying to think. I gave my talk in the morning in Room Twelve, and I definitely had it then because I used the laptop. After that I went to lunch in the main restaurant, and then I attended a session in the auditorium. I'm fairly sure I had it at lunch, so I suspect it was in the auditorium. I remember putting it under the seat.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: The auditorium is cleaned every evening, and anything found there is brought to us. Let me check our records for yesterday. We've had quite a few laptop bags handed in this week, as you can imagine. Do you happen to know the make of the laptop?

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: It's a Lenmark. I don't know the model, I'm afraid, but I do have the serial number at home, written down somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: If you can find it, that would help us confirm it's yours. Now, I can see that a brown bag was handed in by a cleaner at about nine o'clock last night. The description says leather, with a badge. That sounds promising.

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: Oh, thank goodness. Can I come and collect it?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Of course. The lost property office is on the ground floor, behind the main reception desk. We're open from eight in the morning until six in the evening. You'll need to bring some photo identification, and if possible, your conference badge, the one on the lanyard.

dialogue.speaker: Delegate
dialogue.text: Ah, that might be a problem. The thing is, I'm flying home to Brisbane tonight, and I'm in a meeting across town all day. Is there any way someone else could pick it up for me?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Yes, a colleague can collect it, but they'll need a letter or email from you giving permission, as well as their own identification. listeningParts.title: An evening at the observatory
listeningParts.contextDescription: An astronomer introduces a public stargazing evening at a university observatory.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: Good evening, and welcome to the Mount Carrow Observatory. My name's Dr Leo Brandt, and I'm one of the astronomers who works here. Tonight's programme will last about two hours, and I'll start by telling you a little about the observatory and how the evening will work, before we head outside.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: The observatory was built in 1928, when this hill was well outside the city. At that time, the sky here was dark enough to see the Milky Way on any clear night. As the city has grown, though, light from streets and buildings has spread across the sky, and today our research telescopes are used mainly for training students rather than for serious research, which is now done at observatories in remote locations such as the mountains of Chile.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: That said, we're lucky in one respect. Three years ago, the hills to the west of here were designated a dark-sky reserve. That means local councils have agreed to limit outdoor lighting, and many streetlights have been replaced with lamps that point downwards and use a warmer colour. Measurements show the sky to the west is now noticeably darker than it was a decade ago, which is a rare example of light pollution actually being reduced.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: Now, the evening is divided into three parts. We'll begin in the planetarium, which is the dome-shaped building next to this one. There, I'll show you what's visible in tonight's sky, so you know what to look for. That takes about twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: Then we'll go out onto the viewing terrace, where we've set up six smaller telescopes, each operated by one of our volunteers. Each telescope will be pointed at a different object. Tonight, if the clouds stay away, we should be able to show you Saturn and its rings, the Moon, which is half full tonight, and a cluster of stars called the Pleiades. Please wait for the volunteer to adjust the telescope; don't move it yourself, because it takes time to find an object again.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: Finally, at about nine fifteen, we'll open the main dome, where our largest telescope is housed. Groups of ten will go up in turn. It's a narrow spiral staircase, I'm afraid, so if anyone has difficulty with stairs, let one of the staff know and we'll show you the view on a screen downstairs, which is connected to a camera on the telescope.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: A few practical points. It's going to get cold, even though it's been a warm day, so please keep your coats on outside. When you're on the terrace, it takes about twenty minutes for your eyes to adjust fully to the dark, so please don't use your phones. Even a brief glance at a bright screen undoes that adjustment. If you need a light to see your way, use the small red torches we've given you; red light affects night vision much less than white light.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: Children are very welcome, of course, but please keep an eye on them on the terrace, because there's a steep slope beyond the fence. Hot drinks are available in the entrance hall throughout the evening; there's no charge, but donations to the observatory's education fund are very much appreciated.

dialogue.speaker: Astronomer
dialogue.text: And one last thing. If you enjoy tonight, you might like to come back on the twelfth of August, when we're holding a special late-night event for the Perseid meteor shower. The meteors are best seen after midnight, so the observatory will stay open until two in the morning. You don't need a telescope for meteors, just your eyes and a comfortable chair, so we'll be setting up deckchairs on the lawn. Right, let's go through to the planetarium.

listeningParts.title: Interpreting ice-core data
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two earth science students, Hugo and Priya, discuss a lab report on ice cores with their supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Right, Hugo, Priya, I've read the first draft of your report on the Antarctic ice-core data. There's a lot of good work in it, but I'd like to go through a few things.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Thanks. We weren't sure whether the introduction was too long.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Actually, the length is fine. The problem is more that it reads like a general history of ice-core research. The reader needs to know quite early on what specific question your report is trying to answer.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo
dialogue.text: So we should state the research question in the first paragraph?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Ideally, yes, and cut some of the historical detail. Now, your method section. You explain clearly how the cores were drilled and stored, but you don't say much about how the ages of the layers were determined. That's crucial for everything that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We thought that was obvious, because you can count the annual layers, like tree rings.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: In the upper part of the core, yes. But further down, the ice has been compressed so much that individual years can't be distinguished. Below that depth, ages are estimated using models of how ice flows, combined with markers like layers of volcanic ash from eruptions whose dates are known. You need to explain that, and acknowledge that the uncertainty increases with depth.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I remember the lecture saying that at the bottom of some cores, the uncertainty is thousands of years.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, the results. You've used the ratio of oxygen isotopes as your temperature proxy. Can you remind me why that works?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Water containing the heavier oxygen isotope evaporates less easily and falls out of the air sooner as rain or snow. So when the climate is colder, snow reaching the poles contains relatively less of the heavy isotope. The ratio in the ice tells us roughly what the temperature was when the snow fell.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good. But you need to be careful with your language in the discussion. You say that the isotope record 'proves' that temperatures rose by a certain amount at the end of the last ice age. A proxy doesn't prove anything on its own. It's calibrated against modern observations, and that calibration may not hold perfectly in the past.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo
dialogue.text: So 'indicates' or 'suggests' would be better?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Much better. Now, the part I found most interesting was your graph comparing temperature and carbon dioxide. The two lines follow each other very closely.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Yes, that was what surprised us most. Over eight hundred thousand years, whenever temperature goes up, carbon dioxide goes up too.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo
dialogue.text: Although we noticed that in some places, temperature seems to start rising slightly before carbon dioxide. We weren't sure whether to mention that, because some people use it to argue that carbon dioxide doesn't affect temperature.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: You should definitely mention it, and explain it. The current understanding is that the ice ages were triggered by small changes in the Earth's orbit, which warmed the planet slightly at first. That warming caused the oceans to release carbon dioxide, which then amplified the warming. So carbon dioxide acted as a feedback, not the original trigger. That doesn't contradict its role as a greenhouse gas at all.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: That's really useful. Should we put that in the discussion?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Yes, with references. Finally, your conclusion introduces a new idea about future sea-level rise. Interesting, but it isn't supported by anything in your results, so I'd remove it, or move it to a short section on further research.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo
dialogue.text: Okay. When do you need the revised version?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: By the end of next week. And make sure the graphs have proper axis labels and units; two of them don't at the moment.

listeningParts.title: Measuring time
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a history of science course on how humans have measured time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today's lecture is about something we rarely think about but rely on constantly: the measurement of time. I'll trace the main stages in the history of timekeeping and consider how each new level of precision changed society, sometimes in quite unexpected ways.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The earliest timekeepers were natural cycles: the day, the phases of the moon and the seasons. For dividing up the day, the first instrument was the sundial, used in Egypt over three and a half thousand years ago. Sundials work well, of course, only when the sun is shining, and they can't be used at night. The Egyptians and later the Greeks also used water clocks, in which water dripped at a steady rate from one container to another. These had the advantage of working in any weather and at night, and they were used, among other things, to limit the length of speeches in Athenian law courts.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: An important point to bear in mind is that, for most of history, hours were not of fixed length. Many societies divided the period of daylight into twelve equal parts, whatever the season, so a summer hour was considerably longer than a winter hour. Equal hours only became standard with the spread of mechanical clocks in Europe in the fourteenth century. These early clocks, usually installed in church towers, were large iron machines driven by falling weights, and they were not very accurate; they might gain or lose fifteen minutes a day and had to be reset regularly using a sundial.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The great leap in accuracy came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, based on Galileo's observation that a pendulum of a given length always takes the same time to swing, regardless of how far it swings. Huygens's clocks reduced the error to around fifteen seconds a day. For the first time, it made sense for clocks to have minute hands.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Pendulum clocks, however, were useless at sea, where the motion of the ship disrupted the pendulum. And accurate timekeeping at sea was a matter of life and death. Sailors could determine their latitude, their position north or south, quite easily from the height of the sun or stars, but longitude, their position east or west, was another matter. In principle, longitude could be calculated by comparing local time with the time at a reference point such as the home port, but this required a clock that kept accurate time for weeks on a moving ship. After a series of shipwrecks, the British government offered a huge prize in 1714 for a solution. It was eventually won by John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter, whose marine clocks, called chronometers, proved accurate to within a few seconds a day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the nineteenth century, it was the railways that transformed time. Before then, each town kept its own local time, based on the position of the sun, so that noon in Bristol was about ten minutes later than in London. This didn't matter when travel was slow, but it made railway timetables extremely confusing. In 1847, British railway companies adopted a single standard time across the network, and towns gradually followed. Time zones based on the meridian at Greenwich were agreed internationally in 1884.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The twentieth century brought two further revolutions. Quartz clocks, which use the regular vibration of a quartz crystal when an electric current passes through it, were developed in the 1920s and eventually made accurate watches cheap enough for almost everyone. Then, in 1955, the first atomic clock was built, measuring time by the extremely regular vibrations of caesium atoms. Since 1967, the second itself has been officially defined in terms of these vibrations rather than the rotation of the Earth, which is actually slightly irregular.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: You might wonder why we need such extreme precision. The answer is that much of modern technology depends on it. Satellite navigation systems work by measuring how long signals take to travel from several satellites to a receiver, and an error of a single millionth of a second would put your position out by about three hundred metres. Financial markets, mobile phone networks and power grids all depend on precise synchronisation. Next week, we'll turn to the measurement of distance.

readingPassages.title: Reading the rocks: the discovery of deep time
paragraphs: Until the late eighteenth century, most educated Europeans believed that the Earth was only a few thousand years old. The most famous calculation, published in 1650 by the Irish archbishop James Ussher, placed the creation of the world in the year 4004 BC, a date arrived at by carefully adding up the generations recorded in the Bible. Ussher's work was not regarded as eccentric; it was a serious piece of scholarship, and his date was printed in the margins of many Bibles for the next two centuries. Within this short timescale, features of the landscape such as mountains and valleys were usually explained as the result of sudden catastrophes, most notably the great flood described in the Book of Genesis.

The person most often credited with overturning this view is the Scottish naturalist James Hutton. Hutton, who had trained in medicine and then become a farmer, spent years observing how soil was gradually washed away from fields by rain and carried by rivers to the sea. He reasoned that the sediment deposited on the sea floor would slowly be compressed into new rock, which might eventually be pushed up to form new land, to be worn away in turn. The Earth, in Hutton's view, was a kind of machine that continuously destroyed and renewed itself. Crucially, the processes involved, erosion, deposition and uplift, were the same slow ones that could be observed at work in the present.

Hutton's most famous evidence came from a coastal headland called Siccar Point, east of Edinburgh, which he visited by boat in 1788 with two friends. There, nearly vertical layers of grey rock are overlain by gently sloping layers of red sandstone. Hutton recognised that the grey layers must originally have been laid down horizontally on a sea floor, then tilted and lifted above the sea, eroded flat, and finally submerged again so that the red layers could be deposited on top. Each of these stages, if it had happened at the slow rates that could be observed, must have taken an immense length of time. His friend John Playfair later wrote that 'the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time'.

Hutton summarised his conclusion in a phrase that has become famous: the Earth showed 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end'. This was not a claim that the Earth was infinitely old, but rather that the rocks themselves contained no evidence of how long ago it had begun. Nevertheless, his ideas met strong opposition, partly on religious grounds, and partly because his writing was notoriously difficult to read. It was only after Playfair published a clearer account in 1802 that the ideas reached a wider audience.

In the following decades, Hutton's approach was developed by Charles Lyell, whose three-volume Principles of Geology, published between 1830 and 1833, argued that the Earth's history could be explained entirely by processes still operating today, a principle that came to be known as uniformitarianism. Lyell's book had an enormous influence, not least on the young Charles Darwin, who took the first volume with him on the voyage of the Beagle. Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, which required vast periods for small changes to accumulate, would have been almost unthinkable without the geological timescale that Hutton and Lyell had made available.

Yet even the geologists had no reliable way of measuring how old the Earth actually was. Estimates based on the rate at which sediments accumulated, or the time it would take the oceans to become salty, varied wildly. In the 1860s, the physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, calculated the age of the Earth from the rate at which it must have cooled from a molten state, arriving at a figure of between twenty and four hundred million years, which he later narrowed to around twenty to forty million. Kelvin's prestige was such that many geologists accepted his figures, even though they seemed far too short to accommodate the history recorded in the rocks.

The solution came from an unexpected direction. The discovery of radioactivity at the end of the nineteenth century showed that the Earth contained a source of heat that Kelvin had not known about, invalidating his calculations. More importantly, radioactive elements decay at constant, measurable rates, providing a natural clock. In the early twentieth century, scientists began to use this to date rocks directly. Today, using this method on meteorites and the oldest minerals, the age of the Earth is estimated at about 4.54 billion years, a figure that would have astonished even Hutton.

readingPassages.title: The problem of space debris
paragraphs: Since the launch of the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957, humanity has sent more than fifteen thousand satellites into orbit, and the pace is accelerating rapidly. Most of the satellites launched in recent years belong to so-called mega-constellations, networks of thousands of small satellites designed to provide internet access around the globe. Alongside the working satellites, however, orbit an enormous quantity of debris: dead satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments produced by explosions and collisions. Space agencies estimate that there are more than thirty thousand pieces larger than ten centimetres being tracked from the ground, and perhaps a million pieces between one and ten centimetres, too small to track but large enough to cause serious damage.

The danger arises from speed rather than size. In low Earth orbit, objects travel at around seven to eight kilometres per second, roughly ten times as fast as a bullet. At these speeds, even a fragment of paint can damage a spacecraft window, and the windows of the International Space Station have had to be replaced several times because of chips caused by tiny particles. A piece of debris the size of a marble carries as much energy as a bowling ball travelling at motorway speeds, and a collision with an object of ten centimetres or more would be likely to destroy a satellite completely.

In 1978, a scientist at NASA, Donald Kessler, published a paper warning of a possible chain reaction. If the density of objects in a particular orbit becomes high enough, he argued, collisions will produce fragments faster than natural processes remove them, and each fragment will increase the probability of further collisions. In the worst case, certain orbits could become so crowded with debris that they would be unusable for generations. This scenario, now known as the Kessler syndrome, was once regarded as a distant possibility, but some researchers believe that the most crowded orbits may already have passed the point at which the number of fragments will continue to grow even if no further launches take place.

Two events dramatically increased the amount of debris. In 2007, China deliberately destroyed one of its own old weather satellites with a missile as a test of anti-satellite technology, creating more than three thousand trackable fragments, many of which remain in orbit. Two years later, an inactive Russian military satellite collided accidentally with a working American communications satellite above Siberia, the first known collision between two intact satellites, producing more than two thousand further fragments. Further anti-satellite tests by other countries have since added to the problem, prompting widespread international criticism.

Whether debris eventually falls back to Earth depends largely on its altitude. At the lowest orbits, around three or four hundred kilometres, the thin atmosphere gradually slows objects down, and most burn up on re-entry within a few years. At eight hundred kilometres, the process may take centuries, and in the geostationary orbit used by many communications satellites, about thirty-six thousand kilometres above the equator, objects will remain effectively forever. Operators of geostationary satellites are therefore expected to move them, at the end of their working lives, into a higher 'graveyard' orbit where they will not interfere with active spacecraft.

Current international guidelines recommend that satellites in low orbit should be removed within twenty-five years of the end of their mission, either by being lowered so that they burn up or by being moved out of busy orbits. Compliance, however, has been poor, partly because the guidelines are voluntary and partly because older satellites were not designed with the necessary fuel or equipment. Several regulators have recently tightened the rules; the United States, for example, now requires many satellites it licenses to be removed within five years. Critics argue, though, that national rules are of limited value when space is shared by dozens of countries with different priorities.

Engineers are also developing ways to remove existing debris. Proposed methods include nets, harpoons and robotic arms to capture dead satellites, magnetic docking devices fitted to new satellites in advance, and lasers fired from the ground to nudge small fragments into lower orbits. A small number of demonstration missions have already taken place. The difficulty is less technical than economic and legal: removing a single large object is expensive, no company has an obvious financial incentive to do it, and international law gives the original owner continuing ownership of its objects in space, even when they are no longer working, which means that one country cannot simply remove another's debris without permission.

readingPassages.title: Is there anybody out there?
paragraphs: In the summer of 1950, during a lunchtime conversation at the Los Alamos laboratory in New Mexico, the physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have asked a deceptively simple question: 'Where is everybody?' Fermi's point was that the galaxy is extremely old and contains hundreds of billions of stars, many of them billions of years older than the Sun. If even a tiny fraction of them had produced technological civilisations, and if any of those civilisations had developed interstellar travel, then, given enough time, they should have spread throughout the galaxy. Yet we see no sign of them. This apparent contradiction between the high probability of alien life and the absence of evidence for it has become known as the Fermi paradox.

The question gained a more formal structure in 1961, when the astronomer Frank Drake proposed an equation intended not so much to produce an answer as to organise the discussion. The Drake equation multiplies together a series of factors: the rate at which stars form, the fraction of stars with planets, the number of planets suitable for life, and the fractions of those on which life, intelligence and detectable technology develop, together with the length of time such civilisations remain detectable. At the time, only the first of these factors could be estimated with any confidence. The others were, in effect, educated guesses, and depending on the values chosen, the equation could yield anything from a galaxy teeming with civilisations to one in which we are entirely alone.

Since then, one part of the equation has been transformed. In 1995, astronomers confirmed the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star, and space telescopes have since identified more than five thousand such exoplanets. It now appears that planets are the rule rather than the exception, and that a substantial proportion of stars have rocky planets at a distance where liquid water could exist on the surface. In purely astronomical terms, then, potential homes for life seem to be abundant. Yet this progress has, if anything, sharpened the paradox, because it removes one of the most obvious explanations for the silence.

The proposed solutions fall broadly into three groups. The first holds that life, or at least intelligent life, is genuinely rare. Perhaps the origin of life from non-living chemistry is an extraordinarily unlikely event, or perhaps the evolution of complex cells, which on Earth took around two billion years, requires a sequence of improbable accidents. The economist Robin Hanson has described this possibility as a 'Great Filter', some step in the development from simple chemistry to galaxy-spanning civilisation that almost no species manages to pass. I find this explanation the most persuasive of the three, though, as Hanson himself has noted, it carries an uncomfortable implication: if the filter lies ahead of us rather than behind, our own prospects may be bleak.

A second group of explanations accepts that civilisations may be common but argues that we would not have noticed them. Interstellar distances are vast, and radio signals weaken rapidly with distance; a civilisation like ours, broadcasting accidentally, would probably be undetectable beyond a few light years. Advanced societies might communicate by means we have not thought to look for, or might deliberately avoid contact. Supporters of this view also point out that our searches have been remarkably limited. One researcher has calculated that, relative to the volume of space and range of frequencies that might plausibly be searched, the effort so far is comparable to examining a single glass of water from the world's oceans and concluding that the seas contain no fish. This argument has some force, but in my view it does not fully answer Fermi's original point, which concerned not signals but the physical spread of civilisations across the galaxy.

A third group of explanations focuses on the behaviour of civilisations themselves. Perhaps technological societies tend to destroy themselves, through war or environmental collapse, soon after acquiring the ability to do so. Perhaps they lose interest in expansion, turning inward to virtual worlds of their own making. Explanations of this kind are difficult to evaluate, because they require us to assume that all, or almost all, civilisations behave in the same way, an assumption that seems unlikely given the diversity of human cultures alone.

What is striking about the Fermi paradox is that it has stimulated useful research across many disciplines, from the chemistry of the origin of life to the study of planetary atmospheres. In the coming decades, telescopes may be able to analyse the atmospheres of nearby exoplanets for gases, such as oxygen combined with methane, that are difficult to explain without biology. Such a discovery would not settle the question of intelligent life, but it would tell us whether life itself is a common outcome of planetary evolution, and that, I would argue, is the more fundamental question.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering on a wildlife survey
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a conservation charity to sign up for a weekend bird survey.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello, Westmoor Wildlife Trust, Karen speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I read in the local paper that you're looking for volunteers for a bird survey, and I'd like to find out more.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Oh, wonderful. Yes, we're doing our annual count of breeding birds on the Westmoor wetlands. We use the information to see how populations are changing from year to year. Have you done any bird surveys before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Not formally. I've been watching birds as a hobby for about five years, so I can recognise most of the common species, but I've never taken part in a proper survey.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That's absolutely fine. Most of our volunteers start that way. Each new volunteer is paired with an experienced surveyor for the first day, so you'll learn the method as you go.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. When does the survey take place?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We do two visits: one in April and one in June. The April visit is on the weekend of the twelfth and thirteenth. You'd only need to come on one of the days, though, not both.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I could do the Sunday. Saturdays are difficult for me.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Sunday the thirteenth, then. I should warn you, it's an early start. Birds are most active just after sunrise, so we meet at five forty-five in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wow, that is early. Where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: At the car park next to the visitor centre. Don't go to the main entrance on the road, because the gates aren't opened until nine. There's a separate track to the car park from Mill Lane. Look for the sign with a heron on it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Mill Lane, sign with a heron. Got it. How long does the survey last?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Usually about four hours. Each pair walks a fixed route, which we call a transect, and records every bird they see or hear within fifty metres of the path. You'll be back by about ten, and we provide breakfast at the visitor centre afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Breakfast sounds good after that. What do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Binoculars are the most important thing. If you don't have any, we can lend you a pair, but let me know in advance because we only have six. Bring waterproofs, even if the forecast is good, because the wetlands can be very wet underfoot, and wellington boots are better than walking boots.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I have binoculars, so that's fine. Do I need a notebook?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No, we'll give you a recording sheet and a clipboard. Some volunteers like to use an app on their phone instead, but we ask everyone to fill in the paper sheet as well, in case the phone battery runs out.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Is there any cost involved?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No, volunteering is completely free. And all our volunteers get free entry to our nature reserves for the year. If you'd like to become a member of the Trust as well, that's twenty-four pounds a year, but there's no obligation at all.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very generous. Can I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Marcus Delaney. That's D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know, any health issues for example?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm fine, but I'm allergic to bee stings. I carry medication with me.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me. I'll let your survey partner know. And one last thing: there's a short online training video about identifying birds by their songs. It's only twenty minutes, and it's really worth watching before the day, because about half of what you record will be birds you hear rather than see.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll definitely watch it tonight. Will I get the results of the survey afterwards?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes, we send all volunteers a short report in the autumn, showing how the numbers compare with previous years. Last year, for example, we recorded our first pair of breeding bitterns for twenty years, which was very exciting.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's great. Thanks, Karen.

listeningParts.title: Rewilding at Hartwell Estate
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a former farm explains a rewilding project to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, and welcome to Hartwell. My name is Tom Ashby, and my family farmed this land for four generations. Fifteen years ago, we made the decision to stop farming it in the traditional way and to let nature take over instead, a process usually called rewilding. I'll explain why we did that and what has happened since, and then we'll walk down to the river.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The honest answer to why is money. The soil here is heavy clay, which makes it very difficult and expensive to farm. For years, we were losing money on almost every crop, and my father was close to selling the land. A friend suggested we look at what had been done on a similar estate in the Netherlands, and that gave us the idea.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So what did we actually do? First, we stopped ploughing and stopped using fertilisers and pesticides. We took down most of the internal fences, so the land became one large area rather than a lot of separate fields. And we introduced a small number of grazing animals: old breeds of cattle and pigs, as well as ponies and deer. These animals act as a substitute for the large wild herbivores that once lived in Britain. As they graze, browse and dig, they create a mixture of habitats: open grassland in some places, thick scrub in others, and young trees growing up through the thorny bushes.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: One thing that surprised us was how important scrub turned out to be. Most people see thorny bushes as untidy, a sign that land has been neglected. But scrub is actually one of the richest habitats for wildlife. It shelters nesting birds, provides food for insects, and protects young oak trees from being eaten by deer until they're big enough to survive.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The results have been remarkable. We've recorded a large increase in the number of species of butterflies and moths, and populations of several birds that are declining elsewhere in the country have grown here. The most famous example is the nightingale. When we started, we had perhaps two or three pairs. Now we have more than thirty, which makes Hartwell one of the most important sites for nightingales in the country.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Three years ago, with permission from the government, we released a family of beavers into the river. Beavers build dams, which slow down the flow of water. That has created a series of ponds and wetlands, which are fantastic for insects, frogs and fish. It has also helped to reduce flooding in the village downstream, because the water is held back and released more slowly after heavy rain.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, how does the estate make money if we're not farming? Mainly through what we call nature-based tourism. We have a campsite, a few safari tents and some holiday cottages, and we run guided walks like this one. We also sell meat from the cattle and pigs, which is in high demand because the animals live outdoors all year. And recently, we've begun to receive payments for storing carbon in our soils and trees, which may become a more important source of income in the future.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Not everyone has welcomed what we've done. Some of our farming neighbours were worried that weeds from our land would spread into their fields, and a few felt that we were wasting good farmland when the country needs to produce food. We take those concerns seriously. We cut back plants along our borders, and we've shared what we've learned with other farmers, several of whom are now rewilding small areas of their own land, such as field edges and riverbanks.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, before we set off, a couple of requests. Please keep to the paths, and keep dogs on leads, because the cattle have young calves at the moment and may be protective. And if you're lucky enough to hear a nightingale, please stay quiet and don't use recordings to try to attract it, as that can disturb nesting birds.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on urban foxes
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two zoology students, Ellie and Raj, prepare a presentation on foxes living in cities with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, you two have chosen urban foxes for your presentation. Why foxes?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Partly because they're so visible. Almost everyone in the city has a story about seeing a fox in their garden or on the street at night. But when we started reading, we realised how little most people actually know about them, and how many myths there are.

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: And it's a good example of a wild animal adapting to a completely human environment, which links to the theme of the module.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. What's the history? When did foxes start living in cities?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: In Britain, it seems to have started in the 1930s, when lots of new suburbs were built with large gardens. Foxes moved in from the surrounding countryside, and the gardens gave them shelter and plenty of food.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: A lot of people assume foxes came into cities because they couldn't find food in the countryside, but there's no real evidence for that. They simply found that suburbs were a very good habitat.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What do urban foxes actually eat? People often say they live mainly on rubbish.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: That's one of the myths we want to address. Studies that analysed what foxes eat found that food deliberately put out by people, for foxes, birds or pets, makes up a much larger part of their diet than food taken from bins. They also eat a lot of earthworms, insects and fruit, and they catch some rats and mice.

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: And one study estimated that about one household in ten in some cities feeds foxes on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. How have researchers studied their movements?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Mostly with GPS collars, which record the fox's position every few minutes. The results show that urban foxes have much smaller territories than rural ones, because food is so concentrated. In the countryside a fox might need several square kilometres, but in a city it might be less than half a square kilometre.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: And there's a really nice citizen science project where people put camera traps in their gardens. They've collected thousands of video clips of foxes, and they've shown how foxes use fences and walls as routes, almost like roads.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are foxes active during the day as well?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Mostly at night, especially in busy areas, because that's when there are fewer people and less traffic. But in quiet parks and gardens, they're often seen during the day too, particularly in spring when they have cubs to feed. Traffic is actually the biggest cause of death for urban foxes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What about the idea that urban foxes are becoming different from rural foxes?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: There's a study comparing skulls that found urban foxes have slightly shorter, wider snouts than rural ones. The researchers suggested this might be because they don't need to catch fast-moving prey so much, and they eat more food that needs crushing rather than tearing.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: But we want to be careful there. It's one study, and the differences are small. We don't want to suggest that foxes are evolving into a new species.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that's a sensible caution. Now, how are you going to structure the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with a short video clip from the camera traps, to get people's attention. Then the history, then diet, then movement, and finally the question of conflict with people.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What do you mean by conflict?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Things like foxes digging in gardens, or making noise at night. Some people want them removed. But research suggests that killing urban foxes doesn't work, because other foxes quickly move into the empty territory.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point to end on. I'd suggest finishing with some practical advice on living alongside foxes, rather than just the problem. And keep your slides simple; one main idea per slide.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Okay. We'll have a practice run on Friday.

listeningParts.title: The hidden life of trees
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a plant biology course on how trees interact with each other and with fungi.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's topic has attracted a great deal of public attention in the last few years: the idea that trees communicate and cooperate with each other through underground networks. You may have heard the phrase 'wood wide web'. I want to explain what we know, what is still debated, and why it matters for how we manage forests.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with the basics. If you dig into the soil of almost any forest, you'll find that tree roots are surrounded by extremely fine threads. These are the threads of fungi, and the partnership between the fungus and the plant root is called a mycorrhiza, from the Greek words for fungus and root. Around ninety per cent of land plants form these partnerships.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The relationship benefits both sides. The fungal threads are much thinner than roots and can spread far further through the soil, so they're very good at absorbing water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, which they pass to the tree. In return, the tree supplies the fungus with sugars that it produces by photosynthesis. In some forests, trees may give up as much as a third of the sugar they produce to their fungal partners. That tells you how valuable the relationship must be.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, here's where it gets interesting. A single fungus can connect to the roots of several trees at once, and a single tree can be connected to many fungi. So the trees in a forest can be linked together in a network. In the 1990s, the Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard carried out a famous experiment in which she covered young trees with bags and supplied them with carbon dioxide containing a special form of carbon that can be traced. She then found that some of this carbon turned up in neighbouring trees of a different species. This suggested that carbon was moving from tree to tree through the fungal network.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Later studies claimed to show even more remarkable things. One finding was that the largest, oldest trees, sometimes called 'mother trees', are connected to many young trees and may send them carbon, particularly when the young trees are growing in deep shade. Other experiments suggested that when a tree is attacked by insects, chemical signals may travel through the network and prompt neighbouring trees to increase their defences.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: These ideas have been enormously popular. They've appeared in best-selling books and documentaries, often with the message that forests are cooperative communities, a bit like families. However, I need to stress that in recent years a number of scientists have raised serious doubts. A review published in 2023 examined the evidence and concluded that many of the most widely repeated claims are not well supported. The networks certainly exist, but it's much less clear how often carbon is actually transferred in meaningful amounts, and whether this happens because trees are helping each other or simply because the fungi move resources around to suit their own needs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In other words, the fungi are not neutral cables. They're living organisms with their own interests. Some researchers argue that it may be more accurate to think of the fungi as traders, exchanging nutrients for sugar wherever they get the best deal, rather than as a communication system that trees use to cooperate.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever the outcome of this debate, the research has had practical consequences. It has shown that the soil beneath a forest is a vital part of the ecosystem. When forests are clear-felled, meaning all the trees in an area are cut down at once, the fungal networks can be badly damaged, and young trees planted afterwards may grow more slowly. Some forest managers now leave groups of older trees standing when they harvest timber, in the hope that this will help the forest recover. Next time, we'll look at the role of forests in the global carbon cycle.

readingPassages.title: The return of the wolf
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the grey wolf was absent from Yellowstone National Park in the United States. Wolves had been deliberately exterminated across most of the country by the 1920s, hunted, trapped and poisoned because they killed livestock and were widely regarded as dangerous pests. In Yellowstone, even park rangers took part in the campaign, and the last known wolves in the park were killed in 1926. At the time, few people questioned this policy, and some biologists even supported it, believing that an ecosystem without predators would be richer and more stable. Removing large predators was seen as a way of protecting the elk, deer and other grazing animals that visitors came to see.

Over the following decades, however, scientists began to notice changes in the park's ecosystem. Without wolves, the elk population grew dramatically, and the animals spent long periods grazing in river valleys, where they ate young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees before they had a chance to grow. As these trees disappeared from riverbanks, other species that depended on them declined. Beavers, which need willow for food and for building dams, became extremely rare, and the loss of beaver dams changed the way rivers flowed. Some songbirds that nest in riverside trees also declined, and the banks of some streams began to erode more quickly without tree roots to hold the soil in place.

In 1995 and 1996, after years of public debate and legal challenges, thirty-one wolves captured in Canada were released into Yellowstone. The reintroduction was strongly opposed by many ranchers in the surrounding states, who feared that wolves would leave the park and attack their cattle and sheep. To address these concerns, a conservation organisation set up a fund to compensate ranchers for any livestock killed by wolves, and the government allowed wolves that repeatedly attacked livestock outside the park to be shot.

The wolves thrived, helped by an abundant supply of prey. Within a decade, their numbers in the park had risen to more than a hundred, divided among a dozen or so packs. The most obvious effect was on the elk, whose population fell considerably over the following years. But researchers soon began to report changes that went far beyond the direct effect of wolves killing elk. In some river valleys, willow and aspen began to grow again. Beaver colonies increased from one to nine within about a decade, and their dams created ponds that provided habitats for fish, amphibians and birds.

To explain these changes, some ecologists proposed what they called the 'landscape of fear'. According to this idea, elk changed their behaviour in response to the presence of wolves, avoiding open valleys and riverbanks where they could easily be trapped, and spending less time in any one place. This reduced grazing pressure on young trees in those areas, allowing them to recover. The effects of a predator thus spread through the whole food chain, a process ecologists call a trophic cascade.

The Yellowstone story became famous around the world, helped by a popular online video claiming that wolves had literally 'changed the course of rivers'. In recent years, however, many scientists have argued that the story has been oversimplified. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting outside the park, harsh winters and the growing number of other predators, such as bears and cougars. Some studies have found that elk do not avoid areas used by wolves as much as the 'landscape of fear' theory suggests. And in many valleys, willows have not recovered, possibly because without beaver dams, the water table has fallen too far for young trees to establish themselves.

None of this means that the reintroduction of wolves was unimportant. Most researchers agree that wolves have had significant effects on Yellowstone's ecosystem. But the case shows how difficult it can be to separate the effects of a single species from the many other factors that shape an ecosystem, and why it is risky to assume that restoring one missing animal will automatically restore a landscape to its previous state. Nevertheless, the Yellowstone experience has inspired similar projects elsewhere, including the return of wolves to parts of Europe, where their numbers have increased significantly in recent decades.

readingPassages.title: Saving the world's seeds
paragraphs: Deep inside a mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, about a thousand kilometres from the North Pole, lies one of the most unusual storage facilities in the world. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008, holds more than a million samples of seeds from almost every country on Earth, representing thousands of varieties of crops such as wheat, rice, maize, beans and barley. The vault is sometimes described in the media as a 'doomsday vault', but its managers prefer to stress its everyday role. Its purpose is to act as a backup for the world's food supply: if seeds held in other collections are lost through war, natural disaster or simple mismanagement, copies stored in Svalbard can be used to replace them.

The location was chosen for several reasons, after a long search. Spitsbergen is remote and politically stable, and the vault is cut more than a hundred metres into the rock, well above sea level, so that it would remain dry even if the polar ice caps melted completely. The surrounding rock is permanently frozen, which means that even if the electricity supply failed, the seeds would remain below freezing. In normal operation, the vault is cooled to minus eighteen degrees Celsius, a temperature at which many seeds can remain alive for decades or even centuries.

The vault does not own the seeds it holds. It works rather like a safe-deposit box in a bank: the institutions that send seeds, usually national gene banks, retain ownership, and only they can withdraw them. Sending seeds to Svalbard costs them nothing, as the facility is funded by the Norwegian government and an international trust. Each deposit is sealed in a box which is not opened by the vault's staff. The vault is opened only a few times a year, when new deposits arrive, and it has no permanent staff on site; it is monitored remotely from the Norwegian mainland. Countries and organisations of all sizes use it, from large international research centres to small community seed banks run by groups of farmers.

Why is such a facility needed? Over the last century, the genetic diversity of the crops we depend on has declined dramatically. Farmers once grew a huge variety of local types, each adapted to particular soils, climates and uses. As agriculture has industrialised, many of these have been replaced by a small number of high-yielding modern varieties. Although these produce more food and are easier to harvest by machine, relying on them is risky, because a single disease or pest can affect an entire crop. Traditional varieties often carry genes for resistance to disease, drought or heat that plant breeders may need in the future, particularly as the climate changes.

The value of the vault was demonstrated in 2015, when it received its first withdrawal. An important gene bank near Aleppo in Syria, which held seeds of crops adapted to dry conditions, had been forced to stop working because of the civil war in the country. Its scientists, who had relocated to Lebanon and Morocco, requested the return of samples they had deposited in Svalbard, and used them to rebuild their collection. They later sent new copies back to the vault.

The vault has not been free of problems. In 2016, unusually high temperatures caused permafrost near the entrance to melt, and water flowed into the access tunnel. Although no seeds were damaged and the water never reached the storage rooms, the incident drew attention to the potential effects of climate change on the Arctic, which is warming faster than most of the planet. The Norwegian government subsequently spent millions on improvements, including a new waterproof access tunnel.

Some experts warn that a single global vault, however secure, is not a complete solution. Seeds in storage are frozen in time; they do not continue to evolve in response to changing conditions, as crops in farmers' fields do. For this reason, many conservationists argue that it is equally important to support farmers who continue to grow traditional varieties in their own fields, so that these crops can keep adapting to new pests and climates. Seed vaults and living farms, they suggest, should be seen as complementary rather than as alternatives.

readingPassages.title: Should we put a price on nature?
paragraphs: In 1997, a team of ecologists and economists led by Robert Costanza published a paper in the journal Nature that attempted something that had never been done before: to estimate the economic value of all the services that nature provides to humanity. These 'ecosystem services' included the pollination of crops by insects, the purification of water by wetlands, the protection of coasts by coral reefs and mangroves, and the regulation of the climate by forests and oceans. The researchers concluded that these services were worth, on average, around thirty-three trillion dollars a year, considerably more than the total value of the global economy at the time.

The paper provoked fierce debate. Some critics argued that the figure was meaningless, since without these services there would be no human economy at all; in that sense, nature's value is infinite. Others questioned the methods used, pointing out that the calculations relied on combining many different local studies and assuming their results could be applied across the globe. Yet the study was enormously influential. It helped to establish the idea that the destruction of nature is not only an environmental problem but an economic one, and that decisions which appear profitable may actually make society poorer if the loss of ecosystem services is taken into account.

Supporters of valuing nature argue that it corrects a basic flaw in the way economic decisions are made. When a forest is cleared for farmland, the value of the timber and the crops is recorded in national accounts, but the loss of the forest's role in storing carbon, preventing floods and supporting wildlife is not. Because nature's services are usually free, they are easily ignored. Putting a monetary value on them, supporters say, ensures that they are given proper weight. In my view, there is real force in this argument, particularly when decisions are being made by governments and businesses that think mainly in financial terms.

There are well-known examples of the approach influencing policy. In the 1990s, New York City faced a choice about how to protect the quality of its drinking water, which comes largely from the Catskill Mountains north of the city. Building a water treatment plant would have cost an estimated six to eight billion dollars, plus large running costs. Instead, the city chose to spend around one and a half billion dollars buying land and paying farmers and landowners in the catchment area to protect forests and reduce pollution, relying on the natural landscape to filter the water. The decision was presented as a sound financial investment rather than merely an act of conservation.

Critics, however, raise several objections. One is practical: many of nature's benefits are extremely difficult to measure, and different methods can produce wildly different values. How, for example, should one value the existence of a species that has no direct use to humans? A second objection is ethical. Some philosophers and environmentalists argue that treating nature as a collection of services to be bought and sold reduces it to a commodity, and that some things have value in themselves, regardless of their usefulness. If a wetland is worth protecting only because it is profitable to do so, then the case for protection disappears whenever destroying it becomes more profitable.

A further concern is that putting a price on nature may change people's motivations in unexpected ways. Psychologists have found that offering payment for an activity that people previously did for moral reasons can sometimes reduce their willingness to do it. There is a risk, critics argue, that paying landowners to protect nature could weaken the sense that conservation is a duty, so that people come to expect payment for doing what they would previously have done anyway.

These objections are serious, but I do not think they are decisive. Valuing nature need not mean that only financial value counts; it can simply be a way of making visible some of the costs that are otherwise ignored. The most sensible approach is probably to use economic valuation as one tool among several, alongside legal protection for important habitats and recognition of the cultural and spiritual value that many communities place on the natural world. What matters is not whether we put a price on nature, but whether the decisions we make reflect the full range of what we stand to lose.

listeningParts.title: Joining a running club
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a local running club to ask about joining.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Runners, this is Dave.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I found your number on a poster in the library. I'm interested in joining a running club, but I'm a complete beginner. Is your club suitable for someone like me?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Absolutely. We welcome runners of all levels. In fact, we have a special group for beginners called Couch to 5K. It's a nine-week programme that takes you from not running at all to running five kilometres without stopping.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Five kilometres sounds like a lot right now.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Everyone says that at the start. But the programme is very gradual. In the first week, you run for just one minute, then walk for ninety seconds, and repeat that eight times. Each week the running parts get a bit longer.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds possible. When do the sessions take place?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: The beginners' group meets twice a week: on Tuesday evenings at seven and on Saturday mornings at nine. You should try to come to both, but if you miss one, you can do the session on your own.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Tuesday evenings are fine. Saturday might be difficult sometimes because I work every other weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: That's no problem. Lots of people have the same situation.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where do you meet?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: We meet outside the sports centre in Victoria Park. Not the main entrance on Park Road, but the side entrance next to the tennis courts. There's a big green door, and you'll see us there.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Next to the tennis courts. Okay. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: The Couch to 5K programme costs thirty pounds for the whole nine weeks. After that, if you want to stay with the club, the yearly membership is forty-five pounds. That gives you access to all our sessions, and discounts at a local sports shop.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very reasonable. What do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: The most important thing is a good pair of running shoes. You don't need anything expensive, but please don't run in old shoes or fashion trainers, as that can cause injuries. The sports shop on the high street will check how you run and help you choose the right ones. Apart from that, comfortable clothes and a bottle of water.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And in winter, when it's dark at seven?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Good question. In winter, everyone must wear something bright or reflective, like a yellow vest, so drivers can see us. The club can sell you one for five pounds if you don't have one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Do I need to be fit already? I haven't done any exercise for years.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Not at all. Most people in the beginners' group haven't run since they were at school. We go at the speed of the slowest runner, and one of our coaches always stays at the back of the group, so nobody is ever left behind. If you find a session too hard, you can repeat a week before moving on.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's good to hear. Is there anything else I should know?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Each session starts with a ten-minute warm-up and finishes with some stretching. And after the Saturday session, many members go for coffee at the park café, which is a nice way to get to know people.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds lovely. When does the next programme start?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: The next one starts on Tuesday the fourth of March. It would be good if you could register before then, so we know how many people to expect.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can I register now?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Of course. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Jessica Thornton. That's T-H-O-R-N-T-O-N.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: And your phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: Thanks, Jessica. And do you have any health problems I should know about?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I have asthma, but it's not serious. I just carry an inhaler.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: That's fine. Many runners have asthma. Just bring your inhaler to every session, and tell the coach if you feel unwell. We'll see you on the fourth of March!

listeningParts.title: The new community sports centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A manager gives a tour introduction for the opening of a new community sports centre.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the brand-new Oakfield Community Sports Centre. My name's Lisa Moreno, and I'm the manager here. Thank you all for coming to our opening day. I'm going to tell you about the facilities, show you where everything is on the plan, and explain how to join.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: First, a little background. The old sports hall on this site was over sixty years old and in very poor condition. After a long campaign by local residents, the council agreed to build a new centre, and it was finished last month. It cost twelve million dollars, and a large part of the money came from a national sports fund.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, please look at the plan on the screen. We're standing in the reception area, here at the bottom of the plan in the middle. The café is directly behind me. On your left as you look at the plan, there's the swimming pool, which takes up the whole left side of the building. It has six lanes, and there's a separate small pool for children and beginners.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: On the right side of reception, you'll find the changing rooms. We've designed them so that families can change together if they wish, and there are also private cubicles.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you walk straight on past the café, you come to the main sports hall, in the middle of the building. It's big enough for basketball, volleyball, badminton or five-a-side football. The hall can also be divided into two with a curtain, so two groups can use it at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: In the top right-hand corner of the building is the gym, with the latest equipment for cardio and weight training. And next to the gym, in the top left-hand corner, is our climbing wall, which is eight metres high. It's very popular with teenagers, and we run climbing courses for complete beginners every Saturday.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Outside, at the back of the building, there are also two new tennis courts and an outdoor fitness area with exercise machines that anyone can use for free, even if they're not members. We hope this will encourage more people in the neighbourhood to be active, especially older residents and families who may not feel comfortable in a gym.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, upstairs, there's a studio for exercise classes like yoga, dance and spinning. You can reach it by the stairs next to reception, or there's a lift beside the changing rooms.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, how do you join? There are two options. You can pay as you go, which means paying each time you visit. A swim costs four dollars fifty, for example. Or you can buy a monthly membership for thirty-five dollars, which gives you unlimited use of the pool, gym and classes. Students and people over sixty-five pay twenty-five dollars a month.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: To become a member, you'll need to fill in a form at reception and have your photo taken for your membership card. And everyone who joins today gets their first month free.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: A few rules to remember. Children under eight must be with an adult in the pool at all times. You must have an induction before you use the gym for the first time; it's free and takes about forty minutes. And you need to book classes in advance, either at reception or on our app.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Today, all activities are free, and there are taster sessions all day. The first climbing session starts at eleven, and there's a family swim at two. Please enjoy yourselves, try as many activities as you like, and if you have any questions, ask any member of staff in a blue T-shirt.

listeningParts.title: Planning a survey about exercise habits
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two sports science students, Tom and Aisha, plan a survey about students' exercise habits.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Okay, Tom. We need to plan our survey for the sports science project. Our topic is why some students exercise regularly and others don't.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Right. I think first we should decide how many people to ask. Our tutor said at least fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Fifty is the minimum. I'd like to aim for a hundred, so we can compare different groups, like first-year and final-year students, or men and women.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: A hundred is a lot, though. How would we find that many people?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: I think an online survey would be easiest. We could share the link on the student union's social media page. Lots of students follow it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Good idea. But if we only use social media, we'll mainly get people who are already interested in that page. Maybe we should also stand outside the library and ask people to fill it in on a tablet.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Okay, let's do both. Now, what questions should we ask? First, how often they exercise each week.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, and what kind of exercise. Like going to the gym, team sports, running, cycling, or walking.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Should walking count as exercise? Everyone walks a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Let's say walking counts only if it's at least thirty minutes at a fast speed. Otherwise almost everyone will say they exercise.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Good point. Then the most important part: the reasons. For people who don't exercise much, we want to know why not.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: I think we should give them a list of possible reasons to choose from, like lack of time, cost, not enjoying it, or feeling embarrassed at the gym. And then an 'other' box where they can write their own reason.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Yes, a list is easier to analyse than open answers. I read an article which said that for students, lack of time is the most common reason people give, but often the real reason is that they don't have a friend to go with.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Interesting. We could ask a question about that, like 'Would you exercise more if you had someone to exercise with?'

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: I like that. And we should ask about cost too. The university gym is quite expensive, about twenty pounds a month.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We could also ask about the time of day they prefer to exercise. If most students say evenings, but the gym classes are mostly in the morning, that might be part of the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Good idea. The university might find our results useful if we show that. Maybe we could send them a summary at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. How long should the survey be? I hate long surveys. I usually stop halfway.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Me too. Let's keep it to ten questions maximum, so it takes about five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Perfect. Before we send it to everyone, we should test it on a few friends to make sure the questions are clear.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Definitely. Let's test it on five people this week. Then we can change anything that's confusing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And how will we present the results?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Mainly with charts. A bar chart would be good for comparing reasons, and a pie chart could show the types of exercise. And we need to write a short report of about two thousand words.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: When is it due?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: The twentieth of April. So we should send out the survey by the end of this month at the latest.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. I'll write the first draft of the questions tonight and send them to you.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Great. And I'll speak to the student union about sharing the link. I know one of the officers there, so it shouldn't be a problem. Let's meet again on Friday to check the questions together before we test them.
