listeningParts.contextDescription: A talk at a sports museum about the ancient and modern Olympic Games.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the sports museum. Today I'm going to talk about the history of the Olympic Games, from ancient Greece to the present day.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The first Olympic Games that we know about took place in 776 BC, at a place called Olympia in southern Greece. Olympia was not a city, but a religious site dedicated to the god Zeus. The Games were held every four years, and this four-year period was called an Olympiad. The Greeks even used Olympiads to measure time, a bit like we use years.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: At first, there was only one event: a running race of about one hundred and ninety metres, the length of the stadium. Over time, more events were added, including longer races, wrestling, boxing, horse racing and chariot racing. There was also the pentathlon, which had five events: running, jumping, throwing the discus, throwing the javelin and wrestling.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Only free men who spoke Greek could compete. Women were not allowed to take part, and married women were not even allowed to watch. Interestingly, the athletes competed without any clothes. Winners did not receive medals. Instead, they were given a crown made of olive leaves. But when they returned home, they were treated as heroes, and some cities gave them free meals for the rest of their lives.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: During the Games, there was a special truce. This meant that wars between Greek cities were stopped so that athletes and visitors could travel safely to Olympia. The ancient Games continued for more than a thousand years, until they were stopped in the year 393 by the Roman emperor Theodosius, who was a Christian and did not like events connected with the old Greek gods.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The modern Olympic Games were the idea of a Frenchman, Pierre de Coubertin. He believed that sport could help to build character and bring people from different countries together in peace. The first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896, as a way of connecting them with ancient Greece. About two hundred and fifty athletes from fourteen countries took part, all of them men.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Women competed for the first time at the next Games, in Paris in 1900, in sports such as tennis and golf. Since then, the number of women athletes has grown steadily, and at the Paris Games in 2024, for the first time, there were equal numbers of male and female athletes.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Several famous traditions were added later. The five rings, which represent the five continents joined together, were designed by Coubertin in 1913. The Olympic flame was first lit at the Amsterdam Games in 1928, and the torch relay, in which runners carry the flame from Olympia to the host city, began in 1936. The Winter Olympics, for sports on snow and ice, started in 1924 in France. And the Paralympic Games, for athletes with disabilities, were first held in Rome in 1960. Today they take place in the same city as the Olympics, a few weeks later, and they have become one of the largest sporting events in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Today, the Olympics is the biggest sporting event in the world, and the opening ceremony is watched by hundreds of millions of people. More than ten thousand athletes from over two hundred countries take part in the Summer Games. However, hosting the Games is extremely expensive, and some cities have decided not to bid because they worry about the cost and about building stadiums that will not be used afterwards. Now, if there are no questions, please follow me to the next room, where you can see some Olympic torches from different Games.

readingPassages.title: The story of football
paragraphs: Football, known as soccer in some countries, is the most popular sport in the world. It is played by around two hundred and fifty million people, and billions watch the World Cup on television. In many countries, football clubs are an important part of local identity, and families support the same team for generations. Part of its popularity comes from its simplicity: all you need is a ball and some open space, and the basic rules are easy to understand. But the game we know today developed over many centuries, and its early history was much less organised than the modern sport.

Games that involve kicking a ball have been played in many parts of the world for thousands of years. In China, a game called cuju was played more than two thousand years ago, in which players tried to kick a leather ball through an opening in a net. It was used to train soldiers and was later popular at the emperor's court. In ancient Greece and Rome, there were also ball games, although players were allowed to use their hands as well as their feet.

In medieval England, a very rough form of football was played, especially on holidays. These games were often played between whole villages, with no limit on the number of players and very few rules. The goals might be several kilometres apart, and the games could last all day. Players were often injured, and windows and shops were damaged. Sometimes the ball was not even a real ball, but an animal's bladder filled with air and covered in leather. Several English kings tried to ban football, partly because it was so violent and partly because they wanted young men to practise archery instead, which was more useful in war.

The modern game began to take shape in English schools in the nineteenth century. Different schools had different rules: at some, players could pick up the ball and run with it, while at others, handling the ball was not allowed. When former students went to university, they found it difficult to play together because of these different rules. In 1848, a group of students at Cambridge University wrote one of the first sets of common rules, known as the Cambridge Rules.

The most important moment came in 1863, when representatives of several London clubs met in a pub called the Freemasons' Tavern and formed the Football Association. They agreed on a single set of rules, which banned carrying the ball and kicking other players. Some clubs disagreed, because they preferred a game in which players could run with the ball. These clubs went on to develop their own sport, rugby, which still has its own separate rules today.

Football spread very quickly in Britain during the late nineteenth century, especially among working people in the industrial cities of the north of England and Scotland. In 1885, the Football Association allowed clubs to pay players, and three years later, the first professional league was formed. British sailors, workers and teachers took the game to other countries, and by the early twentieth century, it was being played across Europe and South America. The international organisation FIFA, which still organises the World Cup today, was founded in Paris in 1904, and the first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930.

Women have played football for well over a century. In England, women's matches were very popular during the First World War, when many men were away fighting. One famous team, the Dick, Kerr Ladies, played in front of more than fifty thousand people in 1920. However, in 1921, the Football Association banned women's teams from playing on the grounds of its member clubs, saying the game was unsuitable for women. The ban lasted for fifty years. Today, women's football is growing rapidly, and crowds at major women's tournaments have broken records.

Modern football has also been changed by technology. Since 2018, many major competitions have used a video assistant referee, known as VAR, to check important decisions such as goals and penalties. Some fans welcome this because it makes decisions fairer, but others feel it slows the game down and reduces the excitement of celebrating a goal.

readingPassages.title: How exercise helps the brain
paragraphs: Most people know that regular exercise is good for the body. It strengthens the heart and muscles, helps control weight and reduces the risk of many diseases, including diabetes and some types of cancer. In recent years, however, scientists have discovered that exercise is also very good for the brain. Research shows that physical activity can improve memory, help people concentrate and reduce the risk of depression. Some scientists now say that exercise is one of the best things we can do for our mental health, and doctors in some countries now recommend physical activity to patients alongside, or even instead of, medicine.

One of the clearest effects of exercise is on mood. Many people say they feel happier and more relaxed after a run, a swim or a game of football. This is partly because exercise causes the brain to release chemicals called endorphins, which reduce pain and create a feeling of well-being. Exercise also reduces levels of stress hormones in the body. Several studies have found that, for people with mild or moderate depression, regular exercise can be as effective as some medicines, although people with serious depression should always talk to a doctor.

Exercise also seems to help memory and learning. In one study in the United States, older adults were divided into two groups. One group walked for forty minutes three times a week, while the other group did only stretching exercises. After a year, scientists used brain scans to measure a part of the brain called the hippocampus, which is important for memory. In the walking group, the hippocampus had grown by about two per cent, while in the stretching group it had become slightly smaller, as normally happens with age.

Why does this happen? When we exercise, our heart beats faster and pumps more blood to the brain, bringing it more oxygen and nutrients. Exercise also increases the production of a protein that helps brain cells to grow and to make new connections with each other. Some scientists call this protein 'fertiliser for the brain'. In addition, exercise usually improves sleep, and good sleep is very important for memory. Exercising outdoors may bring extra benefits, because daylight helps to regulate the body clock, and spending time in green spaces such as parks has been linked with lower levels of stress.

Exercise may be especially useful for children. Studies have found that children who are physically active tend to concentrate better in class and get better results in tests. Some schools have started giving pupils short exercise breaks during lessons, for example a few minutes of running on the spot or dancing, and teachers report that pupils are calmer and more focused afterwards. In Finland, schools encourage children to be active for at least an hour a day, and many children walk or cycle to school.

How much exercise do we need? The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity every week, such as fast walking or cycling, or seventy-five minutes of more intense activity, such as running. That is about thirty minutes a day, five days a week. The good news is that even small amounts of exercise can help. One study found that people who walked for just ten minutes felt happier and had more energy than people who sat still for the same time.

Unfortunately, many people around the world do not get enough exercise. Modern life often involves sitting for long periods, at a desk, in a car or in front of a screen. The World Health Organization estimates that about a quarter of adults are not active enough. Experts suggest that the best type of exercise is the one you enjoy, because you are more likely to continue doing it. Dancing, gardening, playing with children or walking with friends can all be just as good as going to the gym.

Finally, it is never too late to start. Studies show that people who begin exercising in middle age or even later still gain important benefits for both body and brain. As one researcher put it, if exercise were a pill, it would be the most widely prescribed medicine in the world.

readingPassages.title: Should children play competitive sport?
paragraphs: In many schools around the world, sports days and competitive games are an important part of school life. Children run races, play team games and compete for medals and trophies. But in recent years, some parents and teachers have questioned whether competition is good for children. A few schools have even stopped giving prizes to winners, or have organised sports days where everyone gets a medal. This has led to a lively debate about the role of competition in children's sport. Newspapers have reported on it, and many parents have strong opinions on both sides.

Those who support competitive sport argue that it teaches children important lessons for life. Through competition, children learn how to win without boasting and how to lose without giving up. They learn that hard work and practice lead to improvement, and they discover how to cope with disappointment. Supporters say that adult life is full of competition, in education, in jobs and in business, so it is better for children to learn to deal with it at a young age, when the consequences are small.

Competition can also be highly motivating. Many children enjoy the excitement of trying to win, and the chance to compete may encourage them to train harder and improve their skills. Team sports, in particular, teach children to work together, to support their teammates and to put the success of the group before their own success. Some research suggests that children who play team sports have better social skills and higher self-esteem than those who do not. Competitive sport can also give children a sense of belonging, as they become part of a club or a school team, and many adults remember the friendships they made through sport for the rest of their lives.

However, critics point out that competition can have negative effects, especially when the pressure to win becomes too strong. Children who are less talented may feel embarrassed or useless if they always lose, and some may give up sport completely. Surveys in several countries have found that many children stop playing organised sport around the age of thirteen, and one of the main reasons they give is that it is no longer fun. Too much focus on winning, critics say, can take away the enjoyment that should be at the heart of children's sport.

Parents can also make the problem worse. Most parents simply want their children to enjoy themselves and stay healthy, but some put a great deal of pressure on them, shouting from the side of the field or criticising them after a game. In one study, children said that the worst moment of playing sport was the car journey home, when parents discussed their performance. Some sports organisations now have codes of conduct asking parents to stay positive and to let coaches do the coaching.

Another concern is that very young children may not be ready for competition. Experts in child development explain that children under the age of about seven often find it difficult to understand the idea of winning and losing, and they may become very upset. For this reason, some sports have changed their rules for young children, with the aim of keeping the game fun. In some countries, for example, children's football matches for under-sevens do not record the score, and children play in small teams so that everyone gets plenty of time with the ball.

Perhaps the answer is not to choose between competition and no competition, but to find the right balance. Many experts believe that competition can be healthy if it is combined with an emphasis on effort, improvement and enjoyment, rather than only on winning. Coaches and teachers, for example, can praise children for trying hard and for improving their personal best, not only for coming first. Schools can also offer a wide range of activities at lunchtime and after school, including non-competitive ones like dance or walking, so that every child can find something they enjoy.

The goal of children's sport, most parents and teachers agree, should be to help children develop a lifelong love of physical activity. If competition helps to achieve that, it is valuable. If it makes children give up sport, it is not.

mockExams.title: Mock Exam 9: Art, Archaeology & the Past

listeningParts.title: Enquiring about an archaeology dig
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a heritage trust about volunteering on a summer archaeological excavation.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Northvale Heritage Trust, Gemma speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm calling about the summer excavation at Castle Hill. I saw on your website that you're looking for volunteers, and I'm really interested.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Lovely. Yes, we're recruiting now. Can I ask a little about you first? Have you any experience of archaeology?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Not on a real excavation, but I'm studying history at university, and I did a short course on archaeological methods last year, so I know the basics.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: That's fine. We take complete beginners as well. Everyone gets a full day's training at the start, covering how to use the tools, how to record what you find and, very importantly, health and safety.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Could you tell me a bit about the site? The website said it was a Roman fort.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: That's what we thought originally, because Roman coins were found there in the nineteenth century. But last year's excavation found that the fort was actually built on top of a much older settlement, from the Iron Age, about two and a half thousand years ago. So this year, the main aim is to find out more about the people who lived there before the Romans arrived.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fascinating. When does the excavation take place?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: It runs for four weeks, from the seventh of July to the first of August. Volunteers can sign up for one week or more. Most people do two weeks, which gives you time to really learn the techniques.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I think two weeks would be good. Probably the first two, because I have a family holiday at the end of July.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Perfect. The first fortnight tends to be when we open the new trenches, so it's a good time to start. The working day runs from eight thirty until four thirty, Monday to Friday, with an hour for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is there a cost to volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: There's a contribution of sixty pounds per week, which covers training, insurance and the use of tools. For students, it's reduced to forty pounds a week, so you'd pay eighty in total.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. What about accommodation? I'll be coming from quite far away.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Some volunteers camp at a farm about a mile from the site, which is free, but very basic. There's also a youth hostel in the village, which offers a discounted rate of twenty-two pounds a night for our volunteers. You'd need to book that yourself, though, because it gets busy in the summer.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'll probably go for the hostel. What should I bring?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Strong boots are essential, preferably with steel toe caps. Also a sun hat, sun cream and plenty of water, because there's very little shade on the hill. We provide most of the tools, but many volunteers like to have their own trowel. If you want to buy one, make sure it's a proper archaeological trowel, not a garden one.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. And what happens to the things that are found?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Every find is cleaned, labelled and recorded on site. Then the important ones go to the county museum, where specialists study them. At the end of each week, the site director gives a talk about what's been discovered, and that's open to the public too.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds amazing. How do I apply?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: There's an application form on the website. You'll need to include the name of someone who can give you a reference; for a student, your tutor would be ideal. Applications close on the thirtieth of May.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I give you my name now, so you know to expect it?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's Rebecca Lowenthal. L-O-W-E-N-T-H-A-L.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Thanks, Rebecca. I'll look out for your form. One last thing: if you have any allergies, particularly to insect stings, please mention them on the form, because the site is close to some beehives.

listeningParts.title: A tour of a restored historic house
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a historic house that has recently been restored.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Welcome to Ashcombe Hall. My name's Simon, and I'll be your guide this morning. The house reopened to the public in March, after a restoration project that took six years and cost eleven million pounds. Before we go inside, I'll give you some background and explain what you'll see.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The house was built in the 1720s for a wealthy merchant, Sir Edward Ashcombe, who made his fortune in the textile trade. It remained in the Ashcombe family for nearly two hundred years. Then, after the First World War, the family could no longer afford to keep it. It was sold and used as a school for boys until the 1970s, and then it stood empty for almost twenty years. By the time the Trust bought it, the roof was leaking badly, and some of the ceilings had collapsed.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The aim of the restoration was not simply to make the house look as it did in the eighteenth century. The conservators decided that each room would show a different period in the house's history. So, as you go round, you'll see rooms as they were in the 1720s, the 1850s, and even one classroom from the school period, complete with old wooden desks.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One of the biggest challenges was the Great Hall, which is where we'll start. Its painted ceiling had been covered with white paint when the house was a school, probably because the headmaster thought the images were unsuitable for boys. Conservators spent nearly two years removing the paint, layer by layer, using small scalpels and special solvents. The scenes underneath, showing figures from Greek mythology, were in remarkably good condition.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: From the Great Hall, we'll go up to the Long Gallery on the first floor, where you can see portraits of the Ashcombe family. Most of these were sold when the family left, and the Trust has managed to buy back about half of them, from collectors and auction houses around the world. The portrait of Lady Margaret Ashcombe was found in a private house in Canada, and it was returned only last year.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Many visitors say their favourite part of the house is the servants' quarters in the basement. In the eighteenth century, around thirty servants worked here, and the kitchens show you just how hard their lives were. We know a lot about them because the housekeeper's account books survived, recording everything from wages to the price of candles. There's an interactive display where you can find out about individual servants and what happened to them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Outside, the gardens are still being restored, using a plan from 1760 that was discovered in the county archives. At the moment, only the walled kitchen garden is open, and it's growing the same varieties of fruit and vegetables that would have been grown at the time. The rest of the garden should open next spring.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Long Gallery, because flash can damage the paintings. Please don't touch the furniture or the walls, and stay behind the ropes. The tour takes about an hour and a quarter. Afterwards, the tearoom in the old stables serves lunch, and the shop sells books about the house and its restoration.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: On the second floor, you'll also find a small exhibition about the restoration itself, with photographs showing the state of the house when the Trust bought it, and some of the tools the conservators used. There's a short film too, which many visitors find surprisingly moving, because it shows how close the house came to being lost.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And if you enjoy your visit, you might like to know that the Trust is always looking for volunteers to work as room guides. It's a great way to learn more about the house, and full training is provided. Right, let's go in.

listeningParts.title: Researching art forgery
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two art history students, Marta and Ollie, discuss their research project on art forgery with their supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So, Marta and Ollie, you've chosen art forgery for your project. What drew you to that topic?

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: I watched a documentary about a forger who fooled experts for decades, and I wanted to understand how that was possible. It seems strange that people who've spent their whole lives studying art could be deceived.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: And for me, it raises interesting questions about value. If a forgery is so good that nobody can tell the difference, why is it worth so much less than the original?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's a philosophical question as well as a practical one. Let's start with the practical side. How do experts detect forgeries?

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: There are three main approaches. The first is connoisseurship, which means experts judging a work by its style, the way the artist painted, the brushwork and so on. The second is provenance research: tracing the history of who has owned the painting since it was made. And the third is scientific analysis of the materials.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Which do you think is the most reliable?

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We disagree on that, actually. I think science is the most reliable, because you can't argue with chemistry. For example, if a painting supposedly from the seventeenth century contains a pigment that wasn't invented until the nineteenth century, it must be a fake.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: But science can only prove that something is a fake. It can't prove that a painting is genuine. A clever forger can use old canvas and make their own paints from historical recipes. So I think provenance is more important. If there's a complete record of ownership going back to the artist, that's very strong evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Though provenance documents can themselves be forged. One of the most famous forgers in Britain, John Myatt, worked with a man who created false records and even inserted fake documents into the archives of major museums.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: Yes, we read about that. It's amazing how much effort went into it.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: What about connoisseurship? It's sometimes dismissed as too subjective.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: It can be, but our reading suggested it's still essential, because it's often what raises suspicion in the first place. Experts look at a painting and feel that something isn't quite right, and that leads to further investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, which case studies are you planning to use?

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We're going to focus on Han van Meegeren, the Dutch forger who painted fake Vermeers in the 1930s and 1940s. What's interesting about him is that he was only caught because, after the Second World War, he was accused of selling a national treasure to the Nazi leader Hermann Göring. That was treason, so to save himself, he had to prove the painting was a fake he'd made himself.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: And he actually painted another fake Vermeer in front of witnesses to prove he could do it.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: A wonderful story. Make sure you also discuss why the experts were fooled. Many critics have pointed out that his paintings don't look much like Vermeer to modern eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We think part of it was that experts wanted to believe. Van Meegeren painted religious scenes that filled a gap in Vermeer's known work, which experts had predicted might exist. So they were seeing what they hoped to see.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Excellent. That links to wider research on confirmation bias. For your second case study, I'd suggest something more recent, involving modern scientific methods.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: We were thinking of the case where a painting was exposed because of radiocarbon dating of the canvas fibres, which showed they were too recent.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good choice. And for the final section, return to Ollie's question about value. That would make a strong conclusion. Please send me an outline by the end of next week.

listeningParts.title: Cave art and the origins of creativity
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an anthropology course on prehistoric cave art.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at some of the oldest art in the world: the paintings and engravings made on cave walls during the Palaeolithic period, the Old Stone Age. These images raise fundamental questions about when and why humans began to create art, and what it tells us about the development of the human mind.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The modern study of cave art began in 1879, when a Spanish amateur archaeologist, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, was exploring the cave of Altamira in northern Spain. It was actually his eight-year-old daughter, Maria, who first noticed paintings of bison on the ceiling of a side chamber. When Sautuola published his findings, most experts refused to believe that prehistoric people could have produced such sophisticated work, and he was accused of having faked the paintings. It was only after similar paintings were found in France in the early 1900s that the experts accepted they were genuine, by which time Sautuola had died.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The most famous cave art site is probably Lascaux in south-western France, discovered in 1940 by four teenagers who were searching for their dog. Lascaux contains around six hundred paintings, mostly of animals such as horses, deer and cattle, many of them painted with great skill. The cave was opened to the public after the Second World War, but by the 1960s, the breath and body heat of more than a thousand visitors a day had caused algae and crystals to grow on the walls, and it was closed. Today, visitors see an exact replica built nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do we know how old these paintings are? For paintings made with charcoal, researchers can use radiocarbon dating, which measures the decay of carbon in organic material. Using this method, the paintings at Chauvet Cave in France, discovered in 1994, were found to be around thirty-six thousand years old, far older than anyone had expected for such sophisticated work. They include images of lions, rhinoceroses and mammoths, animals that are rarely shown in later cave art.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For a long time, it was assumed that cave art began in Europe. That assumption has now been overturned. In 2014, researchers used a technique called uranium-series dating, which measures the thin layers of mineral that form over paintings, to date hand stencils in caves on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. A hand stencil is made by placing a hand against the rock and blowing pigment around it. The Sulawesi stencils turned out to be at least forty thousand years old, and a painting of a wild pig found there has since been dated to over forty-five thousand years. This suggests that art may have developed in many places, or that the ability to make it was already present in the early humans who left Africa.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Even more controversially, some researchers have claimed that certain markings in Spanish caves are more than sixty-four thousand years old, which would mean they were made by Neanderthals rather than modern humans, since modern humans had not yet arrived in Europe. If confirmed, this would challenge the long-held view that symbolic thinking was unique to our species. However, other scientists have questioned the dating, and the debate continues.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why did people make cave art? There are many theories. An early idea was 'art for art's sake', simply the pleasure of decoration. Another popular theory was hunting magic: by painting animals, people hoped to ensure success in the hunt. But studies of the bones found in caves show that the animals people actually ate were often different from those they painted. At Lascaux, for example, reindeer were the main food, yet they appear in only one painting.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: More recent theories focus on sound and ritual. Some researchers have found that paintings are often located in parts of caves with unusual acoustics, where echoes are particularly strong, suggesting that the spaces may have been used for ceremonies involving music or chanting. Others note that many of the images are in deep, dark and hard-to-reach parts of the caves, which would have been experienced by flickering lamplight, making the animals appear to move.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever its purpose, cave art shows that, tens of thousands of years ago, humans were capable of abstract thought, planning and communicating through symbols, abilities that underlie language, religion and science. Next week, we'll look at the earliest musical instruments.

readingPassages.title: The terracotta army
paragraphs: In March 1974, a group of farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in central China struck pieces of fired clay. At first they thought they had found fragments of an old water pot, but when archaeologists arrived to investigate, they realised that the farmers had uncovered something far more significant: part of a life-sized clay figure of a soldier. Over the following years, excavations revealed one of the most remarkable archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century, an army of thousands of terracotta warriors, buried for more than two thousand years to guard the tomb of China's first emperor.

The emperor, Qin Shi Huang, came to power as king of the state of Qin at the age of thirteen in 246 BC. Over the following twenty-five years, he conquered the other warring states that made up China at the time, and in 221 BC he declared himself the first emperor of a unified country. His achievements were enormous. He standardised writing, weights and measures and the width of cart axles, built thousands of kilometres of roads and began linking existing defensive walls into an early version of the Great Wall. But he was also a ruthless ruler, who is said to have ordered the burning of books that challenged his authority.

Work on the emperor's tomb began soon after he came to the throne and continued for decades. According to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, around seven hundred thousand workers were involved. Sima Qian described an underground palace containing a model of the empire, with rivers of mercury that flowed mechanically, and crossbows set to fire automatically at anyone who broke in. For centuries, historians assumed these descriptions were exaggerated. However, modern scientific surveys have detected unusually high levels of mercury in the soil above the tomb, suggesting that at least part of the account may be accurate.

The terracotta army itself was found in pits about one and a half kilometres east of the burial mound. Archaeologists estimate that the three main pits contain around eight thousand soldiers, together with horses and wooden chariots. The figures were arranged in military formation, with archers at the front, infantry behind and chariots among them, apparently ready for battle. Most remarkably, no two faces appear to be exactly alike. The figures were made in sections using moulds, but the heads were finished individually by hand, giving each soldier a distinct appearance, and some researchers believe they may have been modelled on real people.

When they were made, the figures were brightly painted in red, green, blue, purple and other colours. Unfortunately, almost all of this paint has disappeared. When the figures are exposed to the dry air after centuries underground, the layer beneath the paint dries out and curls within minutes, and the colours flake off. This is one reason why excavation has proceeded slowly. Chinese archaeologists have worked with conservation experts from other countries to develop methods of preserving the paint, and some figures with their original colours have now been successfully preserved.

Excavating the soldiers has also revealed much about how the army was produced. Many figures carry the names of the workshop foremen who supervised their production, which allowed officials to trace and punish anyone responsible for poor workmanship. The real bronze weapons held by the soldiers, including swords, spearheads and crossbow triggers, were also inscribed with marks indicating where and when they were made. Some of the weapons were coated with a layer of chromium and remained remarkably sharp, although researchers now think the coating may have come from the lacquer of the wooden handles rather than from a deliberate treatment.

Perhaps the most intriguing question concerns the emperor's tomb itself, which has never been opened. The Chinese government has so far decided not to excavate it, partly out of respect, but mainly because archaeologists are concerned that they do not yet have the technology to protect what might be found inside, particularly any painted or organic materials. They point to the loss of the soldiers' colours as a warning. For now, the tomb remains sealed, and the secrets of the first emperor's underground palace continue to wait for a future generation.

readingPassages.title: Why do we value original art?
paragraphs: In 2017, a painting attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, known as Salvator Mundi, was sold at auction for four hundred and fifty million dollars, the highest price ever paid for a work of art. Only a few years earlier, however, the same painting had been sold for less than ten thousand dollars, when it was believed to be the work of one of Leonardo's followers. Nothing about the physical object had changed between the two sales, apart from careful restoration. What had changed was a belief about who had painted it. The case illustrates a question that has puzzled philosophers and psychologists alike: why do we place so much value on originality?

One obvious answer is rarity. There are fewer than twenty paintings generally accepted as Leonardo's, and any object that is unique and cannot be replaced will command a high price. But rarity alone cannot explain the dramatic fall in value that follows when a painting is shown to be a forgery. A convincing forgery may be just as rare as an original, since there may be only one copy, yet once its true origins are revealed, its value collapses, even though people may have admired it for years.

Psychologists have suggested that part of the answer lies in what is called essentialism: the tendency to believe that objects possess an invisible essence connected to their history. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Paul Bloom and his colleagues found that people place great value on objects that have been touched or owned by famous individuals, such as a sweater worn by a celebrity, and that this value falls sharply if the object has been washed. It is as if the person's essence has been transferred into the object through physical contact. An original painting, on this view, is valued partly because it was physically touched by the hand of the artist.

Another explanation emphasises performance. The philosopher Denis Dutton argued that we see works of art not simply as objects but as the outcome of human achievement, in the same way that we admire an athlete's record-breaking run. A forgery may look identical to an original, but it represents a different, and lesser, achievement: copying is not the same as creating. Just as we would feel cheated to discover that a marathon winner had taken a shortcut, we feel deceived when we learn that a painting is not what it claims to be.

A third factor concerns the role of expertise and social status. The art market depends on the judgements of experts, dealers and museums, and the label of a famous name acts as a guarantee of quality and an investment. Some critics argue that this system encourages people to respond to the label rather than to the work itself. In one experiment, participants were shown the same abstract paintings, but some were told the works were in a major museum while others were told they had been generated by a computer. The paintings labelled as museum works were rated as more beautiful, and brain scans showed greater activity in areas associated with pleasure.

Not all cultures, or all periods, have valued originality in the same way. In traditional Chinese painting, copying the works of earlier masters was regarded as an essential part of an artist's training and a way of showing respect, and skilled copies could be highly prized. In medieval Europe, many artists worked in teams within workshops, and the idea of the individual creative genius was much less important than it later became. Some historians argue that the modern obsession with originality emerged largely in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, along with the development of copyright law and the art market.

Digital technology is now challenging traditional ideas once again. High-resolution scanning and three-dimensional printing can produce copies of paintings that reproduce even the texture of the brushstrokes, so accurately that experts find them difficult to distinguish from the original without close examination. Some museums have begun displaying such copies, particularly when the originals are too fragile to travel. Whether audiences will come to accept these reproductions, or will continue to insist on the authentic object, may tell us a great deal about what we really value when we look at art.

readingPassages.title: Lost cities of the rainforest
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, many archaeologists believed that tropical rainforests were unable to support large, complex societies. The soils of the Amazon, for instance, are generally poor in nutrients, because heavy rainfall washes them away and most of the nutrients in the ecosystem are stored in the vegetation rather than the ground. On this view, the rainforest was a hostile environment in which people could survive only in small, mobile groups, and reports by early European explorers of large settlements along the Amazon were dismissed as exaggerations. The dense forest also made it extremely difficult to test these assumptions, since ruins could be hidden beneath the canopy only a few metres from a researcher without being seen.

This picture has been transformed by a technology called LiDAR, which stands for light detection and ranging. A LiDAR instrument, usually mounted on an aircraft or drone, fires hundreds of thousands of laser pulses per second towards the ground and measures how long each one takes to return. Although most pulses are reflected by leaves and branches, a small proportion pass through gaps in the canopy and reach the forest floor. By filtering out the vegetation using computer software, researchers can produce a detailed three-dimensional map of the ground surface, revealing features such as walls, roads and terraces that would be almost impossible to detect on foot.

Some of the most dramatic results have come from Central America. In 2018, a survey of more than two thousand square kilometres of forest in northern Guatemala revealed over sixty thousand previously unknown structures associated with the ancient Maya, including houses, palaces, defensive walls and raised roads connecting cities. On the basis of these results, researchers suggested that the population of the Maya lowlands at its height, around the eighth century, may have been between seven and eleven million people, several times higher than many earlier estimates. The surveys also revealed extensive systems of canals and terraced fields, showing that the Maya had transformed large areas of the landscape to produce food.

Similar discoveries have been made in the Amazon. In Bolivia, a LiDAR survey published in 2022 revealed settlements of the Casarabe culture, which flourished between around 500 and 1400 AD. The surveys showed large platforms and pyramid-like mounds, connected by raised roads running for several kilometres, together with reservoirs and canals for managing water. In the upper Amazon of Ecuador, researchers have mapped a network of settlements more than two thousand years old, linked by long, straight roads. These findings suggest that, contrary to earlier assumptions, some parts of the Amazon supported dense, organised populations long before the arrival of Europeans.

How did such societies manage to farm the poor soils of the rainforest? Part of the answer lies in a remarkable dark, fertile soil known as terra preta, Portuguese for 'black earth', found at many ancient sites in the Amazon. Unlike the surrounding soils, terra preta is rich in nutrients and organic matter, including charcoal, pottery fragments and food waste, and it remains fertile today, centuries after the settlements were abandoned. Researchers believe it was created, at least in part deliberately, by ancient communities who added charcoal and waste to the soil. Some scientists are now studying terra preta in the hope of developing methods for improving soils in tropical regions today.

The discoveries also raise questions about the history of the rainforest itself. If large areas were once cleared, farmed and managed, then parts of what appears to be untouched wilderness may in fact have been shaped by human activity. Many of the tree species most common in the Amazon today are ones that were useful to people, such as Brazil nut and cacao, which some researchers interpret as evidence of ancient forest management. When European diseases devastated indigenous populations after 1492, the forest may have grown back over abandoned fields and settlements, creating the impression of a pristine landscape.

Not all researchers accept the most dramatic interpretations. Some argue that population estimates based on counting structures are uncertain, since it is often impossible to know how many buildings were occupied at the same time. Others warn that the idea of a heavily populated ancient Amazon could be misused to justify modern deforestation, by suggesting that the forest has recovered before and will do so again. In my view, the evidence does not support such a conclusion: ancient societies managed the forest over centuries in ways that maintained its diversity, which is very different from the large-scale clearing for cattle ranching and agriculture that threatens the Amazon today.

listeningParts.title: Booking a diving course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a diving school to book a beginners' course for her holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: G'day, Coral Bay Dive Centre, Ryan speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I'm coming to Coral Bay on holiday next month, and I'd love to learn to dive while I'm there. Could you tell me about your courses for beginners?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Sure thing. We have two options for complete beginners. The first is a Try Dive, which is a single morning. You learn the basics in the pool and then do one shallow dive in the sea with an instructor holding onto you. It doesn't give you a qualification, but it's a good way to see if you like it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And the other option?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: The other is the Open Water course, which is the full beginner's qualification. It takes four days. You do some theory, five sessions in the pool and four dives in the sea. At the end, you get a certificate that allows you to dive anywhere in the world, down to eighteen metres, with a buddy.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Four days. I'm there for ten days, so I think I'd like to do the full course. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: The Open Water course is six hundred and fifty dollars. That includes all the equipment hire, the boat trips and your certificate. The only extra cost is the online theory course, which you should complete before you arrive. That's about a hundred dollars, but it means you spend less time in the classroom and more time in the water.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That makes sense. What dates are available?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: We start a new course every Monday and Thursday. Which week are you here?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I arrive on Saturday the twelfth of April.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Then you could start on Monday the fourteenth, which would finish on the Thursday. That gives you a few days afterwards to do some fun dives with your new certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. Is there anything I need to know about my health?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone has to fill in a medical form. If you answer yes to any of the questions, for example if you have asthma or heart problems, you'll need a letter from a doctor saying you're fit to dive. It's best to sort that out before you travel, because it can be hard to see a doctor here at short notice.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I don't think I have any problems, but I'll check the form. Do I need to be a strong swimmer?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: You need to be able to swim two hundred metres without stopping, any stroke, and float for ten minutes. You don't need to be fast.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. What's the group size?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: We keep it small: a maximum of four students per instructor. So you get plenty of attention.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what will I see on the dives?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Coral Bay is famous for its reef, which starts just a few metres from the beach. You'll see lots of tropical fish, often turtles, and if you're lucky, manta rays. They visit the bay between May and November, so you might be a bit early, but sometimes we see them in April.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, I hope so. Where do I go on the first day?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Come to our shop on Robinson Street at eight o'clock. It's next to the bakery, opposite the post office. Bring your swimming costume, a towel and plenty of sun cream. Please make sure it's reef-safe sun cream, because some chemicals in normal sun cream damage the coral.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Reef-safe sun cream. I'll look for that. Can I book now?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Of course. Can I take your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Laura Whitfield. W-H-I-T-F-I-E-L-D.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.text: Thanks, Laura. We ask for a deposit of a hundred and fifty dollars to hold your place. If you cancel more than fourteen days before, you'll get it back. I'll send you the link to the online course and the medical form by email.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering on a beach clean-up
listeningParts.contextDescription: A coordinator explains a beach clean-up and marine survey day to a group of volunteers.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone! Thanks so much for coming out on a Saturday morning, and especially in this wind. My name is Fiona, and I'm the coordinator for Clean Coasts in this region. Before we get started, I'll explain what we're doing today and how to stay safe.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: First, some background. Our charity organises beach clean-ups all around the country, and last year, volunteers removed over a hundred and twenty tonnes of rubbish from our beaches. But we don't just collect litter. We also record exactly what we find, because that information is really valuable. It's sent to scientists and to the government, and it has helped to change the law. For example, data collected by volunteers like you was used as evidence when the government introduced a charge on plastic bags, and the number of bags we find on beaches has fallen by more than half since then.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: So, how will today work? We're going to divide into teams of four. Each team will be given a section of beach exactly one hundred metres long, marked with flags. Within your section, please collect everything that isn't natural. One person in each team will be the recorder, who fills in the data sheet, noting each item you find. The others collect the litter and call out what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The most common items we find are usually small pieces of plastic, then plastic bottle caps, and then fishing rope and nets. Cigarette ends are also very common, and they're a real problem, because the filters contain plastic and toxic chemicals. Please count them carefully, even though they're small.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, safety. Everyone must wear the gloves we've given you, and please use the litter pickers for anything sharp. If you find anything dangerous, like broken glass, needles or containers of chemicals, don't touch it. Mark the spot with one of the small orange flags and tell me or one of the other team leaders, who are wearing yellow jackets. We'll deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Also, please keep away from the bottom of the cliffs at the northern end of the beach. There have been small rock falls there recently, so that area is closed. And keep an eye on the tide. It's going out at the moment, but it will turn at about half past twelve, so we'll finish by twelve to be safe.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: After the litter collection, those of you who are interested can join our marine biologist, Dr Patel, for a rock pool survey at the southern end of the beach. She'll show you how to identify crabs, starfish and other creatures, and you'll help her count them. This is part of a long-term study looking at how warmer sea temperatures are affecting which species live on our coast. Please remember to put any creatures back exactly where you found them, and turn any rocks you lift back over carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: If you find any animals tangled in litter, such as a seabird caught in fishing line, please don't try to free it yourself, as you could injure it or get hurt. Call me, and we'll contact the local wildlife rescue centre, who are on standby today. Last month, volunteers found a young seal caught in a net, and it was rescued and released back into the sea a week later.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: When you've finished, please bring your bags to the collection point by the café. Separate the recycling, mainly plastic bottles and cans, from the general rubbish. The local council will collect everything this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: And finally, to say thank you, the beach café is offering everyone a free hot drink when you show them your volunteer badge. Right, let's get into teams.

listeningParts.title: Planning a presentation on coral reefs
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two marine biology students, Jack and Leila, plan a seminar presentation on coral reefs with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right, Jack and Leila. You're presenting on coral reefs next week. How are you planning to approach it?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: We want to start by explaining what coral actually is, because when we asked friends, most of them thought coral was a type of rock or a plant.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Right. So we'll explain that each coral is made up of thousands of tiny animals called polyps, and that they build their hard skeletons from calcium carbonate. And then the really important part: inside their tissues live microscopic algae, which provide the coral with most of its food through photosynthesis.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That relationship is key to understanding bleaching. How will you explain that?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: When the water gets too warm, even just one or two degrees above normal for a few weeks, the coral becomes stressed and expels the algae. Because the algae give coral its colour, the coral turns white, which is why it's called bleaching. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can come back, but if the heat lasts too long, the coral starves and dies.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: We were going to show some photos of the Great Barrier Reef before and after a bleaching event. They're really striking.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Photos are effective, but make sure you have permission to use them, and cite the source. What else are you covering?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Ocean acidification. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the water becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for coral to build their skeletons.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: And we want to mention local threats too, like pollution from farms, which causes algae to grow over the coral, and overfishing, which removes fish that normally keep algae under control.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lot to fit into fifteen minutes. I'd suggest you focus on warming and bleaching, since that's the biggest threat, and mention the others more briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Okay, that makes sense. Then for the second half, we wanted to talk about solutions, particularly coral restoration.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What examples have you found?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: There's a technique called coral gardening, where small pieces of coral are grown on underwater frames, a bit like a plant nursery, and then planted onto damaged reefs. It's been used in Florida and the Caribbean.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: And scientists in Australia are trying to breed corals that can survive higher temperatures. They're crossing corals from warmer parts of the reef with corals from cooler parts.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. But be careful how you present these. Some researchers argue that restoration can only work on a very small scale, and that it risks distracting attention from the main problem, which is reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: We did read that. Restoring even a small area is very expensive, and the reefs are enormous.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Maybe we could end with a slide saying that restoration can help buy time, but it can't replace action on climate change.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: And we could mention what ordinary people can do, like choosing reef-safe sun cream or not buying souvenirs made from coral, so the audience doesn't feel the situation is hopeless.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, but keep that short. The main point is the science. That would be a balanced conclusion. How are you dividing the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: I'll do the biology and the threats, and Jack will do restoration and the conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor

listeningParts.title: The deep ocean
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an oceanography course on exploration of the deep sea.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. It's often said that we know more about the surface of the Moon than about the floor of our own oceans. That's something of an exaggeration, but it reflects a real truth: the deep ocean is the largest and least explored habitat on Earth. Today, I want to talk about how we explore it, what we've found, and the new threats it faces.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First, some definitions. The deep sea is usually defined as the part of the ocean below about two hundred metres, the point at which sunlight becomes too weak for plants to photosynthesise. That's more than ninety per cent of the ocean's volume. The average depth of the ocean is around three thousand seven hundred metres, and the deepest point, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, is nearly eleven thousand metres deep.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The biggest challenge of exploring the deep sea is pressure. For every ten metres you go down, the pressure increases by roughly one atmosphere. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, it's over a thousand times the pressure at the surface, equivalent to having several elephants standing on your thumb. Vehicles that go to these depths need extremely strong hulls, usually made of titanium or thick steel.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first people to reach the Challenger Deep were the Swiss engineer Jacques Piccard and the American naval officer Don Walsh in 1960, in a vessel called the Trieste. They spent only about twenty minutes on the bottom, and because their arrival stirred up sediment, they could see very little. Nobody returned for more than fifty years, until the film director James Cameron made a solo dive in 2012. Today, most deep-sea exploration is done not by people but by remotely operated vehicles, controlled from ships by cable, and by autonomous robots that can travel for days without human control.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the most important discoveries came in 1977, when scientists exploring near the Galápagos Islands found hydrothermal vents: openings in the sea floor where water heated by volcanic activity pours out, sometimes at temperatures above three hundred and fifty degrees Celsius. To their amazement, the vents were surrounded by dense communities of life, including giant tube worms over two metres long, clams and shrimps. These animals don't depend on sunlight at all. Instead, the base of the food chain is bacteria that obtain energy from chemicals in the vent water, a process called chemosynthesis. This discovery changed our ideas about where life can exist, and it has even influenced the search for life on other planets.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Another remarkable feature of deep-sea life is bioluminescence: the ability to produce light. It's estimated that around three-quarters of animals in the deep ocean can produce their own light, which they use to attract prey, find mates or confuse predators. The anglerfish, for example, has a glowing lure on its head to attract smaller fish.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Unfortunately, the deep ocean is not as remote from human influence as we might hope. Plastic has been found in the stomachs of animals living in the deepest trenches. And there's growing interest in deep-sea mining. Large areas of the sea floor are covered with potato-sized lumps called nodules, which contain valuable metals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese, needed for batteries in electric cars and phones. Companies argue that mining them would be less damaging than mining on land. However, many scientists warn that we know too little about deep-sea ecosystems to predict the damage, and that recovery would be extremely slow, because life in the deep sea grows very slowly. Some areas disturbed in experiments decades ago have still not recovered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: An international body, the International Seabed Authority, is responsible for regulating mining in international waters, and it's currently discussing rules. Several countries have called for a pause until more research has been done. Next week, we'll look at ocean currents and climate.

readingPassages.title: The great ocean conveyor
paragraphs: Ocean currents have shaped human history for thousands of years. Polynesian navigators used them to cross vast stretches of the Pacific, European sailors relied on them to reach the Americas, and fishing communities have long known that the richest catches are found where currents meet. Yet it is only in the last century that scientists have begun to understand the full extent of the ocean's circulation, and to recognise its importance for the climate of the entire planet.

The most familiar currents are those at the surface, which are driven mainly by the wind. The steady trade winds near the equator push water westwards, while the westerly winds of the middle latitudes drive it eastwards, and the rotation of the Earth deflects these flows into enormous circular patterns known as gyres. One of the best-known surface currents is the Gulf Stream, which carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico northwards along the coast of North America and then across the Atlantic towards Europe. It moves more water than all the world's rivers combined.

Beneath the surface lies a second, slower system of circulation, driven not by wind but by differences in the density of seawater. Water becomes denser when it is colder or saltier. In the far North Atlantic, near Greenland and Iceland, warm water brought north by the Gulf Stream releases its heat to the atmosphere and cools. At the same time, when sea ice forms, it leaves salt behind in the surrounding water. The resulting cold, salty water is so dense that it sinks to the bottom of the ocean and begins a long journey southwards along the sea floor.

This sinking water drives a global circulation pattern often called the 'ocean conveyor belt'. The deep water travels south through the Atlantic, around Antarctica and into the Indian and Pacific Oceans, where it gradually rises to the surface and eventually returns to the North Atlantic. A single body of water may take a thousand years or more to complete the circuit. Along the way, the conveyor transports heat, nutrients and dissolved gases around the world, playing a crucial role in regulating climate.

The Atlantic part of this system, known as the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, has a particularly important influence on Europe. By carrying warm water northwards, it helps to explain why western Europe has much milder winters than places at the same latitude in North America. London, for example, lies further north than Calgary in Canada, yet its average winter temperatures are considerably higher.

Evidence from ice cores and ocean sediments shows that the conveyor has changed dramatically in the past. Around twelve thousand years ago, at the end of the last ice age, temperatures in the North Atlantic region fell sharply for more than a thousand years, an event known as the Younger Dryas. Many scientists believe it was caused by a huge release of fresh water from melting ice sheets in North America, which made the surface water of the North Atlantic less salty, preventing it from sinking and weakening the circulation.

There is now concern that climate change could cause a similar weakening. As the Greenland ice sheet melts and rainfall increases at high latitudes, more fresh water is entering the North Atlantic. Measurements since 2004, made using instruments moored across the Atlantic, suggest that the AMOC has varied considerably, and some studies indicate that it is now weaker than at any time in the past thousand years. However, scientists disagree about how quickly it might decline and whether it could collapse completely this century. A major weakening would not trigger an ice age, as some films have suggested, but it could bring colder winters to northern Europe, changes in rainfall patterns in the tropics and faster sea-level rise along the east coast of North America.

Because the deep ocean is so difficult to observe, much of our understanding comes from computer models and a limited number of measurements. In recent years, an international network of nearly four thousand robotic floats, called Argo, has greatly improved this picture. The floats drift with the currents, sinking to depths of up to two thousand metres and rising every ten days to transmit data on temperature and salinity to satellites. Such observations will be essential for detecting changes in the conveyor before their effects are felt.

readingPassages.title: The secret lives of octopuses
paragraphs: Octopuses have long fascinated scientists, not least because they seem to break so many of the rules that apply to other intelligent animals. Most animals with large brains and complex behaviour, such as primates, dolphins and crows, are social, long-lived and closely related to each other on the tree of life. Octopuses are none of these things. They are molluscs, related to snails and clams, and their evolutionary line separated from ours more than five hundred million years ago. Most species live alone and survive only a year or two, so they have little opportunity to learn from parents or companions. Yet they display problem-solving abilities that rival those of many mammals.

Stories of octopus cleverness are common among aquarium workers. Octopuses have been seen escaping from their tanks at night, crossing the floor to a neighbouring tank to eat the fish inside, and then returning to their own tank before morning. In laboratory experiments, they quickly learn to open screw-top jars to reach food inside, and some have learned to do this from the inside as well. In one well-known study, octopuses were observed carrying coconut shells across the sea floor and assembling them into shelters when needed, which some researchers have described as a form of tool use.

The structure of the octopus nervous system is very different from ours. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, comparable to a dog, but around two-thirds of them are located not in the brain but in its eight arms. Each arm can taste, touch and respond to its surroundings with a considerable degree of independence. Experiments have shown that an arm that has been separated from the body can still reach for food and pass it towards where the mouth would be. This has led some researchers to suggest that an octopus's experience of the world may be very different from that of any vertebrate.

Octopuses are also masters of disguise, a skill that helps them both to hunt and to avoid being eaten. Their skin contains thousands of cells called chromatophores, each filled with pigment and surrounded by tiny muscles, which allow the animal to change colour in a fraction of a second. Other cells reflect light to produce shimmering or white patterns. Octopuses can also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps and spikes to imitate rocks, coral or seaweed. Remarkably, they appear to do this despite being colour-blind, since their eyes contain only one type of light receptor. How they match the colours of their surroundings remains a puzzle, though some studies suggest their skin itself may be able to detect light.

One species, discovered in Indonesia in 1998, has taken disguise even further. The mimic octopus appears to imitate the shape and movement of several other animals, including poisonous lionfish, flatfish and sea snakes, apparently choosing which to copy according to the type of predator nearby. Although some scientists have questioned how deliberate this behaviour is, it is widely regarded as one of the most sophisticated examples of mimicry in the animal kingdom.

Why should a short-lived, solitary animal have evolved such intelligence? One leading theory links it to the loss of the protective shell that the ancestors of octopuses once had. Without a shell, octopuses became vulnerable to predators, but they also gained the freedom to squeeze into small spaces and to explore their environment in new ways. Hunting a wide variety of prey and avoiding many different predators may have favoured flexible behaviour and the ability to learn quickly. Their short lifespan, in contrast, may be linked to the fact that females usually stop eating while guarding their eggs and die soon after they hatch.

The growing recognition of octopus intelligence has had practical consequences. In 2021, a review commissioned by the British government concluded that octopuses, along with crabs and lobsters, are sentient, meaning they can experience pain and distress, and they were subsequently included in animal welfare law. The findings have also fuelled opposition to plans for commercial octopus farming, which some companies are developing to meet rising demand. Critics argue that confining such curious, solitary animals in crowded tanks would cause serious suffering, and several jurisdictions have moved to ban the practice.

readingPassages.title: Who owns the fish?
paragraphs: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay called 'The Tragedy of the Commons', which has been cited ever since in debates about natural resources. Hardin asked his readers to imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding another animal to the pasture, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone. As a result, he argued, each herder will keep adding animals until the pasture is destroyed. Freedom in a commons, Hardin concluded, brings ruin to all. Few resources fit this description better than the ocean's fish, which for most of history belonged to no one until they were caught.

The consequences of open access have been dramatic. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the proportion of fish stocks harvested at biologically unsustainable levels rose from around ten per cent in the 1970s to more than a third today. The most famous collapse occurred off the coast of Newfoundland, in Canada, where cod had supported fishing communities for five centuries. Improved technology, including large trawlers and sonar, allowed catches to rise sharply in the 1960s, and despite warnings from some scientists, quotas remained too high. In 1992, the Canadian government closed the fishery, putting around thirty thousand people out of work. Three decades later, cod numbers have still not fully recovered.

One response to the tragedy of the commons has been to extend national control over the sea. In 1982, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea allowed countries to establish Exclusive Economic Zones extending two hundred nautical miles from their coasts, within which they have the right to manage fishing. Today, these zones cover most of the world's productive fishing grounds. However, national control has not always led to good management, as the Newfoundland case shows, and the high seas beyond these zones remain largely unregulated.

A more radical approach involves giving fishers secure rights to a share of the catch. Under a system known as individual transferable quotas, scientists set a total allowable catch for each species, and this is divided into shares that are allocated to fishers, who can buy, sell or lease them. Supporters argue that because quota holders have a long-term stake in the fishery, they have an incentive to conserve it, rather than racing to catch as many fish as possible before others do. Iceland and New Zealand were among the first countries to adopt such systems in the 1980s, and studies have found that fisheries managed in this way are less likely to collapse.

Critics, however, point out that quota systems can concentrate ownership in the hands of a few large companies. In Iceland, small fishing communities complained that quota shares were sold to larger firms based elsewhere, leaving villages without the right to fish waters their families had worked for generations. Some economists argue that quotas, which were originally given away free, have effectively turned a public resource into private wealth, and that governments should charge for them instead.

Hardin's analysis itself has also been challenged. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who in 2009 became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics, spent decades studying communities around the world that had managed shared resources, such as forests, irrigation systems and fisheries, successfully for centuries without either government control or private ownership. In the lobster fisheries of Maine, in the United States, for example, groups of fishers informally divide the coast into territories and enforce their own rules. Ostrom identified a set of conditions under which such self-management tends to succeed, including clear boundaries, rules adapted to local conditions and ways of resolving disputes cheaply. Her work suggested that the tragedy of the commons is not inevitable.

In practice, many successful fisheries combine elements of all these approaches: scientific limits on the total catch, secure rights for those who fish, and meaningful involvement of local communities in decision-making. Marine protected areas, where fishing is restricted or banned, can also allow stocks to recover and spill over into surrounding waters. In 2023, after nearly two decades of negotiations, members of the United Nations agreed a treaty to protect biodiversity on the high seas, including provisions for creating protected areas there. Whether it succeeds will depend on how many countries ratify it and how effectively it is enforced.
