listeningParts.title: Registering with a medical practice
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a doctors' surgery to register as a new patient.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Parkview Medical Centre, Anita speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I've just moved here to start a postgraduate course at the university, and I'd like to register with your practice.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. First, I need to check that you live within our area. What's your address?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's Flat 7, 22 Belmont Road.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Belmont Road, yes, that's within our boundary. Have you been registered with a doctor in this country before?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: No, this is my first time. I'm from the United States.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's fine. You'll need to fill in a registration form, which you can do online or on paper here at the surgery. We'll also need to see some proof of your address, such as a tenancy agreement or a letter from the university, and your passport.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I have a letter from the university confirming my accommodation. Would that be okay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. Once you've registered, we'll invite you for a short health check with one of our nurses. It's not compulsory, but we recommend it. The nurse will check your blood pressure, ask about any medical conditions and make sure your vaccinations are up to date.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds useful. Actually, that reminds me, I take medication for asthma. How do I get my prescriptions here?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: When you register, please bring the details of your medication, ideally the packaging or a letter from your doctor at home. You'll need to see one of our doctors first, and then you can order repeat prescriptions online through our app, and collect them from any pharmacy.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is there a charge for prescriptions?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In England, there's a standard charge for each item, but if you need a lot of medication regularly, you can buy a prepayment certificate, which works out cheaper. The pharmacist can explain the details.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. And how do I make an appointment to see a doctor?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There are three ways. You can phone us from eight in the morning, use the online booking system, or come to the desk in person. For urgent problems, we keep some same-day appointments, but they go quickly, so it's best to call as soon as we open. For routine appointments, you might have to wait a week or so.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And what if I need medical help in the evening or at the weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The surgery is closed then, but you can call the national helpline, one-one-one, any time of the day or night. They'll tell you where to go, and they can arrange for you to see a doctor if necessary. For a serious emergency, like chest pain or severe bleeding, you should call nine-nine-nine or go straight to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's really helpful. Is there anything for students specifically?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, the university health service runs a mental health and well-being clinic on Wednesday afternoons, here in our building. It's free for students, and you can book directly without seeing a doctor first. A lot of students find it helpful, particularly in the first term.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good to know. What are your opening hours?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Monday to Friday, eight until six thirty. And on Tuesday evenings, we stay open until eight for people who work during the day.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is it easy to get to the surgery by public transport? I don't have a car.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, the number twelve bus stops right outside, and it's about a fifteen-minute walk from the main university campus. There's also a small car park and space for bicycles at the back of the building, if you decide to get a bike later.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And can I choose which doctor I see?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You'll be registered with the practice as a whole, but you can ask to see a particular doctor when you book. We have six doctors, three men and three women, and two of them speak other languages as well as English, if that's ever helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Can I start the registration now?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: I can take some basic details. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Megan Kowalski. K-O-W-A-L-S-K-I.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And your date of birth?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: The fourteenth of March, two thousand and one.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. I'll send you a text with the link to the online form. Once we've received it and checked your documents, it usually takes about three working days to complete the registration.

listeningParts.title: A museum of medical history
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a museum of the history of medicine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Halloran Museum of Medicine. My name is Ciara, and I'll be introducing you to the museum before you explore on your own. The museum is housed in what was once the city's first public hospital, built in 1745, so you're standing in a building that has its own place in medical history.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The collection was started by a surgeon, Dr Thomas Halloran, who worked here in the nineteenth century. He collected instruments, specimens and documents, partly for teaching his students and partly because he believed that future generations should understand how medicine had developed. When he died, he left his collection to the hospital, and it was opened to the public as a museum in 1935, after the hospital moved to a new site.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me explain how the museum is organised. There are five galleries, arranged in chronological order. Gallery One, on the ground floor to your left, covers ancient and medieval medicine, including some remarkable surgical instruments from Roman times that look surprisingly similar to modern ones.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Two is devoted to anatomy. For centuries, doctors' understanding of the body was based on the writings of the ancient Greek physician Galen, many of which turned out to be wrong, because Galen had mainly dissected animals rather than humans. This gallery shows how, from the sixteenth century, anatomists began to study human bodies directly. Some visitors find a few of the exhibits here rather disturbing, so there's a separate route that avoids this gallery if you prefer.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs, Gallery Three is the old operating theatre, which is the highlight for many visitors. Before the discovery of anaesthetics in the 1840s, operations were performed while patients were fully conscious, so surgeons had to work as fast as possible. A good surgeon could remove a leg in under a minute. Students watched from the steep wooden seats around the room, which you can still see today. Every Saturday at two o'clock, we have a demonstration here, with an actor playing a Victorian surgeon. It's very popular, so please collect a free ticket from the front desk.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Four tells the story of the fight against infectious disease, from the first vaccine against smallpox, developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, to the discovery of penicillin in 1928. There's an interactive display where you can look at bacteria through a microscope, which children especially enjoy.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And finally, Gallery Five looks at modern medicine and the future, including robotic surgery and genetic medicine. It also includes a section on the recent pandemic, with objects and personal stories donated by local healthcare workers.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. Photography is allowed in all galleries, but please don't use flash, as it can damage older items. Bags larger than a small backpack must be left in the cloakroom, which is free. There's a café in the courtyard, and the gift shop is next to the exit.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you're visiting with children, we have a free activity trail, which you can pick up at the front desk. Children follow clues around the galleries and collect stamps, and when they finish they receive a small badge. The trail takes about forty-five minutes and is designed for ages six to twelve. We also run family workshops during school holidays, where children can try making their own herbal remedies, using the same plants that apothecaries sold two hundred years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum is fully accessible. There's a lift to the first floor next to the cloakroom, and wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge. Seating is available in every gallery if you need a rest, and the courtyard is a pleasant place to sit on a sunny day.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you'd like to know more about any object, scan the code next to it with your phone for a short audio description. Audio guides are also available to borrow from the front desk for three euros, with versions in six languages. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: Evaluating a public health campaign
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two public health students, Grace and Sam, discuss their evaluation of a campaign to encourage hand-washing in schools.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So, Sam, we need to finish the analysis for our report on the hand-washing campaign. Have you looked at the absence figures?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. Just to remind ourselves, the campaign ran in ten primary schools for one term, and we compared them with ten similar schools that didn't take part. The main outcome we measured was how many days pupils were absent because of illness.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: And the result?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: In the campaign schools, sickness absence fell by about eighteen per cent compared with the same term the previous year. In the comparison schools, it fell by about six per cent.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So the comparison schools also improved. Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Probably because the previous winter had a particularly bad flu season, so absence was unusually high that year. That's exactly why we needed the comparison group. If we'd only looked at the campaign schools, we'd have overestimated the effect.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Right. So the real effect is the difference, roughly twelve percentage points. That's still substantial. What about the observations?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That was more complicated. We observed pupils after break and before lunch to see if they washed their hands properly. At the start of the campaign, about forty per cent did. By the middle of the term, it had risen to over seventy per cent.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: But it dropped again towards the end, didn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, to about fifty-five per cent. It seems the novelty wore off. The posters and songs were exciting at first, but after a few weeks, the children stopped noticing them.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: That's an important finding. It suggests campaigns need to be refreshed regularly, rather than just run once.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. The teachers' interviews were interesting too. Most of them were positive, but a few mentioned practical problems.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The biggest one was soap. In several schools, soap dispensers often ran out, and nobody was clearly responsible for refilling them. One teacher said it was pointless telling children to wash their hands when there was no soap.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: So the campaign was only as good as the facilities. We should definitely recommend that schools assign someone to check supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And another teacher said there weren't enough sinks. With thirty children all trying to wash their hands before lunch, it took ages, and lunch was delayed.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Did any teachers mention how the children themselves reacted?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, several said the younger children were the most enthusiastic. The five- and six-year-olds loved the hand-washing song and reminded each other to use it. The older pupils, especially the ten- and eleven-year-olds, found it a bit childish, and one teacher said they started making fun of the posters.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: That's useful. Perhaps the materials need to be adapted for different age groups. Older children might respond better to something more scientific, like growing bacteria from unwashed hands in a dish and comparing it with washed hands.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Actually, one school did exactly that in a science lesson, and the teacher said it had a much bigger impact on the older pupils than the posters did. They were quite shocked by what grew.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: I'm not surprised. Let's mention that as an example of good practice in the discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Okay. What about the limitations of our study?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Well, the schools weren't randomly chosen. The campaign schools volunteered, so their head teachers may have been especially keen on health, which could affect the results.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Also, one term is quite short. We don't know whether the effect would last over a whole year.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And when pupils knew they were being observed, they may have washed their hands more carefully than usual.

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Good point. That's sometimes called the observer effect. Right, I think our recommendations should be: refresh the campaign regularly, make sure facilities are adequate, and carry out a longer study with randomly selected schools.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sounds good. I'll write the results section, and you do the discussion?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Deal. Let's aim to have drafts ready by Monday.

listeningParts.title: The story of antibiotics
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a microbiology course on the discovery of antibiotics and the problem of resistance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at antibiotics: how they were discovered, how they work, and why their effectiveness is now under serious threat.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: It's hard to imagine today how dangerous bacterial infections were before antibiotics. A small cut or a scratch from a rose thorn could lead to a fatal infection. Pneumonia, tuberculosis and infections after childbirth killed millions of people. Surgery was extremely risky, not because of the operation itself, but because of the infections that often followed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The story of the first antibiotic usually begins in 1928, in the London laboratory of the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming. Fleming was studying bacteria called staphylococci, and before going on holiday, he left several dishes of them on his laboratory bench. When he returned, he noticed that one dish had been contaminated by a mould, and that the bacteria around the mould had been killed. He identified the mould as Penicillium, and named the substance it produced penicillin.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, Fleming found penicillin very difficult to purify and produce in useful amounts, and he eventually turned to other research. For about ten years, little progress was made. Then, at the end of the 1930s, a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain took up the work. They developed methods of extracting and purifying penicillin, and in 1941, they treated their first patient, a policeman suffering from a severe infection. He began to recover, but the supply of penicillin ran out, and he died. The scientists had been so short of the drug that they had even recovered it from the patient's urine to use again.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The Second World War created an urgent need for penicillin to treat wounded soldiers, and production was scaled up enormously, mainly in the United States. A key breakthrough came when researchers found a strain of Penicillium growing on a mouldy melon in a market in Illinois, which produced far more penicillin than Fleming's original mould. By the end of the war, penicillin was being produced in large quantities, and Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Over the following decades, many other antibiotics were discovered, most of them from microorganisms found in soil. Antibiotics work in different ways: some destroy the walls that surround bacterial cells, while others prevent bacteria from making proteins or copying their DNA. Importantly, antibiotics have no effect on viruses, which is why they're useless against colds and flu.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Fleming himself warned of the main danger in his Nobel Prize speech. Bacteria reproduce extremely quickly, and occasionally random changes in their DNA, known as mutations, make some of them resistant to a particular antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, the bacteria that aren't resistant are killed, but the resistant ones survive and multiply. Every time antibiotics are used, therefore, there's a risk of encouraging resistance. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes directly to one another, even between different species.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The problem has been made much worse by overuse. Antibiotics are often prescribed for viral infections, where they do nothing, and in many countries they can be bought without a prescription. Large quantities are also given to farm animals, not only to treat disease but to make them grow faster, although this has been banned in the European Union since 2006. Meanwhile, very few new types of antibiotic have been developed since the 1980s, partly because they're not very profitable for drug companies: a new antibiotic is used for short courses and is often kept in reserve for emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A major study published in 2022 estimated that over a million deaths a year worldwide are directly caused by antibiotic-resistant infections. Solutions include using antibiotics more carefully, improving hygiene and vaccination to prevent infections in the first place, and finding new ways to encourage research. Next week, we'll look at some promising alternatives, including viruses that attack bacteria.

readingPassages.title: The conquest of smallpox
paragraphs: For most of recorded history, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases on Earth. It spread easily from person to person through the air, caused high fever and a painful rash that turned into fluid-filled blisters, and killed around three in every ten people it infected. Those who survived were often left with deep scars on their faces, and some were blinded. In the eighteenth century alone, it is estimated that smallpox killed around four hundred thousand Europeans every year, and in the twentieth century, before it was finally defeated, it caused an estimated three hundred million deaths worldwide.

Long before scientists understood how diseases spread, people noticed that those who recovered from smallpox never caught it again. This observation led to a practice known as variolation, in which material from the blisters of a person with a mild case was deliberately introduced into a healthy person, usually through a small cut in the skin or, in China, by blowing dried scabs into the nose. The person usually developed a mild form of the disease and was then protected for life. Variolation was practised in parts of Asia and Africa for centuries before it reached Europe.

The practice was introduced to Britain in the 1720s, largely through the efforts of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, the wife of the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire. She had survived smallpox herself, and had seen variolation performed in Constantinople. On her return to London, she had her daughter variolated in front of the king's doctors. The method became fashionable among wealthy families, but it carried real risks. Around one or two per cent of those variolated died, and because they had a genuine infection, they could pass the disease to others.

The decisive breakthrough came from an English country doctor, Edward Jenner. It was common knowledge among farmers that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle that caused sores on the hands, seemed to be protected against smallpox. In 1796, Jenner tested this idea. He took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and introduced it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. Some weeks later, he variolated the boy with smallpox material, and the boy did not become ill. Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow.

Jenner's experiment would not be considered ethical today, and he was not the first person to try the method; a farmer named Benjamin Jesty had used cowpox to protect his family more than twenty years earlier. Jenner's contribution was to test the idea systematically, to publish his results and to promote vaccination energetically. Vaccination was far safer than variolation, and it spread with remarkable speed. Within a few years, it was being used across Europe and the Americas. In 1803, the Spanish government sent an expedition to its colonies carrying the vaccine in a living chain of orphan boys, who were vaccinated one after another during the voyage to keep the material fresh.

Not everyone welcomed the new method. Some people objected on religious grounds, arguing that it was wrong to introduce material from animals into the human body. Cartoons of the time showed vaccinated people growing horns or the heads of cows. When the British government made vaccination of infants compulsory in 1853, opposition grew stronger, and anti-vaccination leagues were formed. By the end of the century, the law had been changed to allow parents who objected on grounds of conscience to refuse.

Despite vaccination, smallpox remained common in many parts of the world well into the twentieth century. In 1967, the World Health Organization launched an intensified campaign to eliminate the disease completely. At that time, there were still between ten and fifteen million cases a year, mainly in South America, Africa and South Asia. The campaign was helped by two features of the disease: it only infected humans, so there was no animal reservoir in which it could hide, and its rash made infected people easy to identify.

Rather than trying to vaccinate whole populations, which proved impossible in many areas, the campaign adopted a strategy called surveillance and containment. Teams searched for new cases, isolated the patients and vaccinated everyone around them, creating a ring of immunity that stopped the virus from spreading further. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the World Health Organization officially declared that smallpox had been eradicated. It remains the only human disease ever to have been completely wiped out, although samples of the virus are still kept in two high-security laboratories, one in the United States and one in Russia.

readingPassages.title: The long war against malaria
paragraphs: Malaria has probably killed more people than any other disease in human history. Even today, despite more than a century of scientific effort, it infects around two hundred and fifty million people every year and kills more than six hundred thousand, most of them children under the age of five in sub-Saharan Africa. The story of the fight against malaria is a story of remarkable discoveries, disappointing setbacks and, more recently, cautious hope.

For centuries, people believed that the disease was caused by bad air rising from swamps and marshes, which is where its name comes from: the Italian words mala aria mean 'bad air'. The idea was not entirely foolish, since malaria was indeed most common near stagnant water. The real cause was discovered in 1880 by a French army doctor, Alphonse Laveran, who saw tiny parasites in the blood of a patient in Algeria. Seventeen years later, a British doctor working in India, Ronald Ross, proved that the parasites were carried by mosquitoes, a discovery that earned him the Nobel Prize in 1902.

We now know that malaria is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Plasmodium, and that it is spread only by female Anopheles mosquitoes, which need a meal of blood to produce their eggs. When an infected mosquito bites, parasites enter the bloodstream and travel to the liver, where they multiply. They then invade red blood cells, which burst every two or three days, releasing more parasites. This cycle causes the attacks of fever, shaking and sweating that are typical of the disease. When another mosquito bites the infected person, it picks up parasites and the cycle begins again.

The first effective treatment came from South America. In the seventeenth century, Jesuit missionaries in Peru learned from local people that the bark of the cinchona tree could reduce fever. The active ingredient, quinine, was isolated by French chemists in 1820 and became the standard treatment for more than a century. It was so important that European colonial powers established cinchona plantations in Asia, and it has been said that without quinine, much of the European colonisation of Africa would not have been possible.

In the middle of the twentieth century, it seemed that malaria could be defeated altogether. Powerful new insecticides, particularly DDT, were sprayed inside homes to kill mosquitoes, and a cheap synthetic drug called chloroquine was widely used for treatment. In 1955, the World Health Organization launched a global eradication campaign. Malaria was eliminated from Europe, the United States and several other countries, and cases fell dramatically in parts of Asia. However, the campaign largely excluded sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease was most common.

By the late 1960s, the campaign was in trouble. Mosquitoes had become resistant to DDT, the parasites had become resistant to chloroquine, and concerns about the environmental effects of DDT, raised by books such as Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, led to its use being restricted. Funding dried up, and in 1969 the goal of global eradication was abandoned. In many countries, the disease returned, and by the 1990s malaria deaths in Africa were rising again.

A new effort began around the year 2000, supported by international organisations and large private donors. One of the simplest tools proved to be among the most effective: bed nets treated with insecticide, which protect people while they sleep, when Anopheles mosquitoes are most active. Hundreds of millions of nets have been distributed, and studies suggest they have prevented more cases than any other measure. At the same time, a new family of drugs based on artemisinin, a substance discovered by the Chinese scientist Tu Youyou in an ancient herbal remedy, replaced chloroquine as the main treatment. Between 2000 and 2015, malaria deaths worldwide fell by around sixty per cent.

The most recent development is the arrival of vaccines. Developing a malaria vaccine has proved extremely difficult, partly because the parasite changes its form at different stages of its life cycle. In 2021, the World Health Organization recommended the first vaccine for children, and a second, cheaper vaccine was approved in 2023. Neither is completely effective, and both require several doses, but used together with nets and drugs, they could save tens of thousands of lives each year. Yet challenges remain. Resistance to artemisinin has appeared in parts of Africa, and climate change may allow mosquitoes to spread to higher and cooler areas where malaria was previously rare.

readingPassages.title: Testing the treatments
paragraphs: How do we know whether a medical treatment works? For most of history, the answer depended on the opinion of experienced physicians, who based their judgements on the patients they had personally treated. The problem with this approach is that people often recover from illnesses naturally, so a doctor who gives a treatment and sees the patient improve may wrongly conclude that the treatment caused the recovery. As a result, many treatments that did more harm than good, such as bloodletting, remained popular for centuries.

One of the earliest recorded attempts to compare treatments fairly was made in 1747 by James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon. Sailors on long voyages frequently suffered from scurvy, a disease that caused bleeding gums, weakness and eventually death. Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy and divided them into six pairs, giving each pair a different remedy, including vinegar, seawater and two oranges and a lemon each day. The sailors who ate citrus fruit recovered rapidly, while the others did not. Although Lind's trial was very small, it is often described as the first controlled clinical trial. Surprisingly, it was more than forty years before the British navy began to provide lemon juice to all its sailors.

The modern randomised controlled trial emerged in the mid-twentieth century. Its key feature is that patients are allocated to groups by chance, so that the groups are as similar as possible in every respect except the treatment they receive. A landmark study published in 1948 by the British Medical Research Council tested the antibiotic streptomycin for tuberculosis. Partly because the drug was in short supply, the researchers could justify giving it to only some patients, and they used random numbers to decide who would receive it. The trial demonstrated a clear benefit and is widely regarded as a model of good research design.

Randomisation alone is not enough to guarantee reliable results. If patients know they are receiving a new treatment, their expectations may influence how they feel, and if doctors know, they may unconsciously assess those patients more favourably. To avoid this, many trials are double-blind, meaning that neither patients nor researchers know who is in which group until the trial is over. The comparison group typically receives either a placebo or the best existing treatment.

In the 1970s, a British doctor named Archie Cochrane argued that doctors should base their decisions on the systematic evaluation of all the available evidence, rather than on habit or authority. He criticised the medical profession for failing to organise the results of trials in a way that would allow doctors to use them. His ideas inspired the movement known as evidence-based medicine and led to the founding in 1993 of the Cochrane Collaboration, now an international network of researchers who produce systematic reviews summarising the findings of all the reliable trials on a particular question.

Systematic reviews are important because individual trials can give misleading results. A small trial may find a positive effect simply by chance, and there is a well-documented tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often than those with negative or disappointing ones. This problem, known as publication bias, can make treatments appear more effective than they really are. One partial solution has been to require researchers to register their trials publicly before they begin, so that results which are never published can at least be identified. Since 2005, many leading medical journals have refused to publish trials that were not registered in advance.

The influence of funding is another concern. Most trials of new drugs are paid for by the companies that make them, and several studies have found that industry-funded trials are more likely to reach conclusions favourable to the sponsor's product. This does not necessarily mean that the research is dishonest; companies may, for example, choose to compare their drug with a weak alternative or to test it on patients who are most likely to benefit. Nevertheless, critics such as the British doctor and writer Ben Goldacre have argued that greater transparency, including access to full trial data, is essential if doctors and patients are to trust the evidence.

Randomised trials also have limitations of their own. They are expensive and slow, and they often exclude elderly people, pregnant women and patients with several illnesses, which means that their results may not apply to the patients doctors see in everyday practice. For this reason, researchers increasingly supplement trials with large observational studies using health records from millions of patients. Such studies can reveal rare side effects or long-term outcomes that trials are too small or too short to detect, although they cannot prove cause and effect as convincingly. In my view, the best evidence comes from combining both approaches rather than relying on either alone.

listeningParts.title: Joining a volcano hiking trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a tour company to book a guided hike on a volcano.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Fire Mountain Tours, this is Callum. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm on holiday here next month with my husband, and we'd love to do one of your volcano hikes. Could you tell me what you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Certainly. We have three main trips. The easiest is the Lava Fields Walk. It takes about three hours and goes across old lava flows at the bottom of the mountain. There's not much climbing, so it's suitable for almost anyone, including children over eight.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Okay. And the others?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The second is the Crater Rim Hike, which is our most popular. You drive up to the car park at fifteen hundred metres, and then walk up to the edge of the main crater and around it. It takes around six hours in total, and you need to be reasonably fit, because the path is steep in places and the ground is loose.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And the third one?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's the Summit Sunrise trip. You start at two in the morning and climb to the summit in the dark, so that you reach the top at sunrise. It's spectacular, but it's very demanding: around nine hours of walking, and the summit is at over three thousand metres, so some people feel the effects of the altitude.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think the Crater Rim Hike sounds about right for us. We walk quite a lot at home, but we're not experienced mountaineers.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good choice. That trip runs every day except Sunday. Which date were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Could we do the nineteenth?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The nineteenth is a Wednesday. Yes, there are places available. The price is eighty-five euros per person. That includes transport from your hotel, the guide, a helmet, and a packed lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: A helmet? Is it dangerous?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a precaution. The volcano is active, and occasionally small stones are thrown out of the crater. Our guides check the activity reports every morning with the volcano observatory, and if the risk is too high, we change the route or cancel the trip. If we cancel, you get a full refund, or you can move to another day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. What should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Proper walking boots are essential; we won't allow anyone to join in trainers or sandals, because the volcanic rock is very sharp. You'll also need a waterproof jacket and a warm layer. Even in summer, it can be cold and windy near the crater. And bring at least two litres of water per person, sun cream and sunglasses.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: We don't have walking boots with us. Can we hire them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, we hire boots for ten euros a pair. Just tell me your shoe sizes when you book, so we can have them ready.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Great. And what time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The minibus picks people up between seven and seven thirty, depending on where your hotel is. Where are you staying?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The Hotel Miramar, on the seafront.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's one of our first pick-ups, so it'll be seven o'clock, outside the main entrance. Could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Laura Fairbanks. F-A-I-R-B-A-N-K-S.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know about your health, for example heart or breathing problems?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No, we're both fine. Although my husband is allergic to nuts, if that matters for the lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It does, thank you. I'll make a note so the kitchen prepares a nut-free lunch for him. To confirm the booking, we need a deposit of thirty euros per person, which you can pay online using the link I'll send you by email. The rest is paid in cash or by card to the guide on the day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Perfect. One last question: will we actually see lava?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'm afraid I can't promise that. Sometimes, if there's been recent activity, you can see a red glow inside the crater, but most of the time you'll see steam and smoke, and smell the sulphur. It's still very impressive, though, and the views across the island are amazing.

listeningParts.title: Earthquake preparedness at work
listeningParts.contextDescription: A safety officer speaks to new staff at an office about what to do in an earthquake.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Harbourview Engineering. I'm Nadia, the health and safety officer, and this morning I want to talk to you about earthquakes. As you probably know, this city lies close to a major fault line, and scientists estimate there's a significant chance of a damaging earthquake here in the next fifty years. So it's important that everyone knows exactly what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: First, the building itself. This office was built in 2012, and it was designed to meet the latest earthquake standards. It sits on special rubber bearings, which allow the building to move separately from the ground and reduce the shaking inside. That means it's very unlikely to collapse. However, people are often injured in earthquakes not because buildings fall down, but because objects inside them fall over or are thrown across the room. That's why all our bookcases and filing cabinets are fixed to the walls, and why we ask you not to keep heavy objects on high shelves.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Now, if you feel an earthquake, the rule is: drop, cover and hold on. Drop to your hands and knees before the shaking knocks you down. Take cover under a strong desk or table, protecting your head and neck. And hold on to it until the shaking stops. If there's no table nearby, crouch next to an inside wall, away from windows, and cover your head with your arms.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: What you should not do is run outside during the shaking. Many injuries happen when people are hit by falling glass or pieces of buildings as they leave. And please don't use the lifts, either during an earthquake or afterwards, because they may stop working or be damaged. Some people believe that standing in a doorway is the safest place, but in modern buildings, doorways are no stronger than other parts of the structure, so that advice is out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: When the shaking stops, wait for instructions from your floor warden. Each floor has two wardens, who wear orange jackets. If the building needs to be evacuated, they'll lead you down the stairs. Our assembly point is in the car park of the sports centre across the road, not the main car park behind this building, because that's next to a tall wall which could fall. At the assembly point, your manager will check that everyone from your team is there.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Be aware that a large earthquake is usually followed by aftershocks, which can continue for days or even weeks. Some can be strong enough to cause further damage, so be prepared to drop, cover and hold on again.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: We also keep emergency supplies in the building, in case staff are unable to get home, for example if roads or bridges are closed. There are emergency kits on every floor, in the cupboard next to the kitchen. Each one contains water, food bars, a first-aid kit, a torch and a radio that works without batteries, using a handle that you turn. We check the kits every six months and replace anything that's out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: We also strongly recommend that you prepare a small kit for your own home and agree a plan with your family, for example a place to meet if you're separated and a friend or relative outside the city that everyone can contact, since local phone networks are often overloaded after an earthquake. You'll find a checklist on the staff website.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Finally, we hold an earthquake drill twice a year, in April and October, and the whole building takes part. You'll hear a long, continuous alarm, which is different from the fire alarm, which goes on and off. Right, does anyone have any questions?

listeningParts.title: A field trip to study a volcano
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Hannah and Kofi, discuss a field trip with their lecturer.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Come in, Hannah, Kofi. So, now that you're back from the field trip to Tenerife, I'd like to hear how your research went before you start writing it up.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It went really well, thanks. As you know, our project was about how local people perceive the risk of a future eruption of Mount Teide, and whether they'd know what to do if one happened.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your data?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Mainly through face-to-face interviews. We interviewed eighty-six people in three towns at different distances from the volcano. We'd planned to do a hundred, but it took longer than we expected, because a lot of people wanted to talk for much longer than the fifteen minutes we'd planned.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's actually a good sign. People were interested in the topic, then?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Very. What surprised us most was that most people didn't think an eruption was likely in their lifetime, even though Teide is classified as active. Only about one in four thought there was a real chance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Partly because the last eruption on the island was in 1909, so nobody alive remembers one. Several people said things like, 'It's been quiet for over a hundred years, so why would it erupt now?' Volcanologists would say that's not how volcanoes work, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And there were also some interesting differences between groups. Older people were generally less worried than younger people, which we hadn't expected. We thought older residents might know more about the volcano's history.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Did you find any explanation for that?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: We think it might be linked to social media. Younger people said they'd seen news about earthquake swarms under the island in recent years, and some had been following the 2021 eruption on La Palma, the neighbouring island, very closely online.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's a very plausible connection. La Palma would have made the risk feel much more real. What about preparedness?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That was more worrying. Fewer than a third of people knew where their nearest evacuation route was, and almost nobody had an emergency bag ready. Most people said they'd simply wait for the authorities to tell them what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Which isn't unreasonable, as long as the warning systems work. Did you visit the monitoring centre?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, on the third day. That was one of the highlights. The scientists showed us how they measure small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground and the gases coming out of the volcano. They said changes in gas emissions are often one of the earliest signs that magma is moving.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: They also told us that the biggest challenge isn't detecting activity, but communicating it to the public without causing panic. If they warn too often and nothing happens, people stop listening.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's an important point for your discussion. It's sometimes called the 'cry wolf' effect. Did they say how they deal with it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They use a colour-coded alert system, from green to red, and they publish regular updates even when nothing is happening, so that people get used to trusting one source of information rather than rumours on social media.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sensible. Now, any problems with the fieldwork?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: The main one was language. Our Spanish isn't great, so we relied on a local student, Elena, to help with interviews. She was excellent, but sometimes we weren't sure whether her translations were exactly what people had said.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: You should mention that as a limitation. You could also record the interviews, with permission, and have a sample checked by another translator.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good idea. We did record about half of them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then do that. Right, I'd like your first draft by the end of the month, and please include a map showing the three towns.

listeningParts.title: Tsunamis
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an earth sciences course on the causes of tsunamis and how their effects can be reduced.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. In today's lecture, we're going to look at tsunamis: what causes them, why they're so destructive, and what can be done to reduce the number of people they kill.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The word tsunami comes from Japanese and means 'harbour wave', because fishermen would return to find their harbours destroyed, although they'd noticed nothing unusual out at sea. Tsunamis used to be called tidal waves, but that's misleading, because they have nothing to do with tides.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most tsunamis are caused by large earthquakes under the sea, particularly at subduction zones, where one of the Earth's plates is being pushed beneath another. Pressure builds up over hundreds of years, and when the plates suddenly slip, the sea floor can rise or fall by several metres. This moves the entire column of water above it, from the sea floor to the surface. Tsunamis can also be caused by underwater landslides, volcanic eruptions and, very rarely, by meteorites hitting the ocean.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A tsunami is very different from an ordinary wave. Ordinary waves are caused by wind and only affect the water near the surface. Tsunami waves involve the whole depth of the ocean, and they have an extremely long wavelength; the distance between one wave crest and the next can be over a hundred kilometres. In deep water, they travel as fast as a jet aircraft, at around eight hundred kilometres per hour, but they may be less than a metre high, so ships at sea often don't notice them at all.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: As the wave approaches the coast and the water becomes shallower, it slows down and grows much taller. Often, the first sign is not a wall of water but the sea suddenly drawing back, exposing the sea floor far beyond the normal low tide. Tragically, people sometimes walk out to look at the exposed beach, not realising that the wave will arrive within minutes. Another common misunderstanding is that a tsunami is a single wave. In fact, there's usually a series of waves, and the first is often not the largest.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The deadliest tsunami in recorded history occurred in the Indian Ocean on the twenty-sixth of December 2004, after an earthquake off the coast of Sumatra in Indonesia. It killed around two hundred and thirty thousand people in fourteen countries. One reason the death toll was so high was that, unlike the Pacific, the Indian Ocean had no warning system at the time. In some places, such as Sri Lanka and India, the waves arrived two hours after the earthquake, which would have been plenty of time to evacuate if people had been warned.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Since then, a warning system has been established in the Indian Ocean. Such systems rely on two main types of information. First, earthquake measurements, which show where and how strong an earthquake is. And second, sensors on the sea floor that detect changes in water pressure as a tsunami passes above them. These send signals to buoys on the surface, which transmit the data by satellite to warning centres.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But technology alone isn't enough. The 2011 tsunami in Japan showed this. Japan has the world's most advanced warning system and many coastal defences, including sea walls over ten metres high. Yet the waves were higher than expected and went over many of the walls, and around eighteen thousand people died. Studies afterwards found that some people didn't evacuate because they trusted the sea walls to protect them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So education is crucial. In some communities, traditional knowledge has saved lives. On the Indonesian island of Simeulue, very close to the 2004 earthquake, only seven people died out of around seventy-eight thousand, because people had passed down stories about an earlier tsunami in 1907, which taught them to run to high ground when the ground shook. Today, many coastal areas have signs showing evacuation routes, and schools carry out regular drills. Next week, we'll look at how coastal planning and natural barriers such as mangrove forests can also reduce the impact.

readingPassages.title: The year without a summer
paragraphs: In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, produced the largest eruption in recorded history. The explosions were heard more than two thousand kilometres away, and some people on nearby islands believed they were hearing the sound of cannons. Before the eruption, Tambora was over four thousand metres high; afterwards, about a third of the mountain had disappeared, leaving a crater six kilometres wide.

The immediate effects on the region were catastrophic. Clouds of hot gas, ash and rock, known as pyroclastic flows, rushed down the sides of the volcano at enormous speed, destroying villages and killing almost everyone in their path. Thick layers of ash covered fields across Sumbawa and the neighbouring island of Lombok, ruining crops and poisoning water supplies. Estimates vary, but it is thought that around ten thousand people died during the eruption itself, and that tens of thousands more died in the following months from starvation and disease.

The effects of the eruption, however, were not limited to Indonesia. Tambora blasted huge quantities of sulphur gas high into the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the level at which clouds and weather form. There, the gas combined with water to form tiny droplets, which spread around the globe and reflected part of the sun's energy back into space. Because there is no rain in the stratosphere to wash these particles out, they remained there for several years, causing average temperatures around the world to fall by around half a degree Celsius.

This may not sound like much, but the consequences in 1816 were dramatic. In parts of Europe and North America, it became known as 'the year without a summer'. In New England, in the north-eastern United States, snow fell in June, and frosts in July and August killed crops. In western Europe, it rained almost continuously throughout the summer, and harvests of wheat and potatoes failed. Food prices rose sharply, and there were riots in Britain, France and Switzerland. In Ireland, the cold, wet weather was followed by an epidemic of typhus, which killed tens of thousands of people.

The crisis had long-lasting social effects. In the United States, thousands of farmers left New England and moved west in search of better land, contributing to the settlement of states such as Ohio and Indiana. In Germany, the high price of oats, which were used to feed horses, may have encouraged the inventor Karl Drais to develop a 'running machine', an early form of bicycle that did not need to be fed, which he demonstrated in 1817. Although this connection is difficult to prove, it is often mentioned by historians of transport.

The gloomy summer also left a mark on culture. A group of young English writers, including Mary Shelley and Lord Byron, spent the summer of 1816 at a villa beside Lake Geneva in Switzerland. Kept indoors by the constant storms, they held a competition to see who could write the most frightening story. Mary Shelley's contribution later became the novel Frankenstein, published in 1818. Some art historians have also suggested that the vivid orange and red skies in paintings by the English artist J. M. W. Turner during this period reflect the volcanic particles in the atmosphere.

Remarkably, nobody at the time connected these events with the eruption on the other side of the world. News travelled slowly, and the idea that a volcano could affect the global climate had not yet been developed. It was not until the twentieth century that scientists, studying the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 and later ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica, which contain layers of sulphur from past eruptions, were able to show the link.

Today, Tambora's story is studied not only by historians but also by scientists and governments. It shows how vulnerable food systems can be to sudden changes in climate, and how a disaster in one part of the world can have consequences on the other side of it. Some researchers argue that an eruption of a similar size, which is likely to happen at some point in the next few centuries, could cause serious disruption to global food supplies, and that countries should plan for such an event.

readingPassages.title: Can earthquakes be predicted?
paragraphs: Of all natural disasters, earthquakes are among the most frightening, partly because they strike without warning. Hurricanes can be tracked for days as they cross the ocean, and floods can often be forecast from rainfall, but an earthquake can destroy a city in less than a minute. For more than a century, scientists have searched for a reliable way of predicting when and where earthquakes will occur. So far, despite enormous effort, they have not succeeded.

To understand why, it helps to know what causes earthquakes. The Earth's outer layer is broken into large plates, which move slowly, at roughly the speed at which fingernails grow. Where plates meet, they often become locked together along faults, and stress builds up in the surrounding rock. Eventually, the stress becomes greater than the strength of the rock, and the fault suddenly slips, releasing energy in the form of seismic waves. The difficulty is that scientists cannot directly observe conditions deep underground, where most earthquakes begin, and small differences in the properties of rocks can determine whether a fault slips today or in a hundred years.

Throughout history, people have reported strange events before earthquakes. Animals are said to behave unusually, water levels in wells rise or fall, and lights have been seen in the sky. Some of these reports may reflect real physical changes, but most are collected only after an earthquake has happened, when people are searching for explanations. Scientific studies have generally failed to find signals that occur consistently before earthquakes and rarely at other times, which is what a useful prediction method requires.

There has been one famous apparent success. In February 1975, Chinese authorities ordered the evacuation of the city of Haicheng after a series of small earthquakes, changes in groundwater and reports of unusual animal behaviour. The next day, a powerful earthquake struck, destroying much of the city. Thousands of lives were probably saved. However, the following year, an even larger earthquake hit the city of Tangshan without any warning, killing at least two hundred and forty thousand people. Most scientists now believe that Haicheng was a lucky case, made possible by an unusually long sequence of small earthquakes beforehand.

Prediction attempts have also had serious consequences when they failed. In 2009, a series of small earthquakes worried residents of the Italian city of L'Aquila. At a meeting, experts concluded that a major earthquake was unlikely, and an official reassured the public. Days later, an earthquake killed more than three hundred people. Six scientists and an official were convicted of manslaughter for giving misleading information, though the scientists' convictions were later overturned on appeal. The case alarmed researchers around the world, who feared that scientists would become reluctant to give advice.

Instead of predicting individual earthquakes, seismologists now concentrate on forecasting, which means estimating the probability of earthquakes in a particular area over a period of years or decades. These forecasts are based on the history of past earthquakes, the rate at which plates are moving and measurements of how the ground is deforming. In California, for example, scientists estimate that there is a greater than ninety-five per cent chance of an earthquake of magnitude 6.7 or larger in the next thirty years. Such forecasts cannot tell people when to leave their homes, but they are extremely useful for setting building standards and planning insurance.

A further approach is early warning. When an earthquake begins, it produces two main types of waves: faster primary waves, which cause relatively little damage, and slower secondary waves, which cause most of the shaking. Networks of sensors can detect the primary waves and send an alert electronically, which travels much faster than the seismic waves themselves. Depending on the distance from the earthquake, this can give people between a few seconds and about a minute of warning. Japan, Mexico and parts of the United States already have such systems, which can automatically stop trains, open fire station doors and send alerts to mobile phones.

A few seconds may not sound like much, but it can be enough for people to take cover under a table, for surgeons to stop operating and for trains to slow down. Researchers are also experimenting with using the sensors already built into smartphones to detect earthquakes in countries that cannot afford expensive networks. While the dream of predicting earthquakes may never be realised, these more modest goals are already saving lives.

readingPassages.title: There is no such thing as a natural disaster
paragraphs: Earthquakes, floods, hurricanes and droughts are usually described as natural disasters. The phrase seems obvious: these events are caused by forces of nature rather than by human action. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that the term is misleading, and even harmful. A hazard, they point out, is a natural event; a disaster is what happens when that hazard meets a population that is unable to cope with it. Whether a hazard becomes a disaster, and how severe that disaster is, depends largely on human decisions.

This argument was popularised in the 1970s by a group of geographers, including Phil O'Keefe, Ken Westgate and Ben Wisner, whose article 'Taking the naturalness out of natural disasters' became highly influential. They noted that, while the number of hazards was not obviously increasing, the number of people killed and affected by disasters was rising rapidly, particularly in poorer countries. The explanation, they argued, lay not in nature but in the vulnerability of the people exposed to hazards, which was itself the result of poverty, inequality and poor planning.

Comparisons between countries illustrate the point clearly. In January 2010, an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 struck near Port-au-Prince, the capital of Haiti, killing somewhere between one hundred thousand and three hundred thousand people. A month later, an earthquake in Chile released around five hundred times more energy, yet it killed fewer than six hundred people. The difference was not mainly due to geology. Chile had strict building codes, which were generally enforced, and a long experience of earthquakes, whereas in Haiti many buildings were constructed cheaply without reinforcement, and the government lacked the resources to enforce standards.

Vulnerability also varies within countries. When Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans in 2005, the areas that flooded most severely were largely low-lying neighbourhoods where poorer residents lived. Many of them did not own cars and could not leave the city when an evacuation was ordered. Similarly, during the European heatwave of 2003, which killed around seventy thousand people, the victims were disproportionately elderly people living alone, often in apartments without air conditioning, who had little contact with neighbours or relatives. In each case, social factors determined who lived and who died.

Human activity can also increase the hazards themselves. Draining wetlands and cutting down forests can make floods more frequent and severe, because the land is less able to absorb rainfall. Building on unstable slopes increases the risk of landslides. Extracting large quantities of groundwater has caused parts of cities such as Jakarta and Mexico City to sink, sometimes by more than twenty centimetres a year, making them more vulnerable to flooding. And climate change, driven by human emissions of greenhouse gases, is making some hazards, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall, more intense.

Critics of the 'no natural disasters' argument accept much of this, but they warn against taking it too far. Some events are so extreme that no society could fully protect itself against them; the 2011 tsunami in Japan, a wealthy and well-prepared country, still killed around eighteen thousand people. Others worry that the phrase may be used to blame governments or communities unfairly, or that it may distract attention from the need to understand the natural processes involved. Seismologists and meteorologists, they point out, remain essential to reducing disaster risk.

Nevertheless, the change in thinking has influenced international policy. The Sendai Framework, agreed by United Nations member states in 2015, emphasises reducing risk before disasters occur rather than simply responding afterwards. It encourages governments to invest in safer buildings and infrastructure, early warning systems and land-use planning, and to ensure that the poorest and most vulnerable groups are included in decision-making. Research by the World Bank suggests that every dollar spent on making infrastructure more resilient can save around four dollars in future losses.

In my view, the most important contribution of this way of thinking is that it replaces fatalism with responsibility. If disasters are simply acts of nature, there is little that can be done except to respond when they happen. If, on the other hand, they are the product of choices about where and how we build, who is protected and who is left exposed, then they can be prevented, or at least made far less deadly. The language we use, it turns out, matters a great deal.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering at a music festival
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a festival organiser to ask about volunteering.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, Greenvale Music Festival volunteer office, Martha speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I saw on your website that you're looking for volunteers for this summer's festival, and I'd like to find out more.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Great, thanks for calling. The festival runs for three days, from Friday the eighth of August to Sunday the tenth. Volunteers work three shifts of eight hours during the festival, and in return you get a free ticket for the whole weekend, which normally costs two hundred and forty pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds like a good deal. What kind of jobs are there?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There are several teams. The biggest is the stewarding team, which helps with crowd safety, checking tickets at the gates and giving directions. Then there's the recycling team, which collects and sorts waste around the site. We're trying to reduce the amount that goes to landfill, so it's an important job. We also have volunteers in the information tents and at the children's area.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I think I'd be most interested in the children's area. I've worked at a summer camp before.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's useful experience. For the children's area, you need to be at least twenty-one, and you'll need a background check, which we arrange for you free of charge. How old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm twenty-two.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Perfect. The children's area runs activities like face painting, craft workshops and storytelling, and there's a small stage for children's bands. Shifts there are during the day only, between ten in the morning and six in the evening, so you'd have your evenings free to see the main bands.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Even better. Where do volunteers stay?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There's a separate volunteers' campsite, which is quieter than the main one and has its own showers and a kitchen tent. You need to bring your own tent and sleeping bag. Meals are provided during your shifts, and you'll get a voucher for one hot meal a day from any food stall on site.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Do I have to attend any training?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, all volunteers must attend an induction. There's an online session that takes about an hour, which you need to complete by the end of June. Then there's a short briefing on site on the Thursday afternoon, when you arrive and collect your wristband.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And is there a deposit or anything like that?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There is. We ask for a deposit of the full ticket price when you sign up, which is returned to you after the festival as long as you complete all three shifts. It's unfortunate, but in the past some people signed up just to get a free ticket and then didn't turn up for work.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fair. How do I get to the site? I don't drive.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There's a free shuttle bus for volunteers from Hadley train station on the Thursday, leaving every half hour from twelve o'clock. Just show your volunteer email to the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Can I apply now?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, I can start the form. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Jasmine Whitlock. That's W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And an email address?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's jaswhit22 at mailbox dot com. That's J-A-S-W-H-I-T, then the numbers two, two.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And do you have any special skills that might be useful? First aid, for example, or other languages?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I've got a first-aid certificate from my summer camp job, and I speak some Italian.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Both very useful. I'll make a note. You'll receive an email with the link to the online induction and the deposit payment within the next two days. If you have any questions in the meantime, there's a page of frequently asked questions on the website.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: One more thing. Can I choose who I work with? A friend of mine might apply too.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, just put your friend's name in the comments box on the form, and we'll try to put you on the same shifts, although we can't always guarantee it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Thanks so much, Martha. I'm really looking forward to it.

listeningParts.title: Joining a community choir
listeningParts.contextDescription: The director of a community choir talks to people attending an open evening.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome to the Riverside Community Choir open evening. I'm Grace Holloway, the musical director. It's lovely to see so many new faces. I'll tell you a bit about the choir, and then we'll sing a couple of songs together, so you can see what it's like.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The choir was started twelve years ago by a group of friends who wanted to sing together just for fun. There were eight of them at the first rehearsal, in someone's living room. Today we have over ninety members, aged from eighteen to eighty-seven, and we rehearse here in the church hall every Tuesday evening from half past seven to nine thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The first thing I always want to make clear is that you don't need any experience to join, and there's no audition. Many of our members had never sung in a group before, and some told me they'd been told at school that they couldn't sing. In my experience, almost everyone can learn to sing in tune with a bit of practice and confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: You also don't need to read music. We teach most of our songs by ear, which means I sing each line and you copy it. For those who do read music, we provide sheet music as well. We also record practice tracks for each part, which you can download from our website and listen to at home, in the car or wherever you like. Most members find these really helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The choir is divided into four sections, according to the range of your voice: sopranos and altos, who are usually women, and tenors and basses, who are usually men, although that's not a rule. If you're not sure which section you belong in, don't worry. After the first couple of weeks, I'll listen to you individually and help you decide.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: As for what we sing, we have a very wide range. There's pop, gospel, folk songs from around the world and some classical pieces. This term we're learning a medley of songs from musicals, as well as a traditional South African song, which has some wonderful harmonies.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: We perform about four times a year. Our biggest event is the Christmas concert in December, which raises money for a local charity. Last year we raised over three thousand dollars for the children's hospital. In summer we also sing outdoors at the town's riverside festival, and we occasionally visit care homes to sing for the residents, which is always a very moving experience.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: I'm often asked whether singing in a choir is good for you, and the answer seems to be yes. Research has found that group singing can reduce stress and improve mood, and many of our members say the choir is the highlight of their week. It's also very sociable. After each rehearsal, quite a few of us go to the café across the road.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: I should also mention that we have a small choir committee, made up of six members, who organise our concerts, social events and the annual weekend trip. This year we're going to the coast in May, where we'll take part in a choir festival with groups from all over the region. It's a wonderful chance to hear other choirs and make new friends, and everyone is welcome to come, whether or not they sing in the concert.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Now, the practical details. Membership costs sixty dollars per term, and there are three terms a year. If that's difficult for you financially, please speak to me in private, as we have a fund to help people who can't afford it. Your first two rehearsals are free, so you can try it before deciding.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Finally, please fill in one of the yellow forms on the table by the door before you leave, so we can add you to the email list. Right, let's warm up. Everybody stand up, take a deep breath, and stretch your arms above your head.
