listeningParts.title: A project on music and memory
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Ravi and Ellie, discuss a project on music and memory with their supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So, Ravi, Ellie, tell me where you've got to with your project on music and memory.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We've finished the experiment, and we've just started analysing the results. As you know, we wanted to find out whether listening to background music affects how well students remember information.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Remind me of the design.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: We had sixty participants, all undergraduate students. Each of them read a short article about the history of the Silk Road and then answered twenty questions about it. They did this in one of three conditions: in silence, with instrumental classical music, or with pop music that had lyrics.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: And how did you allocate people to the conditions?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Randomly, using a computer program, so that there were twenty people in each group.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: And did all the participants read the article for the same length of time?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone had exactly ten minutes to read it, and then they did a short puzzle for five minutes before answering the questions, so that they couldn't simply repeat what they'd just read.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: The silent group did best, with an average score of fifteen out of twenty. The classical music group was only slightly lower, at fourteen. But the pop music group scored much lower, with an average of just under eleven.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's quite a big difference. How do you explain it?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We think it's mainly the lyrics. When you're reading, you're processing language, and if you're also hearing words in a song, the two compete for the same mental resources. Instrumental music doesn't have that problem, or at least not as much.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That fits with previous research. Did anything surprise you?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes. We also asked participants whether they usually study with music. Those who said they always listened to music while studying did slightly better in the pop music condition than those who never did, but they still did worse than in silence.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So being used to it helps a little, but doesn't remove the effect. That's interesting. Students often believe music helps them concentrate. Did you ask about that?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We did. Most people in the pop music group thought the music hadn't affected them at all, even though their scores were lower. So people may not be very good at judging how distracting music is.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's a really important point to include in your discussion. Now, what about the limitations?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Well, the sample was quite small, and all the participants were students, so we can't generalise to other age groups. Also, the test was immediately after reading, so we don't know about long-term memory.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We chose the music ourselves. People might be less distracted by music they know and like. Next time it might be better to let participants choose their own music.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good. You might also mention the volume. Did you control that?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone used the same headphones at the same volume.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Excellent. In your literature review, you might also want to look at research on music and memory in people with dementia. There's evidence that people with dementia can often remember songs from their youth long after other memories have faded, and some care homes use music to help residents feel calmer and communicate.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: That's fascinating. Is that because musical memory is stored differently in the brain?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's one theory. Some studies suggest that the areas of the brain involved in musical memory are among the last to be damaged by the disease. But it's a different question from yours, so just mention it briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Okay. When would you like the draft?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Send me the results section by next Wednesday, and we'll meet again the week after.

listeningParts.title: The history of recorded sound
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a media history course on the development of sound recording.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at the history of recorded sound. It's easy to forget that for almost all of human history, music could only be heard when it was performed live. If you wanted to hear a symphony, you had to go to a concert hall, and once the performance was over, the sound was gone forever. Recording changed not only how we listen to music, but music itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first device that could record sound was invented not by Thomas Edison, as many people believe, but by a French printer named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, in 1857. His machine, which he called the phonautograph, used a horn to collect sound and a thin brush, called a stylus, which traced the sound waves as lines on paper covered with soot. However, Scott never intended his recordings to be played back. He wanted to study sound visually. Remarkably, in 2008, researchers in the United States used computer technology to convert some of his tracings into sound, and they were able to hear a person singing a French folk song recorded in 1860.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first machine that could both record and play back sound was Edison's phonograph, in 1877. It used a cylinder wrapped in tin foil. As someone spoke into a horn, a needle cut a groove in the foil, and when the cylinder was turned again, the needle followed the groove and reproduced the sound. The first words Edison recorded were the children's rhyme 'Mary had a little lamb'. Interestingly, Edison originally thought the phonograph would be used mainly in offices, for dictating letters, rather than for entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Tin foil wore out after only a few plays, so it was soon replaced by wax cylinders. But cylinders were difficult to copy in large numbers. The solution came from a German-born inventor working in the United States, Emile Berliner, who in 1887 patented the gramophone, which used flat discs instead of cylinders. Discs could be produced from a master copy by pressing, rather like a stamp, which meant that thousands of identical copies could be made cheaply. This is the origin of the record industry.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Early recordings were made acoustically, without electricity. Musicians had to crowd around a large horn, and loud instruments like trumpets were placed further away than quiet ones. Many instruments simply didn't record well, and recordings could last only around three or four minutes per side. This is one reason why popular songs, even today, tend to be about three minutes long. From the mid-1920s, microphones and electrical recording greatly improved quality, and singers could perform more quietly and intimately, which led to new styles of singing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next major development was magnetic tape, developed in Germany in the 1930s. Tape allowed recordings to be edited by cutting and joining pieces, and later to be recorded on several separate tracks, so that different instruments could be recorded at different times and then combined. This transformed the recording studio into a creative tool, and by the 1960s, bands like the Beatles were producing albums that would have been impossible to perform live.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, records themselves improved. In 1948, the long-playing record, or LP, was introduced, which could hold over twenty minutes of music per side and was made of vinyl, which produced less noise than earlier materials. This made it possible to release albums rather than just single songs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then came the digital age. The compact disc, launched in 1982, stored sound as a series of numbers that were read by a laser. In the 1990s, the MP3 format compressed digital files by removing sounds that the human ear is less likely to notice, making it possible to share music over the internet. Today, most people listen through streaming services, which offer millions of songs instantly. Yet interestingly, sales of vinyl records have grown every year for well over a decade, as some listeners seek a more physical and deliberate experience. Next week, we'll look at how streaming has changed the economics of the music industry.

readingPassages.title: The invention of the piano
paragraphs: The piano is one of the most popular musical instruments in the world, found in concert halls, schools, churches and millions of homes. Yet compared with instruments such as the flute, the harp or the violin, it is a relatively recent invention. Its story is one of gradual technical improvement, driven by the demands of composers and performers and by changes in society.

Before the piano, the most important keyboard instruments were the harpsichord and the clavichord. In a harpsichord, pressing a key causes a small piece of quill or leather to pluck a string. This produces a bright, clear sound, but it has a significant limitation: however hard or softly the player presses the key, the volume stays almost the same. The clavichord, in which the strings are struck by small metal blades, could vary its volume, but its sound was so quiet that it was suitable only for small rooms.

The solution was found by Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument maker employed by the powerful Medici family in Florence, Italy. Around the year 1700, he built an instrument in which the strings were struck by small hammers covered in leather. The key feature of his design was a mechanism that allowed each hammer to strike the string and immediately fall back, so that the string could continue to vibrate. Because the force of the hammer depended on how hard the key was pressed, the player could now control the volume. Cristofori called his instrument the gravicembalo col piano e forte, meaning 'harpsichord with soft and loud', and it is from this name that the word piano comes.

Cristofori's invention attracted little attention at first. Only three of his pianos survive today, in museums in New York, Rome and Leipzig. It was in Germany, rather than Italy, that the instrument began to develop. The organ builder Gottfried Silbermann made pianos based on Cristofori's design and showed one to Johann Sebastian Bach in the 1730s. According to one account, Bach criticised the instrument's heavy touch and weak upper notes, but he later approved of an improved version.

By the late eighteenth century, the piano had become fashionable throughout Europe, and composers such as Mozart and Haydn wrote much of their keyboard music for it. Instruments of this period, now often called fortepianos, were much lighter than modern pianos, with wooden frames and thinner strings. Their sound was softer and faded more quickly. As composers demanded greater power and range, piano makers responded by adding more keys and using thicker strings under greater tension. Beethoven, in particular, was known for pushing the instruments of his time to their limits, and he is said to have broken strings when he played.

The greater tension of the strings created a problem: wooden frames could not withstand it and tended to bend or crack. The answer was iron. In 1825, the American maker Alpheus Babcock patented a frame cast in a single piece of iron, which allowed strings to be tightened much more. Later in the century, the firm founded in New York in 1853 by the German immigrant Henry Steinway combined an iron frame with an arrangement in which the bass strings crossed over the others, producing a richer and more powerful sound. By the 1880s, the piano had taken essentially its modern form, with eighty-eight keys covering more than seven octaves.

The nineteenth century also saw the piano move from the homes of the wealthy to those of the middle classes. Industrial production made instruments cheaper, and they could often be bought in instalments. Owning a piano became a symbol of respectability, and learning to play was considered an important accomplishment, especially for young women. Before the invention of the gramophone and the radio, the piano was the main way in which most people heard music at home, and publishers sold enormous quantities of sheet music, including piano arrangements of popular songs and operas.

In the twentieth century, the piano faced competition from recorded music and, later, from electronic keyboards, which are lighter, cheaper and can be played with headphones. Sales of traditional pianos have fallen in many countries. In China, however, where tens of millions of children are estimated to be learning the instrument, demand has grown enormously, and China is now the world's largest producer of pianos. More than three hundred years after Cristofori, his invention remains at the heart of musical life.

readingPassages.title: Why does music give us chills?
paragraphs: Many people have had the experience: a piece of music reaches a particular moment, and suddenly a shiver runs down the spine, the skin breaks out in goosebumps and the hairs on the arms stand on end. Psychologists call this response 'frisson', from a French word meaning a shiver or thrill. For a long time it was regarded as too personal and unpredictable to be studied scientifically. Today, however, it is the subject of a growing body of research, which is shedding light not only on music but on how the brain experiences pleasure.

Frisson is surprisingly common, but not universal. Surveys suggest that somewhere between half and two-thirds of people experience it at least occasionally when listening to music, although estimates vary considerably depending on how the question is asked. For some people, it happens frequently; others report never having felt it at all. The same piece of music may produce chills in one listener and leave another completely unmoved, and even the same listener may react differently on different occasions.

Researchers have identified several musical features that are particularly likely to produce chills. These include a sudden change in volume, such as a quiet passage followed by a loud one, the entrance of a new instrument or voice, and unexpected harmonies. What these features have in common is that they involve something surprising or that breaks a pattern the listener has come to expect. According to one theory, the brain is constantly predicting what will happen next in a piece of music, and chills occur when those predictions are violated in a way that is surprising but ultimately pleasurable.

The first brain-imaging study of musical chills was carried out in 2001 by Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre at McGill University in Montreal. They asked participants to bring in pieces of music that reliably gave them chills, and scanned their brains while they listened. They found that the experience was associated with activity in regions of the brain that are involved in reward and motivation, the same areas that respond to food, sex and certain drugs. This was a striking finding, because music, unlike food, has no obvious value for survival.

A later study by Valorie Salimpoor, also working with Zatorre, went further. Using a technique that can detect the release of chemicals in the brain, the researchers showed in 2011 that dopamine, a chemical associated with pleasure and reward, was released when listeners experienced the peak emotional moments of a piece. More surprisingly, dopamine was also released in a different area in the seconds before those moments, while listeners were anticipating them. In other words, part of the pleasure of music seems to come from the expectation of what is about to happen.

Why do some people experience chills more than others? Personality appears to play a role. Several studies have found that people who score highly on a personality trait known as openness to experience, which includes imagination, curiosity and a love of art and beauty, are more likely to report chills. There may also be differences in brain structure. A study by Matthew Sachs and colleagues at Harvard University in 2016, though based on only twenty participants, found that people who experienced chills had stronger connections between the areas of the brain that process sound and those that process emotion.

Context and memory matter too. Music that is associated with important events in a person's life, such as a wedding or the loss of a loved one, is especially likely to produce strong emotional responses. Some researchers have also noted that sad music produces chills particularly often. One explanation is that the experience resembles the physical response to separation or loss, combined with a sense of comfort and connection, which may explain why people seek out sad music even though it makes them feel sad.

The study of musical chills has practical as well as theoretical value. Because music can activate the brain's reward system so powerfully, researchers are investigating whether it could be used to help people with depression, a condition in which the ability to feel pleasure is often reduced. Others are interested in how music can motivate people during exercise or rehabilitation. Above all, the research shows that our response to music, far from being trivial, is rooted in some of the most fundamental systems of the human brain.

readingPassages.title: Should the arts be paid for by the state?
paragraphs: In most European countries, governments spend significant sums of public money on the arts. Opera houses, orchestras, theatres, museums and galleries receive grants that allow them to keep ticket prices lower than they would otherwise be, to commission new work and to take risks that commercial organisations might avoid. In the United States, by contrast, direct government funding is relatively small, and the arts depend much more on private donations, which are encouraged by tax relief. Whether, and how much, taxpayers should support the arts is a question that provokes strong opinions on all sides.

The tradition of public support for the arts has deep roots. For centuries, artists and musicians depended on wealthy patrons, such as kings, aristocrats and the Church. Haydn spent most of his career as a court musician employed by the Esterházy family in Hungary, and much of the greatest art of the Italian Renaissance was paid for by bankers and popes. As the power of these patrons declined, governments gradually took on part of their role. In Britain, the Arts Council was established in 1946, inspired partly by the economist John Maynard Keynes, who believed that the arts should be available to all and not only to the wealthy.

Supporters of public funding make several arguments. The first is economic. The cultural sector employs large numbers of people and attracts tourists, who spend money in hotels, restaurants and shops. Cities such as Bilbao in Spain, whose economy was transformed after the opening of the Guggenheim Museum in 1997, are often cited as evidence that investment in culture can bring wider benefits. The second argument concerns access. Without subsidies, it is claimed, tickets for opera, ballet or classical concerts would be so expensive that only the rich could attend.

A third argument is that the arts have value that cannot be measured in money. They help societies understand themselves, preserve cultural heritage for future generations and give people experiences of beauty and meaning. Some research also suggests that taking part in arts activities can improve health and well-being, particularly among older people and those who are socially isolated. In my view, this is ultimately the strongest argument, since it does not depend on the arts paying for themselves.

Critics, however, raise important objections. One is that public funding often benefits those who are already advantaged. Surveys in several countries have found that audiences for subsidised art forms such as opera and classical music are, on average, wealthier and more highly educated than the population as a whole. If this is the case, then taxes paid by people who never attend are effectively being used to subsidise the leisure activities of the better off. Supporters reply that the solution is to widen access, not to cut funding.

Another objection concerns who decides what is worth funding. When government bodies distribute grants, they inevitably make judgements about which kinds of art are valuable. Critics argue that this can favour established institutions and traditional forms over popular culture, or that it can lead to political interference. Others worry that dependence on public money can make arts organisations less responsive to audiences, since their income does not depend on selling tickets.

The economic arguments, too, have been questioned. Some economists point out that claims about the economic benefits of the arts are often based on studies commissioned by arts organisations themselves, and that money spent on culture might produce similar or greater benefits if it were spent on something else. The 'Bilbao effect', they note, has proved difficult to repeat; several cities that built expensive new museums in the hope of attracting tourists have been disappointed.

In practice, most countries now combine public and private funding, and the debate is less about whether the state should support the arts than about how much, and on what terms. Many governments now require funded organisations to demonstrate that they are reaching a wider and more diverse audience, through education programmes, cheaper tickets for young people and performances in schools, hospitals and community venues, and some publish detailed information about who attends their events. Whether such measures can answer the criticism that subsidised culture serves mainly a privileged minority remains to be seen.

listeningParts.title: Joining a course for newcomers
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man who has recently moved to a new city phones a centre that runs courses for new arrivals.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good morning, Riverside Newcomers' Centre, Joanna speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I moved to the city about three weeks ago with my wife, for her job, and someone at the library told me you run courses and activities for people who've just arrived. Could you tell me a bit more about them?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Of course, and welcome to Riverside. We offer quite a few things, but our main service is a free orientation programme called Settling In. It helps people understand how things work here, things like registering with a doctor, opening a bank account, looking for work and using public transport. It's a series of six weekly sessions, and each one lasts two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds really useful. My English is fine, obviously, but there's a lot I don't understand about the local systems. The paperwork alone is confusing. When does it run?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: There are two groups. One meets on Monday mornings, from ten until twelve, and the other meets on Wednesday evenings, from half past six until half past eight, for people who work during the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I haven't found a job yet, so Monday mornings would suit me better.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Fine. Let me see. The next course starts on the fourth of March. Oh, sorry, I'm looking at the wrong list. The fourth is when the Wednesday group starts. The Monday group begins a week later, on the eleventh.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The eleventh of March. Okay, that's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: The sessions take place in our main building, which is at number forty-two Carver Street, in Room 3B on the second floor. There's a lift, if you need it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there anywhere to park near the building?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Not really, I'm afraid. Parking on Carver Street is very limited and quite expensive. Most people come by tram. The stop called Market Square is only a couple of minutes' walk away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. We haven't bought a car yet anyway. Is there anything I need to bring to the first session?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Just a notebook, and some form of identification, such as your passport, because we need to check it when you register. A driving licence from your home country isn't enough, unfortunately. Everything else, including the handbook, is provided.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And is the course really free?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: The course itself is free, because it's funded by the city council. We do ask for a small contribution of two pounds a session for tea and coffee, but that's completely optional.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very reasonable. My wife might want to get involved too, although she's working full-time. Do you run anything at weekends?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Yes, we have a Saturday social club, where newcomers and local volunteers meet for different activities. This month there's a walking tour of the old town, which is free, and a cooking afternoon, where people prepare a dish from their home country and share it. That one costs five pounds per person, to cover the ingredients.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: She'd love the cooking afternoon. She's a brilliant cook. Right, can I book a place on the Monday course?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Certainly. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Marchetti. That's M-A-R-C-H-E-T-T-I.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Thank you. And where have you moved from, Daniel?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: From Perth, in Australia, although my father's family originally came from Italy, which explains the surname.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And what's your address here?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Flat 7, 19 Linden Road. The postcode is RV4 8TN.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Can I also ask what kind of work you're hoping to find? Some of our sessions include talks from local employers, so it helps us to plan.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm a qualified nurse. I worked in a children's hospital for eight years, but I need to get my qualifications recognised here before I'm allowed to work.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: That's very common. In session four, we have a specialist adviser who helps people with exactly that, so make sure you bring copies of your certificates that week.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I will. Thank you, that's a great help.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: One last thing. How did you hear about us? We like to keep a record so we know which kind of advertising works.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I picked up a leaflet at the central library, and the librarian recommended you too.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Wonderful. I'll send you a confirmation email this afternoon with a map and the handbook attached. We look forward to seeing you on the eleventh.

listeningParts.title: A guided visit to a migration museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A volunteer guide introduces a group of visitors to a museum about the history of migration through a port city.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Street Migration Museum. My name's Siobhan, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you start exploring, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the museum and explain what you'll find in each of our galleries.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: First, a little about the building. You may have noticed the old sign above the entrance. In the nineteenth century, this was the office of a shipping company, and it was here that thousands of people bought their tickets before leaving for North America and Australia. When the company closed, the building stood empty for many years, and it was almost demolished in the nineteen-nineties. A group of local residents campaigned to save it, and the museum finally opened in 2009. We chose this building precisely because so many journeys began in this very room.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum tells the story of people who left this city, but also of people who arrived here, because the port has always worked in both directions. Most of our collection, around three-quarters of it, has been donated by local families. People bring us letters, photographs, suitcases and even recipes, and every object comes with a story. We're always happy to receive new donations, but please speak to a member of staff first, because we can't accept everything.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, the galleries. On the ground floor, just behind me, is the Departure Hall. This is where you'll find the original ticket counter, and the walls are covered with copies of the passenger lists from the ships that sailed from here. If you know that an ancestor emigrated from this port, our staff can help you search the lists. The originals are far too fragile to handle, so they're kept in our archive.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to it is The Crossing. Here, we've built a full-size reconstruction of the cheapest part of a nineteenth-century sailing ship, which was called steerage. You can climb into the narrow wooden bunks and get a sense of what it was like to spend six weeks or more at sea with very little light or fresh air. Some visitors find it a little uncomfortable, so you're welcome to skip it if you prefer.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs, on the first floor, is the gallery called Arrivals, which looks at the people who have come to settle in this city over the last two centuries, from many different parts of the world. I'm afraid that gallery is closed this week, because we're installing new lighting, but it should reopen on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Also on the first floor is The Kitchen Table, which is our family gallery. It's full of hands-on activities: children can dress up in historical costumes, pack a suitcase for a long journey, and taste bread made from traditional recipes. It's especially popular with school groups, so it can get quite noisy in the mornings.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, on the top floor, there's the Voices Room. This is a small, quiet space where you can sit and listen to recordings of interviews with people who've migrated, both recently and in the past. The oldest recording was made in 1962. There's also a booth where you can record your own family's story, if you'd like to. With your permission, we add these recordings to our collection, and some have been used in our exhibitions.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Voices Room, out of respect for the people speaking. Please don't touch the objects in the glass cases, but anything with a green hand symbol beside it can be handled. And our café on the ground floor serves dishes inspired by the different communities that have settled here. Today's special, I believe, is a lentil soup from a family recipe that was donated last year.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you have any questions, you'll find staff and volunteers in every gallery, wearing blue lanyards. The museum closes at five, but the shop stays open for another half an hour. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: An oral history project
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two sociology students, Amira and Josh, discuss their project interviewing older migrants with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Amira, Josh. Come and sit down. So, you've finished the interviews for your oral history project. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Really well, I think. As you know, we wanted to record the experiences of people who came to live in this town in the nineteen-sixties and seventies, before those memories are lost. In the end, we interviewed fourteen people, all aged over seventy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How did you find them? That can be the hardest part.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We started by contacting community organisations, but that didn't work very well. We sent emails to about ten groups and only got two replies. What really made the difference was a lunch club for older residents at the community centre. Amira went along a few times and just chatted to people, and once they knew her, they were happy to take part, and they introduced us to their friends.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's quite typical. Trust matters much more than a formal invitation. And how did you run the interviews themselves?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We'd prepared a list of questions, but we soon realised that following it too closely didn't work. People wanted to tell their stories in their own order, so in the end we used the questions more as a checklist and let people talk. Most interviews lasted about an hour and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: And we interviewed most people in their own homes, which helped. Several of them showed us photographs or objects while they were talking, which brought back memories they might not have mentioned otherwise. One man had kept the ticket from the ship he arrived on in 1964.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Did anything in the interviews surprise you?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Quite a lot. We'd expected people to talk mostly about the difficulties of arriving: finding work, the weather, discrimination. And they did talk about those things. But what came up again and again was food. Nearly everyone described how hard it was at first to find the ingredients they were used to, and how important cooking was in keeping a connection with home.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The other surprise for me was how many of them had planned to stay only a few years. Almost half said they'd intended to earn some money and then go back, but then they had children, and their children grew up here, and somehow they never left.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a very common pattern in migration research. It's sometimes called the myth of return. Now, I'd like to talk about the problems of using memory as evidence. How reliable do you think your interviewees' memories were?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: That's something we discussed a lot. Some of the dates people gave were clearly wrong. One woman said she arrived in 1968, but later she mentioned an event that happened in 1971 as if it was just after she came. So we checked dates against other sources where we could.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. But remember that the value of oral history isn't mainly in the precise facts. It's in how people understood and felt about their experiences. A wrong date doesn't make the story worthless.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: That's what we've been arguing in our draft. We're treating the interviews as evidence of how people remember and give meaning to their lives, rather than as a record of exactly what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, what about the practical side? You've transcribed everything?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Almost. Transcription took far longer than we expected. Each hour of recording took us about six hours to type up, partly because some people switched between English and their first language.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's normal, I'm afraid. And you got signed consent forms from everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Yes, from all fourteen. Two people asked us not to use their real names, so we've given them different names in the report. And three people asked to see the transcripts before we use any quotations, so we're posting those to them this week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. One more suggestion: the town museum is collecting recordings like these for its archive. If your interviewees agree, you could offer them the recordings. That way, your work will be useful long after the project is marked.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We'd love that. We'll ask them when we send the transcripts.

listeningParts.title: The demographic transition
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a population geography course on how and why population growth changes as countries develop.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at one of the most influential ideas in population studies, the demographic transition model. It attempts to explain how the population of a country changes as it moves from a traditional society to a modern, industrial one. The basic idea was first set out by the American demographer Warren Thompson in 1929, and it was developed further in the nineteen-forties by Frank Notestein and others.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The model is usually described in four stages. In the first stage, both birth rates and death rates are high. This is typical of an agricultural society before modern medicine. Many children are born, but many also die young, from disease, poor diet and periods of famine. Because births and deaths roughly balance each other, the population grows very slowly, if at all. For most of human history, this was the normal situation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the second stage, the death rate begins to fall. This happens because of improvements in the food supply, in sanitation, particularly clean water and proper sewers, and later in medicine, such as vaccination. But the birth rate stays high, because people's attitudes and habits about family size don't change overnight. The result is a period of very rapid population growth. In England, for example, this happened during the nineteenth century, when the population grew several times over.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the third stage, the birth rate also starts to fall. Demographers have identified several reasons for this. As people move from farms to cities, children are no longer needed to work on the land, and instead become an economic cost, because they have to be fed, housed and educated for many years. As more children survive, parents no longer need to have many children to make sure that some reach adulthood. And perhaps most importantly, as girls and women receive more education and enter paid work, they tend to marry later and have fewer children. Access to contraception also plays a role.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the fourth stage, both birth and death rates are low, and the population is fairly stable again, but at a much higher level than before. An important figure here is what's called replacement level fertility, which is about two point one children per woman in countries with low death rates. That's the number needed for each generation to replace itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One thing that surprises students is that a population can keep growing for decades after fertility has fallen to replacement level. This is known as population momentum. It happens because, after a period of high birth rates, there are very large numbers of young people who are just reaching the age when they start their own families. Even if each couple has only two children, the total number of births stays high for a generation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Some geographers have added a fifth stage, in which the birth rate falls below the death rate and the population starts to shrink. Japan is the clearest example. Its population has been falling since around 2010, and a growing proportion of its people are over sixty-five, which creates serious challenges for healthcare, pensions and the labour market.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So, how useful is the model? It certainly describes the history of many countries quite well, but it has been criticised in several ways. First, it was based on European experience, and it assumes that other countries will follow the same path, which isn't necessarily true. Second, the speed of change has varied enormously. In parts of East Asia, the transition happened much more quickly than in Europe. In South Korea, for instance, the average woman had around six children in 1960, but by the mid nineteen-eighties, fertility had fallen below replacement level. Today, South Korea has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And third, and this leads into next week's topic, the model largely ignores migration. In many countries today, immigration has become the main source of population growth, and in some regions emigration has been the main cause of decline. We'll look at that next week.

readingPassages.title: Ellis Island: gateway to America
paragraphs: For more than sixty years, a small island in New York Harbor was the first piece of American soil that millions of immigrants ever stood on. Between 1892 and 1954, around twelve million people passed through the immigration station on Ellis Island, within sight of the Statue of Liberty. For most of them, the experience lasted only a few hours, but it became one of the defining moments of their lives, and the island has since become a powerful symbol of the United States as a nation of immigrants.

Before Ellis Island opened, immigration to New York was managed not by the national government but by New York State, which ran a reception centre called Castle Garden at the southern tip of Manhattan. By the late 1880s, the system was struggling to cope with the growing number of arrivals, and there were frequent complaints of corruption, with newcomers being cheated by dishonest money changers and agents. In 1890, the federal government took control of immigration and chose Ellis Island as the site of a new station. The island was so small that it had to be enlarged with landfill to several times its original size.

The station opened on 1 January 1892. The first immigrant to be registered was Annie Moore, a teenage girl from County Cork in Ireland, who had travelled with her two younger brothers to join their parents in New York. However, the original wooden buildings did not last long. In June 1897, a fire destroyed them, along with many immigration records dating back several decades. They were replaced by a fireproof building of brick and limestone, which opened in December 1900 and still stands today.

Not every passenger had to visit the island. First- and second-class passengers were usually inspected briefly on board their ship and allowed to go straight ashore, on the assumption that people who could afford expensive tickets were unlikely to become a burden on the state. It was the much larger number of third-class, or steerage, passengers who were taken by ferry to Ellis Island. The volume of traffic was enormous. In 1907, the busiest year in the station's history, more than a million immigrants arrived, and on one day in April of that year, over eleven thousand people were processed.

The inspection began before most immigrants realised it. As they climbed the stairs to the vast Registry Room, doctors watched them carefully, looking for signs of illness or disability. Anyone who seemed unwell had a letter marked on their clothing in chalk: 'H' for suspected heart problems, for example, or 'E' for the eyes. One of the most feared tests was the examination for trachoma, a contagious eye disease, in which doctors turned back the eyelids using a small hook. Those who were marked were taken aside for a more detailed examination, and some were sent to the island's hospital.

Next came the legal inspection. An inspector, often assisted by an interpreter, asked each immigrant around thirty questions, including their name, occupation, destination and how much money they had. The answers were checked against the ship's manifest, the passenger list that had been drawn up at the port of departure. A popular story claims that officials frequently changed immigrants' surnames at this stage, giving them simpler, more 'American' names. Historians have found no evidence for this. Inspectors worked from the lists prepared in Europe, and name changes usually happened later, when immigrants or their children chose to adapt their names themselves.

For the great majority, the process ended well. Only about two per cent of those who arrived were refused entry, most commonly because of serious contagious disease or because officials believed they would be unable to support themselves. Nevertheless, for families separated by such decisions, the island earned a painful nickname: the 'Island of Tears'. From the 1920s, however, its role changed. New laws, especially the Immigration Act of 1924, introduced strict quotas that sharply reduced immigration, particularly from southern and eastern Europe. Inspections were increasingly carried out at American consulates abroad, and Ellis Island was used mainly for detention and deportation until it closed in November 1954.

For many years after its closure, the buildings were abandoned and fell into ruin. In 1965, the island was made part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument, and after a major restoration, the main building reopened as a museum of immigration in 1990. Today, it attracts millions of visitors, many of whom come to search for their own ancestors in the passenger records. It is often estimated that around four in ten Americans have at least one ancestor who entered the country through Ellis Island.

readingPassages.title: Why people move
paragraphs: According to the United Nations, around 281 million people were living outside their country of birth in 2020, roughly 3.6 per cent of the world's population. The figure has risen steadily for decades, and migration is rarely out of the news. Yet it is worth remembering that the vast majority of people never move abroad at all, and that far more people move within their own countries, usually from the countryside to cities, than across international borders. Explaining why some people move while most stay where they are has occupied geographers for well over a century.

One of the first serious attempts was made by Ernst Georg Ravenstein, a German-born geographer working in London, who studied British census data and published his 'laws of migration' in 1885. Ravenstein observed that most migrants travelled only short distances, and that migration often happened in steps, with people moving from villages to small towns and later to large cities. He noted that each flow of migrants tended to produce a smaller counter-flow in the opposite direction, and that large towns grew more through migration than through births. Many of his observations still hold remarkably well today.

In 1966, the American sociologist Everett Lee proposed a more general framework. Migration, he argued, is influenced by factors at the place of origin, such as unemployment or conflict, which 'push' people away, and by factors at the destination, such as jobs or safety, which 'pull' them towards it. Crucially, Lee added that between the two lie 'intervening obstacles', including distance, cost and immigration laws, and that personal circumstances, such as age, family ties and attitudes to risk, determine how each individual responds. The same conditions might drive one person to leave while another stays.

Economists have traditionally explained migration as the result of individual decisions: people move when the wages they expect to earn elsewhere outweigh the costs of moving. In the 1980s, however, economists such as Oded Stark proposed what became known as the new economics of labour migration. In this view, migration is often a decision taken by a household rather than an individual. A family in a rural area, for example, may send one member to work in a city or abroad, not only to increase its income, but to reduce risk. If the harvest fails, the money sent home will help the family to survive.

That money, known as remittances, has become one of the most important financial flows in the world. The World Bank estimates that migrants sent more than six hundred billion dollars to low- and middle-income countries in 2023, considerably more than these countries received in official development aid. In some smaller economies, remittances are equivalent to a fifth or more of national income. Sending money is still expensive, however, with fees averaging around six per cent of the amount sent, and one of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals is to reduce this to below three per cent.

A less obvious finding is that the poorest people rarely migrate internationally. Moving abroad requires money for travel, documents and the period before finding work, as well as education and contacts. As a result, when poor countries begin to develop, emigration often increases rather than falls, at least for a time, because more people can afford to leave. Only when incomes reach a much higher level does emigration usually decline. This pattern, sometimes called the 'migration hump', suggests that development aid is unlikely to reduce migration in the short term, despite what some politicians claim.

Once a migration flow has begun, it often continues because of social networks. Migrants who have settled in a new country can provide information, accommodation and help in finding work to relatives and friends who follow them, reducing both the cost and the risk of moving. This process, known as chain migration, helps to explain why migrants from a particular village or region are often concentrated in particular cities or even particular streets abroad, and why migration flows can continue long after the original economic reasons have disappeared.

Increasingly, researchers are also asking how climate change will affect migration. Droughts, floods and rising sea levels can destroy livelihoods, and a 2021 World Bank report projected that, without strong action, up to 216 million people could be forced to move within their own countries by 2050 because of climate-related pressures. Most experts stress, however, that environmental change rarely acts alone. It interacts with poverty, conflict and government policy, and most people affected by disasters move only short distances, often temporarily. Ravenstein, it seems, would not have been surprised.

readingPassages.title: Between two worlds
paragraphs: For most people, the question 'Where are you from?' has a simple answer. For millions of migrants and their children, it does not. Someone born in Marseille to Algerian parents, or raised in Toronto by a Filipino mother and an Irish father, may feel that a single answer would be incomplete, or even untrue. How people come to understand who they are when they belong to more than one culture is one of the central questions in the study of migration, and the answers researchers have given have changed considerably over the past century.

For much of the twentieth century, the dominant assumption, particularly in the United States, was that immigrants would gradually assimilate. The popular image was the 'melting pot', a phrase made famous by Israel Zangwill's play of that name, first performed in 1908, in which people of different origins were imagined dissolving into a new, shared national identity. On this view, the loss of a heritage language and customs over two or three generations was not only inevitable but desirable, a sign of successful adjustment to a new home.

From the 1970s onwards, the Canadian psychologist John Berry offered a more complex picture. He suggested that people living between cultures face two separate questions: to what extent do they wish to maintain their heritage culture, and to what extent do they wish to take part in the wider society? The combination of answers produces four strategies. Assimilation means giving up one's original culture for the new one; separation means holding on to the original culture while avoiding contact with the wider society; integration means maintaining both; and marginalisation describes people who have lost their connection with their original culture without finding a place in the new one.

Much research has supported the value of integration. A large international study led by Berry and his colleagues, published in 2006, examined more than five thousand immigrant adolescents in thirteen countries. Young people who were involved in both their heritage culture and the national culture generally showed the best psychological well-being and adjusted best at school, while those with no clear attachment to either did worst. Berry himself stressed, however, that integration can only be chosen freely when the receiving society is open to cultural diversity. In my view, this point is too often forgotten: migrants cannot integrate into a society that refuses to accept them.

Language is often where the tension is felt most sharply. The sociolinguist Joshua Fishman, who spent much of his career studying minority languages, described a pattern that has been observed in many immigrant communities in the United States: the first generation speaks the heritage language, the second generation understands it but often prefers English, and by the third generation it has largely been lost. Many grandparents and grandchildren today cannot hold a real conversation. I believe this loss is rarely chosen deliberately; it happens quietly, through the pressures of school, friendship and work.

Some people grow up not between two cultures but among several. In the 1950s, the American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem, who had lived in India with her family, introduced the term 'third culture kids' to describe children who spend a significant part of their childhood outside their parents' home culture. Such children often develop a 'third culture' made up of elements of both, and frequently say that they feel at home everywhere and nowhere. Many adapt easily to new places, but some describe a lasting sense of restlessness and difficulty answering the simple question of where home is.

Theorists of identity have pushed the argument further. The cultural theorist Stuart Hall argued in 1990 that cultural identity is a matter of 'becoming' as well as 'being': something that is constantly produced and transformed, rather than a fixed essence inherited from the past. Even national identities, the political scientist Benedict Anderson famously suggested, are 'imagined communities', since the members of a nation will never meet most of their fellow members, yet feel connected to them. If identities are constructed rather than given, then there is nothing unnatural about building one from more than one source.

None of this means that mixed identities are always comfortable. Second-generation migrants frequently report being seen as foreign in the country of their birth and as foreign again when they visit their parents' homeland. Yet I would argue that the problem lies less in the individuals themselves than in other people's expectations that identity should be single and simple. A person who is both Algerian and French is not half of each, but wholly both. In my view, the sooner societies accept this, the easier it will be for millions of people to answer the question 'Where are you from?' honestly.

listeningParts.title: Joining a product-testing panel
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a market research company to sign up as a product tester.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Brightside Research, Sophie speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I heard an advert on the radio about joining a consumer panel and testing new products. Is that you?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, that's us. We run tasting and testing sessions for food and household companies who want feedback on new products before they go on sale. I can explain how it works and take a few details, if you like.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That would be great.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: So, there are two ways of taking part. The first is online surveys, which you can do at home whenever you like. Those take about twenty minutes and pay fifteen pounds each. The second is our in-person sessions, where you come to our testing centre and try products while our researchers observe. Those last around ninety minutes, and they pay twenty-five pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I think I'd be more interested in the in-person ones. How is the money paid?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We don't pay cash, I'm afraid. Everyone receives shopping vouchers, which you can use in most high street stores. They're emailed to you within a week of the session.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. And where's the testing centre?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We're on the second floor of Carlton House, which is the tall glass building opposite the cathedral. There's no parking at the building itself, but there's a multi-storey car park about two minutes' walk away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, I know where that is. How many people are there in each session?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Usually between eight and twelve, but you each have your own small booth, so you don't talk to each other during the test. That way, nobody's opinion is influenced by anyone else's. Shall I take your details now?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, please.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Could I have your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Marcus Whitlow. That's W-H-I-T-L-O-W.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your age, Mr Whitlow? We ask because many companies want feedback from particular age groups.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm thirty-four. My wife's thirty-one, actually, and she might want to join too, but she can ring you herself.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. And what's your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Twenty-seven Elmwood Road, in Ashford. Elmwood is spelt as it sounds, E-L-M-W-O-O-D.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And what do you do for a living?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm a nurse at the general hospital, so I work shifts.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's useful to know, because sessions run at different times of day. Which days are usually best for you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My shifts change every month, but I'm almost never working on Thursdays, so Thursday would be the safest choice.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thursday, then. Now, we have several categories of product. Are there any you'd particularly like to test?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What sort of things are there?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: At the moment, we're doing a lot of work on breakfast cereals, soft drinks, cleaning products and pet food. Don't worry, you don't have to taste the pet food! For that one, we just ask people to look at the packaging and tell us what they think.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ha! I think I'd go for cereals. I eat them every morning, so I'd have plenty to say.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Perfect, cereals it is. Do you have any food allergies or follow a special diet?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, nothing like that.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good. Just one more thing about the sessions themselves. Because many of the tests involve tasting and smelling, we ask people not to smoke or drink coffee for an hour beforehand. And please don't wear perfume or aftershave on the day, as strong smells can affect other people's results too.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Right, no aftershave. That's no problem.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: And finally, you said you heard about us on the radio?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, on the local station, during the traffic news on my way to work.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. I'll email you a short questionnaire about your shopping habits this afternoon, and once you've completed it, we'll invite you to your first session, probably within the next three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks very much. I'm looking forward to it.

listeningParts.title: Marketing advice for market traders
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a food and craft market gives a talk to new stallholders.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome. I'm Rachel Doyle, the manager here at Riverside Market, and I'm delighted that so many new traders are joining us this season. Tonight, I'd like to share some advice about marketing your stall, because, as our experienced traders will tell you, good products alone aren't enough. You need people to notice you, to stop, and then to come back.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: First, a little about our customers. Last year, we carried out a survey of around nine hundred visitors. The market attracts about six thousand people on a typical Saturday, but only around half that number on Sundays. What surprised us was that more than sixty per cent of visitors said they hadn't planned to buy anything in particular. They came for the atmosphere, to meet friends or to have lunch. In other words, most of your sales will come from people who simply notice something as they walk past. So the way your stall looks really matters.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Shoppers make up their minds very quickly, and you've got only a few seconds to catch their eye. My first piece of advice is to think about height. A table with everything laid flat is very hard to see from a distance, especially when the market is crowded. Use boxes, shelves or baskets to raise some of your products to eye level. And keep your display full. A half-empty table suggests that the best things have already gone, or that business isn't going well.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Second, show your prices clearly. Many new traders don't like doing this, because they worry that people will be put off. In fact, our survey found the opposite: a lot of shoppers, particularly younger ones, said they would rather walk away than ask how much something cost, because they found asking embarrassing.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Third, if you sell food, let people taste it. Free samples are one of the most effective ways of turning a passer-by into a customer. But keep the pieces small, and always have someone standing behind the samples to chat to people. Samples left on a plate with nobody there don't sell nearly as well.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now let me say a few words about different ways of promoting yourselves. Lots of you have asked about social media. It costs nothing except time, and it's excellent for keeping in touch with regular customers, for example by posting what you'll be bringing that weekend. However, don't expect it to bring in large numbers of new people quickly. It usually takes months to build up a real following.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Loyalty cards, where customers get a stamp each time they buy something and a free item after, say, eight purchases, work very well for coffee and bakery stalls, where people buy often. They're much less useful if you sell things people only buy once or twice a year, like furniture or rugs.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Leaflets are something I'd generally advise against. They're expensive to print, and most of them end up in the recycling bin within minutes. Business cards are a much better idea, especially if you take orders for special items like birthday cakes.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Then there's the market's own newsletter, which goes out by email every Thursday to about four thousand subscribers. Every trader can be featured once a season, free of charge, but places are limited, so you'll need to book a slot with my assistant, Owen, well in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, there are our special events. Each month, we hold a themed weekend, such as the chilli festival in August or the children's craft day in October. Taking part does involve extra work beforehand, since you may need to create special products or stay later than usual, but traders tell us these weekends are often their busiest of the whole year.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, that's enough from me. There's tea and coffee at the back of the hall, and I'll be around for the next hour to answer any questions you have.

listeningParts.title: An experiment on packaging
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two business students, Amira and Josh, discuss their packaging experiment with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Amira, Josh, you've finished collecting the data for your packaging experiment. Tell me how it went.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: It went quite well. Just to remind you, we wanted to find out whether the design of a package changes how people judge the product inside, even when the product itself is exactly the same.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We bought one brand of plain chocolate biscuits and put them into two different packets that we designed ourselves. One was plain white with black writing, and the other was bright red and gold, with a photo of the biscuits and the words 'luxury recipe'.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how many participants did you have?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Sixty in the end. We'd hoped for eighty, but it was exam season, and quite a lot of students who'd signed up didn't turn up.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sixty is acceptable for a project of this size, although you should mention the smaller sample as a limitation. How did you find your volunteers in the first place?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We put up posters in the library and the student union, and we offered everyone a free coffee voucher for taking part. That worked quite well, but it does mean that almost all of our participants were students between eighteen and twenty-five.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's worth noting too, since students may not shop in the same way as older consumers. How did you organise the tasting itself?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Half the participants tasted biscuits from the white packet and half from the red one. They didn't know there was another version. Then they rated the biscuits on a scale from one to ten for taste and quality, and told us how much they'd be willing to pay for a packet.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the results?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: The red and gold packet did better on every measure. The average taste score was 7.2, compared with 5.9 for the white packet. But the biggest difference was in the price people would pay. On average, they said they'd pay almost forty per cent more for the biscuits in the luxury packet.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a striking result. Were you surprised?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Not by the direction, because previous research has found similar effects, but we were surprised by how large the difference was. Several people in the white-packet group even described the biscuits as dry, which nobody said about the others.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you check whether the colour itself mattered, or was it the photograph and the words?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: That's the main weakness, I think. We changed three things at once: the colour, the image and the description. So we can't say which of them caused the difference.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. In a follow-up study, you'd need to change one feature at a time. That's something to put in your discussion section. What else did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: At the end, we asked people whether they thought the packaging had influenced their ratings. Almost everyone said no. They believed they were judging only the taste.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Which fits a lot of research on consumer behaviour. People are often unaware of what influences their choices. Did you collect any information about the participants themselves?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Just age and gender, and how often they buy biscuits. We'd planned to compare men and women, but the groups were too small to show anything meaningful.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then I'd leave that out, or mention it only briefly. Now, how are you going to present the results?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We thought a bar chart would be clearest, with the two packets side by side for each measure.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And make sure you include the standard deviations, not just the averages, so that readers can see how much the ratings varied. Also, think about the ethics. Did you tell participants afterwards what the study was really about?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Yes, we explained it to everyone once they'd finished, and gave them the chance to withdraw their data. Nobody did.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. You should describe that procedure clearly in your methods section, because the examiners will look for it. Have you started reading for the literature review yet?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Yes, we've found several studies on colour and taste, mostly with drinks rather than food. We're planning to include about fifteen sources.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds about right. When's your presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: On the fourteenth of next month.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then please send me a draft of your slides a week before, and we can go through them together.

listeningParts.title: The origins of branding and advertising
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a history of marketing course on how branding and advertising developed before the age of television.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today, in our course on the history of marketing, I want to go back to the very beginnings of branding and advertising, and trace how they developed up to the arrival of television. Many people assume that advertising is a modern invention, but as we'll see, its roots go back a very long way.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with the word brand itself. It comes from an Old Norse word meaning 'to burn', and it originally referred to the practice of marking cattle with a hot iron to show who owned them. The idea of a mark that identifies the owner or maker of something is, of course, the basic idea behind branding today. Craftspeople in the ancient world did something similar. Potters in the Roman Empire, for example, often stamped their names on the bottom of oil lamps and other goods, and archaeologists have found products carrying the same maker's mark across large parts of the empire.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Advertising, too, existed in the ancient world. In the Roman town of Pompeii, which was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD, archaeologists found painted notices on walls, announcing everything from gladiator shows to political candidates and rooms to rent.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In medieval Europe, most people couldn't read, so shopkeepers and innkeepers relied on pictures rather than words. A shoemaker might hang up a sign showing a boot, and an inn might use the image of an animal, which is one reason why so many British pubs still have names like the Red Lion or the White Horse.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The real turning point came with the printing press, which Johannes Gutenberg introduced to Europe in the fifteenth century. Printing made it possible to produce handbills and posters cheaply and in large numbers, and by the seventeenth century, newspapers in England were carrying advertisements for products such as coffee, tea and books.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the eighteenth century, one of the most inventive marketers was the English potter Josiah Wedgwood. When Queen Charlotte ordered a tea set from him, he was allowed to call his cream-coloured pottery Queen's Ware, and he used this royal connection to attract wealthy customers. He also opened elegant showrooms in London, where people could see his products beautifully displayed, and he produced illustrated catalogues, so that customers far away could order by post.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The nineteenth century brought industrialisation and mass production. For the first time, identical goods could be made in huge quantities and transported by rail across whole countries. Manufacturers needed a way to persuade shoppers to choose their product rather than an almost identical one made by a competitor, and so the modern brand was born. Packaging played a key role. Instead of buying flour or soap loose, weighed out by a shopkeeper, customers began to buy goods in sealed, branded packets, which promised the same quality every time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Legal protection followed. In Britain, the Trade Marks Registration Act came into force in 1876, and the first mark to be registered was the red triangle of the Bass brewery, which is still in use today.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At the same time, advertising was becoming more sophisticated. The soap company Pears, under Thomas Barratt, is often described as a pioneer. Barratt bought a painting by the famous artist John Everett Millais, showing a little boy blowing bubbles, and used it in advertisements for the soap. Millais was reportedly unhappy that his work was being used to sell a product, but the campaign was enormously successful, and it blurred the line between art and advertising.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, new technologies opened up new possibilities. Radio spread rapidly in the 1920s and 1930s, and in the United States, companies sponsored entire programmes. Daytime dramas aimed at women listening at home were frequently sponsored by manufacturers of soap and washing powder, which is why they became known as soap operas, a name that has stayed with us.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then came television. The first official television commercial in the United States was broadcast in New York in 1941. It was for Bulova watches, it was shown just before a baseball game, and it lasted only a few seconds. In Britain, television advertising began in 1955, with the launch of the commercial channel ITV, and the first advertisement shown was for a brand of toothpaste.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What's striking is that many of the techniques used in these early campaigns, such as royal or celebrity endorsement, attractive packaging and linking a product with a desirable lifestyle, are still at the heart of advertising today. Next week, we'll look at how the internet has changed things, and whether it has really changed them as much as people think.
