readingPassages.title: The self-service revolution
paragraphs: Walk into almost any supermarket in the world today and the routine is the same. Shoppers take a trolley or a basket, wander along aisles lined with thousands of products, choose what they want and pay at a checkout on the way out. It all seems so natural that it is easy to forget how recent this way of shopping is. For most of history, buying food involved a conversation with a shopkeeper, and the idea of customers simply helping themselves would have seemed strange, and possibly even risky.

In a typical grocery store of the late nineteenth century, goods were kept behind a long counter. Customers waited their turn, then told an assistant what they needed or handed over a written list. The assistant fetched each item from the shelves, weighed out loose goods such as sugar, flour and tea, and wrapped them in paper. Many stores also allowed regular customers to buy on credit and pay at the end of the week or month, and some delivered orders to people's homes. The system was personal, but it was also slow and required a large number of staff, which meant that prices were often higher than they needed to be.

The man usually credited with changing this was Clarence Saunders, a grocer from Memphis, Tennessee. In 1916, he opened a store called Piggly Wiggly, in which customers collected a basket at the entrance and followed a set route past shelves of goods, picking out what they wanted themselves. Every item had its price clearly marked, and customers paid at a cashier's desk by the exit. Because the store needed far fewer employees, Saunders could sell at lower prices than his rivals. He patented the design of his store in 1917, and Piggly Wiggly expanded rapidly, with hundreds of branches opening across the United States within a few years. Saunders never gave a clear explanation of the unusual name; when asked, he is said to have replied only that it would make people ask exactly that question.

Self-service changed not only how stores operated but also how products were sold. In a traditional shop, the assistant could recommend one brand rather than another, and many customers relied on that advice. Once shoppers were choosing for themselves, the package on the shelf had to do that job instead. Manufacturers responded by investing in eye-catching designs and memorable brand names, and by advertising heavily so that shoppers would already know what they were looking for when they entered the store. Packaging came to be described as a 'silent salesman', and it has remained one of the most important tools of marketing ever since.

The next development was size. Early self-service stores were relatively small, but in 1930, during the Great Depression, a former grocery manager named Michael Cullen opened King Kullen in the New York borough of Queens. It was far larger than an ordinary grocery, sold a wide range of food under one roof, offered car parking and kept its prices low by buying in very large quantities. Many historians regard it as the first true supermarket. The model suited a population that increasingly owned cars and refrigerators, which allowed families to drive to a store once a week and buy a large amount of food at a time.

Larger shops created a new problem: customers could buy only as much as they could carry in a basket. In 1937, Sylvan Goldman, who owned a chain of supermarkets in Oklahoma City, came up with a solution after watching shoppers struggle with heavy baskets. He attached wheels and two baskets to the frame of a folding chair, creating the first shopping trolley. At first, shoppers were reluctant to use it. Many men felt that pushing a cart made them look weak, while many women said that it reminded them of pushing a pram. Goldman reportedly hired models to push trolleys around his stores until the idea caught on, and within a few years trolleys were common across the country.

Outside the United States, self-service spread more slowly. In Britain, the change came mainly after the Second World War, and it was held back for several years by food rationing, which did not end completely until 1954. Many shoppers were suspicious at first, and some shopkeepers feared that customers would steal goods if they were allowed to handle them freely. By the 1960s, however, supermarkets were opening in towns across the country, and many small independent grocers were beginning to disappear.

Technology has continued to reshape the experience. On 26 June 1974, a packet of chewing gum became the first product to be sold using a barcode scanner, at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio. Barcodes made checkouts faster and gave stores detailed information about which products were selling and when. Today, self-checkout machines and online ordering mean that some customers can complete their entire weekly shop without speaking to a single member of staff. In a sense, this is the logical conclusion of the idea that Saunders introduced more than a century ago, when he first invited customers to help themselves.

readingPassages.title: Hidden in plain sight: product placement
paragraphs: When a character in a film drinks a particular brand of cola, drives a recognisable car or checks the time on a famous make of watch, the choice is often not accidental. Product placement, the practice of including branded products in films, television programmes and other entertainment in exchange for money or other benefits, has become a significant part of the marketing industry. Unlike traditional advertisements, which interrupt a programme and are clearly identified as advertising, placed products appear within the story itself, where viewers may barely notice them.

The practice is far from new. In the early decades of cinema and radio, manufacturers frequently supplied products to producers or sponsored entire programmes, and the boundary between entertainment and promotion was often unclear. For much of the twentieth century, however, product placement in films was arranged informally, usually through personal contacts between studios and companies, and it attracted relatively little public attention or academic study.

That changed in 1982 with Steven Spielberg's film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial. In one well-known scene, a boy uses a trail of sweets to lure the alien into his house. The film-makers had reportedly approached the makers of M&M's first, but the company turned down the opportunity, and the sweets that appeared on screen were Reese's Pieces, made by Hershey. After the film was released, sales of Reese's Pieces rose dramatically. The case convinced many companies that appearing in a successful film could be worth far more than a conventional advertising campaign, and specialist agencies soon appeared to match brands with suitable films. Product placement had become a recognised business rather than an informal favour.

The arrangements involved are not always simple cash payments. In many cases, a company supplies products free of charge, such as cars, clothes or computers, which reduces the cost of making a film. In others, the brand agrees to spend money promoting the film in its own advertising, so that both partners benefit from the publicity. Major film series, such as the James Bond films, have attracted agreements reportedly worth tens of millions of dollars, which can cover a considerable share of the production budget. For the film-makers, such deals reduce financial risk; for the brands, they offer an association with characters whom audiences already admire.

Why does product placement work? One explanation lies in what psychologists call the mere exposure effect: people tend to develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them. Seeing a brand repeatedly, even without paying much attention to it, may make it feel more trustworthy when shoppers later come across it in a store. Placement may also benefit from association. When a product is used by an admired character in an exciting or glamorous situation, some of that character's appeal may transfer to the brand itself.

However, the effects are not always positive. Several studies have found that placements which are very prominent, for example when a character mentions a brand by name and praises it, are remembered better by viewers but may also be disliked, particularly by those who feel that a programme they enjoy is being used to sell to them. Subtle placements, by contrast, are less likely to be noticed but also less likely to cause irritation. For marketers, finding the right balance between being seen and being resented is a constant challenge.

Because viewers may not realise that they are being influenced, product placement has long concerned regulators. In the United Kingdom, paid product placement was not permitted on television until 2011. Under the rules introduced then, programmes containing paid placement must display a small 'P' symbol, placement is not allowed in news or children's programmes, and certain products, such as cigarettes and prescription medicines, may not be placed at all. Some critics argue that such rules do little to help viewers, since many people are unaware of what the symbol means.

New technology is now changing the practice once again. With the rise of streaming services, many of which carry no advertisements, and with viewers increasingly able to skip commercials, placement offers brands a way to reach audiences who avoid traditional advertising. Digital techniques also make it possible to insert products into scenes after filming has finished, so that a bottle on a kitchen table, or a poster on a wall, can show different brands to viewers in different countries, or be updated years after a programme was first broadcast. For audiences, the line between story and advertisement may become even harder to see, and the question of how clearly such placements should be identified is likely to become more pressing.

readingPassages.title: Should advertising to children be restricted?
paragraphs: Children have always been a target for marketers, but the scale of the advertising aimed at them has grown enormously. Today's children encounter commercial messages not only on television but also in games, videos, apps and social media, often in forms that are difficult to distinguish from entertainment. Governments around the world have responded in very different ways, and the debate over whether, and how, children should be protected from advertising shows no sign of being settled. At its heart lies a question about whether children can be treated as consumers in the same way as adults.

The central argument for restriction rests on research into how children understand advertising. Young children can recognise an advertisement from an early age, but recognising an advertisement is not the same as understanding its purpose. A report published by the American Psychological Association in 2004 concluded that children under about eight years old generally do not understand that advertisements are designed to persuade them, and tend to accept advertisers' claims as true. If this is correct, then advertising to young children is, its critics argue, fundamentally unfair.

Some places have acted on this argument. In the Canadian province of Quebec, the Consumer Protection Act has banned commercial advertising directed at children under thirteen since 1980. Sweden went further than most of Europe in 1991, banning television advertisements aimed at children under twelve. However, the Swedish ban was partly undermined by satellite channels broadcasting into Sweden from other countries, which were not bound by Swedish law. This illustrates a recurring difficulty: national rules are hard to enforce in a global media environment.

In the United States, attempts at regulation have been less successful. In the late 1970s, the Federal Trade Commission proposed restricting television advertising to young children, but the plan was abandoned after strong opposition from the advertising and food industries and from members of Congress. Instead, the country has relied largely on self-regulation. The Children's Advertising Review Unit, established by the advertising industry in 1974, sets voluntary guidelines, but critics question how effective a system run by the industry itself can be.

Much recent attention has focused on food. Rising rates of childhood obesity have led many governments to examine the marketing of products high in sugar, salt and fat. In the United Kingdom, advertisements for such foods were banned around children's television programmes from 2007. Chile introduced one of the world's strictest laws in 2016, requiring black warning labels on unhealthy foods and banning their marketing to children under fourteen. Cartoon characters were removed from cereal packets, and toys could no longer be sold with sweets. Studies since then have found significant falls in purchases of sugary drinks, although it is difficult to separate the effect of the marketing rules from that of the warning labels.

Opponents of restrictions raise several objections. Advertisers argue that they have a right to promote legal products, and that responsibility for what children watch and eat lies with their parents. Broadcasters point out that advertising revenue pays for children's programmes, and warn that bans could reduce the quality and quantity of content made for young audiences. Others note that obesity has many causes, including a lack of exercise and family eating habits, and that advertising is only one factor among many. Some also argue that children need to learn to deal with advertising, and that keeping them away from it entirely may leave them less prepared as adults.

In my view, the argument that parents alone should be responsible is not convincing. Parents cannot be present every time a child picks up a tablet, and much of today's marketing is designed precisely to reach children directly, without passing through their parents at all. Nor do I accept that the loss of advertising revenue is a decisive objection; public broadcasters in several countries make excellent children's programmes without any advertising whatsoever. Nevertheless, I recognise that complete bans are a blunt instrument, and that the evidence for their effect on children's health is still developing.

What seems clear is that rules designed for television are no longer sufficient. Online, advertisements can be tailored to individual children using data about their behaviour, and influencers who are paid to promote products may appear to their young followers simply as friends. Any effective approach will need to cover these new forms of marketing as well as the old ones. Ultimately, I believe that a society which accepts that children need protection from many other forms of exploitation should be willing to extend that protection to the commercial pressures they face every day.

listeningParts.title: Enrolling in a robotics holiday club
listeningParts.contextDescription: A mother phones a children's robotics club to book a summer course for her son.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Kingsley Robotics Club, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I'm ringing about your summer holiday courses. My son is absolutely obsessed with building things at the moment, and a friend of mine said her daughter went to one of your courses last year and loved it.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's great to hear. We run two courses for children over the summer, depending on their age. Can I ask how old your son is?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He's eleven. He'll be twelve in October.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Right. So our Junior Builders course is for seven- to nine-year-olds, and that's mostly about building simple moving models with motors and gears. For his age, the better option would be Code Explorers, which is for ten- to thirteen-year-olds. On that course, children build a small wheeled robot from a kit and then learn to program it so that it can follow a line, avoid obstacles and respond to sounds.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That sounds perfect. He's done a bit of coding at school, but nothing with real machines. Does he need any experience?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Not at all. Most children are complete beginners. The instructors are university engineering students, and they're very good at explaining things step by step. We also keep the groups small, with no more than eight children per instructor.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Good. And when do the courses run?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Each course lasts one week, Monday to Friday. Code Explorers runs four times over the summer. I'm afraid the week beginning the twenty-eighth of July is already full, but we still have places in the week beginning the fourth of August, and in the last two weeks of August.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: We're away at the end of August, so the fourth of August would be best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. Now, I should mention that during the summer we don't use our usual building in Kingsley, because it's being repainted. The courses will be held at Ashford Primary School, on Mill Lane. We'll be using the school library, which has plenty of space and good internet access.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I know Ashford, it's not far from us. What about the cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full price for the week is one hundred and seventy-five pounds. If you were a member of the club, it would be one hundred and fifty, but membership is only for children who come to our weekly Saturday sessions during term time. To hold the place, we ask for a deposit of thirty pounds, and the rest is due two weeks before the course starts.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Fine. Does that include the robot kit?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, all the equipment is included, and at the end of the week each child takes their robot home, so they can carry on programming it. Children just need to bring a packed lunch and a drink. Oh, and on Wednesday afternoon we go outside to the school field to fly small drones, so they should bring a sun hat, in case it's hot.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He'll love the drones. What time does it start and finish?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Doors open at a quarter to nine, and sessions start at nine. From Monday to Thursday, pick-up is at quarter past four. On Friday, we finish a little earlier, at half past three, because there's a final competition, and parents are invited to come and watch the robots race around an obstacle course.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, that'll be fun. I'll try to get the afternoon off work.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Now, could I take some details? What's your son's name?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It's Toby Westacott. That's W-E-S-T-A-C-O-T-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know about his health?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He has asthma, but it's mild. He carries an inhaler with him, and he knows how to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's fine, I'll add a note to his form, and the instructors are all trained in first aid. Could I have a phone number for you, in case we need to contact you during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll email you a link so you can pay the deposit online, and a consent form for photographs. We sometimes put pictures of the robots on our website, but only with permission.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That's fine. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A new exhibition about robots
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum curator introduces a new exhibition about robots and artificial intelligence to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to the Northgate Science Museum. My name is Rachel Dumont, and I'm the curator of our new exhibition, Machines Like Us, which opened just last week. Before you go in, I'd like to give you a quick overview, so you can plan your visit and make sure you don't miss anything.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The exhibition took nearly three years to put together. Originally, we planned a small display about the history of factory robots, but as we started talking to researchers, we realised that what visitors really wanted to know was how robots and artificial intelligence are going to affect their everyday lives. So the focus changed, and the exhibition became much bigger. It now fills the whole of the second floor.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The first thing I'd like to stress is that this isn't an exhibition where you just look at objects behind glass. Most of the robots here are working machines, and many of them are interactive. You'll be able to talk to them, play games with them and, in some cases, teach them to do simple tasks. Because of that, some of the displays can get very busy, especially at weekends, so I'd recommend visiting the most popular galleries first.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Let me take you through the galleries in order. The first gallery is called Ancestors. It looks at the long history of machines that imitate living things, from clockwork figures made in the eighteenth century to the first industrial robots of the 1960s. The star object here is a beautiful mechanical writer, a doll that can write short messages with a real pen. It's very delicate, so it's only switched on twice a day, at eleven and at three. If you want to see it move, make sure you're there at the right time.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The second gallery is The Factory Floor. Here you'll find a full-sized robot arm of the kind used in car factories. It's been programmed to sort coloured blocks, and you can challenge it to a race to see who's faster. I should warn you that almost nobody wins. For safety reasons, the arm is behind a transparent screen, and children under eight must be accompanied by an adult in this area.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Next comes the gallery called At Home. This one is about robots that people actually live with, such as robot vacuum cleaners and lawnmowers. What's interesting here is that it shows how often these machines fail. There's a fun section where you can watch videos of robots getting stuck under sofas or falling down stairs. It's a reminder that homes are much more difficult environments for robots than factories, because everything is constantly being moved around.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The fourth gallery, Caring Machines, looks at robots in hospitals and care homes. There's a robotic seal that's used to comfort elderly patients, and you're welcome to stroke it. We've also got a surgical robot, although it's not working, I'm afraid; it's a prototype that was donated by a hospital. Next to it, there's a short film in which surgeons explain how they control these machines from a console a few metres away from the patient.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The fifth gallery is called Thinking Machines, and it's about artificial intelligence. Rather than robots, it's mostly screens. You can play a game against a computer that learns from your moves, and try to tell the difference between poems written by people and poems written by software. Many visitors find that harder than they expect.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The final gallery, Tomorrow, is a little different. It doesn't have many objects. Instead, it asks you questions about the future, for example whether you'd trust a robot to look after a child, and you vote using a touch screen. The results are displayed on a large wall, so you can compare your answers with everyone else's. We're collecting these votes for a research project with the local university.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Just a couple of practical points before you go in. Photography is allowed everywhere except in Caring Machines, because the film there includes real patients. The café on the ground floor is open until four, and there's a shop next to the exit where you can buy simple robot kits. Okay, enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A project on robots in elderly care
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two social care students, Megan and Josh, discuss their research project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Megan, Josh. Come and sit down. So you wanted to talk about your project on robots in elderly care. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, we've done most of the reading, and last week we visited a care home that's been trying out a social robot for six months. We've got a lot of notes, but we're not sure how to organise the report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Let's start with the reading, then. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The most researched robot by far is PARO, the robotic seal that was developed in Japan. It responds to touch and to voices, and it moves its head and makes sounds a bit like a baby seal. There are quite a few studies of it being used with people with dementia.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do those studies show?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Some of them found that residents were calmer and less anxious after sessions with the robot, and that they talked to each other more. But a lot of the studies were quite small, and some were funded by people connected with the company, so we decided we couldn't rely on them too much.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a very sensible thing to notice. Make sure you say that in your literature review. What about the visit?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: That was really interesting. The home we went to is using a different kind of robot. It's about the size of a small child, it has a screen for a face, and it leads activities like quizzes, music sessions and gentle exercises. The manager told us they introduced it because they'd had problems recruiting enough staff, not to replace anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: And what surprised me was that the residents were much more positive about it than I'd expected. I thought older people might be suspicious of technology, but most of the ones we spoke to just found it fun. One woman said it was the only thing in the home that never got tired of her stories.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lovely quotation. Did you get permission to use it?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone we interviewed signed a consent form, and we're not using any real names.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what did the staff think?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Their views were more mixed. The activities coordinator liked it, because it meant she could spend more time with residents who needed one-to-one attention. But two of the care assistants were worried that the management might eventually use robots as an excuse to cut staff. And one nurse said that when the robot broke down for a week, some residents were quite upset, which made her wonder whether they were becoming too attached to it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a really important ethical question. In fact, I'd suggest you make ethics a separate section of the report, rather than mixing it in with the findings. Issues like attachment, privacy and whether it's honest to give someone with dementia a robot animal deserve proper discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Privacy came up too. The robot has a camera, and some families didn't like the idea that it might be recording their relatives.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did the home say what happens to the recordings?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The manager said the camera is only used to recognise faces, and nothing is stored. But she admitted that most families had never asked.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the structure. You could start with a short introduction explaining why this matters, for example the growing number of older people and the shortage of care workers in many countries. Then the literature review, then your method, then the findings from the visit, and then the ethics section. Finish with recommendations.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: How long should it be?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: The limit is four thousand words. Don't go over it, because you'll lose marks. And I'd like to see a draft of the literature review by Friday the fourteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We were also thinking of including some photographs of the robot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as no residents appear in them. Actually, a simple table comparing the different types of care robot would be more useful than photos. Put it in the appendix.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Great, thanks. That's really helpful.

listeningParts.title: The early history of artificial intelligence
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a computer science course on how the field of artificial intelligence developed in the twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to step back from the technical material and look at the history of artificial intelligence. It's a history full of big promises, bitter disappointments and surprising comebacks, and knowing it will help you judge some of the claims you hear about AI today.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A good place to start is 1950, when the British mathematician Alan Turing published a paper called 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. Turing thought that the question 'Can machines think?' was too vague to answer, so he replaced it with a test, which he called the imitation game. A human judge has a written conversation with two hidden partners, one a person and one a machine. If the judge can't reliably tell which is which, Turing argued, we have no good reason to deny that the machine is intelligent. We now call this the Turing test, and it's still discussed, although most researchers no longer think it's a useful goal.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The field got its name a few years later. In 1955, the computer scientist John McCarthy and three colleagues wrote a proposal for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States, and in it they used the phrase 'artificial intelligence'. The workshop took place in 1956, and it's usually seen as the birth of AI as a research field. The organisers were extremely optimistic. They believed that significant progress could be made on problems such as language and learning in a single summer.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For the next twenty years or so, most AI research was what we call symbolic. The idea was that intelligence consisted of manipulating symbols according to rules, so if you could write down the right rules, a computer could reason like a person. And there were some impressive early results. Programs were written that could prove mathematical theorems and play draughts. In the mid-1960s, Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT created a program called ELIZA, which imitated a therapist by turning the user's statements into questions. It was very simple, but some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed Weizenbaum.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, the early optimism didn't last. Problems that seemed easy, like understanding ordinary language or recognising objects, turned out to be extremely hard, and computers at the time were very slow and had tiny memories. In Britain, a government report written by the mathematician James Lighthill in 1973 concluded that AI had failed to achieve its grand aims, and funding was cut sharply. Similar cuts happened in the United States. This period of reduced funding and interest became known as the first AI winter.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the 1980s, interest returned, thanks largely to expert systems. These were programs that tried to capture the knowledge of human specialists, such as doctors or engineers, in the form of thousands of if-then rules. Some were commercially successful, but they were expensive to build and to update, and they were brittle: if they met a situation the rules didn't cover, they failed completely. By the late 1980s, the market had collapsed, and a second winter followed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, a different approach had been developing quietly. Instead of writing rules, researchers built neural networks, which are loosely inspired by the brain, and which learn patterns from examples. Frank Rosenblatt had built an early version, the perceptron, in the late 1950s, but for decades these networks were limited by a lack of data and computing power.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Two famous events showed how much things had changed. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue computer defeated the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a six-game match. Deep Blue mostly relied on enormous speed, examining millions of positions per second. Then, in 2012, a neural network won an image recognition competition by a huge margin, using powerful graphics processors originally designed for video games. That result convinced many researchers to switch to the approach now called deep learning. And in 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo program beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's best players of the board game Go, which had been considered far harder for computers than chess.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what's the lesson? Progress in AI hasn't been steady. It's come in waves, driven as much by data and hardware as by new ideas. Next week, we'll look at how modern language models work.

readingPassages.title: The chess-playing machine that fooled Europe
paragraphs: In 1770, at the imperial palace of Schönbrunn in Vienna, a civil servant named Wolfgang von Kempelen presented a remarkable invention to the Empress Maria Theresa and her court. It consisted of a large wooden cabinet, on top of which sat a life-sized figure of a man dressed in robes and a turban, holding a long pipe in one hand. Kempelen announced that this figure, which soon became known as the Turk, could play chess against any human opponent. To the astonishment of the audience, it did exactly that, moving the pieces with its mechanical arm and usually winning.

Kempelen took great care to persuade spectators that the machine was genuine. Before each game, he opened the doors of the cabinet one by one and held a candle behind them, so that the audience could see an elaborate collection of gears, wheels and levers inside. He then closed the doors, wound up the machine with a key and invited a volunteer to play. During the game, the figure would nod its head when it threatened its opponent's queen, and if a player attempted an illegal move, it would shake its head and move the piece back to its original square.

In reality, the Turk was an ingenious illusion. Hidden inside the cabinet was a skilled human chess player, who could slide from one section to another on a moving seat while the doors were being opened, so that he was never seen. The operator followed the game by watching small metal discs beneath the board, which were pulled upwards by magnets in the chess pieces above. He then controlled the figure's arm using a system of levers, and worked by the light of a candle. The machinery that the audience saw was largely there to distract them.

Curiously, Kempelen himself does not seem to have been particularly proud of the Turk. He regarded it as a clever entertainment rather than a serious achievement, and for long periods he refused to exhibit it, preferring to work on other projects, including a machine that could imitate human speech. However, in the early 1780s, he was persuaded to take the Turk on a tour of Europe, and it attracted large crowds in cities such as Paris and London. Wherever it went, writers and scientists published articles attempting to explain how it worked, although few came close to the truth.

After Kempelen's death in 1804, the Turk was bought by Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, a Bavarian musician and showman who is also remembered for producing and promoting the metronome. Maelzel made the act more theatrical and took the machine on further tours. In 1809, according to a famous account, the Turk played against Napoleon Bonaparte, who had occupied Vienna, and easily defeated him. Among the many people who saw the Turk in action was the English mathematician Charles Babbage, who later designed some of the earliest mechanical computers and who was fascinated by the question of whether a machine could really play chess.

In 1826, Maelzel took the Turk across the Atlantic to the United States, where it toured for more than a decade. There, it inspired one of the best-known attempts to expose it: an essay published in 1836 by the writer Edgar Allan Poe. Poe argued correctly that a human player must be hidden inside, partly because the machine did not always win, which he believed a true machine would. Some of his other reasoning, however, was mistaken.

After Maelzel died in 1838, the Turk passed through several owners and eventually ended up in a museum in Philadelphia. In 1854, a fire swept through the building and destroyed it. A few years later, the son of its last owner published a series of articles that finally revealed exactly how the illusion had been performed, ending more than eighty years of speculation.

Although the Turk was a fraud, its influence was real. It encouraged people to ask whether thinking could be mechanised, a question that would later become central to computer science. In the twentieth century, chess became a standard test for artificial intelligence, and in 1997 a real machine, IBM's Deep Blue, defeated the world champion. Even the Turk's name lives on: in 2005, the company Amazon launched a service called Mechanical Turk, through which businesses pay people to carry out small tasks, such as labelling images, that computers still find difficult. The name is an honest joke, since, like the original, the service relies on human intelligence hidden behind a machine.

readingPassages.title: Why robots struggle with the easy things
paragraphs: In 1961, a machine called Unimate began work at a General Motors car factory in New Jersey. It was a heavy hydraulic arm that lifted hot pieces of metal from a casting machine and stacked them, a dangerous job that had injured many workers. Unimate is generally regarded as the first industrial robot, and it was the product of a partnership between the inventor George Devol, who had patented the idea, and the engineer Joseph Engelberger, who turned it into a business. Within two decades, robot arms were welding, painting and assembling cars in factories across the world.

Today, the most automated economies have astonishing numbers of these machines. According to the International Federation of Robotics, South Korea has around one thousand industrial robots for every ten thousand manufacturing workers, and countries such as Singapore, China, Germany and Japan also have very high densities. Yet if you visit almost any factory, you will notice that robots are concentrated in certain kinds of work. They weld and paint with superhuman precision, but many apparently simple tasks, such as folding a towel, sorting a pile of mixed objects or plugging in a flexible cable, are still done by people.

Researchers noticed this puzzle decades ago. In the 1980s, scientists including Hans Moravec, Rodney Brooks and Marvin Minsky pointed out that the tasks people find difficult, such as playing chess or solving equations, are often relatively easy for computers, while those that even a small child performs without thinking, such as recognising a face or walking across a crowded room, are extremely hard. Moravec wrote in 1988 that it was comparatively easy to make computers perform like adults on intelligence tests, but very difficult to give them the perception and mobility of a one-year-old. This observation is now known as Moravec's paradox.

Moravec offered an evolutionary explanation. Skills such as seeing, grasping and moving have been refined by natural selection over hundreds of millions of years, and the brain devotes enormous resources to them. Because they are so well practised, we perform them unconsciously and therefore underestimate how complex they are. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent development in evolutionary terms. It feels difficult to us precisely because we are not very good at it, and it can often be reduced to a small number of clear rules that a computer can follow.

A related idea comes from the philosopher Michael Polanyi, who wrote in 1966 that 'we can know more than we can tell'. A person can ride a bicycle or recognise a friend's voice without being able to explain how. This kind of tacit knowledge creates a problem for engineers, because traditional programming requires every step of a task to be specified in advance. If nobody can describe precisely how they tie a shoelace, it is very hard to write instructions that a robot can follow.

The difficulty is especially clear in warehouses. In 2015, the online retailer Amazon organised the first of a series of competitions, the Amazon Picking Challenge, inviting university teams to build robots that could pick individual items from crowded shelves. The items ranged from pencils and books to soft toys and packets of biscuits. The winning robots worked, but they were far slower and less reliable than human workers, struggling in particular with objects that were transparent, shiny, soft or partly hidden behind others.

Recent progress has come from two directions. First, machine learning allows robots to learn from experience rather than relying entirely on rules written by programmers. Instead of being told how to grasp each object, a robot can practise thousands of times, sometimes in computer simulations, and gradually improve. Second, engineers have developed new hardware, including soft grippers made of flexible materials and suction devices, which are more forgiving of small errors than rigid metal fingers. Cheaper cameras and sensors have also helped robots to build a more detailed picture of their surroundings.

Even so, most experts believe that general-purpose robots capable of doing household chores in an ordinary home are still some way off. Homes are unpredictable; objects are constantly moved, lighting changes and every room is different. Factories, on the other hand, can be redesigned around the needs of machines. For the foreseeable future, it seems likely that robots will continue to take over tasks in controlled environments, while the jobs that require ordinary human dexterity, such as cleaning, caring and cooking, will remain surprisingly hard to automate.

readingPassages.title: Will the machines take our jobs?
paragraphs: Fear that machines will make human workers unnecessary is almost as old as industry itself. Between 1811 and 1816, groups of textile workers in the English Midlands and the north of England, who called themselves Luddites after a mythical leader named Ned Ludd, broke into factories at night and smashed the new machines that threatened their livelihoods. Today the word 'Luddite' is used to mock anyone who resists technology, but the original Luddites were not opposed to machines as such. They objected to the way machines were being used to cut wages and replace skilled workers with cheaper, less skilled labour.

In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes gave this fear a name. In a short essay entitled 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren', he warned of 'technological unemployment', meaning unemployment caused by our discovering ways of saving labour faster than we can find new uses for it. Yet Keynes was optimistic about the long term. He predicted that within a hundred years, people in wealthy countries would be so productive that they might need to work only around fifteen hours a week, and that the main challenge would be learning how to use their leisure time well.

Keynes was right about productivity, which has risen enormously, but wrong about working hours, which have fallen far less than he expected. And despite two centuries of automation, the long-feared collapse of employment has not occurred. The reason, economists argue, is that technology does not only destroy jobs; it also creates them. When machines make goods cheaper, people spend the money they save on other things, and new industries appear that nobody could have imagined. In 1900, around forty per cent of American workers were employed in agriculture; today the figure is below two per cent, yet unemployment is not remotely forty per cent.

Nevertheless, recent advances in artificial intelligence have revived the old anxiety. In 2013, Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne of the University of Oxford estimated that around forty-seven per cent of jobs in the United States were at high risk of being automated within a decade or two. Their study received enormous publicity. However, other researchers soon pointed out that it assessed entire occupations, whereas most jobs consist of many different tasks, only some of which can be automated. A study for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), published in 2016, took this task-based approach and concluded that only around nine per cent of jobs across OECD countries were at high risk.

A well-known example shows why the task-based view matters. When automated teller machines (ATMs) spread through American banks from the 1970s onwards, many people assumed that bank tellers would disappear. The economist James Bessen found that this did not happen. Because ATMs reduced the cost of running a branch, banks opened many more branches, and the number of tellers remained roughly stable for decades. Their work changed, however: they spent less time counting cash and more time selling financial products and dealing with customers' problems.

This does not mean that automation is harmless. The economist David Autor has shown that, in many wealthy countries, technology has contributed to a 'polarisation' of the labour market. Routine middle-skill jobs, such as clerical and factory work, have declined, while employment has grown in both highly paid professional jobs and in low-paid service work, such as cleaning and care, which is difficult to automate. The result has been rising inequality, as many workers have lost secure, reasonably paid jobs and have been unable to move into better ones.

Will artificial intelligence follow the same pattern? There are reasons to think it may be different. Earlier waves of automation mainly affected physical and routine tasks, but modern AI systems can write, translate, summarise and analyse, which means they may affect educated office workers who previously felt secure. In my view, it would be foolish to assume that, because technology has created more jobs than it destroyed in the past, it will automatically do so again. History is a useful guide, but it is not a guarantee.

At the same time, I believe that the most pessimistic predictions underestimate how much choice societies have. Whether automation leads to shared prosperity or to greater inequality depends heavily on policy: on how education systems prepare people for changing work, on whether workers who lose their jobs are supported while they retrain, and on how the gains from higher productivity are distributed. Technology shapes the possibilities, but it is people who decide which ones become reality. The Luddites lost their battle, but the question they raised, about who benefits from new machines, is as relevant as ever.

listeningParts.title: Opening a student bank account
listeningParts.contextDescription: A new international student phones a bank to arrange a student account.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Bank, you're speaking to Fiona. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi. I've just arrived to start a degree at the university here, and I'd like to open a bank account. Someone told me you have special accounts for students.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: We do, yes. It's called the Student Plus account, and it's designed for people in full-time higher education. I can take some details now and then book you an appointment at a branch to finish things off. Is that all right?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Sure, that's great.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Lovely. First of all, what are you studying, and for how long?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm doing a three-year degree in Accounting. I was going to do Economics, actually, but I changed my mind at the last minute.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Accounting. Well, you'll be good at keeping track of your money, then! Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Daniel Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Thank you, Daniel. And your date of birth?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: The twenty-third of June, 2006.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: And where are you living at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm in a student flat. It's Flat 3, 27 Wharf Street. That's W-H-A-R-F. It's near the river, just behind the old customs house.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: I know it. Now, when you come in to the branch, you'll need to bring two things. The first is your passport, so we can check your identity. The second is something to prove you're a student and that you live at that address. Most people bring a letter from the university, which the student services office can print for you. A bill is no good, I'm afraid, because most students don't have bills in their own name.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay, a letter from student services. I'll get that tomorrow. Can I ask what the account actually offers? Is there a monthly charge?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: There's no monthly fee at all. You get a contactless debit card, online and mobile banking, and an arranged overdraft with no interest.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: How much is the overdraft?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: In your first year, you can borrow up to five hundred pounds interest-free. That goes up to a thousand pounds in your second and third years, if you've managed the account well. But I'd always say, only use it if you really need to, because it does have to be paid back once you graduate.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Right. I'll try not to touch it. What about the card? How long does it take to arrive?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Once the account's open, the card is posted to you and should arrive within five working days. Your PIN comes separately, a couple of days later, for security reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And is there a charge if I use the card abroad? I'll be going home to Canada at Christmas.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: With the Student Plus account, there's no fee for spending abroad, but if you take out cash from a machine overseas, there's a small charge. The other thing I'd recommend is our mobile app. If you lose your card, you can freeze it instantly from your phone, and unfreeze it if you find it again, rather than having to cancel it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's handy. I'm always losing things.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: You're not the only one! Now, let's book that appointment. Our nearest branch to you is on Market Square. I'm afraid Tuesday is fully booked because it's the start of term, but I've got a slot on Thursday at half past two. Would that suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Thursday's fine. I don't have any lectures in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Just so you know, the branch is right next to the bus station, so it's easy to find. If you can't make it for any reason, please ring us at least a day in advance, so we can offer the slot to someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Perfect. The appointment should take about forty minutes. And how would you prefer us to contact you, by email or text?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Text, please. I don't check my email very often, to be honest.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: No problem. I'll send you a reminder by text the day before. Finally, just for our records, how did you hear about us?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: A friend from my course recommended you. She opened an account here last week.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Well, Daniel, that's everything for now. We'll see you on Thursday, and don't forget your passport and the letter.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I won't. Thanks very much for your help, Fiona.

listeningParts.title: Welcome to Castlegate Market
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a historic covered market speaks to a group of new stallholders.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Castlegate Market. My name's Rosa Bellamy, and I've been the market manager here for about six years. I know some of you have run stalls at other markets before, while for others this is your very first business, so I'll try to cover the basics and you can ask questions at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me start with a little history, because people often ask about it. There's been a market on this site since the thirteenth century, when the town was granted a royal charter allowing it to hold a weekly market. For most of that time it was an open-air market, selling mainly livestock and grain. The covered hall we're standing in now was built much later, in 1878, and the iron and glass roof was restored about ten years ago, with help from a heritage grant. If you look up, you can still see the original ironwork, which was made in a foundry just outside the town.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a lot of people assume that markets like ours are dying because of supermarkets and online shopping. In fact, our footfall, that's the number of visitors, has gone up every year since the restoration. What's changed is who comes and why. We get fewer people doing their whole weekly shop here, but far more people coming for things they can't get elsewhere: local cheeses, handmade goods, street food. So my advice is to focus on what makes your stall different, rather than trying to compete on price with the big shops.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Some practical points. The market's open Tuesday to Saturday, from eight until five thirty. Your rent is paid monthly, in advance, and it covers your pitch, cleaning of the common areas and security. You'll be glad to hear that we don't charge extra for heating in winter. What we do insist on is that you're open on at least four of the five market days, because empty stalls make the whole market look less lively and that affects everyone's trade.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Payment's another thing I get asked about. Almost all our traders now accept cards, and I'd strongly encourage you to do the same. We've found that customers who pay by card tend to spend more per visit than those using cash, partly because they're not limited by what's in their wallet. That said, quite a few of our older customers still prefer cash, so please don't go card-only.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the facilities, because there have been some changes recently. Deliveries come in through the loading bay at the back, on Mill Lane. You can use it free of charge, but only before nine in the morning, because after that the lane gets very busy with pedestrians.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: For those of you selling food, there's a cold store next to the office, with refrigerated space for meat, fish and dairy. Space there is limited, so you need to book it in advance through the office, and there's a small weekly fee.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The recycling area used to be inside the hall, near the east entrance, but it's recently moved outside to the yard, because of complaints about the smell in summer. Please sort cardboard, glass and food waste into the right bins.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you need somewhere to keep your stock overnight, there are storage lockers in the basement. You'll need to collect a key from the office, and we ask for a deposit, which you get back when you return it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: And finally, the electricity points. Every pitch has one, but the ones on the north side of the hall are being replaced at the moment, so they're closed for repairs until the end of the month. If you're on that side and you need power, have a word with me and we'll sort out a temporary cable.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Okay, that's the main things. Oh, one last point: we run a monthly late-night market on the first Friday of every month, with music and extra food stalls. It's optional, but it's very popular and it's a great way to attract new customers. There's no extra rent for it, but you do need to let the office know by the Monday before if you'd like to take part. Now, who's got a question?

listeningParts.title: Preparing a seminar on comparative advantage
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two economics students, Priya and Jack, discuss a seminar presentation with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay, Priya, Jack, come and sit down. You're presenting next week on comparative advantage, aren't you? How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the reading, and we've got a rough structure. We thought we'd start with the history, then explain the theory with a simple example, and finish with some criticisms.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds sensible. Who are you starting with?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: David Ricardo. His book, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, came out in 1817, and that's where the idea is usually said to come from. Although we did find that some historians think other writers had similar ideas a bit earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's true, and it's worth a sentence, but don't spend long on it. The audience will want to understand the idea itself. How are you going to explain it?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We were going to use Ricardo's own example: England and Portugal, producing cloth and wine. The surprising part is that, in his example, Portugal is better at producing both goods. It needs fewer workers for cloth and for wine. And yet both countries still gain from trade.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Because what matters isn't absolute advantage, but opportunity cost. For Portugal, making cloth means giving up a lot of wine, so it's better to specialise in wine and buy cloth from England.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. But I've found students often get lost with Ricardo's original numbers. Have you thought about a more modern example?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We had one idea: a top lawyer who's also the fastest typist in her office. Should she do her own typing?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic, and it works well, because everyone can see that her time is more valuable spent on legal work, even though she types faster than her assistant. I'd open with that, actually, before Ricardo, to get people's attention, and then show that the same logic applies to countries.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Okay, so swap the order. That makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Should we include any real figures about trade, like how much of the world's output is exported?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: One or two figures would be fine, as long as they're from a reliable source, such as the World Trade Organization or the World Bank, and you give the year. But don't overload the audience. The aim is to explain the idea clearly, not to impress people with statistics.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Now, the criticisms. What have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: The main one is that the theory assumes workers can move easily from one industry to another. In reality, if a factory closes because of cheap imports, the workers can't just become software engineers overnight. We found research on the effect of Chinese imports on manufacturing areas in the United States, which showed that job losses were concentrated in particular towns, and those places took many years to recover.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's the work by David Autor and his colleagues on what they called the China shock. It's very influential. Make sure you cite it properly. What else?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We also wanted to mention that the model is static. It looks at what countries are good at now, but countries can develop new advantages over time. South Korea, for example, wasn't an obvious place to build ships or electronics in the 1950s.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, and some economists argue that governments helped to create those advantages, by protecting young industries for a while. That's a debate you could leave open for the discussion questions. I'd be careful not to suggest that the theory is simply wrong, though. Most economists still accept the basic logic. The arguments are about who gains, who loses, and what should be done for the losers.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: So maybe we should end with policy, like retraining programmes?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. That gives the presentation a clear conclusion. How long is it at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: About twenty-five minutes, but we're only allowed twenty.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then cut the history section down. And one more thing: last year, several groups put far too much text on their slides. Use a diagram for the England and Portugal example instead. It's much clearer.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We'll do that. Could we send you the slides before Friday?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Send them by Thursday evening, and I'll give you comments on Friday morning.

listeningParts.title: The evolution of money
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory economics course on how money developed over time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to step back from the models we've been looking at and ask a very basic question: what is money, and where did it come from? Economists usually say that money has three functions. It's a medium of exchange, which means we use it to buy things. It's a unit of account, so we can compare the value of very different goods. And it's a store of value, meaning that we can save it and spend it later.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The traditional story, which you'll find in many textbooks, is that before money, people used barter, swapping goods directly. The problem with barter is what the nineteenth-century economist William Stanley Jevons called the double coincidence of wants. If I have fish and want shoes, I have to find someone who has shoes and who, at the same moment, wants fish. Money, the story goes, was invented to solve this problem.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: I should say that many anthropologists are sceptical about this story. They point out that there's very little evidence of whole societies that ran on barter. In small communities, people more often relied on systems of credit and obligation: I give you something now, and you owe me a favour later. So it may be that keeping records of debts came before coins, not after them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever its origins, early money often took the form of commodities that had value in themselves, or were at least scarce and durable. Grain, cattle and salt were all used in different places. One of the most widespread was the cowrie shell, which was used as money across large parts of Africa and Asia for centuries. Shells were ideal in some ways: they're durable, difficult to fake, and easy to count. In some regions, they remained in use until the early twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first coins appeared in the seventh century BC, in Lydia, in what's now western Turkey. They were made from electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver, and stamped with a design to show that their weight and purity were guaranteed. That stamp was important. It meant that people no longer had to weigh metal every time they made a purchase; they could simply count the coins.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next major step happened in China. Carrying large quantities of metal coins was heavy and inconvenient, and during the Song dynasty, around the eleventh century, the government began issuing paper money. Marco Polo, who visited China in the thirteenth century, was astonished that people would accept pieces of paper in exchange for goods. In Europe, banknotes came much later. The first in Europe were issued in Sweden, in 1661, by a bank called Stockholms Banco, although the bank soon got into trouble for printing too many of them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many countries operated a gold standard. Under this system, a banknote could, in principle, be exchanged at the bank for a fixed amount of gold. This limited how much money governments could create, which helped to keep prices stable, but it also made it hard to respond to economic crises.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: After the Second World War, the Bretton Woods agreement of 1944 created a system in which other currencies were fixed to the US dollar, and the dollar itself was linked to gold. That arrangement ended in 1971, when President Nixon announced that the United States would no longer exchange dollars for gold. Since then, the major currencies have been what economists call fiat money: money that has value not because it can be exchanged for anything, but because governments declare it to be legal tender, and because people trust that others will accept it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And that brings us to the central point of today's lecture. Money, ultimately, is a system of trust. A banknote is just paper, and the numbers in your bank account are just entries in a computer. They work only because we're confident that they'll be accepted tomorrow. When that confidence collapses, as it does in a hyperinflation, money can lose almost all its value very quickly. Next week, we'll look at the role of central banks in maintaining that trust.

readingPassages.title: The roads of silk
paragraphs: The phrase 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway along which camels carried bales of silk from China to Rome. The reality was far more complicated. The term itself is relatively modern: it was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, who was mapping possible railway routes across Asia. What he described was not one road but a shifting network of overland routes, linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, that carried goods, people and ideas for well over a thousand years.

The origins of the network are usually traced to the second century BC, when the Han dynasty in China sent an official named Zhang Qian westwards on a diplomatic mission. His aim was to find allies against the Xiongnu, a nomadic people who threatened China's northern frontier. Zhang Qian was captured and held for around ten years before he escaped and continued his journey, finally returning to the Chinese capital some thirteen years after he had set out. He failed to secure an alliance, but the reports he brought back of wealthy kingdoms to the west, and of their powerful horses, encouraged the Han emperors to extend their control along the trade routes.

Silk was certainly one of the most valuable goods traded. Its production was a closely guarded Chinese secret, and in the Roman world it became a symbol of luxury. Roman writers complained about the fashion for silk clothing, which they considered immoral, and the scholar Pliny the Elder grumbled that enormous sums of money were flowing out of the empire to pay for luxury goods from the East. However, silk was only one item among many. Spices, precious stones, glass, paper, horses and metalwork all moved along the routes, in both directions. Chinese buyers, for instance, valued glassware from the Roman world and the Middle East, which was rare and expensive in China.

Surprisingly few merchants ever travelled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, changing owners many times, with each trader covering only one section of the journey. Some peoples became specialists in this middleman role. The Sogdians, from the region around Samarkand in present-day Uzbekistan, established trading communities across Central Asia and China, and their language became widely used in commerce. At each stage, prices rose, so that by the time silk reached the Mediterranean it was many times more expensive than in China.

Travel was slow and dangerous. Caravans crossed deserts, such as the Taklamakan, and some of the highest mountain ranges on Earth. The two-humped Bactrian camel was ideal for these conditions, since it can carry heavy loads and survive both freezing winters and scorching summers. Along the main routes, caravanserais, or roadside inns, offered travellers and their animals shelter for the night. Oasis towns grew rich by providing water, food and markets, and some, such as Kashgar and Dunhuang, became important centres of culture as well as trade.

Ideas travelled along the routes as readily as goods. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China, and the cave temples at Dunhuang contain thousands of Buddhist paintings and manuscripts. Technologies also moved. Knowledge of how to make paper, invented in China, had reached the Islamic world by the eighth century, and later spread to Europe. Silk production itself eventually escaped China's control: according to the Byzantine historian Procopius, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople in the sixth century AD, allowing a silk industry to develop there.

Not everything that travelled was welcome. Historians believe that the Black Death, the plague that devastated Asia, the Middle East and Europe in the fourteenth century, spread partly along the trade routes that connected these regions. Merchants, soldiers and their animals carried not only goods but also the fleas and rats that transmitted the disease. In this sense, the Silk Roads were an early example of a familiar feature of globalisation: the same connections that spread wealth and knowledge could also spread disaster.

From the fifteenth century onwards, the overland routes gradually declined in importance as European sailors opened sea routes around Africa to India and East Asia, which could carry larger quantities of goods more cheaply. Yet the memory of the Silk Roads has never disappeared. In 2014, a 5,000-kilometre section of the network between China and Central Asia was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List, nominated jointly by China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Today, the name is often used for new infrastructure projects, a sign of how powerfully the idea of these ancient connections still shapes the way we think about trade.

readingPassages.title: When money melts away
paragraphs: Most people are used to prices rising slowly. In many countries, central banks aim for inflation of around two per cent a year, a rate at which most people barely notice that their money is losing value. Occasionally, however, inflation spirals out of control. In 1956, the American economist Phillip Cagan proposed a definition that is still widely used: hyperinflation begins when prices rise by more than fifty per cent in a single month. At that rate, prices increase roughly a hundredfold within a year, and money rapidly loses its usefulness.

The most famous case occurred in Germany in the early 1920s. After the First World War, the German government faced enormous debts, including reparation payments to the victorious Allies. When Germany fell behind with these payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, the country's industrial heartland, in January 1923. The government encouraged workers there to go on strike and continued to pay their wages, financing this by printing ever larger quantities of money. By November 1923, one US dollar was worth around 4.2 trillion marks.

Even this was not the worst hyperinflation in history. That record belongs to Hungary, whose economy had been devastated by the Second World War. In July 1946, prices in Hungary were doubling roughly every fifteen hours. Banknotes were printed with ever greater numbers of zeros, until the old currency, the pengő, became practically worthless and was replaced by the forint. More recently, Zimbabwe experienced hyperinflation in the late 2000s, following a collapse in agricultural output and heavy money printing. In 2009, the country's central bank issued a note worth one hundred trillion Zimbabwean dollars, shortly before the currency was abandoned altogether.

Although each case has its own history, the underlying mechanism is usually similar. A government that cannot raise enough money through taxes or borrowing begins to pay its bills by creating new money. As more money chases the same quantity of goods, prices rise. The crucial moment comes when people start to expect further rises. They then try to spend their money as quickly as possible, before it loses more value, and this rush to spend pushes prices up even faster. Inflation, in other words, can feed on itself. At its most extreme stage, people may refuse to accept the national currency at all, and the government finds that even printing money no longer pays its bills, since the notes lose value before they can be spent.

Daily life under hyperinflation becomes exhausting. In Germany in 1923, workers were sometimes paid twice a day so that they could rush out and spend their wages before prices rose again. Restaurants were reported to change their prices while customers were still eating. Many people abandoned money altogether and returned to barter, exchanging goods and services directly, while others used foreign currencies wherever possible. Businesses found it almost impossible to plan, since they could not know what their costs would be from one week to the next. Photographs from the period show children playing with bundles of worthless notes.

Hyperinflation does not harm everyone equally. Those who suffer most are people who depend on savings or fixed incomes, such as pensioners, whose money can become worthless within months. In Germany, many middle-class families who had saved carefully for decades lost almost everything. On the other hand, people who owed money often benefited, because their debts shrank in real terms. Some property owners in Germany were able to pay off their mortgages with money that was worth only a tiny fraction of what they had originally borrowed.

Ending a hyperinflation usually requires more than one measure. In Germany, a new currency, the Rentenmark, was introduced in November 1923, with one Rentenmark replacing one trillion old marks. Just as important, the government strictly limited the number of new notes and took steps to bring its spending under control. The key, economists argue, is credibility: people must believe that the government will not simply print money again. Without that belief, a new currency is likely to suffer the same fate as the old one.

The memory of hyperinflation can last for generations. In Germany, the experience of 1923 is often said to explain why the post-war central bank, the Bundesbank, placed such great emphasis on keeping prices stable, an approach that later influenced the design of the European Central Bank. For economists, the lesson of these episodes is that money depends on trust. When people stop believing that the money in their pockets will hold its value, even a modern economy can find that its currency melts away with astonishing speed.
