readingPassages.title: Should we say goodbye to cash?
paragraphs: For most of history, money meant something you could hold in your hand. Today, in many countries, notes and coins are becoming a rarity. People tap cards and phones to pay for coffee, transfer money to friends with an app, and may go weeks without touching a banknote. Some governments, banks and economists welcome this trend and would like to speed it up. Others worry that a cashless society would leave some people behind and give too much power to those who run payment systems. The question of whether cash has a future is no longer a theoretical one.

Sweden is often described as the country closest to abandoning cash. Surveys by its central bank, the Riksbank, have found that fewer than one in ten Swedes used cash for their most recent purchase in a shop, and many cafés and even some bank branches no longer accept it. Yet the speed of this change has caused concern. Swedish lawmakers have required the largest banks to continue providing cash services, and the Riksbank has investigated issuing a digital currency of its own, partly so that the public would still have access to money issued directly by the state.

In some developing economies, digital payments have spread for different reasons. In Kenya, the mobile money service M-Pesa, launched by the telecommunications company Safaricom in 2007, allows people to send and receive money by text message, even on basic mobile phones and without a bank account. A study by the economists Tavneet Suri and William Jack, published in 2016, estimated that access to M-Pesa had lifted around two per cent of Kenyan households out of extreme poverty, in part because it made it easier for families to receive help from relatives during hard times.

Supporters of a cashless economy make several arguments. Digital payments are fast and convenient, and they leave a record, which makes tax evasion and crimes such as money laundering harder. The Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff, in his 2016 book The Curse of Cash, argued that large-denomination banknotes are used disproportionately in illegal activity and should be phased out, while smaller notes could remain. Rogoff also pointed out that the existence of cash limits the ability of central banks to set negative interest rates, because people can simply withdraw their savings and keep them as notes.

However, attempts to force a rapid move away from cash can cause serious problems. In November 2016, the Indian government suddenly withdrew its 500- and 1,000-rupee notes, which together made up around eighty-six per cent of the cash in circulation by value. The aim was to tackle corruption and counterfeit money. The result was weeks of long queues at banks and severe difficulties for small traders and farmers who relied on cash. A later report by the Reserve Bank of India found that almost all of the withdrawn money had been returned to banks, suggesting that relatively little illegal wealth had been eliminated.

There are also concerns about who benefits from a cashless world. In China, two private platforms, Alipay and WeChat Pay, handle a very large share of everyday transactions, which are usually made by scanning QR codes with a smartphone. This is extremely convenient, but it means that a small number of companies hold detailed information about what hundreds of millions of people buy. In my view, this concentration of data is one of the strongest arguments for keeping cash. A banknote does not record where it was spent, and it does not depend on a company's willingness to process a payment.

The groups most dependent on cash are often those with the least power to complain: elderly people, those on low incomes, people with disabilities and those living in remote areas with poor internet connections. For them, a sudden disappearance of cash would not be a minor inconvenience. Digital systems also fail. Power cuts, technical faults and cyber-attacks can all prevent electronic payments, sometimes for hours or days. In my view, any society that relies entirely on digital payments is taking an unnecessary risk, since cash continues to work when the network does not.

None of this means that the trend towards digital money should be reversed, nor would that be possible. The convenience is real, and services like M-Pesa have brought clear benefits. But I believe the choice should remain with the public. Governments should ensure that cash remains widely available and accepted for as long as people want to use it, and should treat it as a piece of public infrastructure, like roads or libraries, rather than as an outdated technology waiting to be retired. A cashless society may arrive one day, but it should arrive because people choose it, not because they are given no alternative.

listeningParts.title: Booking a desert camping trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a tour company to book a three-day trip into the desert.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Sand Sea Expeditions, Martin speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm hoping to book a desert trip for later this year. I've had a look at your website, but I had a few questions first.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. Which trip were you looking at?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The three-day one that goes out into the dunes. I think it's called the Erg Explorer.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's right. The Erg Explorer is our most popular trip. On the first day we drive about four hours from the city to the edge of the desert, and then you ride camels for the last part of the journey to our camp. The second day is spent exploring the dunes on foot and visiting an oasis where people still grow dates, and on the third morning we watch the sunrise and then drive back.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds perfect. How many people go on each trip?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We keep the groups small, so there's a maximum of twelve people, plus a driver, a cook and a guide.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's three hundred and forty dollars per person. Children under twelve pay half price. That covers all your meals, transport, the camel ride and two nights at the camp. The only thing that isn't included is travel insurance, which you'll need to arrange yourself before you come.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. There would be two of us, me and my brother. We were thinking of going in October.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: October's a very good choice. In the summer months it's far too hot, often over forty-five degrees in the afternoon, so we don't run the trip from June to August at all. What dates were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We arrive in the country on the tenth, so maybe starting on the fourteenth?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me just check. Hmm, the fourteenth is full, I'm afraid, but there are still places on the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The sixteenth is fine. We'll spend a couple more days in the city first.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Now, a few things about the camp. You'll sleep in traditional tents made of goat hair, which keep the heat out during the day surprisingly well, and there are proper beds inside. There's a shared shower block, but please remember that all the water has to be brought in by truck, so we ask guests to keep their showers short.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Of course. Is there electricity?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's solar power for lighting in the evening, but there are no sockets in the tents. If you want to charge your phone, there's a charging point in the dining tent. I'd also recommend bringing a torch, because the camp is very dark at night. That's actually one of the highlights: with no towns nearby, you can see thousands of stars.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. What about clothes? I imagine it's hot.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: During the day, yes, but people are often surprised by how cold it gets at night in the desert, because there are no clouds to keep the heat in. In October it can drop to around eight degrees, so bring a warm jacket. For the daytime, wear loose clothing that covers your arms and legs, and bring a hat and a scarf. The scarf is useful if there's wind, because you can wrap it around your face to keep the sand out of your mouth and eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. And where do you pick people up?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: From your hotel, if it's in the old town. Otherwise, we meet outside the main post office, in Station Square, at half past six in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We're renting an apartment outside the old town, so we'll come to the post office.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Fine. Can I take a name for the booking?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Grace Talbot. That's T-A-L-B-O-T.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Ms Talbot. Do either of you have any dietary requirements?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My brother doesn't eat meat, but I eat everything.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem at all. Our cook makes excellent vegetable dishes, so he'll be well looked after. To confirm the places, we ask for a deposit of twenty per cent, and the rest is paid in cash on the first morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And if we have to cancel?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: If you cancel more than two weeks before the trip, we refund the deposit in full. After that, I'm afraid it isn't refundable. I'll email you all the details and a list of what to pack this afternoon.

listeningParts.title: A guided visit to a desert garden
listeningParts.contextDescription: A volunteer guide welcomes visitors to a botanical garden of desert plants.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsley Desert Garden. My name's Rob, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you start exploring, I'd like to tell you a little about the garden and point out a few things you shouldn't miss.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The garden was created in the 1970s on the site of an old sand quarry. The founder, a retired schoolteacher called Edith Kingsley, noticed that the quarry floor was so dry and sunny that almost nothing from the local countryside would grow there, and she decided to try desert plants instead. She started with a small collection of cactuses she'd been given by friends, and today we have more than three thousand species from deserts on every continent except Antarctica.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Most of the plants are kept in the big glasshouse you can see in front of you, which we call the Dry House. It isn't heated in summer, but in winter we have to keep it above five degrees, because many desert plants are killed by frost. People are sometimes surprised by that, since they think of deserts as cold at night, but in many hot deserts it rarely freezes.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you about the different areas. As you go in, the first section is the Cactus Walk. All the plants here come from the Americas, because cactuses are found naturally only there, with one or two minor exceptions. Look out for our saguaro, the tall cactus with arms that you see in cowboy films. Saguaros grow extremely slowly, and they often don't produce their first arm until they're at least fifty years old. Ours is the oldest plant in the whole garden.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to that is the Succulent Terrace, with plants from southern Africa. Many of them store water in thick leaves, and some look exactly like small stones, which protects them from animals that would otherwise eat them. Unfortunately, the terrace is closed this month while we repair the roof above it, but you can still see most of it through the windows.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Then there's the Sahara Court, which has date palms and other plants from North Africa and the Middle East. It's the warmest part of the glasshouse, so if you're feeling cold, that's the place to go. In the evenings during July, we open late so that visitors can see some of the plants that flower only at night. These are pollinated by moths and bats in the wild, so their flowers open after dark and are often strongly scented.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Outside the glasshouse, behind the café, you'll find the Discovery Zone. That's designed for younger visitors, and it's the only place in the garden where you're allowed to touch the plants. We've chosen ones without spines, of course! Everywhere else, please keep your hands to yourselves, partly for your own safety, and partly because the oils on our skin can damage some plants.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, don't miss the Seed Room, next to the shop. It contains a display about our work with an international seed bank. Many desert plants are threatened by climate change and by people collecting them illegally, so we store their seeds in cold conditions so that they could be grown again in the future if they disappear in the wild.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. Tickets are valid for the whole day, so you're welcome to leave and come back later; just show your ticket at the entrance. The café serves lunch from twelve until two, and I'd recommend the cactus fruit lemonade. And there are free guided walks every day at eleven o'clock and three o'clock, which start from the main door of the Dry House. On a hot afternoon it's a good idea to visit the Dry House early, because it gets very warm inside after about two o'clock. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A project on farming in the Sahara
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two agriculture students, Leila and Sam, discuss their project on desert farming with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Leila, Sam. Come and sit down. You're comparing two types of farming in the northern Sahara for your project, aren't you? How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Quite well, I think. We're looking at traditional oasis farming on the one hand, and the large modern farms that use centre-pivot irrigation on the other. Those are the huge green circles you see on satellite images.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what have you found out about the traditional system so far?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The thing that impressed us most is the way the space is organised. Farmers grow crops in three layers. At the top, there are date palms, which can stand the full heat of the sun. Underneath, in their shade, there are fruit trees, like figs and pomegranates. And at the bottom, there are vegetables and animal feed, such as alfalfa.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: The palms reduce the temperature underneath them by several degrees and protect the lower plants from the wind, so less water evaporates. It's a very efficient use of a small amount of land and water.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's right. And the date palm is central to the whole system. Did you find anything about its importance beyond food?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, almost every part of it is used. The leaves are used for roofs and fences, and to make baskets, and the trunks were traditionally used for building. One source we read said the palm was sometimes described as the tree of life for that reason.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the modern farms?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: They're completely different. They pump water from deep underground, often from hundreds of metres down, and spray it over a circle of land with a long rotating arm. They mainly grow wheat, potatoes and animal feed, and the yields can be very high.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The problem is where the water comes from. Much of it is what's called fossil water. It filled the aquifers thousands of years ago, when the Sahara had a much wetter climate, and very little of it is being replaced by rain today. So in a sense it's like a mine: once it's used, it's gone.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you find any figures on how fast water levels are falling?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: We found several, but they vary a lot from one region to another, and some were quite old. We weren't sure which ones to trust.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then I'd suggest you don't base your argument on a single number. Present the range of estimates and explain why they differ. That's much more convincing than choosing the most dramatic figure.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Okay. Another issue we came across is salt. When water evaporates in such a hot climate, it leaves salt behind in the soil, and over time some fields become too salty to farm. Several farms have had to be abandoned for that reason.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, salinity is a serious problem in irrigated drylands everywhere. Does that affect the oases too?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: It can, especially where the drainage channels aren't kept clean. In some oases, younger people have moved to the cities, so there are fewer people to do that maintenance work.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. That's a social factor rather than a technical one, and it would be worth a section of its own. Now, how are you going to structure the report?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We thought we'd describe each system first, and then compare them using four criteria: water use, yields, effects on the soil and employment.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. I'd add one more thing: a short conclusion on whether the two systems could be combined, for example by using drip irrigation on modern farms, which delivers water directly to the roots of each plant.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: We did read about that. Apparently it can cut water use dramatically compared with spraying.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It can, though it's more expensive to install. Right, could you send me a plan of the report by Friday? And please include a couple of satellite images, with the sources clearly given.

listeningParts.title: How desert animals survive
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course on how animals cope with heat and lack of water in deserts.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at how animals survive in deserts, which are among the most difficult environments on Earth. An animal living in a hot desert faces two connected problems. The first is heat: during the day, the surface of the sand can become hot enough to burn. The second is water: rain may fall only a few times a year, or not at all for several years. And the two problems make each other worse, because the usual way for a mammal to cool down is to sweat or pant, and both of those use water.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The simplest solution is to avoid the heat altogether. The great majority of small desert mammals are nocturnal, meaning they're active at night and spend the day underground. A burrow just half a metre below the surface can be dramatically cooler than the sand above it, and the air inside is more humid, so the animal loses less water as it breathes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Some animals have bodies that are designed to get rid of heat. A good example is the fennec fox of the Sahara, the smallest fox in the world. Its ears are enormous in proportion to its body, and they contain many blood vessels close to the surface, so they work like radiators, releasing heat into the air. The fennec also has thick fur on the soles of its feet, which protects it from the burning sand and helps it to walk on loose dunes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But the more remarkable adaptations are those that deal with water. Consider the kangaroo rat, which lives in the deserts of North America. In the laboratory, kangaroo rats have been kept for long periods on a diet of dry seeds without drinking at all. How is that possible? Well, when any animal breaks down food to release energy, water is produced as a by-product. This is known as metabolic water. For most animals, it's only a small part of their needs, but the kangaroo rat loses so little water that metabolic water is almost enough. Its kidneys produce extremely concentrated urine, and its nose is cooler than the rest of its body, so when it breathes out, much of the moisture in its breath condenses and is recovered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Other animals collect water in ingenious ways. In the Namib Desert in south-western Africa, which lies along the coast, it hardly ever rains, but fog regularly drifts in from the Atlantic Ocean in the early morning. Certain beetles climb to the top of a dune and stand with their heads down and their backs raised into the wind. Tiny droplets of water from the fog collect on their backs and then run down towards their mouths. Engineers have since studied these beetles in the hope of designing materials that can collect water from the air.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In Australia, a small lizard called the thorny devil has a different method. Its skin is covered in tiny channels between the scales. When it stands on damp sand, or when rain or dew touches its body, water is drawn along these channels by capillary action, rather like water moving up a paper towel, until it reaches the corners of its mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Birds face a special challenge, because their chicks can't travel to water. Sandgrouse, which live in the deserts of Africa and Asia, have solved this in an extraordinary way. The male flies to a waterhole, sometimes many kilometres from the nest, and wades in so that his breast feathers soak up water like a sponge. He then flies back, and the chicks drink directly from his feathers.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, some animals simply wait. Spadefoot toads, for instance, spend most of the year buried in the ground in a dormant state, sometimes for many months. When heavy rain finally arrives, they come to the surface, call loudly and breed in temporary pools. Because those pools may dry up within days, their tadpoles develop extremely quickly, in some species turning into young toads in little more than a week. What all of these examples show is that there's no single solution to desert life. In the next lecture, we'll look at desert plants, which face the same problems but cannot move.

readingPassages.title: Ship of the desert: how the camel survives
paragraphs: For thousands of years, camels have made it possible for people to live in and travel across some of the driest places on Earth. There are two domesticated species: the dromedary, which has one hump and is found mainly in North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, and the Bactrian camel, which has two humps and lives in the cold deserts of Central Asia. Together they number in the tens of millions, and they still provide milk, meat, wool and transport for many communities. It is the dromedary, however, that has become the symbol of the hot desert, and it is the dromedary that scientists have studied most closely.

Perhaps the most widespread belief about camels is that they store water in their humps. In fact, the hump is made mainly of fat. Concentrating the body's fat in one place, rather than spreading it under the skin as many other mammals do, allows heat to escape more easily from the rest of the body. When food is scarce, the camel can draw on this fat for energy, and the hump shrinks and may even fall over to one side. Breaking down fat does produce some water, but scientists now believe that this makes only a small contribution to the animal's needs.

Much of what we know about camel physiology comes from the work of the Norwegian-born physiologist Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, who carried out experiments with camels in the Algerian Sahara in the 1950s. One of his most important discoveries was that a camel's body temperature is not fixed. A well-watered camel keeps its temperature fairly constant, but a camel without water allows its temperature to rise by around six degrees during the day, from about 34°C in the early morning to about 40°C in the afternoon. By storing heat in its body instead of sweating, the camel saves a large amount of water, and it then loses the stored heat during the cool desert night.

Camels are also able to tolerate a degree of dehydration that would kill most other mammals. A camel can lose water equivalent to around a quarter of its body weight and survive. Part of the explanation lies in the blood. In most animals, severe dehydration causes the blood to become thick and sticky, so that the heart can no longer pump it around the body fast enough to carry heat away, and death follows quickly. In camels, water is lost mainly from the tissues rather than from the blood, which therefore keeps flowing normally.

When water does become available, camels can drink remarkable quantities very quickly: a thirsty animal may drink more than a hundred litres in around ten minutes. Such a sudden intake would be dangerous for most animals, because water would rush into the red blood cells and cause them to burst. A camel's red blood cells, however, are oval rather than round, and they can swell to more than twice their normal size without breaking. This allows the animal to rehydrate safely in a single visit to a well.

Many other features help the camel to save water or to cope with its environment. Its kidneys produce highly concentrated urine, and its droppings are so dry that they can be burned as fuel almost immediately. Its nostrils can be closed during sandstorms, and its eyes are protected by two rows of long eyelashes. Thick pads of skin on its chest and knees allow it to rest on hot ground, and its broad, flat feet spread out on the sand, preventing it from sinking. Thick fur on its back also protects it from the sun's heat, in the same way that desert peoples traditionally wear loose robes.

Surprisingly, the camel family did not originate in a desert at all. Fossils show that the earliest camels evolved in North America around forty million years ago and spread to Asia much later, before dying out in their original home. In 2013, researchers described fossil bones of a giant camel from Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic, dating from around three and a half million years ago, when the region was forested but still experienced long, cold winters. Some scientists have suggested that features such as the fatty hump and broad feet may first have evolved to cope with these conditions, and only later proved useful in deserts.

Today, the camel's ability to survive heat and drought is attracting new interest. As temperatures rise and droughts become more frequent in parts of Africa, some herders who once kept cattle have begun to keep camels instead, since camels continue to produce milk long after cattle have stopped. Meanwhile, the only truly wild camels, a population of Bactrian-type animals in the Gobi Desert of China and Mongolia, are critically endangered, with only around a thousand thought to survive. Their future may depend on protecting the remote places where they still live.

readingPassages.title: When the Sahara was green
paragraphs: Today the Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering much of northern Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. In many parts of it, years may pass without any measurable rain. Yet the evidence that this was not always so is everywhere. Rock paintings and engravings in the mountains of southern Algeria, Libya and Chad show giraffes, elephants and herds of cattle. Dry valleys wind across the landscape where rivers once flowed, and in the middle of the desert, fossil bones of hippopotamuses and crocodiles have been found lying in the sand.

Scientists now know that between roughly eleven thousand and five thousand years ago, much of the Sahara was covered with grassland, shrubs and scattered trees, and dotted with lakes and wetlands. This period is known as the African Humid Period. The most important cause was a gradual change in the Earth's orbit around the sun. Over a cycle of thousands of years, the tilt of the Earth's axis and the timing of its closest approach to the sun slowly change. During this period, the northern hemisphere received more sunshine in summer, which heated the land and strengthened the West African monsoon, drawing moist air and rain much further north than today.

Orbital change on its own, however, does not seem strong enough to explain such a dramatic transformation, and researchers believe that the effect was amplified by the landscape itself. Green vegetation absorbs more of the sun's energy than pale sand, which reflects much of it back into space, and plants release moisture into the air. Both effects tend to encourage more rainfall, which in turn allows more plants to grow. The American meteorologist Jule Charney proposed in the 1970s that a similar process might work in reverse, with the loss of vegetation leading to less rain, an idea that has influenced research on deserts ever since.

The lakes of the green Sahara were sometimes enormous. Lake Chad, which today is shallow and has shrunk greatly in recent decades, was at times part of a vast body of water known to scientists as Lake Mega-Chad, one of the largest lakes on Earth. Fish, including Nile perch, lived in lakes and rivers that are now completely dry, and people living around them caught fish with bone harpoons and hooks. The evidence for these communities is not only artistic but also archaeological.

One of the most remarkable sites was discovered in 2000 in the Ténéré desert of Niger by a team led by the American palaeontologist Paul Sereno, who had gone there to search for dinosaur fossils. At a place called Gobero, the team found around two hundred human burials on the shores of an ancient lake, together with fish bones, pottery and the remains of animals such as hippopotamuses. The burials belonged to two different cultures, separated by a period of extreme drought, and showed that people had returned to the area when wetter conditions came back.

How the Humid Period ended has been a subject of lively debate. In 2000, a study of sediments from the sea floor off the coast of West Africa, which record how much desert dust was blown out over the ocean, suggested that the change was strikingly abrupt, taking place over perhaps a century or two around five and a half thousand years ago. However, a later study of sediments from Lake Yoa in northern Chad, published in 2008, found evidence of a much more gradual change in vegetation over a period of thousands of years. Many researchers now think that the end may have come at different times and speeds in different regions.

As the rains retreated southwards, people had to adapt. Many herders moved towards the Nile Valley, the Sahel and other areas where water could still be found. Some archaeologists have suggested that the drying of the Sahara may have helped to concentrate people along the Nile, contributing to the rise of the civilisation of ancient Egypt, although this idea is difficult to test. The rock art of the Sahara also seems to record the change: later paintings show camels rather than cattle and giraffes.

The history of the green Sahara is more than an academic curiosity. Dust from the dried-up lake beds of the Sahara, particularly the Bodélé Depression in Chad, is carried thousands of kilometres across the Atlantic, and satellite studies suggest that it delivers nutrients such as phosphorus to the Amazon rainforest. Understanding why the Sahara changed so dramatically in the past may also help scientists to predict how rainfall in the region will respond to climate change in the future, a question of great importance for the millions of people who live along its edges.

readingPassages.title: Can a wall of trees hold back the desert?
paragraphs: In the 1970s and 1980s, a series of severe droughts struck the Sahel, the semi-arid belt that stretches across Africa along the southern edge of the Sahara. Crops failed, livestock died in huge numbers and many thousands of people lost their lives. Photographs of cracked earth and abandoned villages encouraged a powerful image in the minds of the public and of policy-makers: that of a desert advancing southwards, swallowing farmland as it went. The idea of a barrier to stop it, a great wall of trees, followed naturally from this image.

That idea became official policy in 2007, when the African Union launched the Great Green Wall initiative. The original plan was to plant a belt of trees around fifteen kilometres wide and roughly eight thousand kilometres long, from Senegal on the Atlantic coast to Djibouti on the Red Sea. Eleven countries were involved at first, and the number has since grown to more than twenty. The project's targets for 2030 are extremely ambitious: to restore one hundred million hectares of degraded land, to capture large quantities of carbon and to create ten million jobs in rural areas.

Progress, however, has been slow and uneven. A report published in 2020 for the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification estimated that only around four per cent of the target area had been restored, although the authors acknowledged that measuring progress across so many countries was difficult. In many places, seedlings were planted but not cared for, and a large proportion died within a year or two from lack of water or because they were eaten by animals. In 2021, at an international summit in Paris, governments and development banks pledged more than fourteen billion dollars to speed up the work.

Meanwhile, scientists had begun to question the picture of an advancing desert. Satellite images from the 1980s onwards showed that much of the Sahel had in fact become greener after the worst droughts ended, as rainfall partly recovered. The boundary of the Sahara is not a fixed line but a broad zone that moves north and south from year to year with the rains. Researchers now prefer to speak of land degradation: the loss of soil fertility and vegetation caused by a combination of drought, overgrazing, clearing land for fuel and poor farming practices. Degradation can happen anywhere in drylands, often far from the desert edge, and a single line of trees can do little to prevent it.

Some of the most impressive results have come not from planting but from regeneration. In Niger, from the 1980s onwards, farmers working with the Australian agronomist Tony Rinaudo began protecting the tree stumps and roots that remained alive beneath their fields, choosing the strongest shoots and pruning them so that they grew into trees. This approach, known as farmer-managed natural regeneration, spread from village to village, and researchers have estimated that it has helped to restore trees on around five million hectares. The trees protect crops from wind, improve the soil and provide firewood and animal fodder.

Traditional techniques have also been revived. In Burkina Faso, the farmer Yacouba Sawadogo became famous for improving an old method known as zaï, in which farmers dig small pits in hard, crusted soil and fill them with manure before planting. The pits catch rainwater and concentrate nutrients around the seeds, and termites attracted by the manure dig tunnels that help water to soak into the ground. Over several decades, Sawadogo turned barren land into a forest, and in 2018 his work was recognised with the Right Livelihood Award. In Senegal, by contrast, the Great Green Wall has relied more heavily on planting, with millions of trees, many of them acacias valued for producing gum arabic.

As a result of these experiences, the initiative has changed considerably. It is now presented less as a wall than as a mosaic of different projects, including water harvesting, improved grazing management and support for small businesses that make use of products from trees. Its supporters argue that this flexibility is a strength. Critics reply that the name continues to encourage a focus on planting large numbers of trees, which produces impressive headlines but not always lasting results, and that too little of the promised money has reached local communities.

In my view, the story of the Great Green Wall shows how the way a problem is described shapes the solutions that are chosen. An advancing desert suggested a wall; land degradation suggests something slower and less dramatic, but probably more effective: helping millions of farmers and herders to manage their own land better. The original image of the wall was misleading, and I believe that it delayed this change in approach. Yet the initiative deserves credit for bringing international attention and money to the drylands. If that attention is used to support the kind of local work seen in Niger and Burkina Faso, the project may yet achieve much of what it promised.

listeningParts.title: Booking an ancient writing workshop
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a city museum to book a weekend workshop on ancient writing for herself and her daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hallam City Museum, bookings desk. Owen speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I picked up a leaflet about your weekend workshops on ancient writing, and I'd like to book a place for myself and my daughter, if there's still room.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. Where did you find the leaflet, just out of interest? We're trying to work out which kind of advertising actually works.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It was at the library on the high street, on the noticeboard by the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's useful to know, thank you. Right, we have two different workshops running this month. One is called Clay and Reed, where you learn to write cuneiform on clay tablets, the way scribes did in ancient Mesopotamia. The other is called Ink and Papyrus, and that one's about Egyptian hieroglyphs. You paint them with a brush on a sheet of real papyrus.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: They both sound fascinating. Which one would suit a twelve-year-old better?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Both are suitable from age ten, so she'd be fine with either. But I'd say Clay and Reed is the more hands-on of the two. Everyone makes their own tablet from scratch, writes their name on it in cuneiform, and then takes it home to dry. The children usually love that part. The papyrus one is quieter and needs a very steady hand.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: She'd much prefer getting her hands dirty, I think. When is Clay and Reed?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It runs on Saturday mornings. This month there are two sessions, on the eighth and the twenty-second. I'm afraid the eighth is already fully booked, but there are still a few places left on the twenty-second.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The twenty-second is fine. We're free that weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. The session starts at half past ten and finishes at one, so it's two and a half hours altogether, with a short break in the middle. It's worth arriving about ten minutes early, because the tutor starts promptly.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: For adults it's eighteen pounds, and for children under sixteen it's twelve. If you're members of the museum's Friends scheme, you get twenty per cent off, but otherwise it's the standard price.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No, we're not members. So that's thirty pounds for the two of us, is it?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's right, thirty pounds in total.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Fine. Do we need to bring anything with us?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: All the materials are provided: the clay, the reed styluses, and a box to carry your tablet home in. But the clay is quite messy, and it can stain, so I'd strongly recommend wearing old clothes, or bringing an apron if you have one.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Good tip. What about food? Is there anywhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a café on the ground floor, and everyone taking part in a workshop gets a free drink there. You just show your ticket at the counter. It's included in the price, so you might as well use it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Lovely. And where in the building is the workshop held?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It's in the Learning Centre, which is on the second floor, right next to our gallery of Near Eastern antiquities. In fact, the session begins with a short tour of that gallery, and the tutor shows you some genuine tablets that are around four thousand years old, so you can see what you're trying to copy.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's a nice idea. Is there a lift? My daughter's fine, but I've got a bad knee at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, there are two lifts just inside the main entrance. Now, could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Fiona Delacourt. D-E-L-A-C-O-U-R-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your daughter's first name?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Mia.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. I'll email the tickets to you once you've paid. One last thing: will you be coming by car?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Probably, yes. Is there parking at the museum?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Unfortunately we don't have our own car park. The nearest one is the multi-storey car park on Brook Street, which is about five minutes' walk away. There's also some street parking on Mill Lane, but it's limited to two hours, so it wouldn't really be long enough for the workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Brook Street, then. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A new exhibition on the origins of writing
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum guide introduces visitors to a new exhibition about the earliest writing systems.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Signs of the Past, our new exhibition on the beginnings of writing. My name's Ciara, and I'll be giving you a short introduction before you explore on your own. The exhibition has been three years in the making. The idea came about when we were offered a long-term loan of objects from a university collection that had been in storage for decades, and we realised we had the chance to tell a story that most museums can only tell in part.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The exhibition is arranged in four rooms, and each one is devoted to a different region where writing developed early. You'll notice as soon as you go in that the lighting is quite dim. That isn't to create atmosphere, although it does. Many of the objects are made from organic materials, and strong light would fade and weaken them. So please give your eyes a minute to adjust. Photography is allowed throughout, but without flash, for the same reason.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Room One covers Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, where most specialists believe writing first appeared. The highlight here is a small clay tablet from the city of Uruk. It's an account of grain rations, and it's more than five thousand years old, which makes it the oldest object in the whole exhibition. In the same room, you'll find a table with replica cylinder seals. These were small carved stone cylinders that were rolled across wet clay to leave a design, a bit like a signature. You're welcome to pick the replicas up and roll them across the trays of modelling clay.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: In Room Two, we move to Egypt. People often think of hieroglyphs as the only Egyptian script, but in fact, for everyday purposes such as letters and accounts, scribes used a faster, joined-up script called hieratic, and we have some lovely examples on display. The material they usually wrote on, of course, was papyrus, which was made from a plant that grew along the Nile. There's a short film in this room that shows how papyrus sheets were made, using the same methods as in ancient times. It lasts about six minutes and runs continuously.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Room Three is devoted to China. The earliest Chinese writing that has survived is found on what are called oracle bones, from the Shang dynasty, around three thousand two hundred years ago. These were mostly the shoulder blades of oxen and the shells of turtles. A question would be addressed to the royal ancestors, for example whether a harvest would be good, and the bone was heated until it cracked. Specialists interpreted the cracks to predict the future, and the question, and sometimes the answer, was carved into the bone. Many of the characters can still be recognised by people who read Chinese today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, Room Four takes you across the Atlantic to the Maya of Central America. The centrepiece is a full-size replica of the Dresden Codex, one of only four Maya books known to have survived. It's made of bark paper and folds up like a screen. Next to it, there's an interactive display that converts your date of birth into the Maya calendar, and prints it out in Maya numbers for you to take home. Children love it, so there's sometimes a queue.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. The free audio guide is available through the museum's app, which you can download using the museum wi-fi, so you don't need to use your own data. The guide lasts about forty minutes. If you'd prefer a printed booklet, they cost three pounds at the shop. The exhibition is open every day until six, but on Thursdays it stays open until nine, and on those evenings there are short talks by curators at seven o'clock. Right, please do go on in and enjoy it.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on Linear B
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two history students, Zoe and Daniel, discuss their presentation on the decipherment of the Linear B script with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Zoe, Daniel, your presentation's on Linear B. How's the planning going?

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've decided to tell it as a kind of detective story, because that's really what it was. We start in 1900, when Arthur Evans began excavating the palace at Knossos on Crete and found thousands of clay tablets covered in an unknown script.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And we explain that Evans actually identified three scripts on Crete: a hieroglyphic one, Linear A and Linear B. Linear A still hasn't been deciphered, so we're only mentioning it briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. One thing your audience might wonder about is how unbaked clay tablets survived for over three thousand years.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a slide on that. The tablets were only meant to be temporary records, so they weren't baked. Ironically, they survived because the palace was destroyed by fire, which baked them hard. Without that disaster, they'd have crumbled long ago.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, how are you dividing the presentation between you?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm doing the part about Alice Kober. I think she's often left out of the story, and she shouldn't be. She was an American classicist, and in the 1940s she showed that some words appeared in groups of three related forms, with different endings.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Her so-called triplets. And why did that matter?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Because it proved the language had inflections, like Latin or Greek, where the ending of a word changes depending on its grammar. That meant you could start to work out which signs shared the same consonant or the same vowel, even without knowing the language. She did all this on thousands of handmade index cards, at a time when paper was in short supply. Sadly, she died in 1950, just two years before the breakthrough.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: And then I take over with Michael Ventris. What's amazing is that he wasn't a professional scholar at all. He was an architect, and he worked on the script in his spare time. He'd been fascinated by it since he heard Evans give a lecture when he was a schoolboy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what was his great insight?

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: He built on Kober's method and made grids of the signs. For a long time, he was convinced the language was related to Etruscan, not Greek. But when he tried out some sound values on place names from Crete, like Knossos, the words suddenly looked like an early form of Greek. He announced it on BBC radio in 1952, and many people were sceptical at first.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: What convinced them was a tablet found at Pylos, on the Greek mainland. It had pictures of pots with three legs, and the word next to them, using Ventris's values, read as the Greek word for tripod. That was hard to argue with.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Do you deal with what the tablets actually say? People often hope for poetry or history.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Yes, and that's the slight disappointment. They're almost all administrative records: inventories of sheep, wool, chariot wheels, and offerings to the gods. But we want to argue that that's actually valuable, because it tells us how the palace economy worked in detail.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd agree. You might add that the decipherment pushed back the history of the Greek language by several centuries. Now, a word on timing. Your draft runs to twenty-five minutes, and you've only got fifteen.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We know. We were thinking of cutting the section on Linear A completely.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd keep one slide on it, actually. It's a nice way to end, showing that there are still mysteries to solve. Cut some of the background on Evans instead. And practise with a timer.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Okay. And should we mention that Ventris died very young?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Briefly, yes. He was killed in a car accident in 1956, aged only thirty-four, the same year that his book with John Chadwick was published. It's a moving detail, but don't let it take over. Send me the revised slides by Friday.

listeningParts.title: Reading the Maya glyphs
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an archaeology course on how the Maya writing system was deciphered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're looking at one of the great intellectual achievements of the twentieth century: the decipherment of Maya writing. The Maya of southern Mexico and Central America developed the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, one that could record anything their language could express. It was in use from at least the third century BC until after the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most surviving Maya writing is carved in stone, on monuments, temple stairways and altars, but the Maya also painted texts on pottery and wrote books. These books, which we call codices, were made from bark, which was pounded into sheets, coated with a fine layer of lime plaster, and folded like a screen. Thousands must once have existed. Only four survive today, and the best known is the Dresden Codex, named after the German city where it's kept. It contains remarkably accurate astronomical tables, including calculations of the movements of the planet Venus and predictions of eclipses.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why did so few books survive? Partly because bark paper decays quickly in a tropical climate. But there was also deliberate destruction. In 1562, a Spanish friar named Diego de Landa, who later became Bishop of Yucatán, ordered the burning of a large number of Maya books at the town of Maní, because he regarded them as works of the devil. The great irony is that Landa also wrote an account of Maya life, which contains what he believed to be the Maya alphabet. This document would eventually become a key to the decipherment, although it lay forgotten in a Spanish library until the nineteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The problem with Landa's alphabet was that it didn't seem to work. For decades, scholars tried to read texts with it and failed. The reason, we now know, is that the Maya script is not an alphabet. It is what we call a logosyllabic system. Some signs, called logograms, represent whole words, while others represent syllables, usually a consonant followed by a vowel. When Landa asked his informant to write the Spanish letters, the scribe wrote the Maya syllable that sounded most like the name of each letter.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In 1952, a young Soviet scholar, Yuri Knorozov, published an article arguing that Landa's signs should be read as syllables. Knorozov never visited a Maya site until very late in his life; he worked from published drawings in Leningrad. His ideas were rejected for many years, especially by the British scholar Eric Thompson, who was the leading authority in the field and believed the glyphs were mainly symbolic rather than phonetic.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second great step was taken by Tatiana Proskouriakoff, a Russian-born American who had trained as an architect. In 1960, she studied the dates on monuments at the site of Piedras Negras and noticed that they fell into groups, each covering a period no longer than a human lifetime. She concluded that the inscriptions recorded the births, accessions and deaths of real rulers. Until then, most scholars had believed the texts dealt only with the calendar, astronomy and religion. Suddenly, the Maya had a political history, with named kings and queens, wars and alliances.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: From the 1970s onwards, progress was rapid. At a famous conference held at Palenque in 1973, a small group of researchers worked out the sequence of the city's rulers in a single afternoon, including its most famous king, Pakal. Today, specialists can read the great majority of known Maya inscriptions, although some signs are still uncertain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Before we finish, I want to mention numbers. The Maya counted in base twenty rather than base ten, and they wrote numbers using just three symbols: a dot for one, a bar for five, and a shell to represent zero. That makes them one of the very few ancient peoples to have developed the concept of zero independently. And finally, it's worth remembering that the Maya did not disappear. Millions of people speak Maya languages today, and some are now learning to read and write the script of their ancestors. Next week, we'll look at the Maya calendar in more detail.

readingPassages.title: Clay, reeds and the first scribes
paragraphs: Writing is so central to modern life that it is easy to forget how recent an invention it is. Human beings have been speaking for tens of thousands of years, perhaps far longer, but the earliest true writing appeared only about five thousand years ago. Most scholars agree that it emerged first in southern Mesopotamia, the flat, fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq. Writing was also invented independently in at least two other places, China and Mesoamerica, and possibly in Egypt, but the Mesopotamian system, later known as cuneiform, has the longest documented history of development.

The setting for this development was the city of Uruk, which by the late fourth millennium BC was one of the largest settlements in the world, with a population that may have reached several tens of thousands. Its great temples controlled vast quantities of grain, livestock, textiles and labour, and the officials who managed these resources faced a problem that memory alone could not solve: how to keep track of who had delivered what, who was owed rations, and how many animals were in each flock. The oldest tablets from Uruk, dating from around 3200 BC, are overwhelmingly concerned with exactly these matters. Rather than poetry, prayers or history, they record quantities of barley, beer and sheep.

Where did the idea of writing come from? One influential theory was developed by the archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat, who studied thousands of small clay objects, known as tokens, found at sites across the Near East. These tokens, in shapes such as cones, spheres and discs, had been used for several thousand years before writing appeared, and she argued that each shape stood for a particular quantity of a particular commodity. To guarantee a transaction, tokens were sometimes sealed inside hollow clay balls, called envelopes, and their shapes were pressed into the outer surface so that the contents could be checked without breaking the ball. Eventually, Schmandt-Besserat suggested, people realised that the marks on the outside made the tokens themselves unnecessary. Not all scholars accept every part of her account, but most agree that writing grew out of earlier systems of counting and recording.

The earliest signs were mostly pictures, drawn into wet clay with a pointed tool: an ear of grain for barley, a jar for beer, the head of an ox for cattle. Signs for numbers were impressed separately. Over the following centuries, however, scribes began to make their marks by pressing the end of a cut reed into the clay rather than drawing with it. This was quicker, but it produced wedge-shaped strokes, and gradually the pictures became abstract groups of wedges that bore little resemblance to the objects they had once represented. It is from these marks that the script takes its modern name: cuneiform comes from cuneus, the Latin word for a wedge.

An even more important change was the use of signs for their sound rather than their meaning. Sumerian, the language of the early scribes, had many short words, and a sign for one word could be borrowed to write another word, or part of a word, that sounded the same. This principle, often compared to a rebus puzzle, allowed scribes to record personal names, grammatical endings and, eventually, any sentence of the spoken language. By around the middle of the third millennium BC, cuneiform was being used for letters, laws, hymns and literary texts as well as accounts. Among the most famous works later written in cuneiform is the Epic of Gilgamesh, the story of a king of Uruk who searches for immortality.

Learning to write was difficult and took years. Trainee scribes, who were mostly boys, studied at schools known in Sumerian as the edubba, or 'tablet house'. They copied long lists of signs and words again and again, often on small round tablets that could be smoothed and reused. Thousands of these practice tablets have survived, some with the teacher's model on one side and a pupil's imperfect copy on the other. Because clay is easily damaged when wet but extremely durable once dry, and even more so when baked, enormous numbers of cuneiform documents have come down to us, sometimes preserved by the very fires that destroyed the buildings in which they were stored.

Cuneiform proved remarkably adaptable. Over roughly three thousand years, it was used to write a number of quite different languages, including Akkadian, the language of the Babylonians and Assyrians, as well as Hittite in what is now Turkey and Elamite in what is now Iran. For long periods, Akkadian written in cuneiform served as an international language of diplomacy; in the fourteenth century BC, even the rulers of Egypt corresponded with other kings in this script, as shown by the clay letters discovered at Amarna. Gradually, though, cuneiform was replaced by alphabetic scripts written with ink on softer materials, and the last known tablets, which record astronomical observations, date from the first century AD.

The script was then entirely forgotten for nearly two thousand years. Its decipherment in the nineteenth century relied heavily on long inscriptions in more than one language, such as the one carved for the Persian king Darius I on a cliff at Behistun, which the British officer Henry Rawlinson copied at considerable personal risk. In 1857, to test whether the decipherment was reliable, the Royal Asiatic Society in London sent copies of a newly discovered inscription to four scholars, including Rawlinson, and asked them to translate it independently. When their sealed translations were opened and compared, they agreed closely enough to convince most sceptics that the long-dead language could genuinely be read again.

readingPassages.title: The silent script of the Indus
paragraphs: In the 1920s, excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, in what is now Pakistan, revealed a civilisation that had been completely forgotten. At its height, between about 2600 and 1900 BC, the Indus or Harappan civilisation covered an area larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Its cities were laid out on carefully planned grids, with covered drains, large public buildings and houses built from bricks of standardised proportions. Its traders used a uniform system of weights across hundreds of kilometres. Yet, unlike the Egyptians and Mesopotamians, the people of the Indus left no texts that anyone can read, and the language they spoke remains unknown.

This is not because they did not write. Archaeologists have found around four thousand objects bearing signs of the Indus script. The great majority are small square seals carved from soft stone, usually showing an animal, most often a one-horned creature that excavators named the 'unicorn', beneath a short line of signs. Other inscriptions appear on pottery, copper tablets and small clay tags that were probably attached to bundles of goods. What is striking is how brief all of these texts are. The average inscription contains only about five signs, and even the longest have fewer than thirty.

The brevity of the inscriptions is only the first of several difficulties facing anyone who hopes to read them. A second is the absence of a bilingual text, an inscription that gives the same message in a known language as well as in the Indus script. Such texts were crucial in the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform. A third problem is that we do not know which language family the Indus language belonged to, or whether any modern language is descended from it. Successful decipherments have usually depended on at least one of these clues; for the Indus script, none is clearly available.

Nevertheless, careful analysis has established some facts. In 1977, the Indian scholar Iravatham Mahadevan published a concordance, a complete catalogue of the known inscriptions and the signs in them, which identified around four hundred distinct signs. This number is important. Alphabets typically have between twenty and forty letters, and purely syllabic scripts rarely more than about a hundred signs, whereas systems in which signs stand for whole words, such as Chinese, need thousands. A total of around four hundred suggests that, like cuneiform, the Indus script combined signs for words with signs for sounds. Studies of the spacing of signs, which are often squeezed together at the left-hand end of an inscription, also show that the script was normally written from right to left.

Beyond such conclusions, there is little agreement. Dozens of decipherments have been announced, most of which identify the language with one of the major language families of modern South Asia. The Finnish scholar Asko Parpola, among others, has argued for many years that the language was an early form of Dravidian, the family that today includes Tamil and is spoken mainly in southern India. Others have proposed early forms of Sanskrit or entirely different languages. Because the history of the Indian subcontinent is a sensitive political subject, these debates have sometimes become heated, and claims are not always judged on purely scholarly grounds.

In 2004, the debate took a dramatic turn when three researchers, Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel, published a paper arguing that the Indus signs were not writing at all. They pointed out that the inscriptions were extraordinarily short, that many signs appeared only once, and that no example had been found of the kind of long text that literate societies usually produce. In their view, the signs were a system of symbols, perhaps related to religion, family groups or political identity, which could convey meaning without representing a spoken language.

This provocative claim prompted a response from a team led by the computer scientist Rajesh Rao, who in 2009 published a statistical study in the journal Science. The team measured how predictable each sign was given the sign that came before it, and compared the result with known languages and with non-linguistic systems such as DNA sequences and computer code. The Indus script, they reported, fell within the range of linguistic systems, suggesting that it did encode language. Their critics replied that the measure could not reliably distinguish writing from other kinds of structured symbol systems, and the question remains open.

What might settle the matter? Most specialists believe that progress depends on new discoveries. In the 1990s, excavators at Dholavira in western India found a row of ten large signs that had apparently once been fixed above a gateway, perhaps as a kind of public notice, which shows that longer and more public inscriptions may yet be found. Indus seals have also been discovered in Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian texts refer to a distant land called Meluhha, which many scholars identify with the Indus region. If a bilingual document from this long-distance trade were ever unearthed, it could do for the Indus script what the great trilingual inscriptions did for the scripts of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

readingPassages.title: Did writing change the way we think?
paragraphs: Few inventions have been credited with as much influence as writing. It has been said to have made possible history, science, law, philosophy and the modern state. A bolder claim, however, is that writing did not merely give people a new tool but changed the way human beings think. This idea has been argued, attacked and refined for more than half a century, and it remains one of the most interesting questions in the study of the human past.

The debate has a surprisingly ancient starting point. In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, written in the fourth century BC, Socrates tells a story in which the Egyptian god Theuth presents his invention of writing to King Thamus, claiming that it will improve memory and wisdom. The king disagrees. Writing, he says, will make people forgetful, because they will rely on marks outside themselves instead of their own memories, and it will give them the appearance of wisdom without the reality. It is an irony often noted that we know of this criticism of writing only because Plato wrote it down.

The modern version of the debate began with scholars of oral poetry. In the 1920s and 1930s, the American classicist Milman Parry argued that the Homeric epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, showed clear signs of having been composed without writing. Their repeated phrases, such as 'swift-footed Achilles', were not decoration but tools that allowed a singer to compose verse rapidly during performance. To test this theory, Parry and his assistant Albert Lord recorded living oral poets in Yugoslavia, some of whom could perform poems of many thousands of lines. Their work suggested that oral cultures possessed sophisticated techniques of memory and composition that literate cultures had largely lost.

Building on such research, several scholars in the 1960s and later proposed that literacy had transformed human thought. The anthropologist Jack Goody argued that writing made possible new intellectual tools, particularly lists and tables, which allowed information to be detached from its context, compared and reorganised. Walter Ong, in his influential book Orality and Literacy, published in 1982, went further, claiming that writing 'restructures consciousness'. In Ong's account, oral thinking tends to be practical, concrete and closely tied to human situations, whereas literate thinking is more abstract, analytical and detached.

These claims were soon challenged. In a study published in 1981, the psychologists Sylvia Scribner and Michael Cole investigated the Vai people of Liberia, some of whom had learned to read and write an indigenous script outside any school. This allowed the researchers to separate the effects of literacy from those of formal education, which earlier studies had confused. They found that literacy alone did not produce general improvements in abstract reasoning. Instead, it was associated with specific skills linked to the particular ways the script was used, such as writing letters. Schooling, not writing as such, seemed to explain many of the differences that had been attributed to literacy.

More recently, neuroscience has added a different kind of evidence. The French researcher Stanislas Dehaene has shown that reading relies on a small region of the brain's visual system, which in literate people becomes specialised for recognising letters and words. Because writing is far too recent for the brain to have evolved specifically for it, Dehaene proposes that reading 'recycles' circuits that originally evolved for other purposes, such as recognising objects and faces. Learning to read, in other words, physically changes the brain, although this tells us more about perception than about the higher forms of thought that Goody and Ong had in mind.

In my view, the strongest versions of the argument that writing transformed the mind should be rejected. They tended to portray people in oral cultures as less capable of abstract or logical thought, a conclusion that is not supported by the evidence and that sat uncomfortably close to older prejudices about so-called primitive societies. The oral poets recorded by Parry and Lord, after all, were performing feats of memory and composition that few literate people could equal. Yet it would be equally mistaken to conclude that writing changed nothing. Writing allows ideas to be stored, compared and criticised across generations, and over time this has transformed what societies can know, even if it has not transformed the individual mind.

The debate has acquired fresh relevance in the digital age. Many people now worry that search engines and smartphones are weakening memory and attention, in much the same way that Thamus feared writing would. It is tempting to dismiss such fears, as Thamus has been dismissed, as the familiar anxiety that accompanies every new technology. In my view, that would be too easy. The history of writing suggests that new technologies of information rarely make us more or less intelligent, but they do change which skills a society values and which it allows to decline. The real question is not whether our tools change us, but whether we choose those changes wisely.

listeningParts.title: Hiring an electric car
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a car hire company to book an electric car for a weekend trip.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, GreenWheels Car Hire, Martin speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Hi. I'd like to hire an electric car for a long weekend later this month, but I've never actually driven one before, so I've got quite a few questions.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem at all. Lots of our customers are first-time electric drivers. When would you need the car?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: From Friday the fourteenth to Monday the seventeenth. I'd collect it on the Friday morning and bring it back on Monday afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me just check the system. Yes, that's fine, we have cars available on those dates. At the moment we offer two models. The smaller one is the City, which is a five-door hatchback. It can travel about two hundred and eighty kilometres on a full charge. The larger one is the Tourer, which has much more space for luggage and a range of around four hundred and fifty kilometres.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: We're driving to the coast, which is about three hundred kilometres from here, so I suppose the Tourer would be better.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'd definitely recommend it. You could do the trip in the City, but you'd have to stop and charge on the way. And bear in mind that in cold weather the range drops, sometimes by as much as twenty per cent, because the heater and the battery itself use more energy when it's cold.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Oh, I didn't know that. The Tourer, then. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Tourer is sixty-two pounds a day, so for four days that comes to two hundred and forty-eight pounds. The City would have been forty-five pounds a day, just so you know.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's fine. Does the price include insurance?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Basic insurance is included, but there's an excess of eight hundred pounds. That means if the car is damaged, you'd pay up to eight hundred pounds yourself. You can reduce the excess to zero by paying an extra nine pounds a day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think I'll take that. I'd rather not have to worry about it on holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Very sensible. Now, charging. The car will be fully charged when you collect it. Some companies ask you to bring the car back with at least eighty per cent, but we only ask for seventy. If it's below that, there's a fee of fifteen pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And how do I pay when I charge on the road? Do I need to set up accounts with different companies?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, the car comes with a charging card that works at most public chargers in the country. You just hold it against the charger, and the cost is added to your bill when you return the car.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's easy. How long does charging take?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It depends on the charger. At a rapid charger, like the ones at motorway service stations, you can go from ten to eighty per cent in about thirty-five minutes, which is long enough for a coffee and a sandwich. At a normal charger, like the ones you find in hotel car parks, it takes about seven hours, so leaving it overnight is ideal.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think our hotel has chargers. Will I need my own cable?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, there's a cable in the boot. It's stored under the floor panel, so it's easy to miss, but it's definitely there.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Good to know. Is there anything else that's different about driving an electric car?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Two main things. First, it's very quiet, so watch out for pedestrians who might not hear you coming, especially in car parks. Second, when you lift your foot off the accelerator, the car slows down quite strongly, because the motor is recharging the battery. It takes a few minutes to get used to, but most people end up loving it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Okay, I'm convinced. Can I book it now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. Can I take your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Joanna Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Ms Whitcombe. And where would you like to collect the car from? We have two branches, one at the railway station and one on Canal Street.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The station would be easier for me, because I'll be arriving by train.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Fine. The station branch opens at eight. When you come, please bring your driving licence and a credit card. I'm afraid we can't accept debit cards for the deposit, because we need to be able to hold the money for a few days.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No problem. I've got both. Thanks so much for all your help, Martin.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: You're welcome. I'll email the confirmation to you within the hour. Enjoy your trip to the coast.
