listeningParts.title: A tour of a former nuclear power station
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes visitors to an energy centre on the site of a nuclear power station that is being dismantled.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hollins Bay Energy Centre. My name's Declan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a little background about the site and explain what we'll be seeing on the tour.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Hollins Bay power station opened in 1968, and for more than forty years it generated electricity from nuclear power. At its peak, it supplied enough electricity for around one and a half million homes. It stopped generating in 2012, and since then it's been going through a process called decommissioning, which simply means taking the plant apart safely and cleaning up the site. People are often surprised to hear how long that takes.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The fuel was removed from the reactors during the first four years, and that was by far the most important stage, because the fuel contained more than ninety-nine per cent of the radioactivity on the site. Once it had gone, the risks dropped enormously. However, the full process of dismantling the buildings and returning the land to other uses is not expected to finish until the 2080s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Visitors often ask why it takes so long. The main reason is that some of the materials inside the reactor buildings will remain radioactive for decades. It's actually safer, and cheaper, to wait for that radioactivity to decline naturally before workers go in and take the structures apart. So the reactor buildings themselves will be sealed and monitored for many years. You'll see them from outside, but nobody goes into them now except specialist teams.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: But this site isn't only about the past. In 2021, part of the land was used to build a large battery storage facility, which we call the Battery Park. You might wonder why it was put here, rather than somewhere closer to a city. The answer is that because the power station was connected to the national grid, the heavy cables and connections were already in place, which saved a great deal of money and time. The batteries store electricity when there's plenty of wind power, often during the night, and then release it when demand is highest, which is usually in the early evening, when people get home and start cooking.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One more thing before we start. Around a third of our guides used to work in the power station itself, as engineers or technicians, so if you have detailed questions about how it operated, please do ask them. They know far more than I do.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the route. We'll begin in the Exhibition Hall, just behind me. It has lots of interactive displays, including a simulator where you can try to balance supply and demand on the electricity grid. Children love it, though it's much harder than it looks. The entrance building that you came through, by the way, was rebuilt only last year, after a storm damaged the roof.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: From there, we'll go across to the Turbine Hall. This is the largest building on the site, and the giant turbines are still in place. Because it's a working area for the decommissioning team, everybody will need to wear a hard hat, which we'll hand out at the door. Please don't remove it until you're outside again.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next is the Control Room, which has been kept exactly as it was on the day the station closed, right down to the logbooks on the desks. It's quite small, so we'll go in groups of ten. Unfortunately, it's at the top of a narrow staircase and there's no lift, so it can't be reached by wheelchair users. However, there's a video tour of it in the Exhibition Hall, so nobody needs to miss out.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: After that, we'll walk to the Viewing Gallery on the roof of the old administration block. From there, you get wonderful views right along the coast, and on a clear day you can see the offshore wind farm, about twelve kilometres out to sea.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, we'll finish at the Battery Park. For security reasons, we ask you not to take any photographs there, although you're very welcome to take pictures everywhere else on the tour. The whole tour lasts about ninety minutes. Afterwards, the café by the entrance is open, although only at weekends during the winter. Right, if you'd like to follow me.

listeningParts.title: Recycling electric car batteries
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two engineering students, Tom and Mei, discuss their project on battery recycling with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen to look at what happens to electric car batteries at the end of their lives. How's the research going?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We started by trying to work out how big the problem will be. At the moment, the number of electric car batteries reaching the end of their life is still quite small, because most electric cars on the road are fairly new. But by the 2030s, the numbers are expected to rise very steeply.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: And one thing we hadn't realised is that a battery that's no longer good enough for a car isn't actually dead. Car makers usually consider a battery worn out when it can only hold around seventy to eighty per cent of its original charge, because the driving range becomes too short. But it can still be perfectly useful for other things.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: You mean what's called second-life use?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Exactly. Old car batteries can be combined and used for stationary storage, for example to store solar power for a building. Weight and size don't matter much there, so a lower capacity is acceptable. We visited a company that does this, and they said a battery can often work for another ten years or so.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's interesting, but does that simply delay the recycling problem?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It does, yes, and some people argue it's better to recycle straight away, so the materials get back into new car batteries sooner. That's one of the questions we want to discuss in the report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what about the recycling itself? What methods did you look at?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: There are two main ones at the moment. The first is basically smelting: the batteries are put into a furnace at very high temperatures, and metals like cobalt, nickel and copper are recovered. It's a well-established process, but it uses a lot of energy, and most of the lithium ends up in a waste product called slag, where it's difficult to recover.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: The second method is to discharge the batteries, take them apart and shred them. That produces a dark powder that the industry calls black mass, which contains the valuable metals. Then chemicals are used to dissolve the metals and separate them. It uses less energy and recovers more of the lithium, but it involves strong acids, so the waste water has to be treated carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And is there anything newer on the horizon?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, researchers are working on what's called direct recycling, where the cathode material is repaired and reused without breaking it down into separate metals. It could be much cheaper, but it's still mostly at the laboratory stage.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What did you find was the biggest practical obstacle?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Honestly, it's the design of the batteries. Manufacturers use strong glues to hold the cells together, so taking a battery pack apart can take a skilled worker several hours. And every manufacturer's packs are different, so it's very hard to automate.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to make. And there's a safety issue too, isn't there?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Definitely. A damaged battery can catch fire, and the fires are very hard to put out. Actually, recycling centres say the bigger problem at the moment is small batteries from things like phones and vapes that people throw away with their ordinary rubbish. They get crushed in the lorries and start fires.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what's the case for recycling? Why does it matter so much?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Partly it's environmental, of course, but there's also the question of supply. A small number of countries control a large share of the mining and processing of these metals. Around seventy per cent of the world's cobalt, for example, is mined in one country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Recycling could make countries less dependent on imports.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the next stage, I'd like you to compare the costs of the two main methods. And please contact the recycling plant near Coventry. They've helped students before.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: We'll email them this week. Should we include a section on government policy?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, briefly. The European Union has introduced rules requiring new batteries to contain a minimum share of recycled material in future, so mention those. Keep it to about a page, though.

listeningParts.title: The quest for fusion power
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a physics and energy course about nuclear fusion and the challenges of using it to generate electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Last week we looked at nuclear fission, the process used in every nuclear power station operating today, in which heavy atoms such as uranium are split apart. Today I want to turn to the opposite process, nuclear fusion, which many people regard as the ultimate source of clean energy, and explain why it has proved so extraordinarily difficult to achieve.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Fusion is the process that powers the Sun and every other star. In the Sun's core, the pressure created by its enormous gravity forces hydrogen nuclei so close together that they fuse to form helium, releasing huge amounts of energy in the process. The problem for us on Earth is that we can't reproduce the Sun's gravity. To make fusion happen here, we have to compensate by making the fuel far hotter than the centre of the Sun: over a hundred million degrees Celsius, which is several times hotter than the Sun's core.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what fuel do we use? The most promising fuel for a power station is a mixture of two forms of hydrogen, called deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is a heavier form of hydrogen, and it can be extracted from ordinary seawater. There's enough of it in the oceans to supply the world for millions of years. Tritium is more of a problem. It's radioactive, it decays fairly quickly, and there's very little of it in nature. So a fusion power station would have to produce, or breed, its own tritium from lithium inside the reactor itself, and nobody has yet shown that this can be done on the scale required.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At temperatures of a hundred million degrees, the fuel is no longer an ordinary gas. It becomes a plasma, a state of matter in which the electrons have been separated from the nuclei of the atoms. Obviously, no material container could survive contact with something that hot, so scientists have developed two main ways of holding the fuel in place.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first, and the one that's received most investment, is called magnetic confinement. Because a plasma is made of charged particles, it can be controlled by magnetic fields. The most common design is a doughnut-shaped chamber surrounded by powerful magnets, known as a tokamak. The design was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1950s and 1960s, and the word tokamak is in fact a Russian acronym. For forty years, the most successful machine of this type was JET, the Joint European Torus, near Oxford in England, which operated from 1983 until the end of 2023. In its final experiments, it set a world record for the amount of energy released in a single fusion experiment. Its successor, ITER, is now being built in southern France by a collaboration of around thirty-five countries. ITER is designed to produce ten times more fusion power than the power used to heat the plasma, but it has faced long delays and its cost has risen many times over.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second approach is called inertial confinement, and it uses lasers instead of magnets. At the National Ignition Facility in California, a hundred and ninety-two lasers are fired at a tiny capsule of fuel, about the size of a peppercorn. The capsule is crushed and heated so quickly that the fuel fuses before it has time to fly apart. In December 2022, scientists there announced that, for the first time, a fusion experiment had released more energy than the laser energy delivered to the fuel. This is known as ignition, and it was a genuine milestone. However, I should point out that the lasers themselves used around a hundred times more electricity from the grid than the experiment produced, so we're still a long way from a power station.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why go to all this trouble? Well, fusion has some very attractive features. It produces no carbon dioxide. It can't run out of control, because there's no chain reaction as there is in fission. In fact, if anything goes wrong, the plasma simply cools and the reaction stops within seconds. And it doesn't produce the long-lived high-level waste that comes from fission reactors. The walls of the reactor do become radioactive over time, but this material should be safe to handle after decades rather than thousands of years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The challenges, though, are enormous. Engineers need materials that can survive years of bombardment by the high-energy particles released by fusion. They need to breed tritium reliably. And they need to do all this at a cost that can compete with other sources of electricity. There's an old joke among physicists that fusion is thirty years away, and always will be. In recent years, dozens of private companies have entered the field, attracting billions of dollars of investment and promising much faster progress. Even so, most experts believe fusion is unlikely to make a significant contribution to electricity supplies before the second half of this century, which means it can't replace the need to cut emissions with the technologies we already have.

readingPassages.title: The battery that changed the world
paragraphs: Few inventions have changed daily life as quietly as the rechargeable lithium-ion battery. It powers almost every mobile phone and laptop in the world, as well as the great majority of electric cars, and it is increasingly used to store electricity from wind and solar farms. Yet the technology is surprisingly young. The first lithium-ion batteries went on sale only in 1991, and the three scientists who made them possible were not recognised with a Nobel Prize until 2019.

The basic idea of the battery is much older. In 1800, the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta built a stack of alternating copper and zinc discs separated by pieces of cloth soaked in salt water, and showed that it produced a steady electric current. Volta's 'pile' could not be recharged: once the chemical reactions inside it were complete, it was useless. The first practical rechargeable battery, the lead-acid battery, was invented by the French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859, and versions of it are still used to start the engines of petrol and diesel cars today. Lead-acid batteries are cheap and reliable, but they are also very heavy for the amount of energy they store.

Chemists had long known that lithium, the lightest of all metals, was an attractive material for batteries. Because it gives up its electrons very readily, it can produce a high voltage, and because it is so light, a lithium battery could in principle store far more energy per kilogram than a lead-acid one. The difficulty was that lithium is also extremely reactive. It reacts violently with water and can catch fire when exposed to air. For decades, this made it seem far too dangerous to use in a product that ordinary people would carry around with them.

The breakthrough came in the 1970s, when the oil crisis of 1973 had led governments and companies to search urgently for alternatives to fossil fuels. Stanley Whittingham, a British-born chemist working for the oil company Exxon in the United States, developed a battery in which lithium ions moved into and out of a material called titanium disulphide. His battery produced just over two volts, which was promising. However, its other electrode was made of pure lithium metal, and when the battery was recharged repeatedly, thin threads of lithium grew inside it. These could reach the opposite electrode, causing short circuits and even explosions.

The next steps were taken by two other scientists. In 1980, at the University of Oxford, the American physicist John Goodenough showed that a cathode made of cobalt oxide could produce around four volts, making a much more powerful battery possible. Then, in 1985, the Japanese chemist Akira Yoshino, working for the company Asahi Kasei, replaced the dangerous lithium metal with a form of carbon called petroleum coke, in which lithium ions could be stored. Yoshino's design was lighter and safer, could be recharged hundreds of times, and formed the basis of the first commercial lithium-ion battery, which the Japanese electronics company Sony began selling in 1991.

At first, lithium-ion batteries were used mainly in portable electronic devices such as video cameras, mobile phones and laptop computers, where their light weight was a decisive advantage. Their use in cars came later, and it was made possible by a dramatic fall in price. According to industry analysts, the average cost of a lithium-ion battery pack fell by roughly ninety per cent between 2010 and 2020, largely as a result of mass production and steady improvements in manufacturing. As a result, electric cars, which had once been expensive curiosities, began to compete seriously with petrol and diesel vehicles.

The same fall in prices has made it possible to use batteries on a very large scale to support electricity grids. One of the best-known early examples is the Hornsdale Power Reserve in South Australia, which was built by the American company Tesla and began operating in 2017. At the time, it was the largest lithium-ion battery installation in the world. Such facilities can respond to sudden changes in supply or demand within a fraction of a second, which helps to keep the grid stable as a growing share of electricity comes from wind and solar power, whose output varies with the weather.

Lithium-ion batteries are not without problems. Mining lithium, cobalt and nickel can damage the environment and, in some places, has been linked to poor working conditions. Damaged batteries can overheat and catch fire. Researchers are therefore exploring alternatives, including sodium-ion batteries, which use a far more abundant element, and solid-state batteries, which replace the flammable liquid inside current batteries with a solid material. When the Nobel Prize was finally awarded, Goodenough was 97, making him the oldest person ever to receive one. He lived until 2023, by which time the invention he had helped to create had become one of the foundations of the world's effort to move away from fossil fuels.

readingPassages.title: Hydrogen: fuel of the future?
paragraphs: Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe, and for well over a century it has been described as the fuel of the future. In The Mysterious Island, published in the 1870s, the French novelist Jules Verne had one of his characters predict that water would one day be used as fuel, with the hydrogen and oxygen it contains providing an inexhaustible source of heat and light. When hydrogen is burned or used in a fuel cell, the only by-product is water. It is hardly surprising, then, that it has attracted renewed interest as countries try to cut their carbon emissions. Whether it will play a central role in the energy system, or a much more limited one, remains a subject of intense debate.

Hydrogen was first recognised as a distinct substance in 1766 by the English scientist Henry Cavendish, who called it 'inflammable air'. In 1783, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it its modern name, from the Greek for 'water-former', after showing that it produced water when burned. Because it is the lightest of all gases, hydrogen was soon used to fill balloons, and in the early twentieth century it lifted the great passenger airships. That era ended abruptly in 1937, when the German airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing in New Jersey, killing thirty-six people. The disaster gave hydrogen a reputation for danger that it has never entirely lost.

What many people do not realise is that hydrogen is already a major industrial product. Nearly one hundred million tonnes are produced each year, mostly for refining oil and for making ammonia, the basis of most of the world's nitrogen fertilisers. Almost all of it, however, is made from fossil fuels, mainly by reacting natural gas with steam at high temperatures, a process that releases large quantities of carbon dioxide. As a result, hydrogen production today is responsible for more greenhouse gas emissions than some entire countries. Before hydrogen can help to solve the climate problem, in other words, the existing industry must itself be cleaned up.

To describe the different ways of making hydrogen, the industry has adopted a system of colours. Hydrogen made from natural gas without any attempt to capture the carbon dioxide is known as grey hydrogen. If the carbon dioxide is captured and stored underground, the result is called blue hydrogen, although critics point out that capture rates are often lower than promised and that methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, can leak from gas wells and pipelines. Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis, in which an electric current from renewable sources such as wind or solar power is used to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Green hydrogen produces almost no emissions, but it currently costs considerably more than grey hydrogen and makes up only a tiny fraction of total production.

Even when it has been produced cleanly, hydrogen is awkward to handle. Although it contains more energy per kilogram than petrol, it contains very little energy per litre at normal pressure, because it is so light. To be useful as a fuel for vehicles, it must either be compressed to around seven hundred times atmospheric pressure or cooled to minus 253 degrees Celsius to turn it into a liquid. Both processes consume a significant amount of energy. Hydrogen's tiny molecules can also escape through very small gaps, and over time the gas can make some metals brittle, so pipelines and storage tanks must be specially designed.

A further drawback is efficiency. Every time energy is converted from one form to another, some of it is lost. When renewable electricity is used to make hydrogen, which is then compressed, transported and turned back into electricity in a fuel cell, much of the original energy disappears along the way. For this reason, a battery electric car can travel roughly two to three times as far as a hydrogen fuel-cell car on the same amount of renewable electricity. This helps to explain why, despite years of government support in countries such as Japan and South Korea, sales of hydrogen cars remain tiny compared with those of battery electric cars.

None of this means that hydrogen has no future. There are some activities for which batteries are unlikely to be practical and for which few other low-carbon options exist. Steelmaking is one. Conventional blast furnaces use coal both as a fuel and to remove oxygen from iron ore, but hydrogen can do the same chemical job, producing water instead of carbon dioxide. In 2021, a Swedish project known as HYBRIT delivered what it described as the world's first steel made using fossil-free hydrogen to the vehicle manufacturer Volvo. Hydrogen, or fuels made from it such as ammonia, may also be needed for long-distance shipping and for storing energy over many months, which batteries cannot yet do economically.

In 2021, the energy analyst Michael Liebreich proposed what he called a 'hydrogen ladder', a ranking of possible uses from those where clean hydrogen is essential to those where other technologies are likely to win. Fertiliser production and steelmaking are near the top; heating homes and powering cars are near the bottom. The ladder has been widely discussed because it captures a broader point. Hydrogen is a valuable but limited resource, and the challenge for governments is not to promote it everywhere, but to direct it towards the places where it will make the greatest difference.

readingPassages.title: Should nuclear power be part of the answer?
paragraphs: Few energy sources divide opinion as sharply as nuclear power. To its supporters, it is a reliable, low-carbon source of electricity that can run day and night regardless of the weather, and that the world cannot afford to ignore if it is serious about climate change. To its opponents, it is expensive, slow to build and potentially catastrophic when things go wrong, and it leaves behind waste that will remain dangerous for thousands of years. Nuclear power currently generates just under a tenth of the world's electricity, so the question of whether that share should grow or shrink is far from academic.

The strongest evidence of what nuclear power can achieve comes from France. After the oil crisis of 1973 exposed the country's dependence on imported oil, the French government launched an ambitious programme, often called the Messmer plan after the prime minister of the time, to build dozens of reactors in little more than fifteen years. Today nuclear power provides around two thirds of France's electricity, and its power sector produces far less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity than those of neighbouring countries that rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The French experience suggests that when reactors are built in large numbers to a standard design, costs and construction times can be kept under control.

Public fear of nuclear power owes much to two accidents. In 1986, an explosion at the Chernobyl plant in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, spread radioactive material across much of Europe, and a large area around the plant remains largely closed today. In 2011, an earthquake and tsunami in Japan disabled the cooling systems at the Fukushima Daiichi plant, causing meltdowns in three reactors. Yet the number of deaths directly caused by radiation at Fukushima was very small, and studies have found that the hurried evacuation of the surrounding area, particularly of elderly and sick people, caused far more deaths than radiation itself. When deaths from accidents and air pollution are measured per unit of electricity generated, nuclear power turns out to be among the safest sources of energy, comparable with wind and solar power and far safer than coal.

Fukushima nevertheless had dramatic political consequences, and not only in Japan, which shut down all of its reactors for safety checks and restarted only some of them years later. In Germany, the government responded by bringing forward its plans to phase out nuclear power, and the country's last three reactors were closed in April 2023. Germany has expanded its use of renewable energy enormously, but critics argue that, by closing working nuclear plants before its coal plants, it burned more coal than it otherwise would have done, increasing both carbon emissions and air pollution.

The most serious practical objection to nuclear power today concerns cost and time. Several recent projects in Europe and North America have run years behind schedule and far over budget. The Olkiluoto 3 reactor in Finland is a striking example: construction began in 2005, with completion planned for 2009, but the reactor did not begin regular electricity production until 2023. Meanwhile, the cost of solar panels, wind turbines and batteries has fallen dramatically, so that in many countries new renewable capacity is now considerably cheaper to build. Supporters of nuclear power respond that such comparisons ignore the cost of backing up wind and solar power when the weather is calm or cloudy.

Then there is the question of waste. The volume of highly radioactive waste is relatively small, but it must be kept isolated from people and the environment for many thousands of years. For decades, no country had a permanent solution, and spent fuel was kept in temporary stores, often at the power stations themselves. Finland, again, has taken the lead. At Onkalo, near Olkiluoto, it has built a repository in which spent fuel will be sealed in copper canisters and buried in solid rock more than four hundred metres underground. It is expected to be the first facility of its kind in the world to begin operating.

Many hopes for the future rest on new technologies. Small modular reactors, which would be built in factories and transported to their sites, are intended to reduce the costs and delays that have troubled large projects, although only a handful have yet been built anywhere in the world, and none in large numbers. Fusion power, which would join atoms together rather than splitting them, promises abundant energy with far less long-lived waste, but even its supporters admit that it is unlikely to supply significant amounts of electricity for several decades.

In my view, the case against nuclear power on grounds of safety is much weaker than its reputation suggests, and the closure of reactors that were operating safely, while coal plants continued to run, was a mistake. The objection based on cost, however, is a serious one, and supporters of nuclear power too often dismiss it. Money spent on a reactor that takes fifteen years to build cannot also be spent on wind and solar farms that could be producing clean electricity within two or three. The sensible conclusion, I believe, is that existing reactors should be kept running for as long as they are safe, and that new ones should be built only where they can be delivered on time and at a reasonable cost. Nor should the waste problem be seen as unsolvable: Finland has shown that it is a question of political will rather than technical possibility.

mockExams.title: Mock Exam 21: Mountains, Glaciers & the Polar Regions

listeningParts.title: Booking a guided glacier walk
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones the visitor centre of a national park to book a guided walk on a glacier.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Icefield Discovery Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm planning a trip to the national park in August with my sister, and I'm interested in one of your guided glacier walks. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two guided walks on the glacier itself. The first is the Ice Explorer, which is a half-day trip. You spend about three hours on the ice, and it's suitable for anyone aged ten or over who can walk comfortably for a few hours. The second is the Glacier Discovery, which is a full day, roughly seven hours, and it goes much further up the glacier, towards the icefall.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sorry, what's an icefall?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a steep part of the glacier where the ice breaks up into huge blocks and deep cracks, which we call crevasses. You don't go into it, of course, but you get a fantastic view of it. The full-day walk is more demanding, so we ask that people are fit and have done some hill walking before.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We both do a lot of hiking at home, so I think the full day would be fine. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Glacier Discovery is a hundred and sixty-five dollars per person. The half-day trip is ninety-five. The price includes a qualified guide, transport from the centre to the start of the trail, and all the specialist equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What kind of equipment do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Crampons, which are metal spikes that attach to your boots so you don't slip on the ice, as well as a helmet and a harness. You'll need your own boots, though. They have to be stiff mountain boots, because ordinary trainers or soft walking shoes won't hold crampons properly.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I've got proper boots, but my sister only has light walking shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's not a problem. We rent boots here at the centre for fifteen dollars a day. Just let us know her size in advance, so we can have a pair ready.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. And what else should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Layers of warm clothing, gloves and a hat, because it can be cold on the ice even in the middle of summer. And sunglasses are essential. The sunlight reflected off the ice is very strong, and without good sunglasses you can actually damage your eyes. Sun cream too, of course. We provide lunch on the full-day trip, but bring plenty of water.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Which days does the full-day walk run?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: In August it runs on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and groups are limited to twelve people.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Could we book for Wednesday the fourteenth?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me just check. I'm sorry, the fourteenth is already fully booked. But there are still a few places on Friday the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The sixteenth is fine. We're staying in the area for a whole week.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Rachel Dunmore. That's D-U-N-M-O-R-E.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks, Rachel. Now, on the day, please be at the centre by seven forty-five. The bus leaves at eight o'clock sharp, and it's about a forty-minute drive to the trailhead.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there parking at the centre?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a large car park behind the building, and it's free for people on our tours. Just leave a note with your booking reference on the dashboard so the attendant knows you're with us.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what happens if the weather is bad?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Our guides make the decision early on the morning of the trip. If there's heavy rain, strong wind or fog, we cancel, because it isn't safe on the ice when you can't see the crevasses clearly. In that case, you can either have a full refund or move to another date.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That seems fair. Do we need to pay everything now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, we take a deposit of fifty dollars per person to hold the places, and the rest is paid when you arrive. I can take the deposit over the phone by card if you like.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do that. Oh, and one more thing. Is there anything to do at the centre if we arrive early?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a small exhibition about how the glacier has changed over the last hundred years or so. There are photographs taken in the 1920s that show the ice reaching almost down to where the car park is now. Today, the front of the glacier is about two kilometres further up the valley, so it's quite a striking comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds really interesting. Thanks very much for your help, Megan.

listeningParts.title: A welcome talk at a mountain national park
listeningParts.contextDescription: A park ranger gives an evening talk to visitors at a national park visitor centre.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Ben Arran National Park. I'm Fiona, one of the park rangers, and I'm going to spend the next twenty minutes or so telling you a little about the park, how to stay safe in the mountains, and some of the trails and huts you can use during your stay.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The park was established in 1987, and it covers just over nine hundred square kilometres. It contains eleven peaks over a thousand metres high, which makes it one of the most popular areas for hill walking in the country. Around three hundred thousand people visit each year, most of them between May and September. That brings a lot of money into the local villages, but it also causes problems. The biggest one, perhaps surprisingly, isn't litter, because most visitors are very good about taking it home. It's the erosion of the paths. When a path gets muddy, people walk around the edges, and the path gets wider and wider until whole hillsides are scarred. So please stay on the stone surface, even when it's wet.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, safety. The weather in the mountains can change remarkably quickly. It's quite common to set off in sunshine and find yourself in thick cloud an hour later, and the temperature at the summits is usually around eight to ten degrees lower than it is down here in the valley. So whatever the forecast says, carry waterproofs and an extra warm layer. And please don't rely only on your phone for navigation. Batteries run down fast in the cold, and in many parts of the park there's no signal at all. We strongly recommend carrying a paper map and a compass, and knowing how to use them. In fact, we run free map-reading sessions here at the visitor centre every Saturday morning, and you're all very welcome to come along.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Before you set off on a longer walk, leave details of your route and the time you expect to be back with someone, either a friend or the staff at your accommodation. If something does go wrong, call the emergency number and ask for the police, and then for mountain rescue. The rescue teams here are all volunteers, and they're called out around sixty times a year. A surprising number of those call-outs aren't because of injuries at all, but because walkers have simply got lost or been caught out by darkness. So check what time the sun sets and give yourself plenty of time to get down.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about four routes and huts I'd particularly like to mention. The Lochside Trail is the easiest. It's a flat circuit of about eight kilometres around the loch, and it's the only route in the park that's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs along most of its length. There's a café at the halfway point, which is open from Easter until the end of October.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The Corrie Path is a steeper walk up into a corrie, which is a bowl-shaped hollow carved out by a glacier during the last ice age. At the top there's a small lake, and in early summer it's one of the best places in the park to see alpine flowers. The path is steep and rocky in places, so I wouldn't recommend it for young children.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Then there's Stag Ridge, which is the classic route to the highest summit. It's a long day, eight hours or more, and there's a narrow section near the top where you'll need to use your hands to climb over the rocks. In winter conditions it should only be attempted by people with an ice axe and crampons and the experience to use them. We've had several serious accidents there involving people who underestimated it.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Finally, for those of you who'd like to stay overnight in the hills, there's Glenbeg Hut. It's a simple stone shelter, the kind of building known in Scotland as a bothy. It's free to use and you don't need to book, but there's no electricity or running water, so you'll need to bring your own sleeping bag and stove. Please carry all your rubbish out with you. The hut is looked after by a charity whose members are all volunteers, so if you use it, do consider making a donation. Glenbeg is also the best spot in the park for seeing red deer, especially at dawn.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Before I finish, a quick word about wildlife. In spring, several kinds of bird lay their eggs on the ground on the open hillsides, so between April and July we ask dog owners to keep their dogs on a short lead. And please don't feed the deer near the car parks. It encourages them to come close to the roads, and sadly several are hit by cars every year. Right, I'll be at the information desk for the next half hour if you have any questions, and you can pick up a free trail map on your way out.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on shrinking mountain glaciers
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Jake and Amira, discuss their presentation on mountain glaciers with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Jake, Amira. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation on mountain glaciers. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: We've done most of the research, and we've agreed on the structure. We want to start with the evidence that glaciers are shrinking, then look at why it matters for people living downstream, and finish with some of the ways communities are responding.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. What evidence are you planning to use for the first part?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We were going to show a lot of graphs of measurements, but we decided that might be a bit dry for the audience. So instead we're going to open with repeat photography. That's where you take a photo from exactly the same spot as an old historical photograph, so you can compare them directly. There are some amazing pairs from the Alps, where you can see a valley full of ice in about 1900 and then just bare rock today.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Those images are very powerful. But make sure you also give some numbers, so it doesn't seem like you're relying on a few dramatic pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll include figures from the Swiss monitoring network. Switzerland has some of the best long-term records in the world, and their data show that Swiss glaciers lost around ten per cent of their total volume in just two years, 2022 and 2023. Both years had very hot summers and not much snow in the winter before.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a striking figure. Are you going to mention Iceland as well?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Yes, we want to talk about Okjökull. It was officially declared dead in 2014, because it had become too thin to move under its own weight, which is what defines a glacier. In 2019 people held a kind of funeral and put up a memorial plaque, with a message addressed to the future. We thought it would make a memorable ending to the first section.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, the second part, why it matters. What have you found?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: The main issue is water supply. In places like the Himalayas and the Andes, millions of people depend on rivers that are partly fed by meltwater, especially in the dry season. What surprised me was the idea of peak water. As glaciers melt faster, rivers actually get more water at first, so things can look fine. But once the glaciers get small enough, the amount of meltwater starts to fall, and that's when the shortages begin.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, it's a very counterintuitive idea, so you'll need to explain it carefully. A simple diagram might help.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: I'll draw one. The other big risk we're covering is floods from glacial lakes. When a glacier retreats, meltwater often collects behind the loose rock and ice that the glacier left behind. These natural dams can suddenly fail, and the flood can travel a long way down the valley.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the final section, on responses?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: We've got two examples. One is in Switzerland, at the Rhône Glacier, where people cover part of the ice with large white sheets in summer to reflect sunlight and slow down the melting. It works on a small scale, near a tourist ice cave, but it's far too expensive to use on whole glaciers, so we want to be clear that it's not a real solution.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: The other is the ice stupas in Ladakh, in northern India. An engineer called Sonam Wangchuk developed a way of piping stream water down from higher up and spraying it into the freezing winter air, so it builds up into tall cones of ice. Because the cone shape has a small surface area for its volume, the ice melts slowly in spring, just when farmers need water for their crops.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lovely example, because it's cheap and locally designed. How long is the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: Twenty minutes, plus five minutes for questions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then I'd suggest cutting back the first section a little. Audiences generally accept that glaciers are shrinking, so spend more time on the consequences and responses, which are less familiar. And please send me your slides by Thursday, so I can give you feedback before the session on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Okay, we'll do that. Thanks.

listeningParts.title: How glaciers shape the land
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a physical geography course on how glaciers erode and deposit material, and the landforms they leave behind.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at glaciers, and in particular at the way they shape the landscape. Even if you've never seen a glacier, you've almost certainly seen landscapes created by them, because during the last ice age, ice covered much of northern Europe and North America.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with how a glacier forms. A glacier develops wherever more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, so that snow builds up year after year. As new layers are added, the older snow underneath is compressed. The snowflakes lose their delicate shape and become rounded grains, forming a dense material called firn, which is halfway between snow and ice. Over many years, as the pressure increases, the air spaces are squeezed out and the firn turns into solid glacial ice.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Once the ice is thick enough, it begins to move downhill under its own weight. It does this in two main ways. First, the ice itself deforms slowly, rather like very stiff toothpaste. Second, in many glaciers, the whole mass of ice slides over the rock beneath it on a thin layer of meltwater. Most glaciers move at somewhere between a few centimetres and a few metres a day, although some fast-flowing glaciers in Greenland can travel many kilometres in a year.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: As they move, glaciers erode the land, mainly through two processes. The first is called plucking. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the rock under the glacier and then freezes onto it, so that when the ice moves on, it pulls away blocks of rock. The second process is abrasion. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the glacier scrape across the bedrock, a bit like a giant sheet of sandpaper. This leaves long, parallel scratches on the rock surface, which are called striations. They're very useful to geologists, because they show the direction in which the ice was moving.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now let's look at the landforms that result. High in the mountains, glaciers often begin in hollows on the side of a mountain. Over thousands of years, the ice deepens these into steep-sided, bowl-shaped basins called cirques. In Scotland they're known as corries, and in Wales as cwms. When the ice melts, a cirque often contains a small lake, which is called a tarn. Where two cirques form back to back, the ridge between them is worn into a sharp, narrow edge called an arête. And where three or more cirques cut into a single mountain, the result can be a pyramidal peak. The most famous example is the Matterhorn, on the border between Switzerland and Italy.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Further down, glaciers flowing along river valleys change their shape completely. Rivers tend to cut narrow V-shaped valleys, but a glacier fills the whole valley and erodes its sides as well as its floor, producing a wide valley with steep sides and a flat bottom, which we call U-shaped. Smaller side glaciers don't erode as deeply as the main glacier, so when the ice disappears, their valleys are left high above the main valley floor. These are known as hanging valleys, and they're often marked by spectacular waterfalls, like those in Yosemite in California. Along some coastlines, glacial valleys were later flooded by the sea when sea levels rose at the end of the ice age. These are fjords, and the best-known examples are in Norway, where the longest is over two hundred kilometres long.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Glaciers don't only remove material; they also deposit it. All the rock they carry is eventually dropped, often as an unsorted mix of clay, sand and boulders. Ridges of this material are called moraines, and the one at the furthest point the ice reached is known as the terminal moraine. Under the ice, the material can be shaped into smooth, oval hills called drumlins. They're often described as looking like an egg cut in half lengthways, and they usually occur in groups, with their long axis pointing in the direction of ice flow.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, erratics. These are boulders that the ice has carried far from where they originally formed, sometimes hundreds of kilometres, so they're a completely different type of rock from the ground they rest on. In the nineteenth century, erratics were an important part of the evidence used by the Swiss-born scientist Louis Agassiz to argue that large parts of Europe had once been covered by ice. Next week, we'll look at how these features are used to reconstruct past climates.

readingPassages.title: The race to the South Pole
paragraphs: In the first decade of the twentieth century, the South Pole was one of the last great geographical prizes still unclaimed. By 1910 two expeditions were preparing to reach it: a British party led by Robert Falcon Scott, a Royal Navy officer, and a Norwegian party led by Roald Amundsen. Their contrasting fortunes have been debated for more than a century, and the story remains one of the most closely studied episodes in the history of exploration.

Amundsen had not originally intended to go south at all. His plan was to drift across the Arctic Ocean in the Fram, the ship previously used by the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, and to reach the North Pole. In 1909, however, the Americans Frederick Cook and Robert Peary each announced that they had already reached it. Fearing that his sponsors would lose interest, Amundsen quietly changed his destination, revealing the new plan to most of his crew only when the ship stopped at the island of Madeira. From there he sent a brief telegram informing Scott that the Fram was heading for Antarctica.

Scott, by contrast, was an experienced Antarctic leader. He had commanded the Discovery expedition of 1901 to 1904, and his new expedition, which sailed in the Terra Nova, had substantial scientific aims as well as the goal of reaching the Pole. Its members studied geology, meteorology, biology and magnetism, and during the winter of 1911 three of them made a dangerous journey in almost total darkness to collect the eggs of emperor penguins, an episode later described by one of them, Apsley Cherry-Garrard, in his book The Worst Journey in the World.

The two leaders made very different choices about transport. Amundsen relied entirely on dogs and skis. He had spent long periods in the Canadian Arctic during his earlier voyage through the Northwest Passage, and had learned from the Netsilik Inuit how to drive dogs and how to dress in loose fur clothing. Scott used a mixture of motor sledges, ponies and dogs, but planned for his men to pull the sledges themselves for much of the route. The motor sledges broke down early, and the ponies, which suffered badly in the cold, had to be shot.

Amundsen set out from his base at the Bay of Whales in October 1911 with four companions and around fifty dogs. He planned from the outset to kill some of the dogs on the way and use them as food for the remaining animals and the men, which allowed his loads to become lighter as the journey progressed. The Norwegians reached the Pole on 14 December 1911. Before leaving, they put up a small tent and left a letter inside, asking Scott to deliver it to the King of Norway if they did not survive the return journey.

Scott's final party of five reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, only to find the Norwegian tent. 'Great God! this is an awful place,' Scott wrote in his diary. The return journey became a disaster. Edgar Evans died in February after a fall, and in March Lawrence Oates, whose feet were severely frostbitten, walked out of the tent into a blizzard, apparently so as not to slow down his companions. Scott, Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers died in their tent around the end of March, only about eighteen kilometres from a large store of food and fuel. Their bodies were found by a search party in November 1912.

Among the belongings recovered with them were about sixteen kilograms of rock samples, which the men had continued to haul even as they grew weaker. These included fossils of a plant called Glossopteris, which showed that Antarctica had once supported forests and a much warmer climate. The same plant had already been found in South America, Africa, India and Australia, and such fossils later became part of the evidence that the continents had once been joined together.

For decades after his death, Scott was celebrated in Britain as a tragic hero. In 1979, however, the writer Roland Huntford published a highly critical account, arguing that Scott's poor planning had cost the lives of his men. More recently, the atmospheric scientist Susan Solomon has used weather records to argue that the temperatures the party faced in March 1912 were unusually low, and that bad luck with the weather played a larger part than earlier critics allowed. Amundsen himself continued to explore, and in 1926 he flew over the North Pole in an airship. He died in 1928 when his aircraft disappeared during a rescue mission in the Arctic.

readingPassages.title: Archives in the ice
paragraphs: The great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica are, in a sense, the largest libraries on Earth. Each year, snow falls on their surfaces and is buried by the snow of the following year, so that the ice forms a stack of layers stretching back hundreds of thousands of years. By drilling down through these layers and extracting long cylinders of ice, known as cores, scientists can read a detailed record of the Earth's past climate, and even of the air that our ancestors breathed.

The key to this record lies in the way snow turns into ice. Near the surface, fresh snow is loose and full of air. As it is buried, it is slowly compressed into a granular material called firn, through which air can still move. Only at a depth of roughly fifty to a hundred metres do the passages close completely, sealing small bubbles of air inside the ice. Because this happens well below the surface, the air in a bubble is always somewhat younger than the ice that surrounds it, a difference that can amount to thousands of years in places where very little snow falls.

To find out how warm or cold it was when the snow fell, scientists measure the chemistry of the water itself. Water molecules contain either a common, lighter form of oxygen or a rarer, heavier one. In the 1950s the Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard showed that the proportion of the heavier form in rain and snow depends closely on the temperature at which it formed: the colder the air, the less of the heavy form the snow contains. By measuring this ratio layer by layer, researchers can build up a continuous record of past temperatures.

Obtaining the cores has required remarkable feats of engineering. In 1966, at Camp Century, a United States military base built inside the Greenland ice sheet, a drill reached the bedrock for the first time, recovering a core nearly 1,400 metres long. Later projects went much deeper. At the Russian Vostok station in East Antarctica, drilling in the 1990s produced a core more than three and a half kilometres long, covering about 420,000 years. A European project at a site called Dome C then extended the record to around 800,000 years.

The results of this work have been profound. The Antarctic cores show that, over the past 800,000 years, the Earth has swung repeatedly between long, cold glacial periods and shorter, warmer interglacials. Throughout these cycles, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the trapped air rose and fell closely in step with temperature, varying between roughly 180 parts per million in the coldest periods and about 300 in the warmest. Today, the figure is above 420, far outside the range found anywhere in the ice.

Cores from Greenland revealed something equally significant. Two cores drilled in the early 1990s, one by a European team and one by an American team, showed that during the last glacial period the climate of Greenland had repeatedly jumped by ten degrees Celsius or more within a few decades. Until then, many scientists had assumed that major climate changes took thousands of years. The discovery that the climate system could change so abruptly forced a fundamental rethink, and it continues to shape how researchers assess the risks of present-day warming.

The ice also preserves a record of individual events. Large volcanic eruptions leave layers of sulphuric acid that can be detected by passing an electric current along the core, and these layers help scientists to date the ice precisely. Human activity has left its mark too. Greenland ice contains traces of lead released by mining and smelting in the Roman period, and layers from the 1950s and 1960s contain radioactive material from nuclear weapons tests, which provides a convenient marker for dating recent snow.

Two challenges now face the field. The first is to find even older ice. About a million years ago, the rhythm of the ice ages changed, with cycles lengthening from about 41,000 years to roughly 100,000, and nobody yet knows why. Recovering ice from this period, which requires finding places where the deepest layers have not melted or been disturbed, could help to answer the question. The second challenge is more urgent: many mountain glaciers, which hold their own valuable records, are melting so quickly that their archives may be lost. A project called Ice Memory has therefore begun collecting cores from threatened glaciers, such as those in the Alps, to be stored in a cave dug into the snow in Antarctica for future generations of scientists.

readingPassages.title: A continent for peace and science
paragraphs: Antarctica is unlike any other place on Earth. Covering around fourteen million square kilometres, it is almost twice the size of Australia, yet it has no permanent population. The only residents are a few thousand scientists and support staff in summer, falling to around a thousand in the long, dark winter. Equally unusual is the way it is governed. No single country controls Antarctica; instead, it is managed under an international agreement that has, remarkably, survived for more than sixty years.

This was not inevitable. In the first half of the twentieth century, seven countries made formal claims to parts of the continent: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. Most claims took the form of wedge-shaped sectors meeting at the South Pole, and three of them, those of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom, overlap on the Antarctic Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United States and the Soviet Union made no claims of their own but refused to recognise anyone else's, and reserved the right to make claims in the future.

The turning point came with the International Geophysical Year of 1957 to 1958, an eighteen-month programme of scientific cooperation during which twelve countries established dozens of research stations in Antarctica. Building on this spirit, the same twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it came into force in 1961. The treaty states that Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only, guarantees freedom of scientific research, and bans nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste. Any station can be inspected by observers from other treaty nations at any time. Most cleverly, the treaty neither accepts nor rejects existing territorial claims, but simply freezes them, so that no activity carried out while it is in force can strengthen or weaken a claim. In my view, this was a stroke of genius: by setting aside a dispute that could not be solved, it allowed cooperation on everything else.

Since then, the system has grown considerably. More than fifty countries are now parties to the treaty, although only those that carry out substantial scientific research in Antarctica become Consultative Parties with the right to take part in decisions. These decisions are made by consensus, meaning that every Consultative Party must agree. The treaty has also been extended by further agreements, together known as the Antarctic Treaty System.

The most important of these concerns mining. During the 1980s, treaty nations negotiated a convention that would have allowed mineral resources to be exploited under strict controls. In 1989, however, Australia and France announced that they would not sign it, arguing instead for complete protection, and the convention was abandoned. In its place came the Protocol on Environmental Protection, signed in Madrid in 1991, which came into force in 1998. It designates Antarctica as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, and prohibits all activity relating to mineral resources other than scientific research. It is often claimed that this ban will expire in 2048. This is a misunderstanding. After that date, any Consultative Party may request a conference to review the protocol, but lifting the ban would still require broad agreement and a binding system to regulate mining, which seems most unlikely.

The surrounding ocean is managed by another body, the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, established in the early 1980s, largely in response to concern about the growing harvest of krill. These small crustaceans are the main food of many whales, seals and penguins, and the commission was one of the first international bodies to manage fishing with the needs of the whole ecosystem in mind. In 2016 it created a vast marine protected area in the Ross Sea. Since then, however, proposals for further protected areas have been blocked for years because a small number of members objected. I believe this shows the weakness of consensus as well as its strength: it gives every member a sense of ownership, but it also allows a single country to prevent action that most others regard as necessary.

Tourism presents a newer challenge. In recent seasons, more than a hundred thousand visitors a year have travelled to Antarctica, most of them on cruise ships to the Antarctic Peninsula. Much of the industry is self-regulated through the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators, founded in 1991. Under guidelines adopted by the industry and the treaty nations, ships carrying more than five hundred passengers may not land them at all, and no more than a hundred people may be ashore at any one site at the same time. Some campaigners argue that tourism should be banned altogether. I do not believe that a ban would be right. Visitors who have seen Antarctica for themselves often become its strongest defenders, and the industry's rules have so far been largely respected. What is needed is not prohibition but firmer limits that are legally binding, rather than voluntary.

The treaty system now faces pressures its founders could not have imagined, from a warming climate to growing global demand for resources and rising tensions between major powers. Some observers doubt whether an agreement made in 1959 can survive them. In my view, such pessimism is premature. The treaty has already outlasted the Cold War that shaped it, and it has adapted repeatedly when the need arose. Its greatest achievement may be the simplest one: for more than six decades, an entire continent has been devoted to peace and science, and no shot has been fired over it in anger.

listeningParts.title: Arranging a furniture collection
listeningParts.contextDescription: A resident telephones a community reuse service to arrange collection of furniture.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good morning, Northbank Reuse Service. This is Hannah speaking. We collect furniture that can be passed on to another household. How can I help you today?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm moving to a smaller flat next month, and there are a few things I can't take. I would rather someone used them than have them thrown away. Could you explain what you accept and how the collection works?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Certainly. We take tables, chairs and other solid furniture if the items are clean and reasonably sound. We don't collect electrical goods, because we haven't got the equipment to test them. What were you hoping to donate?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: A dining table and four chairs. The table is in good condition apart from a small mark on the top. One chair has a loose leg, although it still stands up. I could probably tighten it if that's necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Please do. Surface marks are fine, but the furniture must be safe to move and use. Could you send us a photograph of the items first? A picture taken in daylight is best. Include the damaged area as well, so our workshop team knows what to expect.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: Yes, I can do that this evening. Does the table need to be taken apart? The legs unscrew, and I still have the little bag that the screws came in. I don't want the collection team to spend ages getting it through the doorway.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: If the legs come off easily, removing them would help. Put the screws in an envelope and tape it underneath the tabletop. People sometimes tape them onto the legs, but envelopes can get torn there when we load the van. Under the top is safer.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: All right. What does a collection cost? A neighbour said you used to charge twelve pounds, but I wasn't sure whether that was still the price.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: It was twelve last year. The current collection fee is eighteen pounds for up to five items from one address, so your table and four chairs fit within that. If you bring furniture to us yourself, there isn't a fee.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: I'd need to hire a vehicle, so collection makes more sense. Could you come on Thursday the twenty-first? I'll be at home in the morning, although I have an appointment later.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thursday is our workshop day, and the vans aren't out. We have a space on Tuesday the nineteenth, or Friday the twenty-second. On Friday we would be in your neighbourhood between two and four in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: Friday the twenty-second works. I can work from home that day. Will you call shortly before arriving, so I can clear the hallway? There's a shared entrance, and I don't want to block it all afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We send a text about thirty minutes before arrival. Please keep the shared entrance clear until then. Now, may I have your surname and address?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: My surname is Kershaw. That's K-E-R-S-H-A-W. I'm at fourteen Willow Lane, in the upstairs flat. The building has a green door, and the bell for my flat is the top one.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. Is there a lift in the building? If there isn't, we need to record how many flights of stairs the team will use. That helps us choose a suitable crew.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: There's no lift, but it's just one flight. The stairs are quite wide. The awkward part is outside: the road is narrow, and vans can't stop directly in front of the door.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Where would you recommend parking? Sometimes there is a side street that our drivers can use without getting in anyone's way.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: There's a loading bay beside the bakery, around the corner. It's closer than the supermarket car park. From the bakery, there's a level path to our entrance, so nobody has to carry furniture up any outdoor steps.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: I'll put that in the booking. Please don't leave the furniture outside overnight. Even a little rain can damage the joints, and we would then have to refuse it. Keep everything indoors until the team arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.text: Understood. Do I pay the driver, or do I pay when the booking is confirmed? I can use a bank card, but I don't normally keep cash at home.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We'll email a payment link after we've checked your photograph. Please use that before collection day; the drivers don't handle payments. The same email contains your booking reference. If anything changes, quote that reference when you contact us.

listeningParts.title: Using the community workshop
listeningParts.contextDescription: A workshop supervisor welcomes new members and explains how the shared space operates.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Welcome to the community workshop. Before you start your first project, I want to explain how the rooms are organised and how we keep the space useful for everyone. You may have seen photographs of people making furniture here, but we also welcome smaller jobs, such as replacing a bag strap or making a simple storage box. You don't need an ambitious project to justify coming in.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: The most important thing to know is that the workshop is a place for learning, rather than a low-cost manufacturing service. Staff can demonstrate a technique and help you plan a safe sequence, but they won't complete your project while you wait. Our aim is for you to leave knowing more than when you arrived. If you need a finished item urgently, a commercial repairer may be more appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: We have three rooms. The clean room is for drawing, measuring, sewing and assembling small pieces. The machine room is beyond the glass doors. You can enter it only after a member of staff has checked your training record. At the back is the finishing room, where painted or glued items can be left on marked shelves. Please don't bring food into any working room; there is a separate kitchen near the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: The machines require individual introductions. Completing the general welcome session today does not qualify you to use every machine. A supervisor will show you one tool at a time, watch you use it, and then sign your record. We do that even if you have used a similar model elsewhere. Controls differ, and we need to know that you understand the equipment that is actually here.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Booking works slightly differently in each area. For a sewing machine, reserve a ninety-minute session online. The machines are popular, so please release your reservation if you cannot attend. Workbenches are not booked: you take the next available one when you arrive. If none is free, leave your name at reception and use the planning table while you wait. For painting, first ask us whether a drying shelf is available. There's no point applying paint if we have nowhere safe to leave your work.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Members sometimes ask whether they can store a half-finished project here. Small pieces can stay for a week if the label shows your name and the collection date. Larger items must go home at the end of each visit. We simply haven't got room for an unfinished wardrobe to occupy a bench for a month. If carrying a project is difficult, speak to us before starting it rather than after you have assembled it.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: You can use the wood in the open racks without paying extra. It consists of clean offcuts donated by local businesses. The locked cupboard contains materials bought for particular classes, so please ask before taking anything from there. The metal box beside the racks is for reusable scraps. The general waste bin is for material that really cannot be used again. Keeping the two separate helps the next person find something suitable.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Before leaving, allow ten minutes to clean your bench, return tools and tell us about damage. You won't automatically be charged for a worn or broken tool.
