readingPassages.title: Apparently empty ground
paragraphs: A dry landscape can appear almost vacant to a visitor accustomed to grass, trees and large flowers. Spaces between shrubs may seem to be nothing more than exposed dirt. In some drylands, however, a community of small organisms lives at the soil surface. Biological soil crusts can include cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, algae and fungi. Their inconspicuous appearance challenges the assumption that visible green vegetation is the only meaningful sign of life. In my view, describing such ground as empty is not a harmless shortcut when that description influences how people think it can be used.

The word crust needs care. A biological soil crust is not simply a hard surface layer produced by physical rearrangement of mineral particles. It is a living community associated with the ground surface. Some young crusts can resemble the surrounding soil, while more developed forms may be darker or rougher. Appearance varies with region and conditions. A visitor should not expect one universal colour or shape. This variability helps explain why a small community can be overlooked even by someone who believes they are paying attention to the landscape.

The organisms and their products can bind soil particles together. That stabilising role matters in environments where the spaces between larger plants might otherwise be vulnerable to disturbance and movement. Biological crusts also participate in ecological processes involving water and nutrients, although their effects depend on the community and setting. The important point is not that every crust performs every function identically. It is that the surface is active. Its significance cannot be inferred solely from the absence of tall vegetation or from how little material can be seen above the soil.

This creates a difficulty for familiar ideas of improvement. People may assume that a useful landscape should look green, smooth or densely planted. I would question that assumption when applied without understanding the existing system. An action intended to make a place look more alive could disturb organisms already performing important roles. That does not establish that every proposed change is wrong. It establishes a responsibility to understand what is present before selecting an appearance as the measure of success. A visually modest surface can have ecological value that an attractive photograph fails to communicate.

Disturbance is therefore more than a matter of leaving a visible mark. Pressure from feet or other activity can damage a community whose small scale makes it easy to miss. Local guidance about routes and suitable surfaces should be followed. In my view, education should explain the reason for such guidance, not merely present an unexplained prohibition. Knowing that apparently bare ground can contain living connections may help visitors understand why stepping around one large plant does not necessarily avoid all sensitive parts of the habitat.

At the same time, communication should resist replacing one simplification with another. It would be misleading to label every bare-looking patch as the same biological community or promise an identical recovery time after every disturbance. Conditions and histories differ. Reliable explanation can acknowledge these differences while still making the general significance clear. I believe uncertainty about a particular patch is a reason to seek appropriate guidance, not a reason to treat the whole idea of small living communities as irrelevant until every detail has been identified.

The lesson extends beyond dryland ecology. Public attention often favours large, colourful or moving organisms, while less conspicuous relationships receive less notice. This preference can influence which changes are celebrated and which losses remain almost invisible. A broader view does not require people to stop appreciating dramatic landscapes. It asks them to recognise that ecological function and visual spectacle are different qualities. A place can be worth understanding even when it does not offer the signs of abundance that a visitor has learned to associate with a flourishing environment.

Biological soil crusts thus provide a concrete challenge to the idea that unoccupied-looking space is unused space. The community may be difficult to distinguish at first, but its role belongs in an account of the ecosystem. In my view, good stewardship begins by learning to see more accurately, then connecting that understanding to practical behaviour. The goal is not to turn every walk into a technical survey. It is to replace a confident but misleading label with enough curiosity and care to avoid treating an inhabited surface as if nothing important were there.

listeningParts.title: Ordering a language reference book
listeningParts.contextDescription: A customer calls an independent bookshop to order a reference book as a gift.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: Bracken Books, good morning. I'm serving at the desk, but I can check a title for you if you have its details. If you want to reserve something already in the shop, we can hold it until the end of the following day without payment.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I'm hoping to buy a language reference book for my nephew. He's starting a course and sent me a photograph of the cover, but it doesn't show the identifying number. The title is Everyday Sounds. There seem to be several editions, and I don't want to choose the wrong one simply because the covers look similar.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: Let me check. There is a pocket edition and a larger student edition. The student edition has a blue cover and includes access to recordings. The pocket edition is green and has a shorter introduction, though the publisher's name is the same. Has your nephew said which one the course recommends?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: He said the student edition, the one with recordings. The photograph is blue, so that sounds right. I saw it advertised for twenty-four pounds somewhere. Is that what you charge, or was that a different version?

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: The student edition is twenty-nine pounds. Twenty-four is the pocket edition. We don't have the student version on the shelf at the moment, but the supplier lists it as available. I can order it today. We normally receive that delivery on Wednesday, although we will call you rather than promise that a supplier's estimate is certain.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I'd appreciate that. His birthday is at the weekend, and I can collect on Thursday if it arrives. If there is a delay, I could give him a card saying the book is on its way. I would rather have the correct edition than substitute one he can't use.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: That's sensible. We need a five-pound deposit for a special order. You pay the balance when you collect. We can take the deposit through a payment link; I wouldn't ask you to read card details aloud on this line while other customers are beside the desk. What name should I put on the order?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Helen Wetherby. That's W-E-T-H-E-R-B-Y. The initial is H, not E, if you're entering it. I can give you my email for the payment link, and my mobile number for the arrival message.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: Thank you, Helen. You mentioned it is a gift. Would you like us to wrap it? We have plain paper and ribbon, and the wrapping service is free for books bought here. We don't put the price on the outside, but we'll give you the receipt separately.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, please. Plain paper would be lovely. Does the recording access require a disc? My nephew uses a small laptop without a disc drive, and I don't want to discover he needs extra equipment just to use the material.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: The current student edition uses a code printed inside the cover to access recordings online. There isn't a disc. Your nephew should follow the publisher's instructions before discarding any inserts. We can't activate the code for you because it is intended for the reader's own account.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That should be fine. Where do I collect a special order? I know the main counter, but last time I came there was building work at the back and another desk upstairs. I don't want to queue in the wrong place.

dialogue.speaker: Bookseller
dialogue.text: Collect it from the downstairs counter, the one beside the staircase. The upstairs desk is for event tickets. If someone else comes for you, give them the order reference from the email. We can find the book by name, but the reference is more reliable when several people have similar names.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I'll collect it myself if possible. Please send the payment link, and I'll wait for the arrival message before making the journey. Thanks for taking the time to check the edition; a different cover colour wouldn't have meant much to me without the explanation.

listeningParts.title: Visiting the local voices exhibition
listeningParts.contextDescription: An exhibition guide introduces displays about regional speech.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Welcome to Local Voices. The exhibition explores ways people speak in and around this region. It is not a competition to find the most authentic speaker, and we do not ask visitors to rank accents. You may hear words you use yourself, words remembered from relatives or unfamiliar expressions from a nearby place. The point is to notice variation and the experiences associated with it, rather than assume that one village or generation owns the only correct form.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The first room contains a listening wall. Each button plays a short recording, and the label identifies the broad area and the date of the recording. The oldest voices and the newest ones are deliberately mixed, so read the date instead of judging age from sound quality. Some modern recordings were made outdoors, while an older studio recording may be clearer. A crackle does not by itself tell you when someone spoke.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Use the headphones hanging beneath each button. The speakers are kept off because several recordings playing aloud at once would make the room difficult to use. If headphones are unsuitable for you, ask at the desk about the quieter listening station. We also provide written versions, but these are a way of finding the subject of a recording, not a complete replacement for hearing its rhythm and pronunciation.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: In the map room, movable word cards can be placed beside areas where visitors have heard an expression. Those cards represent contributions to the exhibition. They are not the results of a completed scientific survey, and we don't remove a card simply because another visitor associates the word with a different place. A word can travel, and people can remember different parts of its history. Tell the volunteer if you would like to add a short explanation with your card.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The third room is about making a recording. There is a demonstration microphone and a sample questionnaire. Visitors can try answering one question, but the practice device does not save their voice. A separate project is collecting recordings for an archive, and that requires a conversation with a member of staff and a consent form. Please don't mistake trying the equipment for agreeing to have your speech kept or published.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: At the end of the corridor is the family table, where people can discuss expressions used at home. Children are welcome, but adults should avoid turning the activity into a test of whether a child remembers the proper family word. We provide prompt cards about food, weather and games, and people can draw as well as write. The activity is intended to encourage conversation between generations, including different recollections. Some families have found that grandparents and grandchildren remember quite different words for the same thing, and those differences often lead to the most interesting conversations of all.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Two talks take place today. The morning talk looks at the work of field collectors and how questions were prepared. The afternoon talk examines the use of local speech in fiction. Both are in the lecture room, and both have free tickets available at reception. We ask you to take a ticket even if a seat seems empty, because a reserved place may belong to someone who has briefly stepped outside.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The exhibition notebook is beside the exit. If you comment, tell us what you noticed or what you would like explained more clearly. Please don't write private contact details there, as other visitors can read it. If you want staff to contact you about contributing to the archive, use the separate enquiry form. We hope you leave with more interest in the voices around you, not a set of judgements about which ones deserve to be heard.

listeningParts.title: Preparing a short phonetic transcription task
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two linguistics students discuss an introductory class exercise with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: For your introductory exercise, you don't need to teach the whole phonetic alphabet. Choose one distinction and build a task around it. The aim is to show classmates how a transcription can make attention to sound more precise, not to reward whoever memorises the largest number of unfamiliar symbols before the session.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.text: We thought of comparing spelling and pronunciation using a few ordinary English words. That would show why copying the letters isn't the same as describing the sounds. We can avoid asking classmates to read a long passage, because reading style might become an extra issue we aren't prepared to analyse.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Our first idea used words from three languages, but neither of us knows enough about two of them. We'd risk presenting our own guesses as accurate examples. So we'll use a small English set we can check with the tutor and a reliable pronunciation source. We should identify which variety the source describes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. A pronunciation example is not a claim that every speaker must sound identical. Also distinguish the sound you are studying from the spelling that suggests it. If you ask for a word ending in a particular letter, you may receive examples whose final sounds differ. Make the question about what is heard, not merely what is written.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.text: We'll start with two recordings and ask people whether the target sound is the same or different. Then we'll show the relevant symbols and explain what contrast we intend them to represent. We don't need to imply that the symbols describe every detail of the voices.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: For the recording, should we use our own voices? That would avoid a permission issue with downloading someone else's sound file, but we still need to be clear that our voices are examples rather than a model of the only acceptable accent.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Using your own recordings is fine for this classroom task. Record in the same room with the microphone at a consistent distance. Otherwise, a difference in loudness or background noise may draw attention away from the feature you want people to compare. Listen back before deciding that a take is suitable.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.text: We'll make a trial recording this afternoon. I think a short pause between words will help people hear the boundaries, but we shouldn't leave such a long pause that the whole exercise becomes slow. We can ask one classmate to try it and tell us whether the instructions are clear.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: What should go on the handout? I was going to print the entire chart, but that may be distracting for a task using only a few symbols. Perhaps a small key would be more useful, with a reference to the full chart for anyone interested.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds appropriate. Make sure the symbols print correctly. A font change can turn a carefully chosen symbol into an empty box or another mark. Check the actual printed sheet, not just the document on your own screen. You should also have a plain-language explanation of the distinction so nobody is excluded simply because the notation is new.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.text: At the end, we can ask what the notation helped them notice. We shouldn't give a band or a language proficiency score from a tiny exercise like this. It is an introduction to a tool for describing speech, not an assessment of someone's general ability to communicate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Then our preparation list is manageable: choose and check examples, record them consistently, test the instructions and print the handout. We'll keep the final discussion focused on the relationship between a notation and a listening task, rather than opening a debate about which accent people prefer. If we finish early, we could play the recordings a second time and ask whether people noticed anything new on a second listening.

listeningParts.title: Words as units in connected speech
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecturer introduces the difference between spaces in writing and the flow of speech.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: On a printed page, spaces help us see where one word ends and another begins. When we listen, the situation is different. Ordinary connected speech does not contain a matching silence at every printed space. A speaker produces a flow in which sounds are influenced by neighbouring sounds and by rhythm. This helps explain why a learner may recognise each word on a page yet find the same sequence difficult to follow when it is spoken naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First, distinguish a pause from a word boundary. A speaker may pause in the middle of an idea to plan what comes next, while several short words can be spoken without a break. If we treat every silence as punctuation and every uninterrupted stretch as one word, we will describe neither the writing nor the speech very well. Listening requires attention to several kinds of information, including the likely grammar and meaning of the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Stress can make some parts more prominent than others. In an ordinary phrase, not every word receives equal emphasis. A speaker can also shift prominence to make a contrast, for example when correcting which object they meant. The written sentence may remain the same while the listener hears a different focus. A transcript that contains only the words can preserve the sequence without recording every aspect of that focus. It is therefore useful to know what kind of detail a transcription is intended to show.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sounds may change in the company of other sounds. For an introductory class, the important point is not to memorise a long list of changes, but to compare a word spoken alone with the same word in a phrase. The isolated version is useful for examining one form, while the phrase shows a different practical setting. Neither should automatically be dismissed as careless. The relationship depends on the language, the variety and the style of the particular utterance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Examples should be short enough for a listener to compare. Repeating a whole paragraph when the question concerns a single junction between words can make the relevant feature difficult to locate. A carefully chosen extract lets the class listen more than once and discuss what they notice. It should still be identified as an extract, because removing its surrounding conversation can remove information that helped the original listener understand it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Recording quality matters, but it does not create a universal model of speech. A quiet room can make a contrast easier to hear, yet a clearly recorded voice remains one person's performance in one setting. Students should not conclude that an unfamiliar accent is defective because it differs from that example. The purpose of phonetic attention is to describe differences more accurately, not to turn personal familiarity into a judgement about a speaker's worth.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For practice, try listening before looking at a transcript. Write down what you think you heard, then compare it with the words and listen again. The point is to locate the source of a difficulty. Was it an unfamiliar word, an unexpected grammatical pattern or the way familiar words joined together? Different difficulties suggest different practice. Simply replaying the same sound without a question in mind can be less informative than a short comparison focused on one feature.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, keep the scale of the conclusion appropriate. Identifying a feature in one phrase shows that the example can be described that way; it does not establish how every person always speaks. A useful listening notebook can collect examples from different situations and connect them to a clear explanation. The goal is a stronger relationship between what is seen on the page and what is heard in an utterance, while recognising that writing and speech organise information through related but different resources.

readingPassages.title: An alphabet for describing speech
paragraphs: An ordinary alphabet is part of a writing system, not a direct inventory of everything speakers do with their voices. English makes the distinction particularly visible: the letters in familiar words can relate to sound in different ways. A reader who knows how to pronounce 'though' cannot simply apply the same ending to 'cough'. For a teacher or researcher wishing to describe pronunciation, ordinary spelling therefore leaves a problem. A phonetic notation offers a way to attend to speech without assuming that the conventional letters of one language provide a sufficient description of another.

The International Phonetic Association was founded in Paris in 1886, with Paul Passy and other language teachers and linguists involved. Its early purpose was closely connected to improving modern-language teaching through phonetics. The first versions of the International Phonetic Alphabet grew from that practical educational interest. The Association's historical chart archive identifies an 1888 alphabet, and later charts show continuing revision. The system did not arrive as an unchanging table delivered outside history. It developed through the work of people trying to make speech more accurately describable across languages and teaching contexts.

The word international is important. If each teacher used only the spelling habits familiar from their own language, the same written explanation could suggest different sounds to different learners. A shared notation provides conventions that can be learned and discussed independently of those habits. That does not make a symbol self-explanatory to someone seeing it for the first time. Like any notation, it requires teaching and examples. Its value lies in making the intended distinction more explicit, rather than relying on a reader to guess what a conventional letter is meant to represent on a particular occasion.

The alphabet's familiar chart groups symbols according to features of speech production. It is not merely a decorative list of unfamiliar letters. Such organisation allows a learner to connect a symbol with a description of how a sound is made, and to compare related possibilities. The chart also contains marks that add detail beyond a basic symbol. A transcription can consequently be more or less detailed depending on its purpose. Recording every audible feature is not the same task as showing the distinctions relevant to a short pronunciation lesson or an introductory account of a language.

A transcription must therefore be read with some knowledge of its conventions. Two accounts may differ because they choose different levels of detail, not because one author failed to listen. In an original classroom example, one teacher might show the sound contrast needed to distinguish two words, while another examines a small variation at the beginning of one sound. The questions are related but not identical. A useful notation makes these choices available for explanation. It does not remove the need to say what the transcription is intended to represent.

Nor does phonetic description establish a single socially superior accent. A notation can describe more than one variety, and a pronunciation guide should indicate the variety it presents. A learner may choose a particular model for a practical purpose without treating other speakers as defective. The distinction between describing a sound and evaluating the person who produces it is essential. A symbol can help specify what is heard, but no row in a chart can by itself justify a judgement about intelligence, courtesy or the cultural worth of a community.

The Association's history describes the widening use of the alphabet beyond language teaching into linguistic description and other fields concerned with speech. That expansion also helps explain the need for shared reference materials and revisions. Users need to know which conventions are being followed, particularly when reading work from different periods. Historical charts can show that a notation has a history, while current reference material supports communication among users. Neither history nor standardisation means that every question about the sound of an individual utterance can be answered simply by pointing to a printed symbol.

A phonetic alphabet is best understood as a disciplined resource for description. It can make a pronunciation question more precise, connect listening with articulatory explanation and allow examples to be compared. Its usefulness depends on appropriate selection of detail and on the listener's learning, not on the visual complexity of a transcription. The achievement is not that speech has been replaced by writing. It is that a shared system of marks can support careful attention to spoken language while leaving room to explain the purposes and limits of each particular representation.

readingPassages.title: Putting dialects on a map
paragraphs: The Survey of English Dialects, associated with the University of Leeds, created a substantial record of regional speech in the mid-twentieth century. Harold Orton and Eugen Dieth had developed the idea before the Second World War, which interrupted the work. The main field investigation took place during the 1950s and was completed in 1961. Its later publications and surviving records allow a reader to examine not merely a collection of unusual words, but an organised attempt to relate forms of speech to places. That purpose shaped both the information sought and the way it was gathered.

Fieldworkers visited a network of 313 localities. They used a substantial questionnaire intended to make responses from different places comparable. A question could prompt a word for an everyday object or activity, enabling researchers to place different answers alongside one another. This is different from waiting for every desired expression to arise spontaneously in a conversation. A questionnaire can make a comparison possible while also shaping what enters the record. The resulting collection must be understood as material produced through particular questions and encounters, not as every possible word spoken in each locality.

The respondents were not a miniature version of the whole population. The survey sought forms associated with local continuity, and the selection of speakers reflected that aim. This makes the record valuable for its question, but it limits an interpretation of it as a complete account of every age group and social setting. A modern reader needs to distinguish the existence of a documented form from a claim that every person in the place used it. A dot on a map can represent a recorded answer without representing an entire community's uniform speech.

Written responses were central to the work, and the surviving response books show the importance of careful notation. The Leeds archive retains a response book for each locality in the national network. Recording speech in writing requires conventions that let another reader interpret the entry. The fieldworker had to attend to the answer and represent relevant features, rather than simply replace it with the nearest ordinary spelling. Such records can preserve distinctions that a standardised written summary would smooth away, though they remain a representation made by a particular listener in a particular encounter.

Sound recording added another kind of material. The Leeds account identifies a decision in 1952 to record samples of casual speech and conversation. These recordings can contain more than the isolated responses needed for a word map. They may preserve rhythm, narrative and accounts of local work or custom. They are not interchangeable with the questionnaire books: each form makes some features easier to examine than others. Their survival together gives later users opportunities to connect language with the circumstances and stories in which it was used, rather than treating every answer as a detached specimen.

Publication required further work after collection. The results appeared through an introduction and volumes of basic material, while the Linguistic Atlas of England was published in 1978. A map transforms a set of records into a visual comparison. The reader can notice a distribution more quickly than by turning through every response book, but the map necessarily selects a feature to display. Its symbols and key matter. A boundary drawn around similar answers should not be mistaken for a wall that prevented speakers from meeting or a claim that no variation existed within the area.

Later interest in the collection can ask questions different from those of the original investigators. A person may recognise a word remembered from a grandparent, while a researcher may compare a historical form with newer recordings. The archive's value does not depend on freezing living speech in the state recorded decades ago. Languages and communities change, and movement can carry expressions beyond the places where a fieldworker first encountered them. The historical record offers a point of comparison, not a rule about who is entitled to use a word today.

The survey consequently illustrates both the power and the selectivity of a language atlas. Shared questions, systematic fieldwork and publication created a resource far beyond an individual's collection of memories. At the same time, locality, speaker selection and methods of recording remain part of its meaning. A careful user can appreciate its detail without turning it into a complete census of speech. Putting language on a map makes patterns visible, provided the reader continues to ask what was recorded, from whom and for the particular purpose the investigation was designed to serve.

readingPassages.title: Should schools make room for local speech?
paragraphs: Schools teach forms of language that allow students to participate in situations beyond their immediate community. This is an important task, but it need not require presenting local speech as a defect. In my view, the educational question is how to expand a learner's repertoire without making them ashamed of the language through which they already know people and places. A school can explain the conventions expected in a formal written task while recognising that a family conversation is a different activity. Treating those activities as identical creates a false choice between opportunity and belonging.

A common argument for excluding local expressions from school is that students need a clear standard. The practical need for shared written conventions is real, particularly when work will be read by people from different areas. Yet a shared convention does not establish that every other form is linguistically empty or morally inferior. I believe teachers should explain what a convention enables and where it is expected. A rule presented as a tool for a particular purpose can be learned without becoming a judgement that the student's relatives speak badly or have nothing worth saying.

This does not mean that every classroom task should accept every form without discussion. If a learner is preparing a formal report, learning its expected register is part of the task. If the class is examining dialogue in a story, local vocabulary or grammar may be central to what the writer is doing. The same feature can therefore be relevant in different ways. In my view, good teaching helps students notice these differences rather than using the simple labels correct and incorrect as if the purpose and audience never changed.

There is also a danger in turning local speech into a display of authenticity. Asking a student to perform an accent for classmates can make them feel exposed, especially if others imitate it for amusement. Nor should a child be appointed the representative of a whole region because of a family connection. Participation in a language activity needs respectful boundaries and choices. A collection of expressions can be studied through willing contributions, published materials or recordings used appropriately, without requiring an individual to prove that their home language is sufficiently traditional to count.

Learning about variation can support close attention to language. Students can compare how a speaker addresses different audiences or how a writer uses a word that is unfamiliar outside one area. Such work need not become a competition between accents. It can make the relationship between form, context and effect more visible. I would value an activity that asks why a choice matters in a text more than one that simply asks students to collect as many unusual words as possible. The educational purpose is understanding, not the accumulation of curiosities.

Assessment should make its requirements clear. A teacher may reasonably evaluate whether a learner uses the conventions specified for a formal assignment. It is less defensible to penalise a feature without explaining that requirement or to let a personal preference about accent stand in for a stated criterion. In my view, students should be able to understand what is being assessed and how to improve it. Expanding access to a standard is different from rewarding those whose home experience happened to make that standard familiar before they entered the classroom.

Practical limits deserve attention. Teachers need suitable resources and time, and not every lesson can become a survey of regional language. Respect does not require an elaborate festival whenever an unfamiliar word appears. It can begin with avoiding ridicule, asking what a form means and connecting the discussion to the lesson's purpose. Where more detailed study is appropriate, resources should present communities as living and varied rather than as museum exhibits whose speech stopped changing at a convenient historical date. Students can learn about heritage without being asked to preserve every feature unchanged.

The strongest case for making room for local speech is therefore not resistance to learning a wider standard. It is the possibility of learning that standard more intelligently, as one part of a flexible repertoire. In my view, a school succeeds when students can recognise the demands of a new situation and choose language purposefully while retaining respect for the people with whom they began speaking. Their education should increase what they can do. It need not reduce the value of what they already bring in order to make that expansion possible.

listeningParts.title: Joining a well-being course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a community centre to sign up for a course in its spring well-being programme.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hillcrest Community Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I'm calling about your Feel Good programme. I'm interested in joining one of the courses, and I wondered if you could give me some details.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. The Feel Good programme is a series of short courses that run throughout the spring. They're all about looking after your mental and physical well-being. At the moment we've got four courses: mindfulness, gardening for health, laughter yoga and a walking group. Did you have one in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I was thinking about the mindfulness course. I've been quite stressed at work recently, and a colleague told me it really helped her when she was going through a difficult time.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's one of our most popular courses. It runs for eight weeks, and the sessions are on Tuesday evenings, from seven until half past eight. The walking group and the gardening course are both during the day, so they tend to suit people who are retired.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Evenings are much better for me. When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The first session is on the fourteenth of March. We did have a course starting at the end of February, but that one's completely full now, I'm afraid.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fourteenth is fine. And where does it take place? Here at the centre?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Usually, yes, in the Garden Room on the ground floor. It's the quietest room in the building, because it looks out onto the back garden rather than the main road. But for the first two weeks we're having some building work done, so those sessions will be in the library next door instead. There'll be a sign on the door to remind people.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, that's no problem. How much does the course cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full course is sixty pounds. If you're a student or over sixty-five, there's a reduced price of forty pounds. And if you'd just like to try it first, you can pay twelve pounds for a single session.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll pay the full price, sixty pounds. I think I'd rather commit to the whole thing, otherwise I'll probably find excuses not to go. Who teaches it?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The teacher is Anna Kowalski. She used to be a nurse, and she's been teaching mindfulness for over ten years now. People really like her because she's very practical. She doesn't expect you to sit in silence for an hour on the first evening; she starts with very short exercises, just two or three minutes long.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's good to hear, because I'm not sure I could manage an hour. Is there anything I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Just wear comfortable clothes. We provide mats and cushions, but quite a few people like to bring their own blanket, because the room can get a bit cold in the evenings. Anna will also ask you to keep a short diary during the week, about how you're feeling and when you practise, so a small notebook is useful.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Right. And do I need any experience?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: None at all. It's designed for complete beginners. Is there anything about your health that Anna should know about?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, I've got a bad back, so I can't sit on the floor for very long.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's no problem at all. Lots of people prefer to use chairs, and we always have plenty in the room. Now, can I take some details to register you? What's your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Hartigan. That's H-A-R-T-I-G-A-N.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Daniel. And could I ask how you heard about the programme? We like to know which kind of advertising works best.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I heard an advert for it on the local radio, on my way to work one morning.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Oh, good. That's the first year we've tried that, so it's nice to know it's working. Is there anything else you'd like to know?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Just one thing. Is there somewhere to park?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a small car park behind the building, but it fills up very quickly in the evening because of the gym classes. Most people park in Station Road, just round the corner, which is free after six o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Station Road. Great. Thanks very much for your help.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You're welcome, Daniel. I'll send you a confirmation by email this afternoon, with a link so you can pay online. We look forward to seeing you on the fourteenth.

listeningParts.title: A community volunteering scheme
listeningParts.contextDescription: The coordinator of a local volunteering scheme speaks to people at an information evening.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello everyone, and thank you for coming along this evening. My name's Siobhan, and I coordinate the Kindness Counts volunteering scheme here in Ashford. Tonight I'd like to explain how the scheme works, tell you a little about the different roles that are available, and then answer any questions you might have.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Kindness Counts was set up four years ago by the local council, together with three local charities. The idea came from a survey of residents, which found that a lot of people wanted to help in their community but didn't know where to start. Some had contacted charities directly, but had been put off by long application forms, or by being asked to commit to several days a week. So our aim was to make volunteering as simple and flexible as possible. You register once with us, and then you can try out different roles without filling in new forms every time.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Since we started, more than eleven hundred people have registered, and around four hundred volunteer with us every month. Interestingly, the biggest group isn't retired people, as many people expect, but people in their twenties and thirties, many of whom are looking for something meaningful to do outside work.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, some of you may know that researchers have found links between volunteering and well-being. People who volunteer regularly tend to report higher life satisfaction and lower levels of depression. However, it's not always clear which comes first: it may be partly that happier people are more likely to volunteer in the first place. What we've noticed, though, is that the benefits seem greatest when people choose a role they really care about, rather than one they feel they ought to do. So please don't feel guilty about picking something you'll enjoy.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Let me run through the main roles. First, there's our telephone befriending service. Volunteers phone an older person who lives alone, once a week, just for a chat. It's ideal if you find it hard to leave the house yourself, or if you work irregular hours, because you can make the calls from home at a time that suits you both. Because you'll be speaking to people who may be vulnerable, you'll need to have a background check before you start, which we arrange free of charge.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Second, there's the Green Team. They meet every Saturday morning in Riverside Park, planting trees, clearing paths and looking after the wildflower meadow. You don't need any experience, and all the tools and gloves are provided. Just bring old clothes and waterproof boots, because it can get very muddy down by the river, especially in winter.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Third, Reading Buddies. Volunteers go into local primary schools and listen to children read, for an hour a week. This role is during school hours, of course, so it tends to suit people who are retired or who work part-time. The teachers tell us that the children's confidence improves enormously, and many of our volunteers say it's the highlight of their week.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Fourth, the food bank on Mill Lane. Volunteers sort donations, pack parcels and help to hand them out. It's busiest before Christmas, so if you can only give a few days a year, that would be the time we need you most.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: And finally, there's the Repair Café, which takes place on the first Sunday of every month in the church hall. People bring along broken items, such as lamps, bicycles and clothes, and volunteers show them how to fix them, rather than throwing them away. It's very sociable, and there's always tea and cake. This is the only role where we ask for a particular skill, so if you're good with a sewing machine or a screwdriver, we'd love to hear from you.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: To register, you simply fill in one form online and come to a one-hour welcome session, which runs on the second Thursday of every month. After that, you can sign up for activities through our app, and you can change roles whenever you like. Right, has anyone got any questions?

listeningParts.title: Planning a presentation on hedonic adaptation
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Maya and Tom, discuss their seminar presentation with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Maya, Tom, come in and sit down. So you're presenting to the seminar group next week on hedonic adaptation. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've done most of the reading, but we wanted to check the structure with you before we make the slides.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sure. Remind me how you're going to start.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We thought we'd begin with a question for the audience: if you won a million pounds tomorrow, how much happier do you think you'd be in a year's time? We'll ask everyone to write down a number from one to ten, and then we'll come back to it at the very end.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I like that. It gets people involved straight away. Then what?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Then we explain the basic idea: that people tend to get used to changes in their lives, both good and bad, so after a while their happiness returns to roughly where it was before. The term 'hedonic treadmill' was introduced by Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell in 1971. The idea is that, like someone on a treadmill, you keep moving, but you don't really get anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And then the classic study?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, that's the 1978 paper by Brickman and two colleagues, which compared lottery winners with people who had been seriously injured in accidents, and with a control group. The winners weren't significantly happier than the control group, and they actually got less pleasure from everyday things, like chatting with friends or hearing a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The authors suggested two reasons. One was contrast: compared with the excitement of winning, ordinary pleasures just didn't seem as exciting any more. The other was habituation, which means they simply got used to their new wealth.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: But we want to be careful not to exaggerate the findings. It's often reported as if the accident victims ended up just as happy as everyone else, and that's not what the study found. They were less happy than the control group, although not as unhappy as people might have expected.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's exactly the kind of critical point I'm looking for. Are you going to say anything about the methods?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll point out that the groups were quite small, and that the study only measured people at one point in time, so it can't really show how anyone's happiness changed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. And that's why the later research matters so much. Have you looked at the long-term studies?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We have. Richard Lucas and his colleagues used data from a German survey that followed thousands of people every year for a long time. They found that, on average, people who became unemployed didn't fully return to their previous level of life satisfaction, even after they found a new job. So adaptation isn't complete for every kind of event.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. And Ed Diener, together with Lucas and another colleague, wrote a well-known paper in 2006 revising the treadmill model. One of their points was that people don't start from a neutral point. Most people are slightly happy most of the time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We hadn't included that. We'll add it to the section on later research.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And you'll finish with some practical implications?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yes, we want to end with ways of slowing down adaptation to positive things. One is variety: for example, changing how you spend your free time rather than doing the same thing every weekend. Another is gratitude. There's a study by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough from 2003, where people who wrote down things they were grateful for each week felt better about their lives than people who wrote about their problems.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a nice way to end, and it links back to your opening question. How long is it at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We've been given twenty minutes, plus five for questions. At the moment it's running at about twenty-five, so we need to cut something.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd shorten the history section. The audience doesn't need every date. And I'd strongly recommend a graph for the German data, rather than a table full of numbers. It'll be much easier for people to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay. Should we give out a handout as well?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, but keep it to one page, with your references on it. And please send me your slides by Friday, so I've got time to look at them before the seminar.

listeningParts.title: How can happiness be measured?
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a psychology course on the methods researchers use to measure happiness and well-being.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at a question that might seem impossible to answer: how can we measure something as personal as happiness? After all, you can't put happiness on a scale or measure it with a ruler. Yet researchers have developed a number of methods, and each has its own strengths and weaknesses.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First, a word about terms. Psychologists usually avoid the word 'happiness', because it means different things to different people. Instead, they tend to talk about subjective well-being, which is usually divided into three parts: how satisfied people are with their lives as a whole, how often they experience positive emotions, and how often they experience negative ones.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The simplest method is just to ask people. One of the best-known questions is the Cantril ladder, developed by the American researcher Hadley Cantril in the 1960s. People are asked to imagine a ladder with steps numbered from zero at the bottom to ten at the top, where the top represents the best possible life for them, and to say which step they're standing on now. This question is used in the Gallup World Poll, and it provides the rankings in the World Happiness Report, which was first published in 2012. You may have seen headlines about it; Finland was ranked first in every edition from 2018 to 2025.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The problem with simple questions like this is that the answers can be influenced by things that have nothing to do with how people's lives are really going. In a famous study published in 1983, Norbert Schwarz and Gerald Clore phoned people and asked them how satisfied they were with their lives. People questioned on sunny days reported higher satisfaction than people questioned on rainy days. Interestingly, the effect disappeared when the interviewer first asked about the weather, as if people then realised that their mood was partly caused by the rain, and ignored it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: To get around this kind of problem, researchers have developed methods that measure feelings as they happen, rather than asking people to sum up their whole lives. In experience sampling, which was developed in the 1970s by the psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and his colleagues, participants carried electronic pagers that beeped at random times during the day. Each time, they wrote down what they were doing and how they felt. Today, the same thing is done with smartphone apps.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One well-known app study, published in 2010 by Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert, found that people's minds were wandering, that is, thinking about something other than what they were doing, almost half the time. And people were generally less happy when their minds were wandering, even when they were thinking about pleasant things.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Experience sampling is accurate, but it's also expensive and disturbs people's daily lives. So Daniel Kahneman and his colleagues developed a simpler alternative, the Day Reconstruction Method, which they described in 2004. Participants, in their first study around nine hundred working women in Texas, filled in a diary of the previous day, dividing it into episodes and rating how they felt during each one. Among the least enjoyable activities was commuting, while socialising with friends was among the most enjoyable.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, some researchers try to avoid self-report altogether by using physical measures. One is cortisol, a hormone that the body releases when we're under stress, which can be measured in saliva. Another is facial expression. In the nineteenth century, the French doctor Guillaume Duchenne showed that a genuine smile involves not only the mouth but also the muscles around the eyes, while a polite smile uses only the mouth. Genuine smiles are now often called Duchenne smiles.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In a study published in 2001, LeeAnne Harker and Dacher Keltner looked at photographs of women in their college yearbook, taken around the age of twenty-one. Those who showed genuine smiles were more likely, decades later, to report being married and to have higher well-being. Of course, physical measures like these have their own limits, so most researchers now combine several methods. Next week, we'll look at what these methods have revealed about the causes of well-being.

readingPassages.title: Eighty years of good lives
paragraphs: In 1938, researchers at Harvard University began following the lives of 268 second-year students. The idea came from Arlie Bock, a doctor at the university's health service, who felt that medicine spent too much time studying people who were ill and too little studying those who were healthy. With funding from the businessman William T. Grant, the owner of a chain of department stores, the Grant Study, as it became known, set out to discover what allowed some young men to thrive. Nobody involved could have imagined that it would still be running more than eighty years later.

The original participants were all men, since Harvard did not admit women as undergraduates at the time, and almost all of them were white. Several went on to have remarkable careers; the most famous was John F. Kennedy, who later became President of the United States. Most, however, led more ordinary lives as lawyers, doctors, teachers and businessmen. At around the same time, a separate study led by Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck, of Harvard Law School, began following 456 boys from some of Boston's poorest neighbourhoods. The Gluecks had originally been interested in why some young people turned to crime while others did not.

In the 1970s, the two groups were brought together into what is now called the Harvard Study of Adult Development. Combining them gave the researchers something unusual: two very different groups of people, one privileged and one from much harder backgrounds, followed over the whole course of their lives. Every two years, the men completed long questionnaires about their work, health, marriages and friendships. Every five years, researchers collected their medical records, and at regular intervals the men were interviewed in their homes. In later decades, the researchers also took blood samples and carried out brain scans.

Keeping a study going for so long has not been easy. Funding has often been difficult to find, because few organisations are willing to pay for research that will not produce results for decades. Some participants stopped replying to questionnaires, and others died in the Second World War. The study has also had several directors. The psychiatrist George Vaillant led it for more than three decades, from 1972 to 2004, and wrote a number of books about its findings. The current director, Robert Waldinger, is the fourth person to hold the role.

So what has the study found? Its most famous conclusion is surprisingly simple: the quality of people's relationships has a greater influence on their health and happiness than almost anything else. In a talk given in 2015, which has since been viewed tens of millions of times, Waldinger explained that the men who were most satisfied with their relationships at the age of fifty were the healthiest at the age of eighty. It was not their cholesterol levels in middle age that best predicted how they would grow old, he said, but how satisfied they were in their relationships.

Importantly, the study suggests that it is the quality of relationships, rather than their number, that matters. Having many friends or being married was not enough on its own; people in marriages with a great deal of conflict often did worse than those who were divorced. On the other hand, people who felt they could rely on a partner or a friend in difficult times tended to keep their memories sharper for longer. Loneliness, by contrast, was associated with poorer health and earlier decline. As Waldinger put it, loneliness turns out to be toxic.

The study has its limitations. Because the original participants were all men, and nearly all white, its findings cannot automatically be applied to everyone. The researchers have tried to address this by extending the study to include the men's wives and, more recently, their children, more than half of whom are women. They have also been careful to point out that a study which simply observes people can show links between relationships and health, but cannot on its own prove that one causes the other.

Even so, the findings are consistent with many other studies, and they have a practical message. Relationships, Waldinger and his co-author Marc Schulz argue in their 2023 book The Good Life, need to be looked after, just as the body does. Small actions, such as getting in touch with an old friend or setting aside regular time for a partner, may have a bigger effect on well-being than a promotion or a pay rise. Very few of the original participants are still alive, but the lives they shared with researchers continue to offer lessons to the generations that have followed them.

readingPassages.title: Can money buy happiness?
paragraphs: Few questions have been debated for as long as whether money makes people happy. Philosophers and religious teachers have often warned that wealth brings anxiety rather than contentment, while most ordinary people, if asked, say that a little more money would make their lives better. Over the past fifty years, economists and psychologists have tried to settle the matter with data, and their answers have turned out to be more complicated, and more interesting, than either side expected.

The modern debate began in 1974, when the American economist Richard Easterlin published a paper that pointed out a strange pattern. Within any one country, he found, richer people were on average happier than poorer people. Yet when he looked at the United States over time, average happiness had hardly changed in the decades after the Second World War, even though incomes had risen substantially. This apparent contradiction became known as the Easterlin paradox, and it has been argued about ever since.

One explanation is that people judge their income not in absolute terms but by comparing it with the incomes of others. If everyone becomes richer at the same rate, nobody feels better off relative to their neighbours. Another explanation is adaptation: as people's incomes rise, their expectations rise too, so that luxuries soon come to feel like necessities. Not all economists accept the paradox, however. Some have argued that, with better data covering more countries, a link between national wealth and average life satisfaction can in fact be seen.

In 2010, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton, both Nobel prize winners, added an important distinction. Analysing more than 450,000 responses to a daily survey of Americans, they separated two aspects of well-being. The first, life evaluation, is what people think about their lives when they reflect on them. The second, emotional well-being, refers to the feelings, such as joy, stress or sadness, that people experience day to day. Life evaluation rose steadily with income. Emotional well-being also rose, but it appeared to level off at an annual income of around 75,000 dollars.

That figure was widely reported, but in 2021 a younger researcher, Matthew Killingsworth, published results that seemed to contradict it. Using more than 1.7 million reports collected from over 33,000 people through a smartphone app, he found that feelings continued to improve as income rose, with no sign of a plateau. Rather than arguing in print, Killingsworth and Kahneman agreed to work together, with the psychologist Barbara Mellers acting as a referee. Their joint paper, published in 2023, concluded that for most people happiness does keep rising with income, but that for the unhappiest group, roughly the least happy fifth, it stops rising at around 100,000 dollars.

Other researchers have asked a different question: not how much money people have, but how they spend it. In a study published in 2008, Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton gave students in Vancouver an envelope containing either five or twenty dollars, and asked them to spend it by five o'clock that afternoon. Half were told to spend it on themselves, and half on someone else or on a charity. That evening, those who had spent the money on others reported feeling happier, while the amount they had been given made no difference.

Spending on experiences may also bring more lasting happiness than spending on possessions. Research by Leaf Van Boven and Thomas Gilovich in 2003 found that people tended to look back on purchases such as holidays, concerts and meals with friends more positively than on material goods. Experiences are often shared with others, they become part of our identity, and they are harder to compare unfavourably with what other people have. More recently, studies have suggested that paying to avoid disliked tasks, such as cleaning, can increase life satisfaction by giving people more free time.

None of this means that money is unimportant. For people living in poverty, extra income can make an enormous difference, reducing stress and allowing them to meet basic needs such as food, housing and healthcare. The research suggests, rather, that beyond a certain point, the way money is used matters as much as the amount. A pay rise is likely to make someone happier, but so too, perhaps, is spending some of it on friends, on experiences, or on a few extra hours of free time.

readingPassages.title: Should governments measure happiness?
paragraphs: For most of the past century, the success of a country has been judged mainly by a single number: gross domestic product, or GDP, the total value of the goods and services it produces. Yet even the economist who did much to create modern national accounts doubted that it should be used in this way. In a report to the United States Congress in 1934, Simon Kuznets warned that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income. GDP tells us how much a country produces, but not whether its people are living good lives.

The best-known alternative comes from Bhutan, a small Himalayan kingdom. In the 1970s, its fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, is reported to have declared that gross national happiness was more important than gross national product. The idea was later written into the country's constitution, adopted in 2008, and Bhutan now carries out regular surveys to calculate a Gross National Happiness Index, which covers nine areas, including health, education, the use of time, community life and the environment.

For many years, Bhutan's approach was seen as a curiosity, but interest grew in wealthier countries after the turn of the century. In 2008, the French president Nicolas Sarkozy asked a group of leading economists, including the Nobel prize winners Joseph Stiglitz and Amartya Sen, to examine how economic and social progress should be measured. Their report, published the following year, argued that governments should pay far more attention to well-being and to whether progress could be sustained for future generations.

The United Kingdom followed. In 2010, the prime minister, David Cameron, announced that the government would begin measuring national well-being, and since 2011 the Office for National Statistics has included four questions in a large annual survey. People are asked, on a scale from zero to ten, how satisfied they are with their lives, how far they feel the things they do are worthwhile, how happy they felt yesterday and how anxious they felt yesterday. In 2019, New Zealand went further, presenting what it called a Wellbeing Budget, in which new government spending was expected to address priorities such as mental health and child poverty.

Critics have raised several objections. Some argue that answers to happiness questions are too easily influenced by culture to be compared between countries. Finland, for example, has regularly topped international rankings of life satisfaction, yet Finns are often described, not least by themselves, as reserved and modest rather than joyful. Others fear that governments might try to raise happiness scores through propaganda rather than real improvements, or that a focus on happiness could encourage politicians to interfere in areas of private life where they do not belong.

These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but in my view they are not a reason to abandon the idea. Cultural differences certainly make it difficult to compare countries, yet they matter much less when a government tracks changes within its own population over time, which is the main purpose of most well-being statistics. Nor is GDP itself free from problems: it counts the cost of cleaning up a disaster as economic growth, and it ignores unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives.

Nobody seriously proposes that governments should simply try to maximise a single happiness score. The more modest aim is to use well-being data to identify problems that GDP hides. The British figures, for example, have consistently shown that unemployment and poor health have a much larger effect on life satisfaction than modest changes in income, and that loneliness is a serious problem for many people. This kind of evidence can help governments decide where public money will do the most good.

In my view, the answer is not to replace GDP but to stop relying on it alone. A country that grows richer while its people become more anxious, lonely and overworked is not, in any meaningful sense, making progress. Measuring well-being will not tell governments exactly what to do, and the numbers must be interpreted with care. But a society tends to value what it measures, and it seems to me that how people feel about their lives is one of the things most worth measuring.

listeningParts.title: Booking a steam railway trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a heritage steam railway to book a day trip for her family.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Good morning, Moorvale Steam Railway, booking office. Gemma speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I'm hoping to book a trip on one of your steam trains for my family. We're staying in the area for a couple of weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Lovely. Are you thinking of our standard return journey, or one of our special events?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: The standard service runs from Moorvale station up the valley to Highcross, at the top of the line, and then back again. The round trip takes around three hours, including a stop of forty minutes at Highcross, where there's a small museum about the history of the line. On certain days we also run special trains, like the Fish and Chip Express in the evening, or the Driver Experience, where you spend an hour on the footplate with the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The standard one sounds right. We've got three children, and I think an evening trip would be too late for the youngest.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: How old are the children?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Twelve, nine and four.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Children under five travel free, so you'd only pay for two of them. Which day were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Friday the fourteenth, if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm sorry, Friday is fully booked, because there's a large school group travelling that day. But I've got plenty of space on Saturday the fifteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday is fine. We're flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: There are three departures from Moorvale on Saturdays: ten fifteen, twelve thirty and half past two. The ten fifteen is pulled by our oldest locomotive, which was built in 1912, so it's very popular with enthusiasts.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My husband would love that. We'll take the ten fifteen.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Good choice. Now, for two adults and two children, the best option is our family ticket, which is fifty-eight pounds. If you bought the tickets separately, it would come to sixty-four, so you save a little.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Can we choose where we sit?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: You can. Most of the train is made up of carriages from the 1950s, but we also have an observation carriage at the back, with large windows at the end, so you can watch the track disappearing behind you. It's an extra three pounds per person, but children usually love it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do that, then. And is there any food on board?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: There's a buffet car serving hot drinks, sandwiches and cakes. Or you're welcome to bring your own picnic. There are picnic tables at Highcross, beside the river, and it's a lovely spot if the weather's good.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. We'll probably bring our own.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Could I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Rachel Hollingworth. That's H-O-L-L-I-N-G-W-O-R-T-H.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My mobile is 0412 556 803. It's an Australian number, I'm afraid.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: That's no problem. We'll only use it if there's a change to the service. Occasionally, in very dry weather, we have to replace the steam engine with a diesel, because sparks from the chimney can start fires in the fields beside the line. If that happens, we'll send you a text and offer you a discount or a refund.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I hadn't thought of that. And how do we get our tickets?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: I'll email you a booking confirmation, and you collect the actual tickets from the booking office at Moorvale on the day. Please arrive at least twenty minutes before departure, as the queue can be quite long on Saturdays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there parking at the station?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a car park right next to it. It costs four pounds for the day, and the machine only takes coins, so make sure you bring some change with you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. Oh, one more thing. My father is coming to stay next month, and he's mad about trains. Do you sell gift vouchers?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: We do. They're available in any amount from ten pounds, and they're valid for a year. You can buy them online or in our shop at the station.

listeningParts.title: A visit to an air museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to an aviation museum and explains its layout.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Northfield Air Museum. My name's Dave, and I'll be your guide for the first part of your visit. Before we set off, I'll give you a bit of background and explain how the museum is laid out, so that you can explore on your own later.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum is built on the site of a real airfield, which opened in 1938 as a training base for pilots. After the war it was used by a flying club for many years, and when the club moved to a larger airport in the 1990s, a group of local residents campaigned to persuade the council to turn the site into a museum rather than sell it for housing. Today we have over sixty aircraft, and more than half of the people who work here are still volunteers, many of them retired engineers and pilots, so if you have a question, please ask them. They love to talk.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere, but please don't use a flash in Hangar Two, because some of the fabric-covered aircraft there are very old, and strong light can damage the materials over time. You're welcome to touch any aircraft that has a green sticker next to it, but please don't climb on anything unless a member of staff is with you.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me explain the layout. We're standing in the entrance hall, and the first building you come to is Hangar One. This tells the story of the early days of flight, from the first balloons in the eighteenth century to the aircraft of the First World War. One of the most popular exhibits here is a full-size copy of a balloon basket, which children can climb into. You'll also find a set of display cases about women in aviation, including pilots who set long-distance records in the 1930s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Hangar Two is our largest building, and it covers the golden age of passenger air travel, from the 1950s onwards. The highlight is the front section of a jumbo jet, which you can walk through, from the cockpit to the first-class cabin. It gives you a good idea of how luxurious flying used to be, and how much the seats have changed. In the same hangar, there's a collection of airline uniforms and a whole wall of old posters advertising holidays abroad, which many of our older visitors find quite nostalgic.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you'd like to see how air traffic was managed, head to the original control tower, at the far end of the site. It's been restored to look exactly as it did in the 1960s, with the original radio equipment. On the top floor, there's a viewing gallery, and on clear days you can watch planes landing at the international airport about twenty kilometres away. There's also a flight simulator up there, which you can book for fifteen-minute sessions at the information desk. It's very realistic, and I'll warn you now: most first-time pilots crash.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the outdoor airfield, where we keep the larger military and cargo aircraft that won't fit inside. On the first Sunday of each month, we start the engines of some of our historic planes, and occasionally one of them actually takes off, weather permitting. That's also where you'll find our picnic area and the children's playground, which is designed to look like a small airport.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: As for food, the café is next to the shop in the entrance hall. It's run by volunteers, and all the money it makes goes towards restoring aircraft. Our current project is a small passenger plane from the 1950s, which was found in very poor condition in a farmer's field. The restoration has already taken four years, and we hope to finish it next summer. You can watch the volunteers at work through a glass window in the workshop behind Hangar One.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, I think that's everything. We'll start in Hangar One, and this part of the tour will take about forty-five minutes. Please stay together, and follow me.
