listeningParts.title: Can trains replace short flights?
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two transport studies students, Maya and Tom, discuss their report on high-speed rail with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Maya, hi, Tom. Come and sit down. So you're about halfway through your report on high-speed rail and short-haul flights. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've done most of the reading, and we've started looking at some case studies of routes where a fast rail line has opened alongside an existing air route.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Remind me what your main question is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Basically, whether high-speed trains can take passengers away from planes on journeys of up to about a thousand kilometres, and what factors make the difference.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what have you found so far?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The clearest finding is that journey time is the most important factor, but it's the total journey time that matters, not just the time spent on the train or in the air. With a flight, you have to get out to the airport, which is often a long way from the city centre, arrive early for security checks, and then travel into the city at the other end. Stations are usually right in the centre.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So several studies suggest that if the train takes less than about three hours, most people choose the train. Once it's more than four or five hours, flying usually wins.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's consistent with what I've read. Which case studies are you using?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The first one is Japan. The original Shinkansen line between Tokyo and Osaka opened in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics, and it's still one of the busiest high-speed lines in the world. What impressed me most wasn't the speed, though, it was the reliability. The average delay is measured in seconds rather than minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Our second case study is France. The first TGV line, between Paris and Lyon, opened in 1981, and air traffic between the two cities fell sharply afterwards. More recently, France has banned some domestic flights on routes where there's a train alternative of less than two and a half hours.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That ban got a lot of attention. Did you find out how much difference it actually made?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Not a huge amount, to be honest. Only a few routes were affected, partly because there are exceptions for passengers who are connecting to other flights. And many people on those routes had already switched to the train anyway. So critics say it was more symbolic than practical.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point to make. A policy can matter symbolically even if its direct effect is small. What about cost?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That was the most surprising part for us. We expected trains to be cheaper, but on many routes in Europe, budget airlines charge less than the train, especially if you book early. Part of the reason is tax. In many countries there's no tax on aviation fuel, whereas rail companies have to pay for electricity and for access to the track.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the cost of building the lines?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It's enormous. High-speed lines need very gentle curves and slopes, so they often require long tunnels and bridges, and in crowded countries buying the land is extremely expensive. That's why some people argue the money would be better spent improving existing railways.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, I'd like you to think about the environmental argument a bit more critically. It's often assumed that trains are always the greener choice.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We were going to say that electric trains produce far lower emissions per passenger than planes, especially where the electricity comes from renewable sources.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's true once the trains are running. But building a new line produces a great deal of emissions, from all the concrete and steel. So the overall benefit depends on how many passengers use the line over its lifetime. A line with very few passengers might take decades to make up for its construction emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We hadn't really thought about that. We could add a section on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Please do. And for your presentation next month, I'd suggest a map comparing the networks in Japan and France. Visuals help a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay. Should we collect any data of our own?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: A short survey of students about how they travel home at the end of term would be a nice addition. Keep it to ten questions at most, or people won't finish it.

listeningParts.title: From the Grand Tour to the package holiday
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a tourism history course on how travel for pleasure developed in Europe.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. In this lecture, I want to look at one of the most important chapters in the history of travel: the Grand Tour, and how it eventually gave way to something we would recognise today as modern tourism.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For most of history, people travelled because they had to. Merchants travelled to trade, soldiers to fight, and pilgrims to visit holy places. The idea of travelling mainly for education and pleasure is much more recent. From around the middle of the seventeenth century until the early nineteenth century, it became fashionable for wealthy young men, particularly from Britain, to spend a long period travelling around continental Europe. This was known as the Grand Tour. The term was popularised by an English priest, Richard Lassels, in a guide to Italy published in 1670.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The typical Grand Tourist was a young man from an aristocratic family, often in his early twenties, who had just finished his studies at Oxford or Cambridge. He would usually be accompanied by a tutor, whose job was to supervise his education and, ideally, his behaviour. These tutors were sometimes jokingly called 'bear-leaders', because they were said to lead their wild young students around like performing bears. The tour could last anything from a few months to several years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The main purpose was education. Young men were expected to improve their knowledge of languages, especially French and Italian, to study art and architecture, and to learn the manners of polite society. The most important destination was Italy, and above all Rome, where travellers could see the remains of the classical world they had read about at school in Latin and Greek texts. Florence, Venice and Naples were also essential stops.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Getting there was far from easy. Travelling through France meant long days in horse-drawn carriages on poor roads. To reach Italy, many travellers crossed the Alps by the Mont Cenis pass. Carriages could not be driven over the pass, so they were taken apart and carried by mules, while the travellers themselves were carried up and down the mountain in chairs by local porters. Many wrote home describing how terrified they had been.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Grand Tourists were also enthusiastic collectors. They brought home paintings, sculptures, books and antiquities, many of which can still be seen in the great country houses of Britain. Views of Venice by the painter Canaletto were especially popular, and in Rome many visitors had their portraits painted by Pompeo Batoni, often posing in front of famous ancient ruins. The excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii, which began in the 1730s and 1740s, added a new attraction, as travellers could watch buried Roman towns being uncovered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: During the eighteenth century, the Grand Tour gradually became less exclusive, and growing numbers of middle-class travellers and women took part. But it was badly interrupted by the French Revolution and the wars that followed, which made travel across much of Europe dangerous until 1815.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The real transformation came with the railways. In 1841, Thomas Cook, a Baptist preacher who campaigned against alcohol, organised a special train to take around five hundred people from Leicester to a temperance meeting in Loughborough. The ticket cost one shilling, and the price included food. This trip is often described as the beginning of the package tour, because one person arranged the transport, the meals and the activities for a whole group. Cook went on to organise tours to Scotland, and later to continental Europe and beyond.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At around the same time, new guidebooks began to appear, such as those published by John Murray in Britain and Karl Baedeker in Germany, which gave practical information about routes, prices and hotels. Together, the railways, the guidebooks and the organised tour made travel for pleasure possible for millions of ordinary people. Next week, we'll look at how cheap air travel in the twentieth century transformed tourism all over again.

readingPassages.title: Lighter than air: the first balloon flights
paragraphs: On 4 June 1783, a crowd gathered in the market square of Annonay, a small town in south-eastern France, to watch an unusual experiment. Two brothers, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, lit a fire beneath an enormous bag made of cloth lined with paper. As it filled with hot smoke, the bag swelled, strained against the ropes holding it down and, when released, rose high into the sky. It stayed in the air for around ten minutes and came down a couple of kilometres away. The age of human flight had begun, not with wings, but with a bag of hot air.

The Montgolfiers were not scientists by training. They came from a family of paper manufacturers, and their knowledge of paper and fabric was essential to their success. According to a popular story, Joseph got the idea while watching clothes drying over a fire billow upwards, although this may be a later invention. What is certain is that the brothers did not fully understand why their balloons rose. They believed that burning produced a special gas, sometimes called 'Montgolfier gas', and they burned damp straw and wool to create as much thick smoke as possible. In fact, the explanation is simpler: hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it, and so it rises.

News of the Annonay experiment reached Paris quickly, and it inspired a rival. The physicist Jacques Charles knew that hydrogen, a gas that had been identified by the English scientist Henry Cavendish in 1766, was far lighter than air. Working with two brothers, Anne-Jean and Nicolas-Louis Robert, he built a small balloon of silk coated with rubber to keep the gas from escaping. On 27 August 1783 it was launched from the Champ de Mars in Paris. It flew for about forty-five minutes before coming down near the village of Gonesse, where frightened villagers, who had never seen anything like it, attacked it with pitchforks and knives.

The Montgolfiers, meanwhile, had been invited to demonstrate their invention at the royal palace of Versailles. On 19 September 1783, in front of King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette, they sent up a balloon carrying a basket containing a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Nobody knew whether living creatures could survive in the upper air, and the animals served as the first test passengers. The flight lasted around eight minutes, and the balloon landed safely about three kilometres away. All three animals survived, which encouraged the brothers to attempt a flight with people on board.

That flight took place on 21 November 1783, from the gardens of the Château de la Muette, on the western edge of Paris. The passengers were Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier, a young science teacher, and the Marquis d'Arlandes, an army officer. It is often said that the king had suggested sending condemned prisoners instead, since the risks were unknown, but that Pilâtre de Rozier objected that such an honour should not go to criminals. The two men stayed aloft for about twenty-five minutes and travelled roughly nine kilometres across the city. They had to keep feeding the fire with straw, and d'Arlandes later described using wet sponges to put out small fires that broke out in the fabric.

Only ten days later, on 1 December, Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert made the first manned flight in a hydrogen balloon, rising from the Tuileries Garden in front of an enormous crowd. They flew for around two hours and landed more than thirty kilometres away. Charles then went up again alone and climbed to around three thousand metres, where he suffered from intense cold and pain in his ears. He never flew again. His balloon, however, included features such as a valve for releasing gas, bags of sand used as ballast and a basket hanging from a net, and this design remained the basic pattern for gas balloons for more than a century.

The flights caused a sensation. Balloons appeared on fans, plates, clocks and furniture, and huge crowds gathered wherever a launch was announced. The American statesman Benjamin Franklin, who was living in Paris at the time, watched the early flights with great interest. When a sceptical observer asked him what use a balloon could possibly be, Franklin is said to have replied, 'What is the use of a newborn baby?' Practical uses did soon appear: scientists took instruments into the air to study the atmosphere, and in 1794 the French army used a balloon for observation at the Battle of Fleurus.

Ballooning was also dangerous. In January 1785, Jean-Pierre Blanchard and the American doctor John Jeffries became the first people to cross the English Channel by air, though they had to throw almost everything overboard, including some of their clothing, to stay up. Later that year, Pilâtre de Rozier tried to cross in the opposite direction in a balloon that combined hydrogen and hot air. It came down soon after take-off, and he and his companion became the first known victims of an air crash. Hot-air ballooning then declined for many years, until engineers developed modern balloons heated by propane burners around 1960, creating the popular sport we know today.

readingPassages.title: The railway that changed the world
paragraphs: On 15 September 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened to the public. It was not the world's first railway: wagons had run on wooden or iron rails for centuries, and the Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened in 1825, had already used steam locomotives to haul coal. But the Liverpool and Manchester was something new. It was the first railway to link two major cities, the first to rely on steam locomotives for all its regular services, and the first to run passenger trains according to a timetable. In many ways, it was the model for every main-line railway that followed.

The railway was built to solve a business problem. In the early nineteenth century, Manchester was the centre of the world's cotton industry, but the raw cotton its mills needed arrived by ship at the port of Liverpool, around fifty kilometres away. Goods travelled between the two cities by canal and river, which was slow and, according to the merchants, unreasonably expensive, since the canal companies faced little competition and could set their own charges. In winter, the canals sometimes froze, and in dry summers the water could run low. A group of Liverpool merchants concluded that a railway would be faster, cheaper and more reliable.

Not everyone agreed. The canal owners, naturally, saw the railway as a threat to their profits, and powerful landowners objected to a line crossing their estates. Opponents spread alarming claims that the smoke would kill birds, that sparks would set fire to crops and that cows would stop giving milk. The first attempt to obtain permission from Parliament, in 1825, failed after the engineer George Stephenson was questioned by lawyers for the opponents and was unable to defend serious errors in the survey of the route. A second application, based on a new route that avoided some of the most difficult estates, was approved in 1826.

Building the line was a major engineering achievement. The most famous obstacle was Chat Moss, a large area of bog so soft that a person could barely walk across it. Experts had declared that no railway could be built there. Stephenson's solution was to lay the track on hurdles of heather and brushwood, so that it effectively floated on the surface, and huge quantities of material disappeared into the bog before the line was stable. Elsewhere, workers cut a deep passage through solid rock at Olive Mount, dug a tunnel beneath Liverpool to reach the docks and built a viaduct of nine arches across the Sankey valley, where, ironically, the railway crossed over a canal.

Even as construction continued, the company's directors had not decided how the trains would be pulled. Some favoured horses, which were familiar and reliable. Others proposed stationary steam engines placed along the route, which would haul trains with long cables. To settle the question, the directors organised a public competition at Rainhill in October 1829, offering a prize of five hundred pounds for the best locomotive. Several machines took part, and one, called Novelty, was a favourite with the crowds because of its speed, but it broke down repeatedly. The winner was Rocket, built by George Stephenson and his son Robert, the only locomotive to complete the trials. Its design, which included a boiler with many small tubes to heat the water more efficiently, influenced locomotives for decades.

The opening day was meant to be a triumph, and the Prime Minister, the Duke of Wellington, travelled on the first train. But it was overshadowed by tragedy. During a stop to take on water, several passengers stepped down onto the line, among them William Huskisson, a Member of Parliament for Liverpool and a strong supporter of the railway. As he crossed the track to speak to the Duke, he was struck by Rocket, which was approaching on the other line. His leg was badly crushed, and he died that evening. His death was reported across the country and made him one of the first widely publicised victims of a railway accident.

Despite this sad beginning, the railway was a remarkable success. Its promoters had expected freight, especially cotton, to provide most of its business, but the number of people wanting to travel far exceeded their predictions. A journey that had taken several hours by stagecoach could now be completed in under two. Investors and engineers came from across Britain and abroad to study the line, and within a few years railways were being planned between all the major cities of Britain. By the 1840s, the country was in the grip of a 'railway mania', with hundreds of new lines proposed.

The influence of the Liverpool and Manchester can still be felt today. Stephenson built it to a gauge, or distance between the rails, of four feet eight and a half inches, a measurement he had used on earlier colliery lines. Because so many early railways were built by Stephenson and his followers, this became known as standard gauge, and it is now used by the majority of the world's railways. Much of the original route is still in use, and the Manchester terminus at Liverpool Road, often described as the world's oldest surviving passenger station, is now part of a museum of science and industry.

readingPassages.title: Should we fly less?
paragraphs: Within a single lifetime, flying has changed from a luxury enjoyed by a wealthy few into a routine part of modern life. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, airlines carried more than four billion passengers a year, and the industry expected that number to keep rising. Yet over the same period, concern about the climate has grown, and aviation has become a symbol of the conflict between personal freedom and environmental responsibility. In Sweden, a new word, flygskam, or 'flight shame', spread around 2018, as some people began to feel uncomfortable about the emissions caused by their travel. The climate campaigner Greta Thunberg, who refuses to fly, made the issue internationally famous when she crossed the Atlantic by sailing boat in 2019.

How large is the problem? Aviation is responsible for roughly two and a half per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions. That may seem modest, but it is not the whole story. Aircraft also release nitrogen oxides and water vapour at high altitude, and under certain conditions they create contrails, the long white lines of ice crystals that can trap heat in the atmosphere. When these effects are included, scientists estimate that aviation's share of human-caused warming is considerably larger. Moreover, while other sectors such as electricity generation are steadily reducing their emissions, aviation is one of the hardest to clean up, so its share is likely to grow.

The emissions are also very unevenly distributed. Most of the world's population has never taken a flight, while a small minority flies many times a year. One widely cited estimate suggests that around one per cent of the world's people are responsible for roughly half of the emissions from passenger flights. For this reason, some campaigners have proposed a frequent-flyer levy, a tax that would be low or even zero for a person's first flight each year but would rise steeply with every additional journey. Supporters argue that this would protect the annual family holiday while discouraging the habits of the most frequent travellers.

The aviation industry, unsurprisingly, prefers technological solutions. The most promising in the short term is sustainable aviation fuel, which can be made from waste materials such as used cooking oil, animal fats and agricultural leftovers, and which can be mixed with ordinary jet fuel without changes to engines. Over their whole life cycle, such fuels can produce far lower emissions than fossil fuels. However, at present they make up only a tiny fraction of the fuel used by airlines, they cost considerably more, and the supply of suitable waste is limited.

Electric aircraft are another possibility, and several small prototypes have already flown. The difficulty is weight. Even the best modern batteries store many times less energy per kilogram than jet fuel, so a battery-powered airliner capable of crossing an ocean is not realistic with current technology. Electric planes are therefore likely to be used first for small aircraft on short routes, such as those connecting islands. Aircraft powered by hydrogen have also been proposed, but they would require new aircraft designs and new infrastructure at airports, and are unlikely to be common for many years.

In the meantime, many airlines invite passengers to offset their emissions by paying a little extra for projects elsewhere, such as planting trees or protecting forests. Offsetting has been heavily criticised. It is often difficult to check whether a project really removes the carbon it claims, or whether the forest would have been protected anyway, and trees that are planted may later be cut down or destroyed by fire. Critics argue that offsets allow people to feel that they have solved the problem without changing their behaviour.

For shorter journeys, the alternative of the train is increasingly attractive. High-speed rail already competes successfully with air travel on many routes in Europe and Asia, and France has gone as far as banning some domestic flights where a train journey of less than two and a half hours is available. In Europe, night trains, many of which were cut in the early twenty-first century because they were losing money, have been making a comeback, allowing passengers to cover long distances while they sleep and to arrive in a city centre in the morning.

In my view, campaigns that rely on making individuals feel guilty are unlikely to achieve much on their own. Most people will continue to fly if flying remains cheap and convenient, and it is unfair to place the burden on the occasional traveller visiting family abroad. Greater responsibility, I believe, should fall on those who fly most often, which is why a frequent-flyer levy seems to me a fair idea. Nor should we forget that flying brings real benefits: it connects families separated by migration, and tourism by air supports jobs in many poorer countries. The aim should not be to end flying, but to make sure that its true environmental cost is reflected in its price.

listeningParts.title: Booking an underground mine tour
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a heritage centre to book a family visit to a historic tin mine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Polgarrow Heritage Mine, this is Jenna speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. We're visiting the area next month, and my wife and I would like to bring our children on one of your underground tours. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two tours. The first is the Surface Trail, which is a guided walk around the old engine houses and the buildings where the tin ore was crushed. It takes about an hour, and it's all outdoors. The second is the Deep Level Tour, where you put on protective equipment and walk through the tunnels the miners dug about two hundred years ago. That one lasts about ninety minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The underground one sounds like the one the kids would really enjoy. Is there a minimum age?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There is. On the Surface Trail anyone's welcome, but for the Deep Level Tour children have to be at least seven years old. We used to take five-year-olds, but some of the passages are quite narrow and low, and younger children found it frightening, so we changed the rule last year. How old are your children?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We've got three, and the youngest has just turned eight, so that's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. So that's two adults and three children. Which day were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping for Saturday the twelfth.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm sorry, the twelfth is fully booked. Saturdays are always busy in the summer. I could offer you Sunday the thirteenth, or the following Saturday, the nineteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We're leaving on the eighteenth, so it'll have to be the Sunday. The thirteenth, then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No problem. On Sundays, the tours run at ten o'clock, half past twelve and three o'clock. The ten o'clock one is full, I'm afraid, so would half past twelve suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Half past twelve is perfect. And how much will it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: For the Deep Level Tour, it's sixteen pounds for an adult and ten for a child, but for a family of five we do a family ticket, which works out cheaper. That's fifty-four pounds for the whole group.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great, we'll take the family ticket. Is there anything we need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We provide a hard hat with a lamp attached, and a waterproof cape, because water drips from the roof in some of the tunnels. It's eleven degrees underground all year round, even in August, so please bring a warm jumper for everyone. And you'll need shoes with a good grip, because the floor can be slippery.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's useful to know. Is there anything else for the children to do after the tour?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, they usually love the gem panning. They get a bag of sand and gravel, wash it in a stream channel, and keep any small stones they find, such as amethyst or quartz. It costs three pounds a bag, and you pay on the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: They'll definitely want to do that. Can I book now?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Certainly. Could I have your surname, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Delaney. D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Delaney. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My mobile is 07946 318 520.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. When you arrive, please don't use the main car park next to the gift shop, because that's for coaches. Use the lower car park, just past the entrance gate on the left. It's free, and it's only a two-minute walk to the ticket office.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And should we arrive early?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Please arrive at least twenty minutes before your tour, so there's time to collect your equipment and watch a short safety film. If you're late, we can't let you join the group once it has gone underground.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Understood. One more question. Is there somewhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a café in the old count house, where the mine managers used to work. It's famous for its pasties, which were the traditional lunch of the miners here. It does get busy at lunchtime, though, so you might want to eat before your tour.

listeningParts.title: A visit to a coal mining museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a museum on the site of a former coal mine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashworth Colliery Museum. My name's Graham, and before you start exploring, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the site and explain what you can see in each part of the museum.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Coal was mined here for almost a hundred and fifty years, and at its busiest, in the nineteen twenties, the colliery employed over two thousand men and boys. The mine finally closed in 1991, and the museum opened five years later. Many of our volunteers are former miners, so if you see someone in a blue jacket, do ask them about their working lives. They tell the story far better than any display.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me say a word about why the museum looks the way it does. When the mine closed, most of the buildings were due to be demolished, and it was actually the local community, rather than the council or the coal company, that campaigned to save them. People felt that if the buildings disappeared, the history of the town would disappear with them. So the museum really belongs to the people of Ashworth.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. The whole site is free to enter, but there's a charge for the underground tour, which leaves from the main gate every hour. Unfortunately, the underground tour isn't suitable for wheelchair users, because the only way down is the original cage, but we have a virtual tour on a large screen in the visitor centre which shows exactly the same tunnels.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let's look at the different buildings. The first one you'll come to is the lamp room. Before electric lamps, miners carried flame safety lamps, like the one invented by Humphry Davy in 1815. The flame was surrounded by a fine metal mesh, which stopped it from lighting the explosive gas that collects in mines. In the lamp room, you can see hundreds of lamps on the walls, and the brass tokens miners collected at the start of every shift. If a token wasn't returned at the end of the day, everyone knew that a man was still underground.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to the lamp room is the engine house, which contains the huge steam winding engine that raised and lowered the cage in the shaft. It's the oldest building on the site, and the engine is still in working order. We run it every Saturday afternoon, and it's well worth seeing. Please don't climb on the railings, though, as the floor below is a long way down.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Across the yard are the pithead baths. Surprisingly, until the nineteen thirties, miners here went home covered in coal dust, and they washed in a tin bath in front of the fire. The baths changed that. Today, the building holds our exhibition on the lives of mining families, including the role of women, who ran the homes and, during strikes, organised kitchens to feed the whole community. There's also a children's activity area in this building, with dressing-up clothes and a model mine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, at the far end of the site are the stables. Ponies worked underground here, pulling wagons of coal, and some of them stayed below ground for most of the year. People are often surprised to learn that the miners became very attached to them, and the ponies were usually well cared for. Today, the stables are home to two retired ponies, Duke and Bramble, and children can help to feed them at eleven o'clock and three o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: In the same building, you'll find the display about canaries. Miners took them underground because the birds react to poisonous gas much more quickly than people do. If the canary became ill, the men knew they had to get out. British mines only stopped using canaries in 1986, when electronic detectors replaced them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The café is in the visitor centre, and the gift shop sells books written by local people about the mine. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A project on responsible gemstone sourcing
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two business students, Maya and Tom, discuss their research on the jewellery supply chain with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Maya, Tom, you've chosen to look at how jewellery companies make sure their gemstones are sourced responsibly. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the background reading, and we've interviewed managers at three jewellery retailers. The main thing we've learned is that the supply chain for gemstones is much longer and more complicated than we'd imagined. A sapphire might be mined in one country, cut and polished in another, set in a ring somewhere else, and pass through several traders before it reaches a shop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And at every stage, information can get lost. One manager told us that by the time a stone arrives at their head office, they often only know which dealer they bought it from, not the mine where it came out of the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you look at the Kimberley Process?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a section on it. It's the international certification scheme for rough diamonds that started in 2003, after the wars in countries like Sierra Leone, where the sale of diamonds was paying for armed groups. Every shipment of rough diamonds between member countries has to have a certificate saying it's conflict-free.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: But the criticism we found most convincing is that its definition of a conflict diamond is very narrow. It only covers diamonds that fund rebel groups fighting governments. It says nothing about diamonds mined using child labour, or where workers are treated badly by governments or companies. So a diamond can be certified even if the conditions at the mine were terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And it only covers diamonds, of course. What about coloured gemstones?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's actually the part of the project that interested us most. There's no equivalent scheme for rubies, sapphires or emeralds, and a large proportion of them come from artisanal miners, people working on their own or in small groups, often with very simple tools.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Some estimates put the number of people working in artisanal mining worldwide in the tens of millions. And it's not all negative. For many families in rural areas, it's the main source of income, so if jewellery companies simply refused to buy from small-scale miners, it could make poverty worse rather than better.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Boycotts can harm the very people they're intended to protect. So what are companies doing instead?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The retailers we spoke to described a few approaches. One of them is working directly with a cooperative of miners in East Africa, paying them a fair price and funding safety training. The other two use digital tracking, where each stone is recorded at every stage, so the customer can see its whole history.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Although, to be honest, we were a bit sceptical about the tracking. The system is only as reliable as the information people put into it at the start. If someone records a stone from one mine as coming from another, the technology can't detect that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that's the kind of critical thinking I want to see. What about the lab-grown stones? Some people argue they solve the whole problem.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We've included them. Two of the three retailers now sell lab-grown diamonds, and they said younger customers in particular are choosing them. They're chemically identical to mined diamonds, and much cheaper. But they need a lot of electricity to produce, so their environmental impact depends on where the power comes from.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the next stage, I'd like you to add a customer perspective. You could run a short survey asking whether people would pay more for a traceable stone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We were thinking about that. We could do it at the university's careers fair next week, as there'll be lots of people around.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine, but remember that students aren't typical jewellery buyers, so mention that as a limitation. And please send me a draft of your questions by Friday, so I can check them before you start.

listeningParts.title: Lithium: the metal behind the battery
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an earth resources course on where lithium comes from and how it is produced.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're turning to a metal that, until quite recently, most people had never thought about, but which is now at the centre of the global shift towards electric vehicles and renewable energy. I'm talking, of course, about lithium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with some basic chemistry. Lithium was identified in 1817 by the Swedish chemist Johan August Arfwedson, who found it while analysing a mineral called petalite. It's the lightest of all metals, and it's so reactive that in the laboratory it has to be stored in oil to stop it reacting with air and moisture. Its lightness, and the ease with which it gives up electrons, are exactly what make it so valuable in rechargeable batteries.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For most of the twentieth century, lithium had fairly modest uses. It was added to glass and ceramics to make them more resistant to heat, and to grease used in engines and machinery. It also has an important medical use: lithium salts have been used since the middle of the century to treat bipolar disorder. But today, the majority of lithium produced goes into batteries, and demand has grown enormously.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So where does it come from? There are two main sources. The first is brine, which is very salty water found beneath salt flats in dry, high-altitude regions. The best-known area is the so-called lithium triangle, where Chile, Argentina and Bolivia meet, which is thought to hold more than half of the world's known lithium resources. Here, the brine is pumped up from underground into huge shallow ponds, and the sun does most of the work. As the water evaporates, the brine becomes more and more concentrated. This takes a long time, often more than a year, and then the concentrated liquid is processed into lithium carbonate.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This method is relatively cheap, but it's controversial. The Atacama region in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth, and local Indigenous communities have raised concerns that pumping brine, along with the fresh water used in processing, may be lowering water levels and harming the lagoons where flamingos feed. The scientific evidence is still being debated, but it's clearly an issue that companies can't ignore.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second source is hard rock. Here, lithium is extracted from minerals, mainly one called spodumene, which is dug out of open-pit mines. Australia is the world's largest producer by this method, and it has also been the world's largest producer of lithium overall in recent years. The rock is crushed and heated to very high temperatures, and much of it has traditionally been shipped to China for refining. Hard-rock mining is faster than evaporation, but it uses more energy and produces more carbon emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Because of these drawbacks, researchers and companies are investing in what's called direct lithium extraction. Instead of waiting for the sun to evaporate the water, these technologies use special filters or chemicals to pull the lithium out of the brine in hours or days, and then the remaining water can be returned underground. Several projects are also testing whether lithium can be recovered from the hot, salty water used in geothermal power plants, for example in California and in Cornwall in south-west England, where the hot springs deep underground turn out to be rich in lithium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, there's recycling. At the moment, only a small proportion of lithium from used batteries is recovered, partly because batteries are complex and difficult to take apart safely. But as the first generation of electric cars reaches the end of its life, the amount of material available for recycling will increase dramatically, and many experts believe that recycled lithium could eventually meet a significant share of demand. In the next session, we'll look at another battery metal, cobalt, and the ethical questions surrounding its supply.

readingPassages.title: From treasure to tin foil: the story of aluminium
paragraphs: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, making up about eight per cent of it by weight. It is found in clays, in many common rocks and in the soil beneath our feet. Yet for most of human history it was completely unknown as a metal. The reason is chemical: aluminium bonds so strongly with oxygen that it never occurs naturally in pure form, and separating the two proved extraordinarily difficult. As a result, a metal that is now used to wrap sandwiches was, for a few decades in the nineteenth century, more valuable than gold.

The first person to produce aluminium was the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted, who in 1825 obtained a tiny lump of the impure metal. Two years later, the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler improved the method, but the quantities remained minute. In 1854, the French chemist Henri Sainte-Claire Deville developed a process that used sodium to release the metal, and for the first time aluminium could be made in bars rather than grains. Even so, it remained so costly that it was treated as a luxury material, and bars of it were displayed to the public at the Paris Exhibition of 1855.

Deville's work was supported by the French emperor Napoleon III, who hoped that the light metal might be used to equip his army. According to a popular story, he also served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery, while less important visitors had to make do with gold. Whether or not this is exactly true, it captures how the metal was regarded. In the United States, the Washington Monument, completed in 1884, was capped with a small aluminium pyramid weighing less than three kilograms, chosen partly because the metal was so rare and admired.

The transformation came two years later. In 1886, two young scientists working on opposite sides of the Atlantic, the American Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, independently discovered that aluminium could be produced by passing an electric current through alumina, a compound of aluminium and oxygen, dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite. By a remarkable coincidence, both men were born in 1863 and both died in 1914. Their method, now known as the Hall–Héroult process, is still the basis of almost all aluminium production today. Hall went on to help found the company that later became Alcoa, one of the world's largest aluminium producers.

A second breakthrough soon followed. In 1888, the Austrian chemist Carl Josef Bayer patented a method for refining bauxite, a reddish rock rich in aluminium, into pure alumina. Bauxite takes its name from the village of Les Baux in southern France, where it was first identified in 1821. Together, the Bayer and Hall–Héroult processes made it possible to produce aluminium on an industrial scale, and its price collapsed. Within a generation, it had gone from a curiosity for emperors to an everyday material used in pots, pans and machinery.

The new metal found its most important role in transport. When the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903, the engine they built had a crankcase made of cast aluminium, which kept it light enough to lift the aircraft. During the twentieth century, aluminium alloys became essential to aviation, and later to cars, trains and the drinks can. However, the electrolysis process requires enormous amounts of electricity, which is why aluminium smelters are often built near cheap sources of hydroelectric power, in countries such as Norway, Canada and Iceland.

Aluminium production also creates environmental problems. The Bayer process leaves behind large quantities of a caustic waste known as red mud, which is usually stored in vast reservoirs. In October 2010, the wall of one such reservoir at an alumina plant near Ajka in Hungary collapsed, releasing a flood of red mud that swept through nearby villages, killing ten people and polluting rivers as far as the Danube. The disaster led to calls for stricter regulation of waste storage across the industry.

One of aluminium's greatest advantages, however, is that it can be recycled again and again without losing its quality. Recycling uses only about five per cent of the energy needed to produce new metal from bauxite, and the industry estimates that around three-quarters of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use. A drinks can thrown into a recycling bin today may be back on a supermarket shelf as a new can within a couple of months. For a metal once prized by emperors, it has become one of the most ordinary, and most sustainable, materials of modern life.

readingPassages.title: Messengers from the deep: how diamonds are made
paragraphs: A diamond is made of nothing more than carbon, the same element that forms the graphite in an ordinary pencil. What makes the two so different is the way their atoms are arranged. In graphite, carbon atoms form flat sheets that slide easily over one another, which is why pencil marks rub off on paper. In diamond, every atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid three-dimensional framework, producing the hardest natural material known. On the scale of mineral hardness devised by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs in 1812, diamond is placed at the top, with a value of ten.

Such a structure can only form under extreme conditions. Most natural diamonds crystallised in the Earth's mantle, roughly 150 to 200 kilometres below the surface, where temperatures exceed 1,000 degrees Celsius and the pressure is tens of thousands of times greater than at sea level. These conditions are found mainly beneath the oldest and thickest parts of the continents. Dating of the tiny mineral grains trapped inside diamonds shows that many of them are extremely old, typically between one and three and a half billion years, which means that most diamonds were already ancient before the first animals appeared.

How, then, do diamonds reach the surface? The answer lies in a rare kind of volcanic eruption. Deep in the mantle, molten rock rich in gas occasionally forces its way upwards at great speed, carrying fragments of the surrounding rock, including any diamonds, with it. The speed is crucial: if diamonds rose slowly, the falling pressure would allow them to turn into graphite. The rock that fills the carrot-shaped pipes left by these eruptions is called kimberlite, and no such eruption has ever been witnessed by human beings.

Kimberlite takes its name from the town of Kimberley in South Africa, the site of one of the most famous mineral rushes in history. In 1867, a boy found a shiny pebble on a farm near the Orange River, which turned out to be a large diamond. Further discoveries followed, and from 1871 thousands of prospectors arrived to dig on a small hill. Working with picks and shovels, they created what became known as the Big Hole, more than two hundred metres deep. By the time mining stopped in 1914, it had produced nearly three tonnes of diamonds.

Not all diamonds, however, are dug from kimberlite pipes. Over millions of years, erosion wears away the rock at the surface, and rivers carry the released diamonds downstream. Because diamonds are hard and dense, they survive this journey and collect in gravels along riverbeds and coasts. Such deposits, known as alluvial deposits, were the source of the first diamonds ever mined, in India more than two thousand years ago. Today, some of the richest are found off the coast of Namibia, where diamonds carried by the Orange River to the Atlantic are recovered from the seabed by specially equipped ships.

For scientists, diamonds are valuable for a reason that has nothing to do with jewellery. Because they are so strong and chemically stable, they act as tiny time capsules, preserving fragments of minerals from parts of the Earth that can never be sampled directly. In 2014, researchers studying a small, worthless-looking diamond from Brazil reported that it contained a mineral called ringwoodite, which forms only at depths of more than 500 kilometres. The ringwoodite contained water, suggesting that this deep layer of the mantle may hold a very large quantity of water locked inside its minerals.

Impurities also give diamonds their colours. A completely pure diamond is colourless, but such stones are rare. Small amounts of nitrogen, the most common impurity, give many diamonds a yellowish tint, while traces of boron produce a blue colour. The famous Hope Diamond, now in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, owes its deep blue colour to boron. Other colours, such as pink and red, are thought to result from distortions in the crystal structure rather than from foreign atoms, and these stones are among the most expensive in the world.

Since the twentieth century, diamonds have also been made in laboratories. In 1954, scientists at the American company General Electric produced the first reproducible synthetic diamonds by recreating the high pressures and temperatures of the mantle. A second method, developed later, grows diamonds from a carbon-rich gas, layer by layer. Synthetic diamonds were first used mainly in industry, for cutting and drilling, but gem-quality stones are now widely sold. Because they are chemically identical to natural diamonds, telling the two apart requires specialised instruments, a challenge that has transformed the work of gem-testing laboratories.

readingPassages.title: Should we mine the deep ocean floor?
paragraphs: Scattered across vast areas of the deep ocean floor, at depths of four to six kilometres, lie billions of dark, potato-sized lumps known as polymetallic nodules. They contain manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper, metals that are in growing demand for the batteries, wind turbines and power networks of a low-carbon economy. The richest known field is the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, an area of the Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico covering several million square kilometres. To mining companies, the nodules represent an opportunity to obtain these metals without the deforestation and community conflicts associated with mines on land. To many scientists, they represent one of the least understood ecosystems on the planet.

Interest in the nodules is not new. They were first brought to the surface in the 1870s by the British research ship HMS Challenger, and in the 1960s and 1970s several companies explored ways of collecting them. One of the most famous projects of that era, the ship Hughes Glomar Explorer, was publicly described as a nodule-mining vessel, but it had in fact been built for the American intelligence agency, the CIA, to secretly recover a sunken Soviet submarine. The publicity surrounding it nevertheless encouraged a belief that deep-sea mining was about to begin. It did not, largely because metal prices fell and the technical difficulties proved immense.

The legal framework was established in the decades that followed. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the seabed beyond national jurisdiction and its mineral resources are declared the 'common heritage of mankind'. Activities there are controlled by the International Seabed Authority, based in Kingston, Jamaica, which has issued exploration contracts to governments and companies but, so far, no licences for commercial mining. In 2021, the Pacific island nation of Nauru, working with a Canadian company, triggered a rule that obliged the Authority to complete its mining regulations within two years. That deadline passed without agreement, and the negotiations have continued.

Supporters of deep-sea mining make a serious case. The world needs enormous quantities of metals to replace fossil fuels, and land-based mining has well-documented environmental and human costs, from polluted rivers to unsafe working conditions. Nodules lie loose on the seabed, so they can be collected without digging or blasting, and a single deposit can contain several valuable metals at once. In my view, these arguments deserve to be taken seriously rather than dismissed; the choice is not between mining and no mining, but between different places and methods of obtaining the materials that a cleaner energy system requires.

The difficulty is how little we know about what would be lost. A study published in 2023 estimated that around five thousand species have been recorded in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and that the vast majority of them have not yet been formally described by science. Many animals depend on the nodules themselves, which provide one of the few hard surfaces on an otherwise soft, muddy floor. Since nodules grow by only a few millimetres every million years, removing them would eliminate that habitat for a period far longer than human history. Early tests also suggest that mining would create clouds of sediment that could smother animals far beyond the area actually mined.

The long-term evidence is sobering. In 1989, German researchers ploughed a section of the seabed off the coast of Peru to imitate the effects of mining. When scientists returned more than twenty-five years later, the plough tracks were still clearly visible, and many forms of life had not recovered. More recently, in 2024, a team led by the marine scientist Andrew Sweetman reported evidence that oxygen may be produced on the sea floor in complete darkness, possibly through electrical activity on the surface of the nodules. The finding is disputed, but it illustrates how much remains to be discovered about these environments.

Opposition has grown accordingly. A number of countries, including France and Germany, have called for a pause or a ban on deep-sea mining until its impacts are better understood. Several major companies, among them car manufacturers and technology firms, have pledged not to use metals from the seabed in their products. Meanwhile, improvements in battery chemistry have reduced the amount of cobalt and nickel needed in some designs, and better recycling could further reduce demand for newly mined metals. In my view, these developments weaken the claim that the ocean floor must be mined urgently.

Where does this leave us? It seems to me that the strongest argument is not that deep-sea mining should never happen, but that it should not begin before we understand what it would destroy. Decisions made now could cause damage lasting thousands or even millions of years, in places that belong, by international agreement, to all of humanity, including generations not yet born. Caution, in this case, is not an obstacle to progress. It is the only responsible way to make a choice that cannot be reversed.

processSteps: Rock containing copper ore is blasted and dug from an open-pit mine

listeningParts.title: Booking a family visit to a castle
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones the visitor bookings office of a historic castle to plan a family day out.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Hawksmoor Castle visitor bookings, Rachel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm hoping to book a visit for my family during the school holidays. We'd like to do one of your guided tours, if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. How many people would that be?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Two adults and three children. The children are six, nine and thirteen.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Our standard ticket gives you entry to the castle, the gardens and the exhibition in the old stables. Adult tickets are fourteen pounds fifty, and children aged five to sixteen are seven pounds. But we also have a family ticket for two adults and up to three children, which is forty pounds, so that would be the best value for you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great, the family ticket, then. And what about the tours?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There are two. The Castle Highlights tour lasts about an hour and covers the great hall, the chapel and the medieval kitchens. Then there's the Hidden Castle tour, which takes you into parts of the building that are normally closed to the public, including the dungeon and the top of the north tower. That one lasts ninety minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The Hidden Castle tour sounds exciting. Is it suitable for children?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It is, but there's a minimum age of eight, because there are a lot of narrow stone staircases. There are a hundred and twelve steps up to the top of the tower alone.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ah. My youngest is only six.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Then I'd suggest the Highlights tour for the whole family. And if your older two would like something extra, they could join our archaeology workshop in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What happens in that?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's run by our education team in the old dairy, next to the walled garden. The children learn how archaeologists work, and they get to handle real objects found during excavations here at the castle, such as pieces of pottery and old coins. It lasts two hours and costs six pounds per child. It's designed for ages nine to fourteen, so both of your older children could take part.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect, they'd love that. Which days does it run?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: During the holidays it's on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Which date were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping for Thursday the twenty-third of August.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm afraid the workshop on the twenty-third is already full, but there are still places on Tuesday the twenty-eighth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The twenty-eighth would work too. We're staying in the area that whole week.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good. On that day, the Highlights tours start at ten thirty, twelve o'clock and half past two. The workshop begins at two, so I'd recommend the first tour of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ten thirty, then. That gives us time for lunch in between. Is there somewhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's a café in the courtyard that serves hot meals and sandwiches, or you're very welcome to bring your own food. The picnic area is down by the lake, and there are tables there.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll probably bring a picnic. What about parking?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Parking is free for visitors. The main car park is closest to the entrance, but it's usually full by about eleven in the holidays, so if you arrive for the ten thirty tour you should be fine. Otherwise there's an overflow car park, which is about ten minutes' walk away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I book everything now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes. Could I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Mark Treloar. T-R-E-L-O-A-R.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Treloar. And a contact phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's oh-seven-seven-one-three, four-eight-two, nine-six-oh.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. So that's a family ticket at forty pounds, plus two places on the workshop at six pounds each, which makes fifty-two pounds altogether. The Highlights tour is included in the ticket price, so there's no extra charge for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very reasonable. Is there anything else we need to know?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'll send you a confirmation email. Please show it at the gatehouse when you arrive, and the staff there will give you wristbands. The children will need to wear theirs for the workshop. Oh, and the castle floors can be uneven, so I'd recommend comfortable shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Will do. Can we bring our dog?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Dogs are welcome in the gardens and the picnic area if they're on a lead, but not inside the castle buildings, I'm afraid, apart from assistance dogs.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Thanks very much for your help, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: You're welcome. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: Training new volunteer guides
listeningParts.contextDescription: The volunteer manager of a historic country house gives a talk to new volunteer room guides.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for coming. My name's Helen Marsh, and I'm the volunteer manager here at Ashcombe Hall. Before you start shadowing our experienced guides next week, I'd like to give you a bit of background about the house and explain what we'll be asking you to do.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: First, a little history. The hall was built in the early seventeenth century for a wealthy wool merchant, and the same family lived here for more than three hundred years. After the Second World War, the family could no longer afford to repair the roof, and the government was asking them to pay very heavy taxes on the estate. So, rather than sell it to a developer, they gave the house and its contents to our heritage trust. That's why so much of the original furniture is still here, which is quite unusual for a house of this age.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, many of you have told me you volunteered because you love history, and that's wonderful. But when I ask our long-serving volunteers what they enjoy most, they rarely mention the history. What they talk about is the conversations they have with visitors, and the feeling that they're helping people to connect with the house. So please don't worry about memorising every date. Visitors would much rather hear a good story than a list of facts.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me say a word about conservation, because it affects almost everything we do. You'll notice that many of the rooms are quite dark, and that the curtains are often partly closed. Visitors sometimes complain about this, so you need to be able to explain it. Light, and especially the ultraviolet part of sunlight, causes permanent damage to textiles, paintings and paper. Colours fade, and fabrics become weak and split. Once that damage is done, it can't be reversed, so keeping light levels low is the best way of protecting the collection.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: On photography, our policy has changed recently. Visitors may now take photographs in all the rooms, but they must not use flash, and tripods and selfie sticks aren't allowed, because they're too easy to knock against objects. If you see somebody touching furniture or a painting, please don't shout at them. Most people simply don't realise that the oils and salts on our skin can damage surfaces. Just explain politely why we ask people not to touch.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you about some of the rooms you'll be working in, so you know what to expect. The Great Hall is the first room visitors see, and it's usually the busiest. It's also where you'll find the oldest object in the house, a carved oak chest that's actually older than the building itself; the family brought it with them from their previous home.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The Library is much quieter. It contains around four thousand books, and it's the room where visitors most often ask questions we can't answer. That's fine. There's a folder of information in a drawer of the desk, and if that doesn't help, write the question down and we'll find out.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: In the Long Gallery upstairs, we have a dressing-up box with copies of seventeenth-century clothes, and children, and quite a few adults, can try them on. It gets noisy, so it's a good room for volunteers who enjoy working with families.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The Kitchen is one of the most popular rooms. Every Sunday, one of our volunteers bakes bread there using a historic recipe, and visitors can taste it. If you're interested in helping with that, let me know, because you'll need a food hygiene certificate first.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: And finally, the Chapel. It's the smallest room open to the public, and because of the stone floor it's always cold, so please bring a warm layer if you're on duty there. It's also the room where the stained-glass windows are, and they're the reason we're raising money at the moment, as two of them need urgent repair.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, I'll hand out your uniforms and name badges now, and then we'll walk round the house together.

listeningParts.title: A visitor survey in a World Heritage city
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two tourism students, Owen and Grace, discuss their visitor survey in the city of Bath with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've finished collecting the data for your survey in Bath. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. As you know, we wanted to find out what visitors think about crowding in the city centre, and whether it affects how much they enjoy their visit. Bath's been a World Heritage Site since 1987, and it's one of the few places where the whole city is included, not just a single monument, so it seemed like a good case.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your responses?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: We did face-to-face questionnaires at four locations: outside the Roman Baths, near the Abbey, in the Royal Crescent and at the railway station. We'd originally planned to use an online survey with a QR code on posters, but in our pilot week almost nobody scanned it, so we changed our approach.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a useful thing to mention in your methodology. How many people did you speak to?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Two hundred and forty in total. We'd hoped for three hundred, but it rained heavily on two of our survey days, and there were far fewer people about.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Two hundred and forty is still a reasonable sample for a project of this size. Did you have any trouble persuading people to take part?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Not really. We kept the questionnaire short, about five minutes, and we told people that at the start. Families with young children were the hardest to stop, understandably, and some tour groups couldn't take part because their guides were keeping them on a strict schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's worth noting, because it means certain types of visitor may be under-represented. What were your main findings?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: The most interesting one was the difference between day visitors and people staying overnight. Day visitors were much more likely to say the city felt overcrowded. We think that's partly because they all tend to visit the same few places at the same times, usually between eleven and three.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Whereas people staying in the city could go to the Roman Baths early in the morning or in the evening, when it's much quieter. Several of them told us that the evening was the best part of their visit.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That fits with what other research has found. Did the crowding actually reduce people's enjoyment?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Less than we expected. Most people said the crowds were annoying, but they still gave their overall visit a high score. The thing that bothered them more was the lack of information about less famous sights. A lot of visitors didn't know there was anything to see beyond the main attractions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point, because spreading visitors around is one of the main strategies that heritage cities use. Did anyone suggest what might help?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Quite a few people mentioned a phone app with suggested walking routes. And some older visitors said they'd prefer a simple printed map, because they didn't want to keep looking at their phones.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you could recommend both. What about residents? Did you speak to any?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Only a few, by accident, really. Some people we stopped turned out to live in Bath, and they had very strong opinions, mostly about coach parking and noise. We didn't include them in the main results, because our questionnaire was designed for visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd mention them in your discussion as a possible area for further research, rather than ignoring them completely. Residents' views are central to the debate about tourism in historic cities. Now, what's the biggest weakness of your study, do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Probably the timing. We only collected data in October, which isn't the busiest season. In August the results might be quite different.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Make that clear, and be careful not to claim that your findings apply all year round. Right, what are your next steps?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: We're going to enter all the data into a spreadsheet this week, and then make some charts comparing the four locations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And include a photograph of each location, so that readers can picture them. I'd like a complete draft by the twelfth of December, please.

listeningParts.title: Intangible cultural heritage
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a heritage studies course about the protection of living traditions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. So far in this course, we've mainly been talking about heritage you can touch: buildings, monuments and landscapes. Today I want to turn to a different kind of heritage, which UNESCO calls intangible cultural heritage. In simple terms, this means living traditions: the practices, skills and knowledge that communities pass from one generation to the next.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For a long time, international heritage protection focused almost entirely on physical sites. The World Heritage Convention of 1972, which we discussed last week, was designed to protect monuments and natural areas. But many countries, particularly in Asia, Africa and Latin America, argued that this approach favoured nations with grand stone buildings, and ignored the heritage that mattered most to their own people, such as music, festivals and oral traditions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One country had in fact been protecting living traditions for decades. In 1950, Japan passed a law that covered not only objects and buildings but also performing arts and craft skills. A few years later, it began recognising individual masters of traditional arts, such as pottery, puppet theatre and sword-making, as what are popularly known as Living National Treasures. The idea was that the skill itself was the treasure, and that the people who held it should be supported so that they could train apprentices.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At the international level, an important step came from an unexpected place: a market square in Marrakesh, in Morocco. The square, called Jemaa el-Fnaa, is famous for its storytellers, musicians and other performers. In the 1990s, there were plans to develop the area, and the Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, who lived in the city, campaigned to protect not just the square as a space, but the activities that took place there. In 2001, it was among the first examples to be recognised in a new UNESCO programme for oral and intangible heritage.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This eventually led to the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, which was adopted in 2003 and came into force three years later. You'll notice that it uses the word safeguarding rather than protection. That's deliberate. A building can be protected by preventing change, but a living tradition must be allowed to change, or it dies. The aim is to make sure the tradition continues to be practised and passed on.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The convention identifies five broad areas. The first is oral traditions, including language as a means of passing them on. The second is the performing arts, such as music, dance and theatre. Third, there are social practices, rituals and festive events. Fourth, knowledge and practices concerning nature, for example traditional medicine or methods of navigation. And fifth, traditional craftsmanship.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Countries can nominate elements for a Representative List, and there's also a separate list for traditions that are in urgent need of safeguarding, often because there are very few practitioners left. Food is a particularly popular category. The French gastronomic meal was inscribed in 2010, and in 2017 the art of the Neapolitan pizza maker was added. In 2020, four North African countries, Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia, made a joint nomination for the knowledge and practices of making and eating couscous, which was seen as a good example of countries sharing a tradition rather than competing over it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, the system isn't without its critics. One concern is that once a tradition is listed, there may be pressure to perform it in a fixed, official version for tourists, which can freeze something that has always varied from village to village. Another is commercialisation: a listed festival or dish can become a marketing brand. And some anthropologists ask a difficult question: who has the right to decide what a community's authentic tradition is? Is it the government, experts, or the community itself?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There's also the question of what happens when a tradition is shared across borders. Several nominations have caused disagreements between neighbouring countries, each claiming a dish, a dance or a musical instrument as its own. That's one reason why joint nominations, like the couscous example, are increasingly encouraged.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For your next seminar, I'd like you to choose one listed element and investigate how listing has affected the community that practises it.
