readingPassages.title: The temples that moved
paragraphs: On the west bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, close to the border with Sudan, stand two of the most extraordinary monuments of the ancient world. The temples of Abu Simbel were cut directly into a sandstone cliff during the reign of the pharaoh Ramesses II, in the thirteenth century BC. The larger of the two is guarded by four colossal seated statues of the king, each around twenty metres high. The smaller temple was dedicated to his principal wife, Nefertari, and to the goddess Hathor. Yet the temples visitors see today are not where Ramesses' builders left them. In the 1960s, they were cut into pieces and moved to higher ground.

For many centuries after the decline of ancient Egypt, the temples were largely forgotten, and sand from the desert gradually buried much of the larger one. In 1813, the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt saw the tops of the great statues emerging from the sand. Four years later, the Italian explorer Giovanni Belzoni cleared enough of the entrance to get inside. European visitors who followed were amazed by the scale of the carvings and by the wall reliefs inside, which show scenes from Ramesses' military campaigns, including the famous Battle of Kadesh.

The threat to the temples came in the twentieth century. In the 1950s, the Egyptian government decided to build a new, much larger dam on the Nile at Aswan, to control the river's annual flood, store water for farming and generate electricity. The Aswan High Dam would create an enormous reservoir, later named Lake Nasser, stretching hundreds of kilometres south into Sudan. The rising water would cover a large part of the region known as Nubia, forcing tens of thousands of people to leave their homes, and it would drown dozens of ancient sites, including Abu Simbel.

In 1959, Egypt and Sudan asked UNESCO for help, and the following year the organisation launched an international appeal to save the monuments of Nubia. The response was remarkable. Around fifty countries contributed money or expertise, and archaeologists from many nations hurried to excavate and record sites before they disappeared under the water. Several temples were dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere, and a number were given to countries that had supported the campaign. The Temple of Dendur, for example, was given to the United States and now stands in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Abu Simbel presented the greatest challenge of all. Various solutions were proposed, including surrounding the temples with a huge dam of their own, or lifting each temple in a single piece using hydraulic jacks. In the end, engineers chose a plan that was cheaper and less risky. Work began in 1964, while a temporary barrier held back the rising water. The temples were cut into more than a thousand blocks, many of which weighed around twenty tonnes. Workers used hand saws for the most delicate cuts, so that the faces of the statues would not be damaged, and the blocks were numbered so that they could be put back in exactly the right order.

The blocks were then reassembled on a site about sixty-five metres higher and around two hundred metres further from the river. Because the original temples had been carved into a natural cliff, the engineers also had to recreate the cliff. They built two huge concrete domes over the reconstructed temples and covered them with rock and sand, so that from the outside the site looks much as it did before. The project was completed in 1968, and the total cost was around forty million US dollars, a very large sum at that time.

One feature of the temples raised a particular concern. The larger temple was aligned so that, on two days each year, in February and October, the rising sun shines along the entire length of the building and lights up statues in the inner sanctuary, around sixty metres from the entrance. Interestingly, one of the four statues, representing Ptah, a god associated with the underworld, always remains in shadow. The engineers worked hard to keep this alignment in the new location, and they largely succeeded, although the event is now thought to occur about a day later than it did originally.

The Nubian campaign had consequences far beyond Egypt. It showed that the world's nations were willing to share responsibility for protecting sites of exceptional importance, wherever they happened to be. This idea helped to shape the World Heritage Convention, adopted by UNESCO in 1972, under which countries agree to identify and protect places of outstanding universal value. In 1979, Abu Simbel and the other Nubian monuments were themselves added to the World Heritage List. Today, hundreds of thousands of tourists visit the temples each year, many of them arriving by plane or coach from Aswan, about two hundred and eighty kilometres to the north.

readingPassages.title: Loved to death: protecting fragile sites from their visitors
paragraphs: Heritage sites face many threats, from war and neglect to pollution and climate change. But for some of the world's most famous places, the greatest pressure now comes from the people who love them most: their visitors. International travel has grown enormously over the past half century, helped by cheaper flights, rising incomes and, more recently, social media, which can turn a little-known beach or village into a global attraction almost overnight. For the managers of fragile sites, the challenge is to allow people to enjoy these places without destroying the very qualities that attract them.

Visitors can cause damage in ways that are not always obvious. Millions of footsteps wear away stone floors and steps, and erode paths on mountains and in national parks. In enclosed spaces, the warmth, moisture and carbon dioxide that people breathe out can change the air, encouraging the growth of algae and mould. Touching walls and statues leaves oils from the skin, and some visitors carve their names into ancient surfaces. Even the infrastructure built for tourists, such as car parks, hotels and souvenir shops, can spoil the setting of a site and place heavy demands on local water supplies.

One of the clearest examples of this kind of damage is the cave of Lascaux in south-west France. Its walls are covered with paintings of horses, deer and bulls, created around seventeen thousand years ago. After four teenagers discovered the cave in 1940, it was opened to the public, and by the late 1950s, more than a thousand people a day were visiting. Their breath and body heat changed the conditions inside the cave, and green algae began to grow on the paintings. In 1963, the cave was closed to the public, and it has remained closed ever since. Instead, visitors can see detailed replicas, the first of which opened nearby in 1983.

Few sites can simply be closed, however, so managers have developed other ways of controlling numbers. Many now require visitors to book tickets for a specific time. At Machu Picchu, the fifteenth-century Inca citadel in Peru, the authorities have introduced timed entry tickets, a daily limit on visitors and set routes through the site, so that people move in one direction rather than crowding into the most popular spots. Some visitors complain that these rules reduce their freedom, but they have made it possible to keep the site open while reducing wear on its stone terraces and stairways.

In some cases, a temporary closure has given nature a chance to recover. Maya Bay, on the Thai island of Ko Phi Phi Leh, became world famous after it appeared in the film The Beach, released in 2000. By the 2010s, thousands of visitors were arriving every day by boat, and the coral reef in the bay had been badly damaged by anchors, pollution and trampling. In 2018, the Thai authorities closed the bay completely. When it reopened in 2022, swimming was banned, boats were no longer allowed to enter the bay itself, and the number of visitors was limited. Scientists have reported that the coral is recovering and that sharks have returned to the shallow water.

Another approach is to use price to manage demand. The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has long followed a policy it describes as high value, low volume, which means attracting fewer visitors who each spend more, rather than large numbers of budget travellers. Most international visitors must pay a daily sustainable development fee, which is used to fund projects such as conservation and free healthcare. Critics argue that such fees make travel a privilege of the wealthy, but supporters say they ensure that tourism pays for its true costs, which are usually borne by local people and the environment.

Technology is also playing a growing role. Some sites now use sensors to count visitors in real time and adjust entry accordingly, while apps can suggest less crowded times or alternative attractions. Detailed digital models, created using laser scanning, allow people to explore places they could never visit in person, such as the interiors of fragile tombs. These tools cannot replace the experience of standing in front of a real monument, but they can reduce pressure on the most vulnerable sites and help to preserve a record of them in case they are damaged in the future.

Ultimately, managing visitors is not only about protecting stones and paintings; it is also about the people who live in and around heritage sites. Residents may benefit from tourism jobs, but they also experience rising rents, crowded streets and the loss of local shops to souvenir stalls. Successful management therefore requires their involvement in decisions. As one principle of sustainable tourism puts it, a place that is good to live in is usually also a good place to visit. The reverse, sadly, is not always true.

readingPassages.title: Should lost heritage be rebuilt?
paragraphs: When a great historic building is destroyed, whether by war, fire or deliberate attack, the first reaction is often a determination to rebuild it exactly as it was. Yet among conservation specialists, reconstruction has long been a controversial idea. A rebuilt monument, critics argue, is not the original but a copy, and treating a copy as if it were the real thing risks deceiving the public and devaluing genuine historic fabric. Others reply that buildings matter not only as old materials but as symbols of identity, and that rebuilding them can help communities to recover from trauma.

The modern conservation movement has generally been cautious. The Venice Charter, an influential international agreement drawn up by architects and conservation experts in 1964, states that restoration should be based on firm evidence and must stop where guesswork begins. Any new work needed should be clearly recognisable as modern, so that nobody confuses it with the original. Behind this approach lies a belief, developed in nineteenth-century Europe, that a building's value comes largely from its authentic materials and the marks that time has left on them.

Nevertheless, some of the most celebrated reconstructions of the twentieth century were made in direct contradiction to this principle. During the Second World War, most of the historic centre of Warsaw was deliberately destroyed by German forces. After the war, Polish architects rebuilt the old town's streets, churches and market square, using pre-war drawings and photographs, as well as eighteenth-century paintings of the city by the Italian artist Bernardo Bellotto. In 1980, the rebuilt centre was added to the World Heritage List, not as an original medieval town, but as an outstanding example of an almost complete reconstruction.

A similar story can be told about the Old Bridge at Mostar, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The elegant stone arch was completed in 1566 under Ottoman rule and stood for more than four centuries, until it was destroyed during the war in 1993. After the conflict, an international team rebuilt it using traditional methods, and divers recovered some of the original stones from the river below. The bridge reopened in 2004 and was added to the World Heritage List the following year. For many people, its reconstruction was a symbol of reconciliation between communities that had been on opposite sides of the war.

In Dresden, the eighteenth-century Frauenkirche, a Protestant church with a great stone dome, collapsed after the bombing of the city in 1945. For decades its ruins were left as a war memorial. Reconstruction began in 1994 and was completed in 2005, and wherever possible, original stones recovered from the ruins were put back in their former positions. Because the old stones are darkened by fire and age, the rebuilt church shows a pattern of dark and light stone, making the history of its destruction visible. In my view, this honest display of old and new is the most convincing answer to the charge that reconstruction is a form of deception.

Not every case of destruction has led to rebuilding. In 2001, the two giant Buddha statues carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan valley of Afghanistan, which had stood for around fifteen hundred years, were blown up by the Taliban. Since then, there has been a long debate about whether they should be reconstructed. Some argue that rebuilding would undo an act of cultural violence; others believe that the empty niches have become an important memorial in their own right, and that a reconstruction based on limited evidence would be largely imaginary. So far, the niches remain empty.

Perhaps the most interesting challenge to the Western emphasis on original materials comes from Japan. The Grand Shrine of Ise, one of the most sacred sites of the Shinto religion, has been rebuilt every twenty years for well over a thousand years, most recently in 2013. Each time, a new shrine is built on a neighbouring site using fresh wood and traditional techniques, and the old one is taken down. Here, what is preserved is not the material but the form and the knowledge of how to build it. Recognition of this kind of thinking led to the Nara Document on Authenticity of 1994, which accepted that ideas of authenticity vary between cultures.

The question returned to public attention after the fire at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 2019, which destroyed its roof and its nineteenth-century spire. After some debate about whether to add a modern design, the French authorities decided to rebuild the spire as it had been, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024. I believe that this was the right decision, because the spire had become part of how people around the world picture Paris. Reconstruction, in short, should not be rejected on principle. It should, however, be honest about what is new, and it should reflect the wishes of the people for whom the building has meaning.

listeningParts.title: Booking a fitness test at a sports science centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a university sports science centre to book a fitness assessment before running his first marathon.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Northgate University Sports Science Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi. I saw on your website that members of the public can book fitness tests in your laboratory, and I'd like a bit more information. I'm training for my first marathon in the spring.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. We offer three assessments for the public. The simplest is the Health Check, which measures your blood pressure, body fat and flexibility. That takes about forty-five minutes. Then there's the Running Profile, where we film you on a treadmill, analyse your technique and record your heart rate at different speeds. And the third is the Endurance Test, which measures how much oxygen your body can use while you exercise. That's the same test our professional athletes do.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: How does the Endurance Test actually work?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You wear a mask connected to a machine that analyses the air you breathe out, and you run on the treadmill while the speed and the slope increase every two minutes, until you can't continue. It's hard work, I won't pretend otherwise, but people find the results really useful, because we can give you training zones based on your own heart rate, rather than on a general formula.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds like exactly what I need. How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The Endurance Test on its own is a hundred and twenty pounds. The Running Profile is eighty, but if you book both together, the total is a hundred and seventy-five, so you'd save twenty-five pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll just do the Endurance Test for now, I think. I had my running technique checked at a sports shop a few months ago.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No problem at all. I should mention that the tests are carried out by our postgraduate students, but always under the supervision of a member of staff. And with your permission, your results may be used anonymously in research projects.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine with me. When could I come?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We do public testing on Tuesday and Friday mornings. The next free slots are Tuesday the fourth at nine o'clock, or Friday the fourteenth at half past ten.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm away for work on the fourth, so the fourteenth would be better.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Right, I'll put you down for Friday the fourteenth at ten thirty. Now, there are a few things you need to do to prepare. Please don't do any hard training for two days before the test, and don't eat a large meal in the three hours beforehand. Also, avoid coffee on the morning of the test, because caffeine raises your heart rate and can affect the results.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, no coffee? That'll be the hardest part! What should I wear?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Normal running clothes and the shoes you usually train in. There are showers and lockers, so bring a towel, and please bring a water bottle as well, although we do have a drinking fountain in the corridor.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And where exactly are you? I've never been to the campus.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We're in the Hamilton Building, right next to the athletics track. If you come by car, use car park C. You'll need a visitor permit, which you can collect from the main reception when you arrive. It's free, but you have to display it on the windscreen.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Do you need my details?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, please. Could I have your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Daniel. And how old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm thirty-four.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And have you had any injuries or health problems recently? We ask everybody, because the test is quite demanding.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I had a problem with my ankle last year, but it's completely fine now. I've been running forty kilometres a week without any pain.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Please mention the ankle on the health questionnaire anyway. I'll email the questionnaire to you today, and you need to complete it and bring it with you on the day. Payment is taken when you arrive, by card or cash.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. And when do I get the results?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You'll receive a written report within a week, and it includes a twenty-minute meeting with the person who tested you, so they can explain what the numbers mean and how to use them in your training. Is there anything else I can help you with?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, that's everything. Thanks very much, Megan.

listeningParts.title: Open day at a national training centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes visitors to an open day at a centre where elite athletes train.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Westvale National Training Centre. My name's Carly, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we start walking, I'll give you a quick introduction, and then I'll explain what you'll see in each part of the centre.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Many visitors are surprised to hear that this site was once an airfield. The runway was closed in the nineteen-nineties, and the centre opened here in 2009. If you look out of the windows on the north side, you can still see the old control tower, which is now used as offices by our coaching staff.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: At any one time, around three hundred athletes train here, in twelve different sports. Some of them live on site in the accommodation block, especially the younger ones who have moved here from other parts of the country, but most live nearby and come in every day. The centre is funded partly by the government and partly by money raised through the national lottery, and in return, we open our doors to the public several times a year, as we're doing today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One thing I'd like to stress is that the athletes are working, not performing for visitors. So please don't ask them for photographs or autographs while they're training. If they're happy to talk to you during a break, that's fine, but let them come to you. And you're welcome to take photos of the buildings, but please don't use flash anywhere indoors, because it can distract athletes at important moments, for example when a gymnast is in the air.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: People often ask me what makes a centre like this different from an ordinary gym. The answer is really the support around the athletes. Each athlete has a team that might include a coach, a physiotherapist, a nutritionist and a sports psychologist, and they all share information, so that the training programme can be adjusted quickly if, say, an athlete isn't sleeping well or has a minor injury.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the places we'll visit. We'll begin at the hydrotherapy pool. This isn't used for swimming training at all; it's a warm pool where injured athletes do exercises, because the water supports their body weight and reduces the pressure on their joints. You'll be able to see the underwater treadmill, which always gets a lot of attention.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: From there we'll go to the biomechanics laboratory. This is where scientists use high-speed cameras and sensors in the floor to measure exactly how athletes move. Today, the scientists will be running a short demonstration, and two volunteers from the group will be able to try the long-jump runway and see their own results on a screen.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next is the altitude chamber. This is a sealed room where the amount of oxygen in the air can be reduced, so that athletes can experience conditions similar to being high up in the mountains without leaving the country. For safety reasons, visitors can't go inside, but there's a large window, and one of the physiologists will explain how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: After that, we'll stop at the performance kitchen. Every athlete's diet is planned individually, according to their sport, their body size and the stage of the season they're in, so meals are prepared here rather than bought from outside. Our chefs will be giving away samples of a recovery smoothie, so you'll get a taste of what the athletes eat. If you have any food allergies, please tell the chefs before you try anything.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And we'll finish at the indoor athletics hall, which has a two-hundred-metre track. This is the only part of the centre that local schools and clubs can book, usually in the evenings and at weekends, when our own athletes aren't using it. Information about booking is available at the main reception.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, there's a café near the entrance, which is open to the public every day, not just on open days. Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll head to the pool.

listeningParts.title: A project on exercising in the heat
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two sports science students, Priya and Tom, discuss their research project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've finished collecting the data for your project on exercise in hot conditions. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. Just to remind you, we compared two ways of cooling athletes down before exercise: drinking ice slurry, which is a mixture of crushed ice and liquid, and drinking the same amount of cold water.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what made you choose that topic in the first place?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It was partly the Tokyo Olympics. We read that the marathon and the race walks were moved to Sapporo, much further north, because of worries about the summer heat in Tokyo. That made us realise how serious the problem is becoming for event organisers, not just for athletes.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: And with summers getting hotter, it seems likely that more competitions will be held in extreme conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Remind me how you set up the experiment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We had ten participants, all members of the university cycling club. Each of them came to the lab twice, a week apart. On one visit they drank ice slurry before cycling, and on the other they had cold water. Then they cycled in the heat chamber, which we set at thirty-five degrees, until they were too exhausted to continue.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did they know which drink they were getting?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Well, obviously they could see and feel the difference between ice and water, so we couldn't hide it from them. That's a weakness we'll have to discuss. But we didn't tell them what we expected to find, and the person recording their times didn't know which drink they'd had.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that helps. And how did you measure body temperature?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: With a small capsule that the participants swallowed a few hours before the test. It sends a radio signal to a receiver, so we could follow their core temperature throughout the ride. Some of them were a bit nervous about swallowing it, but nobody refused.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: On average, the participants cycled for longer after drinking the slurry, by about ten per cent. What was interesting was that they stopped at almost the same core temperature in both conditions, just under forty degrees. So the slurry seemed to give them more room before they reached that point.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That fits with what's been found in published studies. Was the improvement the same for everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: No, it varied a lot. Two participants actually did slightly worse with the slurry. One of them said it gave him a stomach ache, which we hadn't expected at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's worth reporting. Practical problems like that matter if you're advising real athletes. Now, did you look at acclimatisation at all?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Only in the literature review. Most sources say that the body needs between about one and two weeks of training in the heat to adapt properly. Athletes start sweating earlier and more heavily, and their heart rate doesn't rise as much.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then you could argue in your discussion that pre-cooling is a useful extra, but not a replacement for proper acclimatisation. What are you planning for the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with a short video of the heat chamber, because most people in our year haven't seen it. Then Priya will present the results, and I'll talk about limitations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Keep the video short, no more than a minute. And for the results, I'd use a graph showing each participant's times separately, not just the average, because the variation is one of your most interesting findings.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: That's a good idea. We'd only made a bar chart of the averages.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Finally, make sure you mention the sample size. Ten people is fine for a student project, but it's too small to draw firm conclusions. You should suggest repeating it with a bigger group, perhaps including women, since all your participants were men.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We'll add that. Thanks.

listeningParts.title: Technique, technology and the limits of sport
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a sports science course on how changes in technique and equipment have affected athletic performance.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Last week we looked at how training methods have improved athletic performance over the past century. Today I want to focus on two other factors: changes in technique and changes in equipment, and, importantly, how sports organisations decide what's fair.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's begin with the high jump. For much of the twentieth century, jumpers used techniques in which they went over the bar facing it or sideways, and they landed on their feet. That was necessary, because the landing area was often just a pit filled with sand or sawdust. In the nineteen-sixties, however, these pits began to be replaced by thick foam mats, and that opened up new possibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The athlete who took advantage of this most famously was the American Dick Fosbury. He developed a technique in which he ran towards the bar on a curve, turned, and went over head first, on his back, landing on his shoulders. Many coaches thought it looked ridiculous, and some thought it was dangerous. But at the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, Fosbury won the gold medal, and within a few years, the Fosbury Flop, as it became known, was used by almost every top jumper. It remains the dominant technique today. The point here is that the change in technique depended on a change in equipment: nobody would have landed on their back in a sandpit.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The pole vault shows the influence of equipment even more clearly. In the first half of the twentieth century, most vaulters used poles made of bamboo, which was light but could break. After the Second World War, metal poles became common. Then, from the late nineteen-fifties, poles made of fibreglass were introduced. Unlike metal, fibreglass bends a great deal and then straightens, returning much of the energy the athlete puts into it. World records rose rapidly as athletes learned to use the new poles.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: My third example comes from speed skating. In a traditional skate, the blade is fixed firmly to the boot. In the clap skate, the blade is attached only at the front, by a hinge, so that when the skater pushes off, the heel lifts but the blade stays in contact with the ice for longer. Researchers in the Netherlands developed the modern version in the nineteen-eighties, and once top skaters adopted it in the late nineties, times fell sharply. At the 1998 Winter Olympics in Nagano, in Japan, world records were broken in several events.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, in none of these cases did the governing bodies ban the new equipment, because it was available to everyone and it still required skill. But that isn't always the outcome. Consider swimming. Around 2008, new swimsuits were introduced that contained panels of polyurethane, a type of plastic. They compressed the swimmer's body into a smoother shape, reducing drag, and they also trapped air, which increased buoyancy, helping swimmers float higher in the water. Dozens of world records were broken in just two years. Critics began to describe this as 'technology doping'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In response, the international swimming federation introduced new rules, which came into force in 2010. Suits now have to be made of fabric only, and there are limits on how much of the body they can cover. For several years afterwards, very few of the records set in the plastic suits were broken, which suggests just how much of an advantage they had given.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: More recently, the same debate has arisen in running. Since around 2017, road-racing shoes containing a thick layer of new foam and a stiff carbon plate have helped athletes run faster, and many records have fallen. World Athletics, the sport's governing body, responded by setting a maximum thickness for the sole, of forty millimetres for road races, rather than banning the shoes altogether.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what principle should governing bodies follow? A useful question to ask is whether the technology improves the athlete's own ability to perform, or whether it does part of the work for them. We'll come back to that in the seminar. For next week, please read the article on the reading list about artificial limbs in elite sport.

readingPassages.title: The long road of the marathon
paragraphs: Few sporting events have a story as famous as the marathon. According to a popular legend, after the Athenians defeated a Persian army at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, a messenger ran about forty kilometres to Athens to announce the victory, cried out the news and immediately fell dead. It is a moving tale, and it inspired one of the best-known races in the world. The historical evidence for it, however, is surprisingly weak.

The earliest account of the period comes from the Greek historian Herodotus, who wrote several decades after the battle. He describes a professional runner called Pheidippides who was sent from Athens to Sparta before the battle to ask for help, arriving on the day after he set out. That journey was roughly two hundred and forty kilometres, far longer than a modern marathon. Herodotus says nothing about a run from Marathon to Athens. That version of the story appears only in the work of writers living in the Roman period, several centuries later, and they did not agree on the messenger's name.

Whatever its origins, the legend proved useful when the modern Olympic Games were being planned. The French scholar Michel Bréal, a friend of the Games' founder, Pierre de Coubertin, suggested a long-distance race from Marathon to Athens for the first modern Olympics, held in Athens in 1896. Bréal even offered a silver cup for the winner. The Greek organisers welcomed the idea, hoping that a race linked to their ancient history would attract public interest.

Their hopes were more than fulfilled. Greek athletes had won few events at the Games, and when a local water carrier named Spyridon Louis entered the stadium first, finishing in just under three hours, the crowd was overjoyed. Louis became a national hero. Inspired by the race, the city of Boston held its own marathon the following year, and the Boston Marathon, first run in 1897, is now the oldest marathon held every year in the world.

In these early races, the distance was not fixed; it was simply about forty kilometres. The figure used today comes from the 1908 Olympics in London, where the course began at Windsor Castle and finished in front of the royal box in the stadium, a distance of 26 miles and 385 yards, or 42.195 kilometres. That race is remembered for the Italian runner Dorando Pietri, who entered the stadium in the lead but collapsed several times on the track. Officials helped him across the line, and as a result he was disqualified, but his courage made him a celebrity. In 1921, the international athletics federation adopted the London distance as the official length of the race.

For much of the twentieth century, the marathon was considered unsuitable for women, and many doctors believed that such long distances could damage their health. In 1967, Kathrine Switzer entered the Boston Marathon using her initials, and an official famously tried to pull her out of the race. She finished, and the photographs of the incident were published around the world. Boston officially accepted women runners in 1972, but a women's marathon was not added to the Olympic programme until the 1984 Games in Los Angeles, where it was won by the American Joan Benoit.

In the 1970s, the marathon began to change from an event for a small number of specialists into a mass activity. The first New York City Marathon, in 1970, was a few laps of Central Park with just over a hundred runners. Today, more than fifty thousand people finish the race, and the big city marathons attract runners of all ages and abilities, many of whom raise money for charity. For most participants, the aim is not to win but simply to complete the distance.

At the very top of the sport, times have continued to fall. In 2019, the Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run the marathon distance in under two hours, finishing in Vienna in 1 hour 59 minutes and 40 seconds. Because the event used rotating teams of pacemakers and was not an open race, the time was not accepted as an official world record. Even so, it showed how far the event has come from its legendary beginnings, and it raised new questions about the limits of human endurance.

readingPassages.title: Thin air: the science of altitude training
paragraphs: When the 1968 Olympic Games were awarded to Mexico City, many scientists and coaches were worried. The city lies about 2,240 metres above sea level, and nobody was sure how athletes from lowland countries would cope. Their concerns turned out to be justified. In the longer running races, times were noticeably slower than at previous Games, and several athletes collapsed. Yet in short, explosive events such as sprinting and jumping, performances were outstanding. The American Bob Beamon's long jump of 8.90 metres broke the world record by more than half a metre and stood for almost twenty-three years.

The explanation for both results lies in the physics of the atmosphere. As altitude increases, air pressure falls. The proportion of oxygen in the air stays the same, at about twenty-one per cent, but because the air is less dense, each breath contains fewer oxygen molecules. For endurance athletes, whose muscles depend on a steady supply of oxygen, this is a serious handicap. For sprinters and jumpers, whose events last only seconds and rely less on oxygen, the thinner air is actually an advantage, because it offers less resistance to movement.

The human body, however, is capable of adapting. When a person spends time at altitude, the kidneys detect the lower level of oxygen in the blood and release more of a hormone called erythropoietin, usually known as EPO. This hormone stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, which contain haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen around the body. The process is slow, and it generally takes several weeks before the amount of haemoglobin increases significantly. When athletes return to sea level, they may for a time have a greater capacity to carry oxygen than their rivals.

The success of runners from the highlands of Kenya and Ethiopia has often been linked to these effects. Many of the world's best distance runners grew up and train at altitudes of around two thousand metres or more. Most researchers, though, believe that altitude is only part of the explanation. Factors such as an active childhood, a strong running culture, a lightweight body build and the powerful motivation provided by the prospect of escaping poverty are all thought to play a role, and no single cause has been identified.

For athletes from lowland countries, altitude training presents a dilemma. Living high up stimulates the production of red blood cells, but the thin air also makes it impossible to train at the same intensity as at sea level, so fitness may actually suffer. In the 1990s, the American researchers Benjamin Levine and James Stray-Gundersen tested a solution, known as 'live high, train low'. In their study, published in 1997, runners who lived at altitude but travelled down to train at a lower level improved their race times, whereas runners who lived and trained at sea level did not. The approach has since been adopted by many national teams.

Not every athlete can spend weeks in the mountains, and technology now offers alternatives. Altitude tents, which fit over a bed, and specially built rooms can reduce the amount of oxygen in the air, allowing athletes to 'sleep high' in their own homes. Some people have questioned whether this is fair, since it produces an effect similar to that of a banned substance. In 2006, the World Anti-Doping Agency considered prohibiting such devices, but it eventually decided not to, partly because the effect is natural and partly because the rule would have been very difficult to enforce.

Research has also shown that people respond to altitude in very different ways. In some athletes, red blood cell production increases substantially, while in others it hardly changes at all, and scientists sometimes describe these groups as 'responders' and 'non-responders'. Several practical factors also matter. The body needs iron to make haemoglobin, so athletes with low iron levels may gain little benefit, and sleep is often disturbed at altitude, which can interfere with recovery. For this reason, sports scientists now usually monitor athletes closely during altitude camps rather than simply sending them away.

The same biology that makes altitude training effective has also been exploited dishonestly. In the 1990s, a synthetic form of EPO, originally developed to treat patients with kidney disease and anaemia, was widely abused in endurance sports, particularly cycling. Because it was chemically almost identical to the hormone produced by the body, it was very hard to detect, and it was not until the Sydney Olympics in 2000 that a test for it was first used. The contrast is instructive: altitude achieves by natural means what doping achieves artificially, which is why the line between them remains a subject of debate.

readingPassages.title: Are the Olympics worth the price?
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, winning the right to host the Olympic Games was regarded as one of the greatest prizes a city could achieve. In recent years, however, the enthusiasm has faded. When the International Olympic Committee invited bids for the 2022 Winter Games, several European cities, including Oslo, Stockholm and Munich, withdrew or abandoned their plans, in some cases after local residents voted against them. Only Beijing and Almaty remained. A few years later, faced with a shortage of candidates for the Summer Games, the committee took the unusual step of awarding the 2024 Games to Paris and the 2028 Games to Los Angeles at the same time.

The main reason for this reluctance is cost. Hosting the Games requires stadiums, an athletes' village, transport links and enormous security operations, and the final bill almost always exceeds the original estimate. Researchers at the University of Oxford who examined Games held since 1960 found that every one for which reliable data were available had gone over budget, with an average overrun of more than one hundred and fifty per cent. Few other kinds of large project, they noted, perform so consistently badly.

The most notorious example is Montreal, which hosted the Summer Games in 1976. Construction problems, rising prices and an ambitious stadium design caused costs to soar, and the city took about thirty years to pay off the resulting debt. The Olympic Stadium, intended as a symbol of civic pride, became known locally as 'the Big Owe'. For a generation of politicians, Montreal served as a warning of what could go wrong.

Los Angeles, which hosted the next Summer Games but one, in 1984, took a very different approach. It was effectively the only city willing to host the event, which gave it a strong position in negotiations with the International Olympic Committee. The organisers relied heavily on existing venues, including a stadium that had been used for the 1932 Games, and raised much of their income from private sponsors and television rights. The Games ended with a surplus of more than two hundred million dollars, much of which was used to fund youth sport in the region.

Supporters of the Games often point to Barcelona as proof that the event can transform a city. In preparation for 1992, Barcelona invested heavily in new roads, an improved airport and the redevelopment of a run-down industrial area by the sea, which became a new district with beaches open to the public. In the following decades, the city became one of the most visited in Europe. Sceptics reply that much of this investment could have been made without the Games, but it is generally accepted that the deadline imposed by the event helped the city to complete projects that might otherwise have taken decades.

Other host cities have been left with expensive facilities that they do not need. After the 2004 Games in Athens, many of the venues built for sports with little following in Greece were left empty, and photographs of overgrown stadiums and empty swimming pools were widely published. Similar images emerged from Rio de Janeiro only a few years after 2016. Such buildings are costly to maintain even when they are not used, and they have become a powerful symbol for opponents of future bids.

The International Olympic Committee has responded with a series of reforms. Its Olympic Agenda 2020, adopted in 2014, encourages cities to use existing or temporary venues and allows events to be held in more than one city or even country. Paris took this approach in 2024, with the organisers stating that around ninety-five per cent of the venues were either already built or temporary. The selection process has also changed: Brisbane was chosen for 2032 through a new procedure in which the committee holds discussions with preferred candidates, rather than inviting cities to compete in expensive bidding contests.

In my view, these reforms are welcome but do not go far enough. The fundamental problem is that each host is expected to create a huge event almost from scratch, and then has little use for much of what it has built. Some commentators have proposed giving the Games a permanent home, or a small group of cities that would host them in rotation. I believe this idea deserves more serious consideration than it has received. It would certainly reduce the sense of excitement that comes from taking the Games to new places, but the price of that excitement has too often been paid by local taxpayers who were never asked whether they wanted it.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering for a sleep study
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a university research unit to volunteer for a study on sleep and memory.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Sleep Research Unit, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I saw a poster in the student union about a study you're running, and I'm thinking of taking part. I was hoping you could tell me a bit more about it first.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Of course. The study is looking at how a lack of sleep affects memory. Volunteers spend two nights in our sleep laboratory. On the first night you sleep normally, and on the second night we wake you up several times. Each morning you do some short tests on a computer, mostly remembering words and pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Right. And where exactly is the laboratory?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: It's on the third floor of the Kingsley Building, which is the tall brick building next to the hospital car park. There's a lift, and our reception is straight ahead as you come out of it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Sorry to ask, but is it paid?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: No need to apologise, everyone asks. Volunteers receive a hundred and twenty pounds for completing the whole study. If you have to leave early for any reason, we pay forty pounds for each night you've done. We also cover travel costs up to fifteen pounds, as long as you keep your tickets or receipts.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fair. Are there any requirements?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: A few. You need to be between eighteen and thirty-five, and in good general health. We can't accept anyone who works night shifts, because that disturbs the body clock and would affect the results. And we ask people not to have any coffee, tea, cola or energy drinks for twenty-four hours before each night in the lab.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hmm, that'll be the hardest part, to be honest. But I'm twenty-two and I'm a full-time student, so no night shifts.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Great. Then let me take some details. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Megan Thorley. That's T-H-O-R-L-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Thank you, Megan. Now, we only run the study from Monday to Thursday. Which nights would suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I have lectures early on Tuesday mornings, so could I come on a Wednesday and Thursday? Next week, ideally.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Let me look. I'm afraid next Wednesday and Thursday are already full. The earliest I can offer is the following week: Wednesday the fourteenth and Thursday the fifteenth of March.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine, actually. I'd rather get it done before the exams start anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Lovely. On both evenings, you'll need to arrive at eight thirty, so that we have time to prepare you before lights out at eleven. You'll get breakfast in the morning, and you should be free to leave by about nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Just your own pyjamas, a toothbrush and anything else you'd normally use in the morning. We provide the bedding, although some people like to bring their own pillow, which is fine. Please don't bring a laptop, though. We ask volunteers not to use screens for an hour before bed, so bring a book instead if you like to read.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: How do you actually measure the sleep? Is it uncomfortable?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Not at all. We attach small sensors to your head and face, which record the electrical activity of your brain and the movement of your eyes. They're held on with a special paste, which washes out easily with shampoo the next morning. There's also a camera in the room, but it's only there to check that you're safe.

dialogue.speaker: Caller

listeningParts.title: A garden for the senses
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a sensory garden speaks to a group of visitors at the start of a tour.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hartwell Sensory Garden. My name's Siobhan, and I've managed the garden for the last six years. Before you explore on your own, I'd like to give you a short introduction to what we do here and how the garden is laid out.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The garden was created twenty years ago by a group of parents whose children had visual impairments. They felt that ordinary parks were designed almost entirely for the eyes, and they wanted a place where their children could enjoy nature through touch, smell, sound and taste as well. Today, the garden is used by all kinds of people: schools, care homes for older people, people recovering from strokes, and families who simply like a quiet place to sit. In fact, about half our visitors have no disability at all. Many of them tell us that slowing down and paying attention to smells and sounds is the most relaxing part of their week.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The garden is run as a charity. We receive a small grant from the city council, but most of our income comes from donations, our café and the plant sales we hold every spring. We have only three paid staff, so we depend on around forty volunteers, who do everything from weeding to guiding school groups. If any of you would like to join them, there's an information leaflet at the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Everything here has been designed to be accessible. All the paths are wide and completely flat, so they're suitable for wheelchairs, and you'll notice that each path has a different surface: gravel, wood or smooth stone. That's deliberate. It means that people who can't see well can tell where they are from the feeling and the sound under their feet. Most of the plants are in raised beds, about knee height, so you can touch and smell them without bending down.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a few rules. Unlike in most gardens, you are encouraged to touch the plants here. The only exception is in the Scent Walk, where a few plants have red labels; those can irritate the skin, so please just smell them. And although we grow herbs and fruit, please only pick from the beds marked with a green sign, so that there's enough for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about the four areas. If you go left from here, you'll come to the Scent Walk. It's lined with lavender, roses and other fragrant plants. The best time to visit it is in the early evening, when many flowers release more of their scent. At the far end there's a herb bed, where you're welcome to pick a few leaves of mint or rosemary to take home.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Straight ahead is the Water Court. In the centre there's a fountain, which changes height every few minutes, so the sound keeps changing too. Around it is a shallow stream where children can put their hands in the water. It's also where you'll find our café, which serves drinks made with herbs from the garden.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: To the right is the Sound Garden. Here we've planted tall grasses and bamboo, which rustle in the slightest wind, and there are wooden and metal wind chimes hanging from the trees. Our most popular feature is a set of large outdoor drums, which anybody can play. We do ask you to keep the noise down after four o'clock, though, because that's when the garden holds relaxation sessions.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, behind the Sound Garden is the Touch Wall. This is a long stone wall covered in plants with contrasting textures: soft, silvery leaves known as lamb's ears, spiky succulents, and mosses that feel like velvet. There are also carved stone panels showing animals, which visitors can explore with their hands. Our volunteers made the panels themselves, with help from a local sculptor.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you need anything during your visit, our volunteers are wearing yellow jackets. And if you'd like to learn more, we run workshops on designing sensory spaces at home on the first Saturday of every month. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on flavour perception
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Priya and Tom, discuss their presentation on how we perceive flavour with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Priya, Tom, come in. So, your presentation is on flavour perception, isn't it? How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the reading, and we've planned the structure. We wanted to check a few things with you before we start making the slides.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine. Talk me through the structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Well, we want to start with a misunderstanding that most of the audience will probably share: the idea that flavour is the same as taste. In everyday language people use the words interchangeably, but scientifically, taste is only what the tongue detects, and flavour combines taste with smell, texture, temperature and even sound.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's a strong opening. Are you going to mention the tongue map?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Yes, definitely. Lots of people learned at school that different parts of the tongue detect different tastes, sweet at the tip, bitter at the back and so on. But that's a myth. It came from a German paper published in 1901, which found only small differences in sensitivity, and it was later exaggerated in an American textbook. In fact, all five basic tastes can be detected across the whole tongue.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the five are?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. We thought we'd say a little about umami, because people are less familiar with it. It was identified in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, who was trying to work out why a soup made with seaweed tasted so good. He found that the taste came from glutamate.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Nice detail. What comes next?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: The role of smell. Most of what we call flavour actually comes from smell, but not from sniffing. When we chew and swallow, air carries smells from the back of the mouth up into the nose. It's called retronasal smell. That's why food seems tasteless when you have a cold.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How are you going to show that? Demonstrations always work well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We were going to ask volunteers to hold their noses and eat a jelly bean. They can usually tell it's sweet, but they can't identify the flavour until they let go of their nose. We've tried it on our flatmates and it works every time. One of them was convinced his was lemon until he let go, and it turned out to be pear.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic. Just check whether anyone in the audience has an allergy before you hand out sweets. And I'd keep it to three or four volunteers, otherwise it'll take too long.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Good point. After that, we want to look at the influence of the other senses. There's a well-known study from Bordeaux in which wine students were given a white wine that had been coloured red with a flavourless dye, and they described it using words normally used for red wine.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, I know that one. It's a good example of expectations shaping perception. Do you have something on sound?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We do. There's a study by researchers at Oxford in which people bit into crisps while wearing headphones. When the crunching sound was made louder, people rated the crisps as fresher and crisper, even though they were all identical.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Now, my main concern is your conclusion. At the moment, from your plan, it just repeats the main points. I'd like you to think about practical applications.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Well, some hospitals are using this research to help elderly patients, who often lose their sense of smell and stop eating properly. And airlines are interested too, because food tastes different at altitude. Loud engine noise seems to reduce our sensitivity to sweet and salty flavours.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's interesting. We could finish with the hospital example, since it connects to health.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And one more thing: keep the text on your slides to a minimum. Use images and let your talk do the explaining.

listeningParts.title: How we hear
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course on the structure of the ear and how hearing can be damaged and restored.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're turning to hearing, which is in some ways the most mechanical of our senses. I'll begin by tracing what happens to a sound as it travels through the ear, and then we'll look at how hearing is damaged and what can be done about it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sound is simply a series of pressure waves travelling through the air. The visible part of the ear, the outer ear, acts as a kind of funnel, collecting these waves and directing them down the ear canal. Its curved shape also changes sounds slightly depending on whether they come from above, below, in front or behind, which helps the brain work out where a sound is coming from.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At the end of the canal is the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates when sound waves hit it. These vibrations are passed on to three tiny bones in the middle ear, often called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. The stirrup, by the way, is the smallest bone in the human body, only about three millimetres long. Together, these bones act as a lever, increasing the force of the vibrations. This matters because the inner ear is filled with fluid, and without this amplification most of the sound energy would simply bounce off the surface of the fluid, rather as your voice does when you shout at someone who is under water.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The inner ear contains the cochlea, which is coiled like a snail's shell. Inside it, running along its length, is a membrane lined with thousands of hair cells. When the fluid moves, the tiny hairs on top of these cells bend, and this bending opens channels in the cells, producing electrical signals. These signals travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, which interprets them as sound.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What's remarkable is the way the cochlea separates different pitches. The membrane is narrow and stiff at the base of the cochlea and wider and more flexible at the top. High-frequency sounds make the base vibrate most, while low-frequency sounds travel further along and cause the greatest movement near the top. So, in effect, the cochlea works like a piano keyboard rolled into a spiral, with each position responding to a particular note.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, the problem. Hair cells are delicate, and in humans and other mammals, once they are destroyed, they don't grow back. The most common causes of damage are ageing and loud noise. Exposure to very loud sounds, for example at concerts or from machinery, can bend or break the hairs, and repeated exposure causes permanent loss. Often the first cells to go are those at the base, so people tend to lose their ability to hear high frequencies first. Many people with noise damage also develop tinnitus, which is a ringing or buzzing sound in the ears that has no external source.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, birds are able to regenerate their hair cells, and researchers are studying how they do this, in the hope of eventually triggering the same process in humans. For now, though, the main treatments are hearing aids, which simply make sounds louder, and cochlear implants for people with severe hearing loss.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A cochlear implant works in a completely different way from a hearing aid. It bypasses the damaged hair cells altogether. A microphone worn behind the ear picks up sound, a processor converts it into a digital code, and this is sent to a thin wire of electrodes that a surgeon has inserted into the cochlea. The electrodes stimulate the auditory nerve directly. One of the pioneers of the modern multi-channel implant was Graeme Clark in Australia, whose team carried out its first implant operation in 1978.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Implants don't restore normal hearing. Users often describe the sound at first as robotic, and the brain has to learn to interpret it, which can take months of practice. But the results can be dramatic, especially in young children, who can learn spoken language if they receive an implant early. Next week, we'll look at balance, which, as you'll see, also depends on the inner ear.

readingPassages.title: The man with a hole in his head
paragraphs: On 13 September 1848, near the village of Cavendish in Vermont, a twenty-five-year-old railway foreman named Phineas Gage was preparing to blast away rock to make way for a new line. His job involved drilling a hole in the rock, filling it with gunpowder and then packing the powder down with a long iron rod, known as a tamping iron. At some point, probably while his attention was distracted, the iron struck the rock and produced a spark. The powder exploded, and the rod was driven upwards like a missile.

The tamping iron was just over a metre long, about three centimetres wide and weighed around six kilograms. It entered Gage's face below his left cheekbone, passed behind his left eye and left through the top of his skull, landing some twenty-five metres away. Astonishingly, Gage was not killed. According to witnesses, he may have been briefly unconscious, but within minutes he was talking, and he sat upright in an ox cart for the journey back to the town, where he climbed the stairs to his room at a local inn with little assistance.

Gage was treated by a local doctor, John Martyn Harlow, who cleaned the wound, removed fragments of bone and kept a careful record of his patient's condition. For several weeks Gage's survival was in doubt. He developed a serious infection, and at one point a coffin was made ready for him. Harlow drained an abscess and, by the end of the year, Gage was well enough to return to his parents' home in New Hampshire. He had lost the sight of his left eye, but his memory, speech and movement appeared to be largely intact.

What made Gage famous, however, was not simply that he had survived. In 1868, twenty years after the accident, Harlow published a report describing changes in his patient's character. Before the accident, Harlow wrote, Gage had been the most efficient and capable foreman in the company's employment, with a well-balanced mind. Afterwards, he had become impatient, rude and unable to stick to his plans, so much so that his employers would not give him his old job back. His friends, according to Harlow, said that he was 'no longer Gage'.

This account became one of the most cited cases in the history of brain science. At a time when many people still believed that the brain worked as a single unit, Gage seemed to show that a specific region, the frontal lobes, played a special role in personality, judgement and social behaviour. The case was used to support the idea of localisation, the theory that different parts of the brain are responsible for different functions, which gained ground later in the nineteenth century through the work of researchers such as Paul Broca.

Over time, however, the story was retold so often that it became distorted. Textbooks described Gage as a violent drunkard who wandered aimlessly for the rest of his life, claims for which there is little or no evidence. The Australian psychologist Malcolm Macmillan, who spent decades examining the original sources, pointed out that Gage in fact spent several years working as a stagecoach driver in Chile, a demanding job that required him to plan routes, handle horses and deal politely with passengers. Macmillan suggested that Gage may have made a considerable social recovery.

Our picture of Gage has also changed in another way. For more than a century, no photograph of him was known to exist. Then, in 2009, two collectors realised that an old portrait they owned, showing a man with a closed eye holding a metal rod, was in fact Gage. The image shows a smartly dressed, confident-looking man, quite different from the wild figure of popular legend. Researchers have also used scans of his skull, which is kept with the tamping iron at a medical museum at Harvard University, to reconstruct the path of the rod and estimate which areas of the brain were destroyed.

Gage died in San Francisco in 1860, after a series of seizures that were probably a long-term result of his injury. His case is still taught today, but increasingly as a lesson about evidence as well as about the brain. It shows how much a single dramatic example can shape scientific thinking, and how easily a story can grow in the retelling. It also points to a more hopeful idea that modern neuroscience has confirmed: that the brain is capable of significant adaptation, even after severe damage.

readingPassages.title: The map in the brain
paragraphs: Finding our way around is something most of us do every day without thinking about it. We leave home, walk to a bus stop, change to a train and arrive at work, and if a road is closed we can usually work out another route. Yet this everyday skill depends on one of the most sophisticated systems in the brain, and it is only in the last fifty years or so that scientists have begun to understand how it works.

For much of the early twentieth century, many psychologists believed that animals learned routes simply as chains of responses: turn left at the first corner, then right, and so on. In 1948, the American psychologist Edward Tolman challenged this view. He had observed that rats which had explored a maze could find shortcuts when their usual path was blocked, something a simple chain of responses could not explain. Tolman argued that the rats had formed what he called a 'cognitive map', an internal representation of the layout of their environment. However, he had no way of showing where or how such a map might exist in the brain.

The first clue came in 1971. John O'Keefe, an American-born scientist working at University College London, was recording the activity of individual nerve cells in the hippocampus of rats, a curved structure deep inside the brain. He noticed that certain cells became active only when the rat was in a particular part of its enclosure. One cell would fire when the animal was in one corner, another when it was near the centre. O'Keefe called them 'place cells', and he proposed that, together, they formed Tolman's cognitive map.

Over three decades later, in 2005, a further piece of the puzzle was found in Norway. May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser, a married couple working in Trondheim, were studying an area next to the hippocampus called the entorhinal cortex. They discovered cells that fired not in one location but in many, and when the locations were marked on a plan of the enclosure, they formed a remarkably regular pattern of triangles, like the grid on a map. These 'grid cells' seemed to provide a coordinate system that allowed the brain to measure distance and direction. In 2014, O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries.

Research on humans has shown that experience can physically shape this system. In a famous study published in 2000, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues scanned the brains of London taxi drivers, who must pass a demanding examination known as the Knowledge, which requires them to memorise thousands of streets. The drivers had a larger rear section of the hippocampus than people who did not drive taxis, and the longer they had been driving, the larger it was. A later study followed trainees over several years and found that the growth appeared only in those who passed the examination, suggesting that the learning itself had caused the change.

The findings also have medical importance. The entorhinal cortex and the hippocampus are among the first regions to be affected in Alzheimer's disease, which may explain why getting lost in familiar places is often one of the earliest signs of the condition. Some researchers are now investigating whether simple navigation tests, carried out on tablets or in virtual reality, could help doctors identify people at risk years before memory problems become obvious.

Meanwhile, the spread of satellite navigation has raised a new question: what happens to these brain systems when we no longer use them? In a study at University College London in 2017, volunteers' brains were scanned while they navigated a simulation of the streets of Soho. When they planned their own routes, activity in the hippocampus increased whenever they entered a new street. When they simply followed instructions from a navigation system, that extra activity disappeared. The researchers were careful not to claim that sat-navs cause harm, but the study suggested that people who rely on them are giving the brain's mapping system less work to do.

None of this means that we should throw away our phones. Navigation apps have made travel easier and safer for millions of people. But some scientists suggest that it may be worth occasionally switching them off, studying a map before a journey or trying to find our way by landmarks. Like a muscle, the brain's inner map may benefit from regular exercise, and losing our way now and then may be a small price to pay for keeping it in good condition.

readingPassages.title: Can you train your brain?
paragraphs: Few ideas are as appealing as the promise that a few minutes of puzzles a day can make us sharper, protect us against memory loss and even delay dementia. Over the last two decades, this promise has supported a large industry. Smartphone apps and computer games that claim to train the brain have been downloaded by millions of people, many of them older adults anxious about their mental decline. The question is whether the science supports the marketing, and the answer, after many studies and a good deal of public argument, is considerably less encouraging than the advertisements suggest.

The boom began in Japan. In 2005, the games company Nintendo released a handheld game based on the work of the neuroscientist Ryuta Kawashima, who had argued that simple activities such as rapid arithmetic and reading aloud stimulated the brain. The game, which gave players a 'brain age', sold in enormous numbers around the world and inspired many imitators. Within a few years, online companies were offering subscription programmes promising improvements in memory, attention and problem-solving.

Few of these products had been tested properly. In 2010, a team led by the British neuroscientist Adrian Owen published one of the largest studies of brain training ever carried out. Working with a BBC science programme, the researchers recruited more than eleven thousand viewers, who trained online for several weeks using tasks designed to improve reasoning, memory and attention. The volunteers became steadily better at the tasks they practised. However, when they were tested on different tasks, they showed almost no improvement compared with a control group, who had simply spent the same time answering general knowledge questions online.

This distinction between near transfer and far transfer is central to the debate. Near transfer means getting better at the trained task or very similar ones; far transfer means improvements in general abilities that matter in everyday life, such as remembering appointments or managing money. Almost everyone agrees that practice produces near transfer: a person who plays a memory game every day will, unsurprisingly, become better at that game. The disagreement is about far transfer, which is what most brain-training companies imply in their advertising.

In 2014, a group of around seventy scientists organised by the Stanford Center on Longevity and the Max Planck Institute for Human Development issued a public statement warning that claims made for brain games were frequently exaggerated and sometimes misleading. Later that year, a larger group of researchers responded with an open letter of their own, arguing that some forms of training did produce meaningful benefits. Two years later, in 2016, the Federal Trade Commission in the United States reached a settlement with the company behind the popular Lumosity programme, which agreed to pay two million dollars over charges that it had advertised benefits it could not prove. In the same year, Daniel Simons and colleagues published an extensive review of the scientific literature, concluding that there was little evidence that training improved everyday cognitive performance.

Supporters of training often point to the ACTIVE study, a large trial of older adults in the United States that began in the 1990s. Participants who completed one particular kind of training, designed to increase the speed at which they processed visual information, were reported to have a lower risk of developing dementia ten years later. The finding attracted wide attention, but critics have noted that it was not one of the trial's original aims and that it needs to be confirmed by further research.

In my view, the most reasonable conclusion is not that brain training is worthless but that it has been badly oversold. Practising a task will make you better at that task, and for some people, such as patients recovering from brain injuries, carefully designed exercises may be genuinely helpful. But there is no strong evidence that playing a game on a phone will make the average person more intelligent, and it would be wrong for anyone to pay for an app in the belief that it will prevent dementia.

It is worth remembering, too, that the alternatives are often better supported. There is good evidence that regular physical exercise, sufficient sleep, social contact and controlling blood pressure all contribute to a healthy brain in later life. Learning a demanding real-world skill, such as a language or a musical instrument, may also offer more benefits than a game, because it combines memory, attention and social activity. I would argue that the best brain training may not look like brain training at all.
