listeningParts.title: Enrolling on a news-writing course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones an adult education centre to ask about a weekend course in writing for the news.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Riverside Adult Education Centre, Owen speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I picked up one of your leaflets a while ago, and I think there was a course on writing news articles. I was wondering whether there are still places available.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, that'll be our Writing for the News course. It's one of our most popular courses, but we do still have a few places left for the autumn. Would you like me to tell you a bit about it first?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, please. I've never done anything like this before, so I'm a bit nervous.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Don't worry, it's aimed at complete beginners, so you don't need any experience at all. It used to run over eight Saturdays, but a lot of people found that too long, so we've shortened it, and it now runs for six Saturdays. Each session goes from ten in the morning until three in the afternoon, with an hour off for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Six weeks. That sounds manageable. When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The first session is on the fourteenth of September, and the last one is towards the end of October. There's no session on the second Saturday in October, because the building is closed that weekend for repairs, so the course finishes a week later than you might expect.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, I'll make a note of that. And who teaches it?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The tutor is Joanna Marsh. She worked as an editor on a regional daily paper for nearly twenty years, and these days she writes for several magazines. Students always say she's brilliant at giving feedback, and very honest, which is what you want.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what do you actually do on the course?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In the first few weeks, you learn the basics: how to find a story, how to interview people, and how to organise an article so that the most important information comes first. After that, you look at writing headlines, checking facts and taking good photographs on your phone. And for the final assignment, each student writes a complete article about a local festival. The best ones are published on the website of the Riverside Gazette, which is our local paper.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, that would be exciting. What do I need to bring with me?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Most people bring a laptop, because you'll be writing in every session. If you haven't got one, we can lend you one, but you need to ask at least a week in advance, because we've only got a few. A notebook and pen are useful too, for the interview practice.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I've got a laptop, so that's fine. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full fee is one hundred and twenty pounds. There's a reduced fee of ninety-five pounds for students and for people over sixty-five.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm afraid I'm neither of those, so it'll be the full fee for me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's no problem. To keep your place, you just need to pay a deposit of thirty pounds today, and the rest can be paid at any time before the first session. Now, the course isn't held in the main building. It's in the Garden Building, which is the newer one behind the main car park. It's the one with the glass front. You'll be in room twelve, on the ground floor.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there anywhere to park?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, parking is free at weekends, but the car park fills up quickly, so try to arrive by about a quarter to ten. Right, shall I take your details?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, please.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Could I have your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Clare Delaney. That's D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And is Clare spelt with an 'i'?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, just C-L-A-R-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's forty-seven Linden Road. L-I-N-D-E-N. That's in Ashford.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. And just one more question, which we ask everybody. How did you hear about the course?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, my sister mentioned your website a few months ago, but I didn't really think about it until I heard an advert on the local radio last week. That's what made me pick up the phone.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: So I'll put down the radio, then. That's really useful for us to know. I'll send you a confirmation email this afternoon, with a short reading list from Joanna. There's only one book on it, and it's quite short, so don't panic.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's a relief. Thanks very much for your help.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering at a community radio station
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a community radio station speaks to a group of new volunteers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Valley Community Radio. My name's Sophie, and I'm the station manager. Thank you all for coming along this evening. I know some of you have travelled quite a long way, so I'll try not to keep you too long. I'd like to give you a bit of background about the station, explain how volunteering works, and then tell you about some of our programmes, so you can start thinking about where you'd like to get involved.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The station was set up in 2009 by a small group of local residents who felt that the big commercial stations didn't cover anything happening in this valley. For the first two years, we only broadcast for a few weeks each summer, but now we're on air twenty-four hours a day, all year round. Like all community stations, our licence says we must be run on a not-for-profit basis and serve the people of our local area. We do carry a small amount of advertising from local businesses, but most of our income comes from grants and from our listeners' donations.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: People are often surprised to hear that we have only two paid members of staff: me, and a part-time engineer who keeps all the equipment running. Everything else, from presenting and producing to answering the phones and doing the accounts, is done by volunteers. There are around ninety of them at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: As you can see, this building is fairly new. We moved here three years ago from a room above a shop in the high street. That place was actually quite cosy, and the rent was low, but it was up two flights of stairs with no lift, which meant that some of our volunteers simply couldn't get in. Here, everything is on one level.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, I know that most of you are keen to get on air as soon as possible. But before anyone presents a live programme, they have to sit in on at least four shows with one of our experienced presenters and learn how the desk works. Then you do a short practice show, which isn't broadcast, and one of our senior volunteers gives you feedback.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: There are a few rules I want to mention tonight. The most important one is about what you say on air. The thing that gets small stations into serious trouble isn't swearing or playing the wrong song. It's repeating a rumour about a named person, which could be defamatory. So if you're not sure something is true, don't say it. And please never leave the studio during a live show, even for a minute.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: As for our audience, it's changed a lot. When we started, everybody listened on an ordinary radio. Now, more than half our listeners hear us online or through smart speakers, and some of them are former residents who live in other countries but still like to hear what's going on at home.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about some of the programmes where we need help. Our biggest show is the Breakfast Show, from six until nine on weekdays. It's a mix of music, local news and travel, and a big part of it is listeners phoning in to talk about whatever's on their mind that morning, so we need people to answer the calls.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Then there's Farming Week. It's presented by a farmer, Tom Ellis, and because he can't be here at lunchtime during the busy seasons, it's recorded in advance on Sunday evenings. He'd love someone to help with the editing.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Youth Hour, on Friday evenings, is produced and presented entirely by teenagers from the two secondary schools in the valley. It was shortlisted for a national prize this year, although we haven't heard the result yet. They need an adult volunteer to supervise them in the studio.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Our sports programme, Valley Sport, is currently on Saturday afternoons. But from September, it's going to start an hour later, so that our reporters can include the final scores from the local football and rugby matches.

dialogue.speaker: Manager

listeningParts.title: A project on checking online news
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two media students, Megan and Tariq, discuss their research project on how students check news online with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you're going to tell me how your project on checking online news is going. Remind me how you chose the topic.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, it was a bit embarrassing, really. During a hurricane in America last year, I saw a photo of a shark swimming along a flooded motorway, and I shared it with all my friends. Then Tariq pointed out that the same photo had been shared during almost every big flood for years. It was completely fake.

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: And we realised that if a media student could be fooled that easily, it was probably happening to lots of people. So we decided to look at what students actually do when they see a news story online.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And how did you go about it?

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: We did it in two stages. First, there was an online survey about people's habits. Then, we invited some of the people who'd done the survey to come in and do a practical exercise. We gave them a set of ten news stories on a laptop, some real and some false, and asked them to decide which ones they'd trust.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what did the survey show?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Almost everyone said they checked whether a story was true before they shared it. But in the practical exercise, it was a different story. Very few people checked anything. Most of them just looked at whether the website looked professional, and whether the story had lots of likes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That gap between what people say and what they do is a really important finding. Make sure you discuss it properly. How many people did the practical exercise, by the way?

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: Sixty-four. We'd hoped to get a hundred, but it was exam season, so a lot of people dropped out.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's still a reasonable number for a project like this. Did you compare them with anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Not directly, but we read about a study from Stanford University which compared students, historians and professional fact-checkers. The fact-checkers were much faster and more accurate, and the main reason was something called lateral reading.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Explain that for me.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Instead of staying on a website and reading it carefully from top to bottom, the fact-checkers left it almost immediately. They opened new tabs and searched for what other sources said about the website or the organisation behind it. The students tended to stay on the page and were often taken in by how it looked.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. And did any of your participants do that?

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: Only nine of them. And only five used a reverse image search to check where a photo came from, which is the easiest way to spot old pictures being reused, like Megan's shark.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Thanks for reminding everyone, Tariq.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What about the reasons false stories spread? Have you looked at the research on that?

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: Yes, we read the study from MIT that was published in 2018. They looked at millions of posts on Twitter and found that false news spread further and faster than true news. What surprised us was that it wasn't mainly because of automated accounts, which is what we'd assumed. It was ordinary people sharing it, probably because false stories are more surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, that point about novelty is important. Now, were there any problems with your method?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: The main one is that people knew they were taking part in a study about fake news, so they were probably more suspicious than usual. In real life, when you're scrolling quickly on your phone, you'd probably check even less.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly, so your results may actually be optimistic. Mention that in the limitations section. What are you planning to do next?

dialogue.speaker: Tariq
dialogue.text: We'd like to see whether a short training session makes a difference. We're thinking of teaching a group of students lateral reading in about twenty minutes and then giving them the exercise again.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds very worthwhile. But you'll need a control group who don't get the training, otherwise you can't tell whether they've just improved through practice. And please send me a draft of your literature review by Friday.

listeningParts.title: The rise of the news agency
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a media history course about the origins of international news agencies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today, I want to look at an institution that most newspaper readers never think about, but which has shaped the news we receive for nearly two hundred years: the news agency. If you read a story about an election in South America or an earthquake in Asia, there's a good chance that the first report came not from the newspaper's own journalist, but from an agency such as Reuters, the Associated Press or Agence France-Presse.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what exactly is a news agency? Put simply, it's an organisation that gathers news and sells it to other organisations, its subscribers, which include newspapers, broadcasters and, today, websites. The idea is that it's far cheaper for hundreds of newspapers to share the cost of a network of reporters around the world than for each of them to employ its own.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, news could only travel as fast as a horse or a ship could carry it. News from India might take several months to reach London. The first modern agency was founded in Paris in 1835 by Charles-Louis Havas. He began by translating articles from foreign newspapers and selling them to the French press. Havas soon used carrier pigeons to bring news from London and Brussels to Paris, because they were faster than any coach. His agency was the ancestor of today's Agence France-Presse, which was established in 1944.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the people who worked briefly for Havas was a young German called Paul Julius Reuter. In 1850, he spotted a gap in the new telegraph network. There was a telegraph line from Berlin to the German city of Aachen, and another from Paris to Brussels, but nothing in between. Reuter used more than forty carrier pigeons to fly share prices between Aachen and Brussels, and for a time this was the fastest link between the two cities. Of course, once the telegraph line was completed, his pigeons were no longer needed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So in 1851, Reuter moved to London. This was the year that the first undersea telegraph cable was laid across the Channel between Dover and Calais, connecting London directly with the financial markets of continental Europe. Reuter opened an office near the Stock Exchange, and at first his customers were mainly bankers and traders who wanted financial information. Only later did newspapers become his most important clients.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, in the United States, a different model developed. In 1846, five newspapers in New York agreed to share the cost of bringing news of the war with Mexico, which was expensive because reports had to be carried long distances. This cooperative arrangement became the Associated Press. Unlike Reuters, it was owned by its member newspapers, and it still operates as a not-for-profit cooperative today.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: By the 1870s, the three biggest European agencies, Havas, Reuters and the German agency Wolff, had signed an agreement dividing the world between them. Each agency had its own territory, where it collected news and sold it, and they exchanged news with each other. This arrangement lasted, in one form or another, until the 1930s.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The telegraph didn't just change the speed of news; it may also have changed the way news was written. Because sending telegrams was expensive, and lines sometimes failed in the middle of a message, journalists learned to write as briefly as possible and to put the most important facts at the start. This is often given as the origin of the inverted pyramid, the structure in which a story begins with the key facts and adds less important details further down. Historians debate how far the telegraph was really responsible, but the style certainly became standard in the late nineteenth century. It's also why agencies are still sometimes called wire services, after the telegraph wires they once depended on.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today, the agencies face new challenges, as newspapers have less money to spend on subscriptions. But they remain essential. Because their stories are sold to clients with very different political views, agencies have traditionally tried to write in a neutral style, and many people regard them as among the most reliable sources of basic facts. Next week, we'll look at the role of the foreign correspondent.

readingPassages.title: From the Roman Forum to the penny press
paragraphs: People have always wanted to know what is happening beyond their own street, and long before the invention of printing, rulers and merchants found ways of spreading news. In ancient Rome, Julius Caesar ordered in 59 BC that the proceedings of the Senate should be made public. Daily notices known as the Acta Diurna, or 'daily acts', were displayed on boards in busy public places. As well as official announcements, they reported on trials, births, marriages and deaths, and scribes copied them by hand so that they could be sent to officials and wealthy families in distant provinces.

Other early societies developed similar systems. Under the Tang dynasty, the imperial court in China circulated handwritten bulletins among government officials, informing them of decisions, appointments and events at court. In sixteenth-century Venice, which was then one of Europe's great trading centres, merchants depended on handwritten news sheets that reported on wars, shipping and prices in foreign markets. It is often said that these sheets could be read for a small coin called a gazzetta, which is the origin of the word 'gazette', still used in the names of many newspapers today.

The printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg in Germany in the mid-fifteenth century, made it possible to produce hundreds of identical copies of a text quickly. For more than a century, however, printed news appeared mainly in occasional pamphlets describing a single dramatic event, such as a battle, a flood or the appearance of a comet. These pamphlets were often sensational, and readers had no way of knowing when the next one would appear or whether its contents were accurate.

The publication that is usually regarded as the world's first newspaper appeared in Strasbourg, then part of the Holy Roman Empire, in 1605. Its publisher, Johann Carolus, had previously earned his living producing handwritten newsletters for wealthy subscribers. Copying each one by hand was slow, so he bought a printing press and began publishing a weekly paper called the Relation. In a petition to the city council, he asked for protection against other printers copying his work, and this document is one of the main pieces of evidence for the paper's early date. What made the Relation different from earlier pamphlets was regularity: it appeared every week and covered a range of news.

The idea spread quickly. Within a few decades, weekly papers were being published in Amsterdam, Frankfurt and other European cities. In England, the Oxford Gazette was first published in 1665, in Oxford rather than London because the royal court had moved there to escape the plague; a few months later it was renamed the London Gazette, and it is still published today as an official journal of the government. The first daily newspaper in Britain, the Daily Courant, was founded in London in 1702 by Elizabeth Mallet. It consisted of a single sheet and, unusually for the time, promised to report only news, not opinions, so that readers could make up their own minds.

For much of the following century, newspapers remained expensive. In Britain, the government introduced a stamp duty on newspapers in 1712, partly to raise money and partly to limit the spread of criticism. Critics called such charges 'taxes on knowledge', because they kept newspapers out of the reach of ordinary working people. The duty was increased several times, and it was not finally abolished until 1855, after a long public campaign. A separate tax on paper itself was removed six years later, in 1861.

Technology also played a part in bringing prices down. In 1814, The Times of London began printing on a steam-powered press designed by the German engineer Friedrich Koenig, which could produce more than a thousand sheets an hour, several times faster than a hand-operated press. Over the following decades, further improvements, together with cheaper paper made from wood pulp rather than rags, allowed publishers to print much larger numbers of copies at lower cost.

The most dramatic change came in the United States. In 1833, a young printer named Benjamin Day launched The Sun in New York and sold it for just one cent, at a time when most papers cost six. Instead of relying on subscriptions from the wealthy, Day's paper was sold on the street by boys, and it made its money mainly from advertising. To attract large numbers of readers, it concentrated on crime, accidents and human-interest stories rather than politics and business. Its success was rapid, and other 'penny papers' soon followed. For the first time, newspapers had become a mass medium, read by people of almost every social class.

readingPassages.title: What makes a story news?
paragraphs: Every day, millions of things happen around the world: people are born and die, laws are passed, companies make profits and losses, and storms form over the oceans. Only a tiny fraction of these events will ever be reported. Someone, somewhere, has to decide which events become news and which are ignored. For more than seventy years, researchers have tried to understand how these decisions are made, and their answers reveal a great deal about the picture of the world that the media present to us.

One of the earliest attempts to study the question used the idea of 'gatekeeping'. The term had been introduced by the psychologist Kurt Lewin, who used it to describe how certain members of a household decided which foods reached the family table. In 1950, the American researcher David Manning White applied it to journalism. He persuaded the wire editor of a small-town newspaper, whom he called 'Mr Gates', to keep every news agency story he received during one week, along with a note explaining why he had rejected it. The editor used only around a tenth of the material, and many of his reasons were highly personal. White concluded that the news was shaped to a surprising extent by the individual tastes and prejudices of the person at the gate.

Later researchers argued that this picture was too simple, because journalists working in very different organisations tended to make similar choices. In 1965, two Norwegian scholars, Johan Galtung and Mari Holmboe Ruge, published an influential study of how four Norwegian newspapers had reported crises in the Congo, Cuba and Cyprus. They proposed that events were more likely to be reported if they had certain characteristics, which they called 'news factors', and that the more of these factors an event had, the more likely it was to make the news.

Some of their factors will seem obvious to any newspaper reader. Events that are negative, such as disasters, conflicts and accidents, are more likely to be reported than positive ones. Unexpected events attract more attention than predictable ones. Events involving powerful nations or famous people are favoured over those involving ordinary people or distant, less powerful countries. And stories that can be told through the experience of individuals, rather than as abstract processes, are more attractive to editors, because readers find it easier to identify with a person than with a set of statistics.

Galtung and Ruge's list has been tested and revised many times. In 2001, the British researchers Tony Harcup and Deirdre O'Neill examined the main stories in three national newspapers and found that some of the original factors no longer fitted. Stories about celebrities and entertainment, for example, were far more common than the 1965 study would have predicted, and many stories were included simply because they were good news or had striking pictures. In an update published in 2017, the same researchers added a new factor that would have been unimaginable in the 1960s: 'shareability', the likelihood that a story will be shared and commented on through social media.

If gatekeeping and news factors explain which stories are chosen, another theory suggests what effect those choices have on the public. During the 1968 United States presidential election, Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw asked undecided voters in the town of Chapel Hill, North Carolina, which issues they considered most important. They then compared the answers with the amount of coverage each issue had received in the local media and found a very close match. Their theory, known as agenda-setting, echoed a famous remark by the political scientist Bernard Cohen in 1963: the press 'may not be successful much of the time in telling people what to think, but it is stunningly successful in telling its readers what to think about'.

The preference for negative news has consequences of its own. Surveys carried out for the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism in recent years have found that, across many countries, nearly four in ten people say they sometimes or often avoid the news, and one of the most common reasons they give is that it has a negative effect on their mood. In response, some journalists have promoted 'solutions journalism', which reports not only on problems but also on how people are trying to solve them. The Solutions Journalism Network, founded in the United States in 2013, trains reporters in this approach, while insisting that it should be as rigorous as any other kind of reporting.

Today, the gatekeepers are changing once again. Editors still choose which stories to publish, but a large share of the public now meets the news through search engines and social media, where computer programs decide which stories each user sees, based on what they have clicked on, liked or shared before. These algorithms are designed mainly to keep people engaged rather than to inform them, and they are largely hidden from public view. Understanding how they select the news may prove to be one of the most important tasks for researchers in the coming decades.

readingPassages.title: Who will pay for local news?
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, local newspapers were among the most profitable businesses in many towns. They reported on council meetings, courts, schools and sports clubs, and they were paid for largely by advertisers who had few other ways of reaching local customers. In the past two decades, that model has collapsed. In the United States, more than a quarter of all newspapers have closed since 2005, and many of those that survive employ only a fraction of the journalists they once did. Similar declines have been recorded in Britain, Canada and Australia. The researcher Penelope Muse Abernathy helped to popularise the term 'news deserts' to describe the growing number of communities with no reliable local source of news at all.

The main cause is not hard to find. Advertising, which once provided most of a local paper's income, has moved online. Small advertisements for jobs, homes and second-hand goods, which used to fill page after page, migrated to free websites, and much of the remaining advertising money now goes to a small number of technology companies that can target customers far more precisely than any newspaper. At the same time, readers have become used to finding news online without paying for it, so that income from sales has also fallen.

Does it matter? A growing body of research suggests that it does. A study by the economists Pengjie Gao, Chang Lee and Dermot Murphy found that, after a local newspaper closed, the cost of borrowing for the local government tended to rise. Their explanation was that, without journalists watching how public money was spent, lenders saw a greater risk of waste or mismanagement and charged more. Another study, by Joshua Darr and his colleagues, found that after local papers closed, voters became more likely to choose the same party in national and local elections, which suggests that they were relying more on national news, which tends to be more strongly divided along party lines.

Several new models have emerged to fill the gap. One is the non-profit news organisation, funded by charitable foundations, individual donors and events. The Texas Tribune, founded in 2009 in Austin, is one of the best-known examples. It concentrates on state politics and public policy and allows other news outlets to republish its articles free of charge. Critics point out, however, that donors may have their own interests, and that charitable funding tends to flow to wealthier, larger cities rather than to the small towns that have suffered most.

A second approach relies on readers. Some publishers have introduced paywalls, which allow only paying subscribers to read their articles. Others, such as the British newspaper The Guardian, have kept their journalism free to read and instead asked readers to make voluntary contributions; more than a million people have supported the paper in this way. Yet such models seem to work best for large national titles with loyal audiences. Surveys repeatedly find that only a small minority of people in most countries pay for any online news, and very few are willing to pay for several sources.

A third option is support from public money. In Britain, the BBC launched the Local Democracy Reporting Service in 2017, under which it pays for around 150 reporters who work for local news organisations and cover the activities of councils and other public bodies. In Canada, the federal government's Local Journalism Initiative, which began in 2019, funds journalists to report on communities that are poorly served by the media. Supporters of such schemes argue that local news is a public good, like clean water or street lighting, which markets alone will not provide. Opponents worry that journalists who depend on the state for their salaries may be reluctant to criticise it.

Finally, some governments have tried to make the technology companies themselves pay. In 2021, Australia introduced the News Media Bargaining Code, which requires large digital platforms to negotiate payments with news publishers whose content appears on their services. Before the law was passed, Facebook briefly blocked users in Australia from viewing or sharing news on its platform, which also affected the pages of some emergency services. The dispute was resolved after a few days, and the companies have since signed deals worth large sums with Australian publishers, although critics claim that most of the money has gone to the biggest media groups.

In my view, there is no single solution to the crisis, and it would be a mistake to search for one. Each of these models has weaknesses, but together they can support a varied range of local news organisations, which is itself a protection against any one source of funding becoming too powerful. What matters most is that the reporting of local courts, councils and schools continues, because it is precisely in those places, which national journalists rarely visit, that power is most easily abused without anyone noticing. A town without a newspaper is not necessarily a worse place to live, but it is certainly a place where fewer questions are asked.

listeningParts.title: Enrolling on a weather course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A recently retired man phones an adult education centre to book a place on a course about weather.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hilltop Adult Education Centre, Ruth speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I picked up a leaflet about a weather course you're running this winter, and I'd like to find out a bit more about it, and possibly book a place.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. That'll be Reading the Sky, our introductory course on weather and forecasting. It's designed for complete beginners, so you don't need any background in science. Is it for yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. I've just retired, and I spend a lot of my time sailing now, so I'd like to understand the weather properly. At the moment I just look at an app on my phone and hope for the best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Well, you'd be in good company. Last year about half the group were sailors or hill walkers. The course runs for eight weeks, and there are two options. There's a daytime class on Tuesday mornings, or an evening class on Thursdays, from seven until nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Now that I'm not working, the daytime one would suit me better. I'm not at my best in the evenings. What time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Half past nine, and it finishes at twelve, with a short break for coffee in the middle. The first session is on the fourteenth of January. The evening group starts a week later, on the twenty-first.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fourteenth. Right. And where exactly is it held? At your main building on the High Street?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, this course is held at our smaller site, the Ashcombe Building. That's A-S-H-C-O-M-B-E. We use it because it has a flat roof, where the tutor has set up a small weather station. Students take readings from the instruments during every session, so by the end you'll have two months of your own records. It's on Mill Lane, about five minutes' walk from the railway station.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. And what does the course actually cover?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In the first few weeks, you learn to identify the main types of cloud and what they tell you about the weather that's coming. Then you move on to air pressure and wind, and how to read the weather charts you see on television. In the final two weeks, everyone produces their own forecast for the local area, and then compares it with what actually happens. People usually find that part quite humbling.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I can imagine. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full price is ninety-five pounds for the eight weeks. There's a reduced price for people over sixty, which is seventy pounds, and for students, which is fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I turned sixty-two last month, so I think that's me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then it's seventy pounds. There's also a course book, which costs twelve pounds. You'll need it from the first week, although some people borrow a copy from the library instead.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll buy one, I think. I like writing notes in the margins.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Fine. I'll add that to the booking. And you'll need to bring a notebook and a pencil, rather than a pen, because pens don't work very well outside in the rain. Oh, and bring a warm coat. You'll be up on the roof for part of every session, whatever the weather is doing.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Of course. That's the whole point, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Graham Pelling. P-E-L-L-I-N-G.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Pelling. And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Forty-three Orchard Road, Hilltop.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And may I ask how you heard about the course? We like to know which kinds of advertising work.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: As I said, I picked up a leaflet. It was in the café at the sailing club, down by the harbour.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely, I'll make a note of that. Now, there's a maximum of sixteen students, and at the moment there are only three places left on the Tuesday class, so I'd recommend paying today if you want to be sure of your place.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll do that now. Can I pay by card over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, that's fine. And one more thing: at the end of the course there's an optional visit to the regional forecasting office near the airport, where you can watch professional forecasters at work. It's on a Saturday, and there's no extra charge, but you have to arrange your own transport.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Excellent. I wouldn't miss that for anything.

listeningParts.title: A tour of a hilltop weather observatory
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a weather observatory that has been recording the weather for over a century.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Carrick Hill Observatory. My name's Siobhan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we go outside, I'll give you a little background and explain what you'll see on the tour.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The observatory was founded in 1889 by a group of local doctors and teachers who were interested in the weather. You might wonder why they chose such an exposed spot, a good forty minutes' walk from the town. It wasn't for the view, I'm afraid. In those days the town was full of factories, and the smoke from their chimneys affected the readings from the instruments, especially the ones measuring sunshine. Up here, the air was clean, and that's still true today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Since then, the weather has been recorded here every single day, which makes our records among the longest unbroken series in the country. Scientists studying climate change use them a great deal, because they show how temperatures and rainfall have changed over more than a century in the same place, with the same kind of instruments.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Nowadays, most of the measurements are taken automatically and sent to the national weather service every minute. But we still have two human observers on duty every day. People sometimes ask why we need them, and the answer is that there are things machines still don't do well. A computer can measure rainfall perfectly, but it isn't very good at recognising different types of cloud, or judging how far you can see through mist. So our observers go outside every hour and record what they see.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the different parts of the site. First, there's the Instrument Garden, which is the fenced area of grass you passed on the way in. That's where the thermometers are kept, inside white wooden boxes that protect them from direct sunlight. You can look over the fence, but please don't go inside, because even the heat from a group of people standing close by can change the readings.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to that is the Balloon Shed. Twice a day, at exactly the same times as hundreds of other stations around the world, we release a large balloon filled with gas. It carries a small instrument package that measures temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises, and sends the data back by radio. The balloon expands as the air gets thinner, and eventually it bursts, usually more than twenty kilometres up. The package then falls back to earth on a small parachute. There's a label on each one asking whoever finds it to post it back to us, and you'd be surprised how many people do. The next launch is at a quarter past eleven, so you'll be able to watch it.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: After that, we'll go into the main building. On the ground floor is the Old Library, where you can see the original handwritten record books from the 1880s onwards. They're very fragile, so they're kept in glass cases, but some pages have been scanned, and you can turn them on the touch screens.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs is the Forecast Studio. This is the part that children usually love most. We've built a copy of a television weather set, with a green screen, so you can try presenting the forecast yourself and take a video home with you. Do try it. It's much harder than it looks.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the Roof Platform, which has wonderful views across three counties on a clear day. Unfortunately, it's closed this morning, because the wind is too strong. I should mention that the strongest gust ever recorded here was a hundred and sixty-one kilometres an hour, during a storm in January 1974, and the anemometer that measured it is on display in the café.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Speaking of the café, it's open until four, and the hot soup is excellent after a morning in this wind. Right, any questions before we start? No? Then follow me, and please do keep your hats on.

listeningParts.title: Testing traditional weather sayings
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two students, Megan and Daniel, discuss their project on weather folklore with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen weather sayings for your project. Tell me how it's going.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Quite well, I think. The idea came from my grandfather, actually. He was a farmer, and he had a saying for everything. Whenever we went for a walk he'd look at the sky and tell us what the weather would do the next day, and he was right surprisingly often.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: So we wanted to find out two things. First, how well people today still know these sayings, and second, whether any of them actually have a scientific basis.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. How did you approach the first question?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We wrote a short questionnaire listing ten common sayings, and asked people to tick the ones they'd heard of. We collected a hundred and twenty responses, mostly online, although we also stood outside the library for a couple of afternoons to get some older people.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That was sensible. Online surveys tend to attract younger people. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: By far the best known was 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning'. Almost everyone knew it, whatever their age. But with most of the others, there was a clear pattern. People over sixty knew roughly three times as many sayings as people under thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: What surprised us was where people said they'd learned them. We expected the answer to be parents or grandparents, but a lot of the younger people said they'd learned them from books or films.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. And the science?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, the red sky one does seem to have some basis, at least in places like Britain. Weather systems here usually move from west to east. If the sky is red at sunset, it means the sunlight is shining through clear air to the west, where the weather is coming from, so the next day is likely to be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Whereas a red sky in the morning means the clear air is already in the east, moving away, and cloud may be on its way from the west. It's not perfect, but it's not nonsense either.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What about the others?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The one about cows lying down before rain had almost no evidence to support it. We found one study of cattle, but it suggested they lie down mainly when they're tired or the temperature is low, not because rain is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: The most fun part was the pine cones. There's an old belief that pine cones close up before wet weather. We kept three cones on a windowsill for a month and photographed them every morning, and they really did close when the air was damp and open when it was dry.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So they respond to humidity rather than predicting rain, strictly speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Exactly. They tell you what the air is like now, which is often a sign that rain is close, but they can't see into the future.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important distinction, and you should make it clearly in your report. Now, are there any weaknesses in your study that you're aware of?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The main one is the sample. A hundred and twenty isn't very many, and nearly all of them live in the same city. Sayings probably vary from region to region, especially in farming areas.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then say so in your conclusion. It doesn't weaken the project as long as you're honest about it. And for the pine cones, you could compare your photos with the humidity readings from the university weather station. That would make your results much more convincing than just saying the air felt damp.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Good idea. I didn't know the university had a weather station.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It's on the roof of the geography building, and the data's online. Right, I'd like a full draft in three weeks, please, and keep the introduction short. Don't spend two pages on your grandfather.

listeningParts.title: The layers of the atmosphere
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory earth science course on the structure of the Earth's atmosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to look at the structure of the atmosphere, the thin layer of gas that surrounds the Earth and makes life possible. And I do mean thin. If the Earth were the size of an apple, the part of the atmosphere where almost all our weather happens would be no thicker than the apple's skin.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Scientists divide the atmosphere into layers, and the main way they do this is by looking at how the temperature changes as you go up. Within some layers the air gets colder with height, and within others it gets warmer, and the boundaries are where that pattern changes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The lowest layer is the troposphere. This is where we live, and it's where nearly all weather happens: clouds, rain, snow and storms. It contains around three quarters of the total mass of the atmosphere, and almost all of its water vapour. In the troposphere, temperature falls steadily as you climb, by about six and a half degrees Celsius for every kilometre. That's why mountain tops are cold, even near the equator. The troposphere isn't the same thickness everywhere. It's only about eight kilometres deep over the poles, but up to around eighteen kilometres over the tropics, because the warm air there rises much higher.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The top of the troposphere is called the tropopause, and it acts a bit like a lid. Clouds can't easily rise through it, which is why the tops of big thunderstorm clouds often spread out into a flat shape, rather like an anvil. Just below the tropopause, you'll also find the jet streams, which are narrow bands of very fast wind, and which airlines use to save fuel when they fly from west to east.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above the tropopause is the stratosphere, which stretches up to about fifty kilometres. Here, something unexpected happens: the temperature starts to rise with height. The reason is ozone. The stratosphere contains the ozone layer, and ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, which warms the air around it. That absorption is also what protects living things on the surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation. Because warm air sits on top of cooler air, the stratosphere is very stable, with almost no vertical movement and very little cloud, so passenger jets often cruise in its lower part to avoid turbulence.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above the stratosphere, from about fifty to eighty-five kilometres, is the mesosphere. Here the temperature falls again, and the top of the mesosphere is the coldest place in the whole atmosphere, often below minus ninety degrees Celsius. The mesosphere is also where most meteors burn up. Every day, tons of dust and small rocks from space hit the atmosphere, and the friction heats them until they glow and vaporise. Those are the shooting stars you see on a clear night. Oddly enough, the mesosphere is one of the least studied parts of the atmosphere, because it's too high for aircraft and weather balloons, but too low for satellites to orbit.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Above that is the thermosphere, which extends to several hundred kilometres. In the thermosphere, temperatures can reach well over a thousand degrees Celsius, because the few gas molecules there absorb intense radiation from the Sun. But if you were up there, you wouldn't actually feel hot. The air is so thin that there are hardly any molecules to transfer that heat to your body. The thermosphere is where the International Space Station orbits, at around four hundred kilometres, and it's also where the aurora occurs, the spectacular curtains of green and red light seen near the poles, when particles from the Sun collide with gases in the upper atmosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, the outermost layer, the exosphere, gradually fades away into space, with no clear upper edge. For legal and practical purposes, though, many organisations treat a height of one hundred kilometres, known as the Kármán line, as the boundary where space begins.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, why does all this matter to a meteorologist? Well, although weather happens in the troposphere, the layers above it influence what goes on below, for example through the way the stratosphere affects the jet streams. Next week, we'll look at how air moves within the troposphere, and how those movements create the pressure systems you see on weather maps.

readingPassages.title: The man who named the forecast
paragraphs: Today it is difficult to imagine a world without weather forecasts. They appear on our phones, on television and in newspapers, and millions of decisions, from whether to carry an umbrella to whether a ship should leave port, depend on them. Yet the first forecasts to be published regularly in a British newspaper appeared only in 1861. They were the work of a naval officer named Robert FitzRoy, whose determination to save lives at sea brought him public fame, bitter criticism and, eventually, a lasting place in the history of science.

FitzRoy was born in 1805 into an aristocratic family and joined the Royal Navy as a boy. He is best remembered today as the captain of HMS Beagle during its voyage around the world between 1831 and 1836, on which the young Charles Darwin sailed as a naturalist. The voyage made Darwin famous, but it also confirmed FitzRoy's reputation as a skilled surveyor and a careful observer of the weather. Years of commanding ships in dangerous waters had shown him how many sailors lost their lives in storms that, he believed, could have been anticipated. After a short and difficult period as governor of New Zealand in the 1840s, he returned to Britain, where his interest in the weather would shape the rest of his career.

In 1854, FitzRoy was appointed head of a small new department of the Board of Trade, the government body responsible for commerce and shipping. This department, which later became known as the Met Office, had a limited purpose at first. It was not expected to predict the weather at all, but to collect information about winds and currents at sea, so that voyages could be made faster and safer. FitzRoy supplied the captains of merchant ships with reliable instruments and asked them to keep detailed logs of the conditions they met. These records were then gathered in London and turned into charts.

A disaster in October 1859 changed the direction of his work. A violent storm swept across Britain, and the Royal Charter, a ship returning from Australia, was wrecked off the coast of Anglesey in north Wales. Hundreds of passengers and crew drowned, and many other vessels were lost around the coast. Studying the reports afterwards, FitzRoy became convinced that the storm's approach could have been detected in advance. What made this possible was a relatively recent invention: the electric telegraph. For the first time, observations of pressure, wind and temperature from places hundreds of kilometres apart could be collected within hours and compared, rather than arriving days later by post.

In February 1861, FitzRoy began sending storm warnings by telegraph to ports around the British coast. When a warning was received, a large canvas cone was raised on a tall pole where sailors could see it, its position indicating the expected direction of the wind. Later that year, he went further. On 1 August 1861, The Times newspaper printed his first general weather forecasts for different regions of the country. FitzRoy is usually credited with introducing the word 'forecast' in this sense; he wanted a term that sounded like a reasoned scientific judgement rather than a prophecy.

The forecasts quickly became popular with the public, and fishermen in particular came to depend on the storm warnings. FitzRoy also arranged for barometers to be placed in fishing ports, so that crews could check the pressure themselves before putting to sea, and he explained how to interpret the readings in simple language. In 1863 he published The Weather Book, in which he set out his methods and his conviction that the weather, although complicated, followed patterns that could be understood.

However, the forecasts also attracted fierce criticism. When they were wrong, as they often were, newspapers mocked them and questions were asked in Parliament. Many scientists argued that FitzRoy's methods relied too heavily on personal judgement and lacked a proper theoretical basis. Some ship owners complained that the warnings kept their vessels in harbour unnecessarily, costing them money. FitzRoy, who was overworked, in poor health and deeply hurt by the attacks, died in 1865. Shortly afterwards, a committee appointed to review the department concluded that the forecasts could not be scientifically justified, and they were stopped in 1866. The storm warnings, however, were restored after protests from coastal communities, and newspaper forecasts eventually returned more than a decade later.

FitzRoy's reputation has risen steadily since then. Modern forecasting relies on far more data and far more powerful methods than he could have imagined, but the basic idea he championed, that observations gathered quickly from a wide area can be used to warn people of the weather to come, remains at its heart. In 2002, when the sea area called Finisterre in the Shipping Forecast broadcast on BBC radio needed a new name to avoid confusion with a Spanish area of the same name, it was renamed FitzRoy in his honour.

readingPassages.title: Calculating tomorrow
paragraphs: Every day, the world's major weather services feed millions of observations from satellites, aircraft, ships, balloons and ground stations into some of the most powerful computers on Earth. These machines solve the equations that describe how air moves, warms, cools and condenses, and the result is a picture of the atmosphere hours, days and even weeks ahead. The idea behind this process, known as numerical weather prediction, is more than a century old, but it took decades of failure, ingenuity and technological progress before it became the foundation of modern forecasting.

The starting point is usually traced to 1904, when the Norwegian scientist Vilhelm Bjerknes argued that forecasting should be treated as a problem in physics. If the present state of the atmosphere were known accurately enough, he reasoned, the laws governing the motion of fluids and the behaviour of heat could be used to calculate its future state. The principle was elegant, but there was an obvious difficulty. The equations involved were far too complex to be solved exactly, and approximate solutions required an enormous amount of arithmetic, at a time when every calculation had to be done by hand.

The first person to attempt it seriously was the British mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson. During the First World War, while serving as a driver with an ambulance unit in France, he spent his spare time working out, by hand, how the pressure and winds over a small part of central Europe would change over six hours, using observations recorded on a single day in 1910. The task took him many weeks. When he finally finished, his result was spectacularly wrong: he predicted a rise in surface pressure of 145 hectopascals, a change far larger than any ever observed, when in reality the pressure had barely altered. Richardson nevertheless published his method, together with his failed result, in his 1922 book Weather Prediction by Numerical Process.

Rather than abandoning the idea, Richardson imagined how it might one day work in practice. He described a vast hall, shaped like a theatre, in which 64,000 people, each responsible for one part of the globe, would carry out calculations simultaneously, while a conductor in the centre used beams of light to keep them working at the same pace. This 'forecast factory' was never built, but it anticipated with remarkable accuracy the way modern supercomputers divide the atmosphere into a grid of points and process them in parallel. Much later, researchers who repeated his calculations showed that his method had been largely sound; the error came mainly from problems with the starting data, which contained small unrealistic variations that the equations magnified.

The arithmetic finally became manageable with the arrival of electronic computers. In 1950, a team in the United States that included the meteorologist Jule Charney and the mathematician John von Neumann used ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, to produce a series of forecasts for North America. The model was greatly simplified, and producing a 24-hour forecast took roughly 24 hours of computing time, so it was of no practical use. But the forecasts were reasonably realistic, and they proved that the approach could work. By the middle of the 1950s, weather services in Sweden and the United States had begun issuing computer-based forecasts routinely.

Just as the method was proving its worth, a discovery revealed its limits. In 1961, the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz was running a simple weather model on a computer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Wanting to examine one result again, he restarted the run part-way through, typing in a number from a printout, 0.506, instead of the full value of 0.506127 stored in the machine. The tiny difference grew until the new simulation bore no resemblance to the original. Lorenz realised that the atmosphere is chaotic: very small uncertainties in its starting state grow rapidly, so that detailed forecasts eventually become impossible, however good the model. A later talk in which he asked whether the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas gave the phenomenon its popular name, the butterfly effect.

Forecasters responded not by giving up but by changing how they work. Since observations can never be perfect, modern weather centres run their models not once but dozens of times, each starting from slightly different conditions that reflect the uncertainty in the data. This technique, called ensemble forecasting, became part of daily operations in the early 1990s. When the different runs produce similar results, forecasters can be confident; when they spread widely, the forecast is uncertain, and that uncertainty can itself be communicated to the public.

The results of these advances have been striking. Studies suggest that forecasts have gained roughly a day of useful accuracy with each decade, so that a five-day forecast today is about as reliable as a three-day forecast was some twenty years earlier. Most scientists believe, following Lorenz, that the limit for detailed day-to-day forecasts lies at around two weeks. More recently, technology companies and weather centres have developed systems based on machine learning, which are trained on decades of past weather data and can produce forecasts in minutes rather than hours. Whether these will replace traditional models or simply work alongside them is one of the most important questions facing the field.

readingPassages.title: A thirty per cent chance of confusion
paragraphs: Weather forecasts have never been more accurate. Thanks to satellites, supercomputers and decades of research, a forecast for three days ahead is now roughly as reliable as a forecast for the next day was a generation ago. Yet complaints that 'the forecast is always wrong' remain as common as ever. In my view, the main problem with weather forecasting today is not the science, which is remarkably good, but the way its results are communicated to the people who rely on them.

Consider the familiar 'thirty per cent chance of rain'. In a study published in 2005, the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer and his colleagues asked people in five cities, Amsterdam, Athens, Berlin, Milan and New York, what such a forecast actually means. The answers varied enormously. Some people thought it meant that it would rain for thirty per cent of the time, while others believed it would rain over thirty per cent of the region. The meaning intended by forecasters, that it will rain on about thirty per cent of days with a forecast like this one, was far from universally understood. Residents of New York, where forecasts of this kind had been broadcast for decades, were the most likely to choose it.

Confusion is not only the fault of the public. In his 2012 book The Signal and the Noise, the statistician Nate Silver described what forecasters call the 'wet bias'. Examining American forecasts, he found that the national weather service's probabilities of rain were well calibrated, but that many local television forecasters deliberately exaggerated the chance of rain, because viewers who are caught in an unexpected shower are angrier than viewers who stay indoors because of rain that never arrives. I find this understandable, but in my opinion it is self-defeating: an audience that discovers it has been misled, however kindly, has less reason to believe the next warning, which may be one that really matters.

Graphics can mislead as well as words. Forecasts of hurricanes approaching the United States are often shown with a 'cone of uncertainty', a shape that widens over time to show where the centre of the storm is likely to travel, based on the size of past forecasting errors. The cone is a sensible way of displaying uncertainty, but research has repeatedly found that many people read it as a map of the area that will be affected, and conclude that if they live outside it they are safe. In fact, the cone says nothing about the size of a storm, and dangerous winds and flooding often extend far beyond its edges.

Some weather services have tried to address such problems by changing what a warning is about. The UK's Met Office, for example, now issues impact-based warnings, coloured yellow, amber or red. The colour depends not only on how likely severe weather is, but on what it is expected to do: whether it is likely to close roads, cut off power or endanger lives. A heavy snowfall that would be a minor inconvenience in a mountain village might therefore lead to a higher warning in a city where it rarely snows. I believe this is exactly the right approach, because people make decisions about what the weather will do to them, not about rainfall totals.

Another innovation has been less obviously useful. Since 2015, the Met Office and Met Éireann, Ireland's weather service, have given names to major storms, a practice long established for hurricanes. The aim is to raise awareness and make it easier for the media and the public to follow a storm's progress. The names certainly attract attention, and they make headlines easier to write. Whether they actually change how people prepare is, as far as I am aware, much less clear, and I suspect that a memorable name can sometimes make a storm seem like entertainment rather than a threat.

A more radical argument is that the public simply cannot cope with uncertainty, and should be given clear, simple messages: rain or no rain, safe or unsafe. This view is understandable but, I think, mistaken. Research by the psychologist Susan Joslyn and her colleagues at the University of Washington has found that people who are given probability information alongside a forecast tend to make better decisions, and to trust the forecast more, than people who receive a simple prediction. Uncertainty does not confuse people when it is explained clearly; what confuses them is uncertainty presented in ways they cannot interpret.

In my view, the next great advance in forecasting will come not from faster computers but from taking communication as seriously as calculation. Forecasters already know a great deal about how much they do not know. The challenge is to share that knowledge honestly, and in a form that helps people decide whether to cancel a journey, move their livestock or leave their homes. That will require meteorologists to work closely with psychologists, designers and the communities they serve.

listeningParts.title: Booking a young inventors' club
listeningParts.contextDescription: A father phones a science centre to book a place for his daughter on a holiday club for young inventors.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good morning, Brightwater Science Centre, Leanne speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm calling about the Young Inventors club during the summer holidays. My daughter's very keen, and I wanted to find out a bit more and maybe book a place.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Of course. The club runs for five days, Monday to Friday, and it's for children aged nine to thirteen. Each day the children learn about a famous invention, and then they work in small teams to design and build their own. On the last afternoon, they present their inventions to the parents.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That sounds great. She's eleven, so that's fine. What kind of things do they make?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: It varies, but last year they built things like simple robots, water filters and machines for sorting coins. Most of the materials are recycled, things like cardboard, plastic bottles and old toys, because we want the children to see that you don't need expensive equipment to invent something. We do also have a small electronics kit for each team, with batteries, motors and lights, and the children learn how to use it safely on the first morning. There are never more than twelve children in a group, with two members of staff, so everyone gets plenty of help.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Which weeks are available?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We have three sessions. The first one, starting on the twenty-second of July, is already full, I'm afraid. There are still places on the week starting the fifth of August, and on the last one, starting the nineteenth of August.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: We're away at the end of August, so it would have to be the fifth.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No problem. Let me take some details. What's your daughter's name?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It's Isla Pemberton. That's P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And does Isla have any medical conditions or allergies we should know about?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: She has asthma, but it's mild. She carries an inhaler with her.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That's fine. I'll make a note of it, and our staff are all trained in first aid. Now, the price. The full week costs a hundred and forty-five pounds. If you're a member of the science centre, there's a discount, and it comes down to a hundred and twenty.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: We're not members, unfortunately.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Then it's a hundred and forty-five. You can pay a deposit of fifty pounds now to hold the place, and the rest at least two weeks before the start.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Okay. And what are the times?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The club starts at nine thirty and finishes at three thirty. We do offer an early drop-off from eight fifteen, at no extra charge, for parents who work.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That would be really helpful. Does she need to bring lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes, please send her with a packed lunch and a water bottle. We provide a snack in the afternoon, usually fruit. And because they'll be cutting and gluing, it's a good idea to send her in old clothes, or with an apron.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Right. Where do I drop her off? The science centre's quite big.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The club meets in the Discovery Room, which is on the ground floor. Don't use the main entrance; use the side door on Mill Lane, opposite the library. There'll be a member of staff there to sign the children in.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: And is there anything else I need to do before the first day?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Just one thing. We'll email you a consent form for photographs. We like to take pictures of the children's inventions for our website, but we only include children's faces if parents agree. Please return it before the club starts.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Will do. And do the children get to keep what they make?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: They do. And every child also receives a certificate at the presentation on the Friday. Last year one team's invention, a plant-watering machine, was so good that it's now on display in our main hall.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Isla will love that. She's been taking apart old radios at home for months, so it'll be nice for her to build something for a change.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Ha! She sounds like a natural inventor. I'll send the booking confirmation and the payment link to your email this afternoon.

listeningParts.title: A tour of the Museum of Everyday Inventions
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a museum about everyday inventions and explains the galleries.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome to the Museum of Everyday Inventions. I'm Craig, and I'll be giving you a quick introduction before you head off to explore. Most museums of science focus on spectacular inventions like rockets and computers. We decided to do something different and tell the stories behind the ordinary objects that we use every day without thinking about them, things like zips, tin cans and toothbrushes.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum opened in 2009 in what used to be a shoe factory, which seemed appropriate, because the building itself was full of machines that were once new inventions. Some of the original machinery is still in place on the ground floor, and on the first Sunday of every month we switch one of them on, so you can see how shoes were made a hundred years ago. It's very noisy, but people love it, and it gives you a real sense of what working life was like for the hundreds of people who were employed here.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Before I describe the galleries, just a few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Patent Room, where some of the documents are very old and can be damaged by flash. Bags larger than a small backpack need to go in the lockers next to the shop; you'll need a one-dollar coin, but you get it back. And the café on the top floor closes half an hour before the museum, at four thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, the galleries. There are four. Gallery One, here on the ground floor, is called In the Kitchen. It covers everything from the tin can, which was invented in the early nineteenth century, long before anyone had invented a tin opener, to the modern microwave. The highlight for many visitors is a wall of more than two hundred kitchen gadgets, some useful and some completely ridiculous. You can vote for the silliest one on a screen at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Two, on the first floor, is At Home. This is where you'll find our collection of early vacuum cleaners. One of the first ones was so large that it was pulled by horses and parked outside the house, with long hoses going in through the windows. There's also a reconstructed bathroom from the nineteen twenties, where you can see how much plumbing has changed.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Three is called Getting Dressed, and it's all about clothing. It tells the story of the zip, which took several inventors and about twenty years to perfect, as well as buttons, safety pins and waterproof fabrics. Children particularly enjoy the dressing-up area, where they can try on copies of historical clothes and see how long it takes to fasten them without modern zips.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Gallery Four, on the top floor, is the Inventors' Workshop. This is our hands-on space, where you can build your own simple inventions using the tools and materials provided. It's very popular with school groups, so if you want to use it, I'd recommend going this morning, as there are three schools booked in for this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And finally, next to the workshop is the Patent Room, which I mentioned earlier. It contains original patent drawings for many of the objects in the museum. Some of them were drawn by the inventors themselves, and they're surprisingly beautiful. We've also got a small display of inventions that failed, which I personally find the most interesting part of the whole museum. Most inventions never make any money, and it's good to remember that the successful ones are the exception. My favourite is a hat with a built-in umbrella, which was patented more than once and never sold.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you have any questions, our staff are in green shirts. There's also a free audio guide, which you can download onto your phone using the code on the back of your ticket. Enjoy your visit.
