listeningParts.title: A presentation on Hedy Lamarr
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two history of technology students, Nina and Josh, discuss their presentation on the actress and inventor Hedy Lamarr with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Nina, Josh. Have a seat. So, you've chosen Hedy Lamarr for your presentation on overlooked inventors. Why her?

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: Mainly because her story is so surprising. Most people who've heard of her know her as a Hollywood film star from the nineteen thirties and forties. Very few people know that she was also an inventor and held a patent for a communication system.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: And we liked the fact that her invention was ignored for years and then became important much later. It fits the theme of the module really well.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Remind me of the basic facts.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: She was born in Vienna in 1914 and became an actress in Europe before moving to the United States in the late nineteen thirties. During the Second World War, she wanted to help the war effort, and she became interested in radio-controlled torpedoes.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The problem with those torpedoes was that the enemy could jam the radio signal, or take control of it, by finding the frequency it was using. Lamarr's idea was that the signal should jump rapidly between many different frequencies in a pattern known only to the sender and the receiver. So the enemy couldn't follow it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And she didn't do this alone, did she?

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: No, she worked with a composer, George Antheil. He had experience of synchronising mechanical pianos, and they used a similar idea: a strip of paper with holes punched in it, like a piano roll, to keep the transmitter and receiver switching at the same time. They used eighty-eight frequencies, which is the same as the number of keys on a piano.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lovely detail. Make sure you include it. What happened to the patent?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: It was granted in 1942, and they gave it to the US Navy. But the navy didn't use it during the war. They thought the mechanism was too complicated to fit inside a torpedo. Some historians also think that the navy simply didn't take an actress seriously as an inventor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How are you going to handle that point? It's partly speculation.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: We were going to present it as one possible explanation, and make it clear that the technical objections were real as well.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that's the right approach. And what about her later influence? There are some big claims online.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Yes, that's something we wanted to ask about. A lot of websites say she invented Wi-Fi or mobile phones, which isn't really accurate. The idea of switching between frequencies, which is called frequency hopping, was later developed by many engineers, and it's one of the techniques behind some modern wireless systems, such as Bluetooth. But she didn't invent those systems herself.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'd describe her work as an important early contribution rather than the origin of modern wireless technology. Be careful with your sources there. Use books and academic articles rather than popular websites.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: We've found a good biography in the library, so we'll rely mainly on that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine. How are you going to end the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: With the recognition she received. She got very little credit for most of her life, but in 1997 she received an award from an organisation that campaigns for digital rights, and in 2014, after her death, she was added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in the United States.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a nice way to finish. Perhaps you could also ask the audience a question at the end, about why some inventors are remembered and others forgotten. It would link back to the theme of the module.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.text: Good idea. We could show some photos of other forgotten inventors while we ask it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Just don't make it too long. You've got fifteen minutes in total, including questions.

listeningParts.title: Gutenberg and the printing revolution
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a history course on the invention of printing with movable type in Europe and its effects.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at what many historians consider one of the most important inventions of the last thousand years: printing with movable type, developed in Europe by Johannes Gutenberg in the middle of the fifteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First, though, it's important to say that Gutenberg did not invent printing itself. Printing from carved wooden blocks had been used in China for centuries, and around the year 1040, a Chinese craftsman called Bi Sheng created movable type made from baked clay. In Korea, books were being printed with metal type by the fourteenth century. However, Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, which made movable type far less practical there than for European languages, which need only a few dozen letters and symbols.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what was the situation in Europe before Gutenberg? Books were copied by hand, often by monks, and a single book could take months or even years to produce. As a result, books were extremely expensive, and most were owned by churches, universities and wealthy families.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Gutenberg was born in the German city of Mainz, around 1400. He trained as a metalworker, and that background was crucial. His real achievement was not a single machine but a whole system. The first part was a hand mould, a device that allowed individual letters to be cast quickly and accurately, so that thousands of identical pieces of type could be made. The type itself was made of an alloy, mainly lead, with tin and antimony, which melted at a low temperature but was hard enough to survive repeated use.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second part of the system was the ink. The water-based inks used by scribes did not stick well to metal, so Gutenberg developed an oil-based ink, similar to the paints used by artists at the time. And the third part was the press. Here, Gutenberg adapted the screw presses that were already used in the region for making wine and pressing olives. Using a press, rather than rubbing the paper by hand, allowed even pressure to be applied across the whole page, and both sides of the paper could be printed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The most famous product of Gutenberg's workshop is the Gutenberg Bible, completed in about 1455. Around a hundred and eighty copies were printed, some on paper and some on vellum, which is a fine material made from animal skin. About forty-nine copies survive today, and they're among the most valuable books in the world. What's striking is that they were designed to look like handwritten manuscripts, with the same style of lettering, because that's what readers expected a book to look like.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sadly, Gutenberg himself didn't profit much from his invention. He had borrowed large sums of money from a businessman called Johann Fust, and in 1455 Fust took him to court to get his money back. Fust won the case and took over much of the equipment, and he and his partner went on to run a successful printing business.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But the technology spread remarkably quickly. Printers trained in Mainz moved to other cities, and by 1500, there were presses in more than two hundred and fifty towns across Europe. Historians estimate that millions of books had been printed by then. Books became much cheaper, and they could be produced in identical copies, which meant that scholars in different countries could refer to exactly the same text, page by page.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The consequences were enormous. Printing helped to spread the ideas of the Renaissance and, later, of the Scientific Revolution, as scientists could publish their findings and build on each other's work. It also played a major role in religious change. When Martin Luther wrote his criticisms of the Church in 1517, printed copies spread across Germany within weeks. Over the longer term, cheaper books encouraged the growth of literacy, and printing also helped to standardise spelling and grammar in many European languages.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Next week, we'll look at another information revolution, the arrival of the telephone, and ask whether it changed society as much as printing did.

readingPassages.title: The humble pencil
paragraphs: Few objects are as ordinary as the pencil. It is cheap, light and reliable, it works in freezing temperatures and even upside down, and its marks can be rubbed out. Yet the pencil has a surprisingly long and interesting history, involving a lucky discovery in the English countryside, a war between Britain and France, and the work of several inventors whose names are now largely forgotten.

The story begins in Borrowdale, a valley in the Lake District of north-west England. In the sixteenth century, a large deposit of an unusual black mineral was found there. It was soft, left a dark mark and could be cut into sticks. According to local tradition, shepherds were the first to use it, marking their sheep to show who owned them. Nobody at the time knew what the substance was. Because it looked rather like lead, it became known as 'black lead', and this is why we still talk about the 'lead' of a pencil today, even though pencils have never contained lead at all.

In fact, the mineral was graphite, a form of pure carbon. The Borrowdale deposit was exceptionally pure and solid, and for a long time it was the only one of its kind known in the world. Graphite quickly became valuable, not only for writing but also for lining the moulds in which cannonballs were made. The mine was so important that it was guarded, and it was opened only for a few weeks each year to prevent prices from falling. In 1752, the British Parliament made stealing graphite a serious crime, punishable by imprisonment or transportation to a colony.

Early pencils were simply sticks of graphite, which were soft and brittle and left marks on the user's hands. To solve this, people wrapped them in string or sheepskin. Later, craftsmen began placing the graphite inside a holder made of wood. The method that eventually became standard involved cutting a groove in a strip of wood, laying the graphite in it and gluing a second strip on top. Cedar became the most popular wood, because it is soft, has a straight grain and can be sharpened easily.

The next major development was a result of war. In the 1790s, France was at war with Britain and could no longer obtain English graphite. The French government asked an engineer and painter, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, to find an alternative. In 1795, Conté developed a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and water, forming the mixture into thin rods and heating them in a kiln. His process had a great advantage: by changing the proportion of clay, manufacturers could make pencils harder or softer. The same basic method is still used today, and it explains the grading system found on many pencils, in which H stands for hard and B for black.

The pencil industry grew rapidly during the nineteenth century. Germany became a major centre of production, and in the United States, one of the early manufacturers was the family of the writer Henry David Thoreau, who worked in his father's pencil business and helped to improve the quality of its products. In England, a pencil industry developed in the town of Keswick, close to the original Borrowdale mine, and today the town has a museum devoted to the history of the pencil.

Another common feature of the modern pencil, the eraser on the end, also has an interesting history. Rubber had been used to remove pencil marks since the eighteenth century, but in 1858 an American, Hymen Lipman, received a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end. He later sold the patent for a large sum. However, in 1875, the United States Supreme Court ruled that the patent was invalid, because joining two existing objects together did not count as a new invention.

Today, billions of pencils are produced every year, and despite the arrival of computers and tablets, the pencil remains popular with artists, architects, carpenters and schoolchildren. It needs no batteries, no ink cartridges and no software updates. Some modern pencils are even made from recycled newspapers or plastic rather than wood. The pencil is a reminder that some of the most successful inventions are not dramatic breakthroughs but simple objects that are gradually improved by many people over hundreds of years.

readingPassages.title: Happy accidents
paragraphs: We often imagine inventors as people who set out to solve a particular problem and work steadily until they succeed. Many inventions do happen this way. But a surprising number of familiar products were discovered by accident, when someone who was looking for one thing noticed something quite different. The French scientist Louis Pasteur famously observed that, in the field of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind. The stories behind several everyday inventions suggest that he was right.

In 1945, Percy Spencer, an engineer at the American company Raytheon, was working with a magnetron, a device that produces microwaves for radar equipment. Standing near the machine, he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Other people had probably experienced something similar, but Spencer was curious. He placed some popcorn kernels near the magnetron and watched them pop, and later tried an egg, which exploded. Raytheon soon applied for a patent for cooking with microwaves, and in 1947 the first commercial microwave oven went on sale. It was nearly two metres tall and weighed hundreds of kilograms, and it was used mainly in restaurants and ships. Smaller ovens for the home did not become common until the late 1960s.

Another accidental invention began with a walk in the countryside. In 1941, a Swiss engineer, George de Mestral, returned from a hunting trip in the mountains and found that his clothes and his dog's fur were covered with burrs, the seed cases of the burdock plant. Rather than simply removing them, he examined them under a microscope and saw that they were covered in tiny hooks, which caught on anything with loops, such as fabric or hair. He spent years trying to reproduce this in a factory, first with cotton and then with nylon. He received a patent in the 1950s and called his product Velcro, from the French words for 'velvet' and 'hook'.

Sometimes an accidental discovery waits years for a use. In 1968, Spencer Silver, a chemist at the American company 3M, was trying to develop a very strong glue. Instead, he produced an adhesive that was weak and could be removed easily without leaving a mark. For several years, nobody could think of a use for it. Then a colleague, Art Fry, who sang in a church choir, became frustrated that the paper bookmarks in his hymn book kept falling out. He realised that Silver's adhesive could make a bookmark that stayed in place but did not damage the page. After further development, the product was launched across the United States in 1980 as the Post-it Note.

A similar story lies behind one of the most slippery substances ever made. In 1938, Roy Plunkett, a chemist at the company DuPont, was working on new gases for refrigerators. One morning, he opened the valve of a container that should have been full of gas, but nothing came out. When the container was cut open, it was found to contain a white, waxy powder. The gas had turned into a new solid material, later named Teflon, which was extremely slippery and was not affected by heat or most chemicals. It was first used in industry and the military, and only later on the non-stick frying pans for which it is best known.

What do these stories have in common? In each case, the accident alone was not enough. Many people must have had chocolate melt in their pockets or burrs stuck to their clothes. What made the difference was that the person involved had the knowledge to recognise that something unusual had happened, the curiosity to investigate it and, often, the persistence to spend years turning a strange observation into a product that people wanted to buy.

Some organisations have tried to create the conditions in which such discoveries are more likely. 3M, for example, has for decades allowed its technical staff to spend part of their working time on projects of their own choosing. The idea is that if people are free to follow their curiosity, they are more likely to notice unexpected results and to share them with colleagues who may see a use for them. Other technology companies have since adopted similar policies.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that invention is mainly a matter of luck. The stories of happy accidents are memorable partly because they are unusual. For every accidental discovery, there are many inventions that resulted from years of careful, systematic work. Thomas Edison, whose laboratory tested thousands of materials in the search for a long-lasting light bulb filament, is often quoted as saying that genius is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration. Even the luckiest inventors needed plenty of both.

readingPassages.title: Do patents help or hinder invention?
paragraphs: A patent is a legal right that allows an inventor to prevent others from making, using or selling an invention for a limited period, usually twenty years in most countries today. In return, the inventor must publish a detailed description of how the invention works, so that once the patent expires, anyone can use it. The idea is simple: by giving inventors a temporary monopoly, society encourages them to invest time and money in new ideas, and in the long run everyone benefits.

The idea has a long history. One of the earliest patent laws was passed in Venice in 1474, when the city offered ten years of protection to anyone who built a new and useful device. In the United States, the founders considered patents important enough to mention in the Constitution, which gave Congress the power to promote the progress of science and useful arts. When the first patent law was passed in 1790, Thomas Jefferson, then Secretary of State, was one of the officials responsible for examining applications, although he had mixed feelings about granting monopolies.

Supporters of the system point to industries in which patents seem essential. Developing a new medicine, for example, can take more than a decade and cost enormous sums, while copying the final product may be relatively cheap. Without the protection of a patent, the argument goes, no company would take the risk. Patents can also help small inventors, who may be able to raise money from investors or sell their rights to a larger company. In addition, because patent documents must be published, they form a huge public library of technical knowledge, which engineers and researchers can consult to learn how problems have been solved before.

Critics, however, argue that patents can slow down progress rather than speed it up. A frequently cited example is the steam engine. James Watt patented his improved engine in 1769, and in 1775 the British Parliament extended the patent until 1800. Some economists, including Michele Boldrin and David Levine, have argued that Watt used his patent to block other engineers from making further improvements, and that the steam engine developed much faster once the patent expired.

The early history of aviation offers another example. After their first powered flight in 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright spent years in legal battles with other aircraft makers, especially Glenn Curtiss, whom they accused of using their ideas. Many historians believe these disputes held back the American aircraft industry. When the United States entered the First World War in 1917 and needed planes urgently, the government encouraged manufacturers to share their patents so that production could increase. An organisation was set up through which aircraft makers could use each other's inventions in return for a fee, and the legal battles largely came to an end.

Some inventors have chosen not to seek patents at all. When Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was announced in 1955, he was asked in a television interview who owned the patent. He famously replied that there was no patent, and asked whether one could patent the sun. Historians have pointed out that the vaccine might not have been patentable anyway, but his answer has become a symbol of the idea that some discoveries should be freely available to everyone. Similar arguments are heard today in debates about medicines needed in poorer countries, where high prices protected by patents can put treatment out of reach.

In my view, the evidence does not support either extreme. Patents clearly play an important role in some industries, particularly where research is expensive and copying is easy. But the system works poorly when patents are granted too easily or for very broad ideas, because they can then be used to block competitors rather than to reward genuine invention. A particular problem is the rise of companies that produce nothing themselves but buy up patents in order to sue other businesses, a practice that adds costs without creating anything new.

I believe the most sensible approach is not to abolish patents but to make them harder to obtain and narrower in scope, so that they protect real innovation without preventing others from building on it. It is also worth remembering that patents are only one of many reasons people invent. Curiosity, the desire to solve a problem and the satisfaction of being first have driven inventors for centuries, and many of the most important ideas in history were never patented at all.

writingTask1.title: How pencils are made
writingTask1.instructions: The diagram below shows the stages in the manufacture of wooden pencils. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
processSteps: Graphite and clay are ground into a fine powder
The powder is mixed with water to form a paste
The paste is pressed into thin rods and cut to length
The rods are dried and fired in a kiln at about 1,000°C
The rods are soaked in wax to make them write smoothly
Grooves are cut into thin slats of cedar wood
Rods are laid in the grooves and a second slat is glued on top
The slats are cut into individual pencils

listeningParts.title: Booking a ferry and a holiday cottage
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones an island ferry and accommodation office to arrange a short holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Inishkerrow Ferries and Island Holidays, Declan speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. My partner and I are planning a few days on Inishkerrow this summer, and I'd like to book the ferry and somewhere to stay, if that's possible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem at all, we can do both. Are you bringing a car, or travelling as foot passengers?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were thinking of bringing the car. Is that a good idea?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: To be honest, the island's only about six kilometres long, and most people walk or cycle. But you can bring a car on the larger ferry. The vehicle has to be under five metres long, though, because the deck is quite small.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ours is a small hatchback, so that's fine. How long is the crossing?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: On the car ferry it's forty-five minutes. There's also a fast passenger boat that takes about twenty-five minutes, but it doesn't carry vehicles.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll take the car ferry. What are the fares?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: A single ticket is fourteen euros per adult, and a return is twenty-four euros. The car is an extra thirty-five euros return, and that includes the driver's ticket, so you'd pay for one adult return plus the car.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: So fifty-nine euros altogether. That sounds fine. And the accommodation?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We manage four self-catering cottages on the island. When would you like to come?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping to arrive on the twelfth of July and stay four nights.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me check. Ah, the cottages are all booked on the twelfth, I'm afraid, because there's a music festival on the island that weekend. But I could offer you the fourteenth to the eighteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fourteenth works. We're flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. The cottage that's free then is called Seal Cottage. It's right beside the old harbour, and you can often see seals on the rocks from the kitchen window. It has one double bedroom, a small garden, and a wood-burning stove in the sitting room, which is lovely in the evenings, even in July.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds perfect. How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's ninety-five euros a night, so three hundred and eighty for the four nights. Bed linen and towels are included, and there's a basket of firewood for the stove.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what about food? Is there a supermarket?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's one small shop near the pier, which sells most basics, as well as fresh fish and bread from the island bakery. It's open every day except Wednesday afternoons, when it closes at one. But I'd recommend bringing some supplies with you, as prices are a bit higher than on the mainland.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. Can we pay by card on the island?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The shop and the café take cards, but there's no bank and no cash machine on the island, and a few places, like the bike hire, only accept cash. So it's worth bringing some euros with you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where's the bike hire?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's run from the café, just up the hill from the pier. Bikes are twelve euros a day. Honestly, if you're hiring bikes, you might want to leave your car on the mainland and save the money.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hmm, you might be right. Let me talk to my partner about that. Can I book the cottage now and the ferry later?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll just need your name for the booking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Joanna Pruett. That's P-R-U-E-T-T.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My cell number is oh-one-five-five, three-two-nine, eight-four-one.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. We ask for a deposit of one hundred euros to hold the cottage, and the rest is due two weeks before you arrive. I'll email you the payment details today.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Is there anything else we should bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Definitely a good waterproof jacket. The weather out here can change very quickly, even in summer. And if you're walking to the cliffs at the north end, wear proper boots, because the path can be muddy.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks so much, Declan. You've been really helpful.

listeningParts.title: Welcome to Holm Island nature reserve
listeningParts.contextDescription: A ranger speaks to a group of day visitors as they arrive by boat at an island nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Holm Island. My name's Ben, and I'm one of the two rangers who live here from March to October. Before you set off, I'd like to give you some information about the island and a few rules, so that you have a good day and the wildlife isn't disturbed.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Holm Island has been a nature reserve since 1976. Before that, there was a small farming community here, but the last family left in the 1950s, mainly because the children had to go to the mainland for secondary school and the parents didn't want to be separated from them. Since then, the island has belonged entirely to the birds and the seals, and to visitors like you, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Most people come here to see the seabirds, and you've chosen a very good time. In June the colonies are at their busiest. We have around twelve thousand pairs of puffins, which nest in burrows in the grassy slopes above the cliffs. The burrows are only a short distance under the surface, and the ground is easily broken, so it's extremely important that you stay on the marked paths. If you step off the path, you could collapse a burrow with a chick inside.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: You'll also see razorbills, guillemots and kittiwakes on the cliff ledges. A lot of visitors ask whether the numbers are going up or down. The honest answer is that puffins here are fairly stable at the moment, but kittiwakes have declined by about a third in the last twenty years. The main cause seems to be changes in the sea, which mean there are fewer of the small fish they feed their chicks on.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: A few rules. There are no bins on the island, so please take all your rubbish back with you on the boat. Dogs aren't allowed, as you probably saw on the booking website. And please don't feed the gulls, however friendly they look. They've learned that visitors carry sandwiches, and they can be quite bold.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The boat leaves again at four o'clock, and it won't wait, so please be back at the landing stage by a quarter to four. If you miss it, you'll be spending the night with me, and I can promise you the accommodation isn't very comfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you about the main places to visit. If you look at the map on the board here, you'll see the landing stage at the bottom, and the visitor hut just above it. The hut has toilets, which are the only ones on the island, and an exhibition about the island's history, including photographs of the families who once lived here.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: If you follow the main path north for about twenty minutes, you'll reach the North Cliffs. This is the best place to see puffins close up. In fact, they often walk right up to the path. There's a wooden screen with viewing holes, so you can watch them without disturbing them.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: On the west side of the island is Seal Bay. Grey seals rest on the rocks there at low tide, and today low tide is at about one o'clock, so that's the best time to go. Please keep your voices down, because the seals are easily frightened and will go into the water if they hear people.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: In the middle of the island, you'll find the old walled garden, which belonged to the farm. It's sheltered from the wind, so it's a good spot for a picnic, and there are benches there. It's also where we've planted wild flowers that attract butterflies and bees.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: And finally, at the southern tip, there's the lighthouse. It's been automatic since the 1980s, so there are no keepers any more, and you can't go inside. But on Wednesdays and Saturdays, I give a short talk there at two o'clock about the history of the lighthouse, which you're welcome to join. Right, enjoy your day.

listeningParts.title: A project on island depopulation
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Ella and Tom, discuss their research on population decline in small islands with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Ella, Tom, come and sit down. So, how's the island project going?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. As you know, we're looking at why the populations of small islands off the coasts of Scotland and Ireland have fallen, and whether anything can reverse it. We've now finished our background reading and started on the case studies.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. What did you find in the reading?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The general pattern is quite clear. Most of these islands reached their highest population in the nineteenth century, and since then numbers have dropped, sometimes very steeply. The most famous extreme case is St Kilda, where the last thirty-six inhabitants asked to be taken to the mainland in 1930, and the island has had no permanent population since then.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what are the main reasons for decline, generally?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Lack of jobs is always mentioned first. Traditional work like fishing and small-scale farming doesn't support as many people as it used to. But what surprised me was how often education came up. On a lot of islands, once the primary school closes, families with young children leave, and then it's very hard to get them back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It becomes a kind of cycle. Fewer children means the school closes, and without a school, younger families won't move there, so the population gets older and older.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to develop. Have you found any examples of islands where the trend has been reversed?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Yes, a few. The best examples seem to be places where the community itself bought the land. In Scotland, there have been several community buyouts, where residents raised money to buy the island from a private landowner. Afterwards, they were able to build affordable housing and attract new families.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The other big change is broadband. Since fast internet reached some islands, a few people have moved there to work remotely for companies on the mainland, or even abroad. One woman we interviewed runs a graphic design business from her kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you've done interviews as well?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Yes, by video call. We spoke to fourteen people on three islands. We'd hoped to visit one of them, but the ferry was cancelled twice because of storms, so in the end we had to do everything online.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a shame, but it's actually a nice illustration of your topic. Transport problems are part of island life. Did the interviews tell you anything you didn't expect?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The thing that came up most often wasn't jobs or schools, actually. It was housing. Several people said that holiday homes were pushing up prices, so that young islanders couldn't afford to stay, even when they had work.

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: And one man said that some houses are empty for ten months of the year, which makes the villages feel deserted in winter.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important tension, because tourism also brings income. You'll need to present both sides. Now, how are you going to structure the final report?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with the historical background, then the three case studies, and finish with recommendations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd suggest putting a short section comparing the three islands before the recommendations. That way, the reader can see the patterns clearly. And please include a table with the population figures for each island at each census, so the trends are easy to see.

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should we include quotes from the interviews?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Definitely, but keep them short, and make sure you've got permission from everyone you quote. Some of these communities are very small, so even without names, people might be recognised. You could ask them to check the quotes before you submit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Good idea. When do you need the draft?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: By the end of next month, please. And send me the interview questions too, so I can include them in the appendix check.

listeningParts.title: The theory of island biogeography
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an ecology course about why some islands have more species than others.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at one of the most influential ideas in ecology, which tries to answer a simple question: why do some islands have many more species than others?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Naturalists had noticed for a long time that large islands generally support more species than small ones. If you count the species of birds, reptiles or plants on a group of islands, and plot them against the area of each island, you get a fairly regular pattern. This is known as the species-area relationship. As a rough rule, an island ten times larger than another will have about twice as many species.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But it wasn't until the 1960s that two American ecologists, Robert MacArthur and Edward Wilson, offered a full explanation. In 1967 they published a book called The Theory of Island Biogeography, and their central idea was that the number of species on an island reflects a balance between two processes: immigration and extinction.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's take immigration first. New species arrive on islands all the time: birds and bats fly there, seeds are carried by the wind or by birds, and insects and small reptiles may float across the sea on pieces of vegetation. MacArthur and Wilson pointed out that the rate of arrival depends mainly on distance. An island close to the mainland will receive new arrivals much more often than a remote one in the middle of the ocean.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now extinction. Once a species arrives, it may not survive. On a small island, populations are small, and small populations are much more likely to die out, for example after a storm, a drought or a disease. So the rate of extinction depends mainly on the size of the island. Over time, the two rates come into balance, and the number of species stays roughly constant, even though the actual species present may keep changing. They called this an equilibrium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The theory makes two clear predictions. Large islands close to the mainland should have the most species, and small, remote islands the fewest. And these predictions have generally been supported by the evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Wilson also tested the theory directly, together with his student Daniel Simberloff. In the late 1960s, they chose several tiny mangrove islands off the coast of Florida, each only a few metres across, and covered them with tents before removing all the insects and spiders with chemicals. Then they watched as the islands were recolonised. Within about a year, the number of species on each island had returned to roughly its original level, and, as the theory predicted, the nearest islands recovered fastest, although the species were not all the same as before.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Nature has also provided its own experiments. When the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, it destroyed all life on the remaining islands. Scientists who visited in the following decades recorded the return of plants and animals, starting with ferns and grasses. And in 1963, a completely new island, called Surtsey, appeared in the sea off the south coast of Iceland after a volcanic eruption. It was immediately protected, and only scientists are allowed to land, so that they can study how life arrives. The first plant was recorded there in 1965, just two years after the island appeared.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What makes the theory so important today, though, is that it doesn't only apply to real islands. Think of a forest that has been cut into small patches by farmland or roads. Each patch is effectively an island surrounded by an environment that many forest species can't cross. The same is true of many national parks. So the theory helps to explain why species disappear when habitats are fragmented, and it has influenced the design of nature reserves. For example, it suggests that one large reserve may often be better than several small ones, and that corridors of habitat connecting reserves can help species to move between them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That said, the theory has its limitations. It treats all species as if they were equal, and it pays little attention to the evolution of new species on islands, which is particularly important on very remote islands such as Hawaii. We'll come back to that next week, when we look at island evolution.

readingPassages.title: The statues of Rapa Nui
paragraphs: Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth. A triangle of volcanic rock covering only about 164 square kilometres, it lies in the south-eastern Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand five hundred kilometres west of the coast of Chile, to which it belongs. The nearest inhabited island, Pitcairn, is around two thousand kilometres away. Yet this tiny, isolated island is famous throughout the world for the giant stone statues, known as moai, that were carved by its Polynesian inhabitants centuries ago.

The island's first settlers were Polynesian seafarers, who reached it by canoe after a remarkable voyage across open ocean. Exactly when they arrived is still debated. Earlier researchers suggested a date in the first millennium AD, but more recent radiocarbon dating has led many archaeologists to conclude that settlement took place around 1200. The settlers brought with them crops such as sweet potato and taro, as well as chickens. They also brought, probably by accident, the Polynesian rat, an animal that would have important consequences for the island's environment.

Nearly a thousand moai have been recorded on the island. Most are between three and six metres tall, but the largest ever raised, known as Paro, is around ten metres high and is estimated to weigh more than eighty tonnes. Almost all of them were carved from a soft volcanic rock called tuff, at a quarry in the crater of an extinct volcano, Rano Raraku. Hundreds of statues remain at the quarry today, some still attached to the rock in which they were being carved, which gives archaeologists a valuable picture of how the work was done, using hard stone tools.

Once finished, many moai were transported to stone platforms, called ahu, near the coast. Most of these statues face inland, towards the villages, rather than out to sea, and it is widely believed that they represented important ancestors who watched over the community. Some were given red stone 'hats', called pukao, made from a different type of volcanic rock from another quarry. How the islanders moved such heavy objects across the island, sometimes for more than ten kilometres, has been one of the great puzzles of Pacific archaeology.

For many years, the most popular theory was that the statues were laid on wooden sledges and dragged, which would have required large quantities of timber. This idea fitted a well-known account of the island's history, popularised by the geographer Jared Diamond in his 2005 book Collapse. According to this view, the islanders cut down their forests to move statues and clear land, which led to soil erosion, food shortages and conflict, and a dramatic fall in population. The island became a warning about what happens when a society destroys its own environment.

In recent years, however, this story has been strongly challenged. The archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo have argued that the rats introduced by the first settlers, which ate the seeds of the island's palm trees, played a major part in the loss of the forest. They have also suggested that the moai were 'walked' upright, rocked from side to side by teams pulling on ropes. In 2012, they demonstrated this method with a replica statue weighing several tonnes, which a team of fewer than twenty people moved along a road with surprising speed. This method would have required far less wood than dragging.

What is not disputed is that the greatest disaster in the island's history came from outside. Europeans first reached Rapa Nui on Easter Sunday in 1722, when the Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen arrived and gave the island its European name. In the 1860s, raiders from Peru took around fifteen hundred islanders away to work as slaves, and diseases such as smallpox, brought back by a few survivors who were returned, spread rapidly. By 1877, only around one hundred and eleven Rapa Nui people remained on the island.

Today the population is several thousand, and the island's culture is experiencing a revival. Rapa Nui National Park was added to the World Heritage List in 1995, and tourism is now the main source of income. Many islanders have campaigned for the return of statues taken abroad, including one called Hoa Hakananai'a, which has been in the British Museum in London since 1869. For the Rapa Nui people, the moai are not simply archaeological objects, but living links with their ancestors.

readingPassages.title: Giants and dwarfs: the strange evolution of island animals
paragraphs: Islands have long fascinated biologists, and for good reason. Cut off from the mainland, often for millions of years, island plants and animals evolve in isolation, and the results can be remarkable. Charles Darwin's visit to the Galápagos Islands in 1835 helped to shape his ideas about evolution, and islands continue to serve as natural laboratories. One of the most striking patterns they reveal concerns body size: on islands, small animals often become larger, while large animals often become smaller.

This pattern was first described systematically by the Canadian biologist J. Bristol Foster, who published a study of island mammals in the journal Nature in 1964. Foster compared mammals living on islands off the west coast of North America with their relatives on the mainland, and noticed that island rodents tended to be larger, while island deer and carnivores tended to be smaller. Nine years later, the American biologist Leigh Van Valen gave the pattern a name, the island rule, and it has been debated by scientists ever since.

The fossil record provides some dramatic examples of dwarfing. During the last ice ages, elephants reached several islands in the Mediterranean Sea, including Sicily, Malta and Cyprus, probably by swimming, as modern elephants are strong swimmers. Over many generations, their descendants shrank. Some of the dwarf elephants of Sicily and Malta stood barely a metre tall at the shoulder, compared with their mainland ancestors, which were among the largest elephants that ever lived. On Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, a population of woolly mammoths survived until around four thousand years ago, long after mammoths had disappeared from the mainland.

Even humans may not have been an exception. In 2003, archaeologists working in a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores discovered the remains of a previously unknown human species, which they named Homo floresiensis. Adults appear to have been only around a metre tall, and the species was quickly nicknamed 'the hobbit'. Some researchers have suggested that its small size is another example of island dwarfing, although its origins are still the subject of intense debate.

At the other end of the scale, some islands have produced giants. The Komodo dragon of Indonesia, the world's largest living lizard, can grow to around three metres long. The Galápagos Islands and Aldabra in the Indian Ocean are home to giant tortoises, and on Mauritius lived the dodo, a large flightless relative of pigeons. New Zealand, which had no land mammals apart from bats before humans arrived, was once home to the moa, enormous flightless birds, the largest of which could reach a height of more than three metres with its neck stretched upwards.

Why should islands produce these opposite effects? The most common explanation is that islands offer a very different set of challenges from the mainland. Large animals need a great deal of food, and on a small island, resources are limited, so smaller individuals, which need less food, may be more likely to survive and reproduce. Small animals, on the other hand, are often freed from the predators that kept them small and hidden on the mainland, and from competition with other species, which allows them to grow larger. In the absence of predators, many island birds also lost the ability to fly, as flight requires a great deal of energy.

Unfortunately, the same features that allowed island animals to flourish in isolation also made them extremely vulnerable when humans arrived. Animals that had never encountered predators were often unafraid of people, and flightless birds could not escape. The dodo was first described by Dutch sailors in 1598, and within less than a century it had disappeared, hunted by sailors and attacked by the rats, pigs and other animals they brought with them. In New Zealand, all species of moa were hunted to extinction within a few centuries of the arrival of the first Polynesian settlers.

Not all scientists are convinced that the island rule is a true rule. Some studies have found many exceptions, and in 2008, a group of researchers led by Shai Meiri argued that the pattern was much weaker than had been assumed for many groups of mammals. Others have pointed out that the size of an island, its distance from the mainland and its climate all seem to influence the result. However, more recent large-scale analyses, comparing hundreds of island species with their mainland relatives, have found that the general trend does exist across mammals, birds and reptiles, even if it is far from universal.

readingPassages.title: Can the atoll nations survive?
paragraphs: Scattered across the Pacific and Indian Oceans are a handful of countries made up almost entirely of coral atolls: rings of low, narrow islands built from sand and broken coral on top of ancient reefs. Kiribati, Tuvalu, the Marshall Islands and the Maldives are among them. Most of their land lies only a few metres above sea level, and in the case of the Maldives, the great majority is less than a metre above the sea. As global sea levels rise, these nations face a threat that no other country has experienced: the possibility that their entire territory could become uninhabitable.

The dangers are not only a matter of slow flooding. Long before an atoll is permanently under water, it may become impossible to live on. Storms and unusually high tides already push seawater across some islands, damaging homes and roads. Just as seriously, salt water seeps into the thin layer of fresh groundwater on which atoll communities depend for drinking and for growing crops. In Tuvalu, for example, the deep pits in which families have traditionally grown a type of giant taro have been badly affected by salt in some areas.

The leaders of atoll nations have used dramatic gestures to draw the world's attention to their situation. In 2009, the president of the Maldives, Mohamed Nasheed, held a cabinet meeting underwater, with ministers in diving equipment signing a call for cuts in global emissions. In 2021, Tuvalu's foreign minister, Simon Kofe, recorded a speech for an international climate conference while standing knee-deep in the sea. In my view, such images have been more effective than many years of technical reports in making distant governments understand what is at stake.

Some governments have begun to plan for the worst. In 2014, Kiribati bought a plot of land of around six thousand acres on Vanua Levu, one of the islands of Fiji. The government said it would be used mainly to grow food, but the then president, Anote Tong, also spoke of the possibility that his people might one day need to move there. Fiji itself has already relocated several coastal villages to higher ground, beginning in 2014 with the village of Vunidogoloa, and has identified dozens more communities that may need to move in the future.

Others have chosen to build. The Maldives has created an artificial island, Hulhumalé, near the capital, by pumping sand from the sea floor onto a shallow reef. Work began in 1997, and the new island stands about two metres above sea level, higher than most natural islands in the country. It is now home to tens of thousands of people. Critics point out, however, that such projects are expensive, can damage surrounding reefs, and are beyond the means of the poorest atoll states.

Science offers a more complicated picture than the headlines sometimes suggest. Coral islands are not fixed lumps of rock; they are made of sediment that is constantly moved by waves and currents, and new material is supplied by living reefs. A study published in 2018 by a team led by the geomorphologist Paul Kench found that the total land area of Tuvalu's 101 islands had actually increased slightly between 1971 and 2014, even though sea levels in the region had risen. Some islands had shrunk, but more had grown. I would argue that this finding is a reason for careful planning rather than for complacency, because it depends on healthy reefs, which are themselves threatened by warming oceans.

The situation also raises difficult legal questions. Under the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a state is generally understood to require a defined territory and a permanent population. What happens to a country if its people are forced to leave and its land disappears? Would it still have a seat at the United Nations, or control over the fishing grounds around its former islands, which are a vital source of income? In 2023, the leaders of the Pacific Islands Forum declared that the statehood of their members would continue regardless of the impact of sea-level rise, and Tuvalu has begun recording its land, culture and history in digital form.

In the same year, Tuvalu and Australia signed a treaty that allows up to two hundred and eighty Tuvaluans each year to move to Australia to live, work and study. Some welcomed this as a model of how wealthy countries could help, while others worried that it might encourage the slow emptying of the islands. It seems to me that the real test of the international community is not whether it offers new homes elsewhere, but whether it does enough to cut emissions so that people can choose to remain in the homes they already have.

listeningParts.title: Volunteering at a food bank
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a community food bank because she wants to become a volunteer.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Food Bank, this is Gary speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I saw a poster in the library saying you need more volunteers, and I'd like to find out how I can help.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That's great, thank you for calling. We always need more people, especially at this time of year. Have you volunteered anywhere before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Not at a food bank, no. I used to help at my children's school, listening to young children read, but that was a few years ago. I've just retired from my job, so now I've got a lot more free time.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Well, you'd be very welcome. Let me tell you a bit about how we work. People bring us donations of food, mainly tins and packets, and we also collect food from two supermarkets every week. Volunteers check and sort everything, and then we pack it into bags for families who've been sent to us by doctors, schools or social workers.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I see. And when do you need people?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We're open three days a week: Monday, Wednesday and Saturday. Which days would suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wednesdays are difficult, because I look after my grandson that day. But Saturday would be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Saturday's perfect. That's our busiest day, actually. There are two shifts: the morning shift is from nine until twelve, and the afternoon shift is from twelve until three.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'd prefer the morning, if that's possible.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No problem. On Saturday mornings, most volunteers work in the warehouse at the back, sorting donations. We need to check the dates on everything, because we can't give out food that's out of date. Then later in the morning, some people move to the front and help with packing the bags.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fine. Is there anything I need to wear?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Just comfortable clothes. But you must wear closed shoes, like trainers or boots, because people sometimes drop heavy tins. Sandals aren't allowed in the warehouse. We give everyone an apron, so you don't need to bring one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Do I need any training?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes, all new volunteers come to a short induction session first. It takes about ninety minutes, and we explain health and safety, how to lift boxes properly, and how to talk to the people who visit us. The next one is on Thursday evening at six thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ninety minutes. That's fine. Where do I go?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We're at forty-two Mill Lane. That's M-I-L-L, Mill Lane. It's the old church hall, opposite the fire station. If you come by car, you can park in the car park behind the church. It's free on weekdays and Saturdays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Lovely. What else do you need from me?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: I'll take your name and number now, and then I'll send you a form. On the form, you need to give the name of someone who can give you a reference, such as a previous employer. It's just a short note to say you're reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's easy. My old manager will do that.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Great. So, what's your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Margaret Hargreaves.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Hargreaves: H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Lovely. One more thing: we're also looking for drivers to collect food from the supermarkets on Monday mornings. Is that something you might be interested in?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Maybe later. I'd like to start with the sorting first and see how I get on.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Many of our volunteers start with one shift and then do more. Some of them have been with us for over ten years! Well, thank you, Margaret. I'll see you at the induction on Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks, Gary. See you then.

listeningParts.title: A river clean-up day
listeningParts.contextDescription: An organiser gives instructions to volunteers at the start of a community river clean-up.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone! Can you all hear me at the back? Great. Welcome to the fifth Millbrook River Clean-Up. My name's Jess, and I'm one of the organisers. Thank you so much for giving up your Sunday morning. We've got more than eighty volunteers here today, which is a record. Last year we had about fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Before we start, I'll explain how the morning will work and give you some safety information. Please listen carefully, because the river is beautiful, but it can also be dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: First, the plan. We'll work from now until twelve thirty, and then we'll all meet back here at the bandstand for lunch. The lunch is free, and it's been provided by the bakery on the high street, so please thank them if you go in there. There are vegetarian options too.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, safety. Everyone must wear one of the yellow high-visibility vests, which are in the boxes next to me, and everyone must wear gloves. Never pick up anything sharp, like broken glass or needles, with your hands, even if you're wearing gloves. If you find something like that, don't touch it. Just mark the place with one of the small orange flags and tell your team leader, who'll deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Please don't go into the water at all, even where it looks shallow. The river bottom is very muddy, and it's easy to get stuck. If you see something in the water that you'd like us to remove, tell your team leader. And please stay on the path side of the fence near the old mill, because the bank there is not safe.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We have a first-aid tent next to the car park. It's the white tent with a green cross on it. If you cut yourself, even slightly, please go there and get it cleaned, because river water can carry infections.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Right, you've all been put into teams of about ten, and each team has a different job. Your team name is on the sticker you got when you signed in. Let me explain what each team will be doing.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Kingfisher team will be working along the riverbank between the bridge and the old mill, collecting general litter. That's the longest section, so you're the biggest team. You'll each have a litter picker and two bags, a black one for rubbish and a clear one for things that can be recycled, such as cans and plastic bottles.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Otter team will be in the children's playground and the picnic area. This is a good team for families with young children, because it's away from the water. Your job is mainly to collect small items, such as sweet wrappers and bottle tops.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Heron team has a special job this year. You'll be counting and recording everything you collect on a form, so that we can send the information to a national charity that studies river pollution. So it's a bit slower, but it's really useful.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Badger team will be cutting back plants that are growing over the footpath. You'll be working with two staff members from the council's parks department, who'll show you how to use the tools safely.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And finally, the Swan team will stay here at the bandstand. You'll be weighing the full bags as the other teams bring them back, so that we know how much rubbish we've collected in total. Last year it was over six hundred kilograms! Then, at about twelve, you'll help to set up the tables for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: One last thing. We'd love to share some photos of today on our website and in the local newspaper. If you don't want to appear in any photos, please tell the photographer, who's wearing a red cap. Okay, team leaders, please hold up your signs, and let's get started!

listeningParts.title: A survey on student volunteering
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two students, Aisha and Ben, talk to their tutor about a survey they carried out on volunteering at their college.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Aisha, hi, Ben. Come in and sit down. So, you've finished your survey on student volunteering. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We wanted to find out how many students at the college do voluntary work, what kind of work they do, and why some students don't volunteer at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your answers?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We used an online questionnaire. At first we planned to stand in the canteen and ask people questions face to face, but we decided online would be quicker, and people might be more honest if they didn't have to talk to us.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. How many people answered?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We sent it to about six hundred students, and two hundred and twelve people completed it. We were quite pleased with that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So am I. That's a good number for a project like this. How did you get so many replies?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We offered a prize. Everyone who finished the questionnaire could enter a draw to win a voucher for the college café. I think that helped a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay. And what were the main results?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Well, about a third of the students said they'd done some volunteering in the last year. That was more than we expected, actually. We thought it would be around one in five.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. What kind of volunteering was most common?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Sport was the biggest group. Lots of students help to coach children's football or swimming teams at the weekend. The second biggest was helping in charity shops, and then working with animals, for example at the animal rescue centre near the college.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And why did they say they volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We gave them a list of reasons and asked them to choose the most important one. The top answer was that they enjoy helping other people. But the second was that it looks good on a CV, which isn't surprising, because many of them are applying for jobs or university places.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And quite a few said they started volunteering because a friend asked them to come along. We hadn't really thought about that, but it seems to be important.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, research often shows that being asked is one of the main reasons people start. What about the students who don't volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: The biggest reason was lack of time. Lots of students have part-time jobs as well as their studies. The next reason was that they didn't know how to find opportunities. Some of them said they'd like to volunteer, but they didn't know where to start.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a useful finding, because it's something the college could do something about. Did you include any recommendations?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Yes. We suggest the college should have a volunteering fair at the start of each year, where local charities can come in and talk to students. And we'd like a noticeboard on the college website with a list of opportunities.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Both good ideas. Now, were there any problems with the survey?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: One question was confusing. We asked how many hours a month people volunteer, but some people answered in hours a week, so we had to remove some answers.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That happens a lot. Mention it in your report, and explain what you'd change next time. Is there anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We also wondered whether we should have asked about the types of organisation people volunteer for. Quite a few people mentioned animal shelters and sports clubs in the comments box, but we hadn't given those as options.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That would be a useful improvement for a follow-up survey. Include the comments as examples in an appendix.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Not really. Oh, the student magazine asked if they could publish our results. Is that all right?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as you don't include any names. I'd love to see it. Well done, both of you.

listeningParts.title: Henry Dunant and the birth of the Red Cross
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a history course about how the Red Cross movement began.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at the beginnings of one of the largest volunteer organisations in the world: the Red Cross. Its story begins with one man and one terrible day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The man was Henry Dunant, who was born in Geneva, in Switzerland, in 1828. He was a businessman, and in the eighteen-fifties he had business interests in Algeria, in North Africa. In June 1859, he travelled to northern Italy, hoping to meet the French emperor, Napoleon the Third, to ask for help with his business.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At that time, France and its ally were fighting the Austrian army in northern Italy. On the evening of the twenty-fourth of June, Dunant arrived near the small town of Solferino, just after a huge battle had taken place there. Around forty thousand soldiers had been killed or wounded in a single day. What shocked Dunant most was that thousands of wounded men were simply left lying on the battlefield, because the armies had very few doctors and almost no medical supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Dunant forgot all about his business. He went to the nearby town of Castiglione, where many of the wounded had been taken, and organised the local people, many of them women, to help. They brought water and food, washed and dressed wounds, and wrote letters for dying soldiers to their families. Importantly, Dunant insisted that they should care for soldiers from both sides equally. The local women repeated a phrase in Italian which means 'all are brothers'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: When Dunant returned to Geneva, he couldn't forget what he had seen. In 1862, he wrote a short book called A Memory of Solferino. In it, he described the battle and its terrible results, and he made two important suggestions. First, every country should set up a society of trained volunteers who would be ready to care for wounded soldiers in times of war. And second, countries should sign an international agreement to protect these volunteers and the wounded.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The book was a great success and was translated into many languages. In 1863, Dunant and four other men from Geneva formed a committee to put his ideas into action. This group later became the International Committee of the Red Cross. Just one year later, in 1864, the representatives of twelve countries signed the first Geneva Convention, which said that medical staff and the wounded must be protected and treated as neutral.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The volunteers needed a symbol, so that soldiers would recognise and respect them. They chose a red cross on a white background. This is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed, as a way of honouring Switzerland, where the movement began. Later, in the eighteen-seventies, during a war with Russia, the Ottoman Empire began to use a red crescent instead, and today the Red Crescent is used in many countries.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sadly, Dunant's own life did not go well. His business in Algeria failed, and in 1867 he went bankrupt. He had to leave Geneva, and for many years he lived in poverty, almost forgotten. Then, in 1895, a journalist found him living in a small care home in the Swiss village of Heiden and wrote an article about him. People around the world were reminded of what he had done, and in 1901, Dunant was awarded the very first Nobel Peace Prize, which he shared with a French campaigner for peace.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today, the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement has national societies in more than one hundred and ninety countries, and it depends on millions of volunteers. Every year, on the eighth of May, World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day is celebrated. That date was chosen because it was Dunant's birthday. Next time, we'll look at how the movement's work has changed since the two World Wars.

readingPassages.title: The story of the charity shop
paragraphs: Walk down almost any high street in Britain today and you will find at least one charity shop. These shops sell second-hand clothes, books, toys and furniture that members of the public have given away, and the money they make goes to a good cause, such as medical research, help for homeless people or aid for poor countries. There are now more than ten thousand charity shops in the United Kingdom, and they have become a familiar part of everyday life. But how did they begin?

One early example opened in 1899, when the Wolverhampton Society for the Blind started a shop on Victoria Street in the English city of Wolverhampton. It was rather different from a modern charity shop. Instead of selling goods that had been given away, it sold baskets, mats and chair seats that had been made by blind and partially sighted people. The shop gave them a way to earn money from their work, and it also helped to raise money for the society.

The idea of selling donated goods became much more common during the Second World War. In 1941, the Red Cross opened a shop on Old Bond Street in London, where people could give items they no longer needed so that they could be sold to raise money for the war effort. The idea quickly spread. Over the next few years, the Red Cross opened more than two hundred permanent shops, as well as many temporary ones, across the country.

The organisation most closely linked with charity shops today, however, is Oxfam. It began in 1942 as a small group of people in the city of Oxford who called themselves the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief. At that time, Greece was occupied by enemy forces, and the Allied countries had blocked ships from reaching it. As a result, many Greek people were starving. The committee campaigned for food to be allowed through and collected money to help.

After the war ended, the committee continued its work, sending help to people in Europe who had lost their homes. In the late 1940s, it opened a shop on Broad Street in the centre of Oxford, where people could bring clothes and other goods to be sold. The shop was a great success, and it is still open today. Over the following decades, the committee, which officially took the shorter name Oxfam in 1965, opened hundreds of shops, and many other charities copied its example.

Charity shops can make money for several reasons. First, almost everything they sell has been donated, so they do not have to buy stock. Second, most of the people who work in them are volunteers, who give their time for free, although larger shops usually have a paid manager. Third, in the United Kingdom, charity shops pay much lower business taxes than ordinary shops. This means that even when items are sold for low prices, a large part of the money can go to the charity.

Over time, charity shops have changed. Many now sell some new goods, such as cards and fair trade products, as well as second-hand items. Some specialise in one type of product, such as furniture, wedding dresses or books. Oxfam, for example, says that it is the largest seller of second-hand books in Europe. Many charities also sell donated goods online, which allows rare or valuable items to reach buyers who will pay a higher price for them.

Charity shops are not without their critics. Some owners of small businesses say that it is unfair for them to compete with shops that pay lower taxes and do not have to pay most of their staff. However, supporters point out that charity shops give a second life to clothes and other goods that might otherwise be thrown away, which is good for the environment. They also give volunteers, many of them retired people or young people looking for work experience, a chance to meet others and learn new skills. For many people, a charity shop is not just a place to buy a cheap jacket but a small but important part of the community. Whatever the arguments, charity shops remain a familiar part of town centres, and for many shoppers a visit to one is now a normal part of looking for a bargain.
