readingPassages.title: Is volunteering good for you?
paragraphs: Every year, millions of people around the world give up their free time to help others without being paid. They coach children's sports teams, visit elderly neighbours, plant trees, answer phones for helplines and serve food in community kitchens. Most people volunteer because they want to help, but a growing amount of research suggests that the volunteers themselves may also benefit in important ways. Scientists, doctors and governments have become increasingly interested in these benefits, partly because volunteering costs very little and is available to almost everyone. If helping others really does make people happier and healthier, it could be a simple way to improve the lives of millions of people.

One of the most common benefits that volunteers report is a feeling of happiness and satisfaction. Many people describe a warm, positive feeling after helping someone, and this has sometimes been called a 'helper's high'. Studies that ask people about their wellbeing have often found that volunteers say they are more satisfied with their lives than people who do not volunteer. Doing something useful for others seems to give people a sense of purpose. This may be especially important for people who have recently retired from work or whose children have left home, because these changes can leave them feeling that they are no longer needed.

Volunteering can also help people to make friends and feel part of a community. Loneliness is a serious problem in many countries, especially among older people and people who live alone. Working alongside others towards a shared goal gives people a natural reason to talk and spend time together. For people who have recently moved to a new area, volunteering can be one of the quickest ways to get to know their neighbours. Volunteers often say that the friendships they make are among the most valuable things they get from their work, and some of these friendships last for many years.

There is also some evidence of benefits to physical health. In 2013, researchers at the University of Exeter Medical School in England looked at the results of many earlier studies. They found that, in studies which followed people over a number of years, volunteers were less likely to die during the study period than people who did not volunteer. Volunteering was also linked to lower levels of depression. Other studies have suggested that older volunteers, in particular, tend to stay more physically active, perhaps because their work involves walking, carrying things or simply leaving the house more often.

However, the researchers were careful to explain that these results do not prove that volunteering itself makes people healthier. It is possible that people who are already healthy, active and well connected are simply more likely to volunteer in the first place. In other words, good health might lead to volunteering, rather than the other way round. To be more certain, scientists need more studies in which people are chosen at random to volunteer or not, and then followed over time.

For younger people, one important benefit of volunteering is the chance to develop skills that are useful at work. Volunteers may learn how to work in a team, communicate with the public, organise events or handle money. These experiences can give them confidence and can also be mentioned on a CV or in a job interview. Some employers say they value voluntary work because it shows that a person is reliable and willing to take responsibility. For students who are not sure what career they want, volunteering can also be a way to try out different kinds of work, such as teaching, nursing or working outdoors, before making a decision.

Volunteering is not always a positive experience, though. Some volunteers find that they are given boring tasks or that they are not properly trained or supported. Others take on too much and begin to feel tired and stressed, especially if their work involves helping people in difficult situations. Experts say that good organisations should give volunteers clear information about what they will do, offer training and make sure they feel appreciated. Something as simple as saying thank you, or inviting volunteers to a small celebration at the end of the year, can make a big difference to whether people decide to continue.

So, is volunteering good for you? The answer seems to be that it often is, although perhaps not in every case. Most people who volunteer say they get a lot out of it, and there are good reasons to think that helping others can improve our happiness and our connections with other people. Perhaps the best advice is to choose an activity that you enjoy and that fits into your life, rather than one that you feel you ought to do.

readingPassages.title: Should volunteering be compulsory for students?
paragraphs: In many countries, governments and schools are keen to encourage young people to help in their communities. Some have gone further and made a certain amount of community service a requirement for finishing school. Supporters say this teaches young people to care about others, while critics argue that forced 'volunteering' is not really volunteering at all. Looking at some of the programmes that exist around the world can help us to think about this question.

In the United States, the state of Maryland became, in 1992, the first state to require all students to complete community service before they could finish high school. Students there must do seventy-five hours of service, which can include helping at food banks, tutoring younger children or working on environmental projects. Many schools in other states have since introduced their own requirements, although most states have not made it a rule for every school.

In Canada, the province of Ontario introduced a similar rule in 1999. Since then, every student must complete forty hours of community involvement in order to receive a secondary school diploma. Students can choose their own activities, as long as they are unpaid and benefit the community. Some schools help students to find suitable placements, while others leave it to the students and their families.

Service is also part of some international qualifications. Students taking the International Baccalaureate Diploma, which is offered by schools in many countries, must complete a programme called Creativity, Activity, Service, usually known as CAS. As part of this programme, students take part in service activities and write about what they have learned from them. The aim is to help students think about their own role in the wider world.

Other countries have chosen to encourage young people rather than force them. In England, the National Citizen Service, which was introduced in 2011, offers teenagers aged fifteen to seventeen a programme of activities that includes planning and carrying out a project in their local community. It is completely voluntary. In Germany, after compulsory military service was suspended in 2011, a Federal Volunteer Service was created, which gives people of all ages the chance to work for a period in areas such as social care, sport or the environment. Taking part is entirely voluntary, and the programme is designed to be affordable, so that young people from all kinds of families can join.

France has taken a different approach again. In 2019, it launched a programme called the Universal National Service, which brings together young people of around fifteen to seventeen from different backgrounds for a period of group activities, followed by a mission helping an organisation in the community. The government has discussed making it compulsory for all young people, but this has been controversial, and so far it has remained mostly voluntary.

So, do compulsory programmes work? Researchers have reached mixed conclusions. Some studies suggest that students who are required to do community service are just as likely to volunteer later in life as those who are not, or even more likely. Others have found that being forced to help can make some young people less keen to volunteer in the future, especially if the activities feel pointless. Much seems to depend on the quality of the experience and on whether students are allowed to choose what they do. Part of the difficulty is that it is hard to measure the long-term effects of such programmes, since students who choose to volunteer may already be different in important ways from those who do not. Researchers also point out that the quality of the experience seems to matter a great deal: well-organised placements that give students real responsibility appear to have more positive effects than tasks that feel pointless.

In my view, schools are right to make some form of community service part of education. Many young people never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them, and a requirement can open doors that would otherwise stay closed. However, I believe the number of hours should be modest, and students must be given a real choice of activities. It is also important that students have time to talk about what they have done. Without this, I think community service risks becoming just another box to tick, rather than an experience that changes the way young people see the world.

listeningParts.title: Booking a fossil-hunting walk
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a coastal visitor centre to book a guided fossil-hunting walk for her family.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Hello, Seacliff Bay Fossil Centre, Tom speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. We're coming to Seacliff Bay on holiday next week, and my kids are obsessed with dinosaurs. I saw on your website that you do guided fossil walks on the beach. Could I book one?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Of course. Our walks are very popular, especially in the school holidays. They're led by one of our geologists, and they last about two hours. Most people find something, usually ammonites, which are the spiral shells of sea creatures that lived here around two hundred million years ago. Occasionally, someone finds a piece of ichthyosaur, a kind of large marine reptile, but I can't promise that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds brilliant. Which days do you run them?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: This month, we run them on Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays. Which day would you like?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday would be best for us.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm sorry, Saturday's fully booked already. We've still got places on Sunday, though.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sunday's fine. What time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The start time changes every day, because we can only go out when the tide is low. Otherwise, the sea comes right up to the bottom of the cliffs and it isn't safe. Last week the walks started at eleven, but on Sunday it'll be half past nine in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Half nine. Okay. And where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Not here at the centre, but outside the lifeboat station at the eastern end of the beach. The guide will be wearing a bright yellow jacket, so you can't miss her.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It's twelve pounds for adults and six pounds for children. How many of you will there be?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Two adults and two children. The children are seven and ten. Is that old enough?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, the minimum age is five, and all children must be with an adult at all times. Now, there are a few important safety rules. First, footwear. The rocks can be very slippery, so everyone needs to wear strong boots with a good grip. Please don't come in sandals. And you should bring a waterproof jacket, because the weather can change very quickly on the coast.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Do we need any special equipment? Hammers or anything?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: No, you don't. In fact, we ask people not to use hammers at all. The most important rule is that you must never collect anything from the cliffs themselves. They're very unstable, and rocks fall without warning. The best fossils are actually found lying loose on the beach, where the waves have washed them out. We give each child a small bag to keep their finds in, and an identification chart, so they can work out what they've found.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can we keep what we find?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, as long as it's small and common, like most ammonites. But if anyone finds something rare or scientifically important, we ask them to report it to the centre, so experts can record it. Right, can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Siobhan Fitzgerald. That's F-I-T-Z-G-E-R-A-L-D.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number, in case we need to cancel because of bad weather?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Great. You can pay when you arrive, by cash or card. And after the walk, I'd recommend coming back here to the centre. We've got a small exhibition of local fossils, and there's a free talk at one o'clock every day about how the cliffs were formed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll definitely do that. Is there anywhere to park near the lifeboat station?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: There's a small car park there, but it fills up very early. It's usually easier to park at the harbour car park and walk along the seafront, which takes about ten minutes. Oh, and everyone who books a walk gets ten per cent off in our shop, which sells fossils, books and replica dinosaur teeth. The children usually love the teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm sure they will. Thanks very much for your help.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: You're welcome. Enjoy your holiday, and good luck with the fossil hunting.

listeningParts.title: A new dinosaur gallery
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum volunteer introduces a new gallery about prehistoric life to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome to the brand-new Age of Giants gallery here at the Riverside Museum. My name's Kelly, and I'm one of the volunteers. The gallery only opened last month, so you're among the first visitors to see it. Before you go in, I'd like to tell you how it was created and what you'll find in each zone.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The idea for the gallery actually came from our visitors. For years, the most common comment in our visitor book was that people wanted to see more dinosaurs. The old gallery had just two skeletons and a few glass cases, and it hadn't been changed since the 1970s. So, about five years ago, the museum began raising money, and around a third of the cost was donated by members of the public, which we're very grateful for.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: One question people always ask is whether the skeletons are real. The answer is that some are, and some aren't. Real fossil bone is extremely heavy and often fragile, so many museums display casts, which are accurate copies made from the original bones. In this gallery, every label tells you whether you're looking at real fossil material or a cast, so look out for the small red symbol, which means the bones are real.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The gallery is divided into four zones. The first is the Ocean Zone, which shows life in the seas at the time of the dinosaurs. Many people are surprised to learn that the big sea creatures of that period, such as ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs, weren't dinosaurs at all, but marine reptiles. The centrepiece is a plesiosaur skeleton hanging from the ceiling, and there's a large screen where you can watch an animation of it swimming.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Next is the Forest Zone, which is the one most children head for first. It's designed to look like a forest from around seventy million years ago, and it contains our star attraction, a full-size Tyrannosaurus rex. It's a cast, I'm afraid, but it's based on one of the most complete skeletons ever found. Here's a fact that people love: Tyrannosaurus actually lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus. The two are often shown together in films, but they were separated by tens of millions of years.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The third area is the Discovery Lab. This is where you can see how scientists study fossils. Through the large window, you can watch our team cleaning and preparing real fossils, and on weekdays one of the scientists comes out at eleven to answer questions. There are also microscopes you can use yourself, and a sandpit where younger visitors can dig for replica bones.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the Ice Age Hall, which jumps forward to much more recent times, after the dinosaurs had gone. This is where you'll find the mammals, including a woolly mammoth and a sabre-toothed cat. Most mammoths died out around ten thousand years ago, but a small population survived on an island in the Arctic Ocean until around four thousand years ago. That means some mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid in Egypt was built. In this hall, you can also touch a real mammoth tooth, which is about the size of a shoebox.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: A few practical things. Bags can be left in the lockers by the entrance, which take a one-dollar coin that you get back afterwards. Please don't touch the skeletons, except for the objects marked with a hand symbol. And if you'd like a deeper experience, we offer audio guides, which last about forty minutes and are free for museum members.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: We're also looking for more volunteers, especially people who'd like to help in the Discovery Lab at weekends. No experience is needed, as full training is provided. If you're interested, please ask at the information desk. Right, enjoy the gallery, and don't forget to say hello to the T. rex.

listeningParts.title: Are birds living dinosaurs?
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two biology students, Hana and Owen, discuss their presentation on the evolution of birds with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Hana, Owen. So, your presentation is on the idea that birds evolved from dinosaurs. How are you getting on?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Pretty well. We've decided to organise it as a story, going through the main discoveries in the order they happened, because the idea has gone in and out of fashion over the last hundred and sixty years.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sorry, I mean, good. Where does the story start?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: With Archaeopteryx. The first skeleton was found in limestone in Germany and described in 1861, only two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species, in 1859. It had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail, like a reptile. So it looked exactly like the kind of in-between creature Darwin's theory predicted.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: And soon afterwards, Thomas Henry Huxley pointed out how similar birds were to some small meat-eating dinosaurs. But during the twentieth century the idea lost support. One reason was that dinosaurs didn't seem to have collarbones, which birds have, so scientists thought they couldn't be closely related.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what changed?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Two things, really. First, in the late 1960s, John Ostrom described a dinosaur called Deinonychus, which was clearly an active, fast-moving hunter, and its skeleton was remarkably similar to Archaeopteryx. That made people reconsider. And later, collarbones were found in many dinosaur fossils, so that objection disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Then the really big change came in 1996, in north-east China, with Sinosauropteryx. It was a small dinosaur that couldn't fly, but it was covered in simple, hair-like feathers. Since then, dozens of feathered dinosaurs have been found in the same region.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why are the Chinese fossils so well preserved?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Because the animals were buried very quickly in fine volcanic ash and mud at the bottom of lakes. The ash was so fine that even soft parts like feathers left impressions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. I'd make sure you explain that clearly, because the audience may wonder why feathers survive in some places but not others. What's your main argument about why feathers evolved?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: This was the part we found most interesting. If many dinosaurs had feathers but couldn't fly, then feathers can't have evolved for flight in the first place. The most likely explanation is that they first helped animals keep warm, and perhaps later they were used for display, to attract mates. Flight came much later.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Biologists sometimes say a feature was borrowed for a new purpose. And have you included anything about colour?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Yes. We were amazed that scientists can now tell the colours of some dinosaurs. They use powerful microscopes to look at tiny structures inside fossil feathers that once contained pigment. In 2010, researchers showed that Sinosauropteryx had a tail with reddish-brown and white stripes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That always gets a reaction from audiences. Now, the presentation is twenty minutes. How are you dividing it?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Hana will do the history, and I'll do the evidence from the Chinese fossils and the colour research. Then we'll finish together with a few minutes on what it all means.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine. One weakness, though: at the moment, it sounds as if all scientists completely agree. A small number still question parts of the theory, so mention that briefly, to show you've read widely.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Okay, that's fair. What about visuals?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Use a family tree diagram showing where birds fit among the dinosaurs. And I'd avoid putting too much text on your slides. If you can, bring a cast of a fossil for people to look at; the department has several you can borrow.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: That would be great. Could we borrow the Archaeopteryx cast?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'm sure that can be arranged. Ask the technician, and book it at least a week before the presentation.

listeningParts.title: How fossils are formed
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory palaeontology course on the processes that turn living things into fossils.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at how fossils are formed, and why the fossil record gives us such an incomplete picture of past life. The word fossil comes from a Latin word meaning 'dug up', and originally it was used for almost anything taken out of the ground. Today, we use it to mean any preserved evidence of life from the distant past, usually more than about ten thousand years old.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first thing to understand is that fossilisation is extremely rare. When most plants and animals die, they simply disappear. Their bodies are eaten by scavengers, broken down by bacteria, or scattered and worn away by wind and water. Only a tiny fraction of all the living things that have ever existed have become fossils, and only a tiny fraction of those have been found.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what conditions make fossilisation more likely? The most important is rapid burial. If an animal is quickly covered by sediment, such as mud, sand or volcanic ash, it's protected from scavengers, and the supply of oxygen is cut off, which slows down decay. That's why so many fossils come from places that were once at the bottom of seas, lakes or rivers, where sediment builds up steadily. The second factor is the presence of hard parts. Bones, teeth and shells are far more likely to survive than skin, muscles or leaves, so animals with skeletons are much better represented in the fossil record than soft-bodied creatures such as worms or jellyfish.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's look at the main ways fossils form. The most common process is called permineralisation. After burial, groundwater seeps through the sediment and into the tiny spaces inside bone or wood. This water carries dissolved minerals, such as silica or calcite, which slowly crystallise and fill these spaces, turning the original material into stone. Petrified wood, which can preserve the detail of tree rings, is formed in this way.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sometimes, though, the original material dissolves completely, leaving a hollow space in the rock with the exact shape of the organism. This is called a mould. If that space is later filled by other minerals, the result is a cast, which is like a natural copy of the original. Many fossil shells are preserved in this way.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Not all fossils are the remains of bodies. Trace fossils are signs of an organism's activity, such as footprints, burrows, tooth marks and fossilised dung. These can tell us things that bones cannot. For example, long trackways of footprints suggest that some dinosaurs travelled in herds, and the distance between footprints can be used to estimate how fast an animal was moving.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There are also some rare cases of exceptional preservation. Small creatures such as insects and spiders have been trapped in sticky tree resin, which hardened into amber, preserving them in remarkable detail. In the frozen ground of Siberia, woolly mammoths have been found with skin, hair and even stomach contents. And at the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, thousands of animals, including sabre-toothed cats, became stuck in natural asphalt and were preserved.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Perhaps the most famous site of all is the Burgess Shale, high in the Rocky Mountains of Canada, which was discovered by the American scientist Charles Walcott in 1909. It's around five hundred million years old, and it preserves soft-bodied animals that would normally leave no trace at all, giving us a unique window into early animal life in the oceans.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, fossils are not only useful for studying ancient life; they also help geologists date rocks. Certain species existed for a relatively short time but were widespread, so when they're found in a layer of rock, they show its approximate age. These are known as index fossils, and ammonites are a classic example. Next week, we'll look at how fossils are excavated and prepared in the laboratory.

readingPassages.title: The fossil hunter of Lyme Regis
paragraphs: The small town of Lyme Regis lies on the south coast of England, in the county of Dorset, beneath cliffs made of layers of grey clay and limestone. These rocks formed on the floor of a shallow sea around two hundred million years ago, during the early part of the Jurassic period, and they are packed with fossils. Every winter, storms and heavy rain trigger landslides on the cliffs, exposing new remains on the beach below. It was here, in 1799, that Mary Anning was born. Although she had almost no formal education, she would become one of the most important fossil collectors in the history of science.

The Anning family was poor. Mary's father, Richard, was a cabinetmaker, but he also earned extra money by collecting fossils from the beach and selling them as 'curiosities' to wealthy visitors. Lyme Regis was becoming a fashionable seaside resort at the time, partly because the long wars with France made it difficult for the British upper classes to travel to the continent. A famous story is told about Mary's early life: when she was a baby, she was being held by a woman standing under a tree with two others when lightning struck. The three women were killed, but Mary survived. When Richard Anning died in 1810, he left his family in debt, and selling fossils became an important source of income for his widow and children.

The family's first major discovery came in 1811, when Mary's brother Joseph found the skull of a strange animal in the cliffs. About a year later, Mary, who was then only around twelve years old, found the rest of the skeleton. It was a creature unlike anything most people had seen, with a long jaw full of teeth, large eyes and a body shaped rather like a dolphin's. It was sold to a wealthy collector and later displayed in London, and scientists eventually gave it the name Ichthyosaurus, which means 'fish lizard'.

More remarkable finds followed. In 1823, Mary discovered the first nearly complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile with a small head, flippers and an extraordinarily long neck. The neck was so long that the French anatomist Georges Cuvier, the most respected expert of the day, at first suspected that the fossil might be a fake, made by combining bones from different animals. After examining drawings of the specimen more carefully, Cuvier accepted that it was genuine, and the episode greatly increased Mary's reputation among scientists.

In 1828 she found the skeleton of a pterosaur, a flying reptile; it was the first to be discovered outside Germany. She also made an important contribution to the understanding of how ancient animals lived. Collectors had long been puzzled by small stony objects known as 'bezoar stones', which were often found in the region of the abdomen of ichthyosaur skeletons. Mary noticed that when these objects were broken open, they often contained fish bones and scales. The geologist William Buckland concluded that they were fossilised droppings, and in 1829 he named them coprolites. They provided direct evidence of what these animals had eaten.

Fossil hunting was dangerous work. The best time to search was in winter, after storms, when the cliffs were at their most unstable. In 1833, a sudden landslide killed Mary's dog, Tray, which usually accompanied her, and she herself narrowly escaped. Mary was not simply a collector, however. She taught herself anatomy by reading scientific papers, copying their illustrations by hand and dissecting modern fish and cuttlefish to compare them with her fossils. Visitors to her shop were often astonished to find that this working woman understood the subject as well as many professors.

Despite her achievements, Mary Anning received little formal recognition during her lifetime. As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London, and the scientists who bought her fossils often published descriptions of them without mentioning who had found them. She also experienced financial hardship, especially after losing much of her savings in a bad investment, and some of her scientific friends arranged for her to receive an annual payment. She died in 1847, aged forty-seven, and after her death the president of the Geological Society paid tribute to her in a speech, an unusual honour for someone who had never been allowed to be a member.

Her reputation has grown steadily since then. In 2010, the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science. In 2022, a statue of her was unveiled in Lyme Regis, following a campaign started by a local schoolgirl. It is often claimed that the tongue-twister 'She sells seashells on the seashore' was inspired by her, but this link has never been proved. What is certain is that the fossils she found helped to convince scientists that the Earth had once been home to creatures very different from those alive today, and that many of them had become extinct.

readingPassages.title: The day the dinosaurs died
paragraphs: Around sixty-six million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, life on Earth suffered one of the greatest catastrophes in its history. Roughly three-quarters of all plant and animal species disappeared, including every dinosaur except the ancestors of today's birds. For much of the twentieth century, the cause of this mass extinction was one of the great mysteries of science. Dozens of explanations were proposed, from gradual changes in climate to disease, and even the suggestion that early mammals had eaten too many dinosaur eggs. None of them could be properly tested.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In the 1970s, the American geologist Walter Alvarez was studying rocks near the town of Gubbio in central Italy, where a thin layer of clay marks the boundary between the Cretaceous rocks and the younger rocks above. He wanted to know how long the clay had taken to form. His father, Luis Alvarez, a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, suggested measuring the amount of iridium in it. Iridium is extremely rare in the Earth's crust but more common in meteorites, and tiny amounts fall from space at a fairly steady rate, so the quantity in the clay should indicate how long it had taken to build up. To their surprise, the clay contained many times more iridium than expected. Similar results soon came from sites in Denmark and New Zealand.

In 1980, the Alvarezes and two chemists, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, published a bold explanation. They argued that the iridium had come from an asteroid around ten kilometres wide, which had struck the Earth and thrown enormous quantities of dust into the atmosphere. Many palaeontologists were deeply sceptical. For more than a century, geologists had been taught that the Earth changes slowly and gradually, and the idea of a sudden catastrophe from space seemed to belong to science fiction rather than science. There was also an obvious problem: if such an impact had happened, where was the crater?

The answer had, in fact, already been found, although few people knew it. In the late 1970s, geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company had detected a huge circular structure buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula, but their findings received little attention. In 1991, a team of researchers showed that this structure, now known as the Chicxulub crater, was about the right age and size. It is around one hundred and eighty kilometres wide and lies hidden beneath hundreds of metres of younger rock. Grains of shocked quartz, which form only under extreme pressure, and tiny glassy beads created from melted rock were found in boundary layers around the Gulf of Mexico, strengthening the case.

Scientists have since pieced together what probably happened. The impact released more than a billion times the energy of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. Huge tsunamis swept across the surrounding seas, and hot debris thrown into the atmosphere fell back across large parts of the planet, possibly starting widespread fires. Worse still, the asteroid struck rocks rich in sulphur, sending vast amounts of sulphur gases and soot into the upper atmosphere. These blocked sunlight for months or even years, causing global temperatures to fall sharply. Without sunlight, plants and tiny ocean organisms could not grow, and food chains collapsed from the bottom upwards.

Not all scientists accept that the asteroid acted alone. At around the same time, a series of enormous volcanic eruptions was taking place in western India, producing lava flows that today form a region known as the Deccan Traps. Over hundreds of thousands of years, these eruptions released huge quantities of carbon dioxide and sulphur gases, which may have already been disturbing the climate and putting ecosystems under stress before the asteroid arrived. The precise timing of the eruptions is still debated, but many researchers now believe that the impact was the main cause of the extinction, while the volcanoes may have made matters worse.

Just as interesting as the question of why so many species died is the question of why others survived. Survivors tended to be small, which meant they needed less food, and many could shelter from the worst conditions in burrows or in water. Animals with varied diets, able to eat insects, seeds or decaying material, also did better than specialists. Crocodiles, turtles, many small mammals and some birds, probably those living on the ground, all came through the crisis. Life in freshwater was generally less affected than life on land, perhaps because many freshwater food chains depended on dead plant material rather than on living plants.

For the survivors, the disappearance of the dinosaurs created enormous opportunities. Mammals, which had lived alongside dinosaurs for over a hundred million years but had mostly remained small, spread rapidly into the habitats that had been left empty, and within a few million years they had become much larger and more varied. Without this disaster, it is unlikely that humans would ever have evolved. In 2016, an international expedition drilled into the Chicxulub crater itself, recovering rock samples that are helping scientists to understand both the impact and how quickly life returned to the area afterwards.

readingPassages.title: Should we bring back the mammoth?
paragraphs: For most of human history, extinction has been permanent. Once the last member of a species dies, it is gone forever. Recent advances in genetics, however, have led some scientists to suggest that this may no longer be true. The idea of 'de-extinction', bringing extinct species back to life, has moved from science fiction towards the laboratory, and companies and research groups are now working on projects to revive animals such as the woolly mammoth. The question is no longer only whether this can be done, but whether it should be.

The first, and so far only, animal to be brought back from extinction, at least briefly, was the Pyrenean ibex, a wild mountain goat from the border between Spain and France. The last known individual, a female, was killed by a falling tree in 2000, but scientists had already taken and frozen samples of her skin cells. In 2003, they used these cells to produce a clone, which was carried by a goat. The baby ibex was born alive, but it died within minutes because of a serious defect in its lungs. The experiment showed both what might be possible and how difficult it would be.

The best-known project today aims to recreate the woolly mammoth. Most mammoths died out around ten thousand years ago, though a small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until around four thousand years ago. Because mammoth remains have been preserved in frozen ground, scientists have been able to read much of the animal's genetic code. The plan is not to clone a mammoth, since no living cells survive, but to edit the genes of its closest living relative, the Asian elephant, adding mammoth features such as thick hair and a layer of fat to protect against the cold. The result would then need to be carried by an elephant mother, or perhaps one day grown in an artificial womb, and elephant pregnancies last around twenty-two months.

Supporters argue that such animals could benefit the environment. In northern Siberia, the Russian scientist Sergey Zimov has created an area known as Pleistocene Park, where he hopes to show that large grazing animals can turn mossy forest back into grassland. Some researchers suggest that herds of mammoth-like elephants, by trampling snow and knocking down trees, might help to keep the frozen ground below, known as permafrost, from thawing and releasing greenhouse gases. Others have proposed reviving the passenger pigeon, a North American bird whose flocks once numbered in the billions before hunting and forest clearance wiped it out, and whose last member, Martha, died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Similar plans exist for the thylacine, a striped meat-eating marsupial from Tasmania, the last known individual of which died in a zoo in 1936.

Not every extinct animal could be brought back, however. Films may have encouraged the idea that dinosaurs could be recreated from ancient DNA, but this is not possible. DNA breaks down over time, even in ideal conditions. A 2012 study of fossil bones from the moa, a giant extinct bird from New Zealand, estimated that half of the chemical bonds in a DNA sample break down roughly every five hundred years. The oldest DNA ever recovered is around two million years old, while the last non-avian dinosaurs died sixty-six million years ago.

There are also serious scientific doubts about the projects that are possible. An elephant with mammoth genes would not truly be a mammoth, and nobody knows how such an animal would behave without parents of its own kind to learn from. Elephants are highly social animals, and raising a lonely individual in a laboratory raises obvious welfare concerns. Moreover, a revived species would need a suitable habitat, yet the very conditions that caused many extinctions, such as hunting and the loss of habitat, have not gone away.

Some of the techniques being developed may nevertheless help species that are not yet extinct. The northern white rhino, for example, now has only two surviving members, both of them female, and scientists are attempting to use eggs taken from them and frozen sperm from males that have died to produce embryos, which could be carried by a related rhino. Genetic tools might also be used to increase the genetic diversity of small, isolated populations, or to make animals more resistant to disease.

In my view, the strongest argument against de-extinction is a practical one. Conservation budgets are limited, and the money spent on reviving a handful of lost species might achieve far more if it were used to protect the thousands of species that are threatened today. There is also a risk that the promise of de-extinction will make extinction seem less serious, as if any loss could later be reversed. That said, I do not believe that the research should be abandoned. If the technology helps to save animals such as the northern white rhino, it will have been worthwhile, even if no mammoth ever walks the Siberian plains again.

listeningParts.title: Enrolling on a sign language course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a community college to enrol on an evening course in British Sign Language.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good evening, Riverside Community College, Adult Learning. This is Martin. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm interested in your British Sign Language course for beginners. I saw it advertised, and I wanted to find out a bit more before I enrol.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Of course. That's our Level One course. It's for complete beginners, so you don't need any previous experience. By the end, you'll be able to hold simple conversations about everyday topics, like your family, your work and your free time.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds ideal. Can I ask how long it lasts?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: It runs for twenty-four weeks, starting in September, with a break over Christmas. There's one class a week, and each class is two hours long.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And which evening is it on?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: We run two groups. There's one on Monday evenings and one on Thursday evenings. The Monday group is already full, I'm afraid, but there are still a few places left on Thursdays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thursday's fine for me. What time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Classes start at a quarter to seven and finish at a quarter to nine. Most people come straight from work, so we've made it a little later than our other evening courses.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good. And what's the fee?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: The full fee is two hundred and ten pounds. There's a reduced fee of a hundred and forty pounds for students and people receiving certain benefits. Do either of those apply to you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, I'm working full time, so I'll pay the full fee. Does that include the exam?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: It doesn't, unfortunately. At the end of the course there's an assessment, which is optional, and it costs an extra forty-five pounds. If you pass, you get a nationally recognised certificate. Most people do take it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Where are the classes held?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: In the Hartley Building, which is the newer building opposite the main entrance. The room number will be sent to you by email about a week before the course starts.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Is there anything I should buy before the course, a textbook or anything?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: No, you don't need a textbook. The tutor gives out handouts, and there are videos on the college website so you can practise at home. Some people find it useful to practise in front of a mirror, so they can check their hand shapes and facial expressions. In sign language, your face is very important, because expressions show things like questions and emotions.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I didn't know that. That's fascinating.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Can I ask why you're interested in learning? We ask everyone, just for our records.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, a new colleague has just joined my team, and she's deaf. She lip-reads very well, but I'd like to be able to communicate with her properly, and I think it would make her feel more welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: That's a lovely reason. You'll find quite a few people on the course are learning for similar reasons. And the tutor herself is deaf, by the way, so from the very first class, you'll be learning directly from a native signer.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Even better. Can I enrol now?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Certainly. Can I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Aoife Carrick. The surname is C-A-R-R-I-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your date of birth?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The ninth of March, 1994.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And could I ask where you heard about the course?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It was on the radio, actually, on the local station. They had someone talking about deaf awareness week.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: That's good to know. Right, I'll send you a link to pay online, and once that's done, your place is confirmed. You'll get a welcome pack with a guide to fingerspelling, which is the alphabet you make with your hands. It's worth learning it before the first class if you can.

listeningParts.title: A community dialect recording project
listeningParts.contextDescription: A project coordinator talks on local radio about a project to record the dialect of a rural area.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And now I'm joined in the studio by Helen Ward, who's coordinating a new project called Valley Voices. Helen, welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: Thank you. It's lovely to be here.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: So, tell us what the project is about.

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: Well, Valley Voices is an attempt to record the way people in this area speak before it changes beyond recognition. The local dialect has its own words, its own grammar and, of course, its own accent, and a lot of people assume it will always be there. But when we spoke to families, we found that many grandparents use words that their grandchildren simply don't understand. So we're collecting recordings now, while there are still plenty of people who speak the dialect naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Why is it changing so quickly?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: There are several reasons, but the one people mention most often is that young people move away for university or work, and when they come back, their speech has changed. Television and the internet play a part too, but actually the research suggests that face-to-face contact with people from other places has a bigger effect on how we speak than anything we watch.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: That's surprising. So how does the project work?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: We're looking for two kinds of volunteers. First, people who'd like to be recorded. We're especially keen to hear from people over seventy, but we want all ages, because we're interested in how the dialect differs between generations. Each recording session lasts about an hour. We don't ask people to read word lists; we just chat about their memories of school, work and family life, because people speak much more naturally when they're telling a story.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And the second kind of volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: We need people to help with the recordings and, even more importantly, with transcription, which means typing out exactly what's said. It's slow work, and that's where we really need help. One hour of speech can take six or seven hours to transcribe. You don't need any experience, as we'll give you full training.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Where will all this material end up?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: Everything will go into a permanent archive at the county record office, so it's preserved for future generations, and a selection will be available free online, with a map, so you'll be able to click on a village and hear the people who live there. We're also working with local primary schools, and children will be interviewing their own grandparents, which we hope will make them proud of the way their families speak.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: How can people get involved?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: We're running a series of events over the next month. On the fourth, there's an introductory talk at the town library, where I'll explain the project and play some of the recordings we've already made. A week later, we're holding a training day for transcription volunteers at the community centre. That's a full day, and lunch is provided.

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: Then, on the eighteenth, we have what we're calling a word hunt at the farming museum. People bring in old dialect words they remember, and we record them along with their meanings. Last time we did this, someone brought in a list of over two hundred words that her father had written down in the nineteen fifties. And, finally, at the end of the month, we'll have a recording day back at the community centre, where anyone can drop in and be recorded, no appointment needed.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And if people can't make any of those?

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.text: They can still take part. We've set up a page on our website where you can record yourself using a phone or computer, answering a few simple questions. The quality isn't quite as good as in a proper session, but it all helps. We'd also love to hear from people who have old recordings at home, for example cassette tapes of family gatherings, because they give us a picture of how the dialect sounded decades ago.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Helen Ward, thank you very much.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on whistled languages
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two linguistics students, Sofia and Josh, discuss a presentation on whistled languages with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Sofia, Josh, your presentation is on whistled languages. Remind me why you chose the topic.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: Honestly, it started with a video I saw of shepherds on La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, having a conversation across a valley just by whistling. I assumed it was a simple code, like a few signals for 'come here' or 'danger'. But it turns out it's a complete way of speaking Spanish. Almost anything you can say, you can whistle.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: That's the key point we want to make at the start. Whistled languages aren't separate languages. They're a way of transmitting an ordinary spoken language, in this case Spanish, by replacing the voice with a whistle. The whistle copies the changes in pitch and rhythm that are there in normal speech.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Where else are they found?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: In quite a few places, actually. One researcher, Julien Meyer, estimates there are around seventy communities around the world that use or used whistled speech. What they mostly have in common is the landscape: steep mountains or thick forest, where people live and work far apart, and shouting doesn't carry very far.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: A whistle can be heard over several kilometres in the right conditions, much further than a shout. So for farmers or shepherds working on opposite sides of a valley, it saves walking for an hour to deliver a message.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what's happened to Silbo Gomero, the Gomera whistle, in recent times?

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: It nearly died out in the second half of the twentieth century. Roads were built, telephones arrived, and many young people left the island to find work, so there was less need for it. People also started to see it as old-fashioned, something associated with poverty.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: But then the local government took action. Since 1999, it's been a compulsory subject in the island's primary schools, so every child learns at least the basics. And in 2009, UNESCO added it to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity, which gave it a lot of international attention.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Do you think the school programme has been a success?

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: In terms of numbers, definitely. Thousands of children have learned it. But we read some interviews suggesting that many of them only use it at school or for festivals. It's become more of a cultural symbol than a practical tool, because, of course, they all have mobile phones.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a fair point to include. Revival doesn't always mean returning to the original function. What's your second example?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Kuşköy, a village in the mountains near the Black Sea coast of Turkey. The name actually means 'bird village'. People there use whistled Turkish, and in 2017 UNESCO put it on its list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding, because the number of fluent whistlers has fallen sharply.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: And there's a really interesting study connected with Kuşköy. A team led by a German researcher, Onur Güntürkün, tested how people in the village process whistled speech. Normally, we understand language mainly with the left side of the brain. But they found that with whistled Turkish, the two sides of the brain were much more equally involved.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, that was published in 2015, I think. It's a striking result, but be careful how you present it. It was a fairly small study, so don't claim more than the authors did.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Okay, we'll make that clear. We were also planning to include a short audio clip of Silbo Gomero, if that's all right.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Absolutely, audio will make a big difference. Just keep it under a minute, and check the sound in the seminar room beforehand, because the speakers there aren't very good. And I'd like you to finish with a question for the group to discuss, perhaps about whether these languages can survive once their practical purpose has gone.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: That's a great idea. We could link it to other endangered languages too.

listeningParts.title: Pidgins and creoles
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a linguistics course on how new languages are born from contact between peoples.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Much of this course has been about languages disappearing, so today I want to look at the opposite process: how new languages are born. And one of the clearest examples is the development of pidgins and creoles.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with definitions. A pidgin is a simplified form of communication that develops when groups of people who have no language in common need to communicate, usually for a limited purpose, such as trade. Historically, many pidgins grew up around ports, trading posts and plantations. The word pidgin itself is often said to come from the way the English word business was pronounced in Chinese ports, though that explanation isn't certain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A pidgin has two important features. First, most of its vocabulary comes from one dominant language, which linguists call the lexifier. In many cases this was the language of the traders or colonial powers, such as English, French or Portuguese. Second, its grammar is greatly reduced. There are usually no endings on verbs to show tense, and no complicated rules for plurals. And crucially, a pidgin has no native speakers. Everyone who uses it has another first language, and uses the pidgin only when they need to.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Something remarkable happens, though, when a pidgin becomes the main language of a community, and children start to grow up speaking it as their first language. At that point, linguists call it a creole. And in the process, the language changes dramatically. Within a generation or two, it develops a much richer vocabulary and a full, consistent grammar, with ways of marking tense, and of building complex sentences. A creole is a complete language in every sense, capable of expressing anything its speakers need, from jokes to legal arguments.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let me give you some examples. Tok Pisin, spoken in Papua New Guinea, began as a pidgin used on plantations and in trade, but it's now one of the country's official languages and is spoken by millions of people, many of them as a first language. Its vocabulary comes mostly from English, but its grammar is very much its own. Haitian Creole, which is based mainly on French, is spoken by almost the entire population of Haiti, and since 1987 it has been one of the country's two official languages, alongside French.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the best-studied cases is in Hawaii. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, workers arrived on the sugar plantations from China, Japan, Portugal, the Philippines and elsewhere. A pidgin developed so that they could communicate, and the children of these workers turned it into a creole, which is still widely spoken in Hawaii today. The linguist Derek Bickerton, who studied it in detail, argued that children have an inborn ability to create grammar, and that this explains why creoles around the world share many features, even when they developed far apart. That's a controversial theory, and many linguists disagree with it, but it's been very influential.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Some of the strongest evidence for children's role comes from an unexpected place: Nicaragua. Before the late nineteen seventies, deaf children there were mostly isolated at home, using simple gestures with their families. When new schools for deaf children opened in the capital, Managua, hundreds of them were brought together for the first time. The teachers focused on lip-reading Spanish, with little success, but in the playground and on the buses, the children developed their own system of signs. And researchers found that each new group of younger children made the system more complex and more regular. Within a few decades, it had become a full language, now known as Nicaraguan Sign Language.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, a word about attitudes. For a long time, creoles were dismissed as broken or bad versions of European languages, and in many countries children were punished for speaking them at school. Today, linguists recognise them as full languages, and some governments use them in education and the media. But the old prejudices haven't completely disappeared, and that's something we'll come back to next week when we discuss language and identity.

readingPassages.title: The rebirth of Hebrew
paragraphs: Languages that stop being spoken almost never come back. Once a generation of children grows up without hearing a language at home, it usually survives only in books, recordings and the memories of a few elderly speakers. Hebrew is the great exception. For well over a thousand years it was nobody's mother tongue, yet today it is the everyday language of millions of people, used for everything from parliamentary debates to pop songs and text messages. How this happened is one of the most remarkable stories in the history of language.

Hebrew had been the spoken language of the ancient Israelites, but by the early centuries of the Common Era it had largely been replaced in daily life by Aramaic, and later by other languages as Jewish communities spread across the world. It did not disappear, however. It remained the language of prayer, of religious study and of a rich written literature, and educated Jews in different countries could correspond in it. In a sense, it was never dead, but it was a language that people read and wrote rather than one that they spoke at home.

The figure most closely associated with its revival is Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who was born in 1858 in the Russian Empire. Influenced by the national movements of nineteenth-century Europe, he became convinced that the Jewish people needed a shared spoken language, and that it could only be Hebrew. In 1881 he moved to Jerusalem, where he and his wife agreed to speak only Hebrew at home. Their son, born the following year, is often described as the first child in modern times to grow up with Hebrew as his first language. Ben-Yehuda was famously strict: he is said to have tried to stop his son hearing any other language at all.

One obvious problem was that ancient Hebrew had no words for many features of modern life. Ben-Yehuda devoted much of his life to filling these gaps, creating new words, often from ancient roots, and collecting them in a huge dictionary. He could not complete it himself; the final volumes appeared decades after his death in 1922. Among the words credited to him is the Hebrew word for dictionary itself, milon. In 1890 he helped to found the Hebrew Language Committee, which continued the work of creating new vocabulary and became the Academy of the Hebrew Language in 1953.

Historians now stress, however, that the revival was not the achievement of one man. Ben-Yehuda's newspapers and dictionary were important, but the decisive change happened in schools. In the agricultural settlements founded by Jewish immigrants from the 1880s onwards, teachers began to teach all subjects in Hebrew, rather than teaching Hebrew as a separate subject. Children who learned in this way began to use the language with each other in the playground and, eventually, with their own children at home. It was this new generation of native speakers who turned Hebrew into a living language.

The commitment to Hebrew was tested in 1913, in an episode known as the Language War. A new technical college was being established in Haifa, and its organisers, supported by a German Jewish organisation, decided that some subjects would be taught in German, which was then an important language of science. Teachers and students across the country protested and went on strike, arguing that every subject should be taught in Hebrew. The protests succeeded, and when the college finally opened, Hebrew became its language of instruction.

After the First World War, the British authorities who governed Palestine recognised Hebrew as one of the territory's three official languages, alongside English and Arabic, in 1922. When the State of Israel was founded in 1948, Hebrew became the main language of the new country, and an intensive system of language schools was set up to teach it to the hundreds of thousands of immigrants who arrived speaking Arabic, Yiddish, Russian and many other languages. For many of them, Hebrew was the only language they had in common.

Campaigners for other endangered languages have often looked to Hebrew for inspiration, but its circumstances were unusual. The language had never stopped being read and studied, so there was a large body of texts to draw on. Its speakers were immigrants who needed a common language, and many were strongly motivated by a national ideal. Few endangered languages today enjoy all of these advantages. Nevertheless, the story of Hebrew shows that the decline of a language is not always irreversible, and that what happens in classrooms and family homes matters more than anything else.

readingPassages.title: Counting the world's voices
paragraphs: Around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but they are very unevenly shared. A small number of giants, such as Mandarin Chinese, Spanish, English and Hindi, each have hundreds of millions of speakers, and around half of the world's population speaks one of just a couple of dozen languages. At the other extreme, thousands of languages are spoken by communities of a few thousand people or fewer. Diversity is also unevenly spread across the globe: Papua New Guinea alone is home to more than eight hundred languages, while some large European countries have only a handful.

Even counting languages is less straightforward than it sounds, because there is no simple rule for deciding where one language ends and another begins. Linguists often ask whether speakers can understand each other, but this test does not always match how people see themselves. Speakers of Norwegian and Swedish can usually follow each other's speech, yet they are considered separate languages, while the varieties of Chinese known as Mandarin and Cantonese are often called dialects, although their speakers may not understand each other at all. As the linguist Max Weinreich famously remarked, a language is a dialect with an army and a navy.

Languages rarely die because all their speakers die. Far more often, a community gradually shifts to a different language that seems more useful. Parents who want their children to succeed at school or find work in the city may decide to speak to them in the national language rather than their own. In the past, governments often encouraged this directly. In nineteenth-century Wales, for example, some schools punished children for speaking Welsh by making them wear a wooden sign known as the Welsh Not. Within a few generations, a language that was once spoken by everyone can be known only by the elderly.

Researchers have developed several ways of measuring how endangered a language is. UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger places languages in categories ranging from vulnerable to critically endangered. The American sociolinguist Joshua Fishman proposed a scale of eight stages describing how far a language has declined. What these systems share is an emphasis on one factor above all: whether children are still learning the language from their parents. A language with only a few thousand speakers may be perfectly safe if children are acquiring it, while one with a million speakers may be in serious trouble if they are not.

The final stage of decline is often marked by the death of a last native speaker. Ned Maddrell, who died in 1974, is generally regarded as the last person to have spoken Manx, the Celtic language of the Isle of Man, as a first language. In 2008, the death of Marie Smith Jones in Alaska marked the end of Eyak, a language she had helped linguists to record. Such moments attract attention, but by the time they occur, the language has usually been declining for many decades.

How fast is this happening? In 1992, the linguist Michael Krauss warned that as many as ninety per cent of the world's languages might be gone or seriously threatened by the end of the twenty-first century. More recent estimates are less extreme but still worrying. A study led by researchers at the Australian National University, published in 2021, examined fifty-one possible factors and predicted that, without action, around fifteen hundred languages could stop being spoken by the end of this century. Surprisingly, it found that more years of schooling and a higher density of roads were both linked to greater endangerment.

One response has been to record languages before they disappear. Linguists work with speakers to produce dictionaries, grammars and, above all, recordings of everyday speech, stories and songs, which are stored in digital archives. Increasingly, this work is led by communities themselves rather than by outside experts. Smartphones and social media have made it far easier for speakers to record and share their languages, and some communities have produced apps, online courses and even video games in languages with only a few hundred speakers.

Documentation alone, however, does not keep a language alive, and some communities have gone further. On the Isle of Man, a primary school teaching entirely through Manx opened in 2001, and a small number of children are once again growing up with the language. In New Zealand, Māori 'language nests', in which preschool children are cared for entirely in Māori, began in 1982, and a similar movement in Hawaii started the following year. These programmes show that, with enough commitment, the direction of decline can sometimes be reversed.

readingPassages.title: Should every language be saved?
paragraphs: When a language disappears, what exactly is lost? For many linguists, the answer is obvious: something irreplaceable. Each language represents a unique way of organising sounds, words and ideas, developed over thousands of years. Yet the question of whether outsiders should try to prevent languages from dying is more complicated than it first appears, and it has divided scholars for more than three decades. The debate touches not only on science, but on questions of identity, economics and the right of communities to make their own choices.

The modern debate is often traced to 1992, when the American linguist Ken Hale and several colleagues published a set of articles warning of a crisis in the world's languages. Hale, who had worked with Aboriginal communities in Australia and Native American communities in the United States, became one of the most passionate defenders of small languages. In a much-quoted comparison, he said that losing a language was like dropping a bomb on a great museum such as the Louvre. For Hale and his colleagues, linguists had a responsibility not merely to describe endangered languages but to help keep them alive.

Not everyone agreed. In the same year, the British phonetician Peter Ladefoged published a response arguing that linguists should be cautious about telling communities what to do. He described speakers who had chosen to abandon their language because they believed another one would give their children better opportunities, and he argued that it was not the role of a scientist to decide that they were wrong. In my view, Ladefoged's warning remains important. Outsiders, however well-meaning, can easily treat communities as guardians of a museum collection rather than as people with their own needs and ambitions.

Defenders of language preservation offer several kinds of argument. David Crystal, in his book Language Death, published in 2000, set out reasons why the loss of any language should concern everyone, from the value of diversity itself to the role of language in identity and history. The American linguist K. David Harrison has emphasised that small languages often contain detailed knowledge of the natural world, such as names for plants, animals and weather patterns that have no equivalent in the major languages. When the language goes, he argues, this knowledge may go with it, because it has never been written down.

Other researchers have focused on what happens inside communities as a language declines. The American linguist Nancy Dorian, who spent many years studying a dialect of Scottish Gaelic in the north of Scotland, introduced the term 'semi-speakers' for people who understand a language well but speak it only imperfectly. Her work showed that the decline of a language is rarely a simple matter of people speaking it one day and not the next; it is a long, uneven process in which many people are caught somewhere in between, often with feelings of loss or embarrassment.

Perhaps the most practical contribution came from the sociolinguist Joshua Fishman, whose 1991 book Reversing Language Shift argued that the key battleground is the home. Laws, schools and broadcasting can help, he argued, but unless parents pass the language on to their children in everyday family life, it will not survive as a living language. I find this argument persuasive. Too many revival efforts have concentrated on official recognition and signs on public buildings, while the language quietly disappears from kitchens and playgrounds.

It is sometimes claimed that a world with fewer languages would be more peaceful, because people would understand one another more easily. There is little evidence for this. Some of the bloodiest conflicts in history have been fought between people who spoke the same language, and many countries with dozens of languages are entirely peaceful. Nor is there any reason why speaking a small language should prevent someone from also speaking a major one. Most people in the world already speak more than one language, and there is no limit to how many a community can use.

In my view, the right question is not whether every language should be saved, but whether communities that want to keep their languages should be given the means to do so. Many of the languages under threat today are declining not because their speakers freely chose to abandon them, but because of past policies that punished or ridiculed them. Supporting those who want to reverse that damage is not paternalism; it is a matter of fairness. The decision, however, must remain theirs.
