reading.title: Is free will an illusion?
paragraphs: In 1983, the American neuroscientist Benjamin Libet published the results of an experiment that has been debated ever since. Participants were asked to flex their wrist whenever they felt the urge to do so, while watching a special clock and noting the position of a moving dot at the moment they first became aware of the decision to move. At the same time, electrodes on their scalp recorded a pattern of brain activity known as the readiness potential, which was already known to precede voluntary movements. Libet found that the readiness potential began, on average, about a third of a second before participants reported being aware of their decision.

To many commentators, the implication seemed obvious and startling. If the brain begins preparing an action before we are conscious of deciding to act, then our sense of consciously choosing may be an illusion; the real decision, on this view, is made by unconscious brain processes, and conscious awareness merely follows. Later experiments using brain scanning appeared to strengthen this conclusion. In one study, researchers were able to predict, with an accuracy somewhat better than chance, which of two buttons a participant would press up to several seconds before the participant reported making the decision.

Libet himself did not draw such a radical conclusion. He noted that there remained a brief window, around a fifth of a second, between conscious awareness and the movement itself, during which participants could still veto the action. Free will, he suggested, might operate not by initiating actions but by allowing or blocking them, a capacity sometimes described as 'free won't'. Critics have pointed out, though, that if the decision to veto is itself caused by earlier brain activity, this merely moves the problem back a step.

More recent research has challenged the interpretation of the readiness potential itself. In 2012, a team led by Aaron Schurger proposed that the gradual build-up of activity reflects not a decision being made unconsciously, but the random fluctuations of neural activity that occur all the time. In a task where people are asked to move at an arbitrary moment for no reason, they argued, the movement is likely to occur when these fluctuations happen to cross a threshold. Averaged across many trials, this produces a curve that looks like a slow preparation for action, even though no decision was being made in advance. If this is correct, the readiness potential tells us little about when decisions are actually made.

There are also doubts about whether the experiments study the kind of decision that matters. Flexing a wrist at a random moment is a choice with no reasons and no consequences. Most decisions that we care about, such as accepting a job or ending a relationship, involve weighing reasons over hours, days or even months. A study by Uri Maoz and colleagues found that the readiness potential was present when participants made arbitrary choices between two charities, but largely absent when the choice was meaningful because the selected charity would actually receive a donation. It seems unwise, I would suggest, to draw sweeping conclusions about human freedom from laboratory tasks that are so unlike the choices of real life.

Philosophers, meanwhile, point out that the experiments may not address the real question at all. Many philosophers are what is called compatibilists: they argue that free will is compatible with the idea that all events, including our decisions, have prior causes. On this view, an action is free not because it is uncaused, but because it flows from the person's own desires, values and reasoning, rather than from external force or compulsion. Unconscious brain processes are, after all, still processes within the person. For a compatibilist, discovering that decisions begin in neural activity before conscious awareness is no more threatening to freedom than discovering that thoughts are made of neurons.

Does any of this matter outside the laboratory? Some research suggests it might. In one study, participants who read a passage arguing that free will is an illusion subsequently behaved less honestly in a test where cheating was possible than those who read a neutral passage. Although attempts to repeat this finding have produced mixed results, it raises the possibility that how we think about free will may influence how we behave. My own view is that the neuroscience has added valuable detail to our understanding of how actions are produced, but that it has not, so far, settled one of philosophy's oldest questions.

reading.title: The ancient art of finding water
paragraphs: In many of the world's driest regions, people have always faced the same fundamental problem: how to obtain a reliable supply of water in a landscape where rain is scarce and rivers may disappear for much of the year. Over thousands of years, communities developed remarkably sophisticated solutions, many of which are still in use today. These methods were not only ingenious but also sustainable, since they were designed to use water without exhausting the supply on which future generations would depend. One of the most impressive is the qanat, an underground channel that carries water from beneath hills or mountains to settlements and fields sometimes many kilometres away.

Qanats are believed to have been developed in ancient Persia, in what is now Iran, around three thousand years ago. The principle is simple, but building one requires considerable skill. Builders first dig a vertical shaft, known as a mother well, at the foot of a hill to reach the water table, the level below which the ground is saturated with water. They then dig a gently sloping tunnel from the point where the water is needed, back towards the mother well. Because the tunnel slopes downwards very slightly, water flows along it by gravity alone, without the need for pumps. Getting the slope right is critical: if it is too steep, the fast-flowing water will erode the tunnel and may cause it to collapse; if it is too gentle, the water will not flow at all. Builders traditionally used simple tools, such as lamps and plumb lines, to keep the tunnel straight and level underground.

Along the length of the tunnel, a series of vertical shafts is dug at regular intervals, often every twenty to fifty metres. These shafts allow workers to remove the soil as the tunnel is dug, provide fresh air, and give access for cleaning and repairs. From the air, a qanat appears as a line of round mounds stretching across the desert, each one marking the top of a shaft. The longest qanats are more than seventy kilometres long, and some tunnels lie over a hundred metres below the surface at their deepest point.

The advantages of the qanat are considerable. Because the water travels underground, very little is lost to evaporation, which is an enormous benefit in hot, dry climates. The flow is steady throughout the year, as it depends on groundwater rather than on seasonal rainfall. And because qanats do not use pumps, they cannot extract water faster than it is naturally replaced, so they do not exhaust the underground supply. In this sense, they are a model of sustainable water management.

Qanats also shaped the societies that depended on them. Building and maintaining a qanat required the cooperation of the whole community, and complex systems developed to share the water fairly. In some places, each family's share was measured in units of time: a family might be entitled to the full flow of the qanat for a certain number of hours every few days. Specialist diggers, known in Iran as muqannis, passed their skills down from father to son, and their work was highly respected, although it was also dangerous, as tunnels could collapse.

The technology spread far beyond Persia. Similar systems are found across the Middle East and North Africa, where they are known as foggaras in Algeria and khettaras in Morocco, as well as in Central Asia, China and even Spain, where Arab engineers introduced them. In the oasis towns of the Algerian Sahara, foggaras have supported date palm gardens for centuries, and some are still maintained by local communities today.

In the twentieth century, however, many qanats fell into disuse. The introduction of diesel and electric pumps made it possible to extract groundwater from deep wells much more quickly and cheaply. But pumping has often lowered the water table so much that qanats have run dry, and in some regions, groundwater is being used far faster than it can be replaced. In response, there is growing interest in restoring traditional systems. In 2016, eleven Iranian qanats were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, and several countries have launched projects to repair old channels and train a new generation of diggers.

reading.title: Cloud seeding: can we make it rain?
paragraphs: For as long as people have depended on rain, they have tried to influence it, through prayers, rituals and ceremonies. In the twentieth century, scientists began to wonder whether technology could succeed where these methods had failed. The result was cloud seeding, a technique that attempts to increase rainfall or snowfall by adding tiny particles to clouds. Today, more than fifty countries have carried out cloud seeding programmes, and some, such as China and the United Arab Emirates, spend large sums on it every year. Yet after more than seventy years of research and many millions of dollars of investment, scientists still disagree about how well it works.

The basic science behind the technique is well understood. Clouds are made of tiny water droplets, far too small and light to fall as rain. For rain to form, these droplets must grow much larger. In many clouds, especially in cooler regions, this happens when ice crystals form; the crystals grow by attracting moisture from the surrounding droplets, become heavy, and fall, often melting into rain on the way down. However, ice crystals need something to form around, a tiny particle such as dust. In some clouds, there are not enough such particles, so the water remains as liquid droplets even at temperatures well below freezing.

In 1946, scientists working for the General Electric company in the United States discovered that adding particles could trigger this process. One of them, Vincent Schaefer, found that dropping dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, into a cold cloud in the laboratory produced a sudden shower of ice crystals. Shortly afterwards, his colleague Bernard Vonnegut discovered that silver iodide, a chemical whose crystal structure is similar to that of ice, was even more effective. Silver iodide remains the most commonly used seeding material today, released from aircraft or from generators on the ground.

A second approach, used mainly in warm regions, involves seeding clouds with salt particles. These attract water and help droplets to grow by colliding and merging with each other. The United Arab Emirates, one of the driest countries in the world, has invested heavily in this method and has also funded research into new materials, including particles coated with a thin layer of titanium dioxide, which researchers claim are more effective at attracting water.

The difficulty lies in proving that seeding actually makes a difference. Rainfall varies enormously from day to day and from place to place, so if it rains after a cloud has been seeded, it is very hard to know whether it would have rained anyway. To test the effect properly, scientists need to carry out randomised experiments, in which clouds are randomly selected to be seeded or left alone, and the results compared over many years. Such experiments are expensive and time-consuming, often lasting a decade or more, and many early programmes did not follow these methods, so their claims of success are difficult to assess.

Recent research has provided some clearer evidence. In 2017, a project in the mountains of Idaho in the United States used radar to observe clouds as they were seeded. For the first time, researchers were able to watch the seeding material create ice crystals that grew into snow, and to measure the extra snowfall it produced. However, the amount was relatively modest, and the study showed only that seeding can work under particular conditions, not how much additional water it produces over a whole season. Most reviews conclude that seeding can increase precipitation by perhaps five to fifteen per cent in suitable clouds, but that it cannot create rain from clear skies.

Cloud seeding also raises questions beyond science. Silver iodide is toxic in large amounts, though the quantities used in seeding are very small, and most studies have found no harmful effects on the environment. More controversial is the question of who owns the rain. If one region seeds clouds and increases its own rainfall, critics ask, could it reduce rain further downwind, in another region or country? There is little evidence that this happens, but the concern has caused tension in some places. As water shortages become more common with climate change, such questions are likely to become more pressing.

reading.title: Living with floods
paragraphs: For centuries, the dominant approach to flooding in many countries has been to keep water out. Rivers were straightened and confined between high embankments, wetlands were drained for farming and housing, and coastal towns were protected by ever-higher sea walls. This strategy, often described as 'hard engineering', has protected millions of people and allowed cities to grow on land that would otherwise flood regularly. But in recent decades, especially after a series of costly floods in Europe, North America and Asia, a growing number of engineers and planners have argued that it has also created new problems, and that a fundamentally different approach is needed.

One problem is that hard defences can transfer risk rather than remove it. When a river is confined within embankments, the water that would previously have spread across the floodplain is forced downstream more quickly, increasing the danger for communities further along the river. Defences can also create a false sense of security. Because people believe they are protected, more homes and businesses are built in areas at risk, so that when a defence eventually fails or is overtopped by an extreme flood, the damage is far greater than it would otherwise have been. Engineers call this the 'levee effect'.

Climate change is adding to the pressure. Warmer air holds more moisture, which means that heavy rainfall events are becoming more intense in many regions, while rising sea levels increase the risk of coastal flooding. Building defences high enough to cope with every possible future flood would be enormously expensive, and in some places, physically impossible. As a result, many experts now argue that the goal should not be to eliminate flooding altogether, but to reduce its harm and make communities more resilient when it occurs.

The Netherlands, a country where around a quarter of the land lies below sea level, has been at the forefront of this change in thinking. After serious river floods in the 1990s, the Dutch government launched a programme called Room for the River. At more than thirty locations, instead of raising embankments, engineers moved them further back from the river, lowered floodplains, and created side channels that can carry water when river levels are high. In some places, farmers were paid to relocate, and their former land was turned into areas designed to flood safely. The programme was completed in 2015 at a cost of over two billion euros, and it has been widely studied by other countries.

A related idea is often referred to as 'working with nature'. This includes restoring wetlands, which act like sponges, absorbing water during heavy rain and releasing it slowly; planting trees on hillsides to slow the flow of water into rivers; and allowing rivers to return to more natural, winding courses. In the English town of Pickering, which had flooded repeatedly, a project in the surrounding hills built hundreds of small dams from logs and branches, planted thousands of trees and created areas to store floodwater. The town was not flooded during heavy rains in 2015, although some engineers caution that it is difficult to know how much of this was due to the project.

Cities around the world are also being redesigned to cope with water. In Copenhagen, after a severe rainstorm in 2011 caused damage worth hundreds of millions of euros, the city developed a 'cloudburst plan', which includes parks and squares designed to fill with water during heavy storms, and streets that channel water towards the harbour. In China, the government has promoted 'sponge cities', in which green roofs, permeable pavements and urban wetlands are used to absorb rainwater rather than directing it into drains. Such approaches can also bring other benefits, such as more green space and cooler temperatures in summer.

None of this means, however, that hard defences have no place. For dense cities on the coast, such as London or Rotterdam, sea walls and barriers will remain essential. The most effective strategies combine engineering with natural solutions, better planning to avoid building in high-risk areas, and early warning systems that give people time to protect themselves. Accepting that floods will happen, and preparing for them, may ultimately prove more successful than trying to defeat the water entirely.

reading.title: Living with floods
paragraphs: For centuries, the dominant approach to flooding in many countries has been to keep water out. Rivers were straightened and confined between high embankments, wetlands were drained for farming and housing, and coastal towns were protected by ever-higher sea walls. This strategy, often described as 'hard engineering', has protected millions of people and allowed cities to grow on land that would otherwise flood regularly. But in recent decades, especially after a series of costly floods in Europe, North America and Asia, a growing number of engineers and planners have argued that it has also created new problems, and that a fundamentally different approach is needed.

One problem is that hard defences can transfer risk rather than remove it. When a river is confined within embankments, the water that would previously have spread across the floodplain is forced downstream more quickly, increasing the danger for communities further along the river. Defences can also create a false sense of security. Because people believe they are protected, more homes and businesses are built in areas at risk, so that when a defence eventually fails or is overtopped by an extreme flood, the damage is far greater than it would otherwise have been. Engineers call this the 'levee effect'.

Climate change is adding to the pressure. Warmer air holds more moisture, which means that heavy rainfall events are becoming more intense in many regions, while rising sea levels increase the risk of coastal flooding. Building defences high enough to cope with every possible future flood would be enormously expensive, and in some places, physically impossible. As a result, many experts now argue that the goal should not be to eliminate flooding altogether, but to reduce its harm and make communities more resilient when it occurs.

The Netherlands, a country where around a quarter of the land lies below sea level, has been at the forefront of this change in thinking. After serious river floods in the 1990s, the Dutch government launched a programme called Room for the River. At more than thirty locations, instead of raising embankments, engineers moved them further back from the river, lowered floodplains, and created side channels that can carry water when river levels are high. In some places, farmers were paid to relocate, and their former land was turned into areas designed to flood safely. The programme was completed in 2015 at a cost of over two billion euros, and it has been widely studied by other countries.

A related idea is often referred to as 'working with nature'. This includes restoring wetlands, which act like sponges, absorbing water during heavy rain and releasing it slowly; planting trees on hillsides to slow the flow of water into rivers; and allowing rivers to return to more natural, winding courses. In the English town of Pickering, which had flooded repeatedly, a project in the surrounding hills built hundreds of small dams from logs and branches, planted thousands of trees and created areas to store floodwater. The town was not flooded during heavy rains in 2015, although some engineers caution that it is difficult to know how much of this was due to the project.

Cities around the world are also being redesigned to cope with water. In Copenhagen, after a severe rainstorm in 2011 caused damage worth hundreds of millions of euros, the city developed a 'cloudburst plan', which includes parks and squares designed to fill with water during heavy storms, and streets that channel water towards the harbour. In China, the government has promoted 'sponge cities', in which green roofs, permeable pavements and urban wetlands are used to absorb rainwater rather than directing it into drains. Such approaches can also bring other benefits, such as more green space and cooler temperatures in summer.

None of this means, however, that hard defences have no place. For dense cities on the coast, such as London or Rotterdam, sea walls and barriers will remain essential. The most effective strategies combine engineering with natural solutions, better planning to avoid building in high-risk areas, and early warning systems that give people time to protect themselves. Accepting that floods will happen, and preparing for them, may ultimately prove more successful than trying to defeat the water entirely.

reading.title: The bicycle-friendly city
paragraphs: Visitors to Amsterdam or Copenhagen, two of the most bicycle-friendly cities in the world, are often struck by the sight of thousands of cyclists of all ages riding through the city centre: office workers in suits, parents with children in cargo bikes, elderly people doing their shopping. In Copenhagen, around forty per cent of all journeys to work or education are made by bicycle, and in some Dutch cities the proportion is even higher. Many people assume that these high levels of cycling are a natural result of flat terrain or national culture. The history of these cities, however, tells a different story.

In the 1950s and 1960s, the Netherlands and Denmark, like most European countries, were rapidly becoming car-based societies. As incomes rose, car ownership increased dramatically, and planners demolished old neighbourhoods to make room for wide roads and car parks. Cycling declined steeply, and in some cities the number of journeys by bicycle fell by more than half within two decades. In Amsterdam, there were plans to fill in some of the famous canals to create space for traffic, and a motorway was proposed through part of the historic centre. Had these plans been carried out, the cities might look very different today.

The turning point came in the early 1970s. In the Netherlands, the number of people killed in road accidents reached a peak of over three thousand a year, including more than four hundred children. Public anger led to a protest movement called 'Stop de Kindermoord', which means 'Stop the Child Murder'. Protesters held demonstrations, occupied dangerous junctions and organised bicycle rides demanding safer streets. At the same time, the oil crisis of 1973 caused fuel prices to rise sharply, and the Dutch government introduced car-free Sundays to save fuel. Many people discovered that empty streets were pleasant places to cycle and walk.

These events led governments to change direction. Rather than continuing to build for cars, cities began to invest in cycling infrastructure. The most important element was the separated cycle lane, physically divided from traffic by a kerb or a strip of land, so that cyclists did not have to share the road with fast-moving vehicles. Junctions were redesigned so that cyclists could cross safely, often with their own traffic lights that turn green a few seconds before those for cars. In residential areas, streets were redesigned to slow traffic down, and many city centres were closed to through traffic.

Research has shown that safety, and the perception of safety, is the single most important factor in whether people choose to cycle. Surveys in many countries have found that a large proportion of people would like to cycle more, but are deterred by the fear of traffic. When cities build networks of protected lanes, cycling increases rapidly, and the increase is greatest among groups who rarely cycle in car-dominated cities, such as women, children and older people. This has led planners to speak of designing for 'eight to eighty', meaning that streets should be safe enough for anyone between those ages.

Cycling also brings wider benefits. Regular cycling improves physical and mental health, and studies have estimated that the health benefits of cycling in the Netherlands save the country billions of euros each year. Cycling reduces traffic congestion, air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and it takes up far less space than driving: a single car parking space can hold around ten bicycles. Shops in areas with good cycling infrastructure often report higher sales, as cyclists tend to visit local shops more frequently than drivers, even if they spend less on each visit.

In recent years, many other cities have tried to follow the Dutch and Danish example. Paris has built hundreds of kilometres of new cycle lanes and closed a major road along the River Seine to cars. Seville, in southern Spain, built a network of eighty kilometres of protected lanes in just a few years, and cycling increased more than tenfold. However, such changes often face strong opposition at first, particularly from drivers and some businesses who fear losing customers. Experience suggests that opposition usually declines once the new infrastructure is in place and people see the results, but strong political leadership is needed to get through the initial period of resistance.

reading.title: Learning from nature: biomimicry
paragraphs: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral returned from a walk in the mountains with his dog and noticed that both his trousers and the dog's fur were covered in burrs, the small seed cases of the burdock plant. Curious, he examined them under a microscope and saw that each burr was covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops in fabric and fur. It took him several years of experiments, but the result was Velcro, a fastening system made of hooks on one strip and loops on another. De Mestral's invention is one of the best-known examples of biomimicry: the practice of studying nature to solve human design problems.

The idea is not new. Leonardo da Vinci studied the wings of birds and bats when designing flying machines in the fifteenth century. But in recent decades, advances in microscopes and computer modelling have allowed scientists to investigate natural structures in far greater detail, and biomimicry has become an established field. Its supporters point out that living things have been evolving solutions to problems for billions of years, and that many of these solutions are highly efficient, using little energy and producing no waste.

One frequently cited example comes from Japan's high-speed bullet trains. In the 1990s, when trains emerged from tunnels at high speed, they pushed the air in front of them out of the tunnel exit with a loud bang that disturbed residents living nearby. An engineer at the railway company, Eiji Nakatsu, was a keen birdwatcher, and he recalled that the kingfisher dives from the air into water with barely a splash. He and his team redesigned the front of the train to imitate the shape of the kingfisher's long, pointed beak. The new train was not only quieter, but also used about fifteen per cent less electricity and travelled faster.

Buildings have also benefited. The Eastgate Centre, a large office and shopping complex in Harare, Zimbabwe, which opened in 1996, was designed to stay cool without conventional air conditioning. Its architect, Mick Pearce, was inspired by the mounds built by termites, which maintain a remarkably stable temperature inside despite large changes in the outside temperature. The building uses a system of chimneys and vents that draw cool air in at night and release warm air during the day. It uses less than ten per cent of the energy of a conventional building of similar size. Recent research has suggested that termite mounds may actually work rather differently from how scientists originally believed, but the building itself has proved highly successful.

Some of the most promising research involves surfaces. The leaves of the lotus plant stay clean even in muddy water because their surface is covered with microscopic bumps coated in wax, which cause water to form droplets that roll off, carrying dirt with them. This 'lotus effect' has inspired self-cleaning paints, glass and fabrics. Similarly, the skin of sharks is covered with tiny tooth-like scales that reduce drag and also make it difficult for bacteria and algae to attach. Researchers have developed materials with similar patterns for use on ship hulls and on surfaces in hospitals, where they may help to reduce the spread of infection.

Not every attempt has been successful. In 2000, a company released swimsuits inspired by shark skin, claiming they reduced drag. Swimmers wearing similar high-technology suits broke dozens of world records in 2008 and 2009, leading the governing body of the sport to ban them. However, later research suggested that the shark-skin texture itself contributed little to their performance; the main effect came from the tight fabric compressing the swimmer's body. The case illustrates that copying nature successfully requires a precise understanding of how a natural feature actually works.

Critics also warn that biomimicry is sometimes used as a marketing term, applied to products whose connection with nature is superficial. Genuine biomimicry, they argue, involves more than imitating a shape; it means learning from the underlying principles that allow natural systems to function, such as using local materials and energy, recycling everything and adapting to changing conditions. As the biologist Janine Benyus, who popularised the term in the 1990s, has put it, the aim is to ask not what we can take from nature, but what we can learn from it.

Its supporters point out that living things have been evolving solutions to problems for billions of years, and that many of these solutions are highly efficient, using little energy and producing no waste.

Genuine biomimicry, they argue, involves more than imitating a shape; it means learning from the underlying principles that allow natural systems to function, such as using local materials and energy, recycling everything and adapting to changing conditions. As the biologist Janine Benyus, who popularised the term in the 1990s, has put it, the aim is to ask not what we can take from nature, but what we can learn from it.

reading.title: Are driverless cars the future?
paragraphs: For more than a decade, technology companies and car manufacturers have promised that driverless cars are just around the corner. Supporters claim that autonomous vehicles will dramatically reduce road accidents, free people from the stress of driving and transform the design of cities. Some even predicted that, by the early 2020s, most new cars would be able to drive themselves. Yet despite billions of dollars of investment, fully self-driving cars remain rare, operating only in limited areas of a few cities. Understanding why progress has been slower than predicted reveals much about the challenges of introducing complex technology into the real world.

Engineers usually describe vehicle automation in terms of six levels, from zero, meaning no automation, to five, meaning a car that can drive itself anywhere, in any conditions, without a human driver. Many new cars already have features at level one or two, such as systems that keep the car in its lane or maintain a safe distance from the vehicle in front, but the human driver must remain alert and ready to take control at all times. At level four, a car can drive itself without human supervision, but only within a defined area and in certain conditions. Robotaxi services now operating in parts of the United States and China are at this level.

The main argument for autonomous vehicles is improved safety. More than one million people are killed on the world's roads every year, and the great majority of crashes involve human error, such as distraction, tiredness, speeding or drinking alcohol. Computers, by contrast, do not get tired or distracted, and they can monitor their surroundings in all directions at once using cameras, radar and laser sensors. Some early data from robotaxi services suggests that they are involved in fewer injury crashes than human drivers covering similar distances, although the number of miles driven is still too small for firm conclusions.

However, driving turns out to be extraordinarily difficult to automate fully. Real roads are full of unpredictable situations, sometimes called 'edge cases': a police officer directing traffic by hand, a child chasing a ball into the road, roadworks with temporary signs, or a plastic bag blowing across the street, which a computer must distinguish from a solid object. Humans handle such situations by drawing on general knowledge and common sense, abilities that remain very hard to replicate in software. Bad weather presents further problems for the technology, as heavy rain, snow and fog can interfere with sensors.

There are also difficult legal and ethical questions about responsibility. When a human driver causes an accident, the law is relatively clear about who is to blame. But if a driverless car crashes, should responsibility lie with the owner, the manufacturer or the company that wrote the software? Several high-profile accidents involving partially automated cars have shown that drivers often place too much trust in the technology and stop paying attention, even when they are supposed to be supervising. Some experts argue that partial automation may therefore be more dangerous than either full automation or none at all.

The long-term effects on cities are also uncertain. Optimists imagine shared fleets of driverless taxis reducing the need for private car ownership, freeing up land currently used for parking and making transport available to people who cannot drive, such as the elderly and disabled. Pessimists point out that if travelling by car becomes more comfortable and convenient, people may make more and longer journeys, increasing congestion, and that empty vehicles circulating between passengers could add to traffic. Driverless technology could also threaten the livelihoods of millions of professional drivers around the world, including those of taxi, bus and lorry drivers, many of whom have few alternative sources of employment.

In my view, the most likely outcome is gradual change rather than a sudden revolution, much as electric cars took decades to move from experiments to everyday use. Autonomous vehicles may first become common in controlled environments, such as motorways, ports and mining sites, and in particular cities with good weather and well-maintained roads. How they ultimately affect our lives will depend less on the technology itself than on the decisions that governments and societies make about how it is used.

reading.title: Salt: the mineral that shaped history
paragraphs: Today, salt is so cheap and so easy to find that most people never think about it. A packet costs very little in any supermarket, and it is added to almost every kind of processed food. Yet for most of human history, salt was a precious and sometimes expensive substance. Wars were fought over it, cities grew rich from it, and governments relied on it to raise money. Its story tells us a great deal about the relationship between food, trade and power.

Humans need salt to survive. The sodium it contains helps the body control the balance of water in its cells and allows nerves and muscles to work properly. Early hunters obtained enough salt from the meat they ate, but when people began farming around ten thousand years ago and their diet became based on grain, they needed to find other sources. Farm animals also needed salt, and so did one of the most important food technologies of the ancient world: preservation. Before refrigeration, salting was one of the main ways of keeping meat and fish from going bad, because salt draws water out of food and prevents bacteria from growing.

There are three main ways of obtaining salt. The simplest is to let seawater evaporate in shallow pools in the sun, a method that is still used in many hot countries. Where the climate is too cool or wet, people boiled salty water over fires, which required large amounts of wood. The third method is to dig rock salt from underground deposits left behind by ancient seas. The Wieliczka mine near Kraków in Poland was worked for more than seven hundred years, and its miners carved whole chapels, complete with statues and chandeliers, out of the salt itself.

Because salt was essential but found only in certain places, it became one of the first goods to be traded over long distances. In West Africa, camel caravans carried slabs of salt across the Sahara from mines in the desert to markets in cities such as Timbuktu, where it was exchanged for gold. In Europe, a road called the Via Salaria, or Salt Road, was one of the oldest routes into Rome. Many towns in Europe owe their wealth, and sometimes their names, to salt; the German city of Salzburg, for example, means 'salt castle'.

Governments soon realised that taxing salt was an effective way of raising money, since everyone needed it and it was difficult to avoid paying. In ancient China, the state controlled the production and sale of salt for more than two thousand years, and salt taxes paid for armies and for building projects such as parts of the Great Wall. In France, a hated salt tax called the gabelle forced people to buy a fixed amount of salt each year at a price set by the government. It was one of the causes of anger against the monarchy that led to the French Revolution in 1789.

Perhaps the most famous protest against a salt tax took place in India in 1930. Under British rule, Indians were forbidden to collect or sell salt themselves and had to pay a tax on salt sold by the government. Mahatma Gandhi led a march of around three hundred and eighty kilometres to the coast at Dandi, where he picked up a handful of natural salt in defiance of the law. Thousands of people followed his example, and more than sixty thousand were arrested. The Salt March became an important moment in the movement for Indian independence.

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, new methods of mining and transport made salt cheap and plentiful, and the invention of refrigeration meant it was no longer needed so much for preservation. Today, the largest single use of salt is not in food at all, but in the chemical industry, where it is used to produce chlorine and other substances. In cold countries, large quantities are also spread on roads in winter to melt ice.

Ironically, the problem today is not too little salt but too much. Health experts recommend that adults eat no more than five grams of salt a day, about one teaspoon, but in many countries the average is nearly twice that. Most of it comes not from the salt people add at the table but from processed foods such as bread, cheese, ready meals and snacks. Eating too much salt is linked to high blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Several countries, including the United Kingdom, have persuaded food manufacturers to reduce gradually the amount of salt in their products, and in some cases these reductions have been large enough to lower average blood pressure across the population.

reading.title: Friendly bacteria: the science of fermentation
paragraphs: Bread, cheese, yoghurt, soy sauce and chocolate may not seem to have much in common, but they all depend on the same process: fermentation. In fermentation, microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds break down sugars and other substances in food, producing acids, gases or alcohol. Humans have used this process for thousands of years, long before anyone knew that microorganisms existed, and today fermented foods make up around a third of everything people eat.

The oldest evidence of fermentation comes from China, where traces of a drink made from rice, honey and fruit have been found on pottery around nine thousand years old. In ancient Egypt, workers who built the pyramids were paid partly in bread and beer. Fermentation spread to almost every culture, and each developed its own traditions, from Korean kimchi, made from cabbage and chilli, to sauerkraut in Germany and injera, a spongy flatbread eaten in Ethiopia. In many of these cultures, fermentation was carried out in the home, and recipes and techniques were passed down from one generation to the next, often by women. Families sometimes kept the same culture of microorganisms alive for decades, feeding it regularly with fresh flour or milk, and some bakeries today still use sourdough starters that are said to be more than a century old.

Before the invention of refrigerators, the main reason for fermenting food was to preserve it. The acids and alcohol produced during fermentation make it difficult for harmful bacteria to grow. Milk, for example, goes bad within a few days, but when it is turned into cheese, it can be kept for months or even years. Similarly, cabbage that would rot quickly can last through the winter as sauerkraut. For communities that depended on harvests at particular times of year, this could make the difference between eating well and going hungry.

Fermentation also changes the taste and texture of food, often in ways people find very appealing. When yeast ferments the sugars in bread dough, it produces carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles and makes the bread rise. In yoghurt, bacteria turn the sugar in milk into lactic acid, which gives yoghurt its sour taste and thick texture. Many of the complex flavours of foods like cheese, soy sauce and coffee are created during fermentation.

Scientists did not understand what caused fermentation until the nineteenth century. In the 1850s, the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that it was carried out by living microorganisms. He was asked to investigate why some batches of wine and beer were going sour, and discovered that this happened when the wrong microorganisms were present. His work led to the process of pasteurisation, in which liquids are heated to kill unwanted microbes, and laid the foundation for modern microbiology.

In recent years, fermented foods have become increasingly fashionable, partly because of claims about their health benefits. Some fermented foods contain live bacteria, known as probiotics, which may help to support the community of microorganisms that lives in our digestive system. Research suggests that these gut bacteria play an important role not only in digestion but also in the immune system. A study at Stanford University in 2021 found that people who ate fermented foods every day for ten weeks had a greater variety of gut bacteria and lower levels of inflammation.

However, scientists warn that many claims are exaggerated. Not all fermented foods contain live bacteria; bread, for example, is baked at high temperatures, which kills the yeast, and many shop-bought products are pasteurised after fermentation. In addition, the effects of probiotics vary between individuals, and much of the research has been carried out on small groups of people over short periods. Experts generally agree that fermented foods can be part of a healthy diet, but that they are not a cure for illness.

Fermentation is also being used in new ways. Companies are using microorganisms to produce proteins found in milk and eggs without using animals, a technique called precision fermentation. The microbes are given the genetic instructions to make a particular protein and grown in large steel tanks, rather like those used for brewing beer. Supporters say this could reduce the environmental impact of farming, though the products are currently expensive. An ancient technique, it seems, may help to shape the future of food.

Experts generally agree that fermented foods can be part of a healthy diet, but that they are not a cure for illness.

reading.title: The problem of food waste
paragraphs: Every year, around a third of all the food produced in the world is lost or wasted. According to estimates by the United Nations, this amounts to more than one billion tonnes of food, enough to feed hundreds of millions of people. At the same time, around seven hundred million people regularly do not have enough to eat. Food waste is therefore not only an economic problem but also a moral one, and in my view it deserves far more public attention than it currently receives.

Food waste also has serious environmental consequences. Growing, transporting and storing food uses large amounts of land, water and energy, all of which are wasted when the food is thrown away. When food rots in landfill sites, it produces methane, a gas that warms the atmosphere much more powerfully than carbon dioxide. It has been calculated that if food waste were a country, it would be the third largest producer of greenhouse gases in the world, after China and the United States.

Where does the waste happen? The answer depends on the country. In poorer countries, most food is lost before it reaches consumers, because of poor storage, a lack of refrigeration and difficult transport. Grain may be eaten by insects or rats, and fruit and vegetables may rot before they can reach markets. In richer countries, by contrast, the largest share of waste occurs in shops, restaurants and, above all, people's homes. In the United Kingdom, for example, the charity WRAP has estimated that households are responsible for around sixty per cent of all food waste.

Researchers have identified several reasons why households waste so much food. People often buy more than they need, encouraged by special offers, and then fail to use it before it goes bad. Confusion about date labels is another important factor. In many countries, food carries both 'best before' dates, which refer to quality, and 'use by' dates, which refer to safety. Many people do not understand the difference and throw away food that is perfectly safe to eat simply because the best before date has passed.

Supermarkets have also been criticised for contributing to waste. Fruit and vegetables that are the wrong shape or size are often rejected before they even reach the shops, because retailers believe customers will not buy them. Some studies have found that up to a third of a farmer's crop can be left in the field or used as animal feed for this reason. In response, several supermarkets now sell 'wonky' vegetables at lower prices, although critics say these schemes are too small to make a real difference.

Some governments have introduced laws to tackle the problem. In 2016, France became the first country to ban large supermarkets from throwing away or destroying unsold food that was still edible. Instead, they must donate it to charities or use it for animal feed or compost. Italy introduced a similar law the same year, but chose to use tax incentives to encourage donations rather than fines. South Korea has taken a different approach, requiring households to pay for their food waste by weight, using special bags or electronic bins that read residents' identity cards. Since the scheme was introduced, the amount of food waste has fallen considerably, and much of what remains is turned into animal feed or fertiliser.

Technology is also playing a role. Mobile phone apps allow restaurants and shops to sell surplus food cheaply at the end of the day, or enable neighbours to share food they do not need. Researchers are developing packaging that changes colour as food begins to go off, which could give consumers more accurate information than printed dates. Some companies are even turning food waste into new products, such as using unsold bread to brew beer. Others turn fruit peel and coffee grounds into fuel, cosmetics or fertiliser.

However, I would argue that technology and legislation can only go so far. Ultimately, reducing food waste requires changes in people's everyday habits: planning meals, buying only what is needed, storing food properly and using leftovers creatively. Previous generations, who had experienced shortages and rationing during wartime, often regarded wasting food as unacceptable. Rediscovering some of that attitude may be the most effective solution of all.

reading.title: The children's garden: the invention of kindergarten
paragraphs: Today, it is taken for granted in most countries that young children should spend time in some form of early education before they start school. Yet the idea that children under the age of six could benefit from organised learning is relatively recent. One of the most important figures in its development was a German teacher named Friedrich Froebel, who opened the first kindergarten in 1837 and gave the institution its name, which means 'children's garden'.

Froebel was born in 1782 in a small village in Thuringia, in central Germany. His mother died when he was a baby, and he later described his childhood as lonely and unhappy. He spent much of his time alone in the countryside, developing a deep love of nature that would influence all his later work. As a young man, he studied a range of subjects, including mathematics, architecture and mineralogy, before discovering his talent for teaching while working at a school in Frankfurt. He later said that he had felt from his first lesson as though he had at last found his true calling, and that he never seriously considered any other career afterwards.

At the time, most schools relied heavily on memorisation and strict discipline. Children were expected to sit still, repeat what the teacher said and learn by heart. Froebel was strongly influenced by the Swiss educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi, with whom he worked for two years, and who believed that education should develop the whole child, including the hands and the heart as well as the head. Froebel went further, arguing that young children learn best through play, which he described as the highest expression of human development in childhood.

To put his ideas into practice, Froebel designed a series of educational toys, which he called 'gifts'. The first gift was a set of six soft woollen balls in different colours. Later gifts included wooden cubes, cylinders and blocks that could be combined to build shapes and patterns. Through playing with these objects, children were meant to discover basic ideas of form, number and balance for themselves. He also developed 'occupations', such as paper folding, weaving, sewing and modelling with clay, as well as songs and movement games.

Gardens were central to Froebel's vision. In his kindergartens, each child had a small plot of land to look after, as well as a shared garden for the whole group. He believed that caring for plants would teach children patience and responsibility, and help them understand the natural world. The name kindergarten reflected his belief that children, like plants, need the right conditions in order to grow, and that the teacher's role was rather like that of a gardener, providing care and support rather than forcing development.

Froebel's ideas were controversial in his own lifetime. In 1851, the Prussian government banned kindergartens, apparently because officials confused Froebel with his nephew, Karl Froebel, who had written books with radical political and religious views. The ban lasted until 1860, by which time Froebel had died. Ironically, the ban helped to spread his ideas abroad, as many of his followers, a large number of them women, left Germany and opened kindergartens in other countries.

One of these followers, Margarethe Schurz, opened the first kindergarten in the United States in 1856, in Watertown, Wisconsin. It was taught in German, for the children of German immigrants. The first English-language kindergarten in the country was opened in Boston in 1860 by Elizabeth Peabody, who became one of the movement's most energetic supporters. By the end of the nineteenth century, kindergartens had been established in cities across Europe, North America and Japan, and in many places they became part of the public school system. Training colleges for kindergarten teachers were also set up, and for many women at the time, teaching young children offered one of the few respectable careers available to them outside the home.

Several important architects, including Frank Lloyd Wright, said that playing with Froebel's blocks as a child had shaped their understanding of space and form. reading.title: The marshmallow test revisited
paragraphs: In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel began a series of experiments at a nursery school at Stanford University in California that would become some of the most famous in the history of psychology. Children aged between three and five were taken into a room and offered a treat, often a marshmallow. They were told that they could eat it immediately, or, if they waited until the researcher returned, they would receive two treats instead. The researcher then left the room for up to fifteen minutes, and the children were observed through a one-way mirror.

The children's responses varied widely. Some ate the marshmallow as soon as the door closed. Others tried to resist but gave in after a few minutes. Around a third managed to wait the full time and received the second treat. Mischel and his colleagues were particularly interested in the strategies the successful children used. Many covered their eyes, turned away from the table, sang to themselves or kicked the desk. Some invented games. The children who did least well tended to stare at the marshmallow, touch it or even smell it.

The experiment might have remained a minor study of self-control had it not been for a coincidence. Mischel's own daughters attended the same nursery school, and as they grew older, he began to ask them casually how their former classmates were getting on. He noticed what seemed to be a pattern: the children who had waited longest appeared to be doing better at school. This led him to contact the original participants years later, when they were teenagers, and to collect information about their academic achievement and behaviour.

The follow-up studies, published in the late 1980s and 1990, produced striking results. Children who had waited longer as preschoolers were described by their parents as more competent and better able to cope with stress as adolescents, and they had higher scores on the SAT, the test used for university admission in the United States. Later studies even suggested that they had healthier body weights as adults. The findings were widely reported, and the marshmallow test became a symbol of the idea that self-control in early childhood can predict success in life.

This idea had a powerful influence on education. Schools and parenting books promoted programmes designed to teach young children to delay gratification, on the assumption that improving self-control would lead to better outcomes later. The message often given to the public was simple: if you can teach your child to resist the marshmallow, you are setting them up for success.

However, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts at New York University published a study that challenged this interpretation. They repeated the experiment with more than nine hundred children, a much larger and more varied group than Mischel's, whose original participants had mostly been the children of Stanford University staff. Watts and his colleagues found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was only about half as strong as in the original studies. More importantly, once they took into account factors such as the family's income and the mother's level of education, the link almost disappeared.

This suggests that the ability to wait may be, at least partly, a reflection of children's circumstances rather than a fixed personal quality. Other research supports this view. In a 2012 study at the University of Rochester, children were first promised better art materials by a researcher. In one group, the researcher kept the promise; in the other, he did not. When the marshmallow test followed, children who had experienced a reliable adult waited around four times longer than those who had not. For a child who has learned that promises are often broken, or that food may be taken by others, eating the marshmallow immediately may be a perfectly rational choice.

Mischel himself, who died in 2018, always argued that self-control was not fixed and could be learned, and that the most important finding was not who waited, but how children managed to do so. Nevertheless, the revised findings suggest that teaching children individual strategies is unlikely, on its own, to have dramatic long-term effects. Improving the stability and resources of children's environments may matter just as much, if not more.

Mischel's own daughters attended the same nursery school, and as they grew older, he began to ask them casually how their former classmates were getting on. He noticed what seemed to be a pattern: the children who had waited longest appeared to be doing better at school. This led him to contact the original participants years later, when they were teenagers, and to collect information about their academic achievement and behaviour.

The follow-up studies, published in the late 1980s and 1990, produced striking results. Children who had waited longer as preschoolers were described by their parents as more competent and better able to cope with stress as adolescents, and they had higher scores on the SAT, the test used for university admission in the United States. Later studies even suggested that they had healthier body weights as adults. The findings were widely reported, and the marshmallow test became a symbol of the idea that self-control in early childhood can predict success in life.

This idea had a powerful influence on education. Schools and parenting books promoted programmes designed to teach young children to delay gratification, on the assumption that improving self-control would lead to better outcomes later. The message often given to the public was simple: if you can teach your child to resist the marshmallow, you are setting them up for success.

However, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts at New York University published a study that challenged this interpretation. They repeated the experiment with more than nine hundred children, a much larger and more varied group than Mischel's, whose original participants had mostly been the children of Stanford University staff. Watts and his colleagues found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was only about half as strong as in the original studies. More importantly, once they took into account factors such as the family's income and the mother's level of education, the link almost disappeared.

This suggests that the ability to wait may be, at least partly, a reflection of children's circumstances rather than a fixed personal quality. Other research supports this view. In a 2012 study at the University of Rochester, children were first promised better art materials by a researcher. In one group, the researcher kept the promise; in the other, he did not. Mischel himself, who died in 2018, always argued that self-control was not fixed and could be learned, and that the most important finding was not who waited, but how children managed to do so. Nevertheless, the revised findings suggest that teaching children individual strategies is unlikely, on its own, to have dramatic long-term effects. Improving the stability and resources of children's environments may matter just as much, if not more.

reading.title: Is homework worth it?
paragraphs: Few aspects of school life cause as much argument as homework. For many parents, it is a sign that a school takes learning seriously; for others, it is a source of stress that takes away family time and leads to battles at the kitchen table. Teachers, too, are divided. Some see it as essential practice, while others regard it as a burden that widens the gap between children from different backgrounds. The research evidence, as is often the case in education, is more complicated than either side would like.

Homework has been controversial for more than a century. In the early twentieth century, some American doctors and journalists claimed that homework damaged children's health by depriving them of fresh air, exercise and sleep. In 1901, the state of California passed a law banning homework for children under the age of fifteen, although it was later repealed. Attitudes changed after 1957, when the Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik, and Americans worried that their children were falling behind. Homework was promoted as a way of raising standards, and the amount set increased.

The most widely cited research on the subject is by Harris Cooper of Duke University, who has reviewed hundreds of studies. His conclusion is that the effect of homework depends strongly on the age of the student. For secondary school students, there is a clear positive relationship between homework and achievement, up to a point. Beyond around two hours a night, however, the benefits disappear and may even reverse. For primary school children, Cooper found little evidence that homework improves academic achievement at all.

Why should age make such a difference? One explanation is that younger children are less able to study independently and to concentrate on tasks without help. They are also more easily distracted, and their parents may become heavily involved, sometimes in ways that are unhelpful. It is also possible that much of the homework given to young children is not well designed. Cooper himself does not recommend abolishing homework for primary pupils, however. He argues that short, simple tasks, such as reading for pleasure, can help children develop good study habits and show parents what their children are learning.

International comparisons add another dimension to the debate. Data from the OECD's PISA tests, which assess fifteen-year-olds around the world, show that students in countries such as Finland, which consistently perform well, do relatively little homework, whereas students in some lower-performing countries do a great deal. Yet within individual countries, students who do more homework tend to score higher. In my view, this suggests that the quality of teaching in school matters far more than the quantity of work done at home.

A particular concern is the effect of homework on inequality. Children from wealthier families are more likely to have a quiet place to study, access to a computer and the internet, and parents who have the time and education to help them. Children from poorer families may share a crowded room, have caring responsibilities or part-time jobs, or simply lack support. Homework may therefore reward advantages that have nothing to do with ability or effort. Some schools have responded by setting up homework clubs, where students can work after the school day with access to resources and staff.

There is also growing concern about the effect of homework on well-being. A study of students at high-achieving schools in California by Denise Pope of Stanford University found that many students did more than three hours of homework a night and reported high levels of stress, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and a lack of balance in their lives. Pope does not argue that homework should be abolished, but she believes that much of it is set out of habit rather than for a clear purpose.

What, then, makes homework worthwhile? Most researchers agree that it should be purposeful, clearly linked to what is being taught in class, appropriate to the student's age and not excessive. Feedback matters too; homework that is never marked or discussed is unlikely to be taken seriously. Some schools have experimented with giving students choices about their homework, or with 'flipped learning', in which students watch short videos at home and then use class time for practice. These approaches deserve to be studied more carefully, but they suggest that the question is not simply whether to set homework, but how.

reading.title: The builders of the Gothic cathedrals
paragraphs: Between the twelfth and the sixteenth centuries, the towns and cities of Europe built some of the most ambitious structures the world had ever seen. The great Gothic cathedrals of France, England, Germany and Spain, with their soaring stone vaults, pointed arches and enormous stained-glass windows, still impress visitors today. What makes them even more remarkable is that they were designed and built without modern mathematics, engineering calculations or machinery.

The Gothic style is usually said to have begun in the 1140s, with the rebuilding of the abbey church of Saint-Denis, just north of Paris. Its abbot, Suger, wanted a church filled with light, which he believed was a reflection of the divine. The builders achieved this by combining several existing techniques in a new way. Pointed arches, which had been used earlier in the Islamic world, direct the weight of a building downwards more efficiently than the round arches used before, allowing walls to be higher and thinner. Ribbed vaults, a framework of stone ribs supporting the ceiling, concentrated the weight onto a small number of points rather than spreading it along the whole wall.

The most distinctive feature of Gothic architecture, however, is the flying buttress. This is an external arch that carries the outward push of the vault away from the wall and down to a heavy pier standing outside the building. Because the walls no longer had to support all the weight of the roof, large parts of them could be replaced with glass. At Chartres Cathedral, completed in the thirteenth century, more than one hundred and fifty stained-glass windows survive, many of them original.

The person in charge of building a cathedral was the master mason, who acted as both architect and engineer. Master masons usually began as apprentices, learning their craft over many years on building sites. They did not use mathematical formulas to calculate the forces in a structure. Instead, they relied on rules of proportion based on geometry, which were passed down from one generation to the next and often kept secret. Drawings were sometimes scratched into the plaster floors of special tracing rooms, some of which still survive, for example at York Minster in England. Because of this system of training, the same master mason might work on several cathedrals during his career, carrying ideas and techniques from one region to another.

Building a cathedral was an enormous undertaking. Stone had to be cut in quarries, sometimes many kilometres away, and transported by cart or, wherever possible, by river, which was much cheaper. Some cathedrals even owned their own quarries, and the stones were often roughly shaped there before transport, to reduce their weight. Hundreds of workers were needed, including masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, glaziers and labourers. Huge wooden cranes, powered by men walking inside large wheels, lifted the stones into place. Construction often took several generations, and many workers who began a cathedral never saw it finished. Cologne Cathedral in Germany, begun in 1248, was not completed until 1880, after work had stopped for several centuries.

Not every project succeeded. The builders were constantly trying to make cathedrals taller and lighter, and sometimes they went too far. The most famous failure is Beauvais Cathedral in northern France, which was planned to be the tallest in Europe. In 1284, part of its vault, which rose to around forty-eight metres, collapsed. It was rebuilt with extra supports, but the cathedral was never finished, and only the eastern part stands today.

Paying for such buildings was a continuous challenge. Money came from bishops, kings and nobles, but also from ordinary people. Towns competed with each other to build the most impressive cathedral, which brought prestige and attracted pilgrims, who in turn brought money. Some churches encouraged donations by displaying holy relics, such as the remains of saints, and guilds of craftsmen sometimes paid for individual windows, which often show scenes of their members at work.

Gothic cathedrals continue to raise questions for engineers and conservators. When fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame in Paris in April 2019, the stone vaults below largely survived and protected much of the interior. The cathedral reopened in December 2024 after a restoration in which craftspeople used many of the same traditional techniques, including cutting oak beams by hand, that medieval builders had used eight hundred years earlier.

reading.title: How the skyscraper was born
paragraphs: Today, skyscrapers dominate the skylines of cities from New York to Shanghai, and the tallest, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, rises to more than eight hundred metres. Yet for most of history, buildings of more than five or six storeys were rare. Two practical problems stood in the way: how to get people to the upper floors, and how to build walls strong enough to support great height. The solution to both emerged in the United States in the second half of the nineteenth century.

The first problem was solved by the passenger lift, or elevator. Lifting devices had existed for centuries, but people were reluctant to travel in them because of the danger that the rope might break. In 1854, at an exhibition in New York, an American mechanic named Elisha Otis gave a dramatic demonstration. Standing on a raised platform in front of a crowd, he ordered the rope holding it to be cut. Instead of falling, the platform stopped almost immediately, held by a safety device that gripped the sides of the shaft. The first passenger lift using his system was installed in a New York shop three years later.

The second problem was structural. In traditional buildings, the outer walls carry the weight of the floors above. The taller the building, the thicker the walls at the bottom must be. The Monadnock Building in Chicago, completed in 1891, was sixteen storeys high and built with load-bearing brick walls, which were almost two metres thick at ground level. This took up valuable space and reduced the size of the windows, making it clear that this method had reached its practical limit.

The answer was to build a frame of iron and, later, steel, which carried the weight of the building, so that the outer walls became little more than a covering. The building often described as the first skyscraper, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, used this principle. Designed by William Le Baron Jenney and completed in 1885, it was originally ten storeys high. Its metal frame made it far lighter than a stone building of the same size, and some historians report that city officials were so worried it would fall down that they temporarily stopped work while they investigated.

Chicago was a natural place for such experiments. In 1871, a huge fire had destroyed much of the city centre, creating a need for rapid rebuilding. At the same time, the city's population and economy were growing quickly, and land in the business district was extremely expensive. Building upwards allowed developers to make the most of small and costly plots. A group of architects who worked there, later known as the Chicago School, developed a style that expressed the frame of the building, with large windows and little decoration.

New York soon became the centre of skyscraper construction, and the race for height began. The Woolworth Building, completed in 1913, was the tallest in the world for over fifteen years. In 1931, the Empire State Building, with one hundred and two storeys, was completed in just over a year, an astonishingly rapid achievement. It remained the world's tallest building for nearly forty years. The increasing number of tall buildings led to concerns that streets were becoming dark canyons, and in 1916 New York introduced rules requiring tall buildings to step back as they rose, so that light could reach the ground.

Height brought other challenges. Wind becomes a major force on tall buildings, and engineers must ensure that they do not sway enough to make occupants uncomfortable. Some modern skyscrapers contain huge weights, called tuned mass dampers, near the top, which move to counteract the building's movement. Taipei 101 in Taiwan has a steel ball weighing over six hundred tonnes that visitors can see. Fire safety and evacuation are also more complex in buildings where people may be hundreds of metres above the ground.

Skyscrapers remain controversial. Supporters argue that they allow cities to house and employ large numbers of people on limited land, reducing the need for long commutes. Critics reply that very tall buildings are expensive to build and maintain, use large amounts of energy and can create windy, unwelcoming spaces at street level. Many urban planners now argue that medium-rise buildings of six to ten storeys can achieve high density while creating more pleasant streets.

reading.title: Building tall with wood
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, steel and concrete were the obvious materials for any large building. Wood was considered suitable for houses and small structures, but too weak, too likely to burn and too unpredictable for anything bigger. In recent years, however, a growing number of architects and engineers have begun to challenge this view. Around the world, buildings of ten, twenty and even more storeys are now being constructed largely from timber, and supporters claim that wood could play a major role in reducing the environmental impact of construction.

The key to this change is a group of products known as engineered timber, or mass timber. The best known is cross-laminated timber, or CLT, which was developed in Austria and Germany in the 1990s. It is made by gluing layers of wooden boards together, with the grain of each layer running at right angles to the one below. This produces large, solid panels that are strong in both directions and far more stable than ordinary timber, which tends to bend or split along the grain. Another product, glued laminated timber, or glulam, is used to make beams and columns.

The environmental argument for timber is a powerful one. The production of cement and steel together accounts for a large share of global carbon dioxide emissions. Trees, by contrast, absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, and much of this carbon remains stored in the wood for as long as the building stands. If the trees are replaced by new planting, timber can therefore be a renewable material with a much lower carbon footprint. Some studies have found that a mass timber building can produce significantly lower emissions than an equivalent concrete building, although the results depend on how the forests are managed and on what happens to the wood at the end of the building's life.

There are practical advantages too. Mass timber panels are manufactured in factories to precise measurements and then delivered to the site, where they can be assembled quickly with relatively small teams of workers. Construction sites are therefore quieter, cleaner and less disruptive for neighbours. Timber is also much lighter than concrete, which means that smaller foundations are needed, a particular advantage on sites with weak ground or where new floors are being added to existing buildings.

The most obvious concern is fire. Yet engineers point out that large timber elements behave very differently from the thin pieces of wood used in a campfire. When a thick timber beam burns, the outer layer turns to charcoal, which protects the wood inside and slows the spread of fire, allowing the beam to keep its strength for a predictable time. Steel, by contrast, can lose its strength suddenly at high temperatures. Mass timber buildings must nevertheless pass the same fire safety tests as other buildings, and they are usually fitted with sprinklers, while the timber is often partly covered with fire-resistant boards.

The race for height has already begun. In 2019, an eighteen-storey building called Mjøstårnet, in the Norwegian town of Brumunddal, became the world's tallest timber building, at just over eighty-five metres. It was overtaken in 2022 by Ascent, a twenty-five-storey apartment building in Milwaukee in the United States, which combines timber with a concrete core. Architects have proposed far taller wooden towers, including designs of more than three hundred metres, though none has yet been built.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics argue that if demand for timber increases greatly, it could put pressure on forests, encouraging the replacement of natural forests with plantations of a single species, which support far less wildlife. Others point out that the claimed environmental benefits rely on assumptions about forestry and recycling that may not always hold true. There are also concerns about the effects of moisture, insects and long-term durability, since mass timber buildings have existed for only a few decades.

In my view, these concerns are serious but not decisive. Timber is unlikely to replace concrete and steel completely, and it should not be used without careful attention to where the wood comes from. But as part of a broader effort to reduce the carbon cost of buildings, alongside the reuse of existing structures and the development of greener concrete, it offers real promise. The idea of building tall with wood, which once seemed absurd, now deserves to be taken seriously.
