reading.title: One giant leap: the road to the Moon
paragraphs: On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. It was a metal ball about the size of a beach ball, and all it did was send out a simple radio signal as it circled the Earth. Yet its effect in the United States was enormous. Many Americans were shocked that their great rival had beaten them into space, and they feared that the same rockets could be used to carry nuclear weapons. The event marked the beginning of what became known as the Space Race.

The Soviet Union continued to lead for several years. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, completing a single orbit of the Earth in a flight that lasted 108 minutes. Less than a month later, Alan Shepard became the first American in space, but his flight lasted only about fifteen minutes and did not go into orbit. The United States needed a goal that would be so ambitious that neither country would have an advantage at the start.

That goal was announced by President John F. Kennedy on 25 May 1961. Speaking to Congress, he said that the nation should commit itself to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth before the end of the decade. At the time, the United States had a total of just fifteen minutes of experience of human spaceflight, and many of the technologies that would be needed had not yet been invented. Over the following years, the space agency NASA grew rapidly, and in the mid-1960s its budget reached more than four per cent of all federal government spending.

Getting to the Moon required a series of steps. In the Gemini programme of 1965 and 1966, two-person crews practised the skills that would be needed later, such as spending up to two weeks in space, working outside the spacecraft and joining two spacecraft together in orbit. Meanwhile, engineers developed the Saturn V, a rocket around 110 metres tall that remains one of the most powerful ever flown. The programme also suffered a terrible setback. In January 1967, during a test on the launch pad, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 spacecraft, and its three astronauts were killed. The design of the spacecraft was changed significantly as a result.

In December 1968, the Apollo 8 mission carried three astronauts around the Moon for the first time. As they came out from behind the Moon, they saw the Earth rising above its grey horizon, and one of them, Bill Anders, took a photograph that became known as Earthrise. The picture of a small, colourful planet surrounded by the darkness of space was later credited with helping to inspire the environmental movement.

Apollo 11 was launched on 16 July 1969, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Four days later, while Collins remained in orbit, Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module, called Eagle, on a flat area known as the Sea of Tranquility. The landing was more dangerous than many people realised. The computer was giving alarms, and the planned landing area was full of large rocks, so Armstrong took manual control and flew on to find a safer place. When the module touched down, there was very little fuel left.

Some hours later, Armstrong climbed down the ladder and stepped onto the surface, saying the famous words, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Hundreds of millions of people around the world watched the black-and-white television pictures. The two astronauts spent about two and a half hours walking outside, setting up scientific experiments, planting a flag and collecting samples of rock and soil, before returning to orbit and travelling back to Earth. They landed safely in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July.

There were five more successful landings, and in total twelve men walked on the Moon. The last, Apollo 17, took place in December 1972. The rocks they brought back, weighing almost 400 kilograms in total, are still being studied today and have helped scientists to understand how the Moon was formed. Since then, no human has travelled further than a few hundred kilometres from the Earth. Several countries now have plans to send people back to the Moon, more than half a century after the last footprints were left there.

reading.title: Robots on the red planet
paragraphs: Mars is the most explored planet in the solar system apart from our own, yet no human has ever set foot on it. Everything we know about its surface has been learned by robots. Over the past six decades, more than a dozen spacecraft have successfully orbited or landed on Mars, and their story is one of remarkable engineering, painful failures and some unexpectedly long lives.

The first successful mission was NASA's Mariner 4, which flew past Mars in July 1965 and sent back around twenty images. Before then, some people had imagined that Mars might have canals or forests. The photographs showed instead a dry surface covered in craters, more like the Moon than the Earth. In 1976, two American Viking landers became the first spacecraft to operate successfully on the surface for a long period, sending back the first colour pictures and measuring the weather for several years.

Landing on Mars is extremely difficult, and many missions have failed during the final minutes. The planet's atmosphere is thick enough to heat a spacecraft dangerously as it enters, but too thin, at less than one per cent of the pressure on Earth, to slow it down using parachutes alone. Engineers have tried several solutions. In 1997, the Mars Pathfinder mission bounced onto the surface surrounded by giant airbags, and released a small rover called Sojourner, about the size of a microwave oven, which explored the area around the landing site for nearly three months.

In January 2004, two much larger rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, landed on opposite sides of the planet. They were designed to work for about ninety Martian days, but both lasted far longer. Engineers had worried that dust would cover their solar panels and reduce their power, but from time to time, gusts of wind cleaned the panels, giving the rovers new energy. Spirit became stuck in soft ground in 2009 and stopped communicating the following year, while Opportunity kept going until a huge dust storm in 2018. By then, it had travelled more than 45 kilometres, further than a marathon.

Driving a rover on Mars is very different from steering a remote-controlled car. Depending on where the two planets are in their orbits, a radio signal takes between about three and twenty-two minutes to travel from Earth to Mars. A driver cannot react quickly to a rock or a hole in the ground. Instead, teams on Earth plan each day's activities in advance and send a set of instructions, and modern rovers use cameras and software to find a safe route by themselves. Because a Martian day is about forty minutes longer than an Earth day, team members have sometimes lived on 'Mars time', starting work later every day.

The next generation of rovers was much heavier. Curiosity, which landed in August 2012, is about the size of a small car and weighs almost a tonne, too much for airbags. It was lowered to the ground on cables from a hovering platform powered by rockets, a method called the sky crane. Instead of solar panels, Curiosity uses a nuclear power source, which allows it to work through dust storms and the Martian winter. Its instruments have shown that its landing site, Gale Crater, once contained a lake.

In February 2021, Perseverance used the same landing method to reach Jezero Crater, the site of another ancient lake. Its main task is to collect samples of rock and store them in sealed tubes, which a future mission may bring back to Earth for detailed study. Perseverance also carried a small helicopter called Ingenuity. In April 2021, it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It had been expected to make no more than five flights, but it eventually completed seventy-two before damage to its blades ended the mission in 2024.

Mars exploration is no longer limited to the United States. In 2021, China's Zhurong rover landed successfully, making China only the second country to operate a rover on the planet. Several space agencies now hope to send astronauts to Mars in the coming decades. If they succeed, the first human visitors will owe a great deal to the robots that went before them, which have mapped the ground, studied the weather and tested the technology that people will one day depend on.

reading.title: Holidays beyond the sky
paragraphs: For most of the history of spaceflight, going into space was something only governments could arrange. Astronauts were highly trained pilots, scientists or engineers, chosen from thousands of applicants and paid by the state. Today, that is changing. Private companies are now selling seats on rockets to anyone who can afford them, and space tourism, once a subject for science fiction, has become a real, if very expensive, industry. Whether it deserves our enthusiasm is another matter.

The idea of ordinary people travelling into space is not new. The Russian schoolteacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, who worked out many of the basic principles of rocket science in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, famously wrote that the Earth is the cradle of humanity, but that one cannot live in the cradle forever. For him, leaving the planet was a natural step in human development rather than an adventure for a few wealthy individuals.

The first paying space tourist was the American businessman Dennis Tito, who in 2001 travelled to the International Space Station on a Russian Soyuz spacecraft. He reportedly paid around twenty million dollars for the trip, which lasted about a week. Some officials at NASA were unhappy about his visit, arguing that the space station was a place for serious work rather than sightseeing. A small number of other wealthy individuals followed him over the next few years. Each of them had to spend months training in Russia before the flight, learning how to live and work safely in a cramped spacecraft and how to respond in an emergency.

reading.title: The remarkable history of glass
paragraphs: Glass is so much a part of modern life that it rarely attracts attention. We look through it, drink from it and cook in it, and through the optical fibres that carry internet data across the oceans, we even communicate by means of it. Yet glass is a puzzling substance. It is hard and brittle like a solid, but its internal structure resembles that of a liquid, and for thousands of years people made and used it without having any real understanding of why it behaved as it did.

Long before anyone learned to make glass, nature was producing it. When lava from a volcano cools very rapidly, its atoms have no time to arrange themselves into crystals, and the result is obsidian, a dark volcanic glass. Because it breaks into pieces with extremely sharp edges, obsidian was highly prized by prehistoric peoples for knives and arrowheads, and it was traded over remarkably long distances. Natural glass can also form when lightning strikes sand, melting it into fragile, branching tubes known as fulgurites.

How humans first came to make glass is uncertain. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder told a story of merchants who, camping on a beach, rested their cooking pots on blocks of natron, a natural soda, and found next morning that the fire had fused the sand and soda into glass. Modern historians generally doubt this account, since an open fire would hardly have reached the necessary temperature. What is known is that the earliest manufactured glass objects, mostly beads, come from Mesopotamia and date back more than four thousand years. The first glass vessels were produced by a laborious technique called core-forming, in which molten glass was wound around a core of clay and dung that was scraped out once the glass had cooled.

The great turning point came in the first century BCE, when craftsmen somewhere on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that molten glass could be inflated by blowing through a hollow tube. Glassblowing allowed vessels to be made in minutes rather than days, and as the technique spread through the Roman Empire, glass changed from a luxury into an everyday material. Cups, bottles and storage jars became common, and the Romans even began to set small panes of glass in windows, although this early window glass was thick, bubbly and far from transparent.

The chemistry of glass explains many of the challenges early glassmakers faced. Pure silica, the main component of sand, melts only at temperatures above 1,700 degrees Celsius, far beyond the reach of ancient furnaces. Adding soda acts as a flux, lowering the melting point considerably, but glass made only of silica and soda slowly dissolves in water. The solution was to add lime, obtained from limestone or shells, which makes the glass chemically stable. This combination, known as soda-lime glass, still accounts for the great majority of the glass made today, from bottles to windows. In all these glasses, the atoms are arranged randomly rather than in a regular pattern, which is why scientists describe glass as an amorphous solid.

This unusual structure has given rise to a persistent myth. Visitors to medieval churches are often told that the windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is really a very slow-moving liquid that has flowed downwards over the centuries. Calculations show, however, that at room temperature such flow would be undetectable even over billions of years. The real explanation lies in how the glass was made. Medieval window glass was often produced by spinning molten glass into a large disc, which was uneven in thickness, and glaziers usually, though not always, placed the heavier edge at the bottom. Indeed, some old windows have their thicker edge at the top.

During the Middle Ages, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In 1291, the city's glassmakers were ordered to move their furnaces to the nearby island of Murano, partly because of the risk of fire spreading through the crowded city. The craftsmen were valued so highly that they were forbidden to leave the republic, for fear that they would take their secrets with them. In the fifteenth century, Venetian workshops developed cristallo, an exceptionally clear glass. Two centuries later in England, George Ravenscroft found that adding lead oxide produced a heavy, brilliant glass, now called lead crystal, which was ideal for cutting into decorative patterns.

Making large, flat sheets remained difficult and expensive until the twentieth century. Plate glass had to be ground and polished on both sides, a slow process that wasted much of the material. In the 1950s, Alastair Pilkington and his colleagues at the British company Pilkington Brothers developed the float process, announced in 1959, in which molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin. The glass spreads out and floats on the metal, producing a perfectly smooth, flat surface on both sides without polishing. Most of the world's flat glass is now made in this way. Glass also has an environmental advantage: it can be recycled repeatedly without losing quality, and crushed recycled glass melts at a lower temperature than raw materials, saving considerable energy.

Long before anyone learned to make glass, nature was producing it. When lava from a volcano cools very rapidly, its atoms have no time to arrange themselves into crystals, and the result is obsidian, a dark volcanic glass. Because it breaks into pieces with extremely sharp edges, obsidian was highly prized by prehistoric peoples for knives and arrowheads, and it was traded over remarkably long distances. Natural glass can also form when lightning strikes sand, melting it into fragile, branching tubes known as fulgurites.

How humans first came to make glass is uncertain. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder told a story of merchants who, camping on a beach, rested their cooking pots on blocks of natron, a natural soda, and found next morning that the fire had fused the sand and soda into glass. Modern historians generally doubt this account, since an open fire would hardly have reached the necessary temperature. What is known is that the earliest manufactured glass objects, mostly beads, come from Mesopotamia and date back more than four thousand years. The first glass vessels were produced by a laborious technique called core-forming, in which molten glass was wound around a core of clay and dung that was scraped out once the glass had cooled.

The great turning point came in the first century BCE, when craftsmen somewhere on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that molten glass could be inflated by blowing through a hollow tube. Glassblowing allowed vessels to be made in minutes rather than days, and as the technique spread through the Roman Empire, glass changed from a luxury into an everyday material. Cups, bottles and storage jars became common, and the Romans even began to set small panes of glass in windows, although this early window glass was thick, bubbly and far from transparent.

The chemistry of glass explains many of the challenges early glassmakers faced. Pure silica, the main component of sand, melts only at temperatures above 1,700 degrees Celsius, far beyond the reach of ancient furnaces. Adding soda acts as a flux, lowering the melting point considerably, but glass made only of silica and soda slowly dissolves in water. The solution was to add lime, obtained from limestone or shells, which makes the glass chemically stable. This combination, known as soda-lime glass, still accounts for the great majority of the glass made today, from bottles to windows. In all these glasses, the atoms are arranged randomly rather than in a regular pattern, which is why scientists describe glass as an amorphous solid.

This unusual structure has given rise to a persistent myth. Visitors to medieval churches are often told that the windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is really a very slow-moving liquid that has flowed downwards over the centuries. Calculations show, however, that at room temperature such flow would be undetectable even over billions of years. The real explanation lies in how the glass was made. Medieval window glass was often produced by spinning molten glass into a large disc, which was uneven in thickness, and glaziers usually, though not always, placed the heavier edge at the bottom. Indeed, some old windows have their thicker edge at the top.

During the Middle Ages, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In 1291, the city's glassmakers were ordered to move their furnaces to the nearby island of Murano, partly because of the risk of fire spreading through the crowded city. The craftsmen were valued so highly that they were forbidden to leave the republic, for fear that they would take their secrets with them. In the fifteenth century, Venetian workshops developed cristallo, an exceptionally clear glass. Two centuries later in England, George Ravenscroft found that adding lead oxide produced a heavy, brilliant glass, now called lead crystal, which was ideal for cutting into decorative patterns.

Making large, flat sheets remained difficult and expensive until the twentieth century. Plate glass had to be ground and polished on both sides, a slow process that wasted much of the material. In the 1950s, Alastair Pilkington and his colleagues at the British company Pilkington Brothers developed the float process, announced in 1959, in which molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin. reading.title: The age of plastic
paragraphs: Few materials have transformed everyday life as rapidly as plastics. Chemically, plastics are polymers, substances made of extremely long molecules in which small units called monomers are joined together in chains that may contain thousands of links; the word comes from the Greek for 'many parts'. Global production has risen from around two million tonnes in 1950 to more than four hundred million tonnes a year today, and it is now difficult to find a manufactured object that contains no plastic at all.

Polymers themselves are not new. Nature produces them in abundance, and for centuries people shaped materials such as horn, tortoiseshell, natural rubber and shellac, a resin secreted by the lac insect, into combs, buttons and ornaments. These materials, however, were available only in limited quantities, and some, such as ivory, came at a heavy cost to the animals that supplied them. As industrial societies grew, demand far outstripped supply, and inventors began searching for substitutes.

The first steps were taken using plant material. In 1862, the British inventor Alexander Parkes displayed Parkesine, a mouldable material made from cellulose, at the International Exhibition in London, but his business failed within a few years. In the United States, John Wesley Hyatt developed celluloid, reportedly encouraged by a prize offered for a substitute for ivory in billiard balls. Celluloid proved useful for many purposes, most famously photographic and cinema film, despite being highly flammable, a property that caused numerous fires in early cinemas.

The first fully synthetic plastic, made entirely from chemicals rather than modified natural substances, was invented in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, a Belgian-born chemist working in New York. Bakelite, produced by reacting phenol with formaldehyde, could be moulded into almost any shape, and once it had set under heat and pressure, it could not be melted again. Because it did not conduct electricity and resisted heat, it was ideal for telephones, radio cases and electrical plugs, and its makers promoted it as the material of a thousand uses.

Several important plastics were discovered by accident. In 1933, Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson, chemists at the British company ICI, were conducting high-pressure experiments with ethylene gas when they found a white, waxy solid in their apparatus: polyethylene. Light, flexible and an excellent electrical insulator, it became vital during the Second World War for insulating the cables of radar equipment. At around the same time, Wallace Carothers at the American company DuPont produced nylon, which was launched in women's stockings and sold in vast quantities until wartime needs diverted it to parachutes and ropes.

Chemists divide plastics into two broad families. Thermoplastics, which include polyethylene, PET and PVC, soften when heated and harden again as they cool, so in principle they can be melted down and reshaped many times. Thermosets, such as Bakelite and epoxy resins, form a rigid network of chemical bonds as they set, and cannot be remelted. Even thermoplastics, however, are seldom easy to recycle, because most products contain additives, such as colourings, softeners and flame retardants, and many items combine several types of plastic that must be separated before they can be processed.

The scale of the resulting waste problem was quantified in a widely cited study published in 2017 by the American researchers Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law. They estimated that around 8.3 billion tonnes of plastic had been produced up to 2015, and that of the plastic that had become waste, only about nine per cent had been recycled, while around twelve per cent had been burned and the rest had accumulated in landfill sites or the natural environment. Because plastics break down extremely slowly, much of this material persists as fragments, and microplastics, pieces smaller than five millimetres, have now been found from Arctic sea ice to the deepest ocean sediments.

Solutions are being pursued on several fronts, but none is straightforward. Mechanical recycling usually reduces the quality of the material, so that drinks bottles, for instance, are often turned into fibres for clothing rather than into new bottles. Chemical recycling, which breaks polymers back down into monomers, could in theory produce plastic as good as new, but it remains expensive and energy-intensive. Bioplastics made from plant sources are another option, yet many of them break down only under the high temperatures of industrial composting facilities and persist in the sea much like conventional plastics. Meanwhile, the benefits of plastics, from lighter vehicles that use less fuel to sterile medical equipment, mean that simply abandoning them is not a realistic option.

reading.title: Colour from coal tar
paragraphs: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every dye in the world came from a plant, an animal or a mineral. Blue was obtained from indigo plants in India or from woad in Europe, red from the roots of the madder plant, and crimson from cochineal, an insect harvested in the Americas. reading.title: The disappearing sea
paragraphs: In the middle of Central Asia, on the border between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, lies what remains of the Aral Sea. Although it was called a sea, it was really a huge lake, because it had no connection to the ocean. In 1960, it covered about sixty-eight thousand square kilometres and was the fourth-largest lake in the world. Its water was a beautiful blue, and many small islands were scattered across it. It was full of fish, and thousands of people worked in the fishing industry in towns along its shores.

The lake did not get its water from rain, because the region is very dry. Instead, it was fed by two long rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, which carry water from the high mountains far to the south and east. For thousands of years, the amount of water that these rivers brought into the lake was roughly equal to the amount that was lost by evaporation in the hot summer sun, so the size of the lake stayed fairly stable.

This balance changed in the 1960s. At that time, the region was part of the Soviet Union, and the government decided to turn the surrounding deserts into farmland. Its main aim was to grow cotton, a crop that needs a great deal of water. At first, the plan seemed to be a great success. The region became one of the world's major producers of cotton, and the new farms provided work for many people. Engineers built thousands of kilometres of canals to take water from the two rivers to the new fields. Many of these canals were badly built, and large amounts of water leaked out of them or evaporated before reaching the crops.

As a result, much less water reached the Aral Sea, and it began to shrink. By the late 1980s, the water level had fallen so much that the lake divided into two separate parts: a smaller northern lake in Kazakhstan and a larger southern lake, mostly in Uzbekistan. The southern lake continued to get smaller, and in 2014, satellite photographs showed that its eastern part had dried up completely for the first time in modern history.

The effects on the people of the region were very serious. As the water level fell, the lake became much saltier, and most kinds of fish could no longer survive. The fishing industry collapsed, and thousands of people lost their jobs. Former fishing ports, such as Moynaq in Uzbekistan, were left far from the water, and rusty fishing boats now lie on the sand where the lake used to be. For a while, some fish factories stayed open by bringing in frozen fish from far away, but this could not continue for long. Many young people moved away to find work.

The dried-up lake bed also caused new problems. It became a new desert, covered in salt and in chemicals that had been used on the cotton fields and washed into the lake. Strong winds pick up this dust and carry it for hundreds of kilometres, damaging crops and causing breathing problems for local people. Even the local climate has changed: without the large body of water to cool the air in summer and warm it in winter, summers have become hotter and winters colder. Doctors in the region have also reported high levels of illness, and many people still worry about the quality of their drinking water.

However, the story of the northern lake has a more hopeful ending. In 2005, the government of Kazakhstan, with support from the World Bank, completed a dam called the Kok-Aral Dam, which stops water from the Syr Darya from flowing south into the larger lake. The northern lake began to fill up again much faster than scientists had expected. As its water became less salty, fish returned, and fishing has started again in towns such as Aralsk. The water, which had moved many kilometres away from the town, has also come closer again.

The southern lake is unlikely to recover, because so much water is still taken from the Amu Darya for farming. Instead, Uzbekistan has been planting millions of desert shrubs on the dry lake bed to hold the soil in place and reduce the dust storms. Some experts also hope that better ways of watering crops, such as using pipes instead of open canals, will mean that less water is wasted on farms. The Aral Sea is now often used as an example of how human decisions about water can change an entire region, and of how careful planning can sometimes repair some of the damage.

reading.title: Lake Baikal: the blue eye of Siberia
paragraphs: Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia in Russia, is a lake of records. It is the deepest lake on Earth, reaching more than one thousand six hundred metres at its deepest point. It is also believed to be the oldest, having formed around twenty-five to thirty million years ago. Most lakes only last for a few thousand years before they fill up with mud and disappear, so Baikal is extremely unusual. Because of its great age and beauty, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Baikal is not the largest lake in the world by area, but because it is so deep, it holds an enormous amount of water. In fact, it contains around a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water found on the surface of the Earth, more than all five of North America's Great Lakes put together. The lake is about six hundred kilometres long, but in most places it is less than eighty kilometres wide. More than three hundred rivers and streams flow into the lake, but only one river, the Angara, flows out of it.

The lake lies in a deep crack in the Earth's surface, called a rift, where two parts of the Earth's crust are slowly moving apart. This movement is still happening today. Small earthquakes are common in the area, and scientists say that the lake is becoming wider by about two centimetres every year. Some believe that, in millions of years, the rift could become so wide that it turns into a new ocean.

One of the most famous things about Baikal is how clear its water is. In some places, it is possible to see objects more than thirty metres below the surface. On calm days, people in boats can look down and see rocks and fish far below them. One reason for this is a tiny animal, a kind of crustacean less than two millimetres long, which lives in the lake in enormous numbers. These creatures eat algae and bacteria, and in doing so, they help to keep the water very clean. The water also contains few minerals, so it is often described as being almost as pure as distilled water.

Because the lake has been separated from other water for so long, many of the animals and plants that live in it have developed in their own way. Around two-thirds of the species found there live nowhere else in the world. The best known is the Baikal seal, or nerpa, one of the very few seals that live only in fresh water. It is also one of the smallest seals in the world, and it spends much of its life under the water and ice. Scientists are still not sure how seals reached a lake so far from the sea. Another unusual animal is the golomyanka, a fish with a body so pale that it is almost transparent. It lives deep in the lake and, unusually for a fish, gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

In winter, the weather around Baikal is extremely cold, and from January until May the surface of the lake is covered in ice. In many places, the ice is more than a metre thick, strong enough for cars and lorries to drive across. The ice is often very clear, and in some places visitors can see cracks and bubbles of gas trapped inside it. In the early twentieth century, before a railway around the southern end of the lake was completed, railway tracks were even laid across the ice so that trains could cross. Today, thousands of tourists come in winter to walk, skate and cycle on the frozen lake.

Despite its size, Baikal faces several threats. For almost fifty years, a large factory producing paper materials on the southern shore released waste into the lake, until it finally closed in 2013. More recently, scientists have noticed large amounts of green algae growing near the shore in some places, which they link to waste water from towns and tourist hotels. Numbers of the omul, a fish that is an important food for local people, fell so much that commercial fishing for it was banned in 2017.

Many people believe that protecting Baikal is a responsibility for the whole world, not only for Russia. Scientists from many countries study the lake, and local groups organise clean-up days to remove rubbish from its shores. Visitors are also asked to stay on marked paths and to take all their rubbish home with them. Better treatment of waste water and careful control of tourism will be needed if the lake is to stay as clean and unusual as it has been for millions of years.

It is also one of the smallest seals in the world, and it spends much of its life under the water and ice. Scientists are still not sure how seals reached a lake so far from the sea. Another unusual animal is the golomyanka, a fish with a body so pale that it is almost transparent. It lives deep in the lake and, unusually for a fish, gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

In winter, the weather around Baikal is extremely cold, and from January until May the surface of the lake is covered in ice. In many places, the ice is more than a metre thick, strong enough for cars and lorries to drive across. The ice is often very clear, and in some places visitors can see cracks and bubbles of gas trapped inside it. In the early twentieth century, before a railway around the southern end of the lake was completed, railway tracks were even laid across the ice so that trains could cross. Today, thousands of tourists come in winter to walk, skate and cycle on the frozen lake.

Numbers of the omul, a fish that is an important food for local people, fell so much that commercial fishing for it was banned in 2017.

Many people believe that protecting Baikal is a responsibility for the whole world, not only for Russia. Scientists from many countries study the lake, and local groups organise clean-up days to remove rubbish from its shores. Visitors are also asked to stay on marked paths and to take all their rubbish home with them. Better treatment of waste water and careful control of tourism will be needed if the lake is to stay as clean and unusual as it has been for millions of years.

reading.title: Should rivers have rights?
paragraphs: In most countries, the law treats a river as a thing. It can be owned, used and changed, and if it is polluted, it is usually the people who use the river, rather than the river itself, who can go to court. In recent years, however, a new idea has spread around the world: that rivers, lakes and other parts of nature should have legal rights of their own, in the same way that people and companies do.

The best-known example comes from New Zealand. For more than a century, the Māori people of the Whanganui region tried to persuade the government to recognise their special relationship with the Whanganui River, the country's third-longest river. For them, the river is not simply a resource but an ancestor and a living being. A well-known Māori saying from the region expresses this idea: 'I am the river, and the river is me.' In 2017, after many years of negotiation, the New Zealand parliament passed a law that recognised the river as a legal person. Two guardians, one chosen by the Māori community and one by the government, now speak on the river's behalf.

New Zealand was not the first country to move in this direction. In 2008, Ecuador became the first country to include the rights of nature in its constitution, the country's most important set of laws. Then, in 2016, the highest court in Colombia ruled that the Atrato River, which had been badly damaged by illegal gold mining, had rights to protection and restoration. In 2019, the High Court of Bangladesh went even further and declared that all of the country's rivers should be treated as legal persons.

Not every attempt has been successful. In 2017, a court in the Indian state of Uttarakhand declared that the Ganges and Yamuna rivers, which are sacred to Hindus, were legal persons. However, the state government argued that the decision was unclear and could cause practical problems, for example over who would be responsible if the river flooded and caused damage. A few months later, India's Supreme Court suspended the decision. In the United States, voters in the city of Toledo, Ohio, approved a 'Bill of Rights' for Lake Erie in 2019, after pollution had left the city without safe drinking water for several days in 2014. But a judge ruled the following year that the law was not valid.

Supporters of river rights say that traditional laws have failed to protect nature. Pollution laws often set limits on what can be released into a river, but these are frequently broken, and the fines are small. If a river is a legal person, they argue, its guardians can take polluters to court directly, without having to prove that any human has been harmed. In my view, this is the strongest argument for the idea. It changes the question from 'How much damage can we allow?' to 'What does the river need to stay healthy?' Supporters also say that the idea reflects the beliefs of many indigenous peoples, who have long seen themselves as part of nature rather than its owners.

Critics, however, raise several objections. Some say that the idea is mainly symbolic, and that it does little in practice unless the guardians have enough money and power to act. Others point out that a river cannot tell us what it wants, so the people who speak for it may simply use it to support their own opinions. There are also difficult questions about responsibility: if a river has rights, does it also have duties? Finally, some people worry that if rivers could take companies or governments to court too easily, it might become harder to build important projects, such as bridges or water supply systems.

I think these concerns are reasonable, but they are not a good reason to reject the idea completely. The Whanganui case shows that it can work well when it grows out of a long relationship between a community and a river, and when the guardians are given real resources. Problems are more likely when the idea is introduced suddenly by a court, without the support of the government or the people who live along the river.

In the end, giving rights to a river is a way of saying that it matters for its own sake, and not only because it is useful to us. Whether or not more countries follow New Zealand, the debate has already encouraged many people to think differently about the rivers and lakes around them, and that, I believe, is a valuable result in itself.

reading.title: The monarch butterfly's great journey
paragraphs: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies in eastern North America begin one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal kingdom. Leaving southern Canada and the northern United States, they fly south for more than three thousand kilometres to spend the winter in a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico. No other butterfly is known to make such a long, regular two-way migration, and for many years the question of where these insects actually went was one of the great mysteries of natural history.

The answer was found through the persistence of a Canadian zoologist, Fred Urquhart, who began studying monarch migration in the late 1930s. From the 1950s onwards, he and his wife Norah organised thousands of volunteers to attach tiny paper labels to the wings of monarchs, each with a request that anyone finding the butterfly should report it. Gradually, the reports pointed towards Mexico. Finally, in January 1975, two of their collaborators, Ken Brugger and Catalina Aguado, found the overwintering sites high in the mountains west of Mexico City. The discovery was announced to the world in National Geographic magazine in 1976.

The sites are as extraordinary as the journey. The butterflies gather in dense clusters on the trunks and branches of oyamel fir trees, at altitudes of around three thousand metres. So many butterflies may settle on a single tree that branches have been known to break under their weight. The cool mountain climate allows the monarchs to survive the winter in a state of low activity, using up their stored fat slowly, while the forest canopy protects them from the worst of the cold and from rain and snow. The butterflies remain there until the days lengthen and temperatures rise in late winter, when they begin to mate and prepare to leave.

One of the most surprising facts about the migration is that no single butterfly completes the whole round trip. Monarchs born in early summer live for only a few weeks as adults. The generation that flies south in autumn, however, is different: these butterflies do not breed until the following spring, and they can live for up to eight months. In spring, they fly north to the southern United States, where they lay their eggs and die. It then takes several more generations, each living only a few weeks, to recolonise the north.

How the butterflies find their way to a place they have never visited remains a subject of research. Experiments have shown that monarchs use the position of the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, they must also keep track of time, and scientists have discovered that the internal clocks that allow them to do this are located partly in their antennae. There is also evidence that monarchs can use the Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate, which may be particularly useful on cloudy days.

Monarchs are closely linked to a single group of plants. Their caterpillars feed only on milkweeds, which contain poisonous chemicals. The caterpillars are not harmed by these chemicals; instead, they store them in their bodies, and the poisons remain in the adult butterflies. This makes monarchs unpleasant to eat, and many birds learn to avoid them after a single attempt. The butterflies' bright orange and black colouring acts as a warning, advertising to predators that they are not worth attacking.

Unfortunately, the eastern monarch population has declined dramatically. Because the butterflies cluster so tightly together, scientists estimate the population by measuring the area of forest they occupy in winter. In the mid-1990s, the colonies covered around eighteen hectares; in the winter of 2013 to 2014, they covered less than one hectare. Several causes have been identified. The most important is thought to be the loss of milkweed in the United States, much of it due to the increased use of herbicides on farmland. Illegal logging in Mexico and extreme weather events have also played a part.

Efforts to protect the monarch now involve all three countries along its route. In Mexico, the overwintering area is protected as the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, which was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. In the United States and Canada, governments, schools and individual gardeners have been encouraged to plant milkweed and other flowers that provide nectar for adult butterflies. Whether these efforts will be enough to secure the future of this extraordinary migration is not yet clear, but they show how a single insect can inspire cooperation across an entire continent.

reading.title: Farmers in miniature
paragraphs: Humans began farming around ten thousand years ago, and the change transformed our species. Yet we were not the first farmers on Earth. Tens of millions of years earlier, certain groups of ants had already begun to cultivate their own food. The most famous of these are the leafcutter ants of Central and South America, whose long columns of workers, each carrying a piece of leaf above its head, are a familiar sight in tropical forests. For a long time, people assumed that the ants were simply collecting food to eat. The truth turned out to be far more surprising.

Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they collect. Instead, they carry them back to their underground nests, where smaller workers cut them into tiny pieces, chew them into a pulp and use the pulp to grow a fungus. The ants and their fungus depend completely on each other. The fungus produces small, nutrient-rich swellings that the ants harvest and feed to their larvae, while the fungus relies on the ants to supply it with fresh leaves, to protect it, and to carry it to new places. Neither can survive in the wild without the other.

A mature leafcutter colony is an enormous enterprise, and it can take several years to reach its full size. In some species, a single nest may contain several million workers and extend several metres below the ground, with hundreds of chambers connected by tunnels. The work is divided according to size. The largest workers defend the colony, medium-sized workers cut and carry leaves, and the smallest care for the fungus gardens. Some tiny workers even ride on the leaf fragments as they are carried home, where they appear to protect the carriers from parasitic flies that try to lay eggs on them.

Like human farmers, the ants must deal with pests. Their fungus gardens can be attacked by another fungus, called Escovopsis, which can destroy a garden if it is not controlled. In 1999, a team of researchers including Cameron Currie published a discovery that changed the way scientists thought about the ants. They found that the ants carry bacteria on their bodies which produce substances that kill or slow the growth of Escovopsis. In effect, the ants use antibiotics to protect their crops, something humans have only done for less than a century.

The ants are also careful about hygiene. Waste material from the fungus gardens, which may contain harmful organisms, is carried to special waste chambers or to heaps outside the nest. Studies have shown that the workers who handle this waste are kept separate from the rest of the colony. They rarely enter the fungus gardens, and if they try to, other workers may attack them. This strict division reduces the risk that disease will spread to the precious fungus on which the whole colony depends.

The beginning of a new colony depends on a single queen. Before she leaves her birth nest on her mating flight, a young queen places a small piece of the fungus in a pouch inside her mouth. After mating, she digs a small chamber in the soil, spits out the fungus and begins a new garden, which she feeds and tends herself until her first workers are old enough to take over. In this way, the same fungus has been passed down through countless generations of queens, rather like seeds saved from one harvest to plant the next.

Leafcutters are not the only insects that farm. Some termites in Africa and Asia also grow fungus in their mounds, and certain beetles, known as ambrosia beetles, cultivate fungus inside the tunnels they dig in wood. Many other ant species practise a form of animal farming. They tend groups of aphids, small insects that feed on plant sap, and collect the sweet liquid, known as honeydew, that the aphids produce. In return, the ants protect the aphids from predators such as ladybirds, and some even carry them to fresh plants.

These tiny farmers have much to teach us. Because leafcutter ants have managed to grow essentially a single crop for millions of years without it being wiped out by disease, some biologists believe that studying them may help us understand how to make human agriculture more resilient. Others are investigating the bacteria the ants use, in the hope of discovering new antibiotics. Ironically, in parts of Latin America, the same ants are regarded as serious agricultural pests, because a large colony can strip the leaves from crops and fruit trees in a single night.

Studies have shown that the workers who handle this waste are kept separate from the rest of the colony. They rarely enter the fungus gardens, and if they try to, other workers may attack them. This strict division reduces the risk that disease will spread to the precious fungus on which the whole colony depends.

The beginning of a new colony depends on a single queen. Before she leaves her birth nest on her mating flight, a young queen places a small piece of the fungus in a pouch inside her mouth. After mating, she digs a small chamber in the soil, spits out the fungus and begins a new garden, which she feeds and tends herself until her first workers are old enough to take over. In this way, the same fungus has been passed down through countless generations of queens, rather like seeds saved from one harvest to plant the next.

Leafcutters are not the only insects that farm. Some termites in Africa and Asia also grow fungus in their mounds, and certain beetles, known as ambrosia beetles, cultivate fungus inside the tunnels they dig in wood. Many other ant species practise a form of animal farming. They tend groups of aphids, small insects that feed on plant sap, and collect the sweet liquid, known as honeydew, that the aphids produce. In return, the ants protect the aphids from predators such as ladybirds, and some even carry them to fresh plants.

These tiny farmers have much to teach us. Because leafcutter ants have managed to grow essentially a single crop for millions of years without it being wiped out by disease, some biologists believe that studying them may help us understand how to make human agriculture more resilient. Others are investigating the bacteria the ants use, in the hope of discovering new antibiotics. Ironically, in parts of Latin America, the same ants are regarded as serious agricultural pests, because a large colony can strip the leaves from crops and fruit trees in a single night.

reading.title: Are the insects disappearing?
paragraphs: Many people over a certain age remember long summer drives after which the car windscreen was covered in dead insects. Today, they say, the windscreen stays almost clean. This so-called 'windscreen phenomenon' is only an anecdote, and it could be explained by other factors, such as the more streamlined shape of modern cars. But it reflects a growing fear among scientists and the public alike that insects are disappearing. Since the late 2010s, newspaper headlines have warned of an 'insect apocalypse'. The question is how far the evidence supports such dramatic language, and what, if anything, should be done about it.

Concern about the effect of human activity on insects is not new. In 1962, the American biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, which described how widespread use of pesticides was harming birds and other wildlife, and which helped to inspire the modern environmental movement. Twenty-five years later, the biologist E. O. Wilson famously described insects and other invertebrates as 'the little things that run the world', arguing that if they were to disappear, ecosystems would collapse, whereas the world would manage quite well without humans.

The study that brought the issue to wide public attention was published in 2017. For almost three decades, amateur entomologists from a society in the German town of Krefeld had used special tent-like traps to collect flying insects in nature reserves, mainly in western Germany. When the samples were analysed, they showed that the total weight of flying insects caught had fallen by more than three-quarters over twenty-seven years. What made the result so alarming was that the losses had occurred in protected areas, which were supposed to be refuges for wildlife.

Two years later, a review by the scientists Francisco Sánchez-Bayo and Kris Wyckhuys went further, suggesting that more than forty per cent of insect species could face extinction in the coming decades. This claim was widely reported, but it was also strongly criticised by other researchers. Critics pointed out that the authors had searched for studies using the word 'decline', which may have caused them to overlook studies showing stable or increasing populations, and that most of the data came from Europe and North America.

A more cautious picture emerged in 2020, when a team led by Roel van Klink combined data from more than 160 long-term studies around the world. They found that the number of land-dwelling insects was falling by around nine per cent per decade, a serious but less catastrophic rate than some headlines had suggested. Surprisingly, insects that live in fresh water, such as mayflies and midges, had increased, which the researchers linked to efforts to clean up rivers and lakes. In my view, this finding is one of the most encouraging in the whole debate, because it shows that environmental policies can work.

Why should we care? Insects carry out an enormous range of tasks on which humans depend. Around three-quarters of the world's major food crops benefit at least to some extent from animal pollination, most of it carried out by insects. Insects break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil, and they are food for countless birds, fish and other animals. Many insects also control pests: ladybirds and hoverfly larvae, for example, eat large numbers of aphids. A serious decline in insects would therefore have consequences far beyond the insects themselves.

The causes of decline are many, and they interact. The loss of natural habitats to farming and building is generally considered the most important. Pesticides, particularly insecticides, kill insects directly, while herbicides remove the wild plants on which many insects feed. Climate change, light pollution and invasive species add further pressures. In my view, it is a mistake to look for a single cause, as some campaigners do, because this encourages the belief that one simple solution, such as banning one type of chemical, would solve the problem.

What, then, should we conclude? The phrase 'insect apocalypse' is probably an exaggeration, and it risks damaging the credibility of scientists if the worst predictions do not come true. Yet the evidence that many insect populations are declining, especially in heavily farmed regions, is strong. In my view, the greatest problem is not exaggeration but ignorance: we have reliable long-term data for only a tiny fraction of the world's insects, and almost none for the tropics, where most species live. Monitoring insects properly, with the help of volunteers like those in Krefeld, should be a priority.

reading.title: The story of indigo
paragraphs: Of all the colours that people have used to dye cloth, few have such a long and dramatic history as indigo, the deep blue now most familiar from the denim of jeans. The dye has been used on every inhabited continent, and its trade has made fortunes, caused rebellions and helped to launch the modern chemical industry. Remarkably, the blue of a pair of jeans bought today is chemically identical to the blue that was being produced thousands of years ago, although the way it is made has changed completely.

Indigo can be obtained from a number of different plants, but the most important has been Indigofera tinctoria, a shrub that grows in tropical regions and was cultivated especially in India, from which the dye takes its name. In Europe, a similar blue was obtained from woad, a plant of the cabbage family that grows well in cooler climates, though it contains much less of the colouring substance. The oldest known indigo-dyed fabric, however, comes from neither region: in 2016, researchers reported that fragments of cotton cloth found at Huaca Prieta in Peru had been dyed with indigo around six thousand years ago.

Indigo is unlike most natural dyes, because the colouring substance cannot simply be extracted by boiling the plant in water. The leaves do not even look blue. Instead, they are soaked and allowed to ferment, a process that releases a colourless compound which reacts with oxygen to form solid indigo. This is then dried into cakes for transport. Because indigo does not dissolve in water, the dyer must convert it back into a soluble form in a vat. Cloth dipped into this liquid comes out yellowish-green, and only turns blue as it is exposed to the air. Darker shades are produced by dipping the cloth many times.

When Portuguese and Dutch merchants began importing large quantities of Indian indigo into Europe by sea in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the woad growers of France and Germany, whose industry had made some regions extremely wealthy, faced ruin. They campaigned against the foreign dye, claiming that it was harmful and that it damaged cloth, and several governments introduced laws to restrict or even ban its use. In the end, however, indigo was simply too good to resist. It produced stronger colours more cheaply, and by the end of the seventeenth century the woad industry had largely collapsed.

European powers soon began producing indigo in their colonies. In the 1740s, a young woman named Eliza Lucas, who was managing her family's plantations in South Carolina, experimented with growing indigo, and within a few years it had become one of the colony's most valuable exports. This prosperity, however, depended on the labour of enslaved Africans. In India, British planters in Bengal forced local farmers to grow indigo instead of food crops, often on very unfair terms. In 1859, thousands of farmers refused to continue, in a protest that became known as the Indigo Revolt and that eventually led the authorities to investigate the planters' methods.

The end of the natural indigo trade came not from protest but from chemistry. In the nineteenth century, chemists in Europe, and especially in Germany, were learning how to manufacture dyes from substances found in coal tar. The German chemist Adolf von Baeyer succeeded in making indigo in the laboratory in 1880, and he worked out its chemical structure a few years later. Developing a process that was cheap enough for industrial use took much longer, but in 1897 the German company BASF began selling synthetic indigo. Within a few decades, natural indigo had almost disappeared from world markets, with disastrous consequences for growers in India.

Meanwhile, indigo had found a new use. In 1873, a tailor named Jacob Davis and a merchant named Levi Strauss received a patent in the United States for work trousers strengthened with metal rivets, and these were made from tough cotton cloth dyed with indigo. One feature of indigo explains the character of denim. The dye attaches mainly to the surface of the cotton threads rather than penetrating to their centre, so as jeans are worn and washed, the colour gradually rubs away, revealing the white core of the thread. The faded look that once showed long years of hard work later became highly fashionable.

Today, almost all indigo is synthetic and made from chemicals derived from oil. Producing it, and especially converting it into a soluble form for dyeing, involves chemicals that can pollute rivers if waste water is not properly treated, and some textile regions have suffered serious environmental damage as a result. Researchers are now exploring cleaner methods, including the use of bacteria to produce the dye, while a small number of farmers and craft dyers have returned to growing indigo plants. It seems that the long story of this ancient blue is still far from over.

In the nineteenth century, chemists in Europe, and especially in Germany, were learning how to manufacture dyes from substances found in coal tar. The German chemist Adolf von Baeyer succeeded in making indigo in the laboratory in 1880, and he worked out its chemical structure a few years later. Developing a process that was cheap enough for industrial use took much longer, but in 1897 the German company BASF began selling synthetic indigo. Within a few decades, natural indigo had almost disappeared from world markets, with disastrous consequences for growers in India.

Meanwhile, indigo had found a new use. In 1873, a tailor named Jacob Davis and a merchant named Levi Strauss received a patent in the United States for work trousers strengthened with metal rivets, and these were made from tough cotton cloth dyed with indigo. One feature of indigo explains the character of denim. The dye attaches mainly to the surface of the cotton threads rather than penetrating to their centre, so as jeans are worn and washed, the colour gradually rubs away, revealing the white core of the thread. The faded look that once showed long years of hard work later became highly fashionable.

reading.title: The true cost of cheap clothes
paragraphs: For most of human history, clothes were valuable possessions. Fabric was spun and woven by hand, garments were repaired again and again, and good clothing was often left to relatives in wills. Even in the mid-twentieth century, many families in wealthy countries bought only a few new items each year. Today the situation is very different. It has been estimated that global clothing production roughly doubled in the first fifteen years of this century, while the average number of times a garment is worn before being thrown away fell considerably over the same period.

This change is largely the result of a business model known as fast fashion. Traditional fashion companies planned their collections many months in advance and released them in two main seasons each year. Fast-fashion retailers, by contrast, design, manufacture and deliver new styles in a matter of weeks, responding quickly to trends seen on catwalks, in celebrity photographs or, increasingly, on social media. Their shops receive new stock constantly, which encourages customers to visit often and to buy before a style disappears. Prices are kept low by producing in very large quantities in countries where wages are low.

The environmental costs of this model begin with raw materials. Cotton is one of the world's most water-intensive crops: one widely quoted estimate suggests that around 2,700 litres of water are needed to produce the cotton for a single T-shirt. Irrigation for cotton growing contributed to one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century, the shrinking of the Aral Sea in Central Asia. Synthetic fibres, which now make up the majority of the fibre used in clothing, avoid this problem, but they are made from oil, and dyeing and finishing fabric of all kinds uses large amounts of energy and chemicals.

The problems continue long after clothes are sold. A report published in 2017 by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation calculated that the equivalent of one rubbish truck full of textiles is sent to landfill or burned every second, and that less than one per cent of the material used to make clothing is recycled into new clothing. Much of what is donated to charity in wealthy countries is exported, and some ends up in markets in countries such as Ghana, where traders say that a growing share of the bales they buy is of such poor quality that it cannot be sold and must be thrown away.

There are human costs as well. The low prices of fast fashion depend on low wages in countries such as Bangladesh, Cambodia and Vietnam, and working conditions in some factories are poor or dangerous. In April 2013, the Rana Plaza building near Dhaka in Bangladesh, which housed several garment factories, collapsed, killing more than eleven hundred people. Workers had been ordered to return to the building the day after cracks had appeared in its walls. The disaster led many international brands to sign an agreement to fund independent safety inspections of the factories that supplied them.

Faced with growing criticism, the fashion industry has begun to respond. Many companies now offer clothes made from organic cotton or recycled polyester, and some run schemes in which customers can return old clothes to shops. Critics argue, however, that such initiatives are small compared with the volume of new clothing being produced, and that recycling is of limited value while the technology for turning old garments back into fibre of good quality remains in its early stages. Some describe these efforts as 'greenwashing': presenting a business as more environmentally friendly than it really is.

Governments have also begun to act. In France, a law passed in 2020 made it illegal for companies to destroy unsold clothing and other non-food products, requiring them instead to donate or recycle them. Other proposals include making producers financially responsible for collecting and processing their products at the end of their life, and requiring labels that show the environmental impact of a garment. Such measures aim to change the behaviour of companies, but many experts believe that lasting change will also depend on consumers.

There are signs that attitudes are shifting. The market for second-hand clothing has grown rapidly, helped by websites and apps that make buying and selling used items easy, and clothing rental services have appeared for special occasions. Repair is also enjoying a revival. Nevertheless, the simplest solution may be the least fashionable one: buying fewer clothes of better quality and wearing them for longer. One study after another suggests that extending the life of a garment is among the most effective ways of reducing its environmental impact.

This change is largely the result of a business model known as fast fashion. Traditional fashion companies planned their collections many months in advance and released them in two main seasons each year. Fast-fashion retailers, by contrast, design, manufacture and deliver new styles in a matter of weeks, responding quickly to trends seen on catwalks, in celebrity photographs or, increasingly, on social media. Their shops receive new stock constantly, which encourages customers to visit often and to buy before a style disappears. Prices are kept low by producing in very large quantities in countries where wages are low.

The environmental costs of this model begin with raw materials. Cotton is one of the world's most water-intensive crops: one widely quoted estimate suggests that around 2,700 litres of water are needed to produce the cotton for a single T-shirt. Irrigation for cotton growing contributed to one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century, the shrinking of the Aral Sea in Central Asia. Synthetic fibres, which now make up the majority of the fibre used in clothing, avoid this problem, but they are made from oil, and dyeing and finishing fabric of all kinds uses large amounts of energy and chemicals.

The problems continue long after clothes are sold. A report published in 2017 by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation calculated that the equivalent of one rubbish truck full of textiles is sent to landfill or burned every second, and that less than one per cent of the material used to make clothing is recycled into new clothing. Much of what is donated to charity in wealthy countries is exported, and some ends up in markets in countries such as Ghana, where traders say that a growing share of the bales they buy is of such poor quality that it cannot be sold and must be thrown away.

There are human costs as well. The low prices of fast fashion depend on low wages in countries such as Bangladesh, Cambodia and Vietnam, and working conditions in some factories are poor or dangerous. In April 2013, the Rana Plaza building near Dhaka in Bangladesh, which housed several garment factories, collapsed, killing more than eleven hundred people. Workers had been ordered to return to the building the day after cracks had appeared in its walls. The disaster led many international brands to sign an agreement to fund independent safety inspections of the factories that supplied them.

Faced with growing criticism, the fashion industry has begun to respond. Many companies now offer clothes made from organic cotton or recycled polyester, and some run schemes in which customers can return old clothes to shops. Critics argue, however, that such initiatives are small compared with the volume of new clothing being produced, and that recycling is of limited value while the technology for turning old garments back into fibre of good quality remains in its early stages. Some describe these efforts as 'greenwashing': presenting a business as more environmentally friendly than it really is.

Governments have also begun to act. In France, a law passed in 2020 made it illegal for companies to destroy unsold clothing and other non-food products, requiring them instead to donate or recycle them. Other proposals include making producers financially responsible for collecting and processing their products at the end of their life, and requiring labels that show the environmental impact of a garment. Such measures aim to change the behaviour of companies, but many experts believe that lasting change will also depend on consumers.

There are signs that attitudes are shifting. The market for second-hand clothing has grown rapidly, helped by websites and apps that make buying and selling used items easy, and clothing rental services have appeared for special occasions. Repair is also enjoying a revival. Nevertheless, the simplest solution may be the least fashionable one: buying fewer clothes of better quality and wearing them for longer. One study after another suggests that extending the life of a garment is among the most effective ways of reducing its environmental impact.

reading.title: Should fashion designs be protected from copying?
paragraphs: Within days of a new collection appearing on the catwalk, cheaper versions of its most striking pieces often appear in high-street shops. To the designers concerned, this can feel like theft. A novelist whose book is copied, or a musician whose song is reproduced without permission, can usually take legal action. Yet in many countries, a designer whose dress is copied has surprisingly little protection. Whether that situation is unfair, or whether it is actually good for fashion, is a question that has divided lawyers, economists and designers themselves.

The legal position varies considerably from one country to another. In the United States, copyright law has traditionally treated clothing as a 'useful article', meaning that its practical function prevents it from being protected in the way that a painting or a sculpture would be. Brand names and logos can be registered as trademarks, and a small number of genuinely new technical features can be patented, but the overall shape and cut of a garment are generally free for anyone to copy. Several bills that would have created special protection for fashion designs were introduced in the US Congress from 2006 onwards, but none of them became law.

There has been one notable change. In 2017, in a case about cheerleading uniforms, the US Supreme Court ruled that decorative elements of a garment, in that case a pattern of stripes and chevrons, could be protected by copyright if they could be imagined as a work of art separately from the garment itself. The decision was welcomed by many designers, but legal experts disagree about how far it extends, and it does not protect the basic design of clothes.

Europe takes a different approach. Under European Union law, a design that is new and has individual character is automatically protected against copying for three years from the date it is first made public, without any need for registration. Designers who want longer protection can register their designs, which may then be protected for up to twenty-five years. Some European countries go further: France, for instance, has long allowed clothing designs to be protected in a similar way to works of art. Despite this, copying remains widespread in Europe too, partly because legal action is slow and expensive.

Perhaps surprisingly, some researchers argue that weak protection benefits the fashion industry. In an influential article published in 2006, the American law professors Kal Raustiala and Christopher Sprigman described what they called the 'piracy paradox'. They pointed out that the American fashion industry is highly creative and commercially successful despite, or perhaps because of, the freedom to copy. In their view, copying spreads new styles quickly, so that they soon become too common to be exclusive. Fashionable consumers then look for something new, and designers must keep innovating. Copying, in other words, speeds up the cycle of fashion.

Not everyone accepts this argument. Critics point out that it may describe the position of large, established fashion houses well, since they have famous brand names that protect their sales even when their designs are copied. Independent designers are in a much weaker position. A young designer who produces an original garment may see a copy on sale at a fraction of the price before she has had a chance to sell her own, and she is unlikely to have the money to fight a legal battle against a large retailer. For such designers, copying can mean the difference between building a business and abandoning it.

In my view, the critics have the stronger case, although the piracy paradox contains an important truth. Fashion has always depended on borrowing and imitation, and a law that allowed designers to claim ownership of every new sleeve or neckline would be both unworkable and harmful to creativity. But there is a significant difference between being inspired by a trend and producing an almost exact copy of a particular garment within weeks. The current system in countries such as the United States effectively rewards the companies that are best at copying, rather than those that are best at designing.

The European model, which offers short but automatic protection, seems to me a reasonable compromise. Three years is long enough for a designer to benefit from an original idea, but short enough not to prevent the natural spread of styles. What is needed, I believe, is not stronger laws so much as cheaper and quicker ways of enforcing them, so that the protection that exists on paper is available to small designers as well as large ones. Without that, the debate about copying will continue to be decided by those who can afford the best lawyers.

reading.title: Where do the birds go in winter?
paragraphs: Every autumn, millions of birds disappear from the fields and gardens of northern Europe, and every spring they come back. Today, we know that most of them fly south to warmer places, where they can find food during the winter. But for most of human history, nobody really knew where they went, and people had some very strange ideas to explain their disappearance. The story of how the truth was finally discovered is a long one, and it involves thinkers, hunters, teachers and, more recently, scientists with very small machines.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle wrote about birds that seemed to vanish in winter. He believed that some kinds of birds changed into other kinds as the seasons changed. For example, he thought that the redstart, a small bird seen in summer, turned into the robin, which is more common in winter. He also suggested that some birds, such as swallows, hid in holes and slept through the cold months, in the same way that some animals do.

The idea that swallows slept through the winter lasted for a very long time. Some people even believed that they spent the winter at the bottom of lakes and ponds, buried in the mud. Fishermen sometimes claimed that they had pulled sleeping swallows out of the water in their nets, and these stories were repeated in books for many years. In the eighteenth century, the English naturalist Gilbert White, who carefully recorded the birds around his village of Selborne, still wondered whether some swallows might stay hidden in Britain. One writer of the time, Charles Morton, offered an even more surprising answer: he suggested that birds flew to the Moon.

The first clear proof that birds travel very long distances came in 1822, in a village in northern Germany. A hunter shot a white stork that had a long wooden spear through its neck. The spear had been made in central Africa. Amazingly, the bird had survived and flown all the way back to Europe with the spear still in its body. The stork, now known by the German name Pfeilstorch, meaning 'arrow stork', can still be seen in a university museum in the city of Rostock. Since then, around twenty more storks with African spears or arrows have been found in Germany. Together, these birds gave people the first real evidence that storks spend the winter in Africa, thousands of kilometres away.

The next big step came at the end of the nineteenth century. In 1899, a Danish schoolteacher named Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen put small metal rings on the legs of young starlings. Each ring had a number and his address on it. When people found ringed birds and sent the rings back to him, he could see how far the birds had travelled. This method, called bird ringing, soon spread to other countries, and it is still used today. Millions of birds have been ringed, and the results have shown the routes of hundreds of different species.

Ringing has one big problem, however. A ring tells scientists only where a bird started and where it was found. It does not show the route the bird took in between. In recent years, new technology has helped to solve this problem. Scientists now attach tiny tracking devices to birds. Some of these devices weigh less than a gram, so they can be carried even by small songbirds. They record information about the bird's position every day, and some can send it by satellite. When the bird is caught again, or when the information arrives, scientists can draw a map of its whole journey, including every place where it stopped to rest.

This technology has produced some remarkable discoveries. For example, in a study published in 2016, Swedish scientists found that common swifts can stay in the air for about ten months without landing. They eat, drink and even sleep while flying. Other studies have shown that the bar-tailed godwit, a bird that feeds on muddy coasts, can fly from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping, a journey of more than eleven thousand kilometres. During this flight, it does not eat or drink at all.

Even with modern technology, there is still much that we do not understand about migration. Scientists are still studying how birds find their way, how young birds know where to go on their first journey, and how climate change is affecting the timing of migration. But we have come a very long way from the days when people believed that swallows slept under water, or that birds flew to the Moon.
