But for most of human history, nobody really knew where they went, and people had some very strange ideas to explain their disappearance. The story of how the truth was finally discovered is a long one, and it involves thinkers, hunters, teachers and, more recently, scientists with very small machines.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle wrote about birds that seemed to vanish in winter. He believed that some kinds of birds changed into other kinds as the seasons changed. For example, he thought that the redstart, a small bird seen in summer, turned into the robin, which is more common in winter. He also suggested that some birds, such as swallows, hid in holes and slept through the cold months, in the same way that some animals do.

The idea that swallows slept through the winter lasted for a very long time. Some people even believed that they spent the winter at the bottom of lakes and ponds, buried in the mud. Fishermen sometimes claimed that they had pulled sleeping swallows out of the water in their nets, and these stories were repeated in books for many years. In the eighteenth century, the English naturalist Gilbert White, who carefully recorded the birds around his village of Selborne, still wondered whether some swallows might stay hidden in Britain. One writer of the time, Charles Morton, offered an even more surprising answer: he suggested that birds flew to the Moon.

The first clear proof that birds travel very long distances came in 1822, in a village in northern Germany. A hunter shot a white stork that had a long wooden spear through its neck. The spear had been made in central Africa. Amazingly, the bird had survived and flown all the way back to Europe with the spear still in its body. The stork, now known by the German name Pfeilstorch, meaning 'arrow stork', can still be seen in a university museum in the city of Rostock. Since then, around twenty more storks with African spears or arrows have been found in Germany. Together, these birds gave people the first real evidence that storks spend the winter in Africa, thousands of kilometres away.

The next big step came at the end of the nineteenth century. In 1899, a Danish schoolteacher named Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen put small metal rings on the legs of young starlings. Each ring had a number and his address on it. When people found ringed birds and sent the rings back to him, he could see how far the birds had travelled. This method, called bird ringing, soon spread to other countries, and it is still used today. Millions of birds have been ringed, and the results have shown the routes of hundreds of different species.

Ringing has one big problem, however. A ring tells scientists only where a bird started and where it was found. It does not show the route the bird took in between. In recent years, new technology has helped to solve this problem. Scientists now attach tiny tracking devices to birds. Some of these devices weigh less than a gram, so they can be carried even by small songbirds. They record information about the bird's position every day, and some can send it by satellite. When the bird is caught again, or when the information arrives, scientists can draw a map of its whole journey, including every place where it stopped to rest.

This technology has produced some remarkable discoveries. For example, in a study published in 2016, Swedish scientists found that common swifts can stay in the air for about ten months without landing. They eat, drink and even sleep while flying. Other studies have shown that the bar-tailed godwit, a bird that feeds on muddy coasts, can fly from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping, a journey of more than eleven thousand kilometres. During this flight, it does not eat or drink at all.

Even with modern technology, there is still much that we do not understand about migration. Scientists are still studying how birds find their way, how young birds know where to go on their first journey, and how climate change is affecting the timing of migration. But we have come a very long way from the days when people believed that swallows slept under water, or that birds flew to the Moon.

reading.title: How do birds find their way?
paragraphs: Each year, billions of birds migrate between the places where they breed and the places where they spend the winter. Many of them travel thousands of kilometres, often at night and across seas, deserts and mountains. What is even more amazing is that many birds return to exactly the same garden, field or nest every year. Some young birds make their first journey completely alone. The common cuckoo, for example, is raised by birds of other species, and its parents leave for Africa before it is old enough to fly. Yet the young cuckoo still finds its way to the right part of Africa without any help.

Before they can make these long journeys, birds must prepare. In late summer, many migrating birds start to eat much more than usual, and they store the extra energy as fat. Some small birds almost double their body weight in just a few weeks. At the same time, they become restless. Scientists have noticed that birds kept in cages at migration time hop and flutter much more than usual, especially at night, and they often face in the direction they would fly if they were free. This shows that the need to migrate, and even its direction, is partly built into birds from birth.

One of the tools birds use to find their way is the sun. In the 1950s, the German scientist Gustav Kramer kept starlings in round cages with windows. At migration time, the birds faced in the direction they wanted to fly. When Kramer used mirrors to change the direction of the sunlight coming into the cage, the birds changed direction too. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, birds also need an internal clock to use it correctly. They seem to know what time it is, and they adjust for the sun's movement.

Many birds, however, migrate at night, when they cannot see the sun. In the 1960s, the American scientist Stephen Emlen studied this problem using a planetarium, a building where pictures of the night sky are shown on a round ceiling. He put young indigo buntings, small blue songbirds, under the artificial sky. The birds faced in the correct direction for migration. When Emlen changed the position of the stars, the birds changed direction as well. His experiments showed that the birds learn the pattern of the stars around the North Star while they are young.

Birds can also find their way when the sky is completely covered by clouds. This is because many birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, scientists in Germany showed that European robins kept in cages with no view of the sky still faced in the correct direction. When the magnetic field around the cage was changed, the robins changed direction. Scientists are still not sure exactly how birds sense the magnetic field. One idea is that special chemicals in their eyes allow them to 'see' it in some way.

As well as these 'compasses', birds use things they can see on the ground. Rivers, coastlines and mountains are like signposts, and many birds follow them on their journeys. Some birds may even use smell. Seabirds such as shearwaters travel long distances over the open ocean, where there are no landmarks at all. Experiments have shown that when these birds cannot smell, they have much more difficulty finding their way home. It seems that most birds use several different methods together, and if one does not work, they can use another.

Migration is a very dangerous time for birds, and many die on the way. Storms can blow them far off course, and some birds become too tired to continue. In cities, bright lights confuse birds that fly at night, and many are killed when they fly into tall buildings with glass windows. On the ground, birds face hunters and cats. But one of the biggest problems is the loss of stopover sites, the places where birds stop to rest and feed during their journey. For example, large areas of mudflats around the Yellow Sea, between China and Korea, have been lost, and these were important feeding places for many birds.

Fortunately, people are finding ways to help. In several cities in North America, programmes called Lights Out ask building owners to turn off unnecessary lights at night during the migration season. Many countries are working together to protect the wetlands and other places along migration routes, because a bird that breeds in one country may depend on places in many others. Ordinary people can help too. Thousands of birdwatchers record the birds they see and share their records online, and scientists use this information to understand how migration is changing.

Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, birds also need an internal clock to use it correctly. They seem to know what time it is, and they adjust for the sun's movement.

Many birds, however, migrate at night, when they cannot see the sun. In the 1960s, the American scientist Stephen Emlen studied this problem using a planetarium, a building where pictures of the night sky are shown on a round ceiling. He put young indigo buntings, small blue songbirds, under the artificial sky. The birds faced in the correct direction for migration. When Emlen changed the position of the stars, the birds changed direction as well. His experiments showed that the birds learn the pattern of the stars around the North Star while they are young.

Birds can also find their way when the sky is completely covered by clouds. This is because many birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, scientists in Germany showed that European robins kept in cages with no view of the sky still faced in the correct direction. When the magnetic field around the cage was changed, the robins changed direction. Scientists are still not sure exactly how birds sense the magnetic field. One idea is that special chemicals in their eyes allow them to 'see' it in some way.

As well as these 'compasses', birds use things they can see on the ground. Rivers, coastlines and mountains are like signposts, and many birds follow them on their journeys. Some birds may even use smell. Seabirds such as shearwaters travel long distances over the open ocean, where there are no landmarks at all. Experiments have shown that when these birds cannot smell, they have much more difficulty finding their way home. It seems that most birds use several different methods together, and if one does not work, they can use another.

Migration is a very dangerous time for birds, and many die on the way. Storms can blow them far off course, and some birds become too tired to continue. In cities, bright lights confuse birds that fly at night, and many are killed when they fly into tall buildings with glass windows. On the ground, birds face hunters and cats. But one of the biggest problems is the loss of stopover sites, the places where birds stop to rest and feed during their journey. For example, large areas of mudflats around the Yellow Sea, between China and Korea, have been lost, and these were important feeding places for many birds.

Fortunately, people are finding ways to help. In several cities in North America, programmes called Lights Out ask building owners to turn off unnecessary lights at night during the migration season. Many countries are working together to protect the wetlands and other places along migration routes, because a bird that breeds in one country may depend on places in many others. Ordinary people can help too. Thousands of birdwatchers record the birds they see and share their records online, and scientists use this information to understand how migration is changing.

reading.title: Should we feed garden birds?
paragraphs: Feeding wild birds is one of the most popular ways in which people connect with nature. In Britain, it is thought that around half of all households put out food for birds at some time during the year, and people spend large amounts of money on bird seed, peanuts and feeders. Most people do it because they enjoy watching the birds and because they believe they are helping them. But is feeding birds always a good thing? Scientists have discovered that the answer is more complicated than it might seem.

There is good evidence that feeding helps some birds, especially in winter. When the weather is cold and the days are short, small birds have very little time to find enough food to survive the long nights. A full feeder can make a real difference. Some species have done particularly well. The goldfinch, a small, colourful bird, was once quite rare in British gardens, but it has become a common visitor over the last few decades. Many experts think this is partly because people have started to offer new types of food, such as sunflower hearts and nyjer seed, which goldfinches love.

Feeding can even change the way birds migrate. Blackcaps are small birds that breed in central Europe, in countries such as Germany and Austria. Most of them traditionally flew south-west to spend the winter in Spain and Portugal. Since the 1960s, however, a growing number have flown north-west instead, to spend the winter in Britain and Ireland. Researchers believe that garden feeding is one of the reasons why this new route has been successful. The birds that winter in Britain also have a shorter journey back to their breeding areas in spring.

However, feeding also has some disadvantages. When many birds gather at the same feeder, diseases can spread easily from one bird to another. Since 2005, a disease caused by a tiny parasite has killed large numbers of greenfinches in Britain, and the number of greenfinches has fallen sharply. The disease spreads through food and water that have been touched by infected birds. For this reason, experts advise people to clean their feeders and bird baths regularly and to stop feeding for a while if they see sick birds.

Scientists have also found that feeding can have unexpected effects on breeding. In one British study, blue tits that had been given extra fat during the winter went on to raise fewer chicks the following spring than blue tits that had not been fed. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood. One possibility is that the food helped weaker birds to survive the winter, and these birds were less successful at breeding. Another is that the fat lacked some of the nutrients that the birds needed.

The type of food matters too. In the town of Reading, in southern England, thousands of households regularly feed red kites, large birds of prey that were reintroduced to the area in the 1990s after disappearing from England. Many people put out meat from their kitchens, such as chicken. But this food may not be good for the birds, because it does not contain the bones and fur that they would eat in the wild. Bread is another common problem. It fills birds up but gives them very little of the energy and goodness they need.

In my view, the evidence shows that feeding birds is generally helpful, but only if it is done carefully. People should choose good-quality food, keep feeders clean and avoid giving birds food that is unhealthy for them, such as bread or salty leftovers. I also believe that feeding should never be seen as a replacement for protecting the places where birds live. Some species, such as the house sparrow, have declined in many cities, and the main reasons appear to be the loss of nesting places and insects rather than a lack of seed.

Feeding birds has one more important benefit, which is that it is good for people. Watching birds in the garden helps people relax, and many birdwatchers say it was a garden feeder that first made them interested in nature. In my opinion, this may be the greatest value of feeding birds. If people care about the birds they see from their windows, they are more likely to support efforts to protect wildlife in the wider countryside.

reading.title: Capturing light: the birth of photography
paragraphs: The principle of the camera obscura, Latin for 'dark room', had been known since ancient times. When light passes through a small hole into a darkened space, an upside-down image of the scene outside appears on the opposite wall. By the eighteenth century, portable versions in the form of wooden boxes with lenses were widely used by artists as an aid to drawing. But the image they produced vanished as soon as the light changed or the box was moved. The challenge facing inventors in the early nineteenth century was not to form an image, but to find a way of fixing it permanently.

The first person to succeed was a French inventor, Nicéphore Niépce. In the mid-1820s he coated a pewter plate with bitumen, a substance that hardens when exposed to light, and placed it in a camera obscura at an upstairs window of his family home in Burgundy. After an exposure that probably lasted at least eight hours, and possibly several days, he washed away the bitumen that had not hardened, leaving a faint image of buildings and a tree. The result, now known as View from the Window at Le Gras and generally dated to 1826 or 1827, is the oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera.

In 1829 Niépce formed a partnership with Louis Daguerre, a theatre designer who was famous in Paris for his huge painted spectacles known as dioramas. Niépce died in 1833, but Daguerre continued the work and discovered that a silver-coated copper plate, made sensitive to light with iodine, could record an image in minutes rather than hours. The image was then developed with mercury vapour and fixed with a salt solution. In 1839, the French government acquired the rights to the process and presented it as a gift to the world. The daguerreotype caused a sensation. Its images were astonishingly detailed, but each one was unique: it could not be copied, and it had to be held at an angle to be seen properly.

Across the Channel, the English scientist William Henry Fox Talbot had been working on a quite different method. Talbot made images on paper treated with silver salts, and in 1841 he patented an improved process called the calotype. Its great advantage was that it produced a negative, in which light and dark were reversed, from which any number of positive prints could be made. The pictures were less sharp than daguerreotypes, because the fibres of the paper blurred the finest details, but the principle of the negative would dominate photography for the next century and a half.

Talbot's friend, the astronomer John Herschel, made several important contributions to the new art. He had discovered as early as 1819 that a chemical now known as sodium thiosulphate could dissolve silver salts, and in 1839 he suggested using it to fix photographic images, removing the silver that had not been exposed to light. The same method is still used by photographers who develop film today. Herschel also popularised the word 'photography', from the Greek for 'drawing with light', and introduced the terms 'negative' and 'positive'.

In 1851, another Englishman, Frederick Scott Archer, introduced the wet collodion process, in which a sticky chemical solution was spread on a sheet of glass. It combined the sharpness of the daguerreotype with the ability of the calotype to produce many prints, and exposures took only a few seconds. Its disadvantage was that each plate had to be coated, exposed and developed while it was still wet, so photographers working outdoors had to carry portable darkrooms with them. When Roger Fenton photographed the Crimean War in 1855, for example, he travelled with a converted van that served as his darkroom.

Photography remained a specialist activity until an American businessman, George Eastman, introduced the Kodak camera in 1888. It came loaded with a roll of flexible film long enough for one hundred pictures. When the film was finished, the owner sent the whole camera back to the company, which developed and printed the pictures and returned the camera loaded with new film. The advertising slogan summed up the idea: 'You press the button, we do the rest.' In 1900, the company introduced the Brownie, a simple cardboard box camera that sold for just one dollar and was aimed partly at children.

Within little more than seventy years, then, photography had changed from an experiment requiring hours of exposure into something that almost anyone could do. Its effect on society was profound. It changed the way news was reported, how families remembered their past and how scientists recorded the natural world. It also forced painters to reconsider their role: if a machine could record appearances accurately, perhaps art should do something else. Some historians see this as one of the forces that led towards Impressionism and, eventually, to abstract art.

reading.title: When the movies learned to talk
paragraphs: For the first thirty years of their existence, films were silent, but cinemas were not. Most screenings were accompanied by live music, ranging from a single pianist in a small-town hall to a full orchestra in a big city picture palace. Some cinemas employed specialists to produce sound effects, and in Japan, performers known as benshi stood beside the screen, narrating the story and voicing the characters. Silent films had developed their own sophisticated language of gesture, close-up and written intertitles, and many directors regarded the medium as a complete art form in its own right.

Inventors had tried to combine moving pictures with recorded sound almost from the beginning; Thomas Edison's company experimented with the idea in the 1890s. The difficulty was twofold. First, the sound had to be kept precisely in time with the pictures, so that the words matched the movement of the actors' lips. Second, it had to be loud enough to fill a large auditorium, which was impossible before the development of electronic amplification in the 1910s and 1920s.

By the mid-1920s, two competing solutions had emerged. In the sound-on-disc system, the sound was recorded on large gramophone records that were played alongside the film; Warner Bros. adopted this approach under the name Vitaphone. In the sound-on-film system, the sound was printed as an optical track along the edge of the film itself, which made it much easier to keep sound and picture together, even if the film broke and had to be repaired. Although Warner Bros.' early success gave sound-on-disc a head start, sound-on-film proved more reliable and had replaced it within a few years.

The film usually credited with launching the sound era is The Jazz Singer, released by Warner Bros. in October 1927. It was not, in fact, a fully talking picture. Most of it was silent with recorded musical accompaniment, but it included several songs and a few passages of spoken dialogue performed by its star, Al Jolson. Audiences were thrilled to hear him speak, especially his line 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!' The film was a great commercial success, and the first all-talking feature film, Lights of New York, followed in 1928.

The change that followed was remarkably fast. Cinema owners rushed to install sound equipment, and within about three years almost all new Hollywood films had soundtracks. The cost was considerable, and the change came at a difficult moment, as the economic depression that began in 1929 was about to reduce cinema attendance. The transformation also had human victims. Thousands of musicians who had played in cinemas lost their jobs, and although musicians' unions in the United States campaigned against recorded music, they could not stop the change.

Early sound also created new artistic problems. Cameras were noisy, so they had to be shut inside soundproof booths, which made it difficult to move them. Microphones were insensitive, so actors had to stand close to them, and they were often hidden in vases of flowers or lamps on the set. As a result, many early talkies feel static and stagey compared with the fluid camera work of the late silent period. It took several years, and inventions such as the boom microphone and quieter cameras, before directors regained their freedom.

The arrival of sound affected actors in different ways. Stars whose voices did not match their screen image, or who had strong foreign accents, sometimes found their careers in decline, although historians now believe that this was less common than legend suggests, and that changing tastes and studio politics also played a part. Meanwhile, performers trained in the theatre, who were used to speaking lines, were in great demand. The musical comedy Singin' in the Rain, made in 1952, famously exaggerated these difficulties for comic effect.

Sound also created problems for the international film trade. Silent films could be sold anywhere simply by translating their intertitles, but talking films were tied to a single language. Before dubbing and subtitling became common, studios sometimes filmed several versions of the same story in different languages; a Spanish-language version of Dracula, for instance, was shot in 1931 on the same sets as the English version, at night. Some film-makers resisted dialogue altogether. Charlie Chaplin, whose character the Tramp was loved around the world, continued to make films with music and sound effects but almost no dialogue, including City Lights in 1931 and Modern Times in 1936.

In the sound-on-film system, the sound was printed as an optical track along the edge of the film itself, which made it much easier to keep sound and picture together, even if the film broke and had to be repaired. Although Warner Bros.' early success gave sound-on-disc a head start, sound-on-film proved more reliable and had replaced it within a few years.

The film usually credited with launching the sound era is The Jazz Singer, released by Warner Bros. in October 1927. It was not, in fact, a fully talking picture. Most of it was silent with recorded musical accompaniment, but it included several songs and a few passages of spoken dialogue performed by its star, Al Jolson. Audiences were thrilled to hear him speak, especially his line 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!' The film was a great commercial success, and the first all-talking feature film, Lights of New York, followed in 1928.

The change that followed was remarkably fast. Cinema owners rushed to install sound equipment, and within about three years almost all new Hollywood films had soundtracks. The cost was considerable, and the change came at a difficult moment, as the economic depression that began in 1929 was about to reduce cinema attendance. The transformation also had human victims. Thousands of musicians who had played in cinemas lost their jobs, and although musicians' unions in the United States campaigned against recorded music, they could not stop the change.

Early sound also created new artistic problems. Cameras were noisy, so they had to be shut inside soundproof booths, which made it difficult to move them. Microphones were insensitive, so actors had to stand close to them, and they were often hidden in vases of flowers or lamps on the set. As a result, many early talkies feel static and stagey compared with the fluid camera work of the late silent period. It took several years, and inventions such as the boom microphone and quieter cameras, before directors regained their freedom.

The arrival of sound affected actors in different ways. Stars whose voices did not match their screen image, or who had strong foreign accents, sometimes found their careers in decline, although historians now believe that this was less common than legend suggests, and that changing tastes and studio politics also played a part. Meanwhile, performers trained in the theatre, who were used to speaking lines, were in great demand. The musical comedy Singin' in the Rain, made in 1952, famously exaggerated these difficulties for comic effect.

Sound also created problems for the international film trade. Silent films could be sold anywhere simply by translating their intertitles, but talking films were tied to a single language. Before dubbing and subtitling became common, studios sometimes filmed several versions of the same story in different languages; a Spanish-language version of Dracula, for instance, was shot in 1931 on the same sets as the English version, at night. Some film-makers resisted dialogue altogether. Charlie Chaplin, whose character the Tramp was loved around the world, continued to make films with music and sound effects but almost no dialogue, including City Lights in 1931 and Modern Times in 1936.

reading.title: Will the cinema survive?
paragraphs: Ever since the first audiences paid to watch moving pictures in the 1890s, the cinema has faced predictions of its death. Each new technology that brought moving images into the home, from television to video and now streaming services, was expected to empty the auditoriums. Yet cinemas are still with us, and some of the most successful films in history have been released in the last two decades. Understanding how cinemas survived earlier threats may help us to judge whether they can survive the current one.

The first and most damaging challenge came from television. In the United States, cinema attendance reached its highest levels in the 1940s, when a large proportion of the population went to the pictures every week. As television sets spread rapidly through American homes in the 1950s, attendance fell steeply, roughly halving between the late 1940s and the end of the decade, and thousands of cinemas closed. In Britain, admissions peaked in 1946 at more than 1.6 billion and then went into a long decline that lasted almost forty years.

Hollywood's response was to offer what the small black-and-white television screen could not: spectacle. Studios promoted widescreen formats such as CinemaScope, which was introduced in 1953 with the biblical epic The Robe, along with colour and stereo sound. There was also a brief craze for 3D films in the early 1950s, which faded within a couple of years, partly because audiences found the glasses uncomfortable. The format returned with far greater success in 2009, when James Cameron's Avatar became the highest-earning film ever made.

The next threat was home video. When video cassette recorders became widely available in the late 1970s and early 1980s, many in the film industry feared the worst. In 1982, Jack Valenti, the head of the Motion Picture Association of America, told the US Congress that the video recorder was to the film industry what the Boston Strangler was to a woman home alone. In fact, the opposite happened: sales and rentals of videos became one of the studios' largest sources of income, and the chance to watch films again at home seems, if anything, to have increased interest in seeing new ones at the cinema.

At the same time, cinemas themselves were changing. The multiplex, a single building containing many screens, spread across North America in the 1970s and 1980s. In Britain, where admissions fell to an all-time low in 1984, the first multiplex opened in Milton Keynes the following year. By offering a wide choice of films, convenient parking and comfortable seating, multiplexes helped to reverse the long decline in attendance in many countries.

Streaming presents a different kind of challenge. Netflix, which began as a DVD-by-post company, launched its streaming service in 2007, and it has since been joined by many competitors, some of them owned by the studios themselves. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the change. When cinemas around the world closed in 2020, several studios released major films directly online, or online and in cinemas on the same day. Even after cinemas reopened, the period during which a new film is shown only in cinemas, which had traditionally lasted around three months, became much shorter, often just a few weeks.

Supporters of the cinema argue that it offers something streaming cannot: a shared experience. Laughing or gasping together with strangers in a darkened room is, they say, fundamentally different from watching alone on a sofa, where phones and other distractions compete for attention. Cinemas have also diversified, showing live broadcasts of theatre, opera and sporting events, and offering luxury seating and better food to make a visit feel like a special occasion.

In my view, the cinema will survive, but not in the form that most of us grew up with. The habit of going to the cinema every week, which once sustained thousands of small local cinemas, is unlikely to return. Instead, people will go less often, choosing films they regard as events, and they will expect a higher-quality experience when they do. I suspect this will be good news for large spectacular productions and bad news for medium-budget dramas, which may increasingly be made only for streaming. That would be a real loss, because it is often these smaller films that take creative risks. Cinemas that show a broad range of films, and that are valued by their communities, deserve our support.

reading.title: The glass box that moved the world's plants
paragraphs: In the early nineteenth century, moving living plants around the world was extremely difficult. Plant collectors working in Asia, Africa and the Americas could send home dried specimens and seeds without too much trouble, but living plants rarely survived the long sea voyages. They were exposed to salt spray, sudden changes in temperature and a shortage of fresh water, which sailors were usually unwilling to share. It has been estimated that only a small fraction of the living plants sent to Britain by sea at this time arrived alive.

The solution was discovered almost by accident. Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward was a London doctor with a passion for natural history, especially ferns. He had tried to grow ferns in his garden in the east of the city, but they died, poisoned by the smoke that poured from thousands of coal fires. Around 1829, he placed the cocoon of a moth in a sealed glass bottle with some moist soil, intending to watch the adult insect emerge. Some time later, he noticed that a small fern and some grass had begun to grow in the soil inside the bottle.

Ward was fascinated. The plants inside the bottle were thriving, even though he never watered them and the air of the city outside was badly polluted. He realised that the closed container had created its own tiny climate. During the day, water evaporated from the soil and the leaves, then condensed on the cool glass and ran back down into the soil, so that the plants were never short of moisture. At the same time, the glass protected them from the dirty air. According to Ward's own account, the fern lived in the bottle for several years without any attention.

Ward soon began building larger glazed cases made of wood and glass, and he decided to test whether they could protect plants on long journeys. In 1833 he packed two cases with British ferns and grasses and shipped them to Sydney, in Australia. After a voyage of several months, the plants arrived in good condition. The cases were then refilled with Australian plants for the return journey, and despite extreme changes in temperature during the voyage, most of these plants also reached London alive. In 1842 Ward published a book describing his discovery, and the containers became known as Wardian cases.

The consequences were enormous. For the first time, large numbers of living plants could be moved reliably between continents, and botanic gardens, nurseries and governments quickly took advantage of the new technology. The most famous example involves tea. At the time, China controlled almost all of the world's tea production, and the British East India Company was keen to grow tea in its own territories. In the late 1840s, the Scottish plant collector Robert Fortune travelled through parts of China, often in disguise, and sent thousands of tea plants and seeds to the Himalayas in India in Wardian cases. These plants helped to establish the tea industry of India.

Wardian cases were involved in other major transfers too. In 1876, seeds of the rubber tree were collected in Brazil and taken to the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, near London. Only a small proportion of them germinated, but the seedlings were sent in Wardian cases to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, and to what is now Malaysia and Singapore. Within a few decades, plantations in South-East Asia had overtaken Brazil as the world's main source of natural rubber, with serious economic consequences for the Brazilian Amazon.

The cases also changed life at home. In Victorian Britain they became fashionable pieces of furniture, and many middle-class homes displayed decorative cases filled with ferns. Their popularity was helped by the abolition of a tax on glass in 1845, which made glass much cheaper. The result was a national obsession with ferns, which the writer Charles Kingsley named 'pteridomania', from the scientific word for ferns. Collectors stripped some woodlands of rare species, and books on how to identify and grow ferns sold in large numbers.

Wardian cases remained in use until well into the twentieth century, when air transport and plastic packaging gradually replaced them. Their legacy, however, is mixed. They made possible the spread of valuable crops and garden plants across the globe, but they also carried uninvited passengers, such as insects, fungi and weeds, which travelled along with the plants. Today, strict rules on moving plants between countries try to prevent the spread of pests and diseases, while the modern terrarium, a glass container for growing small plants indoors, is a direct descendant of Ward's simple bottle.

reading.title: The hidden partnership beneath our feet
paragraphs: If you dig up a handful of soil from a forest floor and look at it closely, you may see fine white threads running through it. These are the hyphae of fungi, and many of them are connected to the roots of the plants growing above. This association between fungi and plant roots is called a mycorrhiza, from the Greek words for 'fungus' and 'root'. It is one of the most widespread partnerships in nature: the great majority of land plants, including most crops and trees, form mycorrhizas of some kind.

The arrangement benefits both partners. Fungal hyphae are much thinner than even the finest roots, so they can spread through the soil and reach into tiny spaces that roots cannot enter. They are particularly good at absorbing water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, which they pass to the plant. In return, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars that it produces by photosynthesis. Because fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight, this supply is essential to them, and plants may give a significant share of the carbon they produce to their fungal partners.

The term mycorrhiza was introduced in 1885 by the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, who was among the first to suggest that the relationship was beneficial rather than a form of disease. Since then, scientists have identified two main types. In the first, the fungus actually enters the cells of the root, forming tiny branched structures inside them; this type is found in most herbs, grasses and crop plants. In the second, the fungus forms a dense covering around the outside of the root and grows between its cells; this is typical of many trees, including pines, oaks and birches.

The partnership is extremely ancient. Fossils from the Rhynie chert, a rock formation in Scotland about 400 million years old, contain some of the earliest known land plants, and fungi can be seen inside their tissues in structures very similar to those of modern mycorrhizas. Many scientists believe that fungal partners helped the first plants to move from water onto land, at a time when there was no proper soil and nutrients were hard to obtain.

In recent decades, the subject has attracted public attention for a different reason. In 1997, the Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard and her colleagues published a study in the journal Nature showing that carbon could move between birch and Douglas fir trees in a forest in British Columbia, apparently through fungal connections between their roots. The journal described the idea on its cover as the 'wood wide web'. Over the following years, the notion of trees sharing resources and even communicating through underground networks became popular, and it was spread further by best-selling books, including Simard's own Finding the Mother Tree.

Not all scientists are convinced. In 2023, a review led by Justine Karst, with her colleagues Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema, examined the evidence for three widely repeated claims: that fungal networks connecting trees are common in forests, that resources passed through them help young trees to survive, and that older trees send resources preferentially to their own offspring. The authors concluded that the evidence for all three was weak or mixed, and that some popular accounts had gone well beyond what the research actually showed. They did not deny that mycorrhizas are important; their concern was that uncertain findings were being presented as established fact.

There is, however, no dispute about some of the more remarkable relationships. Orchids produce extremely small seeds that contain almost no stored food, and in nature they cannot germinate unless they are infected by a suitable fungus that supplies them with nutrients. Some plants have gone further still. The ghost plant of North America, for example, is completely white because it contains no chlorophyll and cannot carry out photosynthesis at all. Instead, it obtains all its carbon from fungi, which in turn obtain it from nearby trees.

These partnerships also matter for agriculture. Practices such as frequent ploughing and heavy use of chemical fertilisers can reduce the amount of mycorrhizal fungi in farm soils, because the fungal networks are broken up and plants that are given plenty of phosphorus have less need for their fungal partners. Some farmers and researchers are now exploring ways of encouraging these fungi, for example by reducing ploughing, in the hope of growing healthy crops with fewer chemical inputs. As with the debate over the wood wide web, the challenge is to separate promising ideas from proven results.

Many scientists believe that fungal partners helped the first plants to move from water onto land, at a time when there was no proper soil and nutrients were hard to obtain.

In recent decades, the subject has attracted public attention for a different reason. In 1997, the Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard and her colleagues published a study in the journal Nature showing that carbon could move between birch and Douglas fir trees in a forest in British Columbia, apparently through fungal connections between their roots. The journal described the idea on its cover as the 'wood wide web'. Over the following years, the notion of trees sharing resources and even communicating through underground networks became popular, and it was spread further by best-selling books, including Simard's own Finding the Mother Tree.

Not all scientists are convinced. In 2023, a review led by Justine Karst, with her colleagues Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema, examined the evidence for three widely repeated claims: that fungal networks connecting trees are common in forests, that resources passed through them help young trees to survive, and that older trees send resources preferentially to their own offspring. The authors concluded that the evidence for all three was weak or mixed, and that some popular accounts had gone well beyond what the research actually showed. They did not deny that mycorrhizas are important; their concern was that uncertain findings were being presented as established fact.

There is, however, no dispute about some of the more remarkable relationships. Orchids produce extremely small seeds that contain almost no stored food, and in nature they cannot germinate unless they are infected by a suitable fungus that supplies them with nutrients. Some plants have gone further still. The ghost plant of North America, for example, is completely white because it contains no chlorophyll and cannot carry out photosynthesis at all. Practices such as frequent ploughing and heavy use of chemical fertilisers can reduce the amount of mycorrhizal fungi in farm soils, because the fungal networks are broken up and plants that are given plenty of phosphorus have less need for their fungal partners. Some farmers and researchers are now exploring ways of encouraging these fungi, for example by reducing ploughing, in the hope of growing healthy crops with fewer chemical inputs. reading.title: Should we judge plants by where they come from?
paragraphs: Walk along almost any riverbank in Britain in late summer and you are likely to see tall stems of Himalayan balsam, with their pink flowers and exploding seed pods. Nearby, there may be dense stands of Japanese knotweed, and in the woods, thick clumps of rhododendron. All three plants were brought to Britain deliberately, as attractive additions to gardens, and all three are now widely regarded as serious pests. They are examples of what ecologists call invasive species: organisms introduced by humans to places outside their natural range, where they spread and cause harm.

The study of invasions is often traced back to the British ecologist Charles Elton, whose book The Ecology of Invasions by Animals and Plants, published in 1958, warned that the movement of species around the world was one of the great forces changing nature. Since then, the evidence of harm has grown. A major report published in 2023 by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, a United Nations-backed body, concluded that invasive species had been a major factor in around sixty per cent of recorded extinctions of plants and animals, and that they cost the world economy more than four hundred billion dollars a year.

It is important, however, to keep this in proportion. Most introduced species never become a problem. In the 1990s, the ecologists Mark Williamson and Alastair Fitter proposed what they called the 'tens rule': roughly one in ten introduced species becomes established in the wild, and roughly one in ten of those becomes a pest. The figures are only approximate, but they make a useful point. The vast majority of the plants growing in our gardens, from potatoes and tomatoes to roses and tulips, were brought from elsewhere and cause no harm at all.

In 2011, a group of nineteen ecologists led by Mark Davis published a short article in Nature with the provocative title 'Don't judge species on their origins'. They argued that conservationists had become too focused on whether a species was native or not, and that they should instead judge each species by its effects on the environment, on human health and on the economy. Some introduced species, they pointed out, provide benefits; in parts of the south-western United States, for example, an endangered bird, the south-western willow flycatcher, frequently nests in tamarisk, an introduced tree that many land managers have spent large sums trying to remove.

The article provoked a sharp response. Daniel Simberloff, a leading invasion biologist, organised a reply signed by more than a hundred and forty scientists, who argued that the authors had misrepresented the field. Most conservationists, they said, already concentrated on harmful species, and the origin of a species is relevant because introduced species are far more likely than native ones to cause dramatic and unexpected damage. Other writers have taken the opposite side. The British botanist Ken Thompson, in his book Where Do Camels Belong?, questioned whether the distinction between native and alien species is as meaningful as is often assumed, while the ecologist Chris Thomas has argued that, in many regions, human activity has actually increased the number of plant species.

In my view, both sides are partly right. Davis and his colleagues are correct that being non-native is not, in itself, evidence of harm, and that money spent attacking harmless species would be better used elsewhere. Yet Simberloff's group is also right that origin matters, because plants that have arrived without the insects and diseases that controlled them in their native range can spread in ways that native plants rarely do. Japanese knotweed is a case in point. In Britain it has almost no natural enemies, and because the plants here appear to be a single female clone, it spreads not by seed but from small fragments of stem and root, often carried in soil.

The case of knotweed also shows how fear can run ahead of evidence. Its reputation for forcing its way through concrete and damaging houses has made it notorious, and some homeowners have found their properties difficult to sell. Some recent research, however, suggests that its threat to buildings has been exaggerated, and that it causes no more damage than many other large plants. Meanwhile, scientists have released a tiny insect from Japan that feeds only on knotweed, in the hope of controlling it naturally. I believe this careful, evidence-based approach is far more useful than alarm.

Beyond that, however, there is no reason to feel guilty about growing plants from other parts of the world. In my view, the sensible question to ask about any plant is not where it comes from, but what it does. groups.instruction: Questions 1–2. Do the statements agree with the information? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: A packet of seeds can contain several kinds of information, and they should not all be read in the same way. The plant name identifies what the packet is intended to contain. A sowing period gives guidance about timing, while a description of height helps a gardener imagine the mature plant. None of these details guarantees that every seed will develop successfully. Conditions in a particular garden may differ from those assumed by the writer of the instructions.

Imagine two gardeners using seeds from the same packet. One grows them in a sheltered container; the other chooses an exposed bed. Different results would not, by themselves, prove that the label was inaccurate. To investigate a disappointing outcome, the gardener would need to consider preparation, moisture and other conditions rather than selecting a single explanation immediately. The packet is therefore a starting point for a practical decision, not a complete description of every possible growing situation. Clear guidance can acknowledge such limits without becoming so cautious that it provides no useful direction.

paragraphs: An architectural model can make the arrangement of a proposed building easier to understand. A viewer may see how rooms connect or where an entrance sits in relation to a street. But the model's usefulness depends on what it was made to represent. A simple block model may be appropriate for comparing overall shapes, even if it contains no doors or windows. Its missing details do not automatically make it a poor model; they may reflect a deliberately limited purpose.

Problems arise when a viewer treats a representation as evidence for a claim it was not designed to support. A miniature room that looks bright under an exhibition lamp does not establish the amount of daylight the full-sized room will receive. That question needs a method suited to light and the relevant conditions. Designers should explain what a model can and cannot show. Doing so does not weaken the proposal. It allows observers to ask appropriate questions and prevents visual appeal from being mistaken for a completed assessment of performance.

paragraphs: Imagine a school displaying photographs submitted by families for an anniversary exhibition. The pictures may offer rich accounts of particular experiences. They do not necessarily represent every family connected with the school. Some households may have preserved many photographs, while others have none to contribute. The exhibition reflects both the original events and later decisions about what was kept, found and submitted.

This limitation does not make the collection worthless. It changes the questions that can responsibly be asked of it. A photograph can document an occasion or invite further investigation, but counting the activities visible in the collection cannot by itself establish how often all pupils took part in those activities. An organiser could seek additional material from less represented groups and record how contributions were obtained. Even then, the aim should be to broaden understanding rather than announce that every absence has been corrected. Stating how the collection was assembled helps visitors distinguish an engaging set of examples from a representative survey.

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: Two percentages can look directly comparable while referring to different totals. Suppose a hypothetical centre reports that thirty per cent of its workshop participants travelled by bicycle. Another centre reports that twenty per cent of all its visitors cycled. The first figure concerns people attending workshops; the second includes people who came for other reasons. Comparing the figures without noting this distinction would assume that the groups being described were equivalent.

The period covered matters as well. A figure collected during a summer activity programme may not describe behaviour throughout the year. Neither percentage has to be inaccurate for the comparison to be misleading. A careful reader asks what population each number refers to, when the information was collected and how participation was defined. These questions should come before an explanation of why one centre appears more successful. Otherwise, an attractive numerical difference can invite a confident story that the available evidence does not support. The first task is to establish whether the figures answer the same question.

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: A community archive may receive two different accounts of an object. One contributor remembers a wooden box being used to store tools; another recalls seeing it used for sewing materials. These statements need not be mutually exclusive. The box may have served several purposes at different times. An archive that selects one account simply to produce a single neat label risks losing part of the object's history.

However, preserving accounts is not the same as treating every claim as equally well supported. A useful record can identify who supplied an account, when it was recorded and whether other evidence supports it. The archive may distinguish a contributor's recollection from a conclusion reached after examining documents. If new information changes the interpretation, earlier accounts can remain accessible with an explanation of the change. This approach allows visitors to understand how knowledge developed. It also recognises that uncertainty is part of an honest description, rather than a defect that must be concealed by choosing the most confident-sounding story.

reading.title: The value of an unsuccessful prototype

questions.prompt: A prototype may be designed to investigate a limited question.
questions.explanation: A prototype need not test every product feature.
questions.evidenceQuote: answer a narrow question

questions.explanation: The value depends on framing and interpretation.
questions.evidenceQuote: not that every failure proves progress

groups.instruction: Questions 1–2. Do the statements agree with the information? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: A prototype is not necessarily intended to succeed in every respect. It may be built to answer a narrow question before a designer commits to a complete product. Imagine a temporary handle attached to a cardboard model. The assembly might be unsuitable for carrying a heavy load but still useful for investigating where a user's hand naturally falls. Judging it solely by its strength would overlook its intended purpose.

An unsuccessful trial can therefore be informative, provided the result is interpreted carefully. If users cannot find the handle, that may reveal a problem worth addressing. But the designer must consider whether the model differs from the proposed product in ways that affected the result. A missing colour contrast, for example, could influence what users notice. The trial should be described with enough detail to make these limitations visible. The lesson is not that every failure proves progress. It is that a clearly framed trial can produce useful information even when it does not confirm the designer's expectations.

reading.title: Should every instruction include every detail?

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: Instructions can become difficult because they contain too little information, but additional detail is not always the answer. A newcomer may need a clear first step before learning about unusual exceptions. If every exception appears before that step, the reader can struggle to identify what applies to an ordinary case. In my view, guidance should distinguish the usual route from circumstances requiring additional help.

This does not justify hiding information that affects safety or access. A reader must be able to discover relevant alternatives before making a consequential choice. The challenge is to organise detail, not simply to remove it. Headings, examples and a clear route to further assistance can make complexity manageable. I would judge instructions by whether users can complete the intended task and recognise when they need help, rather than by how short the text appears. A brief page that repeatedly sends users in the wrong direction is not an improvement over a longer explanation that supports accurate action.

reading.title: The appeal and limits of a single score

questions.prompt: Why might learners with the same total need different activities?
questions.explanation: Their strengths and weaknesses can be distributed differently.
questions.evidenceQuote: Their totals match, but useful next steps would differ.
options: A. The exercise contains no vocabulary questions.
B. Their performance patterns may differ.

acceptedAnswers: B. Their performance patterns may differ.

questions.explanation: A small sample can support only cautious inferences.
questions.evidenceQuote: too little evidence for confident conclusions
options: A. They always measure too many skills.
B. They cannot produce a raw score.
C. They may be insufficient for a firm judgement.
acceptedAnswers: C. They may be insufficient for a firm judgement.
They may be insufficient for a firm judgement.

groups.instruction: Questions 1–2. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

reading.sourceNote: Original short skill drill. Not a complete IELTS test or an official past paper.
paragraphs: A single score is convenient. It can summarise a result, make a table compact and allow a quick comparison. Yet the convenience can hide differences between the performances being summarised. Imagine two learners receiving the same total on an exercise with several skills. One answers the vocabulary questions well but struggles with inference; the other shows the opposite pattern. Their totals match, but useful next steps would differ.

In my view, an overall result should therefore be accompanied by information that helps a learner act. This need not mean reporting a separate score for every tiny feature. Very small groups of questions may provide too little evidence for confident conclusions. A responsible explanation distinguishes a pattern worth investigating from a secure judgement of ability. The purpose of feedback is not to create the greatest possible quantity of numbers. It is to identify what the available evidence supports, explain its limits and suggest a reasonable next activity. A summary score remains useful when it is treated as a summary rather than a complete diagnosis.

listening.title: Joining a sports centre
listening.contextDescription: A man calls a sports centre to ask about membership options.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Hello, Parkside Leisure Centre, Jenny speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I've just moved to the area and I'm thinking of joining the centre. Could you tell me about the different types of membership?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We have three main options. The first is Off-Peak, which lets you use the gym and the pool on weekdays before four o'clock and all day at weekends. That's twenty-two pounds a month.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Before four on weekdays. That won't really work for me, I'm afraid. I work in an office until half five.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then you'd probably want our Standard membership. That gives you access to the gym, the pool and the sauna at any time the centre is open, which is six in the morning until ten at night. It's thirty-five pounds a month.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And does that include the exercise classes? I'm quite interested in yoga.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Standard members can book classes, but there's a charge of four pounds per class. If you'd like unlimited classes, there's our Premium membership at forty-eight pounds a month. Premium also includes one session a month with a personal trainer and free parking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hmm. How many yoga classes are there each week?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There are five: Monday and Wednesday evenings, Friday lunchtime, and two on Saturday morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: If I went twice a week, Premium would probably be cheaper, wouldn't it? Let me think. I'll go for Premium, I think. Is there a joining fee?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Normally there's a joining fee of thirty pounds, but this month we've got an offer, so there's no fee if you sign up before the end of March.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great timing. Is the pool ever closed to members?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There are swimming lessons for children on weekday afternoons between four and six, when half the pool is reserved, and the whole pool is closed on the first Monday of every month for cleaning. Apart from that, it's open whenever the centre is.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine, I'd be swimming in the evenings anyway. Do you have lockers?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, the lockers in the changing rooms take a one-pound coin, which you get back afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. What else do I need to do?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Before you can use the gym, you have to do an induction. That's a session with one of our instructors, who'll show you how to use the equipment safely and help you plan a programme. It takes about an hour.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Do I need to book that?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, you can book it when you register. Inductions run on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and on Sunday mornings.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sunday morning would suit me best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Fine. Can I take a few details? What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Declan Moynihan. That's M-O-Y-N-I-H-A-N.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Flat 3, 58 Hawthorn Avenue.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: And the postcode?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's NW6 4TR.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. And are there any health conditions we should know about? It's just so the instructor can adapt your programme.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I hurt my knee playing football a couple of years ago. It's fine now, but I avoid running.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: I'll make a note of that, and the instructor will suggest alternatives. Oh, and one more thing. When you come in, please bring a photo for your membership card. Or we can take one here, if that's easier.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll just have it taken there. How do I pay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Membership is paid monthly by direct debit, so you'll need your bank details. The first payment is taken on the day you join.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. And can I cancel if I move again?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, you just need to give one month's notice in writing. There's no minimum contract.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's great. And just to check, can I bring a friend sometimes?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Premium members can bring one guest a month free of charge.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's great. Thanks for your help, Jenny.

listening.title: Volunteering at City Hospital
listening.contextDescription: A volunteer coordinator gives a talk to new hospital volunteers.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Daniel Okafor and I coordinate the volunteer programme here at City Hospital. Some of you have already filled in your application forms, and others are just finding out what's involved, so I'll start with a general overview and then explain the different roles available.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: First of all, why does a hospital need volunteers? The answer is that volunteers don't replace the work of nurses or doctors, and you'll never be asked to give medical care. What you do is free up staff time and make patients' experience a little more comfortable. Research here showed that patients who had regular visits from volunteers felt less anxious and actually rated the quality of their care more highly.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We currently have just over two hundred volunteers, and they range in age from seventeen to eighty-four. The minimum age is sixteen, but anyone under eighteen can only work in certain roles, and needs a signed form from a parent.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: So, what are the roles? Let me run through the main ones. The Welcome Desk is in the main entrance. Volunteers there greet people, give directions and help visitors find their way around, which is more useful than it sounds, because the hospital is a maze. This role is ideal if you're confident talking to strangers, and it's the one most of our younger volunteers start with.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Then there's the Ward Companion role. Companions visit patients on the wards who don't have many visitors of their own, just to chat, read to them or help them with a meal. This is particularly valued on the wards for older patients. Because you're spending time with patients directly, it requires an extra half-day of training, focusing on communication and on confidentiality, which means never discussing patients outside the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The Garden Team looks after the hospital's courtyard garden, which was created by volunteers about ten years ago. You don't need any experience, as long as you don't mind getting your hands dirty, and the team meets every Wednesday morning, whatever the weather.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We also have a Shop and Trolley service. Volunteers run the small shop on the ground floor and take a trolley round the wards twice a day selling newspapers, snacks and toiletries. All the profits go back into the hospital, and last year they paid for new chairs in the children's ward. You'll need to be comfortable handling money for this one.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Finally, Patient Transport. These volunteers use their own cars to drive patients home after appointments, or bring them in from areas with poor public transport. You need to have held a full driving licence for at least three years, and your fuel costs are paid back by the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, practical matters. We ask volunteers to commit to at least one session of three or four hours a week, for a minimum of six months. We know that's a significant commitment, but it takes a few weeks to get to know a role properly, and patients really appreciate seeing familiar faces.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Before you start, we'll need two references and a health check. For the roles involving direct contact with patients, there's also a background check, which can take up to four weeks, so please don't worry if you don't hear from us straight away. Once everything is ready, you'll get a uniform, which is a green polo shirt, and an identity badge, which you must wear at all times while you're in the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Oh, and meals. Volunteers get a free lunch in the staff canteen on any day they do a session of four hours or more. Right, I'll now hand over to Susan, who's been a ward companion for six years, and she'll tell you what a typical day is like.

listening.title: Preparing a presentation on sleep
listening.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Ali and Sophie, plan a seminar presentation on sleep research.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: So, Ali, we've got twenty minutes for the presentation, plus questions. I thought we could start by showing the audience how little sleep students actually get. Maybe a quick poll?

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Good idea. Everyone could put their hand up for how many hours they slept last night. It gets people involved straight away. Then we move into the science.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Right. Shall I do the section on why we sleep? I've read quite a lot about memory.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Yes, go for it. The key point for me is that during sleep, the brain seems to replay what we learned during the day and move it into long-term memory. That's why staying up all night before an exam is such a bad strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I want to mention that study where students who slept after learning a list of words remembered far more the next day than those who stayed awake for the same length of time.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: That's a great example. Then I'll cover the section on teenagers and body clocks. That's what interested me most.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: The idea that teenagers aren't just lazy?

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Right. During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later than in adults or young children. So a fifteen-year-old who can't fall asleep before midnight isn't being difficult; their body clock has genuinely shifted.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: And that's why some schools have experimented with later start times.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Yes. I found a few studies. In one American school district, starting school an hour later led to students sleeping about forty minutes more each night, and their attendance improved. But I need to be careful, because most of these studies are quite small, and it's hard to separate the effect of the start time from other changes the schools made.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Good, you should say that. Our tutor always asks about limitations. What about the section on technology? Everyone talks about phones and blue light.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: I looked into that, and it's more complicated than people think. Some lab studies show that bright screen light delays melatonin, but the effect of a normal phone at normal brightness seems to be quite small. Several researchers now think the bigger problem is what people are doing on the phone, the fact that it keeps the brain alert, rather than the light itself.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Interesting. So we could challenge a popular belief there. Audiences always like that.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Then, to finish, practical advice. Things like keeping regular sleep times, even at weekends.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Actually, I'm not sure we should end on advice. It might sound like a lecture. What if we end by asking the audience a question to start the discussion? Like whether universities should avoid scheduling exams early in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. It connects to the teenage body-clock section, too. Okay, so we end with a discussion question. What about visuals? I was going to put lots of graphs in.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Maybe two or three at most. Our tutor said last time that slides full of data are hard to follow. One clear graph showing sleep by age would be enough for your section.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Fair enough. I'll make sure the axis labels are big enough to read from the back of the room. Last time, nobody could see the numbers on our graph.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Good idea. And let's use the same colours for our slides so it looks like one presentation, not two.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Fair enough. And handouts?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: I'd rather give a one-page summary with our references at the end, so people can follow up if they're interested.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Perfect. Let's have a run-through on Friday, timed, so we know if we're over twenty minutes.

listening.title: Preparing a presentation on sleep
listening.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Ali and Sophie, plan a seminar presentation on sleep research.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: So, Ali, we've got twenty minutes for the presentation, plus questions. I thought we could start by showing the audience how little sleep students actually get. Maybe a quick poll?

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Good idea. Everyone could put their hand up for how many hours they slept last night. It gets people involved straight away. Then we move into the science.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Right. Shall I do the section on why we sleep? I've read quite a lot about memory.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Yes, go for it. The key point for me is that during sleep, the brain seems to replay what we learned during the day and move it into long-term memory. That's why staying up all night before an exam is such a bad strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I want to mention that study where students who slept after learning a list of words remembered far more the next day than those who stayed awake for the same length of time.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: That's a great example. Then I'll cover the section on teenagers and body clocks. That's what interested me most.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: The idea that teenagers aren't just lazy?

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Right. During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later than in adults or young children. So a fifteen-year-old who can't fall asleep before midnight isn't being difficult; their body clock has genuinely shifted.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: And that's why some schools have experimented with later start times.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Yes. I found a few studies. In one American school district, starting school an hour later led to students sleeping about forty minutes more each night, and their attendance improved. But I need to be careful, because most of these studies are quite small, and it's hard to separate the effect of the start time from other changes the schools made.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Good, you should say that. Our tutor always asks about limitations. What about the section on technology? Everyone talks about phones and blue light.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: I looked into that, and it's more complicated than people think. Some lab studies show that bright screen light delays melatonin, but the effect of a normal phone at normal brightness seems to be quite small. Several researchers now think the bigger problem is what people are doing on the phone, the fact that it keeps the brain alert, rather than the light itself.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Interesting. So we could challenge a popular belief there. Audiences always like that.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Then, to finish, practical advice. Things like keeping regular sleep times, even at weekends.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Actually, I'm not sure we should end on advice. It might sound like a lecture. What if we end by asking the audience a question to start the discussion? Like whether universities should avoid scheduling exams early in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. It connects to the teenage body-clock section, too. Okay, so we end with a discussion question. What about visuals? I was going to put lots of graphs in.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Maybe two or three at most. Our tutor said last time that slides full of data are hard to follow. One clear graph showing sleep by age would be enough for your section.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Fair enough. I'll make sure the axis labels are big enough to read from the back of the room. Last time, nobody could see the numbers on our graph.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Good idea. And let's use the same colours for our slides so it looks like one presentation, not two.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Fair enough. And handouts?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: I'd rather give a one-page summary with our references at the end, so people can follow up if they're interested.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.text: Perfect. Let's have a run-through on Friday, timed, so we know if we're over twenty minutes.
