listening.title: How we taste
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course on the science of taste and flavour.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This morning we're looking at taste, one of the senses we probably think about least, even though we use it several times every day. I'm going to look at three things: how the tongue detects taste, why smell is so important for flavour, and what affects individual differences in taste.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So let's start with the tongue. If you look closely at your tongue in a mirror, you'll see it's covered in tiny bumps. These aren't taste buds themselves, as many people think. They're called papillae, and the taste buds are found within them. An adult has somewhere between two thousand and eight thousand taste buds, and each one contains between fifty and a hundred and fifty receptor cells. These cells are replaced roughly every ten days, which is why your sense of taste recovers so quickly after you burn your tongue on hot coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For a long time, scientists recognised four basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty and bitter. In the early twentieth century, a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda proposed a fifth, which he called umami, from the Japanese word for delicious. Umami is the savoury taste found in foods like meat, cheese, mushrooms and tomatoes. It took almost a century for Western scientists to accept it, because it wasn't until around the year 2000 that the specific receptor for umami on the tongue was identified.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, you may have seen a diagram called the tongue map, which shows sweet at the tip, bitter at the back, and so on. I'm afraid this is a myth. It came from a mistranslation of a German paper published in 1901, which said only that some areas were slightly more sensitive than others. In fact, all five tastes can be detected on all parts of the tongue.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why do we have these particular tastes? The usual explanation is evolutionary. Sweetness signals energy-rich food, while salt is needed for our nerves and muscles to work properly. Bitterness, on the other hand, often indicates poison, which is why most people find strongly bitter foods unpleasant, and why young children are particularly sensitive to it. Sourness may warn us of food that has gone bad, although it also helps us identify fruit that's rich in vitamin C.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But the tongue is only part of the story. What we call flavour is actually a combination of taste and smell, and smell contributes far more than taste. When you chew, air carrying aromas from the food travels up the back of your throat into your nose, where it reaches the olfactory receptors. This is why food seems tasteless when you have a cold and your nose is blocked. You can test this yourself: hold your nose and eat a jelly bean, and you'll probably only notice that it's sweet. Let go, and suddenly you can tell whether it's cherry or lemon.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Our perception of flavour is also influenced by our other senses, especially sight. In one well-known experiment, wine experts were given white wine that had been coloured red with a tasteless dye, and they described it using words normally used for red wine. Sound matters too. Crisps are rated as fresher and crunchier when the sound of the crunch is made louder through headphones.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, why do people's tastes differ so much? Part of the answer is genetic. About a quarter of people are what researchers call supertasters. They have more taste buds than average and find bitter foods, such as coffee, dark chocolate or certain green vegetables, much more intense. At the other end, around a quarter are non-tasters, who are less sensitive. Age plays a role as well: the number of taste buds gradually declines, which is one reason older people often add more salt to their food.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But culture and experience are probably the most important factors. Most people dislike bitter or very spicy foods the first time they try them, yet many come to enjoy them after repeated exposure. Children may need to try a new vegetable ten or fifteen times before they accept it, which is a useful thing for parents to know. Next time, we'll look at how food companies use this research when they develop new products.

listening.title: Booking a farm-stay holiday
listening.contextDescription: A woman phones a farm that offers holiday accommodation.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Hello, Brookfield Farm, Sarah speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh hi, I saw your website and I'm interested in booking a farm holiday for my family. Could you tell me a bit about what you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Of course. We've got three holiday cottages on the farm. Two of them sleep four people, and the larger one, which is called the Old Barn, sleeps six.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: There are five of us, me, my husband and three children, so I guess we'd need the Old Barn.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, that would be best. It has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a big kitchen. All our cottages are self-catering, but we do sell eggs, milk and vegetables from the farm shop, and there's a village shop about two miles away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sounds lovely. What sort of farm is it?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Mainly dairy. We milk about a hundred and twenty cows. We also keep a small flock of sheep, some pigs and chickens, and the children usually love the goats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can the kids help with the animals?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: They can. Every morning at eight we have what we call the farm walk. Guests can come with me to collect the eggs and feed the calves and the goats. It lasts about an hour. It's included in the price, but children have to be accompanied by an adult.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can they watch the cows being milked?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a viewing gallery above the milking parlour. Milking happens twice a day, at half past five in the morning and four in the afternoon. Most families prefer the afternoon one, for obvious reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I can imagine. Now, we were thinking about the first week of August. Is the Old Barn available?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Let me look. I'm afraid the first week of August is booked. But it's free the following week, from Saturday the ninth to Saturday the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That should be okay. What's the price for that week?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: In August, the Old Barn is nine hundred and seventy-five pounds for the week. That includes bed linen, towels, heating and electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's within our budget. Is there anything extra to pay for?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Only if you bring a dog, which is fifteen pounds for the week. And we can provide a cot or a high chair if you have a baby, at no extra charge.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No dog and no baby, thankfully. What else is there to do in the area?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lots. The coast is about twenty minutes' drive. There's a lovely sandy beach at Westbay. And if you like walking, there's a footpath that goes right through the farm along the river to the castle. Cycling is popular too. We have bikes guests can borrow, though we don't have any child seats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My youngest is nine, so she can ride her own bike. Do we need a car while we're there?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: It helps, because buses are only every two hours. But if you come by train, I can collect you from the station at Millbridge. There's a charge of ten pounds each way for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll probably drive, but that's useful to know. How do I book?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: You can book online, or I can take your details now. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you book, and the rest four weeks before you arrive. If you cancel more than eight weeks before, you get the deposit back.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do it now. My name's Karen Whitlock, W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lovely, Karen. And how did you hear about us?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A friend of mine stayed with you last year. She said it was the best holiday her kids had ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Oh, that's nice to hear. Let me take your card details for the deposit.

listening.contextDescription: A woman phones a farm that offers holiday accommodation.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Hello, Brookfield Farm, Sarah speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh hi, I saw your website and I'm interested in booking a farm holiday for my family. Could you tell me a bit about what you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Of course. We've got three holiday cottages on the farm. Two of them sleep four people, and the larger one, which is called the Old Barn, sleeps six.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: There are five of us, me, my husband and three children, so I guess we'd need the Old Barn.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, that would be best. It has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a big kitchen. All our cottages are self-catering, but we do sell eggs, milk and vegetables from the farm shop, and there's a village shop about two miles away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sounds lovely. What sort of farm is it?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Mainly dairy. We milk about a hundred and twenty cows. We also keep a small flock of sheep, some pigs and chickens, and the children usually love the goats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can the kids help with the animals?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: They can. Every morning at eight we have what we call the farm walk. Guests can come with me to collect the eggs and feed the calves and the goats. It lasts about an hour. It's included in the price, but children have to be accompanied by an adult.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can they watch the cows being milked?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a viewing gallery above the milking parlour. Milking happens twice a day, at half past five in the morning and four in the afternoon. Most families prefer the afternoon one, for obvious reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I can imagine. Now, we were thinking about the first week of August. Is the Old Barn available?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Let me look. I'm afraid the first week of August is booked. But it's free the following week, from Saturday the ninth to Saturday the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That should be okay. What's the price for that week?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: In August, the Old Barn is nine hundred and seventy-five pounds for the week. That includes bed linen, towels, heating and electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's within our budget. Is there anything extra to pay for?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Only if you bring a dog, which is fifteen pounds for the week. And we can provide a cot or a high chair if you have a baby, at no extra charge.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No dog and no baby, thankfully. What else is there to do in the area?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lots. The coast is about twenty minutes' drive. There's a lovely sandy beach at Westbay. And if you like walking, there's a footpath that goes right through the farm along the river to the castle. Cycling is popular too. We have bikes guests can borrow, though we don't have any child seats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My youngest is nine, so she can ride her own bike. Do we need a car while we're there?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: It helps, because buses are only every two hours. But if you come by train, I can collect you from the station at Millbridge. There's a charge of ten pounds each way for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll probably drive, but that's useful to know. How do I book?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: You can book online, or I can take your details now. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you book, and the rest four weeks before you arrive. If you cancel more than eight weeks before, you get the deposit back.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do it now. My name's Karen Whitlock, W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lovely, Karen. And how did you hear about us?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A friend of mine stayed with you last year. She said it was the best holiday her kids had ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Oh, that's nice to hear. Let me take your card details for the deposit.

questions.explanation: The Old Barn costs £975 in August.

questions.explanation: The beach is at Westbay.
questions.evidenceQuote: a lovely sandy beach at Westbay

listening.title: Opening day at the city farm
listening.contextDescription: The manager of a community city farm speaks to visitors at an open day.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside City Farm's annual open day. I'm Grace Hollis, the farm manager. Thanks for joining us, especially those of you who came despite the rain. I'll tell you a little about the farm and the programme for today, and then you're free to explore.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The farm was started thirty years ago by a group of local residents who wanted to turn an abandoned railway yard into something useful for the community. In the early days, it was run entirely by volunteers. Today we have eight paid staff, but volunteers are still at the heart of everything we do. Last year, over two hundred people gave their time, from schoolchildren to retired engineers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Our main purpose is education. Many children growing up in the city have never seen a cow or a pig up close, and some don't really know where their food comes from. So every week during term time, we welcome school groups, and our education centre runs sessions on everything from bread-making to bees. We also offer apprenticeships for young people who want a career in agriculture or animal care. Three of last year's apprentices have now got full-time jobs on commercial farms.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're particularly proud of our rare breeds. Many traditional breeds of farm animals have almost disappeared because modern farms prefer breeds that grow faster or produce more milk. But these older breeds often have valuable qualities: they may be hardier, more resistant to disease, or better suited to grazing poor land. We keep several, including Tamworth pigs and Bagot goats, and we work with a national charity to help keep these breeds going.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a quick guide to today's activities. The sheep-shearing demonstration takes place in the main barn at eleven o'clock. Please don't be alarmed; it doesn't hurt the sheep at all, and in fact they're much more comfortable without their heavy winter coats.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: At twelve, there's a talk on composting in the vegetable garden by our head gardener, Tom. Everything we grow here is fertilised with compost made from animal manure and garden waste. Tom will explain how you can make your own at home, even if you only have a small balcony.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Children's activities are in the education centre all day. There's pond-dipping, where children can look for insects and small creatures in our pond, and egg-decorating, which is always popular. Please note that the pony rides, which were advertised on our leaflet, have had to be cancelled, because the field is too wet after this week's rain. We're very sorry about that.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: For older children and adults, there's also a guided tour of the farm every hour, starting at the main gate. Our volunteers will explain how we care for the animals and how the farm is run. The tours are free, but numbers are limited to fifteen people, so please collect a ticket from the information tent first.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Food is available at the café, which uses vegetables from our garden and eggs from our own hens. All profits go towards running the farm. There's also a plant sale outside the café, where you can buy seedlings that our volunteers have grown.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, a few requests. Please wash your hands after touching any animals. There are sinks by every animal pen. Don't feed the animals anything you've brought with you, as some ordinary foods can make them quite ill; you can buy bags of suitable animal feed from the shop. And dogs, I'm afraid, must stay outside the farm gates, because they can frighten the animals.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Oh, and if you've enjoyed your visit, we'd love you to think about volunteering. There's a stand by the entrance where you can find out more. Thank you, and enjoy the day.

listening.title: A project on cattle and methane
listening.contextDescription: Two agriculture students, Nadia and Ben, talk to their tutor about a research project on reducing methane from cattle.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Nadia, Ben, you've chosen methane emissions from cattle for your project. Tell me why.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Well, I grew up on a dairy farm, so I'm interested in anything that affects farmers. And we kept reading that cattle are a major source of greenhouse gases. We wanted to understand how much of that is true, and what farmers can actually do about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And it's a topic that combines biology and economics, which suits both of us. Nadia's done more animal science, and I've done more on farm business.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. So what have you found out so far?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: The basic science first. Cattle produce methane in the rumen, the first part of their stomach, where microbes break down grass and other plant material. Most people think the methane comes out the back end, but in fact about ninety per cent is breathed out or belched.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. And what approaches are there to reducing it?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: We've grouped them into three. First, feed additives. There's a lot of research on a type of red seaweed which can cut methane dramatically in trials. The problem is that it's difficult to grow in large quantities, and it isn't clear yet whether the effect lasts over months. There's also a synthetic additive that has been approved in some countries, and it seems to give a reduction of about a third.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the second group?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Breeding. Some animals naturally produce less methane than others, and that seems to be partly inherited. So in theory, farmers could select bulls whose daughters produce less. The advantage is that the change is permanent and cumulative. The disadvantage is that it's slow; it would take many generations to make a big difference.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: And the third is improving efficiency in general. If cows are healthier and produce more milk each, you need fewer cows to produce the same amount of milk, so total emissions fall even if each cow produces the same amount of methane.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Which approach do you think is most promising?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Honestly, I think efficiency is the most realistic in the short term, because farmers already have reasons to do it. It saves them money.

dialogue.speaker: Ben

listening.title: The domestication of animals
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in an archaeology and animal science course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In today's lecture, I want to look at one of the most important developments in human history: the domestication of animals. Almost all the meat, milk, wool and leather people use today comes from a handful of species that were domesticated thousands of years ago. So, I'll consider when and where this happened, how it may have happened, and why so few species were ever domesticated.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's begin with the dog, which was the first animal to be domesticated, long before any farm animal. Dogs descend from a population of wolves, and genetic evidence suggests that domestication began at least fifteen thousand years ago, possibly much earlier, when humans were still hunters and gatherers. One popular theory is that some wolves began following human groups to feed on leftovers, and that the less fearful animals gradually became tamer over many generations. In other words, the wolves may have domesticated themselves to some extent.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The main farm animals came later, after the beginning of agriculture. Sheep and goats were domesticated around eleven thousand years ago in the region known as the Fertile Crescent, which stretches from what is now Iraq through Syria to Turkey. Cattle followed soon after, from a large wild animal called the aurochs, which was much bigger and more aggressive than modern cattle. The aurochs survived in the forests of Europe until 1627, when the last known animal died in Poland. Pigs were domesticated separately in at least two regions: the Middle East and China.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do we know all this? Traditionally, archaeologists relied on bones found at ancient settlements. Domestic animals tend to be smaller than their wild ancestors, so a reduction in the size of bones over time is one sign of domestication. Another clue is age. When people hunt wild animals, they kill animals of all ages, but herders tend to slaughter mainly young males and keep females for breeding. So if most of the bones at a site come from young males, it suggests the animals were being managed. More recently, analysis of ancient DNA has transformed the field, allowing researchers to trace the movement of domestic animals as farming spread.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So why were so few species domesticated? Of the roughly one hundred and fifty large plant-eating mammals in the world, only fourteen were domesticated before the twentieth century. The geographer Jared Diamond argued that a species needs several characteristics to be a good candidate. It must be able to live on food that humans can easily provide, such as grass. It must grow quickly and breed easily in captivity; animals like elephants take too long to reach adulthood. It must not be too aggressive or too nervous; zebras, for example, are notoriously bad-tempered and difficult to handle, and gazelles tend to panic in enclosures and injure themselves. And finally, it helps if the animal lives naturally in herds with a clear social hierarchy, because then humans can take the place of the leader.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Domestication changed the animals in many ways. Over centuries of selective breeding, farmers chose animals with desirable traits, so that modern sheep produce far more wool than wild sheep, and modern dairy cows produce many times as much milk as their ancestors. Interestingly, domestic animals of very different species share certain features, such as floppy ears, patches of white in their coat, and smaller brains relative to body size. Scientists call this the domestication syndrome, and one theory is that selecting animals for tameness accidentally affected other traits at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Domestication changed humans too. Living close to animals exposed people to new diseases, many of which, such as measles, probably originated in livestock. And in populations that relied heavily on dairy farming, adults gradually developed the ability to digest milk, something most mammals lose after infancy. Next week, we'll look at how modern genetics is changing livestock breeding today.

listening.title: Booking a guided city tour
listening.contextDescription: A tourist phones a tour company to book a walking tour.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, City Walks, this is Maria. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Hello. I'd like to book a walking tour for this weekend, please. I'm visiting with my family.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Wonderful. We have three tours at the weekend. The History Walk, the Food Tour and the Night Walk. Which one interests you?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: What's the difference between them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The History Walk visits the old town, the cathedral and the castle. It takes about two hours. The Food Tour goes to the market and five small restaurants where you can taste local dishes. That one lasts three hours. And the Night Walk is about ghosts and old stories. listening.title: Welcome to the summer arts festival
listening.contextDescription: A festival organiser speaks on local radio about this year's summer arts festival.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, and thank you for inviting me. I'm Paul Grant, the director of the Riverside Summer Festival, and I'm delighted to tell your listeners about this year's programme. The festival runs for ten days, from Friday the eighteenth of July to Sunday the twenty-seventh, and this is our twentieth year, so we've planned something special.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The festival has always been about bringing all kinds of art to everyone in the town, and that's still our aim. This year we have more than a hundred and fifty events, including music, theatre, dance, comedy and film, and about a third of them are completely free.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about some of the highlights. The opening concert on the first Friday will take place in Riverside Park. It's free, and we're expecting around five thousand people, so do come early. The music starts at seven, but the gates open at five, and there'll be food stalls selling dishes from around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For theatre lovers, the main event is a new play written by a local writer, Anna Price, about the history of the town's old factory. It will be performed in the Old Mill, which was once part of that factory, so the setting is perfect. Tickets are twelve pounds, and there are eight performances.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Families are very important to us. Every day there will be activities for children in the Library Gardens, including storytelling, face painting and music workshops. These are all free, and you don't need to book. On the middle Saturday, we also have a children's parade, and children are invited to make costumes at workshops during the first week of the festival.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: This year, for the first time, we're also holding an outdoor film festival. Every evening at nine thirty, we'll show a film on a big screen by the river. Bring a blanket or a chair. The films are free, but there are only five hundred places, so you need to get a ticket from the box office first.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For people who want to try something themselves, there are lots of workshops. You can learn to paint, to make pottery or to dance the tango. Most workshops cost five pounds, and all the money goes to help young artists in the town.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And for comedy fans, there are comedy nights every Friday and Saturday in the back room of the Swan Hotel. Some of the comedians are famous, and some are performing for the very first time. These shows are only for adults, and tickets cost eight pounds. Last year they sold out very quickly, so please book early.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Some practical information now. The festival box office is in the Town Hall, and it's open from nine until six every day. You can also buy tickets online on our website, which is the easiest way, especially for popular events. Many events are in the town centre, so we suggest leaving your car at home. There will be extra buses in the evenings, and the last bus leaves the town centre at midnight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We also need help! Every year we rely on around two hundred volunteers. They do all kinds of jobs, from selling programmes to helping artists. Volunteers get a festival T-shirt and free tickets to two events of their choice. If you're interested, please come to a meeting on Monday the seventh of July at the Town Hall.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Finally, the closing event. On the last night, there will be a fireworks display over the river at ten o'clock. It's the biggest fireworks display in the region and it's completely free. We hope to see you all there.

It's free, and we're expecting around five thousand people, so do come early. The music starts at seven, but the gates open at five, and there'll be food stalls selling dishes from around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For theatre lovers, the main event is a new play written by a local writer, Anna Price, about the history of the town's old factory. It will be performed in the Old Mill, which was once part of that factory, so the setting is perfect. Tickets are twelve pounds, and there are eight performances.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Families are very important to us. Every day there will be activities for children in the Library Gardens, including storytelling, face painting and music workshops. These are all free, and you don't need to book. On the middle Saturday, we also have a children's parade, and children are invited to make costumes at workshops during the first week of the festival.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: This year, for the first time, we're also holding an outdoor film festival. Every evening at nine thirty, we'll show a film on a big screen by the river. Bring a blanket or a chair. The films are free, but there are only five hundred places, so you need to get a ticket from the box office first.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For people who want to try something themselves, there are lots of workshops. You can learn to paint, to make pottery or to dance the tango. Most workshops cost five pounds, and all the money goes to help young artists in the town.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And for comedy fans, there are comedy nights every Friday and Saturday in the back room of the Swan Hotel. Some of the comedians are famous, and some are performing for the very first time. These shows are only for adults, and tickets cost eight pounds. Last year they sold out very quickly, so please book early.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Some practical information now. The festival box office is in the Town Hall, and it's open from nine until six every day. You can also buy tickets online on our website, which is the easiest way, especially for popular events. Many events are in the town centre, so we suggest leaving your car at home. There will be extra buses in the evenings, and the last bus leaves the town centre at midnight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We also need help! Every year we rely on around two hundred volunteers. They do all kinds of jobs, from selling programmes to helping artists. Volunteers get a festival T-shirt and free tickets to two events of their choice. If you're interested, please come to a meeting on Monday the seventh of July at the Town Hall.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Finally, the closing event. On the last night, there will be a fireworks display over the river at ten o'clock. It's the biggest fireworks display in the region and it's completely free. We hope to see you all there.

listening.title: Choosing a topic for a tourism project
listening.contextDescription: Two tourism students, Sam and Lina, discuss ideas for a group project.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hi Lina. So, we need to choose a topic for our tourism project by Friday. Have you had any ideas?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: A few. I was thinking about ecotourism, you know, holidays that try to protect the environment. It's very popular at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It is, but I think lots of other groups will choose it. Our lecturer said she's already read about twenty projects on ecotourism. We might find it hard to say something new.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: That's a good point. What about you? Any ideas?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I was thinking about tourism in our own town. Lots of people visit the castle and the old town in summer, but almost nobody comes in winter. We could look at how the town could attract visitors all year.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. And it's local, so we can do our own research. We could talk to people who work in hotels and shops.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. And the tourist information office might give us some numbers on visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Okay, let's choose that. How should we collect information? I think a questionnaire for tourists would be good.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: In winter there won't be many tourists to ask, though. Maybe we should interview people in local businesses instead. Hotel managers would know a lot about the busy and quiet seasons.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: True. But a questionnaire could still work if we put it online. We could ask people who visited last summer why they didn't come in winter.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Okay, let's do both, then. I'll organise the interviews, because I know the manager of the Castle Hotel. My aunt works there.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Great. And I'll write the questionnaire. I did one last term for another course, so I know how to make it short and clear.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What about examples from other places? It would be good to see what other towns have done.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Yes. I read about a town in Austria that started a winter food festival. Now it's one of their busiest times of year. That could be a good case study.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And there's that town in Scotland that has a winter light festival, where they light up old buildings at night. It's a bit like our castle.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Oh, I've seen photos of that. It looks beautiful. Do you think our town could do something similar?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe. The castle would look amazing with lights on it. But we'd need to find out how much it would cost, and who would pay. That could be a question for our interviews.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Good idea. We could ask the hotel managers if they'd be willing to help pay for an event that brings more visitors in winter. After all, they would get more customers.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Let's write that down so we don't forget it. And we could also ask the people at the tourist information office what they think about the idea, because they talk to visitors every day.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Perfect. Two case studies should be enough. Now, how long does the report need to be?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Three thousand words, plus a ten-minute presentation to the class.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: When's the deadline?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The report is due on the fifteenth of December, and the presentations are the week after.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: That doesn't give us much time. We should start the interviews next week.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. Shall we meet every Wednesday to check our progress?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Wednesday is difficult for me, I have a long lecture in the afternoon. Can we do Thursday?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Thursday's fine. Let's say Thursdays at twelve, in the library café.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Okay. And one more thing. Let's share all our documents online so we can both edit them. That way we won't lose anything.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good idea. I'll set it up tonight and send you the link.

listening.title: The history of the bicycle
listening.contextDescription: A talk at a transport museum about how the bicycle developed.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'm going to tell you the story of one of the simplest and most useful machines ever invented: the bicycle. There are more than a billion bicycles in the world today, but the bicycle as we know it is only about a hundred and forty years old.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The first machine that looked something like a bicycle was invented in Germany in 1817 by a man called Karl Drais. It had two wheels and a wooden frame, but no pedals. The rider sat on the seat and pushed along the ground with his feet, a bit like a child's balance bike today. People called it a running machine. One reason Drais was interested in it was that, at the time, horses were very expensive to feed after a series of bad harvests.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The next important step came in France in the 1860s, when pedals were added to the front wheel. These machines were popular, but they were very uncomfortable. The wheels were made of wood with iron around the outside, and on the stone roads of the time, the ride was extremely bumpy. In fact, people gave them the nickname 'boneshakers'.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1870s, a new design appeared that you've probably seen in old photographs: the penny-farthing. It had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. Why such a big wheel? Because the pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, a bigger wheel meant the bicycle travelled further with each turn of the pedals, so riders could go faster. But it was also dangerous. The rider sat very high up, and if the wheel hit a stone, he could easily fall forward over the handlebars. Penny-farthings were mostly ridden by young men who enjoyed the excitement.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The real breakthrough came in 1885, when an Englishman, John Kemp Starley, produced what he called the 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Because of the chain, the wheels didn't need to be large, so the rider sat closer to the ground. It was much safer and easier to ride, and its basic shape is the same as almost every bicycle today.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: A few years later, another important invention made cycling much more comfortable: the air-filled rubber tyre. It was developed by John Dunlop, a vet in Belfast, who wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable to ride. Air-filled tyres made the ride smoother and faster, and soon all bicycles had them.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1890s, there was a bicycle boom. For the first time, ordinary people could travel easily beyond their own town or village, and cycling clubs became very popular. The bicycle was particularly important for women. It gave them a new kind of freedom to travel on their own, and it even changed fashion, because long, heavy skirts were difficult to ride in, so women began to wear shorter skirts and looser clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, the car became more popular in many countries, and cycling declined. But today, the bicycle is having a comeback. Many cities are building cycle lanes, and electric bicycles are making cycling possible for older people and in hilly places. In the Netherlands, there are actually more bicycles than people, and around a quarter of all journeys are made by bike. Cycling is also very good for your health, and it doesn't cause pollution, which is why many governments now want to encourage it.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Now, if you'd like to follow me into the next room, you can see some of these early bicycles for yourselves, including a real boneshaker. And if you're brave, you can even try sitting on our penny-farthing.

One reason Drais was interested in it was that, at the time, horses were very expensive to feed after a series of bad harvests.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The next important step came in France in the 1860s, when pedals were added to the front wheel. These machines were popular, but they were very uncomfortable. The wheels were made of wood with iron around the outside, and on the stone roads of the time, the ride was extremely bumpy. In fact, people gave them the nickname 'boneshakers'.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1870s, a new design appeared that you've probably seen in old photographs: the penny-farthing. It had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. Why such a big wheel? Because the pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, a bigger wheel meant the bicycle travelled further with each turn of the pedals, so riders could go faster. But it was also dangerous. The rider sat very high up, and if the wheel hit a stone, he could easily fall forward over the handlebars. Penny-farthings were mostly ridden by young men who enjoyed the excitement.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The real breakthrough came in 1885, when an Englishman, John Kemp Starley, produced what he called the 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Because of the chain, the wheels didn't need to be large, so the rider sat closer to the ground. It was much safer and easier to ride, and its basic shape is the same as almost every bicycle today.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: A few years later, another important invention made cycling much more comfortable: the air-filled rubber tyre. It was developed by John Dunlop, a vet in Belfast, who wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable to ride. Air-filled tyres made the ride smoother and faster, and soon all bicycles had them.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1890s, there was a bicycle boom. For the first time, ordinary people could travel easily beyond their own town or village, and cycling clubs became very popular. The bicycle was particularly important for women. It gave them a new kind of freedom to travel on their own, and it even changed fashion, because long, heavy skirts were difficult to ride in, so women began to wear shorter skirts and looser clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, the car became more popular in many countries, and cycling declined. But today, the bicycle is having a comeback. Many cities are building cycle lanes, and electric bicycles are making cycling possible for older people and in hilly places. In the Netherlands, there are actually more bicycles than people, and around a quarter of all journeys are made by bike. Cycling is also very good for your health, and it doesn't cause pollution, which is why many governments now want to encourage it.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Now, if you'd like to follow me into the next room, you can see some of these early bicycles for yourselves, including a real boneshaker. And if you're brave, you can even try sitting on our penny-farthing.

listening.title: Applying for a part-time job
listening.contextDescription: A student phones a café about a part-time job advertised in the window.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Hello, Corner Bean Café, Rob speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, my name's Ana. I saw the sign in your window about a part-time job, and I wanted to ask about it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Oh, great, thanks for calling. Yes, we're looking for someone to work behind the counter, making drinks and serving customers. Have you done this kind of work before?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Not in a café exactly, but I worked in a bakery for a year back home, so I'm used to serving customers and handling money.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: That's useful experience. Are you a student?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Yes, I'm studying architecture at the university. I'm in my second year.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Okay. The job is about fifteen hours a week. We need someone mainly at weekends, but also one weekday shift. Our weekend shifts are from eight until two, or two until eight.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'd prefer the morning shifts at the weekend, if possible. I sometimes have group projects in the afternoons.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: That should be fine. And for the weekday shift, we need someone on Wednesday afternoons, from one until four.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Wednesday afternoon... I have a lecture until two on Wednesdays. Would Thursday be possible instead?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Thursday afternoon could work, actually. One of my staff prefers Wednesdays anyway. So, Saturday and Sunday mornings and Thursday afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Perfect. Can I ask about the pay?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Of course. We pay eleven pounds forty an hour to start with. After three months, if everything goes well, it goes up to twelve pounds. And you keep all your tips. On a busy weekend, that can add up to quite a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds good. Do you provide any training?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Yes. You'd start with a two-hour training session with our head barista, Chloe, who'll show you how to use the coffee machine. Making good coffee takes practice, so for the first few weeks you'd mostly work alongside someone experienced. You'd also need a food hygiene certificate, but don't worry if you haven't got one. You can do the course online. It takes about three hours and we pay for it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Is there a uniform?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We give you two aprons and a cap with the café logo. You just need to wear black trousers and comfortable black shoes. No trainers with bright colours, I'm afraid.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: No problem. How busy does it get?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Weekend mornings are very busy, especially between ten and twelve, when we often have a queue out of the door. Weekday afternoons are calmer, so that's when we do most of the cleaning and restocking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. Do staff get free drinks?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Staff can have free drinks during their shifts, and you get fifty per cent off food. It's a small perk, but people appreciate it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's nice. So what's the next step?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: I'd like to invite you for a short interview, and then, if that goes well, a trial shift, which is paid, so you can see if you like the work. Could you come in on Monday?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Monday morning is fine. What time?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: How about ten thirty? It's usually quiet then, after the morning rush.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Ten thirty on Monday. Should I bring anything?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Please bring a copy of your CV, and the contact details of one person who could give you a reference, maybe your manager from the bakery. If you're from outside the UK, I'll also need to see your passport and visa, just to confirm you're allowed to work.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm from Brazil, so I'll bring my passport. Students on my visa can work up to twenty hours a week during term, so fifteen is fine.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Perfect. And just so I have it, can I take your full name and number?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's Ana Carvalho. C-A-R-V-A-L-H-O. And my number is 07945 382 016.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Lovely. See you on Monday, Ana.

listening.title: Starting your own business: a workshop
listening.contextDescription: An adviser at a business support centre gives an introductory talk to people planning to start a small business.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the first session of our Start Your Own Business course. I'm Michelle Tan, and I've been an adviser here at the Enterprise Centre for eight years. Before that, I ran my own catering company for over a decade, so I've made most of the mistakes I'll be warning you about.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Let me start with a sobering fact. Around one in five new businesses close within their first year, and about half don't survive five years. That's not meant to put you off, but to show why preparation matters. And when we look at why businesses fail, the most common reason isn't a bad idea. It's running out of cash.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: This is why we put so much emphasis on cash flow. A business can be making a profit on paper and still go under, because the money from customers arrives later than the bills have to be paid. If you sell to other businesses, for example, they may take sixty or even ninety days to pay you, while your rent and suppliers have to be paid every month. In week three, we'll show you how to create a simple cash-flow forecast, and I'd say that's the single most useful session on the course.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Before that, though, next week, we'll look at market research. Many people skip this because they're convinced their idea is brilliant. But it's essential to find out whether there are enough people who will actually pay for what you're offering, at a price that covers your costs. And I don't mean asking your friends and family. They'll almost always tell you it's a great idea, because they want to be supportive. You need to talk to potential customers who don't know you.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: We'll then spend two sessions on your business plan. A business plan isn't just something you write to get a loan. It's a way of testing your own thinking. But you will need one if you want funding. Banks are often reluctant to lend to brand-new businesses, so many people start with their own savings, or with a government start-up loan. These loans have a fixed interest rate and come with twelve months of free mentoring, which our previous participants have found extremely valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Another decision you'll need to make early on is the legal structure of your business. The simplest option is to be a sole trader. It's easy to set up and involves less paperwork, but you're personally responsible for any debts the business has. The alternative is to set up a limited company, which protects your personal assets, like your house, but involves more administration and stricter rules about accounts. We'll cover this in week five, along with tax.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points about the course. Sessions run every Tuesday from six thirty until eight thirty, for eight weeks. Please try not to miss any, as each session builds on the previous one. If you do have to miss one, the slides and worksheets are available on our website, and you can book a one-to-one appointment with an adviser to catch up.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: In the final week, each of you will give a five-minute presentation of your business idea to a panel that includes a local bank manager and two successful business owners. It's not a test, and there's no pass or fail. The aim is to get honest feedback and practise explaining your idea clearly, which you'll need to do again and again when you talk to customers, suppliers and lenders.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Finally, I'd encourage you to make use of the networking area downstairs. Several past participants found business partners or their first customers simply by chatting to other people on the course. There's tea and coffee available there from six o'clock. Right, let's begin by going round the room. I'd like each of you to tell us your name and, in one sentence, what your business idea is.

I'm Michelle Tan, and I've been an adviser here at the Enterprise Centre for eight years. Before that, I ran my own catering company for over a decade, so I've made most of the mistakes I'll be warning you about.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Let me start with a sobering fact. Around one in five new businesses close within their first year, and about half don't survive five years. That's not meant to put you off, but to show why preparation matters. And when we look at why businesses fail, the most common reason isn't a bad idea. It's running out of cash.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: This is why we put so much emphasis on cash flow. A business can be making a profit on paper and still go under, because the money from customers arrives later than the bills have to be paid. If you sell to other businesses, for example, they may take sixty or even ninety days to pay you, while your rent and suppliers have to be paid every month. In week three, we'll show you how to create a simple cash-flow forecast, and I'd say that's the single most useful session on the course.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Before that, though, next week, we'll look at market research. Many people skip this because they're convinced their idea is brilliant. But it's essential to find out whether there are enough people who will actually pay for what you're offering, at a price that covers your costs. And I don't mean asking your friends and family. They'll almost always tell you it's a great idea, because they want to be supportive. You need to talk to potential customers who don't know you.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: We'll then spend two sessions on your business plan. A business plan isn't just something you write to get a loan. It's a way of testing your own thinking. But you will need one if you want funding. Banks are often reluctant to lend to brand-new businesses, so many people start with their own savings, or with a government start-up loan. These loans have a fixed interest rate and come with twelve months of free mentoring, which our previous participants have found extremely valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Another decision you'll need to make early on is the legal structure of your business. The simplest option is to be a sole trader. It's easy to set up and involves less paperwork, but you're personally responsible for any debts the business has. The alternative is to set up a limited company, which protects your personal assets, like your house, but involves more administration and stricter rules about accounts. We'll cover this in week five, along with tax.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points about the course. Sessions run every Tuesday from six thirty until eight thirty, for eight weeks. Please try not to miss any, as each session builds on the previous one. If you do have to miss one, the slides and worksheets are available on our website, and you can book a one-to-one appointment with an adviser to catch up.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: In the final week, each of you will give a five-minute presentation of your business idea to a panel that includes a local bank manager and two successful business owners. It's not a test, and there's no pass or fail. The aim is to get honest feedback and practise explaining your idea clearly, which you'll need to do again and again when you talk to customers, suppliers and lenders.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Finally, I'd encourage you to make use of the networking area downstairs. Several past participants found business partners or their first customers simply by chatting to other people on the course. There's tea and coffee available there from six o'clock. Right, let's begin by going round the room. I'd like each of you to tell us your name and, in one sentence, what your business idea is.

listening.title: Researching the four-day working week
listening.contextDescription: Two business students, Daniel and Yasmin, discuss their research on four-day working weeks with their lecturer.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So, Yasmin and Daniel, you've been looking at the four-day working week. Tell me what you've found so far.

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: We started with the big trial that took place in the UK, where about sixty companies reduced working hours to four days a week for six months, with no reduction in pay. The idea was that staff would keep the same output in less time.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And the headline results were very positive. Most of the companies decided to continue with the four-day week after the trial ended. Staff reported less stress and burnout, and fewer people left their jobs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's what was reported in the media. What did you make of the methods?

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: That's where we became more cautious. The companies weren't chosen at random. They volunteered to take part, so they were probably companies that already expected it to work and were willing to change how they operated.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And most of them were quite small, and in sectors like marketing, software and charities. There were very few manufacturing firms or hospitals, where it's much harder to cut hours without hiring more people.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good points. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: The measures of productivity were mainly reported by the companies themselves. Some had clear figures, like sales, but for others it was more a feeling that things were going well. And six months isn't very long. Some of the benefits might be a novelty effect.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Exactly the kind of critical thinking I want to see. So what did you do for your own research?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We interviewed managers at four local firms. Two had moved to a four-day week and two had considered it but decided against it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interesting. What did the ones who rejected it say?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The main issue for both was customers. One was an accounting firm, and they said their clients expect someone to answer the phone five days a week. They couldn't see how to do that without staff working different days, which they thought would be too complicated to organise.

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: The other was a small engineering company. The manager said they'd love to try it, but they're already struggling to find skilled staff, and cutting hours would mean they'd need even more people.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And the two that adopted it?

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: Both said the biggest change was cutting unnecessary meetings. One manager told us they reduced most meetings from an hour to thirty minutes, and introduced a rule that no meeting could have more than six people.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The other said the main benefit was in recruitment. They're a design agency, and since they started offering a four-day week, they've had far more applications for every job they advertise. The manager said it's been more effective than offering a higher salary.

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: Both managers also mentioned that staff were more focused on the days they did work. One said people stopped arranging doctor's appointments and other personal things during work hours, because they now had a free day for that.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: But they admitted it was hard at first. A few projects fell behind in the first month, until people got used to the new routine.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's a really interesting finding. Now, how are you going to structure the report?

dialogue.speaker: Yasmin
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with the background and the big trials, then our interviews, and then a discussion section comparing the two.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That's sensible. But make sure your conclusion is proportionate. Four interviews can give you insights, but they can't tell you whether the policy works in general. You could suggest what further research would be needed.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Like a longer trial including larger organisations?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Exactly, and ideally one with a comparison group of similar companies that didn't change their hours. Right, I look forward to reading the draft.

listening.title: The history of money
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in an economics course on how money developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at a question that sounds simple: what is money, and where did it come from? We use it every day, but most people have never thought much about how strange it is that we accept pieces of paper, or numbers on a screen, in exchange for real goods.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Economists traditionally define money by the three functions it performs. First, it's a medium of exchange: something people accept in return for goods and services. Second, it's a unit of account: a common measure that lets us compare the value of very different things. And third, it's a store of value: something that keeps its worth over time, so you can save it and spend it later.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The standard story in economics textbooks is that before money, people bartered, directly exchanging goods. The problem with barter is what's called the double coincidence of wants. If I have fish and want shoes, I need to find someone who has shoes and also wants fish. Money, according to this story, was invented to solve that problem. However, anthropologists have pointed out that there's actually very little evidence that any society ever relied mainly on barter. In small communities, people tended to share goods and keep track of who owed what, a system based on credit and trust rather than immediate exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Over history, many different objects have served as money. Some of the most widespread were cowrie shells, which were used in parts of Africa, South Asia and China for centuries. They were durable, difficult to fake and roughly the same size, all useful qualities for money. Other societies used salt, cattle, or even large stone discs, as on the Pacific island of Yap, where some stones were so heavy that they were never moved; everyone simply knew who owned them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first coins appeared around six hundred BC in Lydia, a kingdom in what is now western Turkey. They were made of a natural mixture of gold and silver and stamped with a design, often a lion's head, which guaranteed their weight and purity. This was important because it meant people no longer had to weigh and test metal every time they traded. The idea spread rapidly across the Greek world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Paper money was first used in China. During the Tang dynasty, merchants who found heavy coins inconvenient began leaving them with trusted dealers in exchange for paper receipts. By the eleventh century, the government had taken over the issuing of these notes. The Italian traveller Marco Polo, who visited China in the thirteenth century, was astonished that people accepted paper in place of gold. However, the Chinese experience also revealed a danger: when governments printed too much paper money, its value fell sharply, leading to rapid rises in prices, what we now call inflation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In Europe, banknotes developed from the receipts that goldsmiths in seventeenth-century London gave customers who stored gold with them. For a long time, notes could be exchanged at the bank for a fixed amount of gold, a system known as the gold standard. Britain formally adopted it in 1821, and many other countries followed. The gold standard was abandoned during the twentieth century, and today's currencies are what economists call fiat money: they have value not because they can be exchanged for gold, but because governments declare them to be legal tender and people trust that others will accept them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Which brings us to the present. In many countries, the use of cash is falling rapidly. In Sweden, for example, fewer than one in ten purchases in shops is now paid for in cash. Some people welcome this, but others worry about people who don't have bank accounts or smartphones, often elderly or poorer people, who could be excluded. Next week, we'll look at the role of central banks.

listening.title: Reporting a problem with a broadband service
listening.contextDescription: A customer calls an internet provider's helpline about a slow connection.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, you're through to FastLink customer support. My name's Siobhán. Can I start by taking your account number, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's F-L-seven-two-zero-four-nine-one.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Thank you. And can you confirm your name and the first line of your address?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Peter Lindqvist, L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T, and the address is 14 Rowan Close.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Thanks, Mr Lindqvist. How can I help today?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: My internet connection has been extremely slow for about two weeks. I work from home, so it's causing real problems. Video calls keep freezing, and sometimes the connection drops completely.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me run a test on your line from here. While I do that, can you tell me which package you're on?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's supposed to be the Superfast package. The advert said up to a hundred megabits per second.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: That's right. Okay, the test shows your line is currently getting around twelve megabits per second, which is far below what it should be. Have you tried restarting your router?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, several times. It helps for an hour or so and then it slows down again.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: And where is the router in your home?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's in a cupboard under the stairs. I put it there because it's quite ugly.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: That might be part of the problem, I'm afraid. Wireless signals are weakened by walls and especially by metal objects. If there's anything like a boiler or a fridge near it, that can make a big difference. I'd suggest moving it somewhere more open, ideally raised off the floor, and for work, connecting your computer with a cable rather than using wireless.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I can try that. But surely the test you just did measures the speed reaching the house, not the wireless?

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: That's a good point. You're right, the test does suggest there's a fault on the line itself as well. So I'm going to book an engineer to visit. The earliest appointment I have is Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Thursday morning would be ideal, if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: I can offer a morning slot between eight and twelve, or an afternoon slot between one and five. Is the morning okay?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, the morning is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Great. The engineer will call you about half an hour before arriving. They may need access to the point where the cable enters the house. Do you know where that is?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think it's in the garage.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Then please make sure the garage is accessible. Also, if the engineer finds that the fault is caused by something inside your home, such as damaged wiring that isn't ours, there could be a charge of sixty-five pounds. But if the fault is on our network, there's no charge.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Understood. And since I've been paying for a service I haven't been getting, will I get any money back?

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: Yes. Under our service guarantee, if your speed drops below the minimum we promise for more than a few days, you're entitled to compensation. For two weeks, that would be a credit of eight pounds fifty a day on your next bill, starting from the day you first reported the problem. Today is the first time you've reported it, so it would start from today, I'm afraid.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That doesn't seem quite fair, but I suppose I should have called earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: I understand. I can also offer you a free mobile data allowance of fifty gigabytes to use until the fault is fixed, so you can work using your phone as a hotspot. Would that help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, that would help a lot, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Advisor
dialogue.text: I'll set that up now. You'll receive a text message confirming the engineer's visit and your reference number, which is FT eight-eight-three-one.

listening.title: A digital skills programme for older adults
listening.contextDescription: The coordinator of a library programme describes free digital skills classes for older people.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello everyone, and thanks for coming along today. My name is Bridget, and I coordinate the Get Online programme here at Eastfield Library. The programme was set up four years ago to help people over sixty who want to become more confident using computers, tablets and smartphones. Since then, more than eight hundred people have taken part, and I'd like to tell you how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The idea came from a survey we did of library users. We found that many older people felt they were being left behind as more and more services moved online, from booking doctors' appointments to paying bills. Some had no device at all, but a surprising number had been given a tablet or smartphone by their children or grandchildren, and simply didn't know how to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: So, what do we offer? First, there are small group classes, with a maximum of eight people, which run for six weeks. Each weekly session lasts ninety minutes. The first course is called Getting Started, and it covers the basics: turning the device on, using the touch screen, connecting to the internet and sending emails. After that, you can choose from a range of follow-on courses on particular topics.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The most popular of these by far is the course on video calls. Since the pandemic, lots of people want to see family members who live far away, and once people have learned how, they tend to use video calls several times a week. We also run a course on online shopping, and one on using the National Health Service app to order prescriptions and book appointments.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: One course I'd particularly encourage everyone to take is Staying Safe Online. Unfortunately, older people are often targeted by scams, such as emails or text messages pretending to be from a bank, asking you to click on a link or give your password. In this course, a police officer comes in to talk about the latest tricks, and you'll learn how to recognise suspicious messages. listening.title: Evaluating sources on social media and teenagers
listening.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Chen and Olivia, discuss sources for an essay on social media and teenage well-being.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: So, Chen, we've each read about ten sources for the essay on social media and teenagers. Shall we go through them and decide which ones to use?

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: Good idea. I started with that book everyone talks about, the one arguing that smartphones have caused a mental health crisis among teenagers. It was very persuasive, and it has lots of graphs showing rates of anxiety rising sharply after about 2012, when smartphones became common.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: I read it too. The trouble is, showing that two things increased at the same time doesn't prove that one caused the other. Lots of other things changed around then too.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: True. And when I looked at reviews of the book by other researchers, several of them said the author had chosen the studies that supported his argument and ignored others. So I think we can mention it as an influential view, but we shouldn't rely on it as evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: Agreed. What about the big survey study, the one with data from over three hundred thousand teenagers?

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: That one was really interesting. The researchers did find a negative link between technology use and well-being, but it was tiny. They compared it with other factors and found that eating potatoes regularly had about the same association with well-being as using technology. Wearing glasses had a bigger association.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: I loved that comparison. It really puts things in perspective. It's a good one to quote in the introduction, I think, to grab the reader's attention.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: Definitely. But one limitation is that it relied on teenagers reporting how much time they spent online, and people are notoriously bad at estimating that. Some studies that tracked actual phone use found that people's estimates were often wildly wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: That's an important point for our methods discussion. Then there was the experiment where university students were asked to limit their social media use to thirty minutes a day for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: Right, and the group that cut down reported feeling less lonely and less depressed than the control group. I liked that one because it's an actual experiment, so it gets closer to showing cause and effect.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: Yes, but it was a small sample, only about a hundred and forty students, and all from one American university. And they were university students, not teenagers, so we can't be sure the results apply to younger people.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: Fair point. What did you think of the article on different types of use?

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: That's the one I found most useful, actually. It argued that it's not the amount of time that matters so much as how it's spent. Passive scrolling through other people's posts seems to be linked with feeling worse, probably because people compare themselves with others. But actively messaging friends or creating things doesn't seem to have the same negative effect, and might even be positive.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: I think that could be the central argument of our essay, that the question 'is social media bad?' is too simple.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: I agree. And there was that report about girls and boys being affected differently. Girls seemed more affected by social media, and boys more by gaming, though both effects were small.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: That was from a charity, wasn't it? We should check whether it was peer-reviewed before we rely on it.

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: Good thinking. I'll look into that. So, how shall we structure it? Introduction with the potato comparison, then the debate about whether social media causes harm, then types of use, then differences between groups, and a conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Chen
dialogue.text: Sounds good. I'll draft the section on causation and methods, since I've got notes on the self-report problem. You do the types of use section?

dialogue.speaker: Olivia
dialogue.text: Perfect. Let's swap drafts on Sunday.
