listening.title: The history of the printing press
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a media history course on the printing press and its effects.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. We often hear that the internet is the most important change in communication since the printing press. Today, I want to look back at the printing press itself and ask what it actually changed, and what lessons it might hold for thinking about our own media revolution.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Before printing, books in Europe were copied by hand, mostly by monks working in monasteries, and later by professional scribes in towns. Copying a single book could take months, and books were therefore very expensive. A large monastery library might contain only a few hundred volumes. It's worth noting, though, that printing was not invented in Europe. Printing from carved wooden blocks was used in China from at least the eighth century, and movable type, individual characters that could be rearranged, was developed in China in the eleventh century and in Korea, using metal type, by the thirteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In Europe, the key figure was Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from the German city of Mainz, who developed his press around 1450. Gutenberg's achievement was not a single invention but the combination of several. He developed a method of casting large numbers of identical metal letters quickly using a hand mould. He created an oil-based ink that stuck to metal type, and he adapted the screw press, which was already used for making wine and pressing olives. His best-known work, the Gutenberg Bible, was completed around 1455. About a hundred and eighty copies were printed, and around fifty still survive.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The technology spread with astonishing speed. By 1500, there were printing presses in more than two hundred and fifty European towns, and an estimated twenty million books had been printed. The price of books fell dramatically, and for the first time, it became possible for people who were not wealthy to own them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What were the effects? One of the most important was on religion. When Martin Luther published his criticisms of the Catholic Church in 1517, printed copies spread across Germany within weeks. Luther also wrote short pamphlets in German rather than Latin, so that ordinary people could read them, and his translation of the Bible into German became one of the best-selling books of the century. Many historians argue that the Protestant Reformation could not have spread so quickly without print.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Printing also transformed science. Before printing, errors crept into manuscripts each time they were copied, so that diagrams and tables became less accurate over time. Printed books, by contrast, were identical, so scientists in different countries could be sure they were looking at the same information, and they could build on each other's work more effectively. Printing also helped to standardise languages, as printers chose particular spellings and forms of words, which gradually became accepted as correct.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, it's important not to exaggerate. Literacy rates rose only slowly. In 1500, perhaps only one in ten people in Western Europe could read, and in many areas it was well into the nineteenth century before a majority could. Many people experienced printed texts by hearing them read aloud. And the early decades of printing produced a great deal of material that was inaccurate or deliberately misleading, from sensational stories about monsters to false accusations against particular groups. Authorities responded with censorship: lists of banned books were published, and printers could be heavily punished.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This should sound familiar. Concerns about information overload, the spread of false information and attempts to control publishing all accompanied the arrival of print. The lesson, perhaps, is that new media technologies bring both opportunities and dangers, and that it takes societies a long time, often generations, to develop ways of dealing with them. Next week, we'll look at the rise of newspapers.

listening.title: Booking a venue for a research conference
listening.contextDescription: A conference organiser phones a hotel events manager to book facilities for an academic conference.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, Kingsway Hotel events team, this is Martin.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, Martin. My name is Dr Helen Kowalczyk, and I'm organising a two-day psychology conference in the autumn. I spoke to one of your colleagues last week, and she suggested I call you to discuss the details.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Of course, Dr Kowalczyk. Could I just take the spelling of your surname?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Certainly. It's K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Thank you. So, how many delegates are you expecting?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We originally planned for about two hundred, but registrations have been much higher than expected, so we're now looking at around two hundred and eighty.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: That's fine. Our main conference room, the Regency Suite, holds up to three hundred and fifty in theatre style, so you'd have plenty of space for your plenary sessions. What dates were you considering?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The fourteenth and fifteenth of October, which is a Thursday and Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Let me check. Yes, the Regency Suite is available on both days. Will you need smaller rooms for parallel sessions?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll have four parallel sessions running at the same time in the afternoons, so we'd need four breakout rooms, each seating about sixty to seventy people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We have five rooms of that size on the first floor, so that's no problem. They all have projectors and screens. Will your speakers need anything else in the way of equipment?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Microphones in every room, please, because some of our speakers have quite quiet voices. And in the main suite, we'd like the plenary talks to be recorded and streamed online for members who can't attend in person.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can do that, but streaming requires one of our technicians to be present throughout, which is an additional charge of three hundred and fifty pounds per day.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's acceptable. Now, catering. We'd like tea and coffee on arrival and twice during the day, and a buffet lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Our standard day delegate package covers exactly that: room hire, refreshments and a hot buffet lunch, at fifty-two pounds per person per day. For groups over two hundred and fifty, we can reduce that to forty-eight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's helpful. About fifteen per cent of our delegates have dietary requirements, mostly vegetarian, but some vegan and a few gluten-free. Is that manageable?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Absolutely. We'll just need a final list two weeks before the event. Are you planning a conference dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, on the Thursday evening. We expect about a hundred and fifty people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: The dinner would be in the Garden Restaurant, which overlooks the river. It seats up to a hundred and eighty, so that works well. A three-course dinner is sixty-five pounds per person, including a glass of wine.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And accommodation? Many delegates will travel from abroad.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can hold a block of rooms at a discounted conference rate. I'd suggest eighty rooms initially. Delegates book directly using a special code, and any rooms not booked six weeks before the conference are released back to us, so you're not charged for them.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's ideal, because we can't predict exactly how many will stay. What about getting here? Some of our delegates won't be familiar with the city.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We're about ten minutes' walk from the central railway station. If you'd like, we can provide a shuttle bus from the airport on the Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, but that needs to be booked at least a month in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Let's do that. And what do you need from me to confirm the booking?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: I'll email you a contract. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you sign, and the balance thirty days after the event. If you need to reduce numbers, you can do so without penalty up to fourteen days beforehand.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll look out for your email.

dialogue.text: Good morning, Kingsway Hotel events team, this is Martin.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, Martin. My name is Dr Helen Kowalczyk, and I'm organising a two-day psychology conference in the autumn. I spoke to one of your colleagues last week, and she suggested I call you to discuss the details.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Of course, Dr Kowalczyk. Could I just take the spelling of your surname?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Certainly. It's K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Thank you. So, how many delegates are you expecting?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We originally planned for about two hundred, but registrations have been much higher than expected, so we're now looking at around two hundred and eighty.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: That's fine. Our main conference room, the Regency Suite, holds up to three hundred and fifty in theatre style, so you'd have plenty of space for your plenary sessions. What dates were you considering?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The fourteenth and fifteenth of October, which is a Thursday and Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Let me check. Yes, the Regency Suite is available on both days. Will you need smaller rooms for parallel sessions?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll have four parallel sessions running at the same time in the afternoons, so we'd need four breakout rooms, each seating about sixty to seventy people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We have five rooms of that size on the first floor, so that's no problem. They all have projectors and screens. Will your speakers need anything else in the way of equipment?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Microphones in every room, please, because some of our speakers have quite quiet voices. And in the main suite, we'd like the plenary talks to be recorded and streamed online for members who can't attend in person.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can do that, but streaming requires one of our technicians to be present throughout, which is an additional charge of three hundred and fifty pounds per day.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's acceptable. Now, catering. We'd like tea and coffee on arrival and twice during the day, and a buffet lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Our standard day delegate package covers exactly that: room hire, refreshments and a hot buffet lunch, at fifty-two pounds per person per day. For groups over two hundred and fifty, we can reduce that to forty-eight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's helpful. About fifteen per cent of our delegates have dietary requirements, mostly vegetarian, but some vegan and a few gluten-free. Is that manageable?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Absolutely. We'll just need a final list two weeks before the event. Are you planning a conference dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, on the Thursday evening. We expect about a hundred and fifty people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: The dinner would be in the Garden Restaurant, which overlooks the river. It seats up to a hundred and eighty, so that works well. A three-course dinner is sixty-five pounds per person, including a glass of wine.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And accommodation? Many delegates will travel from abroad.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can hold a block of rooms at a discounted conference rate. I'd suggest eighty rooms initially. Delegates book directly using a special code, and any rooms not booked six weeks before the conference are released back to us, so you're not charged for them.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's ideal, because we can't predict exactly how many will stay. What about getting here? Some of our delegates won't be familiar with the city.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We're about ten minutes' walk from the central railway station. If you'd like, we can provide a shuttle bus from the airport on the Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, but that needs to be booked at least a month in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Let's do that. And what do you need from me to confirm the booking?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: I'll email you a contract. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you sign, and the balance thirty days after the event. If you need to reduce numbers, you can do so without penalty up to fourteen days beforehand.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll look out for your email.

listening.title: Inside a memory research laboratory
listening.contextDescription: A research coordinator welcomes volunteers who have signed up to take part in memory experiments.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for volunteering to take part in our research. My name is Dr Amara Osei, and I coordinate the participant programme here at the Centre for Memory Research. Before we start, I'd like to explain what we do, what taking part involves, and your rights as participants.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The Centre was established twelve years ago, and our research focuses on how memories are formed, stored and retrieved, and why they sometimes go wrong. One of our main projects at the moment looks at how sleep affects memory. Another investigates false memories: how people can come to remember, quite sincerely, events that never actually happened. And a third project, funded by a national charity, is studying early changes in memory that might help doctors detect dementia sooner.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: You've all been placed in one of three groups, depending on which studies you're eligible for. The largest group will take part in computer-based tasks in our testing rooms on the ground floor. These usually involve learning lists of words or pictures and then being tested on them later. A typical session lasts about an hour, and you'll be paid fifteen dollars for each session.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The second group will take part in our sleep study. This involves spending two nights in our sleep laboratory, which is on the third floor. You'll learn some material in the evening, sleep with sensors attached to your head to monitor your brain activity, and be tested the following morning. Because it's a bigger commitment, participants in this study receive two hundred dollars in total.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The third and smallest group will have a brain scan. The scanner is in the hospital next door, and you'll be taken there by one of our researchers. Scans are completely safe and painless, but they can be noisy, and you need to lie very still inside a narrow tube for about forty-five minutes. If you think you might feel uncomfortable in enclosed spaces, please tell us now, and we can move you to a different study with no problem at all.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, a few important points about your rights. Before you take part in any study, you'll be asked to read an information sheet and sign a consent form. Please read these carefully and ask questions if anything is unclear. Taking part is entirely voluntary, and you can withdraw from any study at any time without giving a reason. If you withdraw, you'll still be paid for the time you've already spent with us.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: All the information we collect is kept confidential. Your results are stored under a code number rather than your name, and they're anonymised before being published, so nobody will be able to identify you. Your personal details are stored separately and are deleted five years after the study ends.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Some of our studies involve a small amount of deception. For instance, in some memory experiments, we can't tell you in advance that you'll be tested later, because knowing that would change how you pay attention. But at the end of every study, a researcher will explain exactly what the study was about and why any information was withheld. This is called debriefing, and you can ask as many questions as you like.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: A couple of practical things. Please arrive ten minutes before your session, and if you can't make it, let us know at least twenty-four hours in advance so we can offer the slot to someone else. Payments are made by bank transfer within two weeks. And if you're interested in the results, you can sign up for our newsletter, which summarises our findings in plain language a few times a year.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Finally, please don't discuss the details of the experiments with friends who might take part later, as that could affect the results. Right, my colleagues will now take each group to complete the paperwork.

listening.title: Discussing the replication crisis
listening.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Felix and Nora, discuss the "replication crisis" with their tutor in preparation for an essay.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, your essay question is about the replication crisis in psychology. Felix, can you start by explaining what the term refers to?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Sure. Basically, replication means repeating a study to see if you get the same result. Around 2015, a large project tried to repeat a hundred studies published in leading psychology journals, and only about a third to a half of them produced results that were statistically significant the second time. That led people to talk about a crisis, because it suggested that many published findings might not be reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And Nora, what are the main explanations for why so many studies failed to replicate?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: There are several. One is small samples. If you only test twenty or thirty people, a result can easily appear by chance. Another is what's called publication bias: journals were much more likely to publish studies with positive, exciting results than ones that found nothing, so the published literature gave a misleading picture.

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: And then there are questionable research practices. Not fraud exactly, but things like collecting more data until the result becomes significant, or testing lots of different measures and only reporting the ones that worked. Each decision might seem reasonable, but together they greatly increase the chance of a false positive.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, one thing I'd warn you about in the essay is suggesting that psychology is uniquely bad. What would you say to that?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: That similar problems have been found in other fields. There was a project in cancer biology that had trouble replicating important studies, and economics has had similar debates. Psychology may just have been more open about investigating the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd agree. In some ways, psychology has led the response. What reforms have been introduced?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: The one I find most convincing is pre-registration. Researchers publish their hypotheses and their planned analysis before they collect any data. That way, they can't change their predictions after seeing the results.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: And there are now journals that offer what are called registered reports, where the journal agrees to publish a study based on its design, before the results are known. That removes the incentive to produce exciting findings.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are there any drawbacks to pre-registration?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Some researchers say it makes it harder to do exploratory research, where you don't know in advance what you'll find. But I think that's a misunderstanding. You can still explore; you just have to be clear about which results were predicted and which were discovered afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I'm a bit more sceptical than Felix. Pre-registration helps, but it depends on people actually following their plans. I read a study that found a lot of pre-registered papers didn't stick to what they'd registered, and nobody noticed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to include, and it shows critical thinking. What about the famous findings that didn't replicate? Did you choose an example?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: We were thinking of power posing, the idea that standing in a confident posture for two minutes changes your hormone levels and makes you take more risks. It became hugely popular after a talk was watched millions of times online, but larger studies didn't find the hormone effects.

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Although some studies still find that people report feeling slightly more confident. So it's not that the whole idea was wrong, just that the original claims were too strong.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That nuance is exactly what I'd like to see. Be careful not to suggest the original researchers were dishonest; there's no evidence of that. For the conclusion, I'd encourage you to argue whether the crisis has ultimately been good for the discipline.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think we both agree it has, in the long run.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then make that case, but acknowledge that it's damaged public trust in the short term. Send me a plan by Wednesday.

dialogue.text: Good. And Nora, what are the main explanations for why so many studies failed to replicate?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: There are several. One is small samples. If you only test twenty or thirty people, a result can easily appear by chance. Another is what's called publication bias: journals were much more likely to publish studies with positive, exciting results than ones that found nothing, so the published literature gave a misleading picture.

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: And then there are questionable research practices. dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, one thing I'd warn you about in the essay is suggesting that psychology is uniquely bad. What would you say to that?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: That similar problems have been found in other fields. There was a project in cancer biology that had trouble replicating important studies, and economics has had similar debates. Psychology may just have been more open about investigating the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd agree. In some ways, psychology has led the response. What reforms have been introduced?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: The one I find most convincing is pre-registration. Researchers publish their hypotheses and their planned analysis before they collect any data. That way, they can't change their predictions after seeing the results.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: And there are now journals that offer what are called registered reports, where the journal agrees to publish a study based on its design, before the results are known. That removes the incentive to produce exciting findings.

listening.title: How we make decisions
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a psychology course on heuristics and biases in human decision-making.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we turn to one of the most influential areas of modern psychology: the study of how people make decisions under uncertainty, and why those decisions so often depart from what we might consider rational. Much of this work began with two Israeli psychologists, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose research in the 1970s challenged the assumption, common in economics, that people generally make logical choices that maximise their own interests.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Kahneman later described the mind as using two different systems of thinking. System One is fast, automatic and intuitive; it's what allows you to recognise a friend's face instantly or to understand a simple sentence without effort. System Two is slow, deliberate and effortful; it's what you use to solve a difficult mathematical problem or fill in a tax form. Most of the time, System One works extremely well. But it relies on mental shortcuts, known as heuristics, which can lead to systematic errors, or biases.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let me give you three examples. The first is the availability heuristic: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Events that are dramatic or widely reported, such as plane crashes or shark attacks, are easy to recall, so people tend to overestimate their frequency. Meanwhile, far more common causes of death, such as heart disease, receive less attention and are underestimated. After a major accident is reported in the news, for example, sales of insurance against that kind of accident often rise sharply, even though the actual risk hasn't changed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second is anchoring. In one famous experiment, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune that had been fixed to stop at either ten or sixty-five. Participants were then asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who had seen the number sixty-five gave much higher estimates than those who had seen ten, even though the number on the wheel was obviously random. Anchoring effects have since been found among experienced professionals, including judges deciding on sentences and estate agents valuing houses.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The third example is framing. People's choices can be influenced by how options are described, even when the underlying facts are identical. In one well-known study, participants were told that a disease was expected to kill six hundred people and asked to choose between two programmes. When the options were described in terms of lives saved, most people chose the certain option. When exactly the same options were described in terms of deaths, most people chose the risky option. This finding has obvious implications for how doctors present information about treatments to patients.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Underlying many of these patterns is a principle Kahneman and Tversky called loss aversion: losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel pleasurable. This helps to explain why people often hold on to investments that are falling in value, hoping to avoid realising a loss, and why they may refuse a bet with a fifty per cent chance of winning a hundred and fifty pounds and a fifty per cent chance of losing a hundred, even though, on average, they would gain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, it would be wrong to conclude from this research that humans are simply irrational. Some psychologists, notably Gerd Gigerenzer, have argued that heuristics are often remarkably effective, especially in real-world environments where information is limited and time is short. A simple rule of thumb may outperform complex calculations when the future is genuinely uncertain. The question, then, is not whether heuristics are good or bad, but in which environments they serve us well.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This research has had a major practical impact. Kahneman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, an unusual honour for a psychologist. Tversky had died in 1996, and the prize is not awarded after death. Their ideas have since influenced fields as diverse as medicine, law, finance and public policy, and we'll look at some of these applications next week.

listening.title: Booking a boat trip to see whales
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a company that runs whale-watching boat trips.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Ocean Spirit Tours, this is Kylie speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi, Kylie. I'm visiting the area next week with my family, and I'd like to book a whale-watching trip.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. You've picked a great time of year. The humpback whales are migrating north at the moment, so we're seeing them on almost every trip. How many people are in your group?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: There are four of us: me, my wife and our two children, who are twelve and seven.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. We have two types of trip. The first is our Classic Cruise on our large catamaran, which takes up to a hundred and twenty people. It lasts three hours, and there's an indoor area with a café, so it's very comfortable. The second is our Adventure Trip on a smaller, faster boat that takes twelve people. You get much closer to the whales, but it can be quite bumpy, and children must be at least ten years old.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Then it'll have to be the Classic Cruise, because of my youngest.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Sure. The Classic Cruise departs twice a day, at nine thirty in the morning and at one thirty in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Which would you recommend?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The morning is usually calmer, because the wind tends to pick up in the afternoon. If anyone in your family gets seasick, I'd definitely go for the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My wife does sometimes, so the morning, please. Could we do Tuesday?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me check. Tuesday morning is fully booked, I'm afraid, but Wednesday morning has plenty of space.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wednesday is fine.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Okay. Adult tickets are seventy-five dollars and children's are forty-five. So for two adults and two children, that's two hundred and forty dollars. But if you book a family ticket, it's two hundred and ten, which includes a free photo of your family on the boat.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The family ticket sounds good.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. And can I take your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Andrew Pemberton. P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks, Andrew. And a mobile number, in case the weather changes?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Now, where we leave from. Please don't go to our office on the main street, because the boats leave from the marina. Go to Pier Four, and check in at our kiosk at least thirty minutes before departure.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Pier Four, thirty minutes early. Got it. What should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Even on sunny days, it can get cold out on the water, so bring a warm jacket. Sunglasses and a hat are a good idea too, and of course a camera. If you think you might get seasick, take a tablet about an hour before the trip; you can buy them at the pharmacy, or at our kiosk.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there food on board, or should we bring our own?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The café on the boat sells sandwiches, snacks and hot drinks, so you don't need to bring anything. But you're welcome to bring your own food if you prefer. We just ask that you take any rubbish home with you, because we don't want anything blowing into the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Of course. And what happens if we don't see any whales?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's very rare at this time of year, but if it happens, you can come on another trip for free, any time in the next twelve months. And if the trip is cancelled because of bad weather, we'll give you a full refund or move you to another day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very fair. Is there anything for the children to do on board?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, we have a marine biologist on every trip who gives a talk about the whales, and there's a quiz for children, with a small prize. Kids usually love it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Brilliant. Can I pay by card now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll send a confirmation email with your booking number once the payment goes through.

listening.title: A talk on saving water at home
listening.contextDescription: A representative of a water company gives a talk to residents about saving water.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Joanna Price, and I work for Eastern Water. As you'll probably know, after two very dry summers, the water levels in our reservoirs are lower than they have been for thirty years. Tonight I want to explain why that matters and share some simple ways you can save water at home.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Some people are surprised that a country with a reputation for rain could ever be short of water. But our region is actually one of the driest in the country, with less rainfall each year than some parts of the Mediterranean. At the same time, the population is growing, and climate change is making summers hotter and drier. The average person here uses around a hundred and forty litres of water every day, and our aim is to bring that down to a hundred and ten by 2030.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: So where does all that water go? The biggest use in most homes is showers and baths, which account for about a third of the total. Next comes toilet flushing, at around a quarter. Then washing clothes and dishes, and finally drinking, cooking and the garden.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Let's start with the bathroom. Simply reducing your shower time to four minutes can save a large amount. We're giving away free shower timers tonight, which you can stick to the wall. You can also fit a water-saving shower head, which mixes air with the water, so it feels just as powerful but uses about half the amount. And of course, a shower generally uses much less water than a bath.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Older toilets can use up to thirteen litres every time you flush. If you have an old toilet, you can put a small bag in the cistern, the tank behind it, which reduces the amount of water used each time. Again, we have these free tonight. Modern toilets have a dual-flush button, where the smaller button uses much less water.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: One of the most important things you can do is check for leaks. A dripping tap might not seem like much, but it can waste over five thousand litres a year. And a leaking toilet can waste even more, often without anyone noticing. Here's a simple test: put a few drops of food colouring in the cistern and wait fifteen minutes without flushing. If the colour appears in the bowl, you have a leak.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the kitchen, only run the washing machine and dishwasher when they're full. Interestingly, a modern dishwasher actually uses less water than washing the same dishes by hand, as long as you don't rinse them under the tap first.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the garden, the best time to water plants is early in the morning or in the evening, when less water is lost to evaporation. Use a watering can rather than a hose, and consider installing a water butt, a large container that collects rainwater from your roof. Plants actually prefer rainwater to tap water. And don't worry if your lawn turns brown in summer; grass is very good at recovering once the rain returns.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Finally, I'd encourage everyone who doesn't already have one to get a water meter. At the moment, around a third of homes in our area still pay a fixed charge, however much water they use. With a meter, you pay only for what you use, and most households who switch save money, and they typically use about fifteen per cent less water. Installation is completely free, and it usually takes less than an hour. You can apply on our website, or speak to one of my colleagues at the table by the door.

listening.title: A geography field trip to a river
listening.contextDescription: Two geography students, Zara and Ben, discuss their field trip to study a river with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Zara, Ben. So, you went on the river field trip last week. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We were lucky with the weather, because it had been raining heavily the week before, so the river was quite high, which made the measurements more interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Although it also made it harder to get into the water safely at one of the sites. We had to change our plans a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Tell me about that. What were you measuring?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We were looking at how the river changes from its source in the hills to where it reaches the town. We measured the width, depth and speed of the water at five sites along the river.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: We measured the speed by timing how long it took a float to travel ten metres. We used an orange, actually, because it floats just below the surface and isn't blown about by the wind as much as something lighter would be.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic technique. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Mostly what we expected: the river got wider and deeper as it went downstream. But the speed was more surprising. We assumed the water would be fastest in the hills, where it's steep, but actually it was fastest at the site nearest the town.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We read that in the upper sections, the river bed is full of large rocks, which create a lot of friction and slow the water down, even though the slope is steep. Further downstream, the channel is smoother and deeper, so there's less friction.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly right. That's a common misconception, so make sure you explain it clearly in your report. What about the site where you had problems?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That was site three, by a footbridge. The water was too deep and fast to stand in safely, so we couldn't measure the depth across the whole width. We only managed to measure near the banks.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what will you do about that in your analysis?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We thought we could estimate it using data from the Environment Agency, which has a monitoring station near there. They publish river levels online.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a sensible approach, but you must state clearly that you've done that, and explain why. Don't present it as your own measurement.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Of course. We'll put it in the limitations section.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We also took photos of the river level marker at the footbridge, so we can compare our observations with the official readings for the same day.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. That will make your estimate more convincing. Did you look at anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: We also collected stones from the river bed at each site and measured their size and roundness. We found that the stones became smaller and rounder downstream, because they're worn down as they're carried along by the water.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And at the last site, we noticed that new houses had been built on the flood plain, quite close to the river. We'd like to include a short section about flood risk, because we saw signs that the river had flooded there in the past.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That would make a good discussion point, but keep it brief, since it's not the main focus of the assignment. How are you going to present your data?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We thought line graphs to show how width, depth and speed change with distance from the source.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And for the stone data, perhaps a scatter graph. Make sure you include photos of each site too, with a map showing where they are.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Okay. When is the report due?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: The end of the month. Come and see me if you have any questions before then.

listening.title: A geography field trip to a river
listening.contextDescription: Two geography students, Zara and Ben, discuss their field trip to study a river with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Zara, Ben. So, you went on the river field trip last week. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We were lucky with the weather, because it had been raining heavily the week before, so the river was quite high, which made the measurements more interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Although it also made it harder to get into the water safely at one of the sites. We had to change our plans a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Tell me about that. What were you measuring?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We were looking at how the river changes from its source in the hills to where it reaches the town. We measured the width, depth and speed of the water at five sites along the river.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: We measured the speed by timing how long it took a float to travel ten metres. We used an orange, actually, because it floats just below the surface and isn't blown about by the wind as much as something lighter would be.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic technique. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Mostly what we expected: the river got wider and deeper as it went downstream. But the speed was more surprising. We assumed the water would be fastest in the hills, where it's steep, but actually it was fastest at the site nearest the town.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We read that in the upper sections, the river bed is full of large rocks, which create a lot of friction and slow the water down, even though the slope is steep. Further downstream, the channel is smoother and deeper, so there's less friction.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly right. That's a common misconception, so make sure you explain it clearly in your report. What about the site where you had problems?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That was site three, by a footbridge. The water was too deep and fast to stand in safely, so we couldn't measure the depth across the whole width. We only managed to measure near the banks.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what will you do about that in your analysis?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We thought we could estimate it using data from the Environment Agency, which has a monitoring station near there. They publish river levels online.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a sensible approach, but you must state clearly that you've done that, and explain why. Don't present it as your own measurement.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Of course. We'll put it in the limitations section.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We also took photos of the river level marker at the footbridge, so we can compare our observations with the official readings for the same day.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. That will make your estimate more convincing. Did you look at anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: We also collected stones from the river bed at each site and measured their size and roundness. We found that the stones became smaller and rounder downstream, because they're worn down as they're carried along by the water.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And at the last site, we noticed that new houses had been built on the flood plain, quite close to the river. We'd like to include a short section about flood risk, because we saw signs that the river had flooded there in the past.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That would make a good discussion point, but keep it brief, since it's not the main focus of the assignment. How are you going to present your data?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We thought line graphs to show how width, depth and speed change with distance from the source.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And for the stone data, perhaps a scatter graph. Make sure you include photos of each site too, with a map showing where they are.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Okay. When is the report due?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: The end of the month. Come and see me if you have any questions before then.

listening.title: How weather forecasting works
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory meteorology course on the history and science of weather forecasting.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about weather forecasting: how it developed, how it works today, and why, despite enormous advances, forecasts are still sometimes wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For most of human history, people predicted the weather by observing nature: the colour of the sky, the behaviour of animals, or the shape of clouds. Some of these traditional sayings have a scientific basis. The saying 'red sky at night, shepherd's delight' reflects the fact that in many places, weather systems move from west to east, so a clear sky in the west at sunset often means fine weather is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Scientific forecasting became possible with the invention of instruments. The thermometer and the barometer, which measures air pressure, were developed in Italy in the seventeenth century. Scientists noticed that falling pressure was often followed by storms, while rising pressure usually brought settled weather. But a single barometer could only tell you what was happening in one place.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The real breakthrough came with the electric telegraph in the nineteenth century, which allowed weather observations from many places to be sent to a central office almost instantly. In Britain, a naval officer named Robert FitzRoy set up a network of weather stations and began publishing forecasts in newspapers in 1861. In fact, he invented the word 'forecast'. His forecasts were often inaccurate, and he was widely criticised, but his storm warnings for ships are credited with saving many lives.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the early twentieth century, scientists realised that the atmosphere follows the laws of physics, so in theory, its future state could be calculated using mathematical equations. A British mathematician, Lewis Fry Richardson, attempted to do this by hand during the First World War. It took him around six weeks to calculate a forecast for just six hours ahead, and the result was completely wrong. He imagined a huge hall filled with sixty-four thousand people doing calculations together to keep up with the weather.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Richardson's dream became reality with computers. The first computer weather forecast was made in 1950, and today, weather services use some of the most powerful supercomputers in the world. These computers divide the atmosphere into a three-dimensional grid of boxes and calculate how temperature, pressure, wind and moisture will change in each one. The starting data comes from thousands of weather stations, as well as weather balloons, ships, aircraft and, most importantly, satellites, which provide information about areas where there are no other observations, such as the oceans.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So why are forecasts still sometimes wrong? The main reason is that the atmosphere is what scientists call a chaotic system. In the 1960s, the meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered that tiny differences in the starting data could lead to completely different forecasts after a few days. This is often called the butterfly effect, from the idea that the flap of a butterfly's wings could, in theory, influence the development of a storm on the other side of the world. Because our observations can never be perfect, there is a limit to how far ahead we can forecast. At present, forecasts are generally reliable for about a week.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: To deal with this uncertainty, modern weather services run what's called an ensemble forecast. Instead of running the computer model once, they run it many times, each with slightly different starting conditions. If most of the runs agree, forecasters can be confident. If they disagree, the forecast is less certain. That's why forecasts often give a probability, such as a seventy per cent chance of rain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Despite these limits, forecasts have improved remarkably. A five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a one-day forecast was in the 1980s. Next week, we'll look at how climate models differ from weather forecasts.

questions.explanation: Barometers measure pressure.

listening.title: Hiring a car for a business trip
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a car hire company to book a car for a business trip.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Swift Car Hire, Natalie speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Hi, I'd like to book a car for a business trip next week, please.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Certainly. Where would you like to pick the car up?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: At the airport, if possible. I'm flying in on Monday morning.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem, we have a desk in the arrivals hall of Terminal Two. What time does your flight land?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's due at nine forty, so if we say ten thirty, that should give me time to get through passport control.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Ten thirty on Monday the seventeenth. And when will you be returning it?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: On Friday. But I won't be flying back from the same airport. I'm taking the train home from the city centre, so could I return it there?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, we have an office near Central Station, on Queen Street. There's a one-way fee of twenty-five pounds for returning it to a different branch, though.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's fine. My company will be paying.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: And what kind of car would you like? We have small, medium and large, as well as electric cars.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I'll be driving quite long distances to visit clients, and I'll have some samples to carry. So I think a medium-sized car with a big boot.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Our medium estate car would be ideal. It has plenty of space for luggage. That's forty-six pounds a day. Alternatively, we have an electric model of a similar size for fifty-two pounds a day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: How far can the electric one go on a full charge?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: About three hundred and fifty kilometres, depending on how you drive.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Some of my client visits are in rural areas, and I'm not sure there'll be charging points. I'd better go for the standard car.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Okay, the estate car for five days. Now, insurance. Basic insurance is included in the price, but there's an excess of one thousand pounds, which is the amount you'd have to pay if the car was damaged. You can reduce that to zero by adding our full cover, which costs twelve pounds a day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: My company has its own insurance policy which covers car hire, so I won't need that.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's fine. You'll just need to show proof of that when you collect the car. What about extras? Would you like satellite navigation?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No, I'll use my phone. But I would like a phone holder for the dashboard, if you have one.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We can provide one free of charge. And our fuel policy is full-to-full, which means you'll get the car with a full tank and should return it full. If you don't, we charge for the fuel plus a refuelling fee.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Understood. What do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Your driving licence, a credit card in your name, and your passport, since you're visiting from abroad. We'll also need the address where you'll be staying. And one thing to be aware of: we'll put a hold of two hundred and fifty pounds on your credit card as a security deposit, which is released when you return the car.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Okay. And I'll be staying at the Riverside Hotel, on Mill Road.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can I have your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Fitzgerald. F-I-T-Z-G-E-R-A-L-D.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Fitzgerald. Is there a mobile number we can reach you on?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's 001 604 559 2187. That's a Canadian number.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Perfect. And one last thing: if your flight is delayed, don't worry. We track flight arrivals, and we'll keep the car for you for up to three hours after the scheduled time.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's very reassuring. And if I need help during the week, for example if the car breaks down?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's a twenty-four-hour breakdown number on the key ring, and on the windscreen. Just call that and they'll send someone, usually within an hour.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Great. Thanks, Natalie.

listening.title: A new tram line for the city
listening.contextDescription: A project manager speaks at a public meeting about plans for a new tram line.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to tonight's meeting. I'm Rachel Owusu, the project manager for the new Eastside tram line. I'll spend about twenty minutes explaining the plans, and then there'll be plenty of time for your questions.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: First, why do we need a tram? As many of you know from your own experience, traffic congestion in the eastern part of the city has become a serious problem. Journey times by bus have increased by around forty per cent over the past ten years, and air pollution on the main road, Eastern Avenue, regularly exceeds legal limits. A tram can carry far more passengers than a bus, it's quicker because it runs on its own tracks, and because it's electric, it produces no exhaust fumes on the street.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The route will be nine kilometres long, running from the city centre to the new hospital at Greenfield. There will be twelve stops along the way. Trams will run every six minutes during the day and every ten minutes in the evening, from five thirty in the morning until midnight. A journey from one end to the other will take about twenty-five minutes, compared with up to fifty minutes by bus at busy times.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: One of the main changes since our first proposal relates to the route through the old town. Originally, we planned to run the tram along the High Street. But after the public consultation last year, where many local businesses expressed concern about disruption during construction, we've moved that section to Station Road instead, which is wider and has fewer shops.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: At the eastern end of the line, near the motorway junction, we'll build a park and ride site with space for eight hundred cars. The idea is that people driving into the city from outside can leave their cars there and take the tram, reducing traffic in the centre. Parking will be free for anyone with a tram ticket.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, I know many of you are worried about the construction work. It will take around three years, starting next spring. We'll work on one section at a time, so no part of the route will be affected for more than about four months. Most of the noisiest work will be done during the day, but some work near the railway bridge will have to happen at night, when trains aren't running. Residents affected by night work will be offered double glazing or, in some cases, alternative accommodation.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We'll also be planting over five hundred new trees along the route, and the section through Greenfield Park will have grass between the tracks rather than concrete, which helps to absorb rainwater and reduces noise.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: All the trams will be fully accessible, with level boarding at every stop, so passengers in wheelchairs or with pushchairs can get on and off easily. Every stop will also have a shelter, real-time information screens and secure cycle parking.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: How much will it cost to use? Fares will be the same as buses, and the same tickets will work on both, so you can change from bus to tram without paying again. Children under sixteen and people over sixty-five will travel free outside the morning rush hour.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The total cost of the project is three hundred and twenty million pounds. Around two-thirds will come from the national government, and the rest from the city council, partly funded by a small charge on businesses in the city centre, which are expected to benefit from more customers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you'd like more information, our project office on Market Street is open every weekday, and there's an exhibition with detailed maps and drawings in the library until the end of the month. Right, I'll now take your questions.

listening.title: A design project on bridges
listening.contextDescription: Two engineering students, Sofia and Marcus, discuss their bridge design project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay, Sofia and Marcus. Your project is to design a footbridge across the river near the university. Where have you got to?

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: We've looked at the site and done some research on different types of bridge. The river is about sixty metres wide at that point, and the banks are quite soft, which affects what we can build.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: We considered three main types: a beam bridge, an arch bridge and a suspension bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what did you conclude?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: A simple beam bridge wouldn't work without supports in the middle of the river, because sixty metres is too long a span. And we were told the river authority won't allow anything in the water, because it would affect boats and could cause flooding.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: An arch bridge was attractive, but arches push outwards at their ends, so they need very solid ground at both sides. With the soft banks, the foundations would have to be very deep and expensive.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you've gone for a suspension bridge?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Actually, we've chosen a cable-stayed design. It's similar to a suspension bridge, but instead of the deck hanging from long main cables, the cables run directly from one or two tall towers down to the deck. It's simpler to build for a span of this length, and it uses less material.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's a sensible choice. How many towers?

dialogue.speaker: Sofia
dialogue.text: Just one, on the university side, where the ground is firmer. We think a single tall tower will also look more striking.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Appearance matters, but don't let it dominate. What material are you using for the deck?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: We originally planned to use steel, but we've changed to a composite material, fibre-reinforced plastic. It's much lighter, it doesn't rust, and it needs very little maintenance.

dialogue.speaker: Sofia

listening.title: The history of flight
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in an aerospace engineering course on early aviation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at how humans finally achieved powered flight, and how aviation developed in the decades that followed. The dream of flying is as old as humanity, but it was only just over a hundred and twenty years ago that it became reality.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For centuries, people tried to fly by imitating birds, attaching wings to their arms and flapping them. These attempts all failed, often with serious injuries, because human muscles are far too weak relative to body weight. The first major step forward came from the English engineer George Cayley in the early nineteenth century. Cayley realised that flight needed to be thought of in terms of separate forces: lift, which holds an aircraft up; weight; thrust, which drives it forward; and drag, the air resistance that slows it down. He understood that a fixed wing could generate lift, and that a separate means of propulsion was needed. In 1853, one of his gliders carried a person across a small valley, apparently his reluctant coachman.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the 1890s, the German engineer Otto Lilienthal made around two thousand flights in gliders of his own design, launching himself from hills. He carefully recorded his results and published them, and photographs of his flights were seen around the world. Sadly, in 1896, he lost control of a glider in a gust of wind, fell and died the next day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Lilienthal's work inspired two brothers from Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright, who ran a bicycle shop. The Wright brothers recognised that the biggest unsolved problem was not lift or power, but control: how to keep an aircraft balanced and steer it in the air. They developed a method called wing warping, twisting the wings slightly to make the aircraft turn, an idea Wilbur is said to have had while twisting an empty cardboard box. They also discovered that much of the published data on wings was inaccurate, so they built their own small wind tunnel and tested more than two hundred different wing shapes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Because no suitable engine was available, they designed and built their own lightweight engine with the help of their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, and they also designed their own propellers, realising that a propeller is essentially a wing that rotates. On the seventeenth of December 1903, at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville made the first controlled, powered flight. It lasted just twelve seconds and covered thirty-seven metres, shorter than the wingspan of a modern passenger jet. By the end of the day, Wilbur had flown for fifty-nine seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Progress after that was remarkably fast. In 1909, the Frenchman Louis Blériot flew across the English Channel. The First World War, beginning in 1914, greatly accelerated the development of aircraft, which were used first for observation and then for combat. In 1919, two British pilots, John Alcock and Arthur Brown, made the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in an open cockpit, flying through fog and snow for nearly sixteen hours.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next revolution was the jet engine, developed independently in the 1930s by Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany. Jet engines allowed aircraft to fly faster and higher, above much of the bad weather. The first commercial jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, entered service in 1952, but a series of crashes revealed a serious problem: metal fatigue around its square windows. That's why aircraft windows today have rounded corners.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today, around four billion passenger journeys are made by air each year. The current challenge is reducing aviation's environmental impact, and engineers are working on more efficient engines, sustainable fuels and, for short flights, electric aircraft. Next week, we'll look at the science of lift in more detail.

listening.title: Booking a cookery class
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a cookery school to ask about evening classes.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Hello, Saffron Kitchen Cookery School. Daniel speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I saw your advertisement in the local newspaper, and I'm interested in your evening classes. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We run three evening courses at the moment. Each one lasts six weeks, with one class a week. The first is Cooking Basics, which is for complete beginners. You learn things like how to use a knife safely, how to cook rice and pasta properly, and how to make simple sauces and soups.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds about right for me, actually. I can make a few things, but I've never really learned properly.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Well, the second course might also suit you. It's called World Kitchen, and each week we cook food from a different country, for example Thai curries, Mexican dishes and Moroccan tagines. It's for people who already have some basic skills. And the third is Baking and Bread, which covers everything from simple loaves to pastry and cakes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I think I'll start with the basics. What day is that course?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Cooking Basics runs on Thursday evenings, from half past six until nine. The next course starts on the fifth of February.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full course is one hundred and eighty pounds. That includes all the ingredients, and of course you get to eat what you cook, or take it home with you. You'll need to bring a container for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Do I need to bring anything else? Knives or anything like that?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, we provide all the equipment, and we give you an apron to use during the class. Just wear comfortable shoes, because you'll be standing for most of the evening, and please tie your hair back if it's long.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. How many people are there in each class?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We keep the groups small, with a maximum of ten students, so the teacher can give everyone individual attention. Students usually work in pairs at a cooking station.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's good. Oh, I should mention, I'm vegetarian. Is that a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Not at all. Just let us know when you book, and the teacher will make sure there's a vegetarian version of every recipe. We can also cater for people with allergies, as long as we're told in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Who teaches the course?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Cooking Basics is taught by Rosa Martinelli. She worked as a chef in restaurants for fifteen years before she started teaching, and our students really like her. She's very patient.

dialogue.speaker: Caller

listening.title: A tour of a chocolate factory
listening.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a tour of a small chocolate factory.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Welcome, everyone, to Hartwell Chocolate. My name's Ben, and I'll be your guide this morning. The tour lasts about an hour and a quarter, and at the end there's a tasting session, so I hope you've left some room.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me begin with a bit of background. Hartwell was founded in 1921 by a husband and wife, George and Edith Hartwell, who started making chocolates by hand in the kitchen behind their sweet shop. Today, we're still a family business, run by their great-granddaughter, and although we're much bigger than we were, we still make everything on this site. We employ around sixty people.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Chocolate begins as cocoa beans, which grow in pods on the cacao tree. The trees only grow in a narrow band around the equator, and most of the world's cocoa comes from West Africa, particularly Ivory Coast and Ghana. We buy our beans from small cooperatives in Ghana, Ecuador and Madagascar, and we visit them every year. We pay above the standard market price, because we believe farmers should earn a fair living.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Before the beans arrive here, they've already been fermented and dried by the farmers. Fermentation is a really important step, because it develops the flavours that we associate with chocolate. Unfermented beans taste bitter and rather unpleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Our first stop will be the roasting room. Roasting is where much of the flavour develops, and our head roaster, Priya, adjusts the temperature and time for each type of bean. Beans from Madagascar, for example, have a fruity flavour, so we roast them quite gently to keep it. After roasting, the beans are cracked open and the thin shells are removed, leaving small pieces called nibs. We don't throw the shells away, by the way. They're sold to local gardeners, who use them on their flower beds.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next, the nibs are ground into a thick paste called cocoa liquor, although it doesn't contain any alcohol. For dark chocolate, we mix this with sugar; for milk chocolate, we also add milk powder. The mixture is then ground for many hours in a machine called a conche, which makes it smooth. Ours run for up to three days. If you've ever eaten chocolate that felt slightly sandy in your mouth, it probably hadn't been conched for long enough.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The final stage is tempering, where the chocolate is carefully heated and cooled to particular temperatures. This is what gives good chocolate its shine and the satisfying snap when you break it. Badly tempered chocolate looks dull and can have white streaks on the surface. After that, the chocolate is poured into moulds and cooled.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few rules before we go in. For hygiene reasons, everyone needs to wear one of these hairnets and a white coat, which you'll find on the rack by the door. Please don't touch any of the machines, as some parts are very hot. Photography is allowed everywhere except the packing room, because some of our new designs haven't been released yet.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: At the end of the tour, we'll go to the tasting room, where you'll try five different chocolates. I'll show you how to taste chocolate properly, a bit like tasting wine. Afterwards, the factory shop will be open, and as a thank-you for joining the tour, everyone will receive a voucher for fifteen per cent off anything in the shop today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Oh, and one more thing. If you enjoy today, we also run chocolate-making workshops on Saturday mornings, where you can make and decorate your own bars to take home. They're very popular with families, so it's best to book a few weeks ahead. Right, if you'd all like to put on your coats and hairnets, we'll start.

listening.title: A survey of student eating habits
listening.contextDescription: Two nutrition students, Lucy and Omar, discuss the results of a survey of first-year students' eating habits with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Lucy and Omar, how did the survey go?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We had two hundred and twelve responses from first-year students living in university accommodation, which was more than we expected.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good number. How did you collect them?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: We put an online questionnaire on the student union's website, and we also handed out paper copies in the dining hall. Most people did it online, but the paper copies helped us reach students who don't usually check the website.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. So what were the main findings?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: Well, the first thing that surprised us was breakfast. Over forty per cent of students said they regularly skip it. The most common reason wasn't that they weren't hungry, but that they didn't have time, because they got up too late.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: Which isn't very surprising if you know how late students go to bed!

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Indeed. What about fruit and vegetables?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: That was quite worrying. The recommendation is at least five portions a day, but only about one in five students said they managed that. The average was just under three portions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you ask why?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: Yes. The main reason they gave was cost. Many students think fresh fruit and vegetables are expensive, although actually things like frozen vegetables, carrots and bananas are quite cheap. The second reason was that they go off quickly, so students end up throwing them away.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So it's partly a question of knowledge. What about cooking?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: We asked students how confident they felt about cooking a simple meal from basic ingredients. About a third said they weren't confident at all. Those students were much more likely to rely on ready meals and takeaways.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: And interestingly, there was a big difference depending on whether they'd cooked at home before coming to university. Students who'd regularly helped with cooking at home were far more confident.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Any findings about takeaways in particular?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: The average was two takeaways a week, but some students were having five or more. Pizza was the most popular, followed by burgers and then Chinese food.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you find any differences between male and female students?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: A few. Female students ate slightly more fruit and vegetables on average, while male students were more likely to have takeaways. But the differences were quite small, and to be honest, the gap between students who could cook and those who couldn't was much bigger than the gap between men and women.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an interesting point to make in your discussion. And did you look at drinks?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: We did. Energy drinks were more popular than we expected, especially during exam periods. About a quarter of students said they drank them at least once a week, usually to help them stay awake while studying.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's worth highlighting. Now, what recommendations are you going to make?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: Our main idea is to run free cooking workshops in the halls of residence, focusing on cheap, quick meals. We thought about producing a recipe booklet too, but we think students are more likely to learn by actually doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: We'd also like the university shop to offer a cheap breakfast bag, with things like fruit and cereal bars, that students can pick up on their way to lectures.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Those sound practical. One thing you should mention in your report is the limitations of your survey. For example, the results are based on what students said about themselves, and people often report healthier habits than they really have.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: That's true. We also only surveyed students in university accommodation, so we can't say anything about students who live at home or in private flats.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Good. Can you send me a draft by the end of next week?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll aim for Friday.
