listening.title: The science of taste
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a food science course on how humans experience taste and flavour.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about taste, or more precisely about the difference between taste and flavour, which are often confused. Understanding this difference is essential for anyone working in food science, whether you're developing new products or trying to make healthy food more appealing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's begin with the tongue. The surface of the tongue is covered with small bumps, and within these are taste buds, of which an adult has somewhere between two and eight thousand. Each taste bud contains around fifty to a hundred receptor cells. You may have seen a diagram, often called the tongue map, showing that different parts of the tongue detect different tastes, with sweetness at the tip and bitterness at the back. This idea has been repeated in textbooks for decades, but it's actually wrong. It came from a mistranslation of a German paper published in 1901. In reality, all areas of the tongue can detect all of the basic tastes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what are these basic tastes? Traditionally, there were four: sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Each has a clear biological purpose. Sweetness signals energy-rich foods. Saltiness helps us maintain the right balance of minerals in the body. Sourness can warn us that food is unripe or has gone bad, and bitterness is often a sign of poison, which is why young children, in particular, tend to reject bitter vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A fifth basic taste is now widely accepted, called umami. It was identified in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, who was trying to understand the savoury taste of a traditional soup made with seaweed. He discovered that it came from a substance called glutamate, which is also found in foods like tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. Umami is thought to help us recognise foods that contain protein. Some scientists have proposed further basic tastes, including one for fat, but there's not yet agreement about this.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, here's the key point: taste is only a small part of what we experience when we eat. Most of what we call flavour actually comes from smell. When you chew, aroma molecules travel from the back of your mouth up into your nose. This is why food seems to have very little flavour when you have a cold and your nose is blocked. You can try a simple experiment: hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You'll probably only notice that it's sweet. When you let go of your nose, the fruit flavour suddenly appears.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Flavour is also influenced by our other senses. Texture matters a great deal; we expect crisps to be crunchy, and if they're soft, we think they're stale, even if they taste exactly the same. Sound plays a role too. In one famous experiment, people rated crisps as fresher when the crunching sound they heard through headphones was made louder. Even colour affects our perception. When drinks are coloured differently from what people expect, they often find it difficult to identify the flavour correctly.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There are also large differences between individuals. About a quarter of people are what are called supertasters. They have more taste buds than average and experience bitter tastes much more strongly, so they often dislike foods like coffee, dark chocolate and cabbage. Our tastes also change with age. The number of taste buds declines as we get older, which is one reason older people sometimes add more salt to their food.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This research has important practical applications. Food manufacturers are under pressure to reduce the amount of sugar and salt in their products, but consumers often complain that healthier versions taste worse. One approach is to use smell to trick the brain. For example, adding a vanilla aroma can make food seem sweeter without adding sugar. Another approach is to change the shape of salt crystals so that they dissolve more quickly on the tongue, giving a stronger salty taste with less salt. In the next lecture, we'll look at some of these techniques in more detail.

listening.title: The science of taste
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a food science course on how humans experience taste and flavour.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about taste, or more precisely about the difference between taste and flavour, which are often confused. Understanding this difference is essential for anyone working in food science, whether you're developing new products or trying to make healthy food more appealing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's begin with the tongue. The surface of the tongue is covered with small bumps, and within these are taste buds, of which an adult has somewhere between two and eight thousand. Each taste bud contains around fifty to a hundred receptor cells. You may have seen a diagram, often called the tongue map, showing that different parts of the tongue detect different tastes, with sweetness at the tip and bitterness at the back. This idea has been repeated in textbooks for decades, but it's actually wrong. It came from a mistranslation of a German paper published in 1901. In reality, all areas of the tongue can detect all of the basic tastes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what are these basic tastes? Traditionally, there were four: sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Each has a clear biological purpose. Sweetness signals energy-rich foods. Saltiness helps us maintain the right balance of minerals in the body. Sourness can warn us that food is unripe or has gone bad, and bitterness is often a sign of poison, which is why young children, in particular, tend to reject bitter vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A fifth basic taste is now widely accepted, called umami. It was identified in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, who was trying to understand the savoury taste of a traditional soup made with seaweed. He discovered that it came from a substance called glutamate, which is also found in foods like tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. Umami is thought to help us recognise foods that contain protein. Some scientists have proposed further basic tastes, including one for fat, but there's not yet agreement about this.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, here's the key point: taste is only a small part of what we experience when we eat. Most of what we call flavour actually comes from smell. When you chew, aroma molecules travel from the back of your mouth up into your nose. This is why food seems to have very little flavour when you have a cold and your nose is blocked. You can try a simple experiment: hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You'll probably only notice that it's sweet. When you let go of your nose, the fruit flavour suddenly appears.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Flavour is also influenced by our other senses. Texture matters a great deal; we expect crisps to be crunchy, and if they're soft, we think they're stale, even if they taste exactly the same. Sound plays a role too. In one famous experiment, people rated crisps as fresher when the crunching sound they heard through headphones was made louder. Even colour affects our perception. When drinks are coloured differently from what people expect, they often find it difficult to identify the flavour correctly.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There are also large differences between individuals. About a quarter of people are what are called supertasters. They have more taste buds than average and experience bitter tastes much more strongly, so they often dislike foods like coffee, dark chocolate and cabbage. Our tastes also change with age. The number of taste buds declines as we get older, which is one reason older people sometimes add more salt to their food.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This research has important practical applications. Food manufacturers are under pressure to reduce the amount of sugar and salt in their products, but consumers often complain that healthier versions taste worse. One approach is to use smell to trick the brain. For example, adding a vanilla aroma can make food seem sweeter without adding sugar. Another approach is to change the shape of salt crystals so that they dissolve more quickly on the tongue, giving a stronger salty taste with less salt. In the next lecture, we'll look at some of these techniques in more detail.

listening.title: Enrolling a child at a nursery
listening.contextDescription: A father visits a nursery to ask about a place for his daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Hello, you must be Mr Okafor. I'm Sophie, the manager here at Little Acorns. Thanks for coming in.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Thanks for seeing me. My wife and I are both going back to full-time work in September, so we're looking for a nursery place for our daughter, Ada.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Lovely. How old is Ada?

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: She'll be two in July.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So she'd join our Squirrels room, which is for children from two to three years old. We have three rooms altogether: Babies, for children up to two, Squirrels, and then Owls, for three- and four-year-olds who are getting ready for school.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: How many children are there in the Squirrels room?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Up to sixteen, with four members of staff, so the ratio is one adult to four children. Each child has a key worker, who's responsible for their care and keeps a record of their development. Parents can see the records and photos through our app.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: That sounds good. What are your opening hours?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're open from half past seven in the morning until six in the evening, Monday to Friday. We're closed for one week at Christmas and on public holidays, but otherwise we're open all year.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: And the fees?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: A full day is sixty-two pounds. If Ada comes five days a week, there's a five per cent discount. The fee includes all meals and snacks, which are cooked here every day by our chef, and nappies as well. The only extra is if you'd like her to join the weekly music class, which is run by an outside teacher and costs four pounds a session.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Okay. Ada is a fussy eater, I'm afraid. Is that a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Not at all, it's very common at that age. We never force children to eat, but we encourage them to try new things, and they often eat better when they see their friends eating. We'll let you know every day what she's eaten.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: And does she still need to sleep during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Most children in Squirrels have a nap after lunch, usually for about an hour and a half. We have a quiet room with little beds, and we follow whatever routine you have at home as far as possible.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: What do the children do during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: A lot of it is play, because that's how young children learn best. There's painting, building, sand and water play, stories and songs. We also spend time outside every day, whatever the weather, so please bring a waterproof suit and wellington boots for Ada. And every Friday, the older children go to the woodland area behind the nursery for forest school.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: She'd love that. How does the settling-in work?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We offer three free settling-in sessions before the start date. For the first one, you stay with her for an hour. For the second, you leave her for an hour, and for the third, she stays for a whole morning. That way she gets used to us gradually.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Great. Is there a place available for September?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Yes, we have two places left in Squirrels. To secure one, we ask for a registration fee of fifty pounds, which isn't refundable, and a deposit of one month's fees, which you get back when she leaves.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I fill in the form now?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll need Ada's full name and date of birth, and the name of your doctor. Which surgery are you registered with?

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: The Riverside Health Centre.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Perfect, that's just round the corner. And finally, we ask for the names of two people, other than you and your wife, who are allowed to collect Ada. We'll take a photo of them, and we won't let her go with anyone else unless you've told us in advance and given us a password.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. I'll put down my sister and Ada's grandmother.

questions.evidenceQuote: So she'd join our Squirrels room

questions.explanation: The ratio is one to four.

listening.title: A new children's discovery centre
listening.contextDescription: A presenter on local radio describes a new science discovery centre for children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, if you're a parent looking for something to do with the kids during the half-term holiday, there's some good news. The new Spark Discovery Centre opens this Saturday in the old tram depot on Canal Street. I went for a preview visit yesterday, and I have to say, I had as much fun as the children did.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: The centre is designed for children aged three to twelve, and the idea is that everything can be touched. There are no glass cases and no signs saying 'Do not touch'. Instead, children learn by experimenting, making mistakes and trying again. The director, Dr Fiona Grant, told me that the aim is to encourage curiosity rather than to teach facts. As she put it, children forget facts, but they remember the feeling of discovering something for themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: The centre is divided into five zones. On the ground floor, the Water Zone is probably the most popular. Children can build dams, control the flow of water using pipes and pumps, and see how boats float. Be warned: they'll get wet, so it's a good idea to bring a change of clothes, although waterproof aprons are provided.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Next to it is the Build Zone, where children can design and construct structures using giant foam blocks, and then test them on an earthquake table that shakes. It's surprisingly difficult to make a tower that survives.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Upstairs, the Body Zone lets children explore how their bodies work. There's a giant model of a heart that you can walk through, and machines that measure how high you can jump or how fast you react. The Light and Sound Zone is in a darkened room, with mirrors, lasers and instruments that make music when you move in front of them.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And finally, for the youngest visitors, there's the Tiny Explorers area, which is reserved for children under five and their parents. It's quieter and softer, with sensory toys and a small sand pit, so toddlers don't get knocked over by the bigger children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Every day, there are also live science shows in the theatre, at eleven and at three. I saw one about air pressure, which involved a lot of loud bangs and exploding balloons, and the children absolutely loved it.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: One thing I particularly liked is that the centre has thought about children with different needs. On Sunday mornings, from nine until ten, there's a relaxed session for children who find noise and crowds difficult. The lights are lower, the sound effects are turned off, and the number of visitors is kept small. All the exhibits on both floors can be reached by wheelchair, and staff have been trained to help children with disabilities take part fully.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, the practical details. The centre is open daily from ten until five, and entry costs nine pounds for children and twelve for adults. Children under two get in free. If you think you'll visit regularly, an annual family membership costs eighty pounds and covers two adults and up to three children, which pays for itself after about two visits. Tickets should be booked online, because numbers are limited to avoid overcrowding.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: There's no car park at the centre, so the organisers recommend using public transport. The number seven bus stops right outside, and the train station is a ten-minute walk away. There's a café on site, but you're also welcome to bring your own food and eat it in the picnic room on the first floor.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Finally, if your children are as excited as mine were, you might be interested in the holiday workshops for eight- to twelve-year-olds. This half term, they're about robotics, and the children build and program a simple robot that they can take home. Places cost twenty-five pounds and are already filling up fast, so book soon if you're interested.

questions.explanation: The aim is to encourage curiosity.
questions.evidenceQuote: the aim is to encourage curiosity rather than to teach facts
options: C. to prepare children for exams

questions.explanation: To protect toddlers from older children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And finally, for the youngest visitors, there's the Tiny Explorers area, which is reserved for children under five and their parents. It's quieter and softer, with sensory toys and a small sand pit, so toddlers don't get knocked over by the bigger children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Every day, there are also live science shows in the theatre, at eleven and at three. I saw one about air pressure, which involved a lot of loud bangs and exploding balloons, and the children absolutely loved it.

listening.title: Researching bilingual children
listening.contextDescription: Two education students, Mei and Tom, discuss a research project on children who grow up speaking two languages.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So, Mei, have you finished the literature review for our project on bilingual children?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Almost. I've read about twenty studies, and there are some really interesting findings, but also a lot of disagreement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Let's start with the basics. When I was growing up, people used to say that learning two languages at once confused children and delayed their speech.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, that was a common belief, especially in the first half of the twentieth century. Some early studies seemed to support it, but they had serious problems. For example, they often tested bilingual children only in their weaker language, or compared poor immigrant children with wealthier monolingual children, so the differences weren't really caused by bilingualism.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So what does more recent research show?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Bilingual children reach the main milestones, like saying their first words and putting two words together, at about the same age as other children. It's true that if you count their vocabulary in each language separately, it's often smaller than a monolingual child's. But if you add the two languages together, the total is usually the same or even larger.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That makes sense. They might know some words only in one language, depending on where they use them.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Exactly. A child might know kitchen words in the language spoken at home and school words in the other one.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: What about mixing languages? I've noticed my cousin's children do that a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: It's called code-switching, and parents often worry about it, but researchers generally see it as normal and even a sign of skill. Adult bilinguals do it too, and they follow quite complex grammatical rules when they switch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. Now, the part I'm most interested in is the so-called bilingual advantage. I read that bilingual children are better at concentrating and switching between tasks.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That's where the disagreement is. In the 2000s, a lot of studies, particularly by Ellen Bialystok in Canada, found that bilingual children performed better on tests of what's called executive function, which includes things like ignoring distractions and switching attention. The theory was that constantly managing two languages exercises these skills.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And now?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: More recent studies with much larger samples have often found no difference at all. Some researchers think the earlier positive results were partly due to small samples and to publication bias, meaning that studies that found an advantage were more likely to be published.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So we should present both sides in our report.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Definitely. What's much less controversial is that bilingualism has social and cultural benefits, like being able to communicate with grandparents, and practical advantages later in life, for example in the job market.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for our own small study, we're going to interview parents of bilingual children at the community language school. How many families have agreed to take part?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Twelve so far. I'd hoped for at least fifteen, but some parents were worried about their privacy. I've explained that we won't use any real names.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Good. What should we ask them about?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I think the most important topic is the strategies they use at home. For example, some families follow the 'one parent, one language' approach, where each parent always speaks a different language to the child. Others speak one language at home and leave the other to school.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And we should ask about challenges. I imagine a lot of children stop using the home language once they start school, because all their friends speak the majority language.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, that's very common, especially in adolescence. It would be interesting to know what parents do to prevent that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. Shall I write the interview questions, and you finish the literature review?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Sounds good. Let's meet again on Thursday to check them.

listening.title: How babies learn language
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a developmental psychology course on how infants begin to acquire language.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at one of the most remarkable achievements of early childhood: learning to speak. By the age of five, most children have a vocabulary of several thousand words and can produce complex sentences, without ever having had a formal lesson. How do they do it?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Surprisingly, language learning begins before birth. From about the twenty-fifth week of pregnancy, a baby can hear sounds from outside the womb, although they're muffled. Experiments have shown that newborn babies prefer their mother's voice to other voices, and that they prefer the language their mother spoke during pregnancy. Researchers discovered this by measuring how fast babies sucked on a special dummy, which tends to increase when they're interested in what they hear. One study even found that the cries of newborn French and German babies have different melodies, which match the patterns of their parents' languages.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the first months of life, babies are what researchers call universal listeners. Every language uses a particular set of sounds, called phonemes, to distinguish words. For example, English distinguishes between 'r' and 'l', but Japanese doesn't. Young babies can hear the difference between almost all the sounds used in the world's languages. But by around ten to twelve months, they gradually lose the ability to distinguish sounds that aren't used in the languages around them. In other words, they become specialists in their own language.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do babies work out where one word ends and another begins? In normal speech, there are no pauses between words. One answer comes from a famous study published in 1996 by Jenny Saffran and her colleagues. They played eight-month-old babies a continuous stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. Within the stream, some syllables always followed each other, forming 'words', while others appeared together only by chance. Afterwards, the babies listened longer to new combinations than to the 'words', showing that they had noticed the patterns. This ability is known as statistical learning.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, babies are practising producing sounds. At around six months, they begin babbling, repeating syllables such as 'ba-ba-ba' or 'da-da-da'. Interestingly, deaf babies who are exposed to sign language babble with their hands, producing repeated movements that resemble signs. This suggests that babbling is not just about controlling the mouth, but a stage in learning language itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First words usually appear at around twelve months, and progress is slow at first. Then, at around eighteen months, many children experience a vocabulary explosion, learning several new words a day. By two, most children are combining words into short phrases, such as 'more milk' or 'daddy gone'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What role do parents play? Across many cultures, adults speak to babies in a special way, sometimes called infant-directed speech, with a higher pitch, exaggerated intonation and simple words. Studies show babies prefer this kind of speech, and it seems to help them learn. Research by Patricia Kuhl also showed the importance of social interaction. Nine-month-old American babies who played with a Mandarin-speaking adult for twelve sessions learned to distinguish Mandarin sounds. But babies who watched exactly the same sessions on video learned nothing. Real human contact appears to be essential.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, is there a critical period for learning language, after which it becomes much more difficult? Evidence from people learning second languages suggests that those who start in early childhood are much more likely to achieve a native-like accent. Grammar also seems easier to master when learning begins early. However, adults often learn vocabulary faster than children at first, so it's not simply a case of 'younger is better'. In the next lecture, we'll look at the debate about whether humans have an inborn ability for grammar.

One answer comes from a famous study published in 1996 by Jenny Saffran and her colleagues. They played eight-month-old babies a continuous stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. Within the stream, some syllables always followed each other, forming 'words', while others appeared together only by chance. Afterwards, the babies listened longer to new combinations than to the 'words', showing that they had noticed the patterns. This ability is known as statistical learning.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, babies are practising producing sounds. At around six months, they begin babbling, repeating syllables such as 'ba-ba-ba' or 'da-da-da'. Interestingly, deaf babies who are exposed to sign language babble with their hands, producing repeated movements that resemble signs. This suggests that babbling is not just about controlling the mouth, but a stage in learning language itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First words usually appear at around twelve months, and progress is slow at first. Then, at around eighteen months, many children experience a vocabulary explosion, learning several new words a day. By two, most children are combining words into short phrases, such as 'more milk' or 'daddy gone'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What role do parents play? Across many cultures, adults speak to babies in a special way, sometimes called infant-directed speech, with a higher pitch, exaggerated intonation and simple words. Studies show babies prefer this kind of speech, and it seems to help them learn. Research by Patricia Kuhl also showed the importance of social interaction. Nine-month-old American babies who played with a Mandarin-speaking adult for twelve sessions learned to distinguish Mandarin sounds. But babies who watched exactly the same sessions on video learned nothing. Real human contact appears to be essential.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, is there a critical period for learning language, after which it becomes much more difficult? Evidence from people learning second languages suggests that those who start in early childhood are much more likely to achieve a native-like accent. Grammar also seems easier to master when learning begins early. However, adults often learn vocabulary faster than children at first, so it's not simply a case of 'younger is better'. listening.title: Booking an architecture walking tour
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a tourist information centre to book a walking tour of the city's buildings.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Westbridge Tourist Information, Priya speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi. I'm visiting the city next week with my partner, and I heard you run walking tours about architecture. Could you give me some details?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Of course. We have two architecture tours at the moment. The first is called Old Town Treasures. It looks at the medieval and Georgian buildings in the historic centre, including the cathedral, the old market hall and some of the merchants' houses along the river. It lasts about two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And the second?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The second is Modern Westbridge, which focuses on buildings from the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It includes the new concert hall, the library, which won an international design prize, and the old docks area, where warehouses have been turned into flats and offices. That one is slightly longer, about two and a half hours, and it finishes with a visit to the viewing platform on top of the Harbour Tower.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My partner's an engineer, so I think he'd prefer the modern tour.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It's very popular with engineers and architects. The guide, Martin, used to work as an architect himself, so he can answer quite technical questions.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. When does it run?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Modern Westbridge runs on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, starting at ten in the morning. Which day would suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thursday would be best.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. Yes, there are places on Thursday. The tour costs fourteen pounds per person, or eleven for students and people over sixty-five. The price includes entry to the viewing platform, which normally costs six pounds on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We're not students, so two full-price tickets, please. Where does the tour start?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It starts outside the main entrance of the Central Library, on Queen's Square. Martin will be wearing a green jacket with our logo on the back. Please arrive ten minutes early, because the tour leaves on time.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Is there a lot of walking? My partner hurt his knee recently.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It's about three kilometres altogether, mostly on flat ground, and there are several stops where you can sit down. There's a lift up the Harbour Tower, so you don't need to climb any stairs. Comfortable shoes are a good idea, though.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That should be fine. What happens if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The tour goes ahead in all weather, except storms. Part of the route is indoors, in the library and the concert hall, but you'll still need a raincoat or an umbrella. If we have to cancel because of severe weather, we'll send you a text message by eight o'clock that morning and give you a full refund.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Can I take photos inside the buildings?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, in most places. The only exception is the concert hall, because there may be a rehearsal going on, and the musicians prefer not to be photographed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Understood. Shall I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Nathan Brightwell. That's B-R-I-G-H-T-W-E-L-L.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a mobile number, for the text message if necessary?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Lovely. Your booking reference is W, T, then four, eight, two, seven. You can pay by card now, or when you collect your tickets from this office.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Just so you know, we also have audio guides for both tours, if you ever want to do one on your own another day. They cost five pounds and are available in eight languages.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. I'll pay now by card. And is there anywhere good to eat near the end of the tour?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The tour finishes in the docks area, and there are lots of cafés and restaurants there. Martin usually recommends the fish restaurant in the old customs house, which has a beautiful glass roof. It's worth booking a table if you want lunch there, as it gets busy.

listening.title: Opening a new public library
listening.contextDescription: The head librarian speaks at the opening of a new city library.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for coming to the official opening of the new Eastfield Library. My name is Dr Helen Park, and I'm the head librarian. Before we cut the ribbon, I'd like to tell you a little about the building and what it offers.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: The old library, as many of you will remember, was in a nineteenth-century building on Station Road. It was much loved, but it was too small, difficult for people with disabilities to use, and very expensive to heat. After a public consultation, in which more than four thousand residents took part, the council decided to build a new library here, on the site of the former bus depot.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: The building was designed by the local firm Harper and Lowe, and one of their main aims was to make it feel open and welcoming. That's why the whole front of the building is made of glass, so that people passing by can see what's happening inside. When you go in, you'll find yourself in a large central atrium, which rises through all four floors, with a roof of glass panels that fills the building with natural light.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: Sustainability was another priority. The building is heated and cooled using a ground source heat pump, which takes heat from deep underground in winter, and there are solar panels on the roof. Rainwater is collected and used to flush the toilets. As a result, the library uses around sixty per cent less energy than the old building, even though it's three times the size. The wooden panels you can see on the outside were made from trees grown in sustainably managed forests in Scotland.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: So what will you find on each floor? The ground floor has the café, the main information desk and a space for exhibitions. At the moment, there's an exhibition of photographs of the town over the last hundred years, which I highly recommend. The children's library is also on the ground floor, with its own garden, where we'll be holding storytelling sessions in the summer.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: The first floor is for adult fiction and non-fiction, and there's also a quiet reading room overlooking the park. The second floor is mainly for study. There are over two hundred desks, as well as twelve study pods, which are small private rooms for one or two people. These can be booked for up to three hours at a time using the library app.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: On the top floor, we have something completely new: a maker space. This is a workshop where anyone can come and learn practical and creative skills. There are 3D printers, a laser cutter, sewing machines and equipment for recording music and podcasts. To use the equipment, you'll first need to attend a free one-hour safety session, which runs every Saturday morning.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: We've also thought carefully about accessibility. There are lifts to every floor, the shelves are lower than in most libraries so that everyone can reach them, and there's a sensory room on the ground floor for children and adults who need a calm space. We've also introduced a home delivery service for residents who are unable to visit the library in person.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: Some practical information. The library is open from eight in the morning until eight in the evening on weekdays, and from nine until five at weekends. That's longer than the old library, which closed at six. Membership is, of course, free, and you can join at the information desk today with proof of your address. New members today will receive a free canvas bag.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.text: Finally, I'd like to thank everyone who made this possible: the architects, the builders, our staff, and particularly our team of volunteers, who spent the last three weeks moving over a hundred thousand books from the old building. Now, without further delay, I'd like to invite the mayor to come forward and officially open the library.

listening.title: A project on tiny houses
listening.contextDescription: Two architecture students, Zara and Liam, discuss their research project on tiny houses with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Zara, Liam. Sorry I'm a few minutes late; my previous meeting ran over. So, how's the project on tiny houses going?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Really well, I think. We've finished the background research and visited three tiny house communities, and now we're working on the analysis.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Remind me how you're defining a tiny house.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: We're using the most common definition, which is a home with a floor area of less than about thirty-seven square metres, or four hundred square feet. Many of them are built on wheels, so they can be moved, although some are on permanent foundations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And why are people choosing to live in them?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: The main reason, according to our interviews, is cost. Most of the residents we spoke to said they couldn't afford a conventional house, or didn't want to spend most of their income on a mortgage. A tiny house typically costs a fraction of an ordinary home, and some people build their own.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: But there were other reasons, too. Quite a few people talked about wanting a simpler life, with fewer possessions. And many were concerned about the environment. Smaller homes use far less energy for heating and lighting, and some of the houses we visited were completely off-grid, with solar panels, rainwater collection and composting toilets.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Were the residents mostly young people?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That's what we expected, but actually there was a real mix. In one community, almost half the residents were retired people who had sold larger family homes. They said they liked having less to clean and maintain.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. What about the problems?

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: The biggest one is finding somewhere to put the house. In many places, the regulations don't really recognise tiny houses. If they're on wheels, they're sometimes treated like caravans, which means people aren't allowed to live in them all year round. So getting planning permission can be very difficult.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That's why communities have become so important. In a community, a group of people share the land and the legal costs, and they often share facilities like a laundry, a workshop or a big kitchen for social events.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What did residents say about living in such a small space?

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: Most were very positive, but storage was a common complaint. Several people said they'd underestimated how hard it would be to give up their belongings. And couples sometimes said they found it difficult to have time on their own.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: One woman told us that she and her husband had added a separate small cabin as an office, because they were both working from home and kept getting in each other's way.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a useful example. Now, for your design proposal, what are you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: We'd like to design a tiny house community for a site near the university. The idea is to provide affordable housing for postgraduate students and young staff. Each house would have its own small kitchen and bathroom, but there'd be a shared common house with a larger kitchen, a study room and guest bedrooms.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I like it. How many houses are you planning?

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: About twenty, arranged around a central garden, with bicycle parking but no space for cars.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Have you thought about materials?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: We're planning to use timber frames, because they're light and can be built quickly in a factory and then brought to the site. We'd also like to use recycled materials where possible.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. In your report, make sure you also discuss whether tiny houses really are a solution to the housing crisis, or just a niche choice. Some critics argue that they use land less efficiently than flats, for example.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.text: That's a good point. We'll include a section comparing the density of tiny house communities with apartment buildings.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Let's meet again in two weeks, when you have some sketches to show me.

listening.title: The story of concrete
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a civil engineering course on the history and future of concrete.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to talk about the most widely used building material on Earth: concrete. After water, it's the most consumed substance in the world. Every year, enough concrete is produced to build a wall around the planet many times over. But despite its importance, it's a material that most people never think about.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First, some basic definitions, because people often confuse concrete and cement. Cement is a fine grey powder that acts as a kind of glue. When it's mixed with water, a chemical reaction takes place, and it hardens. Concrete is made by mixing cement and water with sand and small stones, which are called aggregate. The cement binds the aggregate together into a solid mass.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Concrete is not a modern invention. The ancient Romans were experts in using it. They made their cement from lime mixed with volcanic ash, which they found near the town of Pozzuoli, close to Naples. Roman concrete was used to build harbours, bridges, aqueducts and, most famously, the Pantheon in Rome, completed around the year 125. Its dome, over forty-three metres across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, nearly two thousand years later.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Remarkably, some Roman concrete has lasted far better than modern concrete. Roman harbour walls that have been in seawater for two thousand years are still standing, whereas modern concrete in the sea often begins to break down within decades. Research published in 2023 by a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology suggested one reason. The Romans appear to have mixed their concrete using lime that was still hot, and this left small lumps of lime in the material. When cracks form and water gets in, the lime reacts and fills the cracks, so the concrete can, in effect, repair itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: After the fall of the Roman Empire, the knowledge of how to make concrete was largely lost in Europe, and for over a thousand years, most large buildings were made of stone or brick. The modern history of concrete begins in 1824, when an English bricklayer named Joseph Aspdin patented a new type of cement, which he made by heating limestone and clay together at high temperatures. He called it Portland cement, because he thought the hardened material looked like Portland stone, a popular building stone from the south of England. Portland cement is still the most common type used today.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Concrete has one major weakness: although it's extremely strong when it's squeezed, it's weak when it's stretched or bent, and it tends to crack. The solution was to put steel bars inside it, creating reinforced concrete. One of the pioneers of this idea was a French gardener, Joseph Monier, who wanted to make stronger flower pots. He took out his first patent in 1867. Steel and concrete work well together, partly because they expand by similar amounts when they get hot, so they don't separate.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Reinforced concrete made possible many of the structures of the twentieth century, from dams and motorways to skyscrapers. It's cheap, it can be poured into almost any shape, and it's resistant to fire. But it also has a serious environmental cost. Producing cement requires heating limestone to around fourteen hundred degrees Celsius, which uses huge amounts of energy, and the chemical reaction itself releases carbon dioxide. Altogether, cement production is responsible for around eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, more than the entire aviation industry.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So engineers are looking for ways to make concrete greener. One approach is to replace part of the cement with waste materials, such as ash from power stations or slag from steel production. Another is to capture the carbon dioxide released during manufacture and store it, or even inject it back into the concrete, where it becomes part of the material. Researchers are also trying to learn from the Romans, to make concrete that lasts longer and therefore needs replacing less often. In the next lecture, we'll look at some of the alternatives to concrete, including engineered timber.

listening.title: Booking a school visit to a space centre
listening.contextDescription: A teacher phones a space science centre to book a visit for her class.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Good morning, Northgate Space Centre, bookings desk. This is Oliver speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Hi, good morning. I'm a teacher at a primary school, and I'd like to book a visit for my class next term. We're studying the solar system, and I've heard your centre is excellent for children.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you, that's lovely to hear. I can certainly help with that. How many children would be coming?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: There are thirty-two in the class, but two of them will be away on that week, so it'll be thirty pupils.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thirty pupils. And how old are they?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: They're nine and ten years old.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Perfect. For that age group, we recommend our Explorer Day. It includes a show in the planetarium, a guided tour of the main galleries and one workshop. Did you have a date in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: We were hoping for a Thursday in May. Would the fifteenth be possible?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm afraid the fifteenth is already fully booked, but we have space on Thursday the twenty-second.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: The twenty-second would be fine. That's still before the half-term holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Great. Now, for the workshop, there are three choices. The first is Rocket Science, where the children build and launch small rockets powered by water and air. The second is Life on the Space Station, where they find out how astronauts eat, sleep and exercise. And the third is Mission to Mars, where they work in teams to design a vehicle that could drive on the surface of Mars.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Hmm. They'd all love the rockets, but I think the Mars one fits best with our topic, because we're going to look at the planets in detail.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Mission to Mars it is, then. It's very popular, and the children get to test their designs on our model Martian landscape at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Wonderful. What time does the day start?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: We ask groups to arrive by half past nine. The planetarium show begins at a quarter to ten, and the day finishes at half past two, so that you can get back to school before the end of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: That works. And what about lunch? We'll bring packed lunches.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's what most schools do. We have a lunch room for school groups on the ground floor, next to the shop. You'll have it from twelve until half past twelve. You can also leave bags and coats there during the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Good. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The Explorer Day is eight pounds fifty per child. Adults are free, as long as there's at least one adult for every ten children. Any extra adults pay six pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: So with thirty children, we need three adults. I'll probably bring four, with myself and three parents. Is that a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Not at all. The fourth adult would just pay the six pounds. Now, can I take some details? What's the name of your school?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: It's Hollybank Primary School.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: And your name?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Mrs Karen Lindqvist. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you. Will you be coming by coach?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Yes, we will.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Then please tell the driver to use the entrance on Mill Lane, not the main entrance, because coaches can drop off and park there. And one more thing: please let us know at least a week before your visit if any children need extra support, or use a wheelchair, so that we can make sure everything is ready.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: One of the boys does use a wheelchair, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's no problem at all. The whole building is accessible, and I'll make a note on the booking. We'll send you a confirmation by email, along with a worksheet that the children can complete during the gallery tour.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Lovely. Thanks so much for your help.

listening.title: A summer space camp
listening.contextDescription: The organiser of a week-long summer space camp for teenagers speaks to parents at an information evening.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Rachel Torres, and I'm the director of Orbit Space Camp. Tonight I'd like to tell you what your children will be doing during the week, and answer some of the questions that parents usually ask.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: First, a bit about us. Orbit Space Camp started eleven years ago, with just twenty students in a borrowed school hall. Today we welcome around two hundred young people every summer, aged between twelve and sixteen, and we're based here at the university, which means we can use the science labs, the sports hall and the observatory on the roof. Most of our staff are science teachers or university students studying physics or engineering, and every group of eight campers has its own team leader.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, the programme. The week is built around a single big challenge: each team has to plan and carry out an imaginary mission to the Moon. Everything they do during the week helps them prepare for that.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Monday, after the welcome session, the teams are formed and each one chooses a name and designs a mission badge. In the afternoon, there's a talk about the history of space travel, and we're very lucky this year, because the talk will be given by a retired engineer who worked on satellite design for over thirty years.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Tuesday, the focus is on rockets. Campers learn the basic science of how rockets work, and then they build their own model rockets, which are launched on the sports field. It's always one of the favourite days, although it can get a little muddy if it rains, so please pack an old pair of shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Wednesday is all about living in space. The campers try some of the food that astronauts eat, which, I should warn you, not all of them enjoy. They also find out how astronauts keep fit, and they try our simulator, which gives them an idea of how difficult it is to move around without gravity.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Thursday, the teams finish planning their missions, and in the evening, if the sky is clear, we hold our stargazing session at the observatory. That means a late finish, at about eleven o'clock, so you'll need to collect your children later that day, or they can stay overnight in the university accommodation for a small extra charge. If it's cloudy, we'll show a film in the lecture theatre instead.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And finally, on Friday, the teams carry out their missions. One room becomes mission control, and the teams have to deal with unexpected problems that we give them, just like real flight controllers. In the afternoon, parents are invited to a presentation, where each team explains its mission, and everyone receives a certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical matters. The camp runs from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, apart from Thursday. Lunch is provided every day in the university canteen, and we can cater for all special diets, as long as you tell us on the registration form. Please don't send your children with large amounts of money; there's nothing to buy apart from snacks and a small shop that sells camp T-shirts.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Mobile phones are allowed, but they must be switched off during activities. We find that the campers are usually far too busy to miss them. And if you need to contact your child during the day, please call the camp office rather than their mobile.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Finally, a question I'm always asked: do children need to be good at science? The answer is no. Many of our campers simply have an interest in space, and some of our most creative mission plans have come from students who say they don't like science at school. Right, I'm happy to take your questions now.

listening.title: A presentation on the Voyager missions
listening.contextDescription: Two astronomy students, Lena and Sam, discuss their presentation on the Voyager space probes with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Lena, Sam. So you've chosen the Voyager missions for your presentation. Tell me how you're planning to organise it.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Well, we want to start with the background, explaining why the two probes were launched when they were. Then we'll look at what they discovered at the planets, and finish with where they are now.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. So why were they launched in 1977?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Because of a rare arrangement of the outer planets. In the late nineteen-seventies, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune were lined up in a way that only happens about once every hundred and seventy-five years. That meant a spacecraft could use the gravity of one planet to speed it up and bend its path towards the next one. It's called a gravity assist.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And without that, the journey would have taken far longer?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Much longer, decades longer for Neptune. One thing that confuses people is that Voyager 2 was actually launched first, in August 1977, and Voyager 1 about two weeks later, in September. But Voyager 1 was on a faster route, so it overtook its twin and reached Jupiter first.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We thought we'd use a timeline to show that, because it's easier to follow than just saying the dates.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good idea. Now, the discoveries. There's a huge amount you could say, so you'll have to be selective.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We know. We've decided to choose one discovery for each planet. For Jupiter, it's the volcanoes on its moon Io. Nobody expected to find active volcanoes anywhere except Earth, so that was a real surprise. For Saturn, we're going to talk about the structure of the rings, which turned out to be made of thousands of narrow rings rather than a few wide ones.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And then for Uranus and Neptune, it's important to say that Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft that has ever visited them. It flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. At Neptune, it found a huge storm, which was called the Great Dark Spot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. And will you mention the Golden Record?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Definitely. Both probes carry a gold-plated record with sounds and images from Earth, including greetings in fifty-five languages and different kinds of music. The committee that chose the contents was led by the astronomer Carl Sagan. We'd like to play a short clip from it during the presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That'll certainly keep the audience's attention. Just check that the clip isn't too long; you only have fifteen minutes in total.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We'll keep it under thirty seconds. Then, for the last part, we want to talk about the famous photograph called the Pale Blue Dot, which Voyager 1 took in 1990, looking back at Earth from about six billion kilometres away. Earth is just a tiny point of light in it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a powerful image to show. And where are the probes now?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Both of them have left the bubble of particles from the Sun and entered interstellar space: Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018. They're the most distant human-made objects ever. Radio signals from Voyager 1 now take nearly a day to reach Earth.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The problem is power. They run on a nuclear power source that produces a little less electricity every year, so the engineers have been switching off instruments one by one to save energy. At some point in the next few years, they won't have enough power to send signals at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do you think the main message of your presentation is?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: I suppose that a mission planned to last about five years has been working for nearly half a century, and that's partly thanks to the engineers, who've solved problems from billions of kilometres away.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good way to end. One piece of advice: for the slides, use fewer words and bigger pictures. The images from Voyager are so striking that they'll do a lot of the work for you.

listening.title: A presentation on the Voyager missions
listening.contextDescription: Two astronomy students, Lena and Sam, discuss their presentation on the Voyager space probes with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Lena, Sam. So you've chosen the Voyager missions for your presentation. Tell me how you're planning to organise it.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Well, we want to start with the background, explaining why the two probes were launched when they were. Then we'll look at what they discovered at the planets, and finish with where they are now.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. So why were they launched in 1977?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Because of a rare arrangement of the outer planets. In the late nineteen-seventies, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune were lined up in a way that only happens about once every hundred and seventy-five years. That meant a spacecraft could use the gravity of one planet to speed it up and bend its path towards the next one. It's called a gravity assist.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And without that, the journey would have taken far longer?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Much longer, decades longer for Neptune. One thing that confuses people is that Voyager 2 was actually launched first, in August 1977, and Voyager 1 about two weeks later, in September. But Voyager 1 was on a faster route, so it overtook its twin and reached Jupiter first.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We thought we'd use a timeline to show that, because it's easier to follow than just saying the dates.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good idea. Now, the discoveries. There's a huge amount you could say, so you'll have to be selective.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We know. We've decided to choose one discovery for each planet. For Jupiter, it's the volcanoes on its moon Io. Nobody expected to find active volcanoes anywhere except Earth, so that was a real surprise. For Saturn, we're going to talk about the structure of the rings, which turned out to be made of thousands of narrow rings rather than a few wide ones.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And then for Uranus and Neptune, it's important to say that Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft that has ever visited them. It flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. At Neptune, it found a huge storm, which was called the Great Dark Spot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. And will you mention the Golden Record?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Definitely. Both probes carry a gold-plated record with sounds and images from Earth, including greetings in fifty-five languages and different kinds of music. The committee that chose the contents was led by the astronomer Carl Sagan. We'd like to play a short clip from it during the presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That'll certainly keep the audience's attention. Just check that the clip isn't too long; you only have fifteen minutes in total.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We'll keep it under thirty seconds. Then, for the last part, we want to talk about the famous photograph called the Pale Blue Dot, which Voyager 1 took in 1990, looking back at Earth from about six billion kilometres away. Earth is just a tiny point of light in it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a powerful image to show. And where are the probes now?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Both of them have left the bubble of particles from the Sun and entered interstellar space: Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018. They're the most distant human-made objects ever. Radio signals from Voyager 1 now take nearly a day to reach Earth.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The problem is power. They run on a nuclear power source that produces a little less electricity every year, so the engineers have been switching off instruments one by one to save energy. At some point in the next few years, they won't have enough power to send signals at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do you think the main message of your presentation is?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: I suppose that a mission planned to last about five years has been working for nearly half a century, and that's partly thanks to the engineers, who've solved problems from billions of kilometres away.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good way to end. One piece of advice: for the slides, use fewer words and bigger pictures. The images from Voyager are so striking that they'll do a lot of the work for you.

listening.title: The human body in space
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a human physiology course on how long periods in space affect astronauts' bodies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at what happens to the human body when it spends a long time in space. This isn't just an interesting question. If people are ever going to travel to Mars, a journey that would take several months in each direction, we need to understand these effects and find ways to reduce them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most of what we know comes from astronauts who have lived on space stations in orbit around the Earth, especially the International Space Station, where crews usually stay for about six months. The longest single stay in space was by the Russian doctor Valeri Polyakov, who spent four hundred and thirty-seven days on the Mir space station in the mid nineteen-nineties.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with the most obvious difference: the lack of gravity, or more accurately, microgravity. On Earth, our bones and muscles are constantly working against gravity, even when we're just standing still. In space, they no longer have to do this, and the body responds by losing what it doesn't need. Astronauts can lose around one to one and a half per cent of the mass of their weight-bearing bones, such as the hips and legs, every month. That's similar to the amount an elderly person on Earth might lose in a whole year. Muscles also become weaker, particularly in the legs and back.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: To reduce these effects, astronauts on the space station exercise for about two hours every day. They use a treadmill, with straps that hold them down so they don't float away, an exercise bike, and a machine that allows them to lift weights by using pressure instead of heavy objects. This has made a big difference, although it doesn't completely prevent bone loss.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A second effect concerns the body's fluids. On Earth, gravity pulls blood and other fluids down towards our feet. In space, these fluids move up towards the head. As a result, astronauts' faces look puffy and their legs become thinner, which some astronauts jokingly call 'bird legs'. This movement of fluid may also be connected to changes in vision. Some astronauts find that their eyesight becomes worse during long missions, because of changes to the shape of the eye, and in some cases the changes last after they return.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, astronauts also grow taller in space, by up to about five centimetres, because the spine is no longer being pressed together by gravity. Unfortunately, this often causes back pain, and they return to their normal height soon after landing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Many astronauts also suffer from space sickness during their first few days, because the balance system in the inner ear becomes confused. And sleep can be difficult. Because the space station travels around the Earth about every ninety minutes, astronauts see around sixteen sunrises a day, which can disturb the body's natural daily rhythms. They usually sleep in small cabins, in sleeping bags attached to the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A more serious long-term concern is radiation. On Earth, and even on the space station, we're partly protected by the Earth's magnetic field. On a journey to Mars, astronauts would be outside this protection for much longer, and exposed to higher levels of radiation, which could increase the risk of cancer. Designing better shielding for spacecraft is one of the main challenges for future missions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, an unusual experiment. In 2015, the American astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the space station, while his identical twin brother, Mark, who is also a former astronaut, stayed on Earth. Because they have the same genes, scientists could compare the two men to see how spaceflight had changed Scott's body. They found a number of changes, for example in his immune system and in the way some of his genes were working, but most of them returned to normal within a few months of his return. That's encouraging news for those planning longer missions. Next week, we'll look at the psychological effects of living in a small space, far from home.

listening.title: Booking a glass-blowing class
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a glass studio to book a beginners' glass-blowing session.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Furnace Lane Glass Studio, Niamh speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'm calling about your glass-blowing taster sessions. I saw a leaflet in the library, and I'd like to book one as a birthday present for my sister.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: What a lovely idea. The taster sessions are for complete beginners. They last two and a half hours, and each person works one-to-one with one of our glass artists at the furnace. Was there a particular date you had in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Her birthday's on the twelfth, which is a Friday, so ideally that day.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm afraid Friday the twelfth is fully booked. But we do have places on Saturday the thirteenth, in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday's fine, actually. She doesn't work at weekends, and it means we can go out for lunch together afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. And how many people would that be for?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, originally I was thinking of four: me, my sister, her husband and my nephew. How old do people have to be?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The minimum age is sixteen, I'm afraid. It's because of the temperatures involved: the furnace runs at over a thousand degrees, and our insurance doesn't cover younger participants.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ah, my nephew's only fourteen, so he'll have to wait a couple of years. So it'll be three of us, then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Three people on Saturday morning. Now, the price. On weekdays, it's fifty-five pounds per person, but weekend sessions are sixty-eight pounds, because they're so popular.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's okay. What does that include?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It includes all the materials, the tuition, and a hot drink when you arrive. And everyone makes their own piece to take home. For beginners, that's a paperweight. You choose your colours, and the artist helps you gather the molten glass and shape it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A paperweight. That sounds perfect. Can we take it home straight away?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, and that surprises a lot of people. If hot glass cools too quickly, it develops stresses inside, and it can crack, sometimes days later. So all the finished pieces go into a kiln overnight, where they cool down very slowly. You can collect them from the studio any time after midday the next day, or we can post them to you for a fee of six pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll come and collect them. Will there be time to watch the artists working, too?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes. At the end of the session, one of our artists gives a short demonstration, usually making a vase or a bowl, and explains what's happening to the glass at each stage. People find it fascinating, because the glass changes colour as it cools, from bright orange to its real colour. There's also a small shop where you can buy work made by our resident artists.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. Is there anything we should wear?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, this is important. Please wear clothes made of cotton, or another natural fibre like wool. Synthetic fabrics, such as polyester or nylon, can melt if a spark lands on them. Long trousers are best, and no loose scarves.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Got it. What about shoes?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Closed shoes, please, ideally leather boots. Sandals and open-toed shoes aren't allowed in the hot shop under any circumstances. We provide safety glasses, so you don't need to bring those.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. And is there parking nearby?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's no parking at the studio itself, but there's a free car park behind the library, which is about three minutes' walk away. On Saturdays, it can fill up by ten, so try to arrive early.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's useful, thanks. Shall I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Ashworth. A-S-H-W-O-R-T-H.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Ashworth. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh seven seven oh oh, nine one two, four eight three.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. I'll send you a confirmation email with directions and a short safety form that each of you needs to sign. Payment is due when you arrive. And if your sister enjoys it, we also run a four-week evening course for people who want to take it further.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll let her know. Thanks so much for your help.
