listening.title: Inside a recycling plant
listening.contextDescription: A guide talks to a group of residents visiting a materials recovery facility.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Greenvale Materials Recovery Facility. I'm Joel, and I'll be showing you around this morning. Before we go onto the viewing platform, where it's very noisy, I'd like to explain what happens here and give you some tips that will make our job a lot easier.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Everything that you put in your household recycling bin ends up in this building. We receive about three hundred tonnes of material on an average weekday, and our job is to separate it into streams of paper, cardboard, metals, glass and different types of plastic, which are then sold to manufacturers who turn them into new products.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let's start with plastics, because that's where most of the confusion lies. You'll have noticed that many plastic items have a small triangle printed on them with a number inside, from one to seven. A lot of people assume that the triangle means the item can be recycled, but that's not actually the case. The number simply tells you what type of plastic the item is made of. Number one, for example, is PET, which is used for most drinks bottles, and number two is high-density polyethylene, which is used for milk bottles and many shampoo bottles. Both of those are easy for us to recycle. Others, such as number three, PVC, are much harder.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: So how do we sort everything? First, the material passes over a series of rotating screens, which separate flat items like paper from three-dimensional ones like bottles and cans. Then powerful magnets lift out the steel cans. Aluminium isn't magnetic, so it's removed further along by a machine that creates a changing magnetic field, which actually pushes the cans off the belt.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The plastics are sorted by optical sorters. These shine infrared light onto each item, and because each type of plastic reflects the light in a slightly different way, the machine can identify it, and then a precisely timed jet of air blows it into the right container. It's remarkably fast. The one exception is black plastic, like the trays that meat often comes in. The black colouring absorbs the infrared light, so the sorters simply can't see it, and it ends up being sent for disposal. So if you can avoid buying food in black trays, please do.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, some tips. The biggest problem we face is contamination, meaning things in the recycling that shouldn't be there, or recyclable items covered in food. Containers do need to be empty and reasonably clean, but you don't need to scrub them or use hot water. A quick rinse in your washing-up water is enough.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Please don't put plastic bags or other soft plastics in your bin. They wrap themselves around the rotating screens, and we have to stop the whole line several times a day so that staff can cut them free. Most large supermarkets now have collection points for soft plastics, including carrier bags and bread bags, so take them there instead.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Shampoo bottles and cleaning product bottles are fine in your household bin, but please put the lids back on, because loose lids are too small for our machines and fall through the screens. Black meat trays should go in your general rubbish, for the reason I explained.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And, most importantly, never put batteries in any of your bins. Lithium batteries from phones, toys and electronic cigarettes can be crushed or punctured in the collection lorry or here on the line, and when that happens, they can catch fire. We have small fires here more often than you'd think. The same goes for old mobile phones and other broken electrical items: please take those to the household waste site on Mill Road, which has special containers for them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, if everyone could put on a high-visibility vest and a pair of ear defenders, we'll head up to the platform.

listening.title: A project on natural dyes
listening.contextDescription: Two chemistry students, Priya and Tom, discuss their natural dye experiments with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Priya, Tom. So, you've finished the practical work for your natural dyes project. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Really well, on the whole. As you know, we wanted to compare how well different natural dyes work on wool and cotton, and how resistant the colours are to light.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We deliberately chose dye sources from the kitchen, things that are cheap and usually just thrown away: onion skins, avocado stones and the outer leaves of red cabbage. We also used turmeric, which isn't waste, of course, but it's widely available and gives a really strong yellow.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you prepare the fibres?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We treated all the samples with alum first, as a mordant. It helps the dye molecules bind to the fibres. Then we simmered them in the dye baths for an hour. We kept the temperature just below ninety degrees, because boiling can damage wool fibres and make them felt together.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. What were the colours like?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The onion skins gave a lovely golden orange, and the turmeric a very bright yellow. The surprise was the avocado stones. We'd expected brown, but they produced a soft pink colour, which was beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, people are often surprised by that. Did the wool and cotton behave differently?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Very differently. The wool took up far more colour than the cotton with every dye. Some of the cotton samples were so pale they were hardly coloured at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's what I'd expect. Wool is a protein fibre, and natural dyes generally bond much more readily with protein than with cellulose, which is what cotton is made of. Traditional dyers often treated cotton with tannins first, from oak bark, for example, to help the dye attach. You might try that if you have time, or at least discuss it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We will. Then for the light test, we put a set of samples on a south-facing windowsill, with half of each sample covered by card, so we could compare the exposed and protected parts. We'd planned to leave them for three weeks, but the weather was so cloudy that we extended it to four.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. And which dye was least resistant to light?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Turmeric, by far. It started off the brightest, but after four weeks the exposed half had faded to a pale cream. The onion skin samples hardly changed at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Turmeric is notorious for that, which is one reason it was never highly valued as a textile dye. What about the red cabbage?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That was the most interesting one chemically. In plain water, the dye bath was purple, but when we added vinegar, it turned pink, and with baking soda, it went green. So the colour of the fabric depended on what we added.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. The pigments in red cabbage are called anthocyanins, and they act as natural pH indicators, changing colour depending on how acidic or alkaline their surroundings are. You should definitely include an explanation of the chemistry behind that in your report, with the structures of the molecules if possible. It would strengthen the theoretical side considerably.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Okay. One thing we're not happy with is how we measured the fading. We just compared the samples by eye and gave each one a score.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a fair concern, because judgements by eye are quite subjective. One option would be to photograph all the samples under identical lighting and then use image software to measure the colour values. That would give you numbers you could actually compare.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's a great idea. We could do that next week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And when you write up, remember to say where your dye materials came from and how much you used of each, so that someone else could repeat the experiment.

listening.title: A project on natural dyes
listening.contextDescription: Two chemistry students, Priya and Tom, discuss their natural dye experiments with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Priya, Tom. So, you've finished the practical work for your natural dyes project. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Really well, on the whole. As you know, we wanted to compare how well different natural dyes work on wool and cotton, and how resistant the colours are to light.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We deliberately chose dye sources from the kitchen, things that are cheap and usually just thrown away: onion skins, avocado stones and the outer leaves of red cabbage. We also used turmeric, which isn't waste, of course, but it's widely available and gives a really strong yellow.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you prepare the fibres?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We treated all the samples with alum first, as a mordant. It helps the dye molecules bind to the fibres. Then we simmered them in the dye baths for an hour. We kept the temperature just below ninety degrees, because boiling can damage wool fibres and make them felt together.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. What were the colours like?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The onion skins gave a lovely golden orange, and the turmeric a very bright yellow. The surprise was the avocado stones. We'd expected brown, but they produced a soft pink colour, which was beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, people are often surprised by that. Did the wool and cotton behave differently?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Very differently. The wool took up far more colour than the cotton with every dye. Some of the cotton samples were so pale they were hardly coloured at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's what I'd expect. Wool is a protein fibre, and natural dyes generally bond much more readily with protein than with cellulose, which is what cotton is made of. Traditional dyers often treated cotton with tannins first, from oak bark, for example, to help the dye attach. You might try that if you have time, or at least discuss it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We will. Then for the light test, we put a set of samples on a south-facing windowsill, with half of each sample covered by card, so we could compare the exposed and protected parts. We'd planned to leave them for three weeks, but the weather was so cloudy that we extended it to four.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. And which dye was least resistant to light?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Turmeric, by far. It started off the brightest, but after four weeks the exposed half had faded to a pale cream. The onion skin samples hardly changed at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Turmeric is notorious for that, which is one reason it was never highly valued as a textile dye. What about the red cabbage?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That was the most interesting one chemically. In plain water, the dye bath was purple, but when we added vinegar, it turned pink, and with baking soda, it went green. So the colour of the fabric depended on what we added.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. The pigments in red cabbage are called anthocyanins, and they act as natural pH indicators, changing colour depending on how acidic or alkaline their surroundings are. You should definitely include an explanation of the chemistry behind that in your report, with the structures of the molecules if possible. It would strengthen the theoretical side considerably.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Okay. One thing we're not happy with is how we measured the fading. We just compared the samples by eye and gave each one a score.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a fair concern, because judgements by eye are quite subjective. One option would be to photograph all the samples under identical lighting and then use image software to measure the colour values. That would give you numbers you could actually compare.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's a great idea. We could do that next week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And when you write up, remember to say where your dye materials came from and how much you used of each, so that someone else could repeat the experiment.

listening.title: The story of rubber
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a materials science course on the history and chemistry of rubber.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at a material that most of us use every day without giving it a second thought: rubber. It's in our car tyres, our shoes, our medical gloves and countless seals and hoses. Its history is a fascinating mix of chemistry, accident and global politics.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Natural rubber comes from latex, a milky white fluid produced by certain plants. By far the most important source is the rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, which is native to the Amazon basin. When the bark is cut, latex slowly oozes out and can be collected in a cup, a process known as tapping. Chemically, rubber is a polymer, made up of very long chain molecules, and it's the ability of these tangled chains to stretch out and then spring back that gives rubber its elasticity.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The peoples of Mesoamerica were using rubber more than three thousand years ago. They famously made solid rubber balls for a ritual ball game, which astonished the Spanish when they arrived, since nothing in Europe bounced like that. Researchers have also shown that Mesoamerican craftspeople mixed latex with the juice of a particular vine, a type of morning glory, and that by changing the proportions they could make rubber that was either bouncier or more hard-wearing, depending on what it was to be used for.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Europeans first became aware of rubber after Columbus's voyages, but for a long time it was little more than a curiosity. In 1770, the English chemist Joseph Priestley noticed that a small piece of it could rub out pencil marks, which is how the material got its English name. But raw rubber had serious drawbacks. In hot weather, it became soft and sticky and smelled unpleasant, and in cold weather, it turned hard and brittle. Early waterproof coats and boots made from it were notoriously unreliable.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The breakthrough came from the American inventor Charles Goodyear, who spent years experimenting, often in great poverty. In 1839, he found that heating rubber with sulphur transformed it into a material that stayed elastic and strong over a wide range of temperatures. According to a popular story, he discovered this by accident when a mixture fell onto a hot stove, though the story may have been improved in the retelling. The process became known as vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. In Britain, Thomas Hancock obtained a patent for a similar process shortly before Goodyear's American patent was granted, and Goodyear, sadly, died heavily in debt.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what does the sulphur actually do? It forms short bridges between neighbouring polymer chains. These bridges, which chemists call cross-links, stop the chains from sliding past one another permanently, so the rubber returns to its original shape after being stretched, instead of slowly flowing like a very thick liquid. The more cross-links there are, the harder the rubber becomes, and with a very large amount of sulphur, you get a hard, rigid material that was once used for things like combs and bowling balls.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Vulcanised rubber, combined with the invention of the air-filled tyre and later the motor car, created enormous demand. At first, almost all of it came from wild trees in the Amazon, and the trade made a few people extremely rich, while the workers who collected the latex were often brutally exploited. Then, in 1876, the Englishman Henry Wickham shipped tens of thousands of rubber seeds from Brazil to Kew Gardens in London. The seedlings that grew there were sent to British colonies in Asia, and within a few decades, huge plantations in Southeast Asia had replaced Brazil as the world's main source.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, plantations have never succeeded in the Amazon itself, largely because of a fungal disease called South American leaf blight, which spreads rapidly when rubber trees are planted close together. That's still true today, and the leading producers are countries such as Thailand and Indonesia.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Dependence on Asian plantations became a serious problem during the Second World War, when Japan occupied the main rubber-growing regions and cut off supplies to the Allies. In response, the United States built an enormous synthetic rubber industry in just a few years. Synthetic rubbers are made from chemicals obtained from oil, and today they account for roughly half of all the rubber used in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, natural rubber hasn't been replaced. It still performs better in some demanding applications, for example the tyres of aircraft and heavy trucks, which have to cope with very high loads and heat. Next week, we'll look at the environmental questions this raises, including the problem of recycling the billions of tyres that are thrown away.

listening.title: Booking a canoe trip
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a canoe hire company to book a river trip for his family.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Canoe Hire, Sophie speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'd like to book a canoe trip for my family, please. We're staying near here for the summer holidays, and we've seen people canoeing on the river every day. It looks like a lot of fun.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It is. Have any of you been canoeing before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My wife and I went once, a long time ago, but the children have never tried it.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's no problem. Most of our customers are beginners. Before you set off, one of our instructors gives everyone a short lesson on the bank, so you learn how to hold the paddle, how to steer and what to do if the canoe tips over.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. What trips do you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: We have two routes. The short one is a half-day trip. You start here at the boathouse, by the old stone bridge, and paddle downstream to Hartley Mill. That's about twelve kilometres, and it usually takes three to four hours, with a stop for a picnic. The long route is a full-day trip of twenty-five kilometres, which goes all the way to the town of Ashbury. For a family with young children, I'd recommend the half day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, I think the half day would be enough. How do we get back from Hartley Mill?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Our minibus collects you and the canoes from the mill and brings you back here. That's included in the price.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there somewhere to stop for lunch on the way?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, about halfway there's a small island with a sandy beach, and most families stop there for their picnic. There aren't any shops along the river, so make sure you bring enough food and water with you. There are toilets at Hartley Mill, and there's also a little café there where you can get an ice cream while you wait for the minibus.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: We charge per canoe, not per person. Each canoe takes up to three people. For the half day, it's thirty-eight pounds per canoe. The full day is forty-five. How many people are in your group?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, there were going to be six of us, but my brother can't come now, so it's five: me, my wife and our three children.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: So five people. You'll need two canoes, then. How old are the children?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: They're fourteen, eleven and eight.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's fine. The minimum age is seven, but all children must be able to swim. They don't need to be strong swimmers, but they should be able to swim at least twenty-five metres.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: They can all do that. When can we go?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: When were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is Saturday possible?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. Saturday morning is fully booked, I'm afraid, but there's space on Sunday. Would that be all right?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, Sunday's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Lovely. Trips leave at ten, but please arrive at half past nine, so there's time to get your life jackets on and have the lesson.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Do we need to bring anything?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: We give everyone a life jacket and a paddle, and we provide waterproof bags for phones and car keys. You should wear clothes that can get wet, and old trainers or sandals that stay on your feet. And bring a change of clothes to leave in the car, because most people get wet, even if they don't fall in. Oh, and don't forget sun cream and a hat.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can we bring our dog? He loves the water.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: I'm sorry, but dogs aren't allowed in the canoes. They tend to jump around, and that makes the canoe tip over very easily.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, he can stay at the cottage. And where can we park?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Our car park is very small, so please use the free car park behind the church. It's only a two-minute walk from the boathouse.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Now, can I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Martin Kerrigan. That's K-E-R-R-I-G-A-N.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Kerrigan. And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Great. If the river is too high after heavy rain, we may have to cancel. In that case, we'll call you the evening before and give you your money back. Is there anything else you'd like to know?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, I think that's everything. Thanks very much.

listening.title: Welcome to a lake nature reserve
listening.contextDescription: A park ranger speaks to visitors at the start of a day at a lake nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Linmere Lake Nature Reserve. My name's Ciara, and I'm one of the rangers here. I'm going to tell you a little about the lake and the reserve, and give you some information to help you enjoy your visit.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: First, a bit of history. Many people think Linmere is a natural lake, but in fact it isn't. Until the 1970s, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the company stopped digging, the large holes they left behind slowly filled with water from the ground and from a small river nearby. Over the years, plants grew around the edges, and birds and fish arrived. In 1995, the land was bought by a wildlife charity, and it became a nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Today, the lake is about two kilometres long, and it's an important home for birds, especially in winter. Every year, thousands of ducks and geese fly here from colder countries in the north, because the lake rarely freezes. In summer, you'll see swans with their young, and if you're lucky, you might see a kingfisher. They're small, bright blue birds that dive into the water to catch fish. The best place to see them is near the wooden bridge, where the river enters the lake.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, some information about getting around. There's a path that goes all the way round the lake. It's about five kilometres long and takes most people around two hours. The path is flat, and the first part, from the visitor centre to the bird hide, is suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. After that, it can be muddy, so you'll need good shoes or boots.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Along the path, there are three bird hides. These are small wooden huts with windows, where you can sit quietly and watch the birds without frightening them. Please keep your voices down when you're inside, and close the windows when you leave. The largest hide is on the north side of the lake, and it has a telescope that anyone can use.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: There are a few rules that I need to tell you about. Dogs are welcome, but they must be kept on a lead at all times, because many birds build their nests on the ground near the water. Swimming in the lake is not allowed. The water is very deep in places, and it's colder than people expect, even in summer. You also can't feed the ducks bread, I'm afraid. It isn't good for them, and the bread that they don't eat makes the water dirty. If you'd like to feed them, you can buy special bird food at the visitor centre.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Fishing is allowed, but only on the east side of the lake, and you need a permit, which you can also get from the visitor centre. Cycling is permitted on the main path, but please go slowly and remember that walkers have priority.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: If you'd like to learn more, we run lots of activities. Every Sunday afternoon, there's a guided bird walk with one of our rangers. It's free, but you need to book because there are only fifteen places. During the school holidays, we also run pond-dipping sessions for children, where they use nets to catch small water creatures and look at them under a microscope. Those are very popular, so book early.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: And one more thing. If you find a bird or an animal that seems to be injured, please don't try to pick it up or move it yourself. Make a note of where it is, and tell one of the rangers or the staff at the visitor centre. We work with a local animal hospital, and they know how to handle wild animals safely.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Finally, the visitor centre has a café, toilets and a shop. The café uses vegetables from our own garden, and all the money from the shop goes towards looking after the reserve. The centre closes at five o'clock, and the car park gates are locked at half past five, so please make sure you're back in time. Enjoy your day.

Over the years, plants grew around the edges, and birds and fish arrived. In 1995, the land was bought by a wildlife charity, and it became a nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Today, the lake is about two kilometres long, and it's an important home for birds, especially in winter. Every year, thousands of ducks and geese fly here from colder countries in the north, because the lake rarely freezes. In summer, you'll see swans with their young, and if you're lucky, you might see a kingfisher. They're small, bright blue birds that dive into the water to catch fish. The best place to see them is near the wooden bridge, where the river enters the lake.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, some information about getting around. There's a path that goes all the way round the lake. It's about five kilometres long and takes most people around two hours. The path is flat, and the first part, from the visitor centre to the bird hide, is suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. After that, it can be muddy, so you'll need good shoes or boots.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Along the path, there are three bird hides. These are small wooden huts with windows, where you can sit quietly and watch the birds without frightening them. Please keep your voices down when you're inside, and close the windows when you leave. The largest hide is on the north side of the lake, and it has a telescope that anyone can use.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: There are a few rules that I need to tell you about. Dogs are welcome, but they must be kept on a lead at all times, because many birds build their nests on the ground near the water. Swimming in the lake is not allowed. The water is very deep in places, and it's colder than people expect, even in summer. You also can't feed the ducks bread, I'm afraid. dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Fishing is allowed, but only on the east side of the lake, and you need a permit, which you can also get from the visitor centre. Cycling is permitted on the main path, but please go slowly and remember that walkers have priority.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Finally, the visitor centre has a café, toilets and a shop. The café uses vegetables from our own garden, and all the money from the shop goes towards looking after the reserve. listening.title: Testing the water in a river
listening.contextDescription: Two geography students, Amy and Ravi, talk to their tutor about their fieldwork on a local river.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Amy. Hi, Ravi. So, you've finished your fieldwork on the River Lune. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: It went quite well, I think. We wanted to find out whether the water quality changes as the river flows past the town, so we chose three sites: one upstream, above the town, one in the middle of the town, and one downstream, about two kilometres below it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what did you measure at each site?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We measured the temperature of the water, its pH, and how fast the river was flowing. And we did kick sampling to collect small animals from the river bed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How did you measure the speed of the water?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We used an orange. We measured ten metres along the bank, dropped the orange in the water, and timed how long it took to float that distance. We did it three times at each site and worked out the average. An orange is good because it floats just under the surface, so the wind doesn't push it much.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic method. And the kick sampling?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: One of us stood in the river and kicked the stones on the bottom for one minute, while the other held a net just downstream to catch whatever was washed out. Then we put everything in a white tray and counted the different creatures.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why is that useful for measuring water quality?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: Because some animals can only live in clean water that has lots of oxygen, like mayfly and stonefly larvae. Others, like some kinds of worms, can survive in quite polluted water. So the types of animals you find tell you how clean the river is, not just on one day but over a longer period.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Chemical tests only show you what the water is like at that moment. What about the pH?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We tested it with paper strips. It was between seven and seven and a half at all three sites, so it didn't really change.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's quite normal for a river like the Lune. It's still worth including, though, because it shows that the differences in the animals weren't caused by the water being more acidic in one place. So, what did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: The upstream site was the cleanest. We found lots of mayfly larvae and a few stonefly larvae. In the town, there were far fewer of them, and more worms and snails. We think that's partly because of rubbish and water running off the roads.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: The surprising thing was the downstream site. We expected it to be the most polluted, because there's a water treatment works just above it. But actually, it was nearly as clean as the upstream site.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why do you think that was?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: We're not completely sure. The river is much faster there, because it goes over a lot of small rapids, and fast, rough water takes in more oxygen from the air. That might help the river to recover.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good explanation. You could check it by measuring the oxygen in the water directly. The department has an oxygen meter you can borrow.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: That would be great. We did have one problem, though. On the second day, it rained heavily, and the river rose, so we couldn't safely go into the water at the town site. We had to go back the following week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: You were right not to take risks. But do mention it in your report, because the conditions weren't exactly the same on both days, and that could affect your results.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: Okay. How should we present the results?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: For the animals, I'd use a bar chart for each site, so the reader can compare them easily. And please include a sketch map showing where the three sites are. The report should be about two thousand five hundred words, and I'd like it by the end of next month.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.text: Should we include any photographs?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, a few photographs of each site would be useful, especially of the river bed, but keep them small so they don't take up too much space.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Thanks. We'll book the oxygen meter today.

listening.title: How rivers shape the land
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory geography course about how rivers change as they flow from their source to the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to follow a river on its journey from the mountains to the sea, and look at how it shapes the land along the way. Rivers might seem gentle, but over thousands of years, they can cut deep valleys and build completely new land.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with some basic words. The place where a river begins is called its source. Often, this is a spring, where water comes out of the ground, or a lake, or melting ice high in the mountains. The place where a river ends, usually at the sea or a lake, is called its mouth. Smaller rivers that join a bigger one are called tributaries, and the whole area of land that drains into one river is known as its drainage basin.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Geographers usually divide a river into three parts: the upper course, the middle course and the lower course. In the upper course, near the source, the land is steep, and the river is usually narrow and shallow. The water flows quickly over rocks and stones. Here, the main process is erosion, which means wearing away the land. The river carries stones and rocks, and as these hit the bottom of the river, they cut downwards. Over a very long time, this creates a deep valley with steep sides, which is shaped like the letter V.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Waterfalls are also common in the upper course. They often form where a band of hard rock lies on top of softer rock. The river wears away the soft rock more quickly, so a step forms, and the water falls over it. Slowly, the water cuts back into the cliff, so the waterfall moves upstream over time, leaving a narrow valley called a gorge.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the middle course, the land becomes flatter, and the river becomes wider and deeper, because tributaries have added more water. Here, the river starts to bend from side to side. These large bends are called meanders. On the outside of each bend, the water flows faster, so it wears away the bank. On the inside of the bend, the water is slower, so it drops the sand and mud it is carrying. This dropping of material is called deposition. Over many years, the bends become bigger and bigger.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sometimes, two bends get so close that the river cuts straight through the narrow piece of land between them, especially when there is a lot of water. The river then takes the shorter route, and the old bend is left behind as a separate lake. Because of its curved shape, this is called an oxbow lake, after the U-shaped collar that was once used on oxen.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the lower course, near the mouth, the land is almost flat, and the river is at its widest. It moves slowly and carries huge amounts of fine mud, called silt. When the river reaches the sea, it slows down even more, and much of this silt is deposited. If the sea's waves and currents are not strong enough to carry it away, the silt builds up and forms new land called a delta. The word comes from the Greek letter delta, which is shaped like a triangle, because the ancient Greek writer Herodotus noticed that the land at the mouth of the Nile had this shape.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Deltas are usually very fertile, because the silt is full of nutrients, so they have been important for farming for thousands of years. The Nile delta in Egypt, the Ganges delta in Bangladesh and India, and the Mekong delta in Vietnam are all home to millions of people. However, deltas are low and flat, so they are at risk from rising sea levels.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, a quick fact about the world's great rivers. The Nile is usually described as the longest river in the world, at about six thousand six hundred and fifty kilometres. But the Amazon in South America carries far more water than any other river. In fact, it carries around one fifth of all the river water that flows into the world's oceans. Next week, we'll look at how people use and change rivers, for example by building dams.

listening.title: Booking a bug hotel workshop
listening.contextDescription: A parent phones a nature centre to book places on a children's workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Nature Centre, Ben speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I saw that you're running a bug hotel workshop for children, and I'd like to book places for my two kids, if there's still room.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a few sessions coming up. They're all on Saturday mornings. Which date were you interested in?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I was hoping for the tenth of May.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm afraid the tenth is completely full. It's been very popular. But there are still places on the seventeenth. Would that work?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: The seventeenth. Yes, I think so. We're not doing anything that weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. Can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It's Joanna Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And how old are the children? The workshop is designed for ages six to twelve.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That's fine. My daughter's seven and my son is ten.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. Now, the price. For members of the centre, it's six pounds per child, and for non-members it's eight pounds. Are you members?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: No, we're not, although we've been meaning to join for ages.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Well, if you join on the day, we can take the difference off your membership fee. Adults come free, by the way, and you're very welcome to stay and help.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, I'd love to. Could you tell me a bit about what they'll actually do?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. A bug hotel is a kind of shelter that gives insects and other small creatures somewhere to live, especially over the winter. Each child builds their own small one, using a wooden frame, which we provide. They fill it with natural materials. We use pine cones, dry leaves, pieces of bark and hollow bamboo canes. Solitary bees, for example, like to lay their eggs inside the bamboo tubes, and ladybirds often spend the winter hidden among the pine cones.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That sounds lovely. Can they bring it home?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, each child takes home their bug hotel, along with a leaflet about garden insects, so they can identify who moves in. We suggest putting it somewhere sheltered, facing the sun, about a metre off the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: And where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The workshop takes place in the wooden barn next to the car park, not in the main visitor centre. It starts at ten and finishes at twelve thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Is there somewhere to park? We'll probably drive, because it's quite a long way from our house.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, parking is free for visitors, but it does fill up quickly on Saturdays, so I'd suggest arriving by about a quarter to ten. There's also a café in the visitor centre if you'd like a coffee while you wait, and the children get a drink and a biscuit halfway through the session.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Is there anything they need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We provide gloves and all the tools, but they should wear old clothes, because it can get messy. And part of the session is outside collecting materials, so I'd recommend boots, as the ground near the river is often muddy.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Good to know. Oh, one thing I should mention. My son has quite bad hay fever. He's allergic to grass. Will that be a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me. I'll make a note for the leader. Most of the outdoor part is in the woodland, rather than the meadow, so it shouldn't be too bad, but he might want to bring his medicine just in case.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I'll make sure he does. And is there anything else happening that day?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's an optional pond-dipping session in the afternoon, starting at quarter past two, where children can look at water insects like dragonfly larvae and water boatmen. It's free for anyone who's done the morning workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Brilliant, we might stay for that. How do I pay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You can pay on the day. Just one last question for our records: how did you find out about the workshop?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It was in the school newsletter last week.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely, thank you. So that's two places on Saturday the seventeenth. We look forward to seeing you.

questions.explanation: Places are available on the 17th.
questions.evidenceQuote: But there are still places on the seventeenth.

questions.prompt: Parent's surname: __________
questions.explanation: She spells Whitcombe.
questions.evidenceQuote: It's Joanna Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

questions.prompt: Children's ages: 7 and __________
questions.explanation: Her son is ten.
questions.evidenceQuote: My daughter's seven and my son is ten.

questions.prompt: Price per child (non-members): £__________
questions.explanation: They are not members, so it is £8.
questions.evidenceQuote: for non-members it's eight pounds
questions.distractorNote: £6 is the members' price.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming. My name's Leah Moretti, and I manage Ashgrove Park for the city council. Tonight I want to explain our plans to turn part of the park into a wildflower area for pollinators, and to answer any questions you have.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So, first of all, why are we doing this? When people hear the word 'pollinator', they usually think of honeybees. But in fact, a huge range of insects carry pollen from flower to flower, including bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies, butterflies, moths and even some beetles. Many of these insects have declined in recent decades, and one of the main reasons is the loss of the flower-rich grasslands they depend on. Parks like ours can't solve that problem on their own, but they can provide important stepping stones for insects moving through the city.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, I know that some of you are worried about how this will look. At the moment, the area by the eastern gate is just short grass that we mow every week in summer. Under the new plan, we'll mow that area much less often. Some people have told me they think this will look untidy or neglected. What we're going to do is keep a mown strip, about two metres wide, along the edges and paths. That shows people that the long grass is deliberate, and in our experience, it makes a big difference to how people feel about it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We'll cut the meadow itself just once a year, in late summer, after the flowers have set seed. And this is important: we'll remove the cuttings rather than leaving them on the ground. That might seem strange, but most wildflowers actually grow best in poor soil. If the cuttings rot down, they add nutrients, and then fast-growing grasses take over and crowd out the flowers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The project is being paid for by a grant from a wildlife charity, so it won't cost residents anything extra. We'll be relying on volunteers, though, especially for planting in the autumn, so if you're interested, please leave your details on the sheet at the back.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about some of the plants we're including, because each one has a particular job. Near the entrance, we're planting willow. Its catkins appear very early in spring, and they're one of the first sources of pollen for queen bumblebees coming out of hibernation. Along the old wall, we'll let the ivy grow. People often think of ivy as a weed, but it flowers in autumn, when hardly anything else does, so it's a vital source of food for insects late in the year.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: In the corner by the compost bins, we're deliberately leaving a patch of stinging nettles. I know they're not very popular with dog walkers! But they're the main food plant for the caterpillars of several butterflies, such as the peacock and the small tortoiseshell. In the main flower bed, we'll have foxgloves. Their flowers are long tubes, so they suit bumblebees with long tongues that can reach the nectar deep inside. And finally, we're planting fennel. Its flat clusters of tiny flowers are very popular with hoverflies, which are excellent pollinators and whose larvae also eat aphids, so they help gardeners too.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're also being careful about where our seeds come from. Rather than buying a cheap mixture that might include plants from other parts of the world, we're using seed collected from wildflower meadows in this region. Local plants are better suited to our soil and climate, and the insects here are adapted to them. It does cost a little more, but we think it's worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: To find out whether the project's working, we'll be running insect counts three times a year, in May, July and September, and anyone can join in. You don't need to be an expert; we'll give you an identification guide and a short training session. The results will be published on the council's website. Right, I'll stop there. Does anyone have any questions?

listening.title: Planning a campus insect survey
listening.contextDescription: Two biology students, Megan and Tom, talk to their tutor about an insect survey project.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Megan, Tom. So, you've decided to do your project on insects on the campus. Tell me what you're planning.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, the basic question is whether different types of habitat on campus support different numbers and types of insects. We've chosen three sites: the short grass on the main lawn, the wildflower strip behind the library, and the small wood near the sports hall.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that gives you a nice contrast. What made you choose this topic?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Partly the news stories about insect decline. But mainly, the university's just started managing some areas for wildlife, and the grounds team said they'd like some data to see whether it's making a difference.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's excellent, because it means your project could actually be useful. How are you going to collect the insects?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: We're using two methods. For insects on the ground, mainly beetles and spiders, we'll use pitfall traps. They're just plastic cups sunk into the soil so the rim is level with the surface. Anything walking along falls in.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are you going to put any liquid in them?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We talked about that. Some studies use a preservative, but that kills everything. We'd rather keep the insects alive, identify them, and release them. So we'll leave the cups dry, and check them every twenty-four hours, because otherwise the predators, like the larger beetles, start eating the other insects.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. And make sure you put a cover over each one, a little raised above the cup, or they'll fill with water when it rains.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Yes, we were going to use small squares of wood for that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the second method?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: A moth trap. It's a box with a bright light on top that attracts moths at night. They fall into the box and settle among egg trays inside, and in the morning we identify and release them. The ecology department has agreed to lend us one.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Have you checked that you're allowed to put traps on university land?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, the grounds team were happy for us to go ahead. We just have to mark each trap with a small flag, so that the gardeners don't mow over them or trip on them, and we've filled in a risk assessment form for working outside at night.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's exactly the kind of thing examiners like to see mentioned.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Where will you run it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's a problem, actually. We'd planned to put it in all three sites, but the main lawn is next to the student halls, and we were worried the light would disturb people trying to sleep. So we'll only use it in the wood and behind the library.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as you explain why in your methods section. It does mean you can't compare all three sites for moths, so be careful about the conclusions you draw. How often are you sampling?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Once a week for six weeks, in June and early July.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how will you deal with the weather? Moth numbers can vary enormously depending on temperature.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We hadn't really thought about that. I suppose we could record the temperature each night?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, record the minimum overnight temperature, and also wind and cloud cover, because moths fly much less on clear, cold nights. And try to run the trap on the same nights at both sites, so that the weather is the same for each.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Good idea. The other thing we're unsure about is identification. Some of the beetles are really hard to tell apart.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Don't try to identify everything to species level. For the difficult groups, it's perfectly acceptable to sort them into families. You'll still be able to compare the sites. And take good photographs, so that an expert can check them later if necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Should we share our results with anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Definitely. Send a summary to the grounds team, and you could also submit your records to the national recording website, so they become part of the wider scientific data. Right, I'd like to see a draft of your methods section in two weeks.

listening.title: The science of fireflies
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course about how fireflies produce light and why they are under threat.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're looking at one of the most magical sights in the natural world: fireflies. On summer evenings in many parts of the world, fields and forests light up with thousands of tiny flashing lights. But how do these insects produce light, why do they do it, and why are scientists worried about their future?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with some basic facts. Despite their name, fireflies aren't flies at all. They're beetles, belonging to a family called the Lampyridae, and there are more than two thousand known species. They're found on every continent except Antarctica, but they're most diverse in warm, humid regions of Asia and the Americas. In some places, people call them lightning bugs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The production of light by living things is called bioluminescence. In fireflies, it takes place in special light organs, usually near the end of the abdomen. Inside these organs, a chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen. The reaction is made possible by an enzyme called luciferase, and it also requires a molecule called ATP, which is the main energy carrier in living cells. What's remarkable is how efficient this reaction is. An ordinary old-fashioned light bulb loses most of its energy as heat, but almost all the energy from the firefly's reaction is released as light. That's why it's sometimes described as cold light.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So how does a firefly switch its light on and off? The answer seems to lie in controlling the supply of oxygen to the light organ. Researchers have found evidence that a gas called nitric oxide plays a role in this, allowing oxygen to reach the light-producing cells in short bursts. That's what creates the flash.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, why do they flash? In most species, the main purpose is courtship. Typically, males fly around flashing a particular pattern, and females, waiting on the ground or on plants, respond with their own flash. Each species has its own code, which might differ in the length of the flash, the number of flashes, or the time between them. This allows fireflies to find partners of the right species in the dark.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But this system can be exploited. Females of some species in a group called Photuris have learned to copy the flash responses of females of other species. When a male of the other species arrives, expecting to find a mate, the Photuris female catches and eats him. Scientists sometimes call them femme fatale fireflies. And by eating these males, they also gain chemicals that help protect them from their own predators, such as spiders.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: It's not only adults that glow. Firefly larvae produce light too, and in many species, the glow seems to act as a warning to predators that they taste unpleasant. The larvae live on the ground or in leaf litter, and they're fierce predators themselves. Many feed on snails and slugs, injecting them with digestive chemicals that turn their prey into a liquid.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the most extraordinary displays happens in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park in the United States, where one species flashes in unison. Thousands of males flash together, then go dark together, creating waves of light through the forest. It's become so popular that the park now uses a lottery system to limit the number of visitors. Similar synchronised displays occur in mangrove forests in Southeast Asia.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sadly, there's growing evidence that many firefly populations are declining. A major review by firefly experts identified three main threats. The first is the loss of habitat, as wetlands, meadows and forests are cleared for building and agriculture. The second is light pollution. Artificial lights from streets and buildings make it harder for fireflies to see each other's signals, and so they find mates less successfully. The third is the use of pesticides, which can kill both the adults and the larvae.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, fireflies have also made an important contribution to science. Scientists have learned to insert the gene for luciferase into other organisms, so that cells glow when a particular gene is active. This technique is now widely used in medical research. In the next session, we'll look at other bioluminescent organisms, particularly those in the deep ocean.

listening.title: Enrolling on a dressmaking course
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a community college to enrol on an evening course in dressmaking.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Brookfield Community College, Siobhan speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'm calling about the evening classes in dressmaking. I saw a leaflet about them, and I'd like to find out a bit more before I sign up.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We actually have two dressmaking courses starting this autumn: Introduction to Dressmaking, which is for complete beginners, and Dressmaking Two, for people who already know the basics. Have you done any sewing before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Only very simple things, like sewing on buttons. I've never used a sewing machine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then the introduction course is definitely the right one. It runs on two evenings, but the Thursday group is already full, I'm afraid. There are still a few places on Tuesdays, from seven until half past nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Tuesday would actually suit me better anyway. When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The first class is on the twenty-third of September, and it runs for ten weeks, with a break for one week in the middle of October, when the college is closed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A break in October? I hadn't realised the college closed then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, it's the mid-term holiday for the schools that share the site, so the whole campus shuts for a week. The course still has ten full sessions, though; the final class just finishes a week later, at the beginning of December. Each class is two and a half hours long, with a short tea break halfway through.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Okay. And what does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The standard fee is one hundred and eighty-five pounds. If you're a student, over sixty-five or receiving certain benefits, there's a reduced fee of one hundred and fifty pounds, but you'd need to show proof of that when you enrol.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, I'll be paying the standard fee. Does that include materials?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It includes the use of the sewing machines, the patterns and thread, but you'll need to buy your own fabric. In the first few weeks, you'll learn how to use the machine safely, how to take measurements and how to read a pattern. Your first project is a simple apron, and by the end of the course most people have made a skirt or a pair of loose trousers that fits them properly.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. Is there anything I need to bring to the first class?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The tutor asks everyone to bring a good pair of scissors, the kind that are only used for cutting fabric, because ordinary ones aren't sharp enough and they damage the cloth. And a notebook is useful, too. You don't need fabric for the first week.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where's the best place to buy fabric? I'm new to the area.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Most of our students go to a shop called Thread and Bobbin, on Mill Street, near the bus station. They give a ten per cent discount if you show your college card.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks. And where exactly are the classes held?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In the Harland Building, which is the new building behind the main car park. It's room fourteen, on the ground floor. There's a lift, but you won't need it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I enrol over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, I can take your details now, and then you can pay online. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a contact phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's oh seven seven one two, four eight three, five six oh.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. And just for our records, how did you hear about the course? You mentioned a leaflet.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's right. Actually, my neighbour gave it to me. She did the course last year and loved it, so she recommended it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's good to hear. I'll put down a personal recommendation, then. One last thing: if you need to miss a class, please let the tutor know in advance, because she'll sometimes give you some practice to do at home so you don't fall behind.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Will do. Thanks very much for your help.

listening.title: A sustainable fashion festival
listening.contextDescription: An organiser talks on local radio about a week-long festival on repairing and reusing clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And now, joining me in the studio is Kirsty Doyle, who's organising next month's Wear It Again festival. Kirsty, welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Thanks for having me. Wear It Again is a week of events about making our clothes last longer, through repairing them, swapping them and redesigning them. It's the third year we've held it, and it's grown a lot. In the first year we had about four hundred visitors, and last year we had nearly two thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Why do you think it's become so popular?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: I think people are increasingly uncomfortable about how many clothes are thrown away. But honestly, the main reason people tell us they come is the cost. Prices have gone up so much that learning to repair a favourite jacket, instead of replacing it, makes a real difference to their budget. The environmental side often comes second.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: So what's on the programme this year?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: The week opens on Monday with the Repair Café in the town library. Volunteers with sewing skills will be there all day to help you fix things like broken zips, torn pockets and holes in jumpers. It's not a service where you leave your clothes and pick them up later, though. The idea is that the volunteers show you how to do the repair yourself, so that next time you won't need them.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Tuesday evening, we have a talk at the arts centre by a textile historian, about how people looked after their clothes in the past, when clothing was so expensive that a coat might be passed down through several generations. That's free, but places are limited, so you'll need to reserve a seat on our website.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Wednesday is our clothes swap, which is always the busiest event. It's very simple: you bring up to five items of clothing that are clean and in good condition, and you receive a token for each one, which you can exchange for something someone else has brought. Anything that's left at the end goes to a local charity.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Thursday there's an upcycling workshop for teenagers, run by students from the college's fashion department. Upcycling means turning old clothes into something new and better, so for example cutting up old jeans to make a bag. That workshop's for thirteen to eighteen-year-olds only, and there's a small charge of five pounds to cover the materials.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Then on Friday we're trying something new: a session with a professional tailor, who'll explain what kinds of alterations are worth paying for and which aren't. For example, shortening trousers or taking in a waist is usually straightforward, but changing the shoulders of a jacket is very difficult and often costs more than the jacket itself.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: And we finish on Saturday with a fashion show in the town square, where all the outfits are second-hand or made from old clothes. Children are very welcome at that, and there'll be face painting and music as well.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: It sounds like a full week. Is there anything people should do to prepare?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: For the Repair Café, please bring your own thread if you can, in a colour that matches the item, because we can't possibly have every colour. And for the swap, please wash everything before you bring it. We do check, and we have to turn away a surprising number of things every year.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And if people want to get involved as volunteers?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: We'd love that. We especially need people on Wednesday to help sort the clothes into sizes before the doors open. You don't need any special skills for that, just a bit of patience. There's a form on the website, or you can come to our planning meeting next Thursday at the library.

It's not a service where you leave your clothes and pick them up later, though. The idea is that the volunteers show you how to do the repair yourself, so that next time you won't need them.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Tuesday evening, we have a talk at the arts centre by a textile historian, about how people looked after their clothes in the past, when clothing was so expensive that a coat might be passed down through several generations. That's free, but places are limited, so you'll need to reserve a seat on our website.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Wednesday is our clothes swap, which is always the busiest event. It's very simple: you bring up to five items of clothing that are clean and in good condition, and you receive a token for each one, which you can exchange for something someone else has brought. Anything that's left at the end goes to a local charity.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Thursday there's an upcycling workshop for teenagers, run by students from the college's fashion department. Upcycling means turning old clothes into something new and better, so for example cutting up old jeans to make a bag. That workshop's for thirteen to eighteen-year-olds only, and there's a small charge of five pounds to cover the materials.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Then on Friday we're trying something new: a session with a professional tailor, who'll explain what kinds of alterations are worth paying for and which aren't. For example, shortening trousers or taking in a waist is usually straightforward, but changing the shoulders of a jacket is very difficult and often costs more than the jacket itself.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: And we finish on Saturday with a fashion show in the town square, where all the outfits are second-hand or made from old clothes. Children are very welcome at that, and there'll be face painting and music as well.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: It sounds like a full week. Is there anything people should do to prepare?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: For the Repair Café, please bring your own thread if you can, in a colour that matches the item, because we can't possibly have every colour. And for the swap, please wash everything before you bring it. We do check, and we have to turn away a surprising number of things every year.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And if people want to get involved as volunteers?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: We'd love that. We especially need people on Wednesday to help sort the clothes into sizes before the doors open. You don't need any special skills for that, just a bit of patience. There's a form on the website, or you can come to our planning meeting next Thursday at the library.

listening.title: Designing a sustainable school uniform
listening.contextDescription: Two design students, Priya and Tom, discuss their project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Priya, Tom, your project is to redesign the uniform for a local secondary school so that it's more sustainable. Where have you got to?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've finished the research stage. We started by surveying parents at the school, and we had nearly three hundred replies, which was far more than we expected.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. What did they say?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The thing that came up again and again was durability. Parents said that the school jumpers, in particular, wear out at the elbows within a few months, and that the trousers lose their colour after being washed a lot. Price was mentioned too, of course, but less often than we'd assumed.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: And quite a few parents complained that the uniform can only be bought from one shop, which is expensive. That's not really a design issue, but we've mentioned it in our report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, what about materials? That's the heart of the project.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We compared four main fibres. The current uniform is mostly a polyester and cotton blend. Polyester is cheap and very hard-wearing, and it dries quickly, which parents like. But it's made from oil, and every time it's washed, it releases tiny plastic fibres that end up in rivers and the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: The other problem with blends is recycling. Because the two fibres are mixed together in the same thread, it's very difficult to separate them at the end of the garment's life, so most blended clothing can't be recycled into new fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point, and one that a lot of people miss. What about cotton on its own?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Cotton is comfortable and breathable, but conventional cotton needs a great deal of water and often a lot of pesticides. Organic cotton avoids the pesticides, but it's more expensive, and on its own it's not as hard-wearing as a blend.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We were quite interested in wool for the jumpers. It's naturally resistant to smells, so it doesn't need washing as often, and it lasts a long time if it's looked after. The disadvantage is that it can shrink if it's washed at the wrong temperature, and some children find it itchy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the fourth?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Lyocell, which is made from wood pulp. The chemicals used to dissolve the wood are recovered and reused in what's called a closed-loop process, so it has a much lower impact than most other fibres made from wood. It's soft and strong, but we couldn't find much information on how well it survives years of school use.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what have you decided?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: For the shirts, organic cotton. For the trousers and skirts, we're suggesting a fabric made from recycled polyester, because durability matters most there, and at least that reuses plastic that already exists. And for the jumpers, wool, with patches on the elbows built into the design from the start.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I like the idea of the elbow patches. It turns a weakness into a feature. But I'd question the recycled polyester. It still sheds microfibres, doesn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It does. We've suggested that the school could give families a special washing bag that catches the fibres, but we know it isn't a perfect solution.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then say that clearly in your evaluation. Examiners respect honesty about limitations. What's the next step?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We're making prototypes. We'd like to test them by asking a few pupils to wear them for a month, but we're not sure whether that's allowed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: You'll need permission from the school, and from the parents, as the pupils are under eighteen. Speak to the head teacher first. In the meantime, you could test the fabrics in the lab here; we have a machine that rubs fabric repeatedly to measure how quickly it wears.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That would be really useful. Thanks.
