listening.title: The invention of synthetic fibres
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a design history course on how artificial and synthetic fibres were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at the natural fibres that people have used for thousands of years: cotton, linen, wool and silk. Today we're going to look at what happened when chemists began to make fibres in the laboratory, a development that has completely transformed the clothes we wear. Today, in fact, synthetic fibres account for considerably more than half of all the fibre produced in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The story begins with silk. For centuries, silk was the most desirable fabric in Europe, but it was extremely expensive, and in the nineteenth century European silk production was badly damaged by diseases affecting silkworms. Several inventors therefore tried to create an artificial silk. The first to succeed commercially was a French aristocrat, Count Hilaire de Chardonnet, who made fibres from cellulose, the substance that forms the walls of plant cells. He displayed his fabric at the Paris Exhibition of 1889, where it attracted a great deal of attention. Unfortunately, the chemical process he used made the material dangerously flammable, and it was some time before safer methods were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of these safer methods was the viscose process, patented in 1892 by three British chemists. In this process, cellulose, usually from wood pulp, is dissolved and then forced through tiny holes to form threads. The fibre it produced became known in the 1920s as rayon, and it was widely used for dresses, linings and underwear. It's important to understand that rayon isn't fully synthetic. It's sometimes called semi-synthetic, because it's made from a natural material that has been chemically processed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first truly synthetic fibre, made entirely from chemicals, came from the American company DuPont. In the late 1920s, DuPont hired a young chemist named Wallace Carothers to carry out basic research into polymers, which are very long chain-like molecules. In 1935, his team produced a polymer that could be drawn out into strong, elastic threads. This was nylon. Interestingly, the first product made from it was not clothing at all, but toothbrush bristles, which went on sale in 1938.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Nylon's great success, however, came with women's stockings. Until then, stockings had been made of silk, which was expensive and ran easily. When nylon stockings went on sale across the United States in 1940, they sold out almost immediately. But soon after the United States entered the Second World War, nylon production was redirected to military uses, especially parachutes, which had previously been made of silk, as well as ropes and tents. Nylon stockings became so scarce that some women drew a line down the back of their legs to imitate the seam.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, in Britain, two chemists working for a textile company in Manchester, John Whinfield and James Dickson, developed polyester in 1941. Polyester became enormously popular after the war, because it's strong, cheap and resistant to creasing, which meant clothes didn't need ironing. Today it's by far the most widely used fibre in the world. A further important development came in 1958, when another DuPont chemist, Joseph Shivers, invented elastane, a fibre that can stretch to several times its own length and then return to its original shape. It's better known by its brand name, Lycra, and it made possible the close-fitting sportswear that we now take for granted.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: These fibres brought enormous benefits. Clothing became cheaper, easier to care for and more varied than ever before. But they also brought problems that their inventors couldn't have foreseen. Most synthetic fibres are made from oil, and they don't break down naturally, so discarded clothes can remain in landfill for centuries. And researchers have found that synthetic garments shed tiny fibres every time they're washed, which pass through water treatment plants and end up in rivers and oceans. Next week, we'll look at some of the new materials that designers are developing in response.

questions.evidenceQuote: forced through tiny holes to form threads

listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a design history course on how artificial and synthetic fibres were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at the natural fibres that people have used for thousands of years: cotton, linen, wool and silk. Today we're going to look at what happened when chemists began to make fibres in the laboratory, a development that has completely transformed the clothes we wear. Today, in fact, synthetic fibres account for considerably more than half of all the fibre produced in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The story begins with silk. For centuries, silk was the most desirable fabric in Europe, but it was extremely expensive, and in the nineteenth century European silk production was badly damaged by diseases affecting silkworms. Several inventors therefore tried to create an artificial silk. The first to succeed commercially was a French aristocrat, Count Hilaire de Chardonnet, who made fibres from cellulose, the substance that forms the walls of plant cells. He displayed his fabric at the Paris Exhibition of 1889, where it attracted a great deal of attention. Unfortunately, the chemical process he used made the material dangerously flammable, and it was some time before safer methods were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of these safer methods was the viscose process, patented in 1892 by three British chemists. In this process, cellulose, usually from wood pulp, is dissolved and then forced through tiny holes to form threads. The fibre it produced became known in the 1920s as rayon, and it was widely used for dresses, linings and underwear. It's important to understand that rayon isn't fully synthetic. It's sometimes called semi-synthetic, because it's made from a natural material that has been chemically processed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first truly synthetic fibre, made entirely from chemicals, came from the American company DuPont. In the late 1920s, DuPont hired a young chemist named Wallace Carothers to carry out basic research into polymers, which are very long chain-like molecules. In 1935, his team produced a polymer that could be drawn out into strong, elastic threads. This was nylon. Interestingly, the first product made from it was not clothing at all, but toothbrush bristles, which went on sale in 1938.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Nylon's great success, however, came with women's stockings. Until then, stockings had been made of silk, which was expensive and ran easily. When nylon stockings went on sale across the United States in 1940, they sold out almost immediately. But soon after the United States entered the Second World War, nylon production was redirected to military uses, especially parachutes, which had previously been made of silk, as well as ropes and tents. Nylon stockings became so scarce that some women drew a line down the back of their legs to imitate the seam.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, in Britain, two chemists working for a textile company in Manchester, John Whinfield and James Dickson, developed polyester in 1941. Polyester became enormously popular after the war, because it's strong, cheap and resistant to creasing, which meant clothes didn't need ironing. Today it's by far the most widely used fibre in the world. A further important development came in 1958, when another DuPont chemist, Joseph Shivers, invented elastane, a fibre that can stretch to several times its own length and then return to its original shape. It's better known by its brand name, Lycra, and it made possible the close-fitting sportswear that we now take for granted.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: These fibres brought enormous benefits. Clothing became cheaper, easier to care for and more varied than ever before. But they also brought problems that their inventors couldn't have foreseen. Most synthetic fibres are made from oil, and they don't break down naturally, so discarded clothes can remain in landfill for centuries. And researchers have found that synthetic garments shed tiny fibres every time they're washed, which pass through water treatment plants and end up in rivers and oceans. Next week, we'll look at some of the new materials that designers are developing in response.

listening.title: Booking a bird-watching boat trip
listening.contextDescription: A man phones a wildlife tour company to book a boat trip to see seabirds.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Seaview Wildlife Trips. This is Hannah speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'm visiting the area next month with my wife, and we'd like to go on one of your boat trips to see the seabirds. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two trips. The short one is called the Harbour Cruise. It lasts about an hour and goes along the cliffs near the town. You'll see gulls and cormorants, and sometimes seals on the rocks.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And the other one?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The other one is the Island Trip. That takes three hours, and the boat goes out to Gannet Island, which is about eight kilometres from the coast. In early summer, the island is home to thousands of seabirds, including puffins. Most people choose that one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Puffins! My wife would love to see puffins. When is the best time to see them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Puffins only come to the island to breed, so they're there from April until the beginning of August. After that, they go back out to sea for the winter. If you're coming next month, in June, that's the perfect time.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. We'd like to book the Island Trip, then. Do you have places on the fourteenth of June?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me check. The fourteenth is a Saturday, and I'm afraid that's full. But we have places on the fifteenth, the Sunday.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fifteenth is fine. What time does the boat leave?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It leaves at nine fifteen in the morning from the harbour. Please arrive at least fifteen minutes before, so we can give you a short safety talk. The boat comes back at about a quarter past twelve.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. And how much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Island Trip costs thirty-two pounds per adult. Children are sixteen pounds. The Harbour Cruise is cheaper, only fourteen pounds, but of course you don't see the puffins.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Two adults, then. Is there anything we should bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes. It can be cold and windy on the sea, even in summer, so bring a warm jacket. And if you have binoculars, bring those too. If you don't, you can borrow a pair from us for free, but we only have twenty pairs, so it's better to bring your own.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We've got our own. What about life jackets?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We give everyone a life jacket on the boat, and everyone must wear one. It's the law.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Can we get off the boat on the island?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, I'm sorry. Landing on the island isn't allowed during the breeding season, because it would disturb the birds. But the boat goes very close to the cliffs, so you get a really good view, and you can take great photos.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That makes sense. One more thing. My wife sometimes gets seasick. Is the sea usually rough?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's usually quite calm in June, but if the weather is bad, we cancel the trip and give you your money back. We'll send you a text message by seven o'clock that morning if there's a problem. Some people take a seasickness tablet before they go, just in case. You can buy them at the chemist next to the harbour.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good idea. Shall I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's David Thornton. That's T-H-O-R-N-T-O-N.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Thornton. And can I have a mobile number?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And where do you usually park? There's a car park right next to the harbour, but it's very small. The best place is the car park at the railway station, which is only a five-minute walk away, and it's free on Sundays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. We'll park at the station, then.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. You can pay now by card, or on the day. Which would you prefer?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll pay now by card, please.

listening.title: A visit to a wetland nature reserve
listening.contextDescription: A ranger welcomes a group of visitors to a wetland nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Marsh End Nature Reserve. My name's Kylie, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you go out and explore, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and how to get the most out of your visit.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: First, a bit of history. Fifty years ago, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the company stopped taking out gravel, the holes filled with water, and slowly plants and birds began to arrive. Then, about thirty years ago, a local wildlife group bought the land and turned it into a nature reserve. Today, more than two hundred different kinds of birds have been seen here.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The reserve is a really important stopping place for migrating birds. In spring and autumn, birds that are travelling thousands of kilometres stop here to rest and feed. Some of them, like the waders you'll see on the mud by the lake, are on their way between Africa and the Arctic. They need to eat a lot here to build up energy for the next part of their journey.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you where everything is. We're in the visitor centre at the moment. Here you'll find the café, the toilets and the shop. On the wall behind me, there's a board where visitors write down the birds they've seen today, so have a look at it before you go out, and please add anything interesting when you come back. Yesterday, for example, someone saw a kingfisher by the small pond, which is always exciting, because they're bright blue and very fast.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: There are three main places to watch birds. A hide, if you don't know, is a small wooden building with long, narrow windows. You can sit inside and watch the birds without them seeing you. The biggest one is the Lake Hide. It's only a two-minute walk from here, and it has wheelchair access. From the Lake Hide you can see ducks and swans, and in winter, large groups of geese arrive from Iceland.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Further along the path is the Reed Bed Hide. It looks out over a large area of tall reeds. It's the best place to hear birds rather than see them, because lots of small birds sing in the reeds but they're quite hard to spot. If you're very lucky, you might see an otter there. We have a family of otters on the reserve, but they're very shy.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The third place is the Woodland Trail. It's a circular path through the trees, and it takes about forty-five minutes to walk round. Along the trail, we've put up more than sixty nest boxes, and in spring, many of them are used by blue tits and great tits. There's also a camera inside one of the nest boxes, and you can watch the pictures live on a screen in the visitor centre.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Just a few rules. Please keep to the paths at all times, because some birds nest on the ground and their nests are very easy to step on. Dogs aren't allowed on the reserve, except for assistance dogs. And please keep your voices down in the hides, because noise frightens the birds away.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: If you'd like to borrow binoculars or a bird guide book, you can get them from the shop. They're free, but we ask you to leave your car keys or a phone number with us. And if you're interested in getting more involved, we're always looking for volunteers. Every Tuesday morning, a group of volunteers helps us cut back the reeds and repair the paths. You don't need any experience. Just come and talk to me afterwards. Right, enjoy your visit!

listening.title: A visit to a wetland nature reserve
listening.contextDescription: A ranger welcomes a group of visitors to a wetland nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Marsh End Nature Reserve. My name's Kylie, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you go out and explore, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and how to get the most out of your visit.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: First, a bit of history. Fifty years ago, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the company stopped taking out gravel, the holes filled with water, and slowly plants and birds began to arrive. Then, about thirty years ago, a local wildlife group bought the land and turned it into a nature reserve. Today, more than two hundred different kinds of birds have been seen here.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The reserve is a really important stopping place for migrating birds. In spring and autumn, birds that are travelling thousands of kilometres stop here to rest and feed. Some of them, like the waders you'll see on the mud by the lake, are on their way between Africa and the Arctic. They need to eat a lot here to build up energy for the next part of their journey.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you where everything is. We're in the visitor centre at the moment. Here you'll find the café, the toilets and the shop. On the wall behind me, there's a board where visitors write down the birds they've seen today, so have a look at it before you go out, and please add anything interesting when you come back. Yesterday, for example, someone saw a kingfisher by the small pond, which is always exciting, because they're bright blue and very fast.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: There are three main places to watch birds. A hide, if you don't know, is a small wooden building with long, narrow windows. You can sit inside and watch the birds without them seeing you. The biggest one is the Lake Hide. It's only a two-minute walk from here, and it has wheelchair access. From the Lake Hide you can see ducks and swans, and in winter, large groups of geese arrive from Iceland.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Further along the path is the Reed Bed Hide. It looks out over a large area of tall reeds. It's the best place to hear birds rather than see them, because lots of small birds sing in the reeds but they're quite hard to spot. If you're very lucky, you might see an otter there. We have a family of otters on the reserve, but they're very shy.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The third place is the Woodland Trail. It's a circular path through the trees, and it takes about forty-five minutes to walk round. Along the trail, we've put up more than sixty nest boxes, and in spring, many of them are used by blue tits and great tits. There's also a camera inside one of the nest boxes, and you can watch the pictures live on a screen in the visitor centre.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Just a few rules. Please keep to the paths at all times, because some birds nest on the ground and their nests are very easy to step on. Dogs aren't allowed on the reserve, except for assistance dogs. And please keep your voices down in the hides, because noise frightens the birds away.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: If you'd like to borrow binoculars or a bird guide book, you can get them from the shop. They're free, but we ask you to leave your car keys or a phone number with us. And if you're interested in getting more involved, we're always looking for volunteers. Every Tuesday morning, a group of volunteers helps us cut back the reeds and repair the paths. You don't need any experience. Just come and talk to me afterwards. Right, enjoy your visit!

listening.title: A project on swallows
listening.contextDescription: Two biology students, Emma and Raj, talk to their tutor about their project on swallows that nest on local farms.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Emma, hello, Raj. Come in. So, you're doing your project on swallows. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We've been visiting farms near the town to count swallow nests and to find out how many chicks each pair has.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why did you choose swallows?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Partly because they're easy to find. They build their nests inside barns and other farm buildings, so you know where to look. But also because they make one of the most amazing journeys of any bird. The swallows that nest here in Britain spend the winter in South Africa. That's a journey of about ten thousand kilometres each way.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: And they do it every year. It's incredible for a bird that weighs about the same as two coins.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How many farms did you visit?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: We visited twelve farms in total. We wanted to do fifteen, but three farmers said no, because they were worried we'd frighten their animals.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's understandable. And how did you count the nests?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: We went into each building with the farmer and looked up at the roof beams with a torch. Swallows' nests are made of mud mixed with bits of grass, and they're shaped like a cup, so they're quite easy to see. We found ninety-four nests altogether, but not all of them were being used. Some were old ones from last year.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How did you know which ones were in use?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: We watched the nests from a distance. If an adult bird flew in and out, or if we could hear chicks, we counted it as active. In the end, we found sixty-one active nests.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what was the most interesting result so far?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: I think it's that farms with animals had many more swallows than farms that only grow crops. On farms with cows or horses, we found on average about eight nests. On the crop farms, it was usually only one or two.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why do you think that is?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: We think it's because of insects. Swallows catch flies while they're flying, and there are lots of flies around animals and their waste. Also, farms with animals have more open buildings, like cow sheds, where the birds can get in easily.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds very reasonable. Did you find anything that worried you?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Yes. Two of the farmers told us that they're planning to replace their old wooden barns with modern metal buildings, which are often closed. If they do, the swallows won't be able to get in to nest.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point to include in your discussion. You could suggest some solutions. For example, some farmers leave a small window or a gap open for the birds. Now, what problems have you had?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: The main problem was the weather. In May, it rained a lot, and there were fewer insects, so some chicks died. It meant our numbers were lower than we expected.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Well, that's a result too. You can compare it with other years if you find data from the national bird surveys. What are you going to do next?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: We'd like to go back in August to see if the swallows have a second group of chicks. Many pairs have two families in one summer.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And when you write it up, I'd like you to include a map of the farms and some photos of the nests. But please don't use the farmers' real names. Just call them Farm A, Farm B and so on.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Okay. When do you need the report?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: The first draft by the end of September, please. That gives you time after your August visit. And remember to thank the farmers. They've been very kind to let you in, and you may want to visit them again next year.

listening.title: Great journeys of the animal world
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course about the migrations of animals other than birds.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Last week, we talked about bird migration. Today, I want to show you that birds aren't the only animals that make long journeys. Insects, mammals, fish and reptiles migrate too, and some of their journeys are just as amazing. Let's look at five examples.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: We'll start with an insect: the monarch butterfly of North America. Every autumn, millions of monarchs fly south from Canada and the northern United States to a small area of mountains in central Mexico. Some of them travel up to about four thousand kilometres. They spend the winter there in forests of fir trees, where so many butterflies hang together on the branches that the trees look orange. Scientists have shown that monarchs use the sun to find their direction.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What's really surprising is that no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn live for about eight months, which is very long for a butterfly. In spring, they start flying north, but they lay their eggs on the way and then die. Their children continue the journey, and it takes three or four generations to get back to Canada. Then, at the end of summer, a new long-living generation flies all the way back to Mexico, to a place it has never seen.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Our second example is a mammal: the wildebeest of East Africa. Every year, about one and a half million wildebeest, together with hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, move in a huge circle between the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Masai Mara in Kenya. They aren't following a calendar. They're following the rain, because the rain makes fresh grass grow, and that's what they eat. The most dangerous moment is when the herds cross the Mara River. The water is fast, and crocodiles are waiting for them. Thousands of animals die every year at the crossings.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Next, fish. Salmon have a very unusual life. They hatch from eggs in rivers, swim down to the sea, and spend several years in the ocean, growing big and strong. Then they swim back to the very same river where they were born to lay their own eggs, which we call spawning. How do they find it? Out at sea, they probably use the Earth's magnetic field, but when they get close to the coast, they use smell. Every river has its own special smell, and the young salmon remember it. Sadly, many salmon rivers now have dams, which block the fish from swimming upstream. Some dams have special fish ladders, a kind of staircase of water, to help them get past.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Our fourth example is the grey whale, which makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal. In summer, grey whales feed in the cold waters of the Arctic, where there's lots of food. In autumn, they swim south along the west coast of North America to warm, shallow lagoons in Mexico. There, the females give birth to their calves. The calves have very little fat when they're born, so they need the warm water. In spring, the whales swim back north again. The round trip can be around sixteen thousand kilometres or even more.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, sea turtles. Female sea turtles often return to the beach where they themselves hatched, many years earlier, to lay their eggs. Some swim thousands of kilometres across the ocean to get there. Research suggests that turtles, like salmon, use the Earth's magnetic field as a kind of map. Every beach has a slightly different magnetic signal, and the young turtles seem to remember it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what can we learn from these examples? First, migration is a way for animals to find food, or a safe place to raise their young, at different times of the year. Second, many of these journeys are now in danger. Roads, fences, dams and the loss of forests and wetlands all make migration more difficult. Because migrating animals depend on several different places, protecting just one of them isn't enough. For your assignment this week, I'd like you to choose one migrating animal and find out what's being done to protect it.

dialogue.text: We'll start with an insect: the monarch butterfly of North America. Every autumn, millions of monarchs fly south from Canada and the northern United States to a small area of mountains in central Mexico. Some of them travel up to about four thousand kilometres. They spend the winter there in forests of fir trees, where so many butterflies hang together on the branches that the trees look orange. Scientists have shown that monarchs use the sun to find their direction.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What's really surprising is that no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn live for about eight months, which is very long for a butterfly. In spring, they start flying north, but they lay their eggs on the way and then die. Their children continue the journey, and it takes three or four generations to get back to Canada. Then, at the end of summer, a new long-living generation flies all the way back to Mexico, to a place it has never seen.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Our second example is a mammal: the wildebeest of East Africa. Every year, about one and a half million wildebeest, together with hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, move in a huge circle between the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Masai Mara in Kenya. They aren't following a calendar. They're following the rain, because the rain makes fresh grass grow, and that's what they eat. The most dangerous moment is when the herds cross the Mara River. The water is fast, and crocodiles are waiting for them. Thousands of animals die every year at the crossings.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Next, fish. Salmon have a very unusual life. They hatch from eggs in rivers, swim down to the sea, and spend several years in the ocean, growing big and strong. Then they swim back to the very same river where they were born to lay their own eggs, which we call spawning. How do they find it? Out at sea, they probably use the Earth's magnetic field, but when they get close to the coast, they use smell. Every river has its own special smell, and the young salmon remember it. Sadly, many salmon rivers now have dams, which block the fish from swimming upstream. Some dams have special fish ladders, a kind of staircase of water, to help them get past.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Our fourth example is the grey whale, which makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal. In summer, grey whales feed in the cold waters of the Arctic, where there's lots of food. In autumn, they swim south along the west coast of North America to warm, shallow lagoons in Mexico. There, the females give birth to their calves. The calves have very little fat when they're born, so they need the warm water. In spring, the whales swim back north again. The round trip can be around sixteen thousand kilometres or even more.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, sea turtles. Female sea turtles often return to the beach where they themselves hatched, many years earlier, to lay their eggs. Some swim thousands of kilometres across the ocean to get there. Research suggests that turtles, like salmon, use the Earth's magnetic field as a kind of map. Every beach has a slightly different magnetic signal, and the young turtles seem to remember it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what can we learn from these examples? First, migration is a way for animals to find food, or a safe place to raise their young, at different times of the year. Second, many of these journeys are now in danger. Roads, fences, dams and the loss of forests and wetlands all make migration more difficult. Because migrating animals depend on several different places, protecting just one of them isn't enough. For your assignment this week, I'd like you to choose one migrating animal and find out what's being done to protect it.

questions.explanation: Crocodiles wait at the river.
questions.evidenceQuote: crocodiles are waiting for them

questions.prompt: Near the coast, salmon find their river by __________
questions.explanation: They use smell.
questions.evidenceQuote: when they get close to the coast, they use smell

listening.title: Enrolling on a photography course
listening.contextDescription: A woman phones a community college to enrol on an evening photography course.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Ashford Community College, adult education office. Ellie speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm calling about your evening photography courses. I picked up a leaflet in the library, and I'd like to sign up for one, but I'm not sure which would suit me best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. This term we're running three. There's Portrait Photography, which is mostly studio work, taking pictures of people with professional lighting. Then there's Landscape Photography, which is mainly outdoors, and there's also a course called Smartphone Photography, for people who'd like to take better pictures without buying a camera.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, I already have a camera, and I mostly take pictures when I go walking in the hills, so I think the landscape course would be the right one for me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That sounds ideal. Just so you know, the portrait course is on Tuesday evenings, but Landscape runs on Thursdays, from seven till nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thursdays are fine. I'm free most evenings, actually. When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It was going to start on the fifth of September, but the tutor is away that week, so the first session is now on the twelfth. It runs for eight weeks altogether.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay, the twelfth. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full fee is a hundred and sixty-five pounds, but there's a reduced rate for students, people over sixty and people who are unemployed. That's a hundred and forty pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm a part-time student at the university. Does that count?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, it does. You'd just need to show your student card at the first session, and we'll charge you the reduced rate.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. What kind of camera will I need? Mine's quite old.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It doesn't matter how old it is. The important thing is that it lets you use manual settings, so you can control things like the shutter speed yourself. A fully automatic camera won't really work for this course. Do you know if yours can do that?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm fairly sure it can. There's a little dial on the top with the letter M on it.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's the one. You'll also need a tripod, because several of the sessions are at sunset, and in low light you need to keep the camera completely still. If you haven't got one, the college can lend you one, but we only have a few, so it's much better to bring your own.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I think I've got a small one somewhere. What about memory cards and so on?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Bring at least one spare memory card and a spare battery, because the cold drains batteries surprisingly quickly. And do wear warm clothes. People are always surprised how cold it gets standing still on a hillside as it gets dark.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where does the course take place? In the main college building?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The theory sessions are in the main building, in the computer room, because you'll learn how to edit your pictures there. But on the first evening the class meets in the college garden, behind the café, because the tutor likes to start with a practical exercise straight away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fun. Are there any trips?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, there's one. In the last week there's a full-day trip on the Saturday to photograph the old lighthouse at Shore Point. Transport is included in the fee, but you'll need to bring your own lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Brilliant. Can I enrol now, over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Certainly. Can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Karin Lindqvist. That's K-A-R-I-N, and the surname is L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. That's an unusual name. Is it Swedish?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, my father's family is from Sweden, but I grew up in Canada.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. And would you like to pay by card now, or would you prefer to pay at the first session?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll pay now by card, if that's all right. Then it's done.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll take the details in a moment, and then I'll email you a confirmation with a map of the college and a list of everything you need to bring.

questions.explanation: She chooses the landscape course.
questions.evidenceQuote: Landscape runs on Thursdays

listening.title: A briefing for film festival volunteers
listening.contextDescription: The volunteer coordinator of a town film festival speaks to a group of new and returning volunteers.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello, everyone, and thank you all for coming along this evening. My name's Kirsty Barnes, and I'm the volunteer coordinator for the Riverton Film Festival. Some of you have helped us before, and some of you are completely new, so I'll go through the basics and then tell you a bit about each of our venues.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: This is our ninth festival, and it's going to be our biggest yet. We'll be showing over a hundred and twenty films across ten days. We've still got five venues, the same as last year, and the festival is the same length, but the big change is that, for the first time, we've got a complete programme of films for children, with screenings every morning during the school holidays. We're really excited about that, and we hope it'll bring in lots of local families.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, shifts. Most shifts are four hours long, and you can choose as many as you like through the online system. Please arrive half an hour before your shift begins. That gives the venue manager time to brief you and tell you about any changes to the programme, which happen more often than you'd think.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: A lot of new volunteers think their main job at the door will be checking tickets, but in fact the scanners do that automatically. The most important thing you'll do is count people as they go in. Every venue has a maximum number of people allowed for fire safety reasons, and we must never go over it, even if someone has a ticket. If a screening's full, call the venue manager and let them deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: You may also be approached by journalists, especially during the first weekend. Please don't give interviews or tell them what you think of the films, however tempting it is. Just politely direct them to the press office, which is in the Town Hall.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: And what do you get in return? Well, we can't pay travel expenses, I'm afraid, but every volunteer who does at least three shifts receives a festival T-shirt and two free tickets for any screening. There's also a party for all volunteers on the final night, which is always great fun.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the venues. Our main venue is the Palace Cinema on the High Street, which is the oldest working cinema in the county. That's where the opening night film will be shown, with the director and some of the cast arriving on the red carpet, so volunteers there will be very busy on the first evening.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The Old Corn Exchange is hosting our silent film season this year. Each of the films will be accompanied by live music. Usually it'll be a pianist, but for one of the films we've got a small orchestra, so it's a fantastic place to work if you enjoy music.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Down by the river, on the Riverside Lawn, we'll put up a giant inflatable screen for outdoor screenings every evening, as long as the weather allows. If you're working there, bring a warm coat, because it gets cold by the water once the sun goes down.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator

listening.title: Making a short documentary
listening.contextDescription: Two media students, Sophie and Ravi, discuss their documentary about a local market with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Sophie, Ravi. Have a seat. So, you've finished filming your documentary about Eastgate Market. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Really well, on the whole. We chose the market because the council's planning to redevelop the whole area in the next couple of years, and lots of the traders don't know whether they'll be able to stay. We felt their stories should be recorded before it's too late.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That gives the film a real sense of urgency. What equipment did you use?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We borrowed the department's camera for the interviews, because the picture quality is much better. But for the general scenes of the market, we used our phones.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why was that?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Mainly because people behaved much more naturally. When we walked around with the big camera, people either stopped what they were doing or started performing for us. With a phone, nobody really noticed, so we got much more realistic footage of the market.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a very good observation. What about sound? That's where student films usually go wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: We learned that the hard way. On the first day, we recorded two interviews using the microphone on top of the camera, and you can hardly hear what people are saying because of the noise in the market. So we had to do them again.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It's a common mistake. Audiences will forgive a picture that's a bit dark or shaky, but they'll stop watching very quickly if they can't hear what people are saying. What did you change?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: We borrowed clip-on microphones, and we filmed all the interviews early in the morning, before the market opened to the public. The traders were setting up their stalls, so it was quiet, and they had more time to talk.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And I hope you got everyone's permission.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Yes. Everyone who appears on camera signed a release form. There was one trader, who sells fish, who agreed at first but then changed his mind after we'd filmed him. He was worried about what his landlord might think.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We took him out of the film completely. It was a shame, because he was very funny, but we felt we had to respect his decision.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Quite right. You must never use footage of someone who's withdrawn their consent. Now, how have you structured the film?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: At the moment, it's in chronological order. It starts with the history of the market, using old photographs from the local museum, and then moves on to the present day, and finally the plans for the future.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's logical, but it's not very gripping. I'd suggest you open with your strongest character, someone the audience will immediately care about, and bring in the history later, briefly. Who's the most memorable person you interviewed?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Probably Mrs Okoye, who's run a fabric stall for over forty years. She's got amazing stories.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then start with her. How long is the film at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Our rough cut is eighteen minutes, and the limit for the assignment is ten.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you'll need to lose almost half of it. That's painful, but it almost always improves a film. I'd start by cutting down the history section, because that's where it drags most. And what about music?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We wanted to use a famous song, but we found out we'd need to pay for the rights. So we asked a local band who play at the market on Saturdays, and they gave us permission to use two of their tracks for free.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's perfect, and it suits the subject. Make sure you get that permission in writing and credit them at the end. Right, I'd like to see the new version in two weeks.

dialogue.text: We learned that the hard way. On the first day, we recorded two interviews using the microphone on top of the camera, and you can hardly hear what people are saying because of the noise in the market. So we had to do them again.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It's a common mistake. Audiences will forgive a picture that's a bit dark or shaky, but they'll stop watching very quickly if they can't hear what people are saying. What did you change?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: We borrowed clip-on microphones, and we filmed all the interviews early in the morning, before the market opened to the public. The traders were setting up their stalls, so it was quiet, and they had more time to talk.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And I hope you got everyone's permission.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Yes. Everyone who appears on camera signed a release form. There was one trader, who sells fish, who agreed at first but then changed his mind after we'd filmed him. He was worried about what his landlord might think.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We took him out of the film completely. It was a shame, because he was very funny, but we felt we had to respect his decision.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Quite right. You must never use footage of someone who's withdrawn their consent. Now, how have you structured the film?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: At the moment, it's in chronological order. It starts with the history of the market, using old photographs from the local museum, and then moves on to the present day, and finally the plans for the future.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's logical, but it's not very gripping. I'd suggest you open with your strongest character, someone the audience will immediately care about, and bring in the history later, briefly. Who's the most memorable person you interviewed?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Probably Mrs Okoye, who's run a fabric stall for over forty years. She's got amazing stories.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then start with her. How long is the film at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Sophie
dialogue.text: Our rough cut is eighteen minutes, and the limit for the assignment is ten.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you'll need to lose almost half of it. That's painful, but it almost always improves a film. I'd start by cutting down the history section, because that's where it drags most. And what about music?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We wanted to use a famous song, but we found out we'd need to pay for the rights. So we asked a local band who play at the market on Saturdays, and they gave us permission to use two of their tracks for free.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's perfect, and it suits the subject. Make sure you get that permission in writing and credit them at the end. Right, I'd like to see the new version in two weeks.

listening.title: A short history of animation
listening.contextDescription: A lecture in a film studies course on how animated films developed from optical toys to computer animation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at the history of animation, from simple nineteenth-century toys to the computer-animated films that dominate cinema screens today. The word animation comes from the Latin anima, meaning breath, soul or life, and that's exactly what animators do: they bring drawings and objects to life.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: All film, whether animated or not, depends on the same trick. When we see a series of still images in quick succession, our brains combine them into continuous movement. In the nineteenth century, this was exploited in a number of optical toys. One of the most popular was the zoetrope, a drum with a series of pictures on the inside. When you spun the drum and looked through slits in its side, the pictures appeared to move. These toys were very popular in Victorian homes, but each one could only show a loop of a second or two.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Once cinema was invented in the 1890s, it wasn't long before people began drawing films. A French artist, Émile Cohl, made a film called Fantasmagorie in 1908, which is often described as the first fully animated film. It lasts less than two minutes, but it required around seven hundred drawings, and its simple white figures on a black background constantly change into other shapes.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the United States, the cartoonist Winsor McCay made Gertie the Dinosaur in 1914. McCay used to present the film as part of a live show: he would appear on stage and give instructions to Gertie, who appeared to obey him. Audiences loved it, and it showed that animated characters could have real personality.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Drawing every part of every picture, though, was extremely slow. The solution, which was developed in the middle of the 1910s, was the cel. Cels were transparent sheets of celluloid on which the moving characters were painted. They were laid over a background, so the background only had to be drawn once for each scene, while the characters were redrawn on new cels for each frame. This system made it possible to produce cartoons on an industrial scale, and it remained the standard method for most of the twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The studio most associated with cel animation is, of course, Walt Disney's. In 1928, Disney released Steamboat Willie, starring Mickey Mouse, which was one of the first cartoons with synchronised sound. Then, in 1937, came Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length cel-animated feature film. Many people in Hollywood expected it to fail, and while it was being made, it was nicknamed Disney's Folly. In fact, it was an enormous success and proved that audiences would sit through an animated story lasting well over an hour.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Just to give you an idea of the work involved: film is normally projected at twenty-four frames per second. Animators often draw a new image for every two frames, which means twelve drawings for every second of film. A feature film could therefore need well over a hundred thousand drawings.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Alongside drawn animation, another technique developed, called stop-motion. Here, real objects are photographed one frame at a time, and moved slightly between each frame. One famous early example is King Kong, made in 1933, in which the giant ape was in fact a set of small models. Later, studios such as Aardman in Britain became famous for stop-motion films using plasticine characters, like Wallace and Gromit. It's incredibly slow work: on a good day, an animator might produce only a few seconds of film.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The biggest change of all came with computers. Computer graphics had been used for short sequences since the 1970s and 1980s, but in 1995 Pixar released Toy Story, the first feature film made entirely with computers. Instead of drawing each frame, animators built three-dimensional digital models of the characters and moved them, rather like puppets, while the computer calculated the final images. Today, computer animation dominates the industry, although many animators still begin by sketching their ideas on paper, and hand-drawn and stop-motion films continue to be made and to win awards. Next week, we'll look at the animation industry in Japan.

listening.title: Applying for an allotment
listening.contextDescription: A man phones his local council to ask about renting an allotment to grow vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hillford Council, allotments office. This is Joanne speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I've just moved to Hillford, and I'd really like to grow my own vegetables, but my new flat doesn't have a garden. A neighbour told me the council rents out allotments. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Yes, it is. We have three allotment sites in the town at the moment. The biggest is at Mill Lane, near the river, with about a hundred and twenty plots. Then there's Station Road, which is smaller, and a new site that opened last year on Orchard Hill.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Are there any plots available now?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Not straight away, I'm afraid. There's a waiting list for all three sites. Mill Lane is the most popular, because the soil there is very good, so the wait is around two years. For Station Road it's about eighteen months. But Orchard Hill is much shorter, usually only a few months, because it's further from the town centre.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Orchard Hill would be fine. I've got a bike, so distance isn't really a problem. How big are the plots?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: A full plot is two hundred and fifty square metres, which is a lot of work for a beginner. Most new people start with a half plot, which is a hundred and twenty-five. Have you grown vegetables before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Only a few tomatoes on a balcony, so I think a half plot would be more sensible.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: I'd agree. A half plot at Orchard Hill costs sixty-two pounds a year. A full plot is a hundred and ten. There's also a deposit of twenty-five pounds when you start, which you get back when you leave, as long as the plot is left in good condition.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds reasonable. What facilities are there on the site?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Orchard Hill has water taps around the site, and every plot has its own water butt for collecting rainwater from the shed roof. There are toilets near the main gate, and a car park. Each plot also comes with a small wooden shed for storing tools. What we don't have yet is a communal building, but the allotment association is raising money for one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there anything I'm not allowed to do on the plot?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: A few things. You can't keep animals, except for hens, and you need permission for those. Bonfires aren't allowed between April and September, because of complaints from people living nearby. And you must cultivate at least three quarters of your plot. If a plot isn't looked after, we send a warning letter, and if nothing changes after a month, we can give it to someone else on the list.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Can I put my name down now?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Of course. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Declan Fairweather. That's F-A-I-R-W-E-A-T-H-E-R.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Lovely name for a gardener! And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Flat 3, 48 Kingsley Road.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: And the postcode?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: HF7 2RB.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Thank you. And what's the best way to contact you when a plot becomes available?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Email is best, really. It's declan.fw at mailbox dot com.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Got it. Now, before you start, all new tenants have to go to an induction session, where the site manager shows you around and explains the rules. They're held on the first Saturday of each month, at ten o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there any help for beginners?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Yes. The association runs a mentoring scheme, where an experienced gardener is paired with a new tenant for the first year. They'll help you plan what to grow and when. Most people find it really useful. And there's a seed swap every February, where people exchange seeds they've saved from their own plants.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. I'll definitely sign up for the mentoring scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: I'll add a note to your application. You should get an email confirming you're on the list within five working days.

dialogue.text: Yes, it is. We have three allotment sites in the town at the moment. The biggest is at Mill Lane, near the river, with about a hundred and twenty plots. Then there's Station Road, which is smaller, and a new site that opened last year on Orchard Hill.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Are there any plots available now?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Not straight away, I'm afraid. There's a waiting list for all three sites. Mill Lane is the most popular, because the soil there is very good, so the wait is around two years. For Station Road it's about eighteen months. But Orchard Hill is much shorter, usually only a few months, because it's further from the town centre.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Orchard Hill would be fine. I've got a bike, so distance isn't really a problem. How big are the plots?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: A full plot is two hundred and fifty square metres, which is a lot of work for a beginner. Most new people start with a half plot, which is a hundred and twenty-five. Have you grown vegetables before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Only a few tomatoes on a balcony, so I think a half plot would be more sensible.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: I'd agree. A half plot at Orchard Hill costs sixty-two pounds a year. A full plot is a hundred and ten. There's also a deposit of twenty-five pounds when you start, which you get back when you leave, as long as the plot is left in good condition.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds reasonable. What facilities are there on the site?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Orchard Hill has water taps around the site, and every plot has its own water butt for collecting rainwater from the shed roof. There are toilets near the main gate, and a car park. Each plot also comes with a small wooden shed for storing tools. What we don't have yet is a communal building, but the allotment association is raising money for one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there anything I'm not allowed to do on the plot?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: A few things. You can't keep animals, except for hens, and you need permission for those. Bonfires aren't allowed between April and September, because of complaints from people living nearby. And you must cultivate at least three quarters of your plot. If a plot isn't looked after, we send a warning letter, and if nothing changes after a month, we can give it to someone else on the list.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Can I put my name down now?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Of course. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Declan Fairweather. That's F-A-I-R-W-E-A-T-H-E-R.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Lovely name for a gardener! And your address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Flat 3, 48 Kingsley Road.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: And the postcode?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: HF7 2RB.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Thank you. And what's the best way to contact you when a plot becomes available?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Email is best, really. It's declan.fw at mailbox dot com.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Got it. Now, before you start, all new tenants have to go to an induction session, where the site manager shows you around and explains the rules. They're held on the first Saturday of each month, at ten o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there any help for beginners?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Yes. The association runs a mentoring scheme, where an experienced gardener is paired with a new tenant for the first year. They'll help you plan what to grow and when. Most people find it really useful. And there's a seed swap every February, where people exchange seeds they've saved from their own plants.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. I'll definitely sign up for the mentoring scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: I'll add a note to your application. You should get an email confirming you're on the list within five working days.

listening.title: A guide to the botanic garden
listening.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a botanic garden and describes its main areas.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Botanic Garden. My name's Daniel, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you head off to explore, I'd like to give you a quick introduction to the garden and tell you about some of the areas you might like to visit.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The garden was founded in 1862 by a group of local doctors, who wanted a place to grow medicinal plants and teach students about them. In fact, for the first thirty years or so it was used almost entirely for teaching. It only opened to the public in the 1890s. Today, we have more than twelve thousand different kinds of plants, and around a quarter of a million visitors a year. But we're still a scientific institution, and much of our work is about conservation. We grow a number of plants that are rare or even extinct in the wild, and we share seeds with other gardens around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Entry to the garden is free, but we do ask for donations, and there's a box by the main gate. All the money goes towards caring for the plants. You'll find the café and the shop next to the car park, and toilets are at the entrance and beside the lake.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. Please stay on the paths, especially in the woodland area, because many plants there are only just coming up at this time of year and they're easily damaged. Dogs are welcome, but they must be kept on a lead. And please don't take cuttings or seeds from any of the plants. I know it's tempting, but some of our plants are very rare, and taking even a small piece can harm them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: So, let me tell you about the main areas. Straight ahead of us is the Palm House. It's the oldest building in the garden, built in the 1870s from iron and glass, and it's kept at a constant tropical temperature all year round. Inside you'll find palms, bananas and orchids. One of the highlights is a cycad, a very ancient type of plant, which was brought here as a small specimen over a hundred and fifty years ago. It's probably the oldest pot plant in the country. The Palm House is closed on Mondays for maintenance, so if you're coming back another day, bear that in mind.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: To the left of the Palm House is the Rock Garden, where we grow alpine plants from mountain regions all over the world. These plants are adapted to cold, windy conditions and very thin soil, so they tend to be small and low-growing. Late spring is the best time to see them, when many of them are in flower. The rock garden was rebuilt last year using stone from a local quarry, and it now has a small waterfall.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Beyond that you'll come to the Medicinal Garden, which is a reminder of how the garden began. It's laid out in beds according to the part of the body the plants were traditionally used to treat. There are labels explaining how each plant was used in the past and, in some cases, which modern medicines have been developed from it. Please don't touch the plants in this area, though, because several of them are poisonous.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you have children with you, I'd recommend the Sensory Garden, which is to the right of the main lawn. It's designed to be explored with all the senses, not just the eyes. Visitors are encouraged to touch the plants, which have interesting textures, and to smell the herbs. There's also a sound trail, with bamboo and tall grasses that rustle in the wind. The paths are wide and flat, so it's very easy to get around with a wheelchair or a buggy.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, down by the lake, there's the Herbarium. That's a collection of over two hundred thousand dried and pressed plant specimens, some of them collected in the eighteen hundreds. Scientists from all over the world use it for research. It's not usually open to the public, but on the last Sunday of every month, the staff offer free tours, and they're well worth booking.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, I think that's everything. Maps are available from the information desk, and I'll be leading a guided walk at two o'clock if anyone would like to join me. Enjoy your visit.

listening.title: Can houseplants clean the air?
listening.contextDescription: Two environmental science students, Leo and Hannah, discuss a research project on houseplants and indoor air quality with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Leo, Hannah. Come and sit down. So, your project is on houseplants and indoor air quality. Tell me where you've got to.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, we started with the literature review. Almost every article we found on garden websites says that plants clean the air in your home, and most of them refer back to the same source, a NASA study from 1989.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Ah yes, the famous NASA study. What did it actually do?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: NASA was interested in how to keep the air clean in space stations, so the researchers put plants inside small sealed chambers and added chemicals that are common indoor pollutants, like benzene and formaldehyde. Over the next twenty-four hours, the levels of those chemicals went down quite a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And they found that much of the effect wasn't actually from the leaves, but from microorganisms living in the soil around the roots.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. So what's the problem with using that study to give advice to people at home?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: The main problem is scale. The chambers were tiny, with no air coming in from outside, so a single plant had a big effect. But a real house is much bigger, and air is constantly being exchanged with the outside through windows, doors and gaps in the walls. We found a review from 2019 that looked at a lot of the later studies and calculated that, to match the cleaning you get from normal ventilation, you'd need somewhere between ten and a thousand plants per square metre of floor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Per square metre? That's quite a jungle.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. So in a normal room, a few pot plants make almost no measurable difference to air quality. Opening a window does far more.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So is your conclusion that the popular claim is simply wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Not exactly. We think it's been exaggerated rather than invented. The original experiments were fine for what they were testing. The problem is that the results were applied to situations they weren't designed for.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a nice distinction, and it's an important point to make in your discussion. Now, I understand you also want to do some practical work?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. We'd like to measure carbon dioxide levels in two similar student rooms in the hall of residence, one with ten plants and one with none, over a period of four weeks. We've borrowed two carbon dioxide monitors from the engineering department.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do you expect to find?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Probably very little difference, to be honest. But that's still a useful result.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It is. A few suggestions, though. First, you'll need to make sure the two rooms are as similar as possible. Things like the size of the room, which way the windows face and how often the students open them could have a much bigger effect than the plants. I'd ask the students living there to keep a simple diary of when they open the window.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's a good idea. We hadn't thought about the windows.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Second, four weeks is rather short. Could you extend it?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: We could probably manage six, if we start next week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Do that. And finally, don't forget that there are other benefits of houseplants that might be worth mentioning, even if they're outside the focus of your project.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, we found several studies suggesting that having plants around can improve people's mood and reduce stress. We thought we'd include those briefly in the introduction.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Just be careful to keep the focus on air quality. Now, when can I see a draft?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: We'd planned to finish the literature review by the end of this month.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine. Email it to me, and we can meet again after that to look at your results.

listening.contextDescription: Two environmental science students, Leo and Hannah, discuss a research project on houseplants and indoor air quality with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Leo, Hannah. Come and sit down. So, your project is on houseplants and indoor air quality. Tell me where you've got to.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, we started with the literature review. Almost every article we found on garden websites says that plants clean the air in your home, and most of them refer back to the same source, a NASA study from 1989.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Ah yes, the famous NASA study. What did it actually do?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: NASA was interested in how to keep the air clean in space stations, so the researchers put plants inside small sealed chambers and added chemicals that are common indoor pollutants, like benzene and formaldehyde. Over the next twenty-four hours, the levels of those chemicals went down quite a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And they found that much of the effect wasn't actually from the leaves, but from microorganisms living in the soil around the roots.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. So what's the problem with using that study to give advice to people at home?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: The main problem is scale. The chambers were tiny, with no air coming in from outside, so a single plant had a big effect. But a real house is much bigger, and air is constantly being exchanged with the outside through windows, doors and gaps in the walls. We found a review from 2019 that looked at a lot of the later studies and calculated that, to match the cleaning you get from normal ventilation, you'd need somewhere between ten and a thousand plants per square metre of floor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Per square metre? That's quite a jungle.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. So in a normal room, a few pot plants make almost no measurable difference to air quality. Opening a window does far more.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So is your conclusion that the popular claim is simply wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Not exactly. We think it's been exaggerated rather than invented. The original experiments were fine for what they were testing. The problem is that the results were applied to situations they weren't designed for.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a nice distinction, and it's an important point to make in your discussion. Now, I understand you also want to do some practical work?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. We'd like to measure carbon dioxide levels in two similar student rooms in the hall of residence, one with ten plants and one with none, over a period of four weeks. We've borrowed two carbon dioxide monitors from the engineering department.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do you expect to find?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Probably very little difference, to be honest. But that's still a useful result.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It is. A few suggestions, though. First, you'll need to make sure the two rooms are as similar as possible. Things like the size of the room, which way the windows face and how often the students open them could have a much bigger effect than the plants. I'd ask the students living there to keep a simple diary of when they open the window.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's a good idea. We hadn't thought about the windows.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Second, four weeks is rather short. Could you extend it?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: We could probably manage six, if we start next week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Do that. And finally, don't forget that there are other benefits of houseplants that might be worth mentioning, even if they're outside the focus of your project.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, we found several studies suggesting that having plants around can improve people's mood and reduce stress. We thought we'd include those briefly in the introduction.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Just be careful to keep the focus on air quality. Now, when can I see a draft?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: We'd planned to finish the literature review by the end of this month.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine. Email it to me, and we can meet again after that to look at your results.
